===== PAGE 10 =====
Preface
I am particularly pleased to present a new edition of the Guide to Treaties on Copyright 
and Related Rights Administered by WIPO. Since the first edition was published in 2003, the 
international framework for copyright and related rights has continued to evolve. Over 
the years, new treaties have been adopted, including the Beijing Treaty on Audiovisual 
Performances in 2012 and, in 2013, the Marrakesh Treaty to Facilitate Access to Published Works 
forPersonsWhoAreBlind,VisuallyImpaired,orOtherwisePrintDisabled.
Given the growing importance of copyright around the world, both in public policy and 
commercial practice, this work is especially useful. The strong upward curve of accession 
to WIPO treaties in the field of copyright over the last decade clearly illustrates that these 
instruments have become a global benchmark. It attests to the central role of copyright, now 
recognized as a strategic asset for growth, particularly in developing and transition countries, 
and is part of the emergence of the concept of the creative economy.
I would like to pay tribute to Dr. Mihály Ficsor, my distinguished predecessor and dear friend, 
whose scholarship and vision have contributed so much to the consolidation and adaptation of the 
international legal framework in the era of new digital technologies. My gratitude also goes to the 
eminentexperts – JørgenBlomqvist,JaneGinsburg,PierreSirinelli,andFernandoZapata – who
reviewed this edition and enriched its content with their complementary perspectives, ensuring 
that it reflects the diversity of approaches inherent in the discipline of copyright and the 
understanding of its fundamental principles at the international level.
We hope that this edition will be useful to governments, creators, lawyers, businesses, 
academics, and all users, and that it will contribute to strengthening a balanced and dynamic 
environment where copyright protection goes hand in hand with creativity, innovation, 
and development.
Sylvie Forbin  
Deputy Director General  
Copyright and Creative Industries Sector
NOTE: The views expressed in this Guide are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect 
those of WIPO.

===== PAGE 12 =====
Introduction
Objective, structure and style of the guides
This collection of guides is composed of five parts:
 – Part I. Guide to the Berne Convention;
 – Part II. Guides to the older generation of related rights treaties (Rome Convention; 
Phonograms Convention and Brussels, or Satellites, Convention);
 – Part III. Guides to the three “Internet Treaties” (WCT, WPPT and BTAP);
 – PartIV.GuidetotheMarrakeshVIPTreaty;and
 – PartV.Glossary.
The objective of these guides is to offer analysis of the above-mentioned copyright and related 
rights treaties administered by WIPO and guidance in their interpretation and application. This 
publication may be regarded as the second edition of a previous work written by the same 
author and published by WIPO under the title “Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights 
Treaties Administered by WIPO and Glossary of Copyright and Related Rights Terms” 1 published 
in 2003, which, of course, did not yet contain guides to the Beijing Treaty on Audiovisual 
Performances(BTAP)andtheMarrakeshVIPTreaty.ThiscompendiumwasnotthefirstWIPO
guide on copyright and related rights. WIPO published in 1978 the Guide to the Berne Convention2 
and in 1981 the Guide to the Rome Convention and the Phonograms Convention,3 both written by 
Claude Masouyé, who was at that time the Director of the Organization’s Copyright Department.
The 1978 and 1981 Guides were published “for the authorities of developing countries”, many of 
which were still at the initial stages of “the development of legislations and institutions in the fields 
of copyright and related rights”, as Árpád Bogsch, the then Director General of WIPO, stressed in 
his preface to the Berne Guide.4 As to its objective, the Director General stated that “[t]he sole aim 
of the Guide is to present, as simply as possible, the contents of the Berne Convention”,5 and the 
purpose of the Guide to the Rome Convention and Phonograms Convention was the same.
The decision to prepare new guides was taken in 1985 at a meeting organized by Director 
General Bogsch in which both Claude Masouyé and the author of the present guides 
participated and the purpose of which was to outline a new copyright program at WIPO in 
general.6Threereasonshademergedtojustifyanewedition.First,theViennaConventionon 
theLawofTreaties(VCLT)–originallyadoptedin1969–hadatlonglastenteredintoforcein
1980withitsdetailedprovisionsinArticles 31and32ontheinterpretationoftreaties.Second, 
developing countries had made progress in the establishment of their copyright infrastructure 
1 Mihály Ficsor, Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO and Glossary of Copyright and 
Related Rights Terms, publication No. 891(E) (Geneva: WIPO, 2003).
2 Claude Masouyé, Guide to the Berne Convention , publication No. 615(E) (Geneva: WIPO, 1978) (hereinafter: Masouyé, 
1978 Berne Convention Guide ).
3 Claude Masouyé, Guides to the Rome Convention and the Phonograms Convention , publication No. 617(E) (Geneva: 
WIPO, 1981).
4 Masouyé, 1978 Berne Convention Guide , 4.

Beyond (Cheltenham: Edward Elgar Publishing, 2020) (hereinafter: Ficsor, WIPO 50 Years),73–74.

===== PAGE 13 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
14 and were engaging in the preparation of more sophisticated legislation, for which they did not 
always find sufficient guidance in the simple narrative description of the Berne Convention 
and the related rights treaties in the Guides published in 1978 and 1981. Third, spectacular 
technological developments were taking place in the 1980s.
The objectives of the Organization’s copyright activities in the coming decades were determined 
at this 1985 meeting. Under the new program, two series of committees of governmental experts 
were to be organized: one to review certain new forms of creation and new uses of works and 
subject matters of related rights, followed by another series to review all the relevant issues 
of the various categories of works to be analyzed. Two desired end products of the program 
were projected by the end of the 1980s for which the results of these meetings were to be used: 
a Model Law on Copyright and new guides to the conventions. The latter would analyze the 
provisions of the WIPO treaties more thoroughly by also referring to the various sources of their 
interpretation, including the records of the diplomatic conferences and the related preparatory 
work, as well as the findings of the series of meetings of governmental experts. The two series of 
meetings took place as planned; on the basis of detailed studies prepared for and considered by 
them, the experts adopted guidance for the interpretation and application of copyright norms in 
the form of recommendations, guiding principles, model provisions and the like. The preparation 
of a Model Law on Copyright had also reached an advanced stage, and the next step would 
have been the preparation and publication of new guides; but at the end of the 1980s all these 
activities were put on hold when the Uruguay Round of General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade 
(GATT) negotiations and, in parallel, the preparation of new WIPO norm-setting activities began.
The preparation of new guides, however, became timely and urgent in 2002, when the two 
“InternetTreaties”–theWIPOCopyrightTreaty(WCT)andtheWIPOPerformancesand 
PhonogramsTreaty(WPPT)–enteredintoforce.WIPOhonoredthisauthorwiththetask 
of preparing this second edition. The guides, published in 2003, as determined in the WIPO 
program adopted in 1985, were not prepared in so simple a style as the 1978 and 1981 Guides; 
thenewguidesanalyzedthetreatiesinaccordancewiththeinterpretationrulesoftheVCLT;
the analysis also intensively took into account the guidance worked out by the governing bodies 
ofWIPOandthevariouscommitteesofgovernmentalexpertsinthe1970sand1980s–inthe
so-called“guideddevelopment”perioddescribedbelow–onagreatnumberofaspectsof 
copyright and related rights. 
This second edition has been created with the same objectives and in the same style as the 
first. Although its nature has been preserved, its size has necessarily increased. The first edition 
comprised a glossary and guides to six legal instruments: the Berne Convention; the Rome 
Convention; the Phonograms Convention; the Brussels, or Satellites, Convention; the WCT; and 
the WPPT. In this second edition, these have been joined by the guides to the BTAP and the 
MarrakeshVIPTreaty,bringingthenumberoflegalinstrumentstoeight.Whileitishopedthat
the guides and the glossary may still fit in to one volume, this edition has been prepared so that 
the various parts of the collection can also be consulted separately. For this reason, following 
this introduction, the publication is divided into the five parts outlined above.
Each of the four guides contained within this volume begins with an introduction reviewing 
the historical background, objectives, preparatory work and main features of the treaty or 
treaties covered. The relationship of the WIPO-administered treaties to each other and to the 
two related treaties not administered by WIPO is also described briefly. The latter two treaties 
are the Universal Copyright Convention (UCC) administered by the United Nations Educational, 
Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) and the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of 
Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS Agreement), which is binding for all Members of the World 
Trade Organization (WTO). Although these two treaties are not analyzed in the form of guides, it 
is mentioned how the UCC has served as a “bridge” for various countries to accede to the Berne 
Convention and, at certain points of the analysis of the three “Internet Treaties”, the guides 
quitefrequentlyrefertotheTRIPSAgreement.
In the guides, the provisions of the treaties are reproduced and analyzed step by step, but 
the compact texts of the treaties are not attached, in order to keep this second edition to a 
manageable size as a handbook. Nor do the guides contain a list of the contracting parties or 
any of their reservations and declarations. All this material is, however, available in an up-to-
date form on the WIPO website.

Introduction
Historical background
What exists now as the international system of copyright and related rights protection has 
developedfrombilateralagreementsconcludedmainly–althoughnotexclusively–between
European countries in the 19th century (at the time, only in respect of copyright, since related 
rights came into being only in the 20th century). The bilateral agreements were, in general, based 
on the principle of national treatment combined with some minimum obligations. This structure 
–thatis,theobligationtograntnationaltreatmenttothenationalsofothercontractingparties
combined with a minimum level of protection that each contracting party must grant to those 
nationalsirrespectiveoftheprotectiongrantedtoitsownnationals–becameakeybuilding
element of the international treaties on copyright and related rights. This was necessary due 
to the differences between the various national systems, not only as to the level of protection 
granted, but also with respect to the legal philosophy on which they were based. From the very 
beginning of national legislation on copyright, there were two fundamentally different systems; 
one taking the form of common law and the other rooted in civil law.
The common law system of copyright had grown out of the printing privileges granted by 
English monarchs. It was Queen Anne who brought about the Copernican turn in 1709/17107 
when she gave authors the right to authorize the printing (copying) of their works. Under the 
common law system, not the relationship between the author and his work, but rather the work 
itself as a product is the central element of protection. The objective of the protection is to offer 
incentives for further creative activity; it is conceptualized as a kind of agreement between 
society and the authors: if you create, you may make available your works to the public since you 
will enjoy protection for a limited time.
The civil law system has more than one root, but the most decisive one goes down as deep as 
the French Revolution, when authors’ rights in their literary and artistic works were recognized 
asamatterofnaturalrights.Authors’rightsintheirworks–asexpressionsofhumancreativity 
andoftheirownpersonalities–wereregardedevenas“themostsacredproperty”. 8
Several differences derived from these two philosophies still characterize the copyright systems. 
They are manifested concerning such fundamental issues as authorship, the concept of “work”, 
the originality test, the protection of authors’ moral rights, the borderline between copyright 
per se and related rights, and the original ownership and the transferability of economic rights. 9
These differences had to be taken into account when the various countries strove to ensure 
international protection for their authors through bilateral agreements. In the second part of 
the 19th century, the number and complexity of such agreements reached such a level that it 
was found desirable to regulate the protection of copyright in a multilateral treaty. The bilateral 
agreementsofferedcertainlegaltechniquesandmodels,butthetaskofworkingoutsucha 
multilateral instrument was more complex; the preparation of norms intended for worldwide 
applicationmadeitdesirabletotrytoestablishassolidalegal–philosophicalfoundationas 
possible. The preparatory work necessary for the establishment of a treaty to satisfy these 
requirementswasbegunandbroughtveryclosetoconclusionbytheInternationalLiteraryand 
Artistic Association (ALAI) during several of its congresses.
ItwasatthesuggestionofALAIthattheSwissConfederationconvenedthreesubsequent 
Diplomatic Conferences in Berne in 1884, 1885 and 1886, at the third of which the Berne 
Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works was adopted. The Convention was 
7 There is some uncertainty as to the exact year in which it happened, but both dates may be correct due to the 
difference at that time between the common and regal calendars.
8 ItwasIsaacRenéGuyLeChapelierwho,inhisfrequentlyquotedspeechonJanuary13,1791,inthedebateaboutthe 
decree on the right of theatrical representation, referred to authors’ rights as “the most sacred, the most legitimate, 
the most unassailable, and […] the most personal of properties, is the work that is the fruit of a writer’s thought (“ La 
plus sacrée, la plus légitime, la plus inattaquable et […] la plus personnelle de toutes les propriétés est l’ouvrage, le fruit de 
la pensée d’un écrivain ”).
9 For a more detailed characterization of the basic copyright systems, seeSamRicketsonandJaneC.Ginsburg,

NewYork:OxfordUniversityPress,2019)(hereinafter:GoldsteinandHugenholtz),13–24(Chapter2:Thelegaltraditions).

===== PAGE 15 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
16 based on the principle of national treatment, but it also fixed a minimum level of protection 
which all the member countries of the newly established Union had to grant to the nationals of 
other member countries.
The Berne Convention was revised several times between 1896 and 1971. The Diplomatic 
Conferences that took place in Paris in 1896, in Berlin in 1908, in Rome in 1928 and in Brussels 
in1948inordertoadapttheConventiontotechnologicaladvancements–suchastheadvent
ofphonographs,photography,radio,andcinematography–andalsotothedevelopmentof
the law of copyright (which had led, for example, to the recognition of moral rights, to the 
abolishment of formalities as a condition of protection and to the determination of a minimum 
term of protection). As a result of this, the 1948 Brussels Act of the Convention contained 
alreadyquitedetailedregulationonalltheimportantaspectsofcopyrightprotection.
In the 1950s and 1960s, the Berne Convention received partners in the system of international 
norms. First, a new copyright convention was adopted; then also a convention for the protection 
of related rights (or, as they were called at that time, “neighboring rights”).
The Universal Copyright Convention (UCC) was worked out and adopted under the aegis 
of UNESCO in 1951. This took place mainly on the initiative of the United States of America 
(US), which, due to certain specific features of its legislation not in accordance with the 
requirementsoftheBerneConvention(suchasformalitiesasaconditionofprotectionanda
complex regulation on the term of protection of copyright) was not able to accede to the Berne 
Convention. Several Latin American countries shared this initiative since they were not members 
of the Berne Convention but had established conventions between themselves and with the 
UnitedStates.InthedeterminingthelevelofprotectionrequiredbytheUCC,thedecolonization
process was also taken into account, and the fact that the emerging newly independent 
countries–the“developingcountries”–wouldhesitatetoaccedetoaninternationaltreatythat
requiredthemtoimmediatelyenforceahighlevelofprotection.Thevariouscriteriathathad
to be taken into account led to the adoption of a convention that differed in many important 
aspects from the Berne Convention. The UCC contained only some very general obligations 
concerning the rights to be granted; it prescribed a much shorter term of protection; and it 
allowed the application of formalities (but simplified their fulfillment by providing that the 
indication of a simple standardized copyright notice was sufficient). Aclose connection has been 
established between the UCC and the Berne Convention to the advantage of the latter. Under 
theAppendixDeclarationtoArticle XVIIoftheUCC,ifacountryispartytobothconventions, 
only the Berne Convention applies; and, if it has withdrawn from the Berne Union, works 
originating in that country are not protected by either the UCC or the Berne Convention. 10 Due to 
these self-destructing provisions, with the growth in membership of the Berne Union, the scope 
of application of the UCC has shrunk ever more, and no longer has any real relevance.11
TheothernewpartneroftheBerneConvention(andtheUCC)–theInternationalConvention
for the Protection of Performers, Producers of Phonograms and Broadcasting Organisations, 
adoptedinRomein1961knownas(theRomeConvention)–wasworkedoutunderthejoint
aegis of the United International Bureaux for the Protection of Intellectual Property (BIRPI) (the 
predecessor organization of WIPO), UNESCO and the International Labour Organization (ILO). 
Theneedforprotectionforthesenewcategoriesofbeneficiarieshademergedasaconsequence
of technological developments. Already sound recording was raising problems for performers 
which were then aggravated by ever more numerous radio programs and the advent of 
television. The phonograms embodying performances and the radio and television transmissions 
of both phonograms and live performances appeared as competitors, which undermined the 
employment opportunities of performers. These performers demanded the recognition of 
theirrights–rightsofauthorization,“rightstoprevent”or,atleast,rightstoremuneration–
with respect to these new forms of exploitation of their performances. Phonogram producers

Introduction
requiredprotectionagainsttheunauthorizedcopyingoftheirphonograms.Finally,broadcasting
organizations also joined the first two groups of interested parties in demanding protection for 
their broadcast programs against unauthorized rebroadcasting. 
The first idea was to try to grant protection for these subject matters within the copyright system; 
and this was discussed at some revision conferences of the Berne Union. In fact, several countries 
–mainlythosethatfollowedthecommonlawtradition–applied,andsomeofthemstillapply,
this solution, at least for phonograms and broadcasts. However, this has not been found to be 
acceptableingeneral–inparticularnotbythosecountriesfollowingthecivillawtradition–andthis
insight led, through a long period of preparatory work, to the adoption of the Rome Convention.
TheRomeConventionischaracterizedfrequentlyasa“pioneerconvention”because,atthetime
of its adoption, the legislation of only avery few countries provided specific rights for the three 
categories of beneficiaries it covered. This was also the reason why, in addition to the obligation to 
grant national treatment as under the Berne Convention, the minimum obligations under the Rome 
Convention were fixed at a relatively low level (in general, much lower than in the Berne Convention).
The number of countries party to the Rome Convention grew slowly. One of the main reasons 
for such a limited adherence was that the countries following the common law tradition 
were not interested in acceding to the Convention since, under their laws, phonograms and 
broadcasts were eligible for copyright protection (and many of them also granted some 
protection for performers). In respect of related rights, for some time there was no movement 
towards working out a “bridging convention” similar to the UCC in the field of copyright 
(this only took place with the drafting and entry into force of the Agreement on Trade-
Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) Agreement and the WPPT). However, 
technological developments constrained countries following different legal traditions to 
combinetheireffortstosolveatleastcertainurgentquestions.Thisledtotheadoptionoftwo 
new conventions, the Phonograms Convention and the Brussels, or Satellites, Convention.
The Phonograms Convention12 became necessary because new, more easily applicable 
reproductiontechniqueswereleadingtoincreasinglywidespreadpiracyofphonograms.The 
objectiveofthePhonogramsConvention–adoptedafterveryquickpreparatoryworkinGeneva 
in1971–wastoofferprotectionagainstthismenacingphenomenon.TheConventiondoesnot
provide for any specific rights; it only identifies the acts of phonogram piracy and obligates the 
Contracting States to grant appropriate protection against them, but allows freedom as regards 
thelegaltechniquesthroughwhichthisobligationisfulfilled.
The Satellites Convention13 adopted in Brussels in 1974, may also be regarded as an anti-piracy 
treaty. Its purpose was to provide protection against piracy of “programme-carrying signals” 
transmitted by telecommunication satellites. Like the Phonograms Convention, it is very flexible; it 
likewise allows Contracting Parties the freedom to choose the legal means through which protection 
is granted. However, only relatively few countries have acceded to the Convention, due to its narrow 
coverage. It does not apply to direct broadcasting satellites; and now, with the increase of the 
capacity and power of telecommunication satellites and the growing possibility for consumers to 
pick up signals directly, ever more satellites are falling outside the protection of the Convention.
In the meantime, the last two revisions of the Berne Convention had taken place, first in 
Stockholmin1967andtheninParisin1971.Theyarefrequentlyreferredtoas“twinrevisions”.
By 1971, only the administrative provisions and final clauses of the Stockholm Act (1967) had 
entered into force (these related to the administrative reform of the Convention in connection 
with the transformation of BIRPI into WIPO) and it became clear that its substantive provisions 
(Articles 1to21andtheProtocol)wouldnotbeadheredtobyasufficientnumberofcountries.
The substantive provisions, with the exception of the Protocol on preferential treatment for 
developing countries, were adopted without any substantive changes into the Paris Act (1971). 
The latter introduced real changes in only one respect: the Protocol adopted at Stockholm was 
replacedwithanAppendix(servingthesamepurpose–toofferpreferentialnormsinfavorof 
developingcountries–butatalessgenerouslevel).
12 Convention for the Protection of Producers of Phonograms Against Unauthorized Duplication of Their Phonograms. 
13 Convention Relating to the Distribution of Programme-Carrying Signals Transmitted by Satellite.

18 At the 1967 Stockholm revision conference, in addition to certain other modifications of the 
text(whichmaybecharacterizedaslegal–technicalimprovements),themoreimportant 
amendments took place in respect of two groups of issues: first, those concerning the rights 
in audiovisual works and the original ownership, exercise and transfer of those rights; second, 
those that developing countries had raised. As a result of the acceleration of the decolonization 
process around the beginning of the 1960s, the developing countries were represented in a 
muchgreaternumberthaninanypreviousdiplomaticconference.Thesecountriesrequested
that two particular issues of major concern be addressed: first, the protection of folklore 
creations; and second, their need for easier access to works to be used for education, scientific 
activities and research. The Stockholm Diplomatic Conference ended with the understanding 
that both these issues had been settled. This was not, however, really the case. As discussed in 
thecommentsonArticle 15(4)oftheBerneConventioninthiscollectionofguides,ithasturned
out that the provision which was alleged to offer copyright protection for artistic folklore is not 
suitabletofulfillthisobjective.TheProtocoltotheStockholmAct–whichwasanintegralpart 
ofthesubstantiveprovisionsoftheAct–wasmuchmorepromisingfordevelopingcountries;
it provided for the possibility of compulsory licensing under fairly favorable terms. Indeed, in 
theopinionofthepublishersbasedincertainindustrializedcountries–whoseaccessiontothe 
Stockholm Act had been fixed as a specific condition for the entry into force of the new norms 
–thetermsweretoofavorable.Thisopinionprevailed;thenecessaryaccessionsdidnottake
place; therefore, the substantive provisions of the Stockholm Act did not enter into force.
The 1971 Paris Diplomatic Conference of the Berne Union was convened due to the failure of the 
Protocol, and the only substantive change it brought about was the replacement of the Protocol 
withanAppendix.TheothersubstantiveprovisionsoftheStockholmAct(Articles 1to21)were 
simply reproduced in the new act without any change. The revision conference of the Berne 
Union was organized jointly with a conference of the UCC. In the latter, in substance, the same 
provisions as in the Appendix to the Berne Convention were included concerning the newly 
adopted compulsory licensing system in favor of developing countries. In addition, some other 
amendments were made which resulted in a slight increase in the minimum level of protection 
prescribed in the UCC.
Asmentionedabove,theBerneConvention,afteritsadoptionin1886,wasrevisedquite 
regularly, more or less every 20 years, until the “twin revisions” in Stockholm in 1967 and in 
Paris in 1971. The revision conferences were generally convened to find responses to new 
technological developments (such as sound recording, photography, radio, cinematography 
and television). In the 1970s and 1980s, a great number of important new technological 
developments took place, such as reprography, video technology, compact cassette systems 
facilitating “home taping” (private copying), satellite broadcasting, cable television, the 
increasing importance of computer programs, computer-generated works, electronic databases 
and more. For a while, the international copyright community followed the strategy of “guided 
development”,14 rather than trying to establish new international norms. The same strategy 
was followed in respect of the related rights covered by the Rome Convention, which has never 
been revised. The recommendations, guiding principles and model provisions worked out by 
thevariousWIPObodies(atthebeginning,frequentlyincooperationwithUNESCO)offered 
guidance to governments on how to respond to the challenges of the said new technologies. 
They were based, in general, on the interpretation of existing international norms (for example, 
concerning computer programs, databases, private copying, satellite broadcasting and cable 
television); but they also included some new standards (for example, concerning the distribution 
and rental of copies).
14 Sam Ricketson coined this term to describe this form of development in 1986 in his seminal book on the Berne 
Convention: “In essence, ‘guided development’ appears to be the present policy of WIPO, whose activities in 
promoting study and discussions on problem areas have been of fundamental importance to international copyright 
protection in recent years”. See Sam Ricketson, Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works: 
1886–1986(TheHague:Kluwer,1986)(hereinafter:Ricketson),919–921; SeealsoRicketsonandGinsburg,126–128.

===== PAGE 18 =====
19
Introduction
The guidance thus offered in the “guided development” period had a significant impact on 
national legislation, and contributed to the development of copyright all over the world. 15 
At the end of the 1980s, however, it was recognized that mere guidance would no longer be 
sufficient; new binding international norms had become indispensable. One of the most 
important reasons for this was that, as a result of the insufficiently harmonized responses to 
the challenges of new technologies, differing elements began to appear between national laws 
not only in certain details which traditionally had been left to national legislation, but also in 
certain fundamental elements of the international copyright norms (categories of works, rights 
and exceptions). This led to growing tensions in the fulfillment of the obligation to grant national 
treatment; the countries that guaranteed more generous, higher-level protection in the new 
aspects wanted to avoid what they perceived as an unjustified unilateral burden.
In addition to the revision of the substantive copyright and related rights norms, two other 
requirementsemerged.First,asaresultofthespectaculardevelopmentofreproduction 
technologies (with the attendant possibility of making a great number of perfect copies at 
extremely low cost), piracy had become a phenomenon that was undermining the whole system 
of the protection of copyright and related rights; much more efficient enforcement procedures 
and sanctions were needed. Second, it was felt that the only possibility for dispute settlement 
offered in the existing intellectual property conventions in case of purported violations of 
obligationsunderthoseconventions–tobringthedisputebeforetheInternationalCourtof
Justice–wasnotsufficienttoachievecompliancewithinternationalnorms.
Thepreparationofnewnormsbeganintwoforums–intheframeworkoftheUruguay
Round (GATT) of negotiations, and at WIPO, first in one committee of experts and later in two 
parallel committees (one was to work out a protocol to the Berne Convention, the other a new 
instrument to update the international norms on the rights of performers and producers of 
phonograms). For a while, the preparatory work in the WIPO committees was delayed, since 
the governments wanted to avoid any undesirable interference with the much more complex 
negotiations on the trade-related aspects of intellectual property rights (TRIPS) taking place 
within the Uruguay Round.
The TRIPS Agreement, along with the other agreements linked to the Marrakesh Agreement 
Establishing the World Trade Organization (WTO), was adopted in April 1994. It did not bring 
about many changes in the substantive norms on copyright and related rights. The level of 
protectionrequiredbytheAgreementispracticallytheBerne/Romelevel(thesubstantive 
provisionsoftheBerneConvention–exceptthoseonmoralrights–wereincludedbyreference
in the Agreement). Certain clarifications were added on how the existing norms should be 
applied (such as in respect of computer programs and databases). There are only two aspects 
in connection with which truly substantive amendments were made: first, the recognition of 
rentalrights–withcertainconditionsandexceptions–forcomputerprogramsandaudiovisual 
works, and for phonograms; and, second, the extension of the minimum term of protection for 
the rights of performers and producers of phonograms from 20 years (as provided in the Rome 
Convention) to 50 years.
The TRIPS Agreement, however, includes two new elements of historical importance that had 
beenmissingfromtheinternationalsystemofintellectualpropertyprotection.First,itsPart III 
(Articles 41to61)containsdetailednormsonenforcementofintellectualpropertyrights; 
second, it extends the efficient WTO dispute settlement system to intellectual property rights 
(which also includes the possibility of trade sanctions if a Member of the WTO does not follow 
the findings of the Dispute Settlement Body).
15 The case of computer programs is a good example. In February 1985, a Group of Experts on the Copyright Aspects of 
the Protection of Computer Software met at WIPO; see Copyright (WIPO'smonthlyreview),April1985issue,146–157. 
At that time, there were only five countries that in their legislation explicitly recognized the copyright protection of 
computer programs: Australia, Hungary, India, the Philippines and the United States of America (it is another matter 
that, in some other countries, such protection was granted on the basis of case law). That meeting, on the basis of 
a comprehensive study prepared by Michael Keplinger (U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, Washington, D.C.) and of 
a thorough discussion, brought a decisive breakthrough towards the copyright protection of computer programs. 
SufficeittomentionthatinJuneandJulyofthesameyearthefollowingfourcountriesprovidedforthecopyright 
protectionofcomputerprogramsintheirstatutorylaws:France,Germany,JapanandtheUnitedKingdom.

Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
20 After the adoption of the TRIPS Agreement, a new situation emerged. The TRIPS negotiations 
were, in fact, concluded in December 1992, and it was after that that the Internet started 
its spectacular expansion, due to the exponential increase of storage and communication 
capacities and the improvement of compression and error-correction systems and other 
technological developments. Emerging as an important market of cultural and information 
products, the Internet was also becoming a distribution channel for pirates. There was no 
chance to reopen the trade negotiations that had just been concluded. Therefore, the forum of 
WIPO was used for the further updating of the international norms on copyright and related 
rights which had suddenly again become necessary.
WIPO started dealing with the impact of digital technology on copyright and related rights 
quiteintensivelyasearlyasMarch1993,whenitorganizedtheWIPOWorldwideSymposium
on this topic at Harvard University. This was also the focus of attention at the WIPO Worldwide 
SymposiumontheFutureofCopyrightandNeighboringRightsorganizedinParisinJune
1994. Discussions continued at the WIPO Worldwide Symposium on Copyright in the Global 
Information Infrastructure, which took place in Mexico City in May 1995. Finally, the WIPO World 
Forum on the Protection of Intellectual Creations in the Information Society, held at Naples in 
October 1995, served as an opportunity to sum up ideas on what kinds of responses might be 
given to the challenges posed by digital technology and the Internet. The concrete preparatory 
work was carried out in the two WIPO committees of experts (the “Berne Protocol Committee” 
and the “New Instrument Committee”) mentioned above.
Inspiteofthecomplexityoftheissuesinvolved,thepreparatorywork–acceleratedafterthe
adoptionoftheTRIPSAgreement–ledwithinarelativelyshorttimetotheconvocationofaWIPO
Diplomatic Conference in Geneva in December 1996. This diplomatic conference adopted the WIPO 
Copyright Treaty (WCT) and the WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty (WPPT), which, once 
30 instruments of ratification or accession had been deposited with the Director General of WIPO 
for each of them, entered into force on March 6, 2002, and May 20, 2002, respectively.
The WCT and the WPPT were referred to as the “Internet Treaties”, and this expression has 
become so commonly used that they are also mentioned in this way in certain WIPO documents. 
However, although the main purpose of the WCT and the WPPT is to offer responses to the 
most urgent challenges posed by digital technology, and in particular by the Internet, they do 
notconsistsolelyofprovisionstoaddressthoseissues.Thesametechniquewasusedfortheir
negotiation and adoption as in the case of the TRIPS Agreement, in the sense that the new 
WIPO treaties obligate the Contracting Parties to comply with existing substantive international 
normswiththeadditionofnewcomplementaryones.Thelevelofprotectionrequiredbythe
two treaties may be characterized as “Berne/Rome plus” or “TRIPS plus”, but in the WCT and the 
WPPT only the small number of substantive copyright and related rights norms within the TRIPS 
Agreement were adopted, not the detailed enforcement provisions nor the effective dispute 
settlement mechanism. The really important new elements of the WCT and the WPPT are those 
provisions worked out in accordance with the so-called “digital agenda” of the preparatory work 
in the above-mentioned two Committees and at the 1996 Diplomatic Conference.
The “digital agenda” covered basically four issues: (i) the concept of reproduction and the 
application of the right of reproduction within the online digital environment; (ii) the right or 
rights to be applied for interactive digital transmissions; (iii) the application of exceptions and 
limitations within the new environment; and (iv) obligations concerning technological protection 
measures and rights management information. These issues on the digital agenda, and the 
solutions adopted by the Diplomatic Conference in respect of them, are discussed below in the 
Guides to the WCT and the WPPT (and the Guide to the BTAP reviews how the same issues were 
settled in the same way 16 years later in that Treaty).
The Basic Proposal for the treaty which was to become the WPPT contained two alternatives. 
One–whichwasadopted–providedprotectionfortherightsofperformersonlyconcerninglive
performancesandperformancesfixedonphonograms;andtheother–whichwasnot–extended
that protection to “audiovisual performances”. The main obstacle to the adoption of the latter 
alternativewasthedisagreement–inviewofthegreatdifferencesbetweenthelegalnormsof
thevariouscountries–concerningtheprovisionsontheoriginalownershipandtransferofrights
of “audiovisual performers” to the producers. After the 1996 Diplomatic Conference preparatory 
work continued and, in 2000, another Diplomatic Conference was convened which, although it

Interpretation of the conventions and treaties in the guides
For the interpretation of the eight instruments analyzed in this collection of guides the relevant 
provisionsoftheVCLTareused.Theprovisionsinquestionreadasfollows:
Article 31.Generalruleofinterpretation
1. A treaty shall be interpreted in good faith in accordance with the ordinary meaning to be 
given to the terms of the treaty in their context and in the light of its object and purpose.
2. The context for the purpose of the interpretation of a treaty shall comprise, in 
addition to the text, including its preamble and annexes:
(a) any agreement relating to the treaty which was made between all the parties in 
connection with the conclusion of the treaty;
(b) any instrument which was made by one or more parties in connection with the 
conclusion of the treaty and accepted by the other parties as an instrument 
related to the treaty.
3. There shall be taken into account, together with the context:
(a) anysubsequentagreementbetweenthepartiesregardingtheinterpretationof
the treaty or the application of its provisions;
(b) anysubsequentpracticeintheapplicationofthetreatywhichestablishesthe
agreement of the parties regarding its interpretation;
(c) any relevant rules of international law applicable in the relations between 
the parties.
4. A special meaning shall be given to a term if it is established that the parties so intended.
Article 32.Supplementarymeansofinterpretation
Recourse may be had to supplementary means of interpretation, including the 
preparatory work of the treaty and the circumstances of its conclusion, in order to confirm 
themeaningresultingfromtheapplicationofarticle 31,ortodeterminethemeaning
whentheinterpretationaccordingtoarticle 31:
(a) leaves the meaning ambiguous or obscure; or
(b) leads to a result which is manifestly absurd or unreasonable.

TheVCLTappliesonlytotreatiesadoptedafteritsentryintoforcein1980.Therefore,in

AnotherquestionthatarisesintheapplicationoftheVCLTconcernsthestatusofthe
substantive provisions of the Berne and Rome Conventions that are reproduced in mutatis 
mutandis manner or included by reference in the WCT, the WPPT and the BTAP (and, in some 
aspects,alsointheMarrakeshVIPTreaty).Thatis,arethesourcesofinterpretationmentioned 

practice”, the “special meaning” of certain words and expressions, and “the preparatory work 
of[a]treatyandthecircumstancesofitsconclusion”–applicablesolelywithrespecttothenew 
treaties or also to the Berne and Rome Conventions?
It is submitted that the answer should be in the affirmative; all these sources should be 
taken into account in a reasonable way. Otherwise, it would be impossible to satisfy the most 
important objective and principle of the interpretation of treaties: namely, that a treaty must 
be interpreted in good faith. This is particularly clear with respect to the substantive provisions 
of the Berne Convention, since the text of these provisions was not simply adopted in the 
WCT; it is made an obligation of the Contracting Parties to comply with these provisions of the 
Berne Convention.

PART I. Guide to the 
Berne Convention
Introduction
What exists now as the international system of copyright and related rights protection has 
grownfrombilateralagreementsconcludedmainly–althoughnotexclusively–between 
European countries in the 19th century (at that time, only in respect of copyright, since related 
rights only came into being in the 20th century). The bilateral agreements were, in general, 
based on the principle of national treatment combined with some minimum obligations. This 
kindofstructureforinternationalagreementsinthefieldofcopyrightandrelatedrights–that 
is, the obligation of granting national treatment to the nationals of the other contracting parties, 
combined with a minimum level of protection that each contracting party must grant to such 
nationals–hasprevailedsincethen.
This structure of international norms became necessary due to the differences between 
the various national systems, not only as to the level of protection granted, but also from 
the viewpoint of the legal philosophy on which they were based. From the beginning of the 
existence of national legislation on copyright, there were two differing systems; these are now 
referred to in general as the common law and the civil law systems.
As pointed out above, the key objective of the protection of the common law system is to offer 
appropriate incentives for further creative activity. It is conceptualized as a kind of agreement 
between society and authors: you create and make available your works to the public, and you 
will enjoy protection for a limited time.
The civil law system has more than one root, but the most decisive one goes down as deep 
as the time of the French Revolution, when authors’ rights in their literary and artistic works 
were recognized on the basis of a natural right approach. The rights in authors’ works were 
regarded as “the most sacred property” ( la propriété la plus sacrée); their works were considered 
as the products of the human mind and as expressions of their personality. Several differences 
have followed from these two philosophies which are still present in the copyright systems. 
They concern such fundamental issues as authorship, the concept of a work, originality, 
the borderline between copyright per se and related rights, original ownership, and the 
transferability of economic rights. In addition to the differences related to the underlying 
philosophies, there are others, because the various countries developed their emerging 
copyright legislation independently. However, the big differences in the technological, economic 
and social developments between the various countries were and have remained at least 
as relevant, and in certain aspects are even more significant, and they necessitate specific 
requirementsintheoperationandupdatingoftheinternationalcopyrightsystem.
ThehistoryoftheBerneConventiongoesbacktothefourthquarterofthe19 th century. The 
International Literary Association, which later was transformed into the International Literary 
and Artistic Association (ALAI), 19foundedin1878inParis–thefirstpresidentofwhichwas
19 ALAI is the acronym of its original French title: Association littéraire et artistique internationale.  ALAI is still an active 
non-governmental organization. It has a permanent observer status at WIPO, holds congresses every year as well 
as Executive Committee sessions regularly, and adopt resolutions and opinions on the key current copyright issues, 
which are published on its website www.alai.org .

===== PAGE 23 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
24 theFrenchwriterVictorHugo–wastheinitiatoroftheadoptionofamultilateralconvention
for the protection of “literary and artistic property”. It held one of its first congresses in 
Bern in September 1883 where the participants adopted a draft multilateral treaty with the 
title “Convention Establishing a General Union for the Protection of the Rights of Authors in 
their Literary and Artistic Works”. At the suggestion of ALAI, the Federal Council of the Swiss 
Confederation sent this draft, on December 3, 1883, to the governments of the participating 
countries with the proposal to hold a diplomatic conference in 1884 to adopt a treaty. In fact, 
three conferences were held in Bern, in 1884, 1885 and 1886, the last of which took place from 
September 6 to 9, 1986, where the Berne Convention on Literary and Artistic Works was adopted 
along with an “Additional Article” and a “Final Protocol”. It was signed by ten countries: Belgium, 
France, Germany, Great Britain, Haiti, Italy, Liberia, Spain, Switzerland and Tunisia.
The original 1886 text of the Convention was composed of 19 articles, and it was based on 
the principle of national treatment with certain minimum obligations. Among the rights to be 
granted, the right of translation received special attention, but the Convention also contained 
provisions on the right of public performance and the right of adaptation (characterized 
as “indirect appropriation” of works) and provided for certain exceptions, such as for 
educational purposes.
The Convention has since been revised six times, in 1896 in Paris, in 1908 in Berlin, in 1928 in Rome, 
in 1948 in Brussels, in 1967 in Stockholm and in 1971 in Paris. Through the revisions, it was adapted 
step by step to emerging new technologies, such as phonographs, cinematography, radio and 
television broadcasting. In addition to the recognition of new economic rights and moral rights, and 
providing for a minimum 50-year term of protection, the revision conferences also paid attention to 
maintaining an appropriate balance of interests by allowing specific exceptions and limitations.
Thelasttworevisions,doneinStockholmandParis,arefrequentlyreferredtoas“twinrevisions”.
In Stockholm, the substantive provisions of the Convention were updated, and its administrative 
provisions adapted to the WIPO Convention by which the international intellectual property 
system was reformed at the same Diplomatic Conference. The most important amendments made 
concerned the right of reproduction, the “three-step test” on the conditions for the application of 
exceptions to and limitations of the right, and an overall regulation of cinematographic adaptation 
of works as well as the protection of cinematographic works, including the complex issues of 
original ownership and transfer of rights by co-authors to the producers.
The Stockholm Diplomatic Conference was the first conference at which, as a result of the 
decolonization process in the late 1950s and the 1960s, developing countries participated in 
significant numbers. These countries had two main demands: preferential treatment for their 
educational and research purposes and intellectual property protection for folklore, which 
in many of those countries was a living tradition and main form of creativity. In response to 
thefirstdemand,theConferenceadoptedaProtocoland,tothelatter,thenewArticle 15(4).
However, neither of the issues was settled satisfactorily. As regards folklore, the comments on 
Article 15(4)inthisGuidediscusswhycopyrightprotectionisnotsuitablefortheprotectionof 
expressions of folklore. The Protocol might have been helpful for the developing countries, but 
the rightholders and publishers concerned strongly opposed it because according to them it 
went too far in restricting their legitimate interests. Under this pressure, the Paris Diplomatic 
Conference was convened with the specific purpose of revising the Protocol, which was replaced 
by an Appendix, which is reproduced and commented on below. 
Since 1971 no revision of the Berne Convention has taken place although the number and 
significance of the technological and social changes since that time has been greater than 
during the entire previous history of the Convention: satellite broadcasting, cable television, 
a spectacular increase of communication capacities, computer programs, databases, and the 
culmination of all this: online digital technology.
The main reason for the absence of Berne revisions since 1971 is the unanimity principle, which 
waslaiddowninArticle 27(3)and,in1886,whentheConventionwasadoptedbytencountries,
seemedtobeappropriate.AsmembershipintheBerneUnion2hasgrown,however–andalso
in view of the significant differences among its members with respect to technological and 
socialdevelopmentsandtocertainaspectsoftheirlegalsystems–thisprinciplehasprovento 
be an obstacle to updating the international copyright norms.

===== PAGE 24 =====
25
PART I. Guide to the Berne Convention
The international copyright community tried to respond to the new challenges by interpreting 
the existing norms, for a while with promising results. In the “guided development” 20 period 
in the late 1970s and 1980s, solutions were worked out in such forms as model provisions and 
guiding principles concerning the copyright protection of computer programs and databases, 
reprography, cable television, satellite television, rental, and certain exceptions and limitations, 
such as for reprographic reproduction by educational institutions and libraries or facilitating 
access to works by blind and visually impaired people. Many of the guiding principles and model 
provisions were transformed later into binding norms in the new generation of international 
treaties: the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS 
Agreement), the WIPO Copyright Treaty (WCT), the WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty  
(WPPT),theBeijingTreatyonAudiovisualPerformances(BTAP)andtheMarrakeshVIPTreaty.
When the new technologies led to widespread piracy, and important differences were emerging 
between national laws concerning certain core aspects of copyright protection, the adoption 
of new binding norms became inevitable. The process took place in parallel: in the Uruguay 
Round of negotiations of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), and in two WIPO 
Committees of Governmental Experts, leading to the adoption of the TRIPS Agreement in 1994 
andthefirsttwoWIPO“InternetTreaties”–theWCTandtheWPPT–in1996.
In the meantime, the membership of the Berne Convention grew substantially. For a long while, 
such large countries as China, the Soviet Union and the United States were not party to the 
Convention and India was bound only by the substantive provisions of the Brussels Act and 
the administrative provisions of the 1967 and 1971 Acts. But, in 1984, India acceded fully to the 
1971 Act, then the United States acceded in 1989, China in 1989, and the Russian Federation 
in 1995. The overwhelming majority of developing countries have also become parties to 
the Convention.21
The updating of the international norms took place so that the substantive provisions of the 
BerneConvention(Article 1to21andtheAppendix)wereincludedbyreferenceintheTRIPS 
Agreement (with the exception of the provisions on moral rights) and in the WCT, and the 
Members of the World Trade Organization (WTO) and the Contracting Parties of the WCT 
are obligated to comply with those Berne provisions, which, in this way, have remained key 
elements of the current international system of copyright protection. Certain provisions of the 
TRIPSAgreementandtheWCTinterprettheBerneConvention.Forexample,Article 10.1ofthe
TRIPSAgreementandArticle 4oftheWCTprotectcomputerprogramsasliteraryworks“within 
themeaningofArticle 2oftheBerneConvention”.Article 10.2.oftheTRIPSAgreementand 
Article 5oftheWCTincludesimilarinterpretativeprovisionsontheprotectionofcompilations 
of data (databases). As mentioned above, and discussed in more detail in the Guide to the WCT 
concerningArticle 4oftheTreaty,thecompetentbodiesofWIPOclarified–andstatedinthe
formofsoft-lawguidance–evenbeforetheadoptionoftheTRIPSAgreementthatcomputer
programs are protected by copyright. The commentary explains how the soft-law guidance was 
transformed into treaty interpretation in the Agreement and how it was further fine-tuned (in 
accordancewithArticle 2(1)oftheBerneConvention)intheWCTinawaythatitwas,inturn,a
kind of interpretation of the interpretative provision of the Agreement.

Preamble
ThecountriesoftheUnion,beingequallyanimatedbythedesiretoprotect,inaseffectiveand
uniform a manner as possible, the rights of authors in their literary and artistic works,
Recognizing the importance of the work of the Revision Conference held at Stockholm in 1967,
Have resolved to revise the Act adopted by the Stockholm Conference, while maintaining 
withoutchangeArticles 1to20and22to26ofthatAct,
Consequently,theundersignedPlenipotentiaries,havingpresentedtheirfullpowers,

Introductory remarks
BC-Pr.1.Article 31.2oftheViennaConventionoftheLawofInternationalTreaties(hereinafter:
VCLT)makesitclearthatapreambletoatreatyisanintegralpartofthetext of a treaty.22 That 
is, in principle, in terms of the interpretation of a treaty, the preamble has the same status as 
thearticles andotherpossibleelementsofthetreaty.Inpractice,however,apreambledoes
not contain concrete normative elements; it usually indicates the object and the purpose of the 
treaty, and may describe certain facts relating to its preparation and adoption. The elements of a 
preamble that may play a role in the interpretation of the treaty are mainly those that refer to its 
objectandpurpose.ThisalsofollowsfromArticle 31.1oftheVCLT,whichprovidesthat“[a]treaty
shall be interpreted in good faith in accordance with the ordinary meaning to be given to the 
terms of the treaty in their context and in the light of its object and purpose” (emphasis added).
BC-Pr. 2. The Preamble of the Berne Convention contains fewer paragraphs than those of the 
more recent WIPO-administered copyright and related rights treaties. 23 Of the four paragraphs 
of its Preamble, only the first one is substantive; the other three paragraphs are of a more 
descriptive nature, stating which provisions of the 1967 Stockholm Act are left intact (the 
great majority thereof) and reflecting the agreement of the delegations that signed the act. 24 
Therefore,itisonlythefirstparagraph whichwarrantscomment.
First paragraph of the Preamble
BC-Pr.3.Thefirstparagraph ofthePreambledeterminestheobjectandpurposeofthe
Convention by declaring the “desire” of “the countries of the Union” “to protect, in as effective 
and uniform a manner as possible, the rights of authors in their literary and artistic works”. 25 
The purpose (“the desire”) of the countries of the Union (see 1.1 below) is an “as effective and 
uniform” protection “as possible” of the “rights of authors in their literary and artistic works”.
BC-Pr. 4. One element of the purpose of the Convention is that the norms on the protection of 
the rights to be granted should be “as uniform as possible”. Uniformization seems to be a more 
ambitiousobjectivethan“harmonization”.Itreferstotheideaofsomedelegationsatthe1884–
1886BerneDiplomaticConferencesthattheConventionshouldthroughsubsequentrevisions
emerge as a kind of “universal copyright law”. This level of uniformity has not been achieved in 
the long history of the Berne Convention (and the development of international copyright norms 
in general), and it does not seem to be a truly realistic idea. Uniformization may be regarded 
as an ideal and abstract result towards which the international copyright community may 
converge, but which it might never fully reach.

comprise, in addition to the text, including its preamble and annexes ”; emphasis added.

PART I. Guide to the Berne Convention
BC-Pr. 5. The objective of granting protection “in as effective […] a manner as possible” indicates the 
intention of granting strong protection for authors’ rights. This is important to keep in mind when it 
comestotheinterpretationofthesubstantiveprovisionsoftheConvention.Itisquiteclear,however,
that “as effective” protection “as possible” does not necessarily mean the highest possible level of 
protectionthattheimaginationandlegaltechniquemightproduce.Theexpression“aspossible”
seems to refer to two possible reasons for the international community to grant protection at a level 
that is lower than the highest possible: first, the economic and social conditions of many countries do 
not allow the adoption of the highest possible standards; and, second, there is a need for balancing 
the public interest of granting effective protection to authors with other public interests.
BC-Pr. 6. These factors have been considered throughout the history of the Berne Convention. 
ProofofthisisfoundinthedeclarationmadebyNumaDroz,theChairmanoftheveryfirst–
1884–BerneDiplomaticConference,inhisclosingspeech:
Whereas, for one thing, certain delegations might have wished for more extensive and 
more uniform protection of authors’ rights, due account did also have to be taken of the fact 
that the ideal principles whose triumph we are working towards can only progress gradually 
in the so-varied countries that we wish to see joining the Union. Consideration also has to be 
given to the fact that limitations on absolute protection are dictated, rightly in my opinion, by 
the public interest. The ever-growing need for mass instruction could never be met if there 
were no reservation of certain reproduction facilities, which at the same time should not 
degenerate into abuses. These were the various viewpoints and interests that we have 
sought to reconcile in the draft Convention.26
Article 1
[Establishment of a Union] 27
The countries to which this Convention applies constitute a Union for the protection of the 
rights of authors in their literary and artistic works.
BC-1.1.Thisarticle doesnotcontainasubstantiveprovision;itwouldhavenoimpactonthe
rights and obligations under the Convention if it had not been included. It might be considered 
necessary to indicate the subject matter and purpose of the Convention: “the protection of the 
rights of authors in their literary and artistic works”. This may not be the case, however, since 
the Preamble already states this.
BC-1.2. “The countries to which this Convention applies” are the countries party to the 
Convention, and the “Union” is the totality of the parties. In the various provisions of the 
Convention,theexpression“thecountriesoftheUnion”isusedfrequently.Bothphrasesmean 
contracting parties of the Convention. 
BC-1.3.InthisArticle,thesameexpressionisusedasinthefirstparagraph ofthePreamble:
“rights in literary and artistic works”. The use of this neutral expression is not by chance. The 
drafters of the Convention wanted to avoid the use of ideologically charged expressions and 
concepts which would only correspond to certain copyright schools and not others.

(1) The expression “literary and artistic works” shall include every production in the literary,

“Literary and artistic works” as a general concept
BC-2.1.Paragraph (1)ofArticle 2containstwoelements:first,ageneraloutlineoftheconceptof
“literaryandartisticworks”–thoughnotaformaldefinition–andsecond,anon-exclusivelistof 
such works.
BC-2.2.AlthoughthisisnotstatedexplicitlyinArticle 2(1),thecontextinwhichthewords“work” 
and“author”areusedintheConventionindicatethatonlythoseproductionsqualifyasworks 
that are intellectual creationsand,consequently,onlythosepersonsqualifyasauthorswhose
intellectual creative activity brings such works into existence. This is the first basic element of the 
concept of literary and artistic works.
BC-2.3. The records of various diplomatic conferences that adopted and revised the Berne 
ConventionreflectthatthereasonArticle 2(1)oftheConventiondoesnotstateexplicitlythat 
works are intellectual creations is that this element of the concept of “works” was considered to 
be evident. This was stated explicitly at the 1948 Brussels Diplomatic Conference. The General 
Report, in referring to certain categories of works, included the following clarification: “You have 
not considered it necessary to specify that those works constitute intellectual creations because 
[...] if we are speaking of literary and artistic works, we are already using a term which means that 
we are talking about [...] an intellectual creation within the sphere of letters and the arts. ”28
BC-2.4.Thetextofonearticle oftheConventioncontainsadirectreferencetothefactthat
onlyintellectualcreationsqualifyasworks.ItisincludednotinArticle 2(1)oftheConvention
on“literaryandartisticworks”,butinArticle 2(5)concerningcollections.Hereitwasevidently 
found necessary to stress this element of the concept of “literary and artistic works”.
BC-2.5. It is also obvious, on the basis of the records of the various diplomatic conferences which 
adoptedandrevisedtheConvention,thattherequirementthataproductionberecognizedas
a work because it is an intellectual creation does not mean that it has to be new according to 
the concept of “novelty” (used in the field of industrial property), but rather that it should be 
original.29 The concept of originality, however, is not used in a uniform manner in the countries 
oftheUnion.Undercertainnationallaws–mainlyamongthosethatfollowthecommonlaw
tradition(butnotincludingtheUnitedStatesofAmerica(US))–itissufficientthataproduction 
in the literary and artistic field be the result of “skill and labor” or “sweat of the brow”, while 
othernationallaws–ingeneral,thoseofthecountriesfollowingthecivillawtradition–apply
a more demanding originality test. Under the latter laws, sometimes it is not sufficient that a 
production is a result of intellectual creation; it must also be an individual creation reflecting 
the personality of the author. There is, however, a trend of some convergence (although it is 
still far from complete harmonization) between the different legal systems. The direction of the 
trend may be summed up as follows: mere “sweat of the brow” is not sufficient for a production

because, if it is not, it is not a work); rather it is to clarify that the derivative works and the audiovisual works are protected

toqualifyasawork;30 for this, it must also be an intellectual creation, which, in turn, is the only 
condition.No“higher”levelofcreativityisrequired. 31
BC-2.6.TheBerneConventiondoesnotcontainanyspecificprovisionconcerningthe“idea–
expressiondichotomy”,asdotheTRIPSAgreement,inArticle 9.2,andtheWCT,inArticle 2. 
However, the principle that mere ideas are not protected by copyright, but only concrete original 
expressions of ideas are, may be deduced from the basic meaning of the generic expression 
“production”. A mere idea is obviously not yet a production; it is only transformed into a 
production when it is developed into a concrete form of expression.
BC-2.7. The phrase “whatever may be the mode or form of its expression” may also be regarded 
asareferencetotheidea–expressiondichotomy,sincetheunderlyingprinciplethatamere
idea is not sufficient for copyright protection follows from what is mentioned in the preceding 
paragraph, and the use of the word “expression” indicates the way in which intellectual creations 
take form. Another basic principle is expressed here as well: “whatever may be the mode and 
form” indicates that copyright protection does not depend on some aesthetic evaluation, or on 
thenatureorqualityoftheconcreteformofexpression.
BC-2.8. The second basic element of the concept of literary and artistic works is referred to by the 
adjectives “literary” and “artistic”. It should be noted that, while in general, the Berne Convention 
uses the expression “literary and artistic works” to indicate the subject matter of protection, in 
Article 2(1)oftheConvention,inadditiontotheseadjectivesathirdoneappears:“scientific”.
The records of various diplomatic conferences reflect that this third adjective is only intended to 
indicate that the concept of literary and artistic works should not be interpreted in a restrictive way, 
for example, to include only “belles-lettres”, “fiction” or the “fine arts”. The adjective “scientific” is 
not necessary for expressing the concept of “literary and artistic works”, the term used throughout 
the Convention; it may even be misleading, given that a work in the scientific domain is protected 
not due to its scientific nature, but rather because it is an intellectual creation expressed in the form 
of writing, drawing, audiovisual creation or some other production.
BC-2.9. The adjective “literary” is to be understood as meaning all language- and information-
oriented productions expressed in letters, numbers or other symbols, irrespective of whether 
they are legible to everyone or are coded. The adjective “artistic” covers all possible modes and 
forms of expression other than what is “literary”.
BC-2.10. The overwhelming majority of the provisions of the Convention apply to “literary and 
artistic works” in general. It is very rare that a provision only relates either to literary works or 
to artistic works, or to a given category or subcategory of works. Although some works may 
be regarded as being exclusively “literary works” (such as short stories, poems or scientific 
studies) or exclusively “artistic works” (such as paintings or sculptures), this is not necessarily the 
case. This has never been so, and this is even less so in the era of multimedia productions. The 
expression“literaryandartisticworks”shouldbeunderstoodasalegal–technicalexpression;in
thecaseofagivenwork,itisnotgenerallynecessarytoqualifywhetheritisaliteraryworkoran
artistic work. The expression includes all intellectual creations, whether literary, artistic, or both.
Non-exhaustive list of “literary and artistic works”
BC-2.11.Inparagraph (1),afterthegeneraloutlineoftheconceptof“literaryandartisticworks”,
a list of such works follows. The non-exhaustive nature of the list is indicated by the words “such 
as”, which introduce the list.

30 BC-2.12. Before going through the various categories of works in this list, it is necessary to 
discuss what the non-exhaustive nature of the list means with regard to the coverage of the 
concept of “literary and artistic works”. First, the list indicates more concretely what kinds 
of “productions” are included “in the literary […] and artistic domain”; all those mentioned in 
the list must be protected as literary and artistic works (provided that they are original in the 
sense that they are the result of intellectual creation). Second, although it is a very broad list, it 
should not be regarded as complete. If a category of “production in the literary […] and artistic 
domain” is not mentioned in the list but corresponds to the general concept of “literary and 
artisticworks”inaccordancewithArticle 2(1),itwouldnotbeappropriatetoconcludethat 
there is no obligation under the Convention to protect that category by copyright. This would 
be in conflict with the provision that “[t]he expression ‘literary and artistic works’ shall include 
every production in the literary, scientific and artistic domain” (emphasis added). If such a 
production is not included in the list, its recognition as falling within this category is a matter of 
interpretationofArticle 2(1)oftheConvention.
BC-2.13. If a majority of contracting parties (“countries of the Union”) recognize a category of 
productionsasliteraryandartisticworks,itispossibletospeakofa“subsequentpractice” 
which,assuch,isarelevantsourceofinterpretationoftreatiesunderArticle 31.3(b)oftheVCLT.
However, in case of a dispute on whether certain productions should be protected by copyright, 
only one possible method is available under the Berne Convention for the settlement of such a 
dispute:itmaybesubmittedtotheInternationalCourtofJustice.This,however,hasnotturned
out to be a workable mechanism. Therefore, the revision conferences preferred to eliminate any 
doubts about certain new categories by including them in the non-exhaustive list as soon as 
there was sufficient agreement on their copyright protection.
BC-2.14.AsregardstheproductionslistedinArticle 2(1),thefollowingparagraphsprovideonlya
generaloverview,sincethecoverageofmostofthesecategoriesofworksisquiteclear.
Main categories of works
BC-2.15.Theworksmentionedinthenon-exhaustivelistofArticle 2(1)maybedividedintoten
groups as follows.
BC-2.16. Books, pamphlets and other writings form the first group. What deserves analysis here 
is the general subcategory “other writings”. It is extremely broad, and there is no reason to try 
to interpret it in a restrictive way. It covers all kinds of writings, irrespective of their means of 
fixation, subject matter (whether fiction, non-fiction, scientific, technical, medical or similar 
professional writings, or the description of information) and whether they may be understood 
directly by everybody who understands the given natural language or are expressed by codes, 
orsomeequipmentisneededfortheirperception.Thisiswhyithasbeenfoundthatcomputer
programs must also be regarded as “writings” (which is discussed in more detail in the comments 
onArticle 4oftheWCTintheGuidebelow).Otherwise,itgoeswithoutsayingthata“book”
does not mean the physical object containing a novel or other writings, nor the manuscript as a 
tangible object, but the novel or other writing as an intellectual creation embodied within it.
BC-2.17. The works in the secondgroup–lectures, addresses, sermons and other works of the same 
nature –insubstancedonotdifferfromwritings,andwhentheyarefixed,theyusuallytake
written form. They are mentioned separately for two reasons: first, because they are often created 
orally(forthequestionoffixationofworksasapossibleconditionofcopyrightprotection,see
paragraph (2)andthecommentsonit,below);and,second,becausespecificexceptionsmayapply
totheuseofsomeoftheseworksbyvirtueofArticle 2bis of the Convention.
BC-2.18. The common element of the thirdgroup–dramatic or dramatico-musical works; 
choreographic works and entertainments in dumb show –isthattheyareintendedforstage
presentation. Dramatic works are normally fixed in writing and may thus be regarded as 
belongingtoboththefirstgroupandthethirdgroupofcategoriesofworkslistedinArticle 2(1).
Dramatico-musical works usually are fixed both in writing and in musical notation. The fixation 
of choreographic works and “entertainments in dumb show” is more difficult (and for this there 
are no such well-established and standardized methods of fixation as there are for writings 
andmusicalworks),butitispossible(asmentionedbelowinthecommentsonparagraph (2)
of this article). The works in this group of productions, in general, contain aleatoric elements:

for the directors of stage presentations, there is room for their own contributions. If those 
contributions are of a creative nature, the stage presentations as such may also be protected by 
copyright.(Fortheprotectionofadaptationsandotheralterationsofworks,seeparagraph (3) 
ofthisarticle,andfortherightofadaptation,seeArticle 12,below.)
BC-2.19. Musical compositions with or without words form the fourth group. These works are also 
usually fixed in musical notation along with the accompanying text (the “lyrics”) in writing, 
butcertainpopularmusicalworksevermorefrequentlyarefixedonlyinsoundrecordings, 
nowadays mainly in digital form. Musical compositions may also be created through live 
presentation as improvisations that include original elements. In the case of such works, the 
issue of fixation as a possible condition of copyright protection may also emerge (see below).
BC-2.20. Cinematographic works to which are assimilated works expressed by a process analogous 
to cinematography is the fifthcategory.Innewerinternationalandnationalnorms–aswell
asinthelegalliterature–theyareoftenreferredtoas“audiovisualworks”. 32 This expression, 
however, in certain specific cases, may not be regarded as fully precise because exclusively 
“visual”works–withoutany“audio”elements–alsofallintothiscategory.
BC-2.21. The sixth group includes works of drawing, painting, sculpture, engraving and lithography 
which are also referred to as “works of fine art”. It would have been more appropriate to add 
after the word “lithography” the word “and” and the general term “other works of fine art”, 
because there are a great variety of ways and means to create works expressed in lines, colors 
and forms. The use of the expression “works of fine art” is also useful to differentiate this 
category of works from the category of works of applied art (see below).
BC-2.22.Inthetextofparagraph (1),thecategory“works of architecture ” appears in the middle 
ofthelistofworksreferredtointheprecedingparagraph as“worksoffineart”.Theseworks, 
however, have certain special features which justify their mention as a seventh group on their 
own. First, they serve a utilitarian purpose; and, second, they are technical constructions. Since, 
however, works of architecture are mentioned among genuine works of fine art, it is clear that 
not the technical, but the artistic aspects are relevant as regards their copyright protection.
BC-2.23. The eighth group is formed by “photographic works to which are assimilated works 
expressed by a process analogous to photography ”. It took several revisions of the Berne 
Convention for photographic works to be considered for assimilation to other categories of 
literary and artistic works. This process was not completed even in the 1971 Paris Act of the 
Convention;onedifferencehasremained:underArticle 7(4),theminimumtermofprotection
oftheseworksisshorter.FullassimilationtookplacethroughArticle 9oftheWCT,which
eliminated the last remaining difference: The development of the international copyright norms 
ontheseworksisdescribedinthecommentsonthatarticle intheGuidetotheWCT.
BC-2.24. It is particularly justified to refer to works of applied art asaseparatecategory–the
ninthone–sincetheyhaveaspecialregimeundertheConvention.Thisisreflected, inter alia, in 
theprovisionsofArticle 1(7)oftheConvention;thiscategoryofworksisanalyzedthere.
BC-2.25. Illustrations, maps, plans, sketches and three-dimensional works relative to geography, 
topography,architectureorscienceformthetenth–andlast–groupofproductionsincludedin
the non-exhaustive list of literary and artistic works. The inclusion of these works in the list may 
beregardedasconfirmationoftheprinciplethataestheticqualityisnotaconditionofcopyright 
protection,andthatthepurposeofaproduction–aslongasitotherwisefulfillstheconditions 
toqualifyasawork–isnotrelevanteither.
BC-2.26. Computer programs, databases, and multimedia productions such as videogames are the 
most important newly identified categories of literary and artistic works. All of them relate to 
the development of information technology; none of them appears in the non-exhaustive list 
inparagraph (1).Asmentionedabove,computerprogramsarerecognizedasliteraryworksin
Article 10.1oftheTRIPSAgreementandinArticle 4oftheWCT,and,therefore,theirprotection
is discussed in the comments on the latter provision in the Guide to the WCT. The protection

32 ofdatabasesisanalyzedinthecommentsonArticle 2(5)oftheBerneConventionbelowandin
