theyaretobeprotectedunderparagraph (1)and/orparagraph (5)ofArticle 2oftheConvention.
BC-2.27. Artificial intelligence productionsrequirespecificcomments.Artificialintelligence–that 
is“computersystemsabletoperformtasksnormallyrequiringhumanintelligence” 33–raises
three kinds of issue concerning copyright protection, two of which relate to the concept of 
literary and artistic works. The issue that does not relate to this concept itself is the training 
of artificial intelligence systems for which a great deal of material and data is used, including 
protectedworks.Thisrequiresauthorization,oritmayjustifytheapplicationofcertain 
exceptions or limitations in accordance with the three-step test. The other two issues, however, 
asmentionedabove,concerntheconceptofworksprotectedbycopyright.Thefirst–andthe 
lessdisputed–oneistheprotectionofartificialintelligencemodels,towhichtheprotection 
of computer programs and databases seems to apply. The second such issue has received 
muchmoreattention,inparticularamongthegeneralpublic:namely,thequestionofthe
copyright protection of artificial intelligence productions. It follows from the general concept 
ofworksdiscussedabove–accordingtowhichaworkisanoriginalcreationofthehuman
intellect–thatthegenerativeproductionsofartificialintelligencethatdonotincludeoriginal 
humancontributionsdonotqualifyasworksprotectedbycopyright.Undercertainnational 
laws following the common law tradition, however, the concept of works is broader than under 
theBerneConvention;italsoincludescertaincategories–inparticularsoundrecordings 
(phonograms)andbroadcasts–whichunderthelawsofcountriesfollowingthecivillaw
tradition are protected by related, or “neighboring”, rights. In the same vein, some of those 
national laws also include provisions on “computer-generated works” produced without creative 
human contributions.34
(2) It shall, however, be a matter for legislation in the countries of the Union to prescribe 
that works in general or any specified categories of works shall not be protected unless 
they have been fixed in some material form.
Fixation as a possible requirement
BC-2.28. It was in connection with choreographic works and entertainments in dumb show 
thatthequestionoffixationasaconditionofcopyrightprotectionfirstemerged.Fixationwas
found necessary to be able to identify and prove the existence of these works. Thus, when 
choreographic works and entertainments in dumb show (pantomime) were included in the non-
exclusive list of literary and artistic works at the 1908 Berlin Diplomatic Conference, the condition 
was added that their presentation (“mise en scene”) must be fixed “in writing or otherwise”. The 
issue of fixation was reconsidered at the 1967 Stockholm Diplomatic Conference. By that time, 
thecriticismthatitwasnotlogicaltorequirefixationforcertaincategoriesofproductionsand
not for others had been found justified. Therefore, the condition concerning these two categories 
ofworkswasremovedfromparagraph (1),andparagraph (2)includedinArticle 2.
BC-2.29.BehindtheideaofleavingittothecountriesoftheUniontodecidewhethertorequire
fixation as a condition of protection was the intention of opening the way to accession to the 
Conventionbythosecountries–notablytheUnitedStates–whoselegislationcontainedsuch
acondition.However,thisrequirementmay,andingeneralis,appliedinareasonableway.
Simultaneous fixation of a live presentation may also be sufficient. Fixation as a condition of 
copyright protection is not a formality, because the protection of productions that otherwise 
qualifyasworksdoesnotdependonthefulfillmentofafurtherrequirement;rather,itmaybe 
considered to make certain productions suitable for protection in the first place (since, without 
it, the subject matter of protection could not be duly identified).
(3) Translations, adaptations, arrangements of music and other alterations of a literary or 
artistic work shall be protected as original works without prejudice to the copyright in 
the original work.

Derivative works
BC-2.30.Theproductionsmentionedinparagraph (3)ofthearticle mustbeprotected“as
original works”. In this expression, the meaning of the adjective “original” does not appear 
correspondtotheconceptof“originality”asdiscussedinthecommentsonparagraph (1)above.
A work is original by definition, since, if a production in the literary and artistic domain does not 
satisfy the originality test, it simply is not a work protected by copyright. 
BC-2.31. The use of the expression “as original works” closely relates to the nature of 
theproductionslistedinthisparagraph asderivativeworks:“translations,adaptations, 
arrangements of music and other alterations” of literary and artistic works. They are derivative 
in that they are derived from pre-existing works such that certain elements of those works are 
present in them. Those elements are supposed to be more than just the underlying ideas of the 
pre-existing works (since such ideas alone, as discussed above, are not protected by copyright). 
At the same time, these productions must also contain some extra elements other than those 
“borrowed” from the pre-existing works that constitute intellectual creations and are, thus, 
original. To the extent that they add some new original elements to the pre-existing works, they 
are protected in the same way as the pre-existing works from which they have been derived. 
Therefore, in this paragraph, the adjective “original”, in the expression “original works”, is a 
synonym of “pre-existing” or “non-derivative”.
BC-2.32. In the phrase “without prejudice to the copyright in the original work”, the adjective 
“original” has the same meaning as in the expression “original works” as discussed in the 
precedingparagraph.Here,however,referenceismadetotheconcretepre-existing–“original”
–workfromwhichatranslation,adaptation,etc.hasbeenderived,andthephraseclarifiesthe 
relationshipbetweentheprotectionofaderivativeworkandthepre-existing–“original”–work 
from which it has derived. The protection of the derivative work “without prejudice to the 
copyright in the original work” means that there are two sets of rights in such a work: the rights 
in the pre-existing work and the rights in the derivative work.
BC-2.33.Inpractice,theauthorizationofderivativeworksisfrequentlysimplified.Thisisbecause,
based on the right of translation and the right of adaptation, arrangement and other alteration 
(Articles 8and12oftheConvention),noderivativeworkofaprotectedpre-existingworkmay
be created without the authorization of the author of the latter. In a contract including such 
an authorization it may then be agreed, inter alia, howthederivativework–withtheimplied
protectionoftheelementsofthepre-existingworkusedfortheircreation–maybeused.
BC-2.34.Thequestionmayemergewhetheraderivativeworkcreatedwithouttheauthorization 
oftheauthorofthepre-existingworkmightenjoycopyrightprotection.Thisquestionshould 
be answered in the affirmative. Although the derivative work is the result of an infringement 
of the rights in the pre-existing work, this fact alone does not justify the use of the derivative 
work without authorization. Sometimes the principle that “the theft from the thief is also a 
theft” is referred to in this respect, but this parallel is not completely fitting, since what is 
“stolen” from the author of the derivative work is more than what he has “stolen” from the 
author of the original work. The records of the diplomatic conferences to revise the Convention 
confirm that this interpretation is correct. The original, 1886 Act of the Convention provided 
only for the protection of “lawful” translations (in that act, there were no provisions yet on the 
protection of adaptations). However, when the 1908 Berlin Diplomatic Conference adopted, in 
substance,whatisnowArticle 2(3)oftheConvention(intheBerlinAct,itwasstillArticle 2(2)in 
which only some non-substantive wording changes were made at the 1948 Brussels Diplomatic 
Conference), it removed the adjective “lawful” from the text, explaining that it had not been 
justified to allow the use of unauthorized derivative works “with impunity”. 35
BC-2.35. Although in the 1971 Paris Act, the copyright status of translations and adaptations 
seems to be the same, this does not mean that the real relationship of translations with the 
works translated is the same as that of adaptations with the works adapted. The task of a 
translation is to offer a new language version of a literary work as faithful to the pre-existing 
work as possible. It should be able to find the work’s original elements recreated in another 
35 Actes de la Conférence de Berlin 1908 (Berne: International Office, 1909), 232.

===== PAGE 33 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
34 language–thesametextureofthoughts,thesame(substantive)expressionsoffeelings,the 
samekindofpresentationofinformation–inanewouterform.Itverymuchdependsonthe
nature of the original text whether translation allows any room for creativity. The translation of 
apoem,forexample,ingeneralrequirescreativeeffort.Ontheotherhand,apurelytechnical 
text may not offer the possibility of choosing different options when it is faithfully translated; 
thus,itstranslationmaynotqualifyasanintellectualcreationand,thus,asawork.
BC-2.36. The nature of adaptations, arrangements and other similar alterations is different. They 
do not leave intact the concrete texture of thoughts, expressions of feelings or presentation 
of information in the way in which translations do. Whether they are created in the same 
language or in a language different from that of the pre-existing work, they by definition 
change these elements. It is the inclusion of creative elements that justifies separate protection 
ofsuchderivativeworks.Thisdifferingnatureofthetwosubcategoriesofderivativeworks– 
translationsandadaptations–inturnjustifiestheirseparateregulationwithintheConvention.
BC-2.37.Theconceptof“translation”isquiteself-evidentwhenoneconsidersthetransposition
of a text from one language to another. It is, however, less evident with regard to the 
transformation of a computer program into another computer “language” or from source code 
into object code. Whether this is also regarded as translation, or rather as an adaptation or 
“other alteration”, is left to national laws to decide; in any case, their copyright status does not 
differ greatly depending on which of these categories they fall into.
BC-2.38. The concept of “adaptation” is also sufficiently clear. It means the transformation of a 
work into another genre (for example, a novel into a dramatic work), or for the purpose of new 
ways of using it (for example, the creation of an “abridged” version of a work). Cinematographic 
adaptationofaworkisalsoadaptation,butspecificprovisionsapplytoit(seeArticles 14and 
14bis oftheConvention).Theconceptof“arrangementsofmusic”doesnotrequiredetailed
explanation either. What does need interpretation is the meaning of “other alterations of a 
literary or artistic work”. It goes without saying that this does not mean any alterations, but 
only those that result in new original elements in relation to the previous, unaltered form of the 
work. It is not easy to find obvious examples of this subcategory of derivative works. Caricatures 
and parodies are sometimes mentioned, and the transformation of a computer program into 
another computer “language” or from source code into object code, as mentioned above, may 
also be included in this broader subcategory.
(4) It shall be a matter for legislation in the countries of the Union to determine the 
protection to be granted to official texts of a legislative, administrative and legal 
nature, and to official translations of such texts.
Official texts
BC-2.39.Thereasonsbehindtheprovisioninparagraph (4)seemtobeevident.Article 19of
the Universal Declaration of Human Rights stipulates that “[e]veryone has the right […] to seek, 
receive and impart information and ideas through any media and regardless of frontiers”. This 
freedom particularly applies to legislative norms determining rights and obligations, and to the 
decisions of administrative authorities and judicial bodies. 
BC-2.40. The text of the provision is also clear. The only thing that needs to be pointed out 
is that only official texts of a legislative, administrative or legal nature are covered by this 
exception, that is, those that are created and adopted by the respective organs (such as laws, 
administrative decisions or court decisions).
(5) Collections of literary or artistic works such as encyclopaedias and anthologies which, 
by reason of the selection and arrangement of their contents, constitute intellectual 
creations shall be protected as such, without prejudice to the copyright in each of the 
works forming part of such collections.
Collections
BC-2.41. For the first time, the 1908 Berlin Act of the Convention provided for the protection of 
collections; but at that time, collections were still protected as a category of derivative works.

===== PAGE 34 =====
35
PART I. Guide to the Berne Convention
TheywerementionedinArticle 2(2)alongwithtranslationsandadaptations.Then,atthe1948
BrusselsDiplomaticConference,aseparateparagraph wasinsertedoncollections.Inthe
BrusselsAct,theprovisionwasincludedinparagraph (4),whichatthe1967StockholmDiplomatic
Conferencewasrenumbered,withoutanysubstantivechange,tobecomeparagraph (5).
BC-2.42.Thecollections–encyclopedias,anthologies,collectionsofprofessionalstudies,and 
soon–forwhichprotectionistobegrantedunderparagraph (5)arecollectionsof literary and 
artistic works. However, the basis of their protection is that they constitute intellectual creations 
by reason of the selection and arrangement of the works; therefore, it is not a further condition 
of the protection that the works selected and arranged in that way enjoy copyright protection. 
Collectionsofworksthathaveneverenjoyedprotection–forexample,intheabsenceoftreaty 
obligations,orancientworksfrombeforecopyrightprotectionexisted–andofworksthathave 
fallen into the public domain are also protected under this provision. 
BC-2.43. Collections not containing literary and artistic works are not protected under 
paragraph (5).Since,however,thecreativityofcollectionsisindependentfromtheworkswhich 
are included in them, and since it consists exclusively in the selection and arrangement of their 
contents, although they are not protected by virtue of this paragraph, they correspond to the 
criteriaofcopyrightprotectionunderparagraph (1)ofArticle 2,becausetheyareintellectual 
creationsintheliteraryandartisticdomains.Therefore,Article 10.2oftheTRIPSAgreementand 
Article 5oftheWCTontheprotectionofcompilationsofdataandanyothermaterialsshouldbe
regarded as mere clarification of the obligation to also protect such collections and compilations 
asworksinaccordancewithArticle 2(1)oftheBerneConvention.
BC-2.44.Itisalsoonthebasisofparagraph (1)ofArticle 2oftheConventionthatthequestion
of how the word “and” should be understood in the expression “selection and arrangement” 
inparagraph (5)ofthearticle maybeanswered.Thequestionmorepreciselyiswhetherboth 
the selection and the arrangement of the contents need to be of an original nature in order 
thatacollectionmayberecognizedasaworkprotectedbycopyright.Underparagraph (1),
anyproductionsqualifyasprotectedworksregardlessofwhytheyareoriginalcreations. 
Consequently,ifacollectionisonlyoriginalduetotheselectionofitscontentsorduetothe
arrangement thereof, this originality is sufficient for its copyright protection. Therefore, 
inparagraph (5),theword“and”intheexpression“selectionandarrangement”shouldbe 
understoodas“and/or.”InArticle 5oftheWCT,aswellasinArticle 10.2oftheTRIPSAgreement,
the word “or” appears, and in that way, the text is clearer.
(6) TheworksmentionedinthisArticle shallenjoyprotectioninallcountriesoftheUnion.
This protection shall operate for the benefit of the author and his successors in title.
Obligation to protect works; protection for the benefit of authors and their successors in title
BC-2.45. Paragraphs (1) to (5) outline the concept of literary and artistic works and include a non-
exhaustivelistthereof.Thefirstsentenceofparagraph (6)makesitclearthatitisanobligation
toprotectsuchworks.Whilethefirstsentenceoftheparagraph isself-explanatory,thisisnot 
the case with the second sentence of the paragraph. Two aspects need interpretation: (i) the 
concept of “author”; and (ii) the scope of “successors in title”.
BC-2.46. It is important who is recognized as an “author”. Otherwise, the sentence could be 
readinquiteanabsurdway;itwouldsuggestanybodyandanybody’ssuccessorsintitleenjoy 
protection.AlthoughthisisnotstatedexplicitlyinArticle 2(1)oftheBerneConvention,only 
natural persons can be “authors”. The context in which the words “work” and “author” are used 
in the Convention indicates that, because only those productions are works that are intellectual 
creations, also only those persons are authors of those works whose intellectual creative activity 
brings them into existence. It may be deduced that legal entities, which do not have intellect, 
do not correspond to the concept of “author”. As discussed above, it is clear from the records 
of the diplomatic conferences adopting and revising the Convention that the reason it was 
not explicitly stated that only natural persons may be recognized as authors was that this was 
regarded as evident. It is also mentioned above that, nevertheless, at one point, the text of the 
Conventionitselfalsoindicatesthatonlyintellectualcreationsareworks;namelyinArticle 2(5) 
concerning collections, where it was found advisable to stress that element of the concept of 
worksand,consequently,ofauthors.

===== PAGE 35 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
36 BC-2.47. Throughout the Berne Convention, the word “author” is used with the meaning outlined 
above.ThisisfurtherconfirmedbythebasicprovisiononthetermofprotectioninArticle 7(1),
which determines the death of the author as the basis for the calculation of the term. Where the 
Convention allows national laws to recognize physical persons other than the authors or legal 
entities as original owners of rights, it uses not “authors” but a neutral expression: “the owners 
ofcopyright”(seeArticle 14 bis).
BC-2.48.Itshouldalsobenoted,however,thatthesecondsentenceofArticle 14bis(1) of the 
Convention states that “[t]he owner of copyright in a cinematographic work shall enjoy the same 
rights as the author of an original work.” This sentence not only indicates that an “owner of 
copyright” and an “author” are not necessarily the same, but also makes it clear that, in this case, 
the rights of the owners of copyright, even if they are natural persons other than authors, or legal 
entities,arethesameastherightsofauthors.Therefore,thequestionmaybeaskedwhether
there is really any substantive difference if an original owner of copyright other than the “author”, 
such as the producer, which may be a legal entity, is simply called “author”. There are a number 
of countries of the Berne Union which follow the common law tradition in which certain legal 
entities–suchasproducersofphonogramsandbroadcastingorganizations–enjoyprotection
as“authors”(ofproductions,suchasphonogramsandbroadcasts,whichdonotqualifyasworks
under the Berne Convention), and the other member countries of the Union have not expressed 
oppositionagainstthis.Itmayberegardedasa“subsequentpractice”accordingtoArticle 31.3(b)
oftheVCLTthatsuchprovisionsareacceptedbytheothercountriesoftheUnion.Itisanother
matter that such productions do not attain protection by the Berne Convention in this way; in the 
Berne member countries, they are protected as subject matters of related rights. 
BC-2.49. The report of Main Committee I of the 1967 Stockholm Diplomatic Conference makes it clear 
thattheinterpretationoutlinedintheprecedingparagraph isdefensible.Itreflectsthefollowing
proposal: “The United Kingdom proposed […] adding [...] a sentence to the effect that the countries 
of the Union should be free to treat the maker of a cinematographic work as its author”. It is to be noted 
thatwhatwasproposedwasnotthatthemaker(thatis,theproducer)frequentlyalegalentity,
should be treated as the original owner of copyright, but that the maker should be treated as the 
“author”.36 Concerning this proposal, the report reflects the following agreement: “As regards the 
United Kingdom proposal, it was agreed that it was not necessary to insert the proposed sentence, as 
it was generally admitted that the Convention had always been interpreted in the manner suggested in that 
proposal, andasthesituationwouldbeclarifiedintheproposednewArticle 14bis”.37
BC-2.50. It nevertheless remains true that it corresponds better to the spirit of the Berne 
Convention if only physical persons are recognized as “authors”. Furthermore, this also 
corresponds better to the text of the Convention, given the distinction in it between authors 
and“ownersofcopyright”.TheclarificationinthesecondsentenceofArticle 2(6)statingthat 
not only authors but also their successors in title benefit from protection seems superfluous. It 
would have to be understood in that way even if it were not stated explicitly; this is clear, inter 
alia,fromArticle 6bis(1) on moral rights, which confirms that the economic rights of authors 
may be transferred inter vivos,andoftheprovisionsofArticle 7(1)and7bis (as well as 6bis(2)) 
of the Convention, which provide for post mortem auctoris (p.m.a) terms of protection. Thus, 
successors in title include both assignees of rights and heirs or other mortis causa successors.
BC-2.51. In the Convention, the term “author” means the authors as human creators and, as 
statedinArticle 2(2),theprotectionoperatesforthemandtheirsuccessorsintitle.Itisanother 
matterthat,underArticle 14 bis(2)(a), also legal entities or natural persons other than the 
authors may be original owners of rights in cinematographic works created by authors.

country to designs and models; however, if no such special protection is granted in

Works of applied art and industrial designs
BC-2.52. Works of applied art have a double nature: they may be regarded as artistic works, and 
yet their exploitation and use do not take place in the specific cultural markets, but rather in 
the market of general-purpose products. This places works of applied art in the borderline area 
between copyright and industrial property. Thus, although works of applied art are mentioned 
inthenon-exhaustivelistofworksinparagraph (1),paragraph (7)leavesthecountriesofthe 
Unionquitebroadfreedominhowtheyprotectsuchproducts.
BC-2.53. Leaving it to the legislation of the countries of the Union “to determine the extent of 
the application of their laws to works of applied art and industrial designs and models, as well 
as the conditions under which such works, designs and models shall be protected” means two 
things: freedom of granting protection for such borderline productions under copyright or 
under specific industrial design protection, and freedom for fixing the conditions of copyright 
protection if it is granted (the latter freedom allowing countries of the Union to disregard certain 
elements of the minimum protection prescribed by the Convention).
BC-2.54.Nevertheless,paragraph (7)limitsthisfreedomwherecopyrightprotectionisgranted; 
namely,althoughcountriesarenotrequiredtoprovideforthesametermofprotectionasfor
literary and artistic works in general, the term must not be shorter than what is provided for in 
Article 7(4)oftheConvention(25 yearsfromthemakingofthework).
BC-2.55. It follows from the possibility of providing only design protection for such productions 
that a restriction of the principle of national treatment was found justified in this respect. This is 
providedinthesecondsentenceofparagraph (7).Thelastphraseofthissentencewasincluded
at the 1967 Stockholm Diplomatic Conference to address the specific cases in which one country 
provides only design protection and another, only copyright protection, for the same products. 
In such a case, in the latter country, copyright protection must be granted.
(8) The protection of this Convention shall not apply to news of the day or to miscellaneous 
facts having the character of mere items of press information.
No copyright protection for mere facts and data
BC-2.56.Thebestwaytointerpretthemeaningoftheprovisioninparagraph (8)istoquote
thereportofMainCommittee Iofthe1967StockholmDiplomaticConference.Thetextof
theprovisionhadbeenincludedintheBrusselsActinArticle 9(3)oftheConvention.The 
“Programme”oftheStockholmConferenceproposeditstransfertoArticle 2,asparagraph (2) 
without modifying it in substance (but with some minor wording changes). The report of Main 
Committee Iquotesthe“Programme”asfollows:
[T]he Convention does not protect mere items of information on news of the day or 
miscellaneous facts, because such material does not possess the attributes needed to 
constitute a work. That implies a fortiori that news items or the facts themselves are not 
protected.Thearticles ofjournalistsorotherjournalisticworksreportingnewsitemsare,
on the other hand, protected to the extent that they are literary or artistic works. It did not 
seem essential to clarify the text of the Convention on this point.38
BC-2.57. The report reflects the agreement of the Diplomatic Conference with this 
understanding, indicating that the proposals included in the “Programme” had been adopted 
and that the Brussels text had been transferred as proposed with only some non-substantive 
wording changes,39 but it has been completed with this clarification. 40

38 BC-2.58.ThereportofMainCommitteeIconcerningArticle 2(8)confirmsthatthesemerepieces 
of information, data and facts, are outside the scope of copyright protection. Therefore, like the 
provisionsofArticle 9.2oftheTRIPSAgreementandArticle 2oftheWCT,whichconfirmthat 
mere ideas are not protected, this is likewise just clarification that mere information is beyond 
the scope of copyright protection; that is, the provision does not provide for exceptions to 
copyrightprotectionthatwouldotherwiseexist.However,asstatedinthereportquotedabove, 
this only applies to mere news items and facts as pieces of information. If they are presented 
inanoriginalmannerinanarticle,thearticle isprotected;iftheyareselectedand/orarranged 
–oranalyzed–inanoriginalway,theyalsoenjoyprotectionunderparagraph (2)ofArticle 2as
discussedinthecommentsonparagraph (5)ofthesamearticle.
BC-2.59.InArticle 2(8)oftheConvention,adichotomysimilartotheidea–expressiondichotomy
is recognized that may be characterized as the information–presentation dichotomy  in the sense 
that mere information is not protected but its original presentation is.
BC-2.60.Article 2(8)doesnotleavethecountriesoftheUnionthefreedomtoexcludesuchnews
itemsandfacts–asakindofexception–fromcopyrightprotection,butitmakesitclearthatthe
protection granted by the Convention does not apply to them. It is possible that, on the basis 
oflegalnormsotherthanthoseoncopyright–suchasasui generis system for the protection 
ofdatabasesandtheircontents,orunfaircompetitionlaw–theinvestmentsintheacquisition, 
verification and presentation of such pieces of information are protected in the countries of the 
Berne Union. In such a case, the obligation to grant national treatment does not apply, because 
the subject matter is beyond the coverage of the Convention.
BC-2.61. In the legal literature, however, the view has been expressed that an alternative 
interpretationmaybejustified.ItisoutlinedinthetreatisebySamRicketsonandJaneGinsburg 
under the title of “Mandatory exclusion: news of the day and miscellaneous facts”:
Thewordingofarticle 2(8)makesitdifficulttodiscernitspurpose.Isitapublic-policy
exception to the Convention in the sense that it excludes news items from the scope of 
the Convention in the interests of freedom of information? Alternatively, does it embody 
a juridical conception of the nature of authors’ rights, which excludes these items from 
protection on the basis that they are incapable of constituting literary or artistic works? 
If the latter is the correct view, it could then be said that such an exclusion is strictly 
unnecessary as these items are not, in any event, covered by the Convention, as they 
fall within the category of facts and items of information which cannot be the subject of 
copyright protection, expressions ‘news of the day’ and ‘miscellaneous information’ do not 
in themselves indicate which view is correct.41
BC-2.62. Then the authors outline the following problems of interpretation:
1. Ifarticle 2(8)isapublic-policyexception,itcouldoperatetoexcludeaccounts
or reports of daily news that would otherwise be capable of being regarded as 
literaryworkswithinthemeaningofarticle 2(1).Thismight,inturn,besomething
of a slippery slope, because news reports differ greatly in their form, from bald 
‘telegraphic’ dispatches to sophisticated analyses of the events reported. […]
2.  If the second interpretation is to be preferred, this would not cause as much 
difficulty, as it simply embodies the basic principle that copyright protection does 
not extend to facts and information per se, but only to the form in which those facts 
are presented. Even if such a statement is strictly unnecessary, its inclusion in the 
Convention could then be defended on two grounds: 
 – As the basic principle is not expressly stated elsewhere in the Convention, 
itsinclusioninarticle 2(8)providesausefulconfirmationofthefactthatthe
principle is generally applicable under the Convention.

 – If a member country of the Union does, in fact, accord protection to bear items 
of news and press information, the authors of such items have no right to claim

BC-2.63. The authors go on to detail how the various diplomatic conferences to revise the Berne 
Convention and the Paris Convention have dealt with the intellectual property status of press 
information (as regards the Paris Convention, under the aspect of unfair competition). Then, 
making reference to the above-cited Programme of the Stockholm Diplomatic Conference, 
which “embodies an authentic interpretation of article 2(8)  which can be followed in national 
legislation” (emphasis added), the authors summarize their analysis:
By way of conclusion, it should be noted that efforts to protect news items have not been 
confined to the Berne Convention, and that there were proposals at several Paris Convention 
revision conferences in the 1920s and 1930s to provide that this should be a specific head of 
protectionavailableundertheunfaircompetitionregimeembodiedinarticle 10terofthatI
agreement. […] Such proposals were unsuccessful, as was a later proposed treaty providing 
sui generis or neighbouring rights protection that was adopted by an ad hoc committee of 
experts […]. Protection of ‘hot’ news has nonetheless remained a topic of concern for news 
organizations in the post-war period […] and continues to be so, in the age of Google and 
other news aggregators. […] At the international level, however, it falls between the twin 
stools of Berne and Paris and remains a matter for domestic laws which may, of course, 
provide relief under their own unfair competition, copyright or other regimes. 
BC-2.64.Astheanalysisunder“mandatoryexclusion”quotedaboveshows,infact,theauthors 
use the word “exclusion” in such a way that it corresponds only to one of the alternative 
interpretations discussed by them. They outline another possible interpretation which is in 
accordance with what is outlined above; namely, that the provision “simply embodies the basic 
principle that copyright protection does not extend to facts and information per se, but only to 
the form in which those facts are presented”. In connection with the latter, however, they raise 
the argument that, if this is the intended meaning of the provision, it is unnecessary, since there 
isnoneedtoexcludefromnon-existentcopyrightprotectionwhat–becauseitdoesnotqualify 
asliteraryorartisticworks–isnotprotected.
Article 2 bis
[Possible Limitation of Protection of Certain Works: 1. Certain speeches; 2. Certain uses of 
lectures and addresses; 3. Right to make collections of such works]
(1) It shall be a matter for legislation in the countries of the Union to exclude, wholly or 
inpart,fromtheprotectionprovidedbytheprecedingArticle politicalspeechesand
speeches delivered in the course of legal proceedings.
(2) It shall also be a matter for legislation in the countries of the Union to determine the 
conditions under which lectures, addresses and other works of the same nature which 
are delivered in public may be reproduced by the press, broadcast, communicated 
to the public by wire and made the subject of public communication as envisaged in 
Article 11bis(1) of this Convention, when such use is justified by the informatory purpose.
(3) Nevertheless, the author shall enjoy the exclusive right of making a collection of his 
works mentioned in the preceding paragraphs.
Paragraphs (1) and (2): freedom of excluding certain speeches from protection
BC-2bis.1.Thecategoryoforalworks–“lectures,addresses,sermons,andotherworksof
thesamenature”–isincludedinthenon-exhaustivelistofworksinArticle 2(1).However,
paragraph (1)ofArticle 2bis introduced into the Convention at the 1928 Rome Diplomatic 
Conference allows countries of the Union to exclude certain speeches from “the protection 
provided by the preceding Article” in order that they may be used freely for informatory

40 purposes.Thisreferenceisprimarilytoparagraph (1)andthefirstsentenceofparagraph (6)of
Article 2.Acompleteexclusionofthesespeechesfromprotectionwouldleadtonocopyright 
protection at all, including economic rights and moral rights. Some commentators, however, 
point out that, while the informatory purpose may truly justify allowing the denial of economic 
rights, this is not the case with the respect to moral rights. Here, the informatory purpose does 
notrequirelimitation,butjusttheopposite:moralrightsalsoserveaninformatorypurpose, 
theyguaranteeadequateindicationofsourceandauthenticityofthetextofthespeeches. 43
BC-2bis.2.Paragraph (3)wasintroducedintothearticle atthe1948BrusselsDiplomatic
Conference,anditwasthelogicalconsequenceoftherecognitionthatthepurposeofallowing
countries of the Union to exclude political speeches and speeches delivered in the course of 
legalproceedingsistoallowquickandobstacle-freeinformationaboutthecontentsofsuch 
speeches.Thispurposeisnotpresent–oratleastitsimportancefadesaway–bythetimethe
author wishes to make a collection of his speeches or to authorize others to do so.
Paragraphs (2) and (3): freedom of determining conditions for the protection of lectures, 
addresses and other works of the same nature
BC-2bis.3. There are similarities and differences between the copyright status of speeches 
coveredbyparagraph (1)andthestatusofotheroralworksmentionedinparagraph (2)interms
of how the possible exclusion or limitation of their protection is regulated.
BC-2bis.4.Paragraph (2)isalsosupposedtoserveaninformatorypurpose,butthereare
differences between the two provisions. While the nature of speeches justifies their free 
availabilityforsuchpurpose,amongtheoralworkscoveredbyparagraph (2)therearedifferent 
kindsofworks.Thisisthereasonparagraph (2)explicitlystatesthatitisonlyapplicableifitis 
justified by the informatory purpose. It does not apply to oral works that are not relevant from 
the viewpoint of public information. For this reason, sermons, which were still mentioned in the 
previousactsoftheConvention,weredeletedfromparagraph (2).
BC-2bis.5.Asubstantialdifferenceisthat,whileparagraph (1)allowstheexclusionofspeeches
mentionedinitfromcopyrightprotection(withtherestrictionsdiscussedabove),paragraph (2) 
only provides for the possibility of “determining the conditions” subject to which certain acts 
may be performed in respect of oral works listed in the paragraph. The acts are: reproduction by 
the press, broadcasting, communication to the public by wire and making the work “the subject 
ofpubliccommunicationasenvisagedinArticle 11bis(1)”. These acts are covered by the rights 
providedforinArticle 9(1)(reproduction),Article 11ter(1)(ii) (communication to the public by wire 
oftherecitationofaliterarywork)andArticle 11bis(1) (broadcasting and other related acts of 
communication). The freedom to “establish conditions” does not apply to other economic rights 
or any moral right.
BC-2bis.6.Paragraph (3)isalsoapplicabletothemakingofcollectionsoforalworksmentioned
inparagraph (2).Thisprovisionappearstobelessnecessaryinthecaseofsuchoralworks
than in the case of speeches. This is so for two reasons: first, the uses mentioned there do not 
seem to be relevant for the making of collections of such oral works (reproduction in the press 
relates to an oral work of current informatory value, and entire collections of speeches are 
hardly included in a broadcast program); and, second, even if these uses were relevant to the 
collectionsofsuchoralworks,paragraph (2)explicitlystatesthattheconditionsthatmaybe 
determined by the countries of the Union may only relate to the uses mentioned there if they 
arejustifiedbytheinformatorypurpose–andthesubsequentmakingofacollectionoforal 
works, by its very nature, goes beyond such a purpose.

Article 3
[Criteria of Eligibility for Protection: 1. Nationality of author; place of publication of work; 2. 
Residence of author; 3. “Published” works; 4. “Simultaneously published” works]
(1) The protection of this Convention shall apply to:
(a) authors who are nationals of one of the countries of the Union, for their works, 
whether published or not;
(b) authors who are not nationals of one of the countries of the Union, for their 
works first published in one of those countries, or simultaneously in a country 
outside the Union and in a country of the Union.
(2) Authors who are not nationals of one of the countries of the Union but who have 
their habitual residence in one of them shall, for the purposes of this Convention, be 
assimilated to nationals of that country.
(3) The expression “published works” means works published with the consent of their 
authors, whatever may be the means of manufacture of the copies, provided that the 
availabilityofsuchcopieshasbeensuchastosatisfythereasonablerequirementsof 
the public, having regard to the nature of the work. The performance of a dramatic, 
dramatico-musical, cinematographic or musical work, the public recitation of a literary 
work, the communication by wire or the broadcasting of literary or artistic works, the 
exhibition of a work of art and the construction of a work of architecture shall not 
constitute publication.
(4) A work shall be considered as having been published simultaneously in several countries 
if it has been published in two or more countries within thirty days of its first publication.
Eligibility for protection on the basis of nationality and habitual residence
BC-3.1.Articles 3and4oftheConventionfixthecriteriaofeligibilityforprotection(orthepoints
ofattachment)ofliteraryandartisticworks.Article 3determinesthegeneralcriteria,while 
Article 4addssomesubsidiaryones.
BC-3.2. Before the 1967 Stockholm Act of the Convention, the criterion of nationality was applied 
only to unpublished works (which were protected if the author was a national of a country of the 
Union). From the moment of publication, a work was only eligible for protection if it had been 
publishedinacountryoftheUnion.Inprinciple,thisentailedtheabsurdconsequencethatawork
of a “Berne national” was protected until the moment of publication, but lost protection if it was 
published in a non-union country (in principle only, because authors were generally sufficiently 
cautious to avoid such a situation). At the Stockholm Diplomatic Conference, the possibility of such 
aconsequencewaseliminatedbydeterminingnationalityasthebasiccriterionofeligibility(with
the place of publication having become only truly relevant in the case of nationals of a non-Union 
country).ItwasalsoinStockholmthat,throughtheadoptionofparagraph (2),authorswhoare
not nationals of a country of the Union (including stateless persons), but who have their habitual 
residence in one of those countries, were assimilated to nationals.
BC-3.3. In the case of double or multiple nationalities, it is sufficient if the author is linked by 
one of the nationalities to a country of the Union. It is a more complex issue how the criterion of 
nationalitymaybeappliediftheauthorchangesnationality.Thesamequestionemergesinthe
case of a change of habitual residence, which is the more likely situation. Which nationality or 
habitual residence is decisive for determining the eligibility of the works created by the author 
depends on a time factor. This differs depending on whether the time of making the work; the 
time of making the work available in whichever way; the time of publication; or the time of claiming 
protection (practically, the time of an act of using the work) is taken into account. The determination 
oftherelevanttimealsodependsonwhetherornottheworkhasbeenpublished.Viewsdiffer,
inrespectofbothpublishedworksandnon-publishedworks,onthequestionofwhichofthe
above-mentioned points in time should be regarded as decisive. The records of the 1967 Stockholm 
Diplomatic Conference, however, offer some guidance in the form of interpretative statements.

===== PAGE 41 =====

42 BC-3.4. The report of Main Committee I indicates that the time regarded as relevant by the 
Diplomatic Conference for the determination of which of the changing nationalities or habitual 
residences is decisive is the time of publication 44 in the case of published works, and, in the case 
of non-published works, the time of the first making available of a work to the public (such as by 
public performance or broadcasting). 45
Eligibility for protection on the basis of the place of first publication
BC-3.5. Paragraphs (1)(b) and (4) are self-explanatory and do not seem to raise any interpretation 
problem. The place of first publication serves as a basis for eligibility when the author is not a 
national of, and does not have habitual residence in, a country of the Union. The concept of “first 
publication”alsocovers“simultaneouspublication”,andparagraph (4)definesthelatterconcept 
in a somewhat extensive manner, declaring publications in different countries “simultaneous” 
thattakeplacewithin30 days.
Definition of “published works”
BC-3.6.Thefirstsentenceofparagraph (3)defines“publishedworks”,whilethesecondsentence 
–intheformofafurtherclarification–listscertainactscoveredbyeconomicrightsbywhich 
the works concerned do not become “published”.
BC-3.7. It was the 1896 Paris Act of the Convention which first offered a definition, in point 2 of 
the Interpretative Declaration, of “published works”. 46 It had the same kind of positive-negative 
structureasArticle 3(3)inthe1971ParisAct,butitslanguage–inparticularasregardsthe 
decisivefirstsentence–wassimplerand,asaconsequence,itleftopencertainaspects.Itread: 
“The expression 'published works' (oeuvres publiées) means works of which copies have been 
made available to the public (oeuvres éditées) in one of the countries of the Union.” The 1908 
Berlin Diplomatic Conference did not introduce any substantive change in this sentence; it only 
transferred the definition of “publication” from the Interpretative Declaration into the body of 
the Convention. At the 1948 Brussels Diplomatic Conference, however, the concept was clarified 
in the sense that making available copies in sufficient quantities became a condition. It was also 
added “whatever may be the means of manufacture of the copies”, by which a further possible 
doubt was eliminated. (But, as discussed in Part III on the three “Internet Treaties,” in the online 
digitalenvironment,theconceptofpublicationrequiresspecificconsiderations.) 
BC-3.8. The definition received its present form in the 1967 Stockholm Act, where, in addition to 
theclarificationthatmakingavailablecopiesmayonlyqualifyas“publication”ifittakesplace
“with the consent of the author” (a condition which until this clarification had been only based on 
an interpretation of the text), the decisive second part of the first sentence was added: “provided 
thattheavailabilityofsuchcopieshasbeensuchastosatisfythereasonablerequirementsofthe
public,havingregardtothenatureofthework”.Theinclusionofthetwonewelements–fixing
thelevelofrequiredavailabilityat“reasonablerequirementsofthepublic”,andtheobligation
of“havingregardtothenatureofthework”–hadtwoeffects:itfurtherclarifiedtheconceptof
“publication”, and it established the basis for a more extensive interpretation of the concept (and 
thusbroadercoverage).ThereportofMainCommittee Ipointsoutthat“[t]hisnewandwider
definition implies, inter alia, new conditions for the publication of cinematographic works, including 
television films”.47 The new conditions make it clear that a work is to be considered published even if

added.], 841, para. 514. This is a relevant guidance even if after this clarification the Director of BIRPI [the predecessor 
organization of WIPO], indicated that [as in respect of any other provisions of the Convention] the interpretation of 
the text of the Convention is up to the countries and especially to the national judiciaries.

the Courts in the country in which protection is claimed. It is probable, however, that the decisive date will be the date 
when the work, without having been published, was first made available to the public. If at that date the author has 
his habitual residence in a country of the Union, he is protected in respect of his work under the Convention. If the 
work was first made available to the public by an unauthorized person, the author can claim protection against that 
unauthorized person, if he has his habitual residence in a country of the Union at that date.”

the members of the public do not normally obtain possession of copies; it includes the distribution 
of copies of cinematographic works for cinema presentations, or the making available of copies of 
sheet music to orchestras to perform the musical works to the public. Mere making available is the 
decisive factor. If, for example, copies of a book are on the shelves of bookshops, the work is to be 
consideredtohavebeenpublished–regardlessofwhetheranyonebuysit.
BC-3.9.Thesecondsentenceofparagraph (3)confirmsthepositivedefinitionof“publication”
contained in the first sentence by underlining that the making available of works to the public 
in such a way that multiple copies are not circulated is not “publication”. This is obvious in the 
case of non-copy-related uses, such as the “performance of a dramatic, dramatico-musical, 
cinematographic or musical work, the public recitation of a literary work, [and] the communication 
by wire or the broadcasting of literary or artistic works”. As regards “the exhibition of a work of art 
and the construction of a work of architecture”, it is undeniable that what is involved is the original 
or a copy of the work, but such acts do not correspond to the positive definition of “published 
works” because these are isolated individual embodiments of the works concerned which may 
come into someone’s possession without being made available to the public at large in the form 
of copies. Members of the public, however, generally may do the same as in the case of the above-
mentioned non-copy-related acts; that is, they may only watch them.
BC-3.10. At the Diplomatic Conference that adopted the WCT and WPPT in 1996, an attempt was 
madetoadapttheconceptof“publishedworks”totheonlinedigitalenvironment.Article 3of 
the draft WCT contained the following provision:
(1) When literary or artistic works are made available to the public by wire or wireless 
means in such a way that members of the public may access these works from a 
place and at a time individually chosen by them, so that copies of these works are 
available,ContractingPartiesshall,undertheconditionsspecifiedinArticle 3(3)of
the Berne Convention, consider such works to be published works.
(2) WhenapplyingArticle 5(4)oftheBerneConvention,ContractingPartiesshall
considerworksreferredtoinparagraph (1)ofthepresentArticle tobepublished
in the Contracting Party where the necessary arrangements have been made for 
availability of these works to members of the public.
BC-3.11. These draft provisions had not been discussed previously in the Committee that carried 
out the preparatory work. The reception of the proposal at the Diplomatic Conference was 
mixed; for example, the delegation of the United States supported the proposed text, while 
the delegation of the European Community opposed it. This issue was related to the more 
fundamental difference of opinions concerning the legal characterization of digital interactive 
transmissions (which finally was resolved with the “umbrella solution” discussed in the Guide to 
theWCTinthecommentsonArticle 8).Theproposedprovisionsofferedquitestrongarguments 
forthedelegationsinfavoroftheapplicationoftherightofdistribution.JukkaLiedes,the 
ChairmanofMainCommittee I,withreferencetothedivisionofopinion,proposedthatno
further debate take place “until clear options were identified”. 48 The positions did not become 
closer, however, even during the informal consultations, and the proposed new provisions were 
“forgotten”. Therefore, the concept of publication as defined in the Berne Convention (and thus 
under the WCT) has not changed.
BC-3.12.  While the concept of “published works” was made more appropriate at the 1967 Stockholm 
Diplomatic Conference, at the same Conference the primary criterion of the place of publication for 
eligibility of protection dramatically lost its importance; it was demoted by nationality and habitual 
residence, which took precedence. The importance of the criterion has continued to decrease with 
the broadening of the membership of the Berne Union because, with the increasing number of 
countriesapplyingtheprovisionsofArticle 3oftheConvention,thereareevermorecasesinwhich
nationality or habitual residence alone is sufficient for eligibility of protection.49

44 Article 4
[Criteria of Eligibility for Protection of Cinematographic Works, Works of Architecture and Certain 
Artistic Works]
TheprotectionofthisConventionshallapply,eveniftheconditionsofArticle 3arenotfulfilled,to:
(a) authorsofcinematographicworksthemakerofwhichhashisheadquartersorhabitual
residence in one of the countries of the Union;
(b) authors of works of architecture erected in a country of the Union or of other artistic 
works incorporated in a building or other structure located in a country of the Union.
BC-4.1. These subsidiary criteria for eligibility of protection were introduced at the 1967 
Stockholm Diplomatic Conference.
BC-4.2.Thecriteriaunderpoint(a)–theheadquartersorhabitualresidenceofthemakerofa
cinematographic work (which in general is a legal entity, which is why the criterion of nationality, 
whichwouldhavebeendifficulttoapplyhere,hasbeenleftout)–areapplicableonlyifthe 
authors of the film are not nationals of, or do not have their habitual residence in, a country 
of the Union, and the work has not been published in such a country. In the practice of the 
audiovisualindustry,co-productionsarequitefrequent.ThereportoftheStockholmMain 
Committee Istatesthat“acinematographicworkwhichistheresultofjointmakingisprotected
intheUnionifoneofthejointmakershas[its]headquartersor[its]habitualresidenceina
country of the Union.”50
BC-4.3.Theothersubsidiarycriterionunderpoint(b)–theplacewhereaworkofarchitecture
has been erected or where other artistic works have been incorporated in a building or other 
structure–isonlyapplicablewheretheauthorofaworkisnotanationalorhabitualresident
of any country of the Union, and furthermore, where the work has not been published in such a 
country (publication, in practice, may take place in the case of works of art also incorporated in 
abuildingorotherstructure).ThereportofMainCommittee Icontainsaclarificationinrespect 
of this subsidiary criterion. It takes the form of a kind of agreed statement and reads as follows: 
“It was decided that the Report should state that the criterion for the location of works of 
architecture and other artistic works in a country of the Union would apply only in respect of the 
original work. No protection under the Berne Convention could be claimed in respect solely of a 
copy of the work erected in a country of the Union if the original were still located in a country 
outside the Union.”51

[Rights Guaranteed: 1. and 2. Outside the country of origin; 3. In the country of origin; 4. “Country 
of origin”]
(1) Authors shall enjoy, in respect of works for which they are protected under this 
Convention, in countries of the Union other than the country of origin, the rights which 
their respective laws do now or may hereafter grant to their nationals, as well as the 
rights specially granted by this Convention.

PART I. Guide to the Berne Convention
Principle of national treatment and minimum protection
BC-5.1.Paragraph (1)containsoneofthemostfundamentalprovisionsoftheConvention.It
provides for the obligation to grant national treatment in respect of works to be protected under 
the Convention. National treatment means that, in countries other than the country of origin of 
awork(definedinparagraph (4)),theauthorsofworkseligibleforprotectionunderArticles 3 
and4oftheConventionmustenjoythesamerights–withthesamepossibleexceptions–asthe
nationals of those countries. “Rights” means both exclusive rights of authorization and a mere 
right to remuneration.
BC-5.2. It is obvious, however, that national treatment without a reasonable level of harmonization 
among the countries of the Union would create unbalanced relations; more generous countries 
wouldhavetobearunilateralburdens.Thisisthereasonparagraph (1)ofthearticle providesthat
theauthorsofworkseligibleforprotectionmustenjoy–atleast–therightsspecificallygrantedby
the Convention; in other words, the minimum level of protection under the Convention (in fact, the 
majority of the provisions of the Convention fix such a harmonized minimum).
BC-5.3. There are four exceptions provided for in the Convention to the obligation to grant 
national treatment:
(i) works of applied art: if, in the country of origin, they are protected solely as industrial designs, 
a country which grants protection under both copyright law (for “works of applied art”) and 
industrial design law (for “industrial designs”) may deny protection under its copyright law 
(buthastograntprotectionunderitsindustrialdesignlaw(Article 2(7)));
(ii) works that are eligible for protection on the basis of the place of publication: the country of 
publication may restrict the protection of such works (in the form of so-called “backdoor 
protection”)undertheconditionsprovidedforinArticle 6(1);ifitdoesso,theothercountries
oftheUnionarenotrequiredtograntmoregenerousprotectiontosuchworksthanis
granted to them in the country of first publication;
(iii) comparison of terms: if a country of the Union provides protection longer than the minimum 
termrequiredbytheConventionandthecountryoforiginoftheworkgrantsprotection
that is shorter than in the first-mentioned country, the first-mentioned country may apply 
theshortertermfortheworkswhosecountryoforigingrantsashorterterm(Article 7(8)).
(ThereisaspecificexceptioninArticle 30(2)concerningthetermofprotectionoftherightof
translation, but from practical viewpoint it is not significant.)
(iv) resale right (droit de suite): a country that recognizes the resale right is allowed to only 
apply it to works whose authors are nationals of another country that also recognizes this 
right(Article 14ter(2)).
(2) The enjoyment and the exercise of these rights shall not be subject to any formality; 
such enjoyment and such exercise shall be independent of the existence of protection 
inthecountryoforiginofthework.Consequently,apartfromtheprovisionsofthis
Convention, the extent of protection, as well as the means of redress afforded to the 
author to protect his rights, shall be governed exclusively by the laws of the country 
where protection is claimed.
Principle of formality-free protection
BC-5.4.ThefirstsentenceofArticle 5(2)laysdowntheprincipleofformality-freecopyright 
protection, which is also called “automatic” protection, since, in the absence of formalities, the 
creation (and, where it is a condition, the fixation) of a work automatically brings copyright 
protection into being.
BC-5.5. The original 1886 Berne Act and the 1896 Paris Act of the Convention did not prohibit 
the application of formalities as conditions for the protection of literary and artistic works; they 
merelycontainedsomeprovisionsabouttheconsequencesoftheirapplication.Whatisnow 
paragraph (2)ofArticle 5wasincludedbythe1908BerlinDiplomaticConference,andithas
remainedthesamesincethen(exceptthat,intheBerlintext,itwasnumberedasArticle 4(2)).
BC-5.6. The principle of formality-free protection is provided in the first part of the first sentence 
ofparagraph (2):“Theenjoymentandtheexerciseoftheserights[thatis,therightsgranted

===== PAGE 45 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
46 under the principle of national treatment and the minimum protection under the Convention 
asprovidedforinparagraph (1)]shallnotbesubjecttoanyformality.”Formalitiesareany
conditionsormeasures–otherthanthecriteriaofrecognizingaproductionaswork(suchasthe
substantiveconditionthataproductionmustbeoriginalinorderforittoqualifyasaprotected 
work)orthefixationthereof(whereitisaconditionundernationallaw)–withoutwhichawork
is not protected or loses protection. Registration, deposit of the original or a copy, and the 
indication of a notice are typical examples of formalities.
BC-5.7. The application of measures like registration of the work, deposit of copies or the use of 
a notice may only be regarded as formalities prohibited by the Convention if they are conditions 
of the enjoyment and/or exercise of rights. If registration has the sole effect of a rebuttable 
presumption that the facts registered are valid, it is not such a formality (it is another matter 
that a measure may become a de facto formality because, for example, the courts only deal 
with an infringement case if a certificate of registration is presented). Also, if deposit is a 
mere administrative obligation (for example, with the objective of maintaining an appropriate 
national library or archive of published works) possibly with some administrative sanctions for 
non-fulfillment, but leaving the enjoyment and exercise of copyright intact, it is not inconsistent 
with the principle of formality-free protection. Likewise, the indication of a copyright notice 
identifying the year of publication and the owner of copyright may be a useful source of 
information and may facilitate the enjoyment and exercise of rights; it is not a forbidden 
formality if it is not made a condition of enjoyment and/or exercise of rights.
Principle of independence of protection
BC-5.8. The principle of independence of protection is laid down in the second part of the first 
sentenceofparagraph (2):“suchenjoymentandsuchexerciseshallbeindependentoftheexistence
of protection in the country of origin of the work”. There was in the past a close interrelationship 
between the principle of formality-free protection and this principle, because for a time the main 
practical example was that of a work not enjoying protection in its country of origin, but in the 
country where protection was claimed.52 A current possible case may be that the 50-year minimum 
term of protection has expired in the country of origin, while a longer term of protection has not 
yet expired in the country where protection is claimed. In this case, the Convention allows the 
restriction of the principle of national treatment, and the reason for the restriction is exactly that it 
is justified to take the shorter term into account in the country of origin.
BC-5.9.Thesecondsentenceofparagraph (2)providesasfollows:“Consequently,apartfrom
the provisions of this Convention, the extent of protection, as well as the means of redress 
afforded to the author to protect his rights, shall be governed exclusively by the laws of the 
country where protection is claimed.” This is, in a way, a confirmation of the independence of 
protection, and underscores that there is no need to refer to the law of the country of origin in 
these respects. The provision only covers “the extent of protection” and “the means of redress”. 
Thesedonotcovercertainaspects,suchasthequestionoftransferandlicensingofrightsand 
the related issues (the duration of the validity of a contract, the level of remuneration and the 
methodsofitsestablishment).Inthiscase,itispossible–inparticular,iftheinterestedparties 
soagreebycontract–toapplythelawofthecountryoforiginor,onthebasisoftheprinciples
of private international law, even the law of a third country.53
“The country where protection is claimed” as a private international rule
BC-5.10.AccordingtothesecondsentenceofArticle 5(2),“theextentofprotection,aswellasthe
means of redress afforded to the author to protect his rights, shall be governed exclusively by the 
laws of the country where protection is claimed”. This reads like a private international law rule to 
determinetheapplicablelaw,and–althoughithasemergedthatitmightalsobeunderstoodasa
non-discriminationrule,whichalsofollowsfromArticle 5(1)onnationaltreatment54–ingeneral,it
isinterpretedinthatway.Viewsdiffer,however,onwhatkindofruleitis;whether“thelawsofthe
52 Itispossiblebecause,asdiscussedbelowinconnectionwithparagraph (3),itisnotanobligationtoapplythe 
Convention to domestic works, and thus formalities may be prescribed for those works.

country where protection is claimed” are the laws of the forum; that is, the place of litigation (lex 
fori), or rather where an act covered by copyright or related rights and its infringement has taken 
place; that is, the laws of the country for which protection is claimed (lex loci protectionis).
BC-5.11.AhugeamountoflegalliteraturehasdealtwiththeinterpretationofArticle 5(2)from
thisviewpoint;itscompletereviewcannotbetheambitionofthisGuide.Itmaybestatedquite 
confidently,however,that–althoughreasonabledoubtsmayberaisedaboutthis,andcertain
valid arguments may be made in favor of interpreting the provision as a lex fori rule55–the
dominantpositionisthatArticle 5(2)providesa lex loci protectionis rule.56
BC-5.12. The lex loci protectionis rule is closely related to the territoriality of copyright protection, 
asBlomqvistpointsout:
This assumption makes common sense. National sovereignty implies that national law 
regulates which acts can lawfully be done in the national territory, and the lawful or unlawful 
character of such acts once committed should not change depending on where the matter 
is adjudicated. ‘[T]he country where protection is claimed’ must therefore be understood as 
‘the country for which protection is claimed’ (emphasis added) just as it has been written out, 
forexample,inArticle 8(1)oftheRomeIIRegulationoftheEuropeanUnion.57
BC-5.13.Article 8(1)oftheRomeIIRegulation58showshowdominanttheviewisthatArticle 5(2)
of the Berne Convention provides for a lex loci protectionis. Recital (26) of the Regulation states: 
“Regarding infringements of intellectual property rights, the universally acknowledged principle 
of the lex loci protectionis shouldbepreserved.”Inaccordancewiththis,Article 8(1)readsas
follows: “The law applicable to a non-contractual obligation arising from an infringement of an 
intellectual property right shall be the law of the country for which protection is claimed.”
BC-5.14. The Kyoto Guidelines on Intellectual Property and Private International Law adopted by 
the International Law Association (ILA) further confirm the applicability of lex loci protectionis 
forthoseaspectsthatarecoveredbyArticle 5(2).IntheEditorialofthespecialissueofthe
Journal of Intellectual Property, Information Technology and Electronic Commerce Law , where the 
Guidelines are published with detailed comments, it is noted that they were prepared by a group 
of35 scholarsfrom20 jurisdictionslastingfortenyearsundertheauspicesofILA.TheKyoto 
Guidelines have been approved by the plenary of the ILA 79 th Biennial Conference, held (online) 
inKyotoonDecember 13,2020.TheKyotoGuidelinesprovidesoft-lawprinciplesontheprivate
international law aspects of intellectual property, which may guide the interpretation and 
reform of national legislation and international instruments. 59

protectionis whereas the law of the closest connection is applied to determine the 
ownership of copyright. For contracts, freedom of choice is acknowledged. With regard

(3) Protection in the country of origin is governed by domestic law. However, when the

(4) The country of origin shall be considered to be:
(a) in the case of works first published in a country of the Union, that country; in the

Protection in the country of origin
BC-5.20.Paragraph (3)confirmsthatprotectioninthecountryoforiginisgovernedbythe
domesticlaw(thecountryoforiginisdeterminedinparagraph (4)).Inotherwords,fordomestic
works, the minimum level of protection under the Convention is not obligatory (whether it is 
advisable to discriminate to the detriment of such works is another matter). This follows from 
the fact that the Convention regulates obligations only in international relations.
BC-5.21. The second sentence of the paragraph, however, provides for the application of national 
treatment for authors who are not nationals of the country concerned; they should enjoy the 
same right as national authors. This means in practice: those non-national authors who publish 
their works first in the given country (since, if they published their works first in another country 
oftheUnion,then,underparagraph (4),thatothercountrywouldbethecountryoforigin).
Definition of “country of origin”
BC-5.22.Although,inparagraph (4),thevariouselementsofthedefinitionofthecountryoforigin
seemquiteclearandself-explanatory,intheonlinedigitalenvironmentspecificproblemshave
emerged.Whensimultaneouspublicationoccursinmultiplecountries–assumingthatonline
makingavailabletothepublicontheInternetcountsas“publication”–underArticle 5(4)(a), 
the rule of the shortest term would apply. Since, in many copyright-producing countries the 
termofprotectionisnow70 yearsp.m.a., this would mean that a country applying the minimum 
termof50 yearsp.m.a. having little relationship to the creation of a work or its author might end 
up being designated the country of origin. The Executive Committee of ALAI has worked out a 
solution to avoid such an anachronistic situation; the key points are these: 
1.  A work disclosed only in immaterial form over a digital network is not “published” 
within the meaning of Berne art. 3(3).

50 2.  Such a work’s country of origin will be the country of nationality of its author at the

BC-5.23. One may ask why the two exceptions were included in point (c). However, the answer 
seemsquitesimple.Theplaceoftheheadquartersorthehabitualresidenceofthemakerofa
cinematographic work (which is usually also the place of production) and the place where an 
architectural work has been erected certainly have at least that strong relationship with the 
country concerned as the place of first publication. Thus, it is logical that, with respect to a 
regulation with the place of the first publication as the most decisive factor, these alternative 
criteria have been given preference rather than the nationality of the author.
BC-5.24. While, in traditional circumstances, the application of the provisions on the “country 
of origin” has not raised major problems, in the online digital environment, certain issues have 
emerged concerning the concept of publication which have raised the possibility of too broad 
proliferation of “countries of origin” (where, therefore, the provisions of the Convention would 
not be applicable). These issues are discussed in the light of an ALAI resolution in the Guide to 
theWCTinthecommentsonArticle 3.Here,onlythetwobasicpointsofconclusionsoftheALAI 

Article 6
[Possible Restriction of Protection in Respect of Certain Works of Nationals of Certain Countries 
Outside the Union: 1. In the country of the first publication and in other countries; 2. No 
retroactivity; 3. Notice]
(1) WhereanycountryoutsidetheUnionfailstoprotectinanadequatemannerthe
works of authors who are nationals of one of the countries of the Union, the latter 
country may restrict the protection given to the works of authors who are, at the date 
of the first publication thereof, nationals of the other country and are not habitually 
resident in one of the countries of the Union. If the country of first publication avails 
itselfofthisright,theothercountriesoftheUnionshallnotberequiredtograntto
works thus subjected to special treatment a wider protection than that granted to 
them in the country of first publication.
(2) Norestrictionsintroducedbyvirtueoftheprecedingparagraph shallaffecttherights
whichanauthormayhaveacquiredinrespectofaworkpublishedinacountryofthe
Union before such restrictions were put into force.
(3) The countries of the Union which restrict the grant of copyright in accordance with 
thisArticle shallgivenoticethereoftotheDirectorGeneraloftheWorldIntellectual
Property Organization (hereinafter designated as “the Director General”) by a written 
declaration specifying the countries in regard to which protection is restricted, and 
the restrictions to which rights of authors who are nationals of those countries are 
subjected. The Director General shall immediately communicate this declaration to all 
the countries of the Union.

PART I. Guide to the Berne Convention
BC-6.1.Thepurposeofthearticle istopreventtheuseof“backdoorprotection”bycountries
not members of the Union whose nationals could enjoy protection on the basis of the criterion 
offirstpublication.Paragraph (1)containsthebasicprovisiononthepossiblemeasuresof
retaliation by the country of first publication against such non-union countries; it goes along 
with the logical corollary that other members of the Union may deny national treatment and 
decreasethelevelofprotectionthesamewayasthecountryoffirstpublication.Paragraph (2) 
providesfortransitionalmeasuresandparagraph (3)foranotificationsystem.
BC-6.2.TheArticle doesnotrequiredetailedcomments;itisself-explanatoryanditsimportanceis
decreasing in proportion to the increase of the membership of the Berne Union (and, thus, with the 
fading away of the importance of the first publication as the criterion of eligibility of protection).
Article 6 bis
[Moral Rights: 1. To claim authorship; to object to certain modifications and other derogatory 
actions; 2. After the author’s death; 3. Means of redress]
(1) Independently of the author’s economic rights, and even after the transfer of the said 
rights, the author shall have the right to claim authorship of the work and to object 
to any distortion, mutilation or other modification of, or other derogatory action in 
relation to, the said work, which would be prejudicial to his honor or reputation.
(2) Therightsgrantedtotheauthorinaccordancewiththeprecedingparagraph shall,after
his death, be maintained, at least until the expiry of the economic rights, and shall be 
exercisable by the persons or institutions authorized by the legislation of the country 
where protection is claimed. However, those countries whose legislation, at the moment 
of their ratification of or accession to this Act, does not provide for the protection after 
thedeathoftheauthorofalltherightssetoutintheprecedingparagraph mayprovide
that some of these rights may, after his death, cease to be maintained.
(3) ThemeansofredressforsafeguardingtherightsgrantedbythisArticle shallbe
governed by the legislation of the country where protection is claimed.
The right of “attribution" and the right to protect the “integrity” of works
BC-6bis.1.Theprovisioninparagraph (1)wasincludedintheConventionatthe1928Rome
Diplomatic Conference, and since then, with one change of lesser importance made at the 1948 
Diplomatic Conference, it has remained the same. Two kinds of “moral rights” are granted in 
paragraph (1):therightof“attribution”andtherightof“integrity”(or“respect”). 66
BC-6bis.2. The right of “attribution” is the right of authors to claim authorship of their works. 
Usually authors “claim” authorship by indicating on the copies, or in connection with non-copy-
related use, of their works, that they are the authors. Based on the right of attribution, they have 
the right to insist on being thus identified as far as is practicable in the given circumstances. 
Authors are also free to make their work available anonymously or to use pseudonyms.
BC-6bis.3. The right to protect the “integrity” of works (or the right of “respect”) referred in 
the original Rome version to an author’s right “to object to any distortion, mutilation or other 
modification of the said work, which would be prejudicial to his honor or reputation”. At the 1948 
Brussels Diplomatic Conference, the following addition was made: “to object to any distortion, 
mutilation or other modification of, or other derogatory action in relation to, the said work, which 
would be prejudicial to his honor or reputation”.
BC-6bis.4. The right does not apply to all kinds of alterations of a work, but only to a deleterious 
alteration that is prejudicial to the honor or reputation of the author.67 One reason for naming 
66 Forthequestionsofwaivabilityandtransferabilityofmoralrights, see in more detail Ricketson and 
Ginsburg,595–596.
67 However, because the Convention prescribes only a minimum level of protection, the countries of the Berne Union 
have the freedom to be more protective and consider a deleterious alteration of the work alone a violation without a 
further condition that it be prejudicial to the author’s honor or reputation.
