52 the concept of honor and reputation as basic values the protection of which is the raison d’être 
of the right was that in this way it also became possible for countries following the common 
law tradition to apply it. Those countries were only willing to protect this right on the basis of 
such existing legal institutions as protection of general personality rights, protection against 
defamation or protection against unfair competition.
BC-6bis.5. At the 1948 Brussels Diplomatic Conference, it was clarified that the protection of 
honor and reputation should apply not only to the honor and reputation of the author in close 
relationshipwiththequalityofhisworkassuchbutalsotohishonorandreputationasahuman
being.Thismayrelatetosuchaspectsasthecontext–forexample,apornographic,otherwise 
derogatory,orpoliticallychargedcontext–inwhichtheworkisused.Itwasemphasizedthat
one of the reasons for the inclusion of the new phrase was to underline this. The following 
clarification was made in the records of the Conference: 
The author will have the right to bring action against any acts prejudicial to his honor and 
reputation, and the discussion revealed that the author has to be protected not only in his 
capacity as a writer, but also in the role he plays on the literary stage: it is for that reason 
that you have added that he could object to any derogatory action, that being understood to 
mean any action that would be liable to harm the person through distortion of his work.68
Independence of moral rights from economic rights; the question of waivability and 
transferability of moral rights 
BC-6bis.6.Itisworthnotingthat,althoughthisisnotthemainsubjectmatterofparagraph (1),
it confirms two principles of the Berne Convention. First, economic rights and moral rights are 
independent of each other (this follows from the first phrase of the paragraph: “[i]ndependently 
of the author’s economic rights”, which in turn is an indication that the Convention follows the 
principle of “dualism” (rather than the principle of “monism”, according to which these two 
categories of rights are considered as parts of one inseparable unity of rights). Second, under 
the Convention, economic rights are transferable. This, however, is not an obstacle to a country 
of the Union restricting the transferability of economic rights in certain cases, which, in general, 
is done with the objective of protecting authors who are regarded as weaker parties in their 
contractual relations with the users of their works.
BC-6bis.7.Thearticle doesnotaddressthequestionoftransferabilityofmoralrights.Thereare
nationallaws–mainlythosethatfollowthecivillawtradition–underwhichmoralrightsareboth
inalienable and unwaivable. This follows from the personality rights nature of moral rights in 
those legislations; after all, the authors’ honor and reputation may hardly be assigned to others 
such that not their but someone else’s honor and reputation is protected. However, nothing in 
Article 6bis rulesouttheauthors’decidingnottoexercise–thatis,towaive–theirrights.Italso
goes without saying that they may trust others to exercise their rights on their behalf (to claim their 
authorship or to object to derogatory actions in relation to their works). Furthermore, “ghostwriter” 
agreementsarealsoallowedinmanycountries(forexample,whenathirdpartycomposesabook–
suchasamemoir–forawell-knownpersontobepublishedunderthelatter’sname).69
Protection of moral rights after the author’s death
BC-6bis.8.Paragraph (2)wasadoptedasquotedaboveatthe1967StockholmDiplomatic
Conference. The 1928 Rome Act and the 1948 Brussels Act allowed even greater freedom to 
the countries party to the Convention in their choice of how to protect moral rights after the 
author’sdeath.Thefirstsentenceofparagraph (2),inprinciple,obligatescountriesoftheUnion 
to protect moral rights “at least” until the expiry of the protection of economic rights. The words 
“at least” refer to the possibility of “perpetual” protection of these rights, which is declared in 
the law of certain countries. The provision leaves it to the countries of the Union to determine 
who or which institution may exercise moral rights after the author’s death.

BC-6bis.9. The second sentence of the paragraph, however, weakens the obligation by providing 
that “those countries whose legislation, at the moment of their ratification of or accession to this 
Act, does not provide for the protection after the death of the author of all the rights set out in 
theprecedingparagraph mayprovidethatsomeoftheserightsmay,afterhisdeath,ceasetobe
maintained”. This is the result of another compromise facilitating the application of moral rights 
by countries following the common law tradition (to allow those countries to fulfil the obligation 
of protecting the “right of integrity” by means of protection against defamation). 
Freedom of determining the means of safeguarding moral rights
BC-6bis.10. It is a general principle that the countries of the Union are free to choose the ways 
through which they fulfil their obligations under the Berne Convention. 70Paragraph (3)–which
hasremainedthesamesincethe1928RomeAct–byemphasizingthefreedomtochoosethe
means of redress mentioned in it, further confirms for countries following the common law legal 
tradition that they may implement their obligations through certain existing legal institutions, 
such as those mentioned above.
Article 7
[Term of Protection: 1. Generally; 2. For cinematographic works; 3. For anonymous and 
pseudonymous works; 4. For photographic works and works of applied art; 5. Starting date of 
computation; 6. Longer terms; 7. Shorter terms; 8. Applicable law; "comparison" of terms]
(1) The term of protection granted by this Convention shall be the life of the author and 
fifty years after his death.
Standard term of protection
BC-7.1.Paragraph (1)ofthearticle includesthebasicruleconcerningthetermofprotection.
Theveryconceptofthetermofprotection–namely,thatitlastsforacertainperiodoftime
andthat,whenthatperiodexpires,theprotectionceasestoexist–justifiessomecomments. 
Copyright is covered by the concept of “intellectual property”, and thus one may ask why it 
mustendafteranyperiod;whyitcannotbeinheritedbysubsequentgenerationsaslongas
thesubjectmatterofsuchpropertyexists;whyitisnotperpetuallikeother–traditional– 
categories of property, such as land or physical objects.
BC-7.2. A practical reason to limit the duration of copyright protection is that, with the passing of 
time, it becomes ever more difficult to identify and locate the potential successors in title, and, 
with ever new generations of heirs, an extreme fragmentation of the rights would take place . 
It seems, however, that this is not a decisive reason. It is true that it would be impossible, or at 
least very difficult, to find the heirs of the authors of some classical works, but there would be 
noobstacle–inviewoftherichpossibilitiesofferedbycomputertechnologyofestablishinga 
registration system (with the effect of a rebuttable presumption) for newer works to solve the 
problem of identification and location.
BC-7.3. There are, however, much more substantial reasons. These relate to the fact that what 
is involved is intellectual property–andnottraditionalpropertysuchaspropertyinlandor
tangible objects. The subject matters of traditional property are, in general, possessed, owned 
and used only by a limited number of persons. The subject matters of copyright as intellectual 
property are literary and artistic works that, in contrast, may be multiplied and distributed; copies 
ofthemmaybepossessedand–evenonthebasisofoneorfewcopies,throughevermore
advancedcommunicationnetworks–maybeusedbyagreatnumberofpeopleatthesame
time. Furthermore, the possession and use of these works and copies serve important social 
purposes, such as education, research, information, entertainment and so on. The most valuable 
and time-resistant works may become common heritage of a nation or all of humanity. In view 
of these reasons, it has special relevance that, with the passing of time, the relationship between 
the works and the potentially identifiable successors in title becomes less and less close. One, 
70 AccordingtoArticle 36(1)oftheConvention,“[a]nycountrypartytotheConventionundertakestoadopt,in 
accordance with its constitution, the measures necessary to ensure the application of the Convention.”

===== PAGE 53 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
54 two and perhaps even three generations of heirs still may have a specific personal relationship 
with the author and with his literary and/or artistic heritage. For later generations, however, this 
relationshipfadesawayanddisappears;whatremains–alsotothem–isbasicallythenameof
their ancestor, the respect towards whom and the cherishing of whose memories they share with 
other people. When the loosening of this kind of special contact reaches such a stage, it is justified 
that the private rights of successors in title cease to exist and the works fall into the public domain.
BC-7.4. The limitation of the duration of copyright protection may be regarded as a logical element 
of the common law system, which conceptualizes copyright protection as a legal tool to serve a well-
determined objective; namely, to offer incentive for the creation of works and for their dissemination 
to the public. This concept of copyright involves not a natural right, but the result of a sort of deal 
–asocialcontractbetweenthecreatorsandsocietysimilartothetypicalscenariointhefieldof
industrial property such as with patents. From this kind of legal-political foundation of copyright 
protection, it follows that it is only justified to grant copyright protection as long as it is necessary 
to achieve the above-mentioned social objective. In fact, in common law countries, in the past, 
the term of protection of copyright was shorter than in many civil-law countries, and it was linked 
to a registration system with the possibility of renewing the registration and thereby extending 
somewhatthetermofprotection–afeaturewhichistypicalofcertainindustrialpropertyrights.
The necessity of balancing between, on the one hand, the public interest in granting appropriate 
protection to authors as incentive for their creative activity and, on the other hand, the broader public 
interest that has also been recognized in civil-law “authors’ rights” systems since the beginning of 
copyright protection. This has consisted not only in providing for certain exceptions to and limitations 
of economic rights, but also in the limitation of the duration of protection, which was also regarded as 
alimitationofauthors’rights,alogicalconsequenceofthenatural-lawjustificationofthissystem.
BC-7.5.Theoriginal1886ActoftheConventiondidnotfixanystandard–orminimum–termof
protection. This was left to national legislation, and the term of protection was exempted from 
the obligation to grant national treatment. The provision which, as of the 1971 Paris Act, is now 
Article 7(1),appearedforthefirsttimeinthe1908BerlinActoftheConvention;however,its
application only became mandatory under the 1948 Brussels Act. At the time of the adoption of 
theoriginalActoftheConventioninBerne,therewereonlythreecountries–Belgium,France
andTunisia,followingthesamecopyrightschool–thatadopteda50-year p.m.a. term; the other 
countries provided for shorter terms, with the exception of Spain, which had an 80-year p.m.a. 
term. The 50-year p.m.a. term of protection later became a more generally adopted standard, 
such that, in the 1948 Brussels Act, it was transformed into obligatory minimum (in principle: the 
“grandfathering”clauseinparagraph (7)providedforatransitionalexception).
BC-7.6. There were two reasons why the 50-year p.m.a. term of protection emerged as an 
internationalstandard.First,itwasfounddesirable–andinaccordancewiththeobjectives 
reflectedinthePreambleoftheConvention–tochooseanupwardtrendforinternational
harmonization. Second, and more substantially, this length of term, considering the average life 
expectancy at that time, corresponded to the idea of fixing a minimum term to guarantee that 
at least the closest relatives of the authors may enjoy the results of their creative activity.
BC-7.7. The 50-year p.m.a. term of protection has been maintained as an international standard 
since the 1948 Brussels revision of the Convention. It was confirmed as such not only in the latest 
1971 Act of the Convention, but also in the TRIPS Agreement and in the WCT. Nevertheless, recently, 
the need for a reassessment of the application of the above-mentioned criteria has emerged to 
take into account certain new developments (in particular a significant increase of life expectancy, 
at least in many countries), resulting in a new trend towards a 70-year p.m.a. standard.
BC-7.8.Ifparagraph (1)ofthearticle isreadalone,itmaybeunderstoodasifitfixed,inan
obligatory manner, not only the minimum, but also the maximum of the term of protection. 
However,paragraphs (2)to(8)makeitclearthatthisisnotthecase.Theseprovisionsallow
shortertermsincertaincases,andtheyalsoclarifythatwhatisprovidedforinparagraph (1)
andinotherprovisionsofthearticle isonlyaminimumtermofprotection.
(2) However, in the case of cinematographic works, the countries of the Union may provide 
that the term of protection shall expire fifty years after the work has been made 
available to the public with the consent of the author, or, failing such an event within 
fifty years from the making of such a work, fifty years after the making.

===== PAGE 54 =====
55
PART I. Guide to the Berne Convention
Term of protection of cinematographic works
BC-7.9.Paragraph (2)readsasifitcreatedanalternativetermofprotectiontothatprovidedin
paragraph (1),becauseparagraph (1)uses“shall”language–todenoteanobligation–while,
underparagraph (2),acountryoftheUnion“may”dowhatismentionedthere.Furthermore, 
thefirstwordofparagraph (2)–“however”–connectstheprovisiondirectlytoparagraph (1). 
Infact,whatisinvolvedisratheranalternativetothetermprovidedforinArticle 7 bis of the 
Convention for works of joint authorship, since cinematographic works are usually such works. 
(It is to be noted that the term “cinematographic works”–whichreferstocinematographyas
a specific technology to create works expressed in moving images usually accompanied by 
sounds–shouldbeunderstoodtomeanallkindsofaudiovisual works.)
BC-7.10. While for literary and artistic works in general, the 50-year p.m.a. term of protection 
became a minimum obligation under the 1948 Brussels Act, for cinematographic works the term 
remained an issue to be settled by national legislation. It was only in the 1967 Stockholm Act 
that minimum standards were established in this respect. This was done in the framework of 
the complex compromise worked out between civil-law and common-law countries (discussed in 
thecommentsonArticles 14and14bis, below). For the latter countries, where “film copyright” 
wasapplied,normallywiththeproducertheoriginalownerofrights–whoorwhichinsome
nationallawswasevencalledthe“author”–the50-year p.m.a. term of protection calculated as 
the lifetime and 50 years after the death of the authors would not fit well.
BC-7.11.Thealternativetermofprotectionprovidedforinparagraph (2)seemstobeinharmony
with the 50-year minimum, but it is to be calculated from the “making available to the public” 
of the work rather than from the authors’ death or from the making of the work. This usually 
resultsinashortertermthanprovidedforunderArticle 7 bis.
BC-7.12. The concept of “making available to the public” is broader than the concept of 
“publication”asdefinedinArticle 3(3)oftheConvention.Inadditiontomakingaworkavailable 
to the public through distribution of copies (as in the case of publication), it also means such acts 
as public performance, broadcasting and communication to the public by wire; that is, “making 
available” works without reproduction or distribution of copies. It also covers interactive 
makingavailabletothepublicofworksasprovidedforinArticle 8oftheWCT(inwhichcase,as
discussed in the Guide to that Treaty below, the elements of copy-related and non-copy-related 
aspects of uses of works may be more complex).
BC-7.13. Two additional remarks seem necessary concerning the concept of “making available”. 
First,inthecontextofparagraph (2),whatisrelevantisthe first making available of the work 
tothepublic.Thisisjustifiedbecauseotherwiseanysubsequentactofmakingavailable,by 
whatever means, could be regarded as a new starting point of a 50-year term of protection. 
Second, making a cinematographic work available to the public is only applicable as a starting 
pointforthetermofprotectionunderparagraph (2)ifittakesplace“withtheconsentofthe
author”. Here too, the reference to the author is to be understood as meaning the owner of 
copyright,asdiscussedinthecommentstoArticle 2(6),above.Itisparticularlyimportantto 
notethisinrespectofaprovisiononcinematographicworks:inthisregardtheConvention–
underitsArticle 14bis(2)(a)–leavesittothenationallegislationofthecountrywhereprotection
is claimed to determine who is to be recognized as the original owner of copyright (which means 
that the producers of such works may be the owners).
BC-7.14. In view of the sometimes great number of creative contributors to a cinematographic 
work, the calculation of the p.m.a. termmaybedifficult;theprovisionofArticle 7(2)ofthe
Convention offers a simpler solution. The countries following the civil law tradition, however, do 
not necessarily make use of this possibility for solving this problem; instead, they merely reduce 
the scope of those joint authors who may be taken into account in the calculation of the term 
of protection.
BC-7.15.TheWCT–byvirtueofitsArticle 1(4),alongwiththeothersubstantiveprovisionsof
theBerneConvention(Articles 1to21andtheAppendix)–obligatestheContractingPartiesto 
complywithArticle 7oftheConvention;thus,alsoparagraph (2)isapplicablebytheContracting 
States. The TRIPS Agreement provides for a slightly different system for the calculation of the 
termofprotectionofcinematographicworks.ItsArticle 12providesasfollows:

===== PAGE 55 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
56 Whenever the term of protection of a work, other than a photographic work or a work of 
applied art, is calculated on a basis other than the life of a natural person, such term shall 
be no less than 50 years from the end of the calendar year of authorized publication, or, 
failing such authorized publication within 50 years from the making of the work, 50 years 
from the end of the calendar year of making.
Cinematographic works are one such category of works where the calculation of the term on a 
basis other than the life of a natural person (an author) is possible.
BC-7.16. However, as discussed above, the concept of “publication” is narrower than the concept 
of“makingavailable”.Asaconsequence,incertaincases,theminimumtermofprotection
will be longer under the TRIPS Agreement than under the Berne Convention; namely, in those 
cases where the first lawful making available of a cinematographic work to the public is not 
through publication, but in another way (such as public performance). In such cases, the 50-year 
term of protection starts under the Berne Convention, but does not start yet under the TRIPS 
Agreement; under the latter, it only starts with the eventual authorized publication of the work 
and, thus, ends later. In other, less typical cases, the minimum term of protection will be longer 
under the Berne Convention than under the TRIPS Agreement; namely, when no authorized 
publication takes place within 50 years from the end of the calendar year of the making of a 
cinematographic work, but the work is made available to the public, with the consent of the 
author, within that period in another way (such as public performance). In such a case, the term 
of protection expires under the TRIPS Agreement 50 years after the making of the work, while 
under the Berne Convention it expires later; 50 years after the making available of the work to 
the public with the consent of the author.
BC-7.17. This means that a Member of the WTO which is also party to the Berne Convention and/
or to the WCT may only make its legislation fully compatible with both the TRIPS Agreement, 
on the one hand, and the Berne Convention and the WCT, on the other hand, if it provides that, 
in the case of a cinematographic work, (i) the term of protection is at least 50 years calculated 
from the end of the calendar year of the first authorized publication of the work; (ii) failing 
such publication within 50 years from the end of the calendar year of the making of the work, 
the term of protection is 50 years calculated from the end of the calendar year of any other 
first making available to the public of the work with the consent of the author; and (iii) failing 
both an authorized publication and any other making available to the public with the consent 
of the author within 50 years from the making of the work, the term of protection is 50 years 
calculated from the end of the calendar year of making the work.
(3) In the case of anonymous or pseudonymous works, the term of protection granted by 
this Convention shall expire fifty years after the work has been lawfully made available 
to the public. However, when the pseudonym adopted by the author leaves no doubt 
astohisidentity,thetermofprotectionshallbethatprovidedinparagraph (1).Ifthe
author of an anonymous or pseudonymous work discloses his identity during the 
above-mentioned period, the term of protection applicable shall be that provided in 
paragraph (1).ThecountriesoftheUnionshallnotberequiredtoprotectanonymous
or pseudonymous works in respect of which it is reasonable to presume that their 
author has been dead for fifty years.
Term of protection of anonymous and pseudonymous works
BC-7.18. The 1928 Rome Act of the Convention included specific provisions on the term of 
protection of anonymous and pseudonymous works. At that time, the 50-year term still was to 
be calculated from the time of publication. At the 1967 Stockholm Diplomatic Conference, the 
same system was introduced as for the basic alternative term for cinematographic works: the 
term became calculable from the “making available to the public” of such works.
BC-7.19.Whileparagraph (2)providesforapossiblealternativetermofprotectionfor
cinematographicworks,theprovisioninparagraph (3)isnotofanalternativenature.Inthecase
of anonymous or pseudonymous works, it contains the minimum obligation. This is so because 
inthecaseofanonymousandpseudonymousworks–intheabsenceofanyknownauthor–itis
simply impossible to apply a p.m.a. system.

===== PAGE 56 =====
57
PART I. Guide to the Berne Convention
BC-7.20. It follows from this that, where the identity of the authors is disclosed, or otherwise 
not in doubt, it is not justified to apply this specific term. For such cases, the second and third 
sentencesreferbacktothegeneralruleunderparagraph (1)ofthearticle.Inthecaseofjoint
authorship, this means that the p.m.a. termmustbecalculatedasprovidedforinArticle 7 bis of 
theConvention.Furthermore,paragraph (4)–whichprovidesforaspecifictermofprotection 
forphotographicworksandworksofappliedart–isalsoapplicablewheresuchworksare
anonymous or pseudonymous since that shorter term is not calculated on a p.m.a. basis.
BC-7.21.Thequestionmayemergewhythereisnoreferenceinparagraph (3)backto
paragraph (2).Tworeasonsmaybefoundforthis.First,itisunlikelythatacinematographic
work will be produced and then made available to the public anonymously or under a 
pseudonym. Second, the basic rule for the calculation of the term of protection is the same 
underbothparagraph (2)andparagraph (3).Theonlydifferenceisthat,underparagraph (2),
if the cinematographic work is not made available to the public within 50 years, the 
alternative term is 50 years from its making. This fallback variant for the term of protection of 
cinematographicworkshasthesamefunctionasthelastsentenceofparagraph (3)(seebelow):
the avoidance of an undesirable perpetual protection. Thus, in the imaginable exceptional cases 
ofanonymousorpseudonymouscinematographicworks,itwouldseemjustified–incountries 
havingchosenthealternativetermprovidedforinparagraph (2)–toapplybyanalogythe
fallbackvariantratherthanwhatfollowsfromthelastsentenceofparagraph (3),which,ina
country not following the p.m.a. system would be illogical and anachronistic.
BC-7.22.Thelastsentenceofparagraph (3)isnecessarytoavoidperpetualprotection.Withoutit,
theapplicationofparagraph (3)mightleadtoanabsurdsituationthat,inprinciple,noworkcreated
–evenseveralhundredyearsagobyanunknownauthor–couldbeusedfreely.Thissentence
shouldbecomparedwithArticle 15(4)oftheConvention.Asdiscussedbelowinthecommentson
that article, the intention behind that provision was to grant some kind of copyright protection 
for folklore, which, however, is referred to as “unpublished works where the identity of the author 
is unknown, but where there is every ground to presume that he is a national of a country of the 
Union”. This is a specific category of anonymous works, in the case of which, although it may be 
presumed that 50 or even many more years have elapsed since the death of the author or authors, 
in principle, some protection is granted under that provision of the Convention.
BC-7.23.Whileparagraph (2)isaboutthemakingavailableofacinematographicworktothe
public“withtheconsentoftheauthor”,paragraph (3)mentionsworks“lawfullymadeavailable 
to the public”. The difference in wording is not by chance. The reason why the 1967 Stockholm 
Diplomatic Conference found it necessary to use the concept of lawful making available rather 
thanthatofmakingavailable“withtheconsentoftheauthor”wasthat,underArticle 15(4),
folklore was to be recognized as a special category of anonymous works in the case of which 
copyright may be exercised and enforced by a “competent authority” rather than by the authors 
of, or other owners of copyright; the neutral wording was intended to simplify application.
BC-7.24. Because the basic rule of calculation of the term of protection of anonymous and 
pseudonymousworksunderparagraph (3)isthesameasinparagraph (2)forcinematographic
works, the comments made above concerning those works are also relevant here, mutatis mutandis.
(4) It shall be a matter for legislation in the countries of the Union to determine the term 
of protection of photographic works and that of works of applied art in so far as they 
are protected as artistic works; however, this term shall last at least until the end of a 
period of twenty-five years from the making of such a work.
Term of protection of photographic works and works of applied art
BC-7.25.Paragraph (4)providesforthesameshorterminimumtermofprotectionfor
photographicworksandworksofappliedart–25yearsfromtheirmaking“insofarastheyare
protected as artistic works”. There are, however, different reasons behind this specific term for 
each category of works.
BC-7.26. As regards photographic works, there had long been hesitation surrounding the 
questionofwhethertheydeservedthesameprotectionand,ifso,underthesameconditions 
as other artistic works. Their assimilation to artistic works was a long process, as referred to in

===== PAGE 57 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
58 thecommentsonArticle 2(1)oftheConventionaboveandonArticle 9oftheWCTintheGuide
tothatTreaty.TheprocesswascompletedbythatArticle oftheWCT,sinceitobligatesthe
ContractingPartiesoftheWCTtodisapplyArticle 7(4)oftheBerneConvention.Asaresultof 
this the general provisions of the Convention on the term of protection became applicable.
BC-7.27. The reasons for the special regime for the protection of works of applied art are 
discussedinthecommentsonArticle 2,and,inparticular,onitsparagraph (7),above.These 
reasons, in particular the intention to avoid undue interference in the general markets of 
utilitarian products, justify a shorter term of protection for such works. As these reasons were 
consideredtostillbevalidwhenitwasconcluded,theWCTdidnotmodifyArticle 7(4)forworks 
of applied art in the same way as for photographic works.
(5) Thetermofprotectionsubsequenttothedeathoftheauthorandthetermsprovided
byparagraph (2),paragraph (3)andparagraph (4)shallrunfromthedateofdeathor
of the event referred to in those paragraphs, but such terms shall always be deemed to 
beginonthefirstofJanuaryoftheyearfollowingthedeathorsuchevent.
Starting date for the calculation of the terms
BC-7.28.Theprovisioninparagraph (5)isself-explanatoryanddoesnotrequirespecificcomments.
(6) The countries of the Union may grant a term of protection in excess of those provided 
by the preceding paragraphs.
Possible longer terms
BC-7.29.Article 19oftheConventionstates,ingeneral,thatthecountriesoftheUnionmay
grantprotectiongreaterthanwhatisrequiredasaminimumundertheConvention;therefore,
theprovisioninparagraph (6)isunnecessary.Since,however,itmaybearguedthatlonger 
protection is not necessarily the same as greater protection, it is a useful clarification.
(7) Those countries of the Union bound by the Rome Act of this Convention which grant, 
in their national legislation in force at the time of signature of the present Act, shorter 
terms of protection than those provided for in the preceding paragraphs shall have the 
right to maintain such terms when ratifying or acceding to the present Act.
“Grandfathering” clause; possible shorter terms
BC-7.30.Theprovisionofparagraph (7)isself-explanatory,anditisbecomingahistoricrelic.It
doesnotrequirespecificcomments.
(8) In any case, the term shall be governed by the legislation of the country where 
protection is claimed; however, unless the legislation of that country otherwise 
provides, the term shall not exceed the term fixed in the country of origin of the work.
Applicable law; “comparison of terms”
BC-7.31.Thefirstphraseofparagraph (8)confirms,inrespectofthetermofprotection,the
generalprinciplestatedinArticle 5(2)thattheextentofprotectionisgovernedbythelawof 
the country where protection is claimed. The second phrase provides for the most important 
exception to the obligation of granting national treatment. The principle on which it is based 
is called “comparison of terms”. It means that no country is obligated to provide for a term of 
protection longer than in the country of origin of the work. This restriction of national treatment 
normally may be applied by a country granting a term of protection longer 71 than the minimum 
prescribed by the Convention, because the minimum term is obligatory. If a country wants 
toapplytheprincipleof“comparisonofterms”,theConventiondoesnotrequireaspecific
71 In many countries now the term of protection is 70 years, but there are some countries where it is even longer, such 
as in Mexico: 100 years; or in Côte d’Ivoire: 99 years.

provisioninitsnationallaw;underparagraph (8),thisprincipleisappliedunlessthelegislation
of the country concerned otherwise provides.
Article 7bis
[Term of Protection for Works of Joint Authorship]
TheprovisionsoftheprecedingArticle shallalsoapplyinthecaseofaworkofjointauthorship,
provided that the terms measured from the death of the author shall be calculated from the 
death of the last surviving author.
BC-7bis.1.Thisarticle containsthenecessaryclarificationwithrespecttoworksofjointauthorship
(the definition of which is left to the countries of the Union, but which presupposes a joint creative 
activity). It provides for a logical method of calculating the term of protection of such works: since 
underArticle 7thetermistobecalculatedfromthedeathoftheauthor,inthecaseofaworkof
joint authorship, the calculation should be made from the death of the last surviving author.
Article 8
[Right of Translation]
Authors of literary and artistic works protected by this Convention shall enjoy the exclusive 
right of making and of authorizing the translation of their works throughout the term of 
protection of their rights in the original works.
Development and current regulation of the right of translation
BC-8.1. The right of translation was the first right to be recognized under the Convention. This 
is understandable because the use of foreign works in translation was one of the most obvious 
issues in international relations. There was a provision on this right in the original 1886 Act of the 
Convention:Article 5oftheBerneActprovidedforarightoftranslationforaperiodoftenyears
from the publication of the original work. This was a compromise between net exporter countries, 
which were in favor of the fullest possible protection for the right of translation, and net importer 
countries, which wanted to maintain the free availability of foreign works as much as possible.
BC-8.2.Article 5wasmodifiedatthe1896ParisDiplomaticConference;thetermofprotection 
of the right of translation was assimilated to the general term of protection provided in the 
countries of the Union (although, at that time, the Convention did not fix yet an obligatory 
minimum term), but with the proviso that an authorized translation had to be published in the 
language concerned within ten years of the first publication of the work. This provision of the 
1896 Act, which in principle still plays a role even in the 1971 Paris Act of the Convention, under 
Article 30(2)(b),readasfollows:
Authors who are nationals of any of the countries of the Union, or their successors 
in title, shall enjoy in the other countries the exclusive right of making or authorizing 
the translation of their works throughout the term of their right in the original work. 
Nevertheless, the exclusive right of translation shall cease to exist if the author shall not 
have availed himself of it, during a term of ten years from the date of the first publication 
of the original work by publishing or causing to be published, in one of the countries of the 
Union a translation in the language for which protection is to be claimed.
BC-8.3.Theprovisionsontherightoftranslationweremodifiedstepbystepatthesubsequent
diplomaticconferences.TheprovisioninArticle 8achieveditsfinalformatthe1948Brussels
Diplomatic Conference, and it has remained the same since then. This, however, went along with the 
possibility,underArticle 25(2)oftheConvention,ofsubstituting,“temporarilyatleast”,forArticle 8,
theprovisionsofArticle 5ofthe1896ParisAct(ontheunderstandingthatthissubstitutionwasto
extend only to translations into the language or languages of the country concerned). The essence 
of the provision allowing this reservation was maintained in the above-mentioned provision of the 
1971 Paris Act, but in a different form, due partly to its combination with the possibility provided for 
in the Appendix to the Convention of limiting the right of translation in developing countries through 
a compulsory licensing system under the complex conditions fixed there.

===== PAGE 59 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
60 Implied exceptions to the right of translation
BC-8.4. At the 1967 Stockholm Diplomatic Conference, there was an intensive debate about 
potentialimpliedexceptionstothetranslationright.ThereportofMainCommittee Ireflectsthe 
results of the debate in the following way:
As regards the right of translation in cases where a work may, under the provisions of the 
Convention, be lawfully used without the consent of the author, a lively discussion took 
place in the Committee and gave rise to certain statements on the general principles of 
interpretation.WhileitwasgenerallyagreedthatArticles 2bis(2),9(2),10(1)and(2),and
10bis(1) and (2), virtually imply the possibility of using the work not only in the original 
form but also in translation, subject to the same conditions, in particular that the use is 
in conformity with fair practice and that here too, as in the case of all uses of the work, 
therightsgrantedtotheauthorunderArticle 6bis(moralrights)arereserved,different
opinionswereexpressedregardingthelawfulusesprovidedforinArticles 11bisand
13.SomedelegationsconsideredthatthoseArticles alsoappliedtotranslatedworks,
provided the above conditions were fulfilled. Other delegations, including those of 
Belgium,FranceandItaly,consideredthatthewordingofthoseArticles intheStockholm
text did not permit of the interpretation that the possibility of using a work without the 
consent of the author also included, in those cases, the possibility of translating it.72
BC-8.5. These statements are clear in respect of the applicability of the exceptions and 
limitations under the Convention to translations. The only cases where the possibility of 
differentinterpretationswasidentifiedaretheprovisionsofArticle 11 bis (this no doubt meant 
paragraphs (2)and(3))andArticle 13.Thereport,describingthetwopossibleinterpretations 
without indicating any preference for one or the other, confirms the freedom of the countries of 
the Union to choose either of the two.
Article 9
[Right of Reproduction: 1. Generally; 2. Possible exceptions; 3. Sound and visual recordings]
(1) Authors of literary and artistic works protected by this Convention shall have the 
exclusive right of authorizing the reproduction of these works, in any manner or form.
(2) It shall be a matter for legislation in the countries of the Union to permit the 
reproduction of such works in certain special cases, provided that such reproduction 
does not conflict with a normal exploitation of the work and does not unreasonably 
prejudice the legitimate interests of the author.
(3) Any sound or visual recording shall be considered as a reproduction for the purposes of 
this Convention.
Implicit recognition of the right of reproduction in previous acts of the Convention
BC-9.1. Before the 1967 Stockholm Act, there was no explicit provision in the Berne Convention 
on the right of reproduction. Nevertheless, the right was recognized implicitly under the 
previous acts. This followed partly from certain provisions that indirectly referred to the 
existence of a right of reproduction and partly from the application of the a contrario principle of 
interpretation in view of the exceptions permitted to the right of reproduction.
BC-9.2. At the 1948 Brussels Diplomatic Conference, the Austrian and French delegations proposed 
the explicit recognition of a general right of reproduction in the text of the Convention, along 
with a right of distribution (“putting into circulation”) of the copies made.73 The French delegation 
stressedthattheConventionhadalreadyprovidedforcertainrights–inrespectoftranslation,
mechanicalreproductionandcinematographicreproduction–whichhadbeen“derivedfromthe
72 Records of the 1967 Stockholm Diplomatic Conference , 1165, para. 205.
73 Records of the 1948 Brussels Diplomatic Conference ,230–233.

===== PAGE 60 =====
61
PART I. Guide to the Berne Convention
fundamental right of reproduction”.74 The proposals did not receive sufficient support, and the two 
delegations withdrew them.75 However, the doubts about, and the opposition against, the proposals 
did not relate specifically to the explicit recognition of the right of reproduction, but rather to its 
combination with the proposed recognition of a right of distribution; furthermore, as regards the 
French proposal, it related to the proposed extension of a full exclusive right of reproduction (and 
thecorollaryrightofdistribution)tonewspaperandperiodicalarticles,inrespectofwhichArticle 9
oftheConventionallowed(andbyArticle 10bis(1) of the 1971 Paris Act even now allows) exceptions.76
Paragraphs (1) and (3): explicit recognition of the right of reproduction
BC-9.3. The study group preparing the Stockholm revision of the Berne Convention proposed 
again the explicit recognition of the right of reproduction. The proposal for the recognition 
of a general right of reproduction was linked, from the very beginning, to a parallel proposal 
to regulate the permissible exceptions to it. The extensive debate on this right during the 
preparatory work and at the Diplomatic Conference related less to the issue of its explicit 
recognitionthantothequestionofwhatexceptionstoitshouldbeallowed.
BC-9.4.Theexplicitrecognitionoftherightofreproductionislaiddowninparagraph (1)of
Article 9.Thecoverageoftherightofreproductionunderparagraph (1)isabsolute;itextendsto
reproduction “in any manner or form”. Therefore, it cannot be extended any further. If an act is 
reproduction,Article 9coversit.Itisadifferentmatterthatexceptionstoandlimitationsofthe 
rightarepermittediftheconditionsdeterminedinparagraph (2)aremet.
BC-9.5. Due to the full coverage of the right, one may ask why it is then necessary to clarify 
inparagraph (3)ofArticle 9thatsoundorvisualrecordingofaworkisalsoreproduction.
Theinclusionofparagraph (3)canbetracedbacktothedevelopmentofthetextofthe
Convention. The Brussels Act of the Convention still contained specific provisions on mechanical 
reproduction of musical works and cinematographic reproduction of works. 77 Since this was 
alreadyinthetextoftheConvention,itwasfounddesirabletomaintainit–consideringthat
its simple deletion might have created misunderstanding and inappropriate interpretations 
–andmorespecifically,toincludeitinthearticle ontherightofreproduction. 78 The inclusion 
ofparagraph (3)maybeusefulforanotherpurposeaswell;namely,topreventanyrestrictive
interpretation of the concept of reproduction based on the assertion that no reproduction takes 
place unless a copy of a work is made that allows direct perception of the work.
Concept of reproduction under the Berne Convention
BC-9.6. The text of the Berne Convention does not contain any explicit definition of 
“reproduction”. Certain elements of the concept of reproduction may, however, be identified in 
theprovisionsoftheConvention.TheclarificationofferedinArticle 9(3)isofthisnature,since 
it makes it obvious that it is not a condition that, on the basis of the reproduction, the copy of 
the work be directly perceivable; it is sufficient that the reproduced work is made perceivable 
throughappropriateequipment.
BC-9.7. At the 1967 Stockholm Diplomatic Conference, the delegation of Austria submitted the 
following proposal to define “reproduction”:
Reproduction shall consist in the material fixation of the work by all methods that permit [its] 
indirect communication to the public. It can be accomplished, in particular, by printing, drawing,

75 Ibid., 234–235.

77 Article 13(i)providedfortheexclusiverightofauthorizationof“therecordingof[musical]worksbyinstruments 

In the comments, it was added that the definition would make clear that “recording by means of 
instruments recording sounds or images likewise constitutes a form of reproduction”.
BC-9.8. In Main Committee I of the Stockholm Diplomatic Conference, the Austrian delegation, 
having seen that the proposal would not receive sufficient support, withdrew it, under the 
condition (accepted by the Committee) that two things would be reflected at least in the report: 
first, that the concept of reproduction did not include oral lectures or public performances (that 
is,fixationinamaterialformhadtobearequirement);andsecond,thatreproductionbymeans
of recording sounds and images was covered.80Therewasnodelegationtoquestionthatthe
acts listed in the Austrian proposal were not covered by the concept of reproduction. Several 
delegations, however, opposed the idea of including a list of acts considered to be reproduction, 
either because they did not consider it necessary, considering that the draft provision covered 
reproduction “in any manner or form”, or because they saw in it a potential danger of the 
weakening of copyright protection. 81 Interestingly, some delegations opposed the Austrian 
proposal because they believed the meaning of the term “reproduction” to be self-evident, 82 or 
at least unlikely to give rise to confusion.83
BC-9.9. No delegation opposed the basic element of the Austrian proposal that reproduction be 
defined as “material fixation of the work by all methods that permit [its] indirect communication 
to the public”. It is also notable that the delegation of the United Kingdom expressed agreement 
with the Austrian proposal in that reproduction had to be regarded as a fixation, but it also 
referred to the possibility of making further copies on the basis of the fixation , and 
suggested that this understanding be reflected in the report. 84 In its summary statements, 
which were not contested by any delegation, the Chairman of the Committee stressed that 
it is not sufficient to define reproduction as a fixation (as opposed to a mere representation 
or execution of the work) on the basis of which the work may be communicated to the public 
indirectly; it should also be taken into account and expressed that, on the basis of the fixation, 
further copies may be made; here he referred to copying by such processes as photocopying. 
Then, the Chairman stated the understanding of the Committee that a reproduction, in that 
sense, is a fixation of a work.85
BC-9.10.OnthebasisofthedebateandthesummaryoftheChairmaninMainCommittee Iof
the Stockholm Conference, it is possible to outline the concept of reproduction that was taken 
into account by the Committee. According to this concept, reproduction is a fixation of a work on 
the basis of which the work may be indirectly communicated to the public and may be further 
copied (reproduced).
The three-step test for exceptions and limitations
BC-9.11.Article 9(2)oftheConventioncorrespondstotherequirementstatedintheveryearly
stages of the preparatory work of the Stockholm Diplomatic Conference and consistently 
taken into account during the Conference; namely, that the recognition of a general right of 
reproduction must be accompanied by general provisions concerning the scope and conditions 
of the application of exceptions to and limitations of this right. No further specific exceptions 
have been allowed; the three-step test has been provided instead of a closed list, determining 
the conditions to be fulfilled where the countries of the Berne Union find it justified to introduce 
exceptions to or limitations of the right of reproduction. The origin of the expression three-
steptestmaybefoundinthedescriptioninthereportofMainCommittee IoftheStockholm
DiplomaticConferenceofhowtoapplyArticle 9(2).

If it is considered that reproduction conflicts with the normal exploitation of the work, 
reproduction is not permitted at all. If it is considered that reproduction does not conflict 
with the normal exploitation of the work, the next step would be to consider whether it 
does not unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of the author. Only if such is not 
the case would it be possible in certain special cases to introduce a compulsory license, or 
to provide for use without payment.86
BC-9.12.Thetechnologicalaspects,thenatureandtheimpactofreprographicreproduction–
thereport’schosenexamples–havechangedfundamentallysince1967,so,theseexamplesmay
notbevalidtoday.Thedescriptionofthewayparagraph (2)shouldbeappliedcontinuestobe
valid, however, with respect to the structure of the test. Although the condition that an exception 
or limitation may be allowed only in special cases is mentioned last, in fact, it is the first one to 
be checked. If it is found that the coverage of a proposed exception is broader than just a special 
case, the other two conditions need not be considered; in such a case, the exception is not 
allowed under the Convention.
BC-9.13.Nothingprovesbettertheadequacyofthethree-steptestfortheapplicabilityof
exceptions and limitations than its steady expansion over the years. In view of its successful 
application concerning the right of reproduction, it has been extended to several other rights: 
byArticle 13oftheTRIPSAgreementandArticle 10oftheWCTtoallrightscoveredbycopyright;
andbyArticle 16oftheWPPTandArticle 13oftheBTAPtotherightsofperformersand
producers of phonograms. Furthermore, the TRIPS Agreement has also extended the test, with 
certainadaptations,toindustrialpropertyrights.UnderArticles 26(1)and30oftheAgreement, 
WTO Members may provide (i) limited exceptions to the protection of industrial designs and to 
the exclusive rights conferred by patents (no mention is made of “special cases”); provided that 
(ii) such exceptions do not unreasonably conflict with a normal exploitation of the protected 
industrial designs or the patents; and that (iii) they do not unreasonably prejudice the legitimate 
interests of the owners of protected designs and patents, taking into account the legitimate 
interest of third parties (the differences in comparison with the copyright test are emphasized). 
Although the present Guide discusses exceptions and limitations specifically in the context of 
copyright and related rights, the first truly thorough analysis of the test took place in a patent 
case by a WTO dispute settlement panel which had an impact on a copyright WTO dispute a 
short time later. Therefore, it is justified to analyze the test in a way that takes into account its 
interpretation and application in this broader field as well; the more so because, as is discussed 
below, certain commentators base their interpretation of some elements of test on the finding 
of a report adopted by a WTO panel.
Addressees of the three-step test; the test as interpretation tool
BC-9.14. The legislation of a country party to the Berne Convention, the TRIPS Agreement and/
or the WIPO “Internet Treaties” must be in accordance with the three-step test. The legislators 
of such a country may only provide for exceptions and limitations that fulfill the three conditions 
ofthetest.Thequestionisinfactwhetherthecourtsalsohavetotakethetestintoaccountto
decideabouttheapplicabilityofexceptionsorlimitationsinconcretecases.Thisquestionis 
mainly relevant for civil-law countries where, in general, the statutory law determines the scope 
of exceptions and limitations in a more or less exhaustive manner. 87
BC-9.15.Thisquestionshouldbeansweredintheaffirmative,evenincivil-lawcountries,for
atleasttworeasons.First,Article 13oftheTRIPSAgreementandArticle 10(2)oftheWCT 
prescribe the application of the three-step test not only for the rights newly provided or clarified 
in them, but also for the specific exceptions and limitations already existing under the Berne 
Convention, and, thus, the test has become an interpretation tool in respect of those exceptions 
and limitations as well.88 Second, the accelerating technological, social and business-model

BC-9.16.Concerningthelatteraspect,anagreedstatementadoptedconcerningArticle 10ofthe
WCT clarifies that the provisions on the three-step test “permit […] to carry forward and appropriately 
extend into the digital environment limitations and exceptions” [emphasis added]. The key element of 
this statement is that the extension must take place “appropriately”. As is pointed out in this Guide 
inthecommentsonArticle 10oftheWCT,althoughtheexistingexceptionsandlimitationsmaybe
carried forward to the new environment, when this happens, it should be guaranteed that they still 
correspond to the conditions of the three-step test under the new circumstances.
BC-9.17.Therecognitionthatitisindispensablethatthefilterofthethree-steptest–oratleast,
its second and third steps, in general leaving the decision regarding the first step to national 
legislation–beusedbycourtswhennumbertheyapplycertainexceptionsandlimitations 
provided in statutory law is duly reflected in the legislation of a growing number of civil-law 
countries.89 For example, the decision of the French Supreme Court (Cour de cassation), in the 
Mulholland Drive case,90 has confirmed that the test may have to be applied by courts.
BC-9.18. As mentioned above, WTO panels have also dealt with the three-step test in two dispute 
settlement cases. Both panel reports were adopted in 2000. The first was a patent case where the 
adaptedversionofthetestprovidedinArticle 30oftheTRIPSAgreementwasconcerned,andthe
legislativehistoryofArticle 9(2)oftheBerneConventionwasalsotakenintoaccount91 (hereinafter: 
the WTO patent panel).92 The second, somewhat more than three months later, was a copyright 
caseinterpretingArticle 13oftheAgreement93 (hereinafter: the WTO copyright panel).
Interpretation of the three-step test – first step: “certain special cases”
BC-9.19. The WTO copyright panel, in interpreting the first condition of the test as provided 
inArticle 13oftheTRIPSAgreement,didnotgobeyondwhatitbelievedtobetheordinary
meaning of the terms “certain” and “special” on the basis of dictionary definitions. In respect of 
the term “certain”, it cited its ordinary meaning as “known and particularised, but not explicitly 
identified”, “determined, fixed, not variable; definitive, precise, exact”. 94Afterquotingthese
dictionary definitions, the panel concluded as follows:
In other words, this term means that, under the first condition, an exception or limitation in 
national legislation must be clearly defined. However, there is no need to identify explicitly each 
and every possible situation to which the exception could apply, provided that the scope of the 
exception is known and particularised. This guarantees a sufficient degree of legal certainty.95
BC-9.20.Thenthepanelturnedtotheterm“special”andquotedfromtheOxfordDictionarythat 
it connotes “having an individual or limited application or purpose”, “containing details; precise, 
specific”,“exceptionalinqualityordegree;unusual;outoftheordinary”or“distinctiveinsome 
way”.96 It deduced from this the following meaning:

This term means that more is needed than a clear definition in order to meet the standard 
of the first condition. In addition, an exception or limitation must be limited in its field of 
application or exceptional in its scope. In other words, an exception or limitation should be 
narrow in quantitative as well as a qualitative sense. This suggests a narrow scope as well as 
an exceptional or distinctive objective.97
BC-9.21.AfterhavinginterpretedArticle 13oftheTRIPSAgreementonthebasisofanOxford
Dictionary, the panel made the following remarks (footnotes omitted):
As regards the parties’ arguments on whether the public policy purpose of an exception is 
relevant,webelievethattheterm‘certainspecialcases’shouldnotlightlybeequatedwith
“special purpose”. It is difficult to reconcile the wording of Article 13 with the proposition that 
an exception or limitation must be justified in terms of a legitimate public policy purpose in 
order to fulfill the first condition of the Article.98
The meaning of the adjective “certain”
BC-9.22. The copyright panel does not give sufficient explanation as to why it has based the 
interpretation of the word “certain” on one of the dictionary definitions: “determined, fixed, not 
variable; definitive, precise” and “known and particularised, but not explicitly identified”. While 
certain commentators 99 consider the panel’s interpretation as appropriate, several others 100 are 
of the view that the adjective “certain” before the words “special cases” does not have a separate 
normative meaning, that it is used rather as a synonym of “some”, and that the adjective 
“special” alone is decisive, which refers to both a limited and a normative nature of the cases 
that may be covered by exceptions and limitations; normative in the sense that they must be 
justifiedbysoundlegal–politicalreasons.
BC-9.23. It is the latter interpretation that may be confirmed by means of the application of the 
provisionsoftheVCLTontheinterpretationoftreaties.Whatratherrequiresexplanationisthe
questionofwhytheWTOcopyrightpanelfoundit“difficulttoreconcilethewordingofArticle 13 
with the proposition that an exception or limitation must be justified in terms of a legitimate 
public policy purpose”. The panel’s explanation was that, in the context of the GATT–WTO dispute 
settlement practice, such a public-policy-free approach is justified. It notes that “in interpreting 
other WTO rules, such as the national treatment clauses of the GATT and the General Agreement 
on Trade and Services  (GATS), the Appellate Body has rejected interpretative tests which were 
based on the subjective aim or objective pursued by national legislation.” 101
BC-9.24.Themethodappliedbythecopyrightpanel–tryingtoestablishthe“ordinarymeaning” 
oftreatyterms(thekeycriterionunderArticle 31.1oftheVCLT)basedondictionarydefinitions
–isnotreliable.Arbitrarilyselectingonedefinitionfromamongthoselistedwithoutfurther 
analysis is not sound practice. A word’s meaning arises from its use in context. If the copyright 
panel had examined the given context of “certain”, it would have ascertained that it is used here 
as a determiner of “special cases” to mean limited in number and further defined. 102 That is, 
“certain special cases” refers to an unspecified but limited number of cases where exceptions 
and limitations may be applied. The criteria for defining and limiting these special cases are 
indicated in the second and third “steps” of the test.

basis of this assertion is that the U.S. Copyright Act does not fulfill the condition of “certainty”, 
sinceitdoesnotcontainasufficientlycleardefinitionasrequiredbytheabove-mentioned 

on the basis of the interpretation adopted by the WTO copyright panel, because they would 
bebasedonanoveremphasisofanisolatedelementofthepanel’sfinding:therequirement

explicitly each and every possible situation to which the exception could apply”. 104
The meaning of the adjective “special”
BC-9.26. There is also a dispute in the legal literature about the meaning of the adjective “special” in 
the term “special cases”, in particular regarding whether the WTO panel was right to stress that its 
finding that the word “suggests a narrow scope as well as an exceptional or distinctive objective” 
does not mean that the objective should be to achieve legitimate public policy purposes.105 
AlthoughneitherthetextoftheConventionnorthereportofMainCommittee Iofthe1967
Stockholm Diplomatic Conference contains a precise definition of what cases may be regarded 
“special”, the records of the Stockholm Conference and the context of the Convention (specifically, 
the provisions on exceptions to the right of reproduction) offer sufficient orientation.
BC-9.27. These sources of interpretation indicate that the concept of “special cases” includes two 
aspects: first, any exception or limitation must be limited in its coverage; no broad exception or 
limitation with a general impact is permitted; and, second, it must also be special in the sense 
thattheremustbesomespecificandsoundlegal–politicaljustificationforitsintroduction.The 
firstaspectiseasilyunderstandableandcannotreasonablybecalledintoquestion.Itisthe 
secondaspectthatrequiresexplanation.
BC-9.28. The provisions of the Berne Convention on special cases of exceptions to the right 
of reproduction and other rights show that the revision conferences have always introduced 
exceptions on the basis of some clearly identifiable reasons of public policy; the basic proposal 
submitted to the Stockholm Diplomatic Conference, referring to the suggestions of the Study 
Group, stresses the consideration of “various public and cultural interests”. 106
BC-9.29. The text and the negotiating history of the Convention indicate that certain specific 
public and cultural policy purposes not only have served as the basis for the adoption of 
provisions on exception, but also must be kept in mind constantly in the application of the 
relevant provisions. Some examples of this follow.
Article 10(1)–onexceptionsforquotation–provides,inter alia,thatfreequotationsare
only possible if “their extent does not exceed that justified by the purpose”. “Purpose” 
refers here to the public policy purpose of guaranteeing study, criticism and free speech.
Article 10(2)allowsthe“utilization,to the extent justified by the purpose, of literary 
and artistic works by way of illustration in publications, broadcast or sound or visual 
recordings for teaching, provided such utilization is compatible with fair practice” 
(emphasis added). Here, illustration for teaching purposes and, in broader terms, 
promoting education, are the public policy purposes.
PublicinformationistheclearpurposeofArticle 2(4)onthepossibilityofexcluding
official texts of a legislative, administrative and legal nature and official translations 
thereof,aswellasoftheexceptionsallowedunderArticle 10bis(1) for the reproduction 
by the press, the broadcasting or the communication to the public by wire of certain

articles andbroadcastworksofthesamecharacter,respectively,andArticle 10bis(2) for 
reporting current events by means of photography, cinematography, broadcasting or 
communicationtothepublicbywire.InArticle 10bis(2), it is explicitly stated that this is 
only allowed “to the extent justified by the informatory purpose”.
The above-mentioned provisions do not just determine certain special purposes that justify 
the given exceptions, they also limit the applicability of the exceptions to the extent that those 
special purposes justify them. 
BC-9.30. The public policy foundation of the purposes serving as a basis for special cases 
coveredbyexceptionsandlimitationsundertheConventionrequiresmorejustification 
than that policy makers wish to achieve any kind oflegal–politicalobjective.Thereisaneed
for appropriate justification, such as freedom of expression, public information, or public 
education; it is not allowed to curtail authors’ rights in an arbitrary way. It has been argued that 
public policy considerations are not involved in the determination of “certain special cases”, but 
only in the application of the two other conditions of the three-step test. Those steps, however, 
only imply public policy considerations in an indirect way, because their text focuses on the 
impact of the exceptions and limitations on the rightholders’ interests.
BC-9.31.However,theabove-mentionedWTOcopyrightpanel,ininterpretingArticle 13ofthe
TRIPS Agreement, adopts another interpretation of the adjective “special ”. Its findings have 
two elements: first, it tries to determine the meaning of the adjective and, second, it rejects the 
criterion that exceptions and limitations may only be applied to the extent justified by certain 
specific purposes.
BC-9.32. The findings of the panel are based on dictionary definitions. Its analysis begins: “We 
also have to give full effect to the ordinary meaning of the second word [“special”] of the first 
condition”.107ThisisundoubtedlyareferencetoArticle 31.1oftheVCLT,accordingtowhich“[a]
treaty shall be interpreted in good faith in accordance with the ordinary meaning to be given 
to the terms of the treaty in their context and in the light of its object and purpose”. Then it 
continues as follows:
The term ‘special’ connotes ‘having an individual or limited application or purpose’, 
‘containingdetails;precise,specific’,‘exceptionalinqualityordegree;unusual;outofthe
ordinary’ or ‘distinctive in some way’.108 This term means that more is needed than a clear 
definition in order to meet the standard of the first condition. In addition, an exception 
or limitation must be limited in its field of application or exceptional in its scope. In other 
words,anexceptionorlimitationshouldbenarrowinquantitativeaswellasaqualitative
sense. This suggests a narrow scope as well as an exceptional or distinctive objective. To 
put this aspect of the first condition into the context of the second condition (‘no conflict 
with a normal exploitation’), an exception or limitation should be the opposite of a non-
special, i.e., a normal case.109
BC-9.33.Theparagraph inwhichthepanelrejectstheinterpretationthattheterm“special 
cases” also means that an exception or limitation should be justified by some special purpose 
consistsofthreesentences,eachofwhichrequiressperateanalysis–alongwiththefootnotes
added to them in which the panel attempts to justify its findings.
BC-9.34. In the first sentence, the panel states that “the term ‘certain special cases’ should not 
belightlyequatedwith‘specialpurpose’”.Tothisitaddsthefollowingfootnote:

BC-9.35. The “teaching” to which the panel refers in Ricketson’s commentary on the Berne 
Convention reads as follows:
[T]he words ‘in certain special cases’ embody a general criterion, and this can be seen 
aspossessingtwodistinctaspects.First,theuseinquestionmustbeforaquitespecific
purpose: a broad kind of exception would not be justified. Secondly, there must be 
something ‘special’ about the purpose, ‘special’ here meaning that it is justified by some 
clear reason of public policy or some other exceptional circumstance.111 
BC-9.36. The panel’s rejection of Ricketson’s interpretation is not persuasive. First, its 
referencetothesimilarwordingofArticle 9(2)oftheBerneConventionandArticle 13ofthe
TRIPSAgreementisamajor–andmisleading–understatement:thetwoprovisionsarein 
fact identical in all substantive aspects. 112 Second, the panel does not attempt to explain how 
the same conditions change if they are applied not only to the right of reproduction but also 
tootherexclusiverights.Third,theWTOMembersalsomustcomplywithArticle 9(2)ofthe 
Berne Convention, and in this connection it seems that the panel has not necessarily rejected 
Ricketson’s interpretation; therefore, some clarification is needed about the relationship of the 
two provisions within the TRIPS Agreement. Fourth, it should also have been clarified whether 
thepanel’sinterpretationistobeapplied–andifso,how–toArticles 10(1)and(2)and11bis(2) 
oftheBerneConvention–underwhichthegivenexceptionsareapplicableonlytotheextent
justified by certain special purposes–byvirtueofArticle 9.1oftheAgreement.
BC-9.37.ThePanelconsidersit“difficulttoreconcilethewordingofArticle 13withtheproposition
that an exception or limitation must be justified in terms of a legitimate public policy purpose 
in order to fulfill the first condition of the Article”. No explanation is offered as to why this is the 
case,butprobablythethirdsentenceoftheparagraph isintendedtoindicatethereason:“We
also recall in this respect that, in interpreting other WTO rules, such as the national treatment 
clauses of the GATT and the GATS, the Appellate Body has rejected interpretative tests which 
were based on the subjective aim or objective pursued by national legislation.” The Panel refers 
totwocaseswheretheAppellateBodyhasrejectedsuchatest–oneonalcoholicbeveragesand
the other on bananas.113However–andthepanelrecognizesthis–thetwocasesrelatedtoother 
WTO rules; they have no relationship with copyright or intellectual property rights.
BC-9.38.Article 31.2oftheVCLTclarifiesthatthetextofatreatyincludesthepreamble and 
annexes.114 The preamble of a treaty tends to determine its “object and purpose” in the light 
of which its provisions must be interpreted. In view of this, it is important that, although

Article 9.1oftheTRIPSAgreementobligatestheWTOMemberstocomplywithArticles 1to
21 and the Appendix of the Berne Convention, this obligation does not apply to the Preamble 
oftheConvention.Asaconsequence,inrespectofbothcontextand“objectandpurpose”,
theAgreementsignificantlydiffersfromtheConvention.Thefirst–andonlysubstantive–
paragraph oftheBernePreambledeterminesthe“objectandpurpose”oftheConventionas
“to protect, in as effective and uniform a manner as possible, the rights of authors in their 
literary and artistic works”. None of the seven substantive paragraphs of the long Preamble of 
theTRIPSAgreementoritsArticles 7and8on“Objectives”and“Principles”correspondfullyto
thisparagraph.Thefirstpreambleparagraph oftheTRIPSAgreement,incontrast,hastheWTO
Membersmerely“takingintoaccounttheneedtopromoteeffectiveandadequateprotectionof
intellectual property rights” without the desire to make it as effective as possible. What they are 
“desiring” is “to reduce distortions and impediments to international trade”, as well as “to ensure 
that measures and procedures to enforce intellectual property rights do not themselves become 
barrierstolegitimatetrade.”Theparagraph clearlyindicates–andthenthefollowingparagraphs
confirm–thattheAgreementdiffersfromtheBerneConventionandtheotherWIPOtreatiesin
respect of the context in which, and the object and purpose in the light of which its provisions 
may be interpreted. In contrast with the author- and creation-centric nature of the Berne 
Convention, the provisions of the TRIPS Agreement are rather product- and trade-centric.115 
Also, the context in which the provisions of the Agreement are to be interpreted also includes its 
Part VonDisputePreventionandSettlement.Article 64.1ofPartVextendstheapplicationofthe
DisputeSettlementUnderstandingelaboratedunderGATT1994suchthat,fromArticle 22ofthe
Understanding it becomes evident that, in the context of the TRIPS Agreement, the fulfillment 
of the obligation to protect intellectual property rights is considered as a matter of trade 
“concession” which may be “suspended” as a trade sanction in case of a WTO covered agreement 
–incertaincases,evenifithasnothingtodowithintellectualpropertyrights.Itisinthiscontext
thatArticle 13oftheTRIPSAgreementhasbeeninterpretedbythecopyrightpanel.
BC-9.39. It is on the basis of these arguments that the WTO copyright panel concludes:
Inourview,thefirstconditionofArticle 13requiresthatalimitationorexceptionin
national legislation should be clearly defined and should be narrow in its scope and reach. 
On the other hand, a limitation or exception may be compatible with the first condition 
even if it pursues a special purpose whose underlying legitimacy in a normative sense 
cannotbediscerned.ThewordingofArticle 13’sfirstconditiondoesnotimplypassinga
judgment on the legitimacy of the exceptions in dispute. However, public policy purposes 
stated by law-makers when enacting a limitation or exception may be useful from a 
factual perspective for making inferences about the scope of a limitation or exception or 
the clarity of its definition.116 
BC-9.40. This finding may be appropriate in the context of the TRIPS Agreement in the light of 
its object and purpose, but it does not mean that the term “in certain special cases” should be 
interpretedinthesamewayunderArticle 9(2)oftheBerneConventionandthecorresponding
provisions of other WIPO treaties on the three-step test in a different context and in the light of 
their different objects and purposes.

notarticle 9(2)ofBerne,[…]theycarrysomeforcewithrespecttoarticle 9(2).” 117 This may be

BC-9.42. The authors recognize that the different objects and purposes of the TRIPS Agreement 
and the Berne Convention “may […] support that the expression bears a different meaning in 
thecontextofarticle 9(2)”,buttheyaddthatthepreparatoryworkfortheStockholmDiplomatic
Conference tends to bear out the position that for a case to be “special”, it need not have an 
underlying justification in public policy.118 It seems that two points are made in this sentence: first, 
that, in principle, due to the different object and purpose, the term may have a different meaning; 
andsecond,that–althoughtheWTOpanelhasnottakenthisintoaccount–thepreparatorywork
ofArticle 9(2)rathersupportstheinterpretationadoptedbythepanelintheBernecontext.
BC-9.43. There appears to be agreement concerning the first point, but not necessarily with 
respect to the significance of the difference between the two treaties and of what impact it 
mayhaveontheinterpretationoftheterm“specialcases”.ApplyingArticle 31.1oftheVCLT,the
differences between the Agreement and the Convention are not just of a relative importance; 
they are of a fundamental nature. The interpretation adopted by the WTO panel seems to be in 
accordance with the trade-centric foundation of the TRIPS Agreement, but the context in which 
Article 9(2)istobeinterpretedintheBerneConventionhaslittletodowiththeenvironment 
of trade rules under which books, symphonies and film dramas may have the same status as 
alcoholic beverages, bananas, and online gambling services. 119 In the Berne context, it follows 
fromthespecificobjectandpurposeoftheConvention–toguaranteeaseffectiveprotectionof 
authors’rightsaspossible–thatexceptionstoandlimitationsoftheserightsareonlyapplicable 
where, and to the extent that, they are justified by special legal-political purposes. The specific 
exceptions and limitations permitted by the Convention form the most direct context of 
Article 9(2)inwhichitshouldbeinterpreted,andtheyservespecialpurposeswhicharenamed 
explicitly in some of the provisions. All this is sufficient basis to conclude that, no matter how it 
is interpreted by virtue of a trade treaty, in the context of the Berne Convention there are good 
reasons to find that the condition according to which an exception or limitation may be applied 
only “in certain special cases” should be interpreted to mean that certain well-founded legal-
politicalreasonsarerequiredtojustifyit.
BC-9.44. Under these circumstances, it may not be necessary to turn to supplementary means 
ofinterpretationunderArticle 32oftheVCLT,suchasthepreparatorywork.Therearethree
possible reasons to do so. Two of them are hardly applicable, because it would be difficult to 
claimthattheinterpretationaccordingtowhichsomesoundlegal–politicalreasonshaveto
justify the application of exceptions and limitations “in certain special cases” either “leaves 
the meaning ambiguous or obscure” or “leads to a result which is manifestly absurd or 
unreasonable”. Therefore, only the third purpose may be relevant: “to confirm the meaning 
resultingfromtheapplicationofarticle 31”.
BC-9.45. Ricketson and Ginsburg give three kinds of reasons to justify the interpretation that 
there is no need for specific purposes in applying exceptions and limitations. Two of these 
reasonsdonotrelatetothepreparatoryworkofArticle 9(2);anditisevennotclearwhether
they may be regarded as supplementary means of interpretation.
BC-9.46. Nevertheless, the authors do refer to the preparatory work by pointing out that “not 
alloftheexceptionsrecognizedundernationallawspriortotheadoptionofarticle 9(2)were
characterized by a clear public-policy justification” and that “of the list of exceptions formulated 
by the 1964 Study Group […], the exceptions for ‘private use’, ‘ephemeral use’, and ‘texts of songs’ 
do not immediately suggest any rationale for their recognition other than convenience for the
