user or the fact that they are possibly de minimis uses that will not affect the copyright owner”.120 
Three comments should be made in this connection. First, although it may be true that the 
rationale–thatis,asoundlegal–politicaljustification–cannotbeidentifiedimmediatelyforall
such exceptions, this does not mean that it does not exist. Take for example “private copying”, 
which is certainly the most significant special case mentioned: to a certain extent, an exception 
may be justified by the protection of privacy; or a limitation to a mere right to remuneration 
by the extreme difficulty of controling use; or also by the purpose of facilitating research, 
private study or “scientific use”.121 Concerning “ephemeral use (recording)” by broadcasting 
organizations, Masouyé refers in his 1978 Guide to the Berne Convention to a reason which justifies 
an exception: “the use of recordings depends on progamming and time factors; and fortuitous 
reasons of this kind do not call for any additional remuneration”122 (that is, within a certain 
reasonably determined limited period, it is justified to use the recordings without the need for 
newauthorization).Thethirdexample–useof“textsforsongs”–ismorecomplex.Suchause
obviously involves reproduction or adaptation, both acts covered by exclusive rights; thus, if a 
national law somewhere in the world might apply such an exception to allow the use of texts for 
songs,itmayonlyavoidaconflictwithArticles 9and12oftheConventionifitislimitedtoavery
small part of the text of a protected work, which may pass as a de minimis use, to which Ricketson 
and Ginsburg also refer as a possible basis for such an exception. Allowing a de minimis free use is 
notwithoutasoundlegal–politicaljustification;itisbasedontheprincipleofde minimis non curat 
praetor. It is submitted, therefore, that the preparatory work does not contain sufficiently clear 
elements which would justify accepting, in the context of the Berne Convention, what a WTO 
panel has found under the TRIPS Agreement, a trade treaty. Otherwise, an atypical exception, 
such as for “texts of sounds” could be considered not just as a de minimis use, but also accepted 
as a “grandfathering clause” to be applied in those countries where it already existed.123
BC-9.47. The authors present two other reasons to accept the interpretation of the WTO panel 
in the Berne context. One is based on an analysis of the assumed logic of the three-step test. 
Theystatethat“itisdifficulttoescapethelogicoftheargumentthatnormativequestions,
i.e. justifications, are more appropriately considered under the second and third steps”,124 
adding:“thefirststepassumesamorecoherentroleasprovidingathresholdrequirementfor
consideration of the real normative issues under the second and third step”.125 This is an apt 
description of the structure of the test, but it does not follow from it that the first step has no 
normative effect. The test should be considered an organic whole composed of three conjunctive 
conditions,thepurposeofwhichistoestablishanadequatebalanceofinterestsbetween
the relevant public private interests. In this structure, the first condition that an exception or 
limitationmaybeappliedonlyin“certainspecialcases”justifiedbysomesoundlegal–political
reasonsisreallyathresholdrequirement;ifitisfulfilled,thesecondandthirdstepsdetermine
further conditions and fine-tune the scope of application of such restrictions of authors’ rights.
BC-9.48. The second reason presented by Ricketson and Ginsburg that is not based on the 
preparatoryworkofArticle 9(2)isthis:“Finally,thereisnoapparentreasonwhythisstepshould 
beinterpreteddifferentlyforarticle 9(2)oftheBerneConventionandarticle 13oftheTRIPS 
Agreement: different interpretations would introduce considerable complexity for no good 
reason.” With due respect to the intention to avoid different interpretations, there are weighty 
reasonstointerpretArticle 9(2)inthecontextoftheBerneConventionandinthelightofits
stated object and purpose, which fundamentally differ from the context, object and purpose 
of the TRIPS Agreement. The more so because the WTO panel has itself justified its differing 
interpretationbythedifferentcontextofArticle 13intheTRIPSAgreementandhasbasedthe 

that have nothing to do with intellectual property rights, in particular not with the rights of 
authorsundertheBerneConvention.Thereareseveralotheraspects–andquiteimportant 
ones–wheredifferentrulesandinterpretationsapplytothesameactsandthesamefactual 
situationswithdifferentlegalconsequencesinthetwotreaties.Itistruethatthisleadsto 

72 considerable complexity, but it does not justify applying the interpretation of Berne provisions

BC-9.49. Therefore, the interpretation of the first condition of the three-step in the context of 
theBerneConvention,asprovidedinArticle 9(2),differsfromitsinterpretationadoptedbya 
WTOpanelinthecontextoftheTRIPSAgreementasitappearsinArticle 13.UnderArticle 9(2)of 
the Berne Convention and the other copyright and related rights treaties administered by WIPO, 
there is good reason to consider the three-step test composed of three conjunctively applicable 
conditionsasawholewithinwhichthefirstcondition–thatexceptionsandlimitationsmay 
onlybeappliedin“certainspecialcases”–alsohasanormativeroleinthesensethatitrequires
areasonablelegal–politicaljustificationforsuchrestrictionoftheeffectiveprotectionof 
authors’ rights.
Interpretation of the three-step test – second step: no conflict with a normal exploitation of 
the works
BC-9.50. The different provisions of the international treaties on the three-step test contain both 
identical and different elements concerning the second condition of the three-step test. While 
the copyright norms uniformly provide that there must be no conflict with a normal exploitation 
of works, performances and phonograms, the industrial property provisions of the TRIPS 
Agreementcontaintherequirementofno unreasonable conflict with the normal exploitation of 
industrial designs and patents.
BC-9.51. WTO patent panel interpreted first the expression “normal exploitation”, which is a 
common element of all the international provisions on the three-step test. The panel considered 
that “exploitation” refers to the commercial activity by which patent owners employ their 
exclusive patent rights to extract economic value from their patents. Concerning the ordinary 
meaning of the word “normal”, the panel referred to the dictionary definition: “regular, usual, 
typical, ordinary, conventional”,126 and stated that the term can be understood to refer either to 
an empirical conclusion about what is common within a relevant community , or to a normative 
standard of entitlement. Thepanelconcludedthattheword“normal”isusedinArticle 30ofthe
TRIPS Agreement in a sense that combines the two meanings.127
BC-9.52. The patent panel further comments: “The normal practice of exploitation by patent 
owners, as with owners of any other intellectual property right, is to exclude all forms of 
competition that could detract significantly from the economic returns anticipated from a patent’s 
grant of exclusivity.”128 As regards the concept of “normal exploitation” as a common element of 
the second condition of each of the various TRIPS provisions, it did not come as a surprise that 
theWTOcopyrightpaneladoptedasimilarinterpretationlaterwhenitinterpretedArticle 13 
of the TRIPS Agreement. The copyright panel, however, also clarifies certain further details; in 
particular on the issue of the exploitation of an exclusive right. Here it makes even clearer what 
has been stated by the patent panel: that the second condition of the test is both of an empirical 
and of a normative nature:
6.165 The ordinary meaning of the term “exploit” connotes “making use of” or “utilising 
for one’s own ends”.129 We believe that “exploitation” of musical works thus refers to the 
activity by which copyright owners employ the exclusive rights conferred on them to 
extract economic value from their rights to those works.
6.166 We note that the ordinary meaning of the term “normal” can be defined as 
“constituting or conforming to a type or standard; regular, usual, typical, ordinary, 
conventional […]”.130 In our opinion, these definitions appear to reflect two connotations:

the first one appears to be of an empirical nature, i.e., what is regular, usual, typical or 
ordinary. The other one reflects a somewhat more normative, if not dynamic, approach, 
i.e., conforming to a type or standard. We do not feel compelled to pass a judgment on 
whichoneoftheseconnotationscouldbemorerelevant.BasedonArticle 31oftheVienna
Convention, we will attempt to develop a harmonious interpretation which gives meaning 
and effect to both connotations of “normal”.131
BC-9.53.ThecopyrightpanelhastakenintoaccountthepreparatoryworkofBerneArticle 9(2) 
and found a “persuasive guidance” in the statements of the Study Group set up for the 
preparation of the 1967 Stockholm Diplomatic Conference, which proposed “[to] limit the 
recognition and the exercising of that right, for specified purposes and on the condition that 
these purposes should not enter into economic competition with these works ” in the sense that 
“all forms of exploiting a work, which have, or likely to acquire, considerable economic or practical 
importance, must be reserved to the authors ”.132
BC-9.54. Under the interpretation of the two WTO panels, “normal exploitation” does not cover 
all kinds of exploitation of works. However, it does cover all forms of exploitation that have, 
orarelikelytoacquire,considerableeconomicorpracticalimportance,andanexceptionor
limitation is to be regarded to conflict with such exploitation if it would enter into economic 
competition with it.
BC-9.55. The WTO copyright panel summarizes the interpretation of the second criterion of the 
test as follows:
We believe that an exception or limitation to an exclusive right in domestic legislation rises 
to the level of a conflict with a normal exploitation of the work (i.e., the copyright or rather 
the whole bundle of exclusive rights conferred by the ownership of the copyright), if uses, 
that in principle are covered by that right but exempted under the exception or limitation, 
enter into economic competition with the ways that right holders normally extract economic 
value from that right to the work (i.e., the copyright) and thereby deprive them of significant 
or tangible commercial gains.133
BC-9.56. This seems to be a reasonable interpretation of the second condition of the test. The 
authoritative commentaries on the Berne Convention and the WIPO Internet Treaties 134 present 
the same interpretation as that adopted by the WTO panels under the TRIPS Agreement.
Interpretation of the three-step test – third step: no unreasonable prejudice to the legitimate 
interests of authors
BC-9.57. The international copyright norms, on the one hand, and the TRIPS provisions 
concerning industrial designs and patents, on the other, with one exception, contain the same 
criteria in the case of the third condition of the three-step test; namely that an exception 
or limitation must not unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of owners of rights. 
Articles 26(6)and30oftheTRIPSAgreementonexceptionstoindustrialdesignandpatent 
rights, respectively, only differ in that they contain the following additional phrase: “taking 
account of the legitimate interests of third parties”. It is submitted, however, that the addition of 
this phrase only consists in the clarification of something that also follows from an appropriate 
interpretation of the copyright provisions; namely that, in the application of the third step, the 
questionofwhetherapossibleprejudicetothelegitimateinterestsoftheownersofrightsis 
stillreasonablemayonlybeansweredadequatelyifittakesplaceonthebasisofduebalancing
withtheinterestsofothers(thirdparties–includingsocietyatlarge). 135

74 BC-9.58. The WTO copyright panel interprets the third step on the basis of the dictionary 
definitions of the key terms; in particular, the adjectives “legitimate” and “unreasonable” 
(sincethoserequirethegreatestattentionfromtheviewpointofbalancingofinterests).The
panel judges the concept of legitimacy of the interests of owners of rights both from a legal 
positivist perspective (an interest recognized and protected by law), and from a more normative 
perspective, in the context of calling for the protection of interests that are justifiable in the light 
of objectives that underlie the protection of exclusive rights. 136 It finds that a prejudice is to be 
regarded as unreasonable “if an exception or limitation causes or has the potential to cause an 
unreasonable loss of income to the copyright owner”.137 At the same time, the panel also states 
that the unreasonable nature of a prejudice may be eliminated in those cases “where there 
would be a serious loss of profit for the copyright owner”, but where “the law [...] provide[s] him 
with some compensation”.
BC-9.59. It should be stressed, however, that according to the panel report, such compensation 
may only make an exception or limitation acceptable from the viewpoint of the third step. It is 
not suitable to do the same in respect of the second step. If an exception or limitation were in 
conflict with a normal exploitation of an exclusive right, the conflict could not be eliminated 
by transforming the exclusive right into a mere right to remuneration (in such a case, the acts 
covered could be performed without the authorization of the owners of rights, and since a 
normal exploitation of an exclusive right consists precisely in the right to authorize or prohibit 
such acts, it would be illogical to speak of restoring the chance for such exploitation).
BC-9.60. The commentaries seem to agree with the essence of the above-outlined interpretation 
of the third condition of the three-step test adopted by the WTO copyright panel concerning 
Article 13inrespectofboththeBerneConventionandtheWIPOInternetTreaties.138
The three-step test and “externalities”
BC-9.61. The finding of the WTO patent panel adopted in 2000 on the role of so-called 
“externalities” warrants comment. It concerns those elements of the provisions of TRIPS 
Article 13(oncopyright)andArticle 30(onthepatentright)thatarethesame;therefore,itmay
also be considered relevant for the exceptions and limitations in the area of copyright.
BC-9.62.Theparties–theEuropeanCommunitiesandCanada–haddiametricallyopposite
viewsonthequestionofwhatroletheprovisionsofArticles 7ontheobjectivesandArticle 8 
on the principles of the TRIPS Agreement may have in the application of the three-step test. 
Article 7providesthattheprotectionandenforcementofIPrightsshouldbe“conduciveto 
socialandeconomicwelfare,andtoabalanceofrightsandobligations”,andunderArticle 8,the
WTO Members, in their national laws “may adopt measures necessary […] to promote the public 
interest in sectors of vital importance to their socio-economic and technological development”. 
Canada’s position was that, in addition to analyzing whether or not an exception fulfills the 
three cumulative conditions, it should also be considered whether or not it is also in accordance 
with these “external” criteria. In contrast, the European Community was of the view that these 
provisions are of the same nature as the preamble paragraphs; they have already been taken 
intoaccountinthearticles oftheAgreement,includingthoseonthethree-steptest;thus,for 
the application of the test, they should not be taken into account again.
BC-9.63. The WTO patent panel adopted a finding that differs from both above-mentioned 
positions; namely, that these development and competition aspects should be taken into 
account; however, not as ”externalities” in addition to, but as an integral part of, the application 
of the three-step test.139 This confirms that, if the three-step test is applied appropriately, it is 
suitablefortakingintoaccountandabsorbingallpossibleaspects–letthembehumanrights, 
competition,developmentoranyotherconsiderations–inordertoestablishaduebalanceof
interests. It was adopted for this purpose.

The three-step test and “fair use”
BC-9.64. Irrespective of the order in which the three conditions are taken into account, the 
bottom line is that they are cumulative. If any of the three conditions is not fulfilled, an 
exception or limitation is not applicable. In this aspect, the three-step test differs from the “fair 
use” system where a court may also find that there is fair use in a given case even if not all the 
fair use factors (such as those codified in section 107 of the U.S. Copyright Act 140) fully support 
suchafinding.Thatis,thefairusefactors–incontrastwiththeconditionsofthethree-steptest 
–arenotnecessarilycumulative.Thefactorsmustallbeweighedtogether;asaresult,afinding 
for one party with respect to one factor will not preclude ruling for the other party if the other 
factors receive more weight altogether.
BC-9.65. It is to be recognized, however, that these open forms of limitations or exceptions rather 
than specific targeted provisions in the statutory law may only be an appropriate option if they are 
based on well-established court practice. For example, in the United States, the “fair use” system 
is the result of two centuries of development of case law. Simply copying the statutory codification 
of the voluminous case law on fair use in section 107 of the U.S. Copyright Act into the legislation of 
anothercountrywheresuchasystemhasnotexistedbeforeandtryingtosettlethequestionsof
limitations and exceptions on that basis might lead to conflicts with the Berne Convention.
Article 10
[Certain Free Uses of Works: 1. Quotations; 2. Illustrations for teaching; 3. Indication of source 
and author]
(1) Itshallbepermissibletomakequotationsfromaworkwhichhasalreadybeen
lawfully made available to the public, provided that their making is compatible with 
fair practice, and their extent does not exceed that justified by the purpose, including 
quotationsfromnewspaperarticles andperiodicalsintheformofpresssummaries.
(2) It shall be a matter for legislation in the countries of the Union, and for special 
agreements existing or to be concluded between them, to permit the utilization, to 
the extent justified by the purpose, of literary or artistic works by way of illustration 
in publications, broadcasts or sound or visual recordings for teaching, provided such 
utilization is compatible with fair practice.
(3) Where use is made of works in accordance with the preceding paragraphs of this 
Article, mention shall be made of the source, and of the name of the author if it 
appears thereon.
Paragraphs (1) and (3): free use for quotations
BC-10.1. It was only at the 1948 Brussels Diplomatic Conference that a specific provision on 
quotationswasincludedinthetextoftheConvention,butthepermissiblenatureofsuchause
had been recognized implicitly since the Berne Diplomatic Conferences. At the 1885 conference, 
whenthedraftArticle 8onthepermissibilityof“freetaking”ofexcerptsofworksfor 
educational and scientific publications was discussed, agreement was reached that, on the basis 
ofthatprovision,quotationswouldalsobeallowed.141 At the 1928 Rome Diplomatic Conference, 
aproposalwasdiscussedforaspecificprovisiononquotations,butthedelegationswere 

PART I. Guide to the Berne Convention
BC-10.5.Paragraph (1)isoneofthefewprovisionsoftheConventionwherethe“makingavailable
to the public” of a work appears as a condition rather than its “publication”. The result of the use of 
this concept is more flexibility and broader applicability. Quotations may be made not only from 
lawfully published works (that are made available to the public through distribution of copies), but 
also from those which have been made available to the public in non-copy-related forms, such as 
throughpublicperformanceorrecital.Thismakesthescopeofworksthatmaybequotedquite
broad,themoresobecauseparagraph (1)doesnotcontainanylimitationastothegenresofthe
worksconcerned.Also,thereisnolimitationregardingtheworksinwhichquotationsmaybe
included.Quotations,nevertheless,mustcorrespondtotheconditionslaiddowninparagraph (1).
BC-10.6.Underparagraph (1),quotationsmustbecompatiblewith“fairpractice”.Therecords
of the 1967 Stockholm Diplomatic Conference do not contain any specific reference to what 
sort of practice may be considered “fair”. Nevertheless, the text of the Convention offers some 
guidance.ThecriteriaofpermissibleexceptionsincludedinArticle 9(2)atthesameconference 
(thethree-steptest)arealsoapplicablehere;itisobviousthatnoquotationisfairifitconflicts 
with a normal exploitation of works or if it unreasonably prejudices the legitimate interests of 
ownersofrights.Thecriterionthattheextentofquotationsmustnotexceedwhatisjustified 
bythepurposeoffersfurtherguidance,alongwiththeconceptof“quotation”,whichinitself 
involves some factors restricting the scope of this free use.
BC-10.7.Theconditionthataquotationmust not go beyond the extent justified by the purpose and the 
conditionthatquotationsmustbeinharmonywithfairpracticeareinterrelated:fairpracticemay
beaguidanceindeterminingwhatmaybejustifiedbythepurpose,andthefactthataquotation
goes beyond its purpose may be a clear indication that it is not compatible with fair practice either.
BC-10.8. There are also other provisions of the Convention allowing free uses where the 
expression“justifiedbythepurpose”appears.Inthoseprovisions,however,thepurposeisquite 
clearlyidentified.InArticle 10(2),itis“utilization[…]bywayofillustration[…]forteaching”and,
inArticle 10bis(2),“theinformatorypurpose[…]ofreportingcurrentevents”.Article 10(1),in 
contrast, does not at first glance seem to identify any specific purpose. What may it then mean 
thatquotationisonlyfreetotheextent“justifiedbythepurpose”?Ifaquotationmightbeused 
for any purpose whatsoever, the purpose-related condition would be meaningless, since then 
itwouldnotinitselfinvolveanytruelimitationofthefreeuse;onlytherequirementofbeingin
harmony with fair practice would.
BC-10.9. A more reasonable interpretation may be found if the purpose of free use is related to 
theconceptofquotationitself.Thereisgoodreasontoconsiderthatthereare,infact,botha
formal purpose and certain possible substantive purposes involved here. The formal purpose is 
quotation,whilethesubstantivepurposesarethoseusualpurposesofquotationswhichfollow 
from its very meaning, such as criticism, political or scholarly debate, illustration and the like. 
Thisinterpretationgivesanappropriatemeaningtothetextandalsobringsparagraph (1)into
harmony with the structure and nature of the above-mentioned other two provisions of the 
Convention with similar purpose-related conditions. 148
BC-10.10.Paragraph (1)referstoaparticularkindofquotation,namely,to“quotationsfrom
newspaperarticles andperiodicalsintheformofpresssummaries”.A“summary”itselfisobviously
notaquotation,sincethefaithfulrepetitionofapartofthequotedtextisanindispensableelement
oftheconceptofquotation.Insteadofapossibleself-contradictoryinterpretationaccordingto
whichaquotationcouldtaketheformofasummary,anothermorereasonableinterpretation
wouldbethat,inthiscase,quotations–inharmonywiththeabove-mentionedjustifiedpurposesof
quotations–maybepartsofsuchsummaries(ratherthanbeingsummariesthemselves).
148 During the preparatory work before, and at the sessions of, the 1967 Stockholm Diplomatic Conference, some draft 
texts and proposals were discussed in which certain second-level purposes of this free use would have been identified. 
These texts referred to scientific, critical, informatory or educational purposes, judicial, political and entertainment 
purposes, or the purpose of “artistic effect” ( Records of the 1967 Stockholm Diplomatic Conference,116–117,860–861).
These texts were not adopted, however, and this was the right decision, because these second-level “purposes” would 
hardly contribute to an appropriate determination of the extent “justified by the purpose”; just the opposite, they 
mighthavebeenmisleadingifithadbeentakenseriouslythatthepurposesofquotationcouldbeconsideredjust 
“information,” “education,” or “entertainment”. These are obviously not the direct purposes ofquotations.Theseare
simply the most typical fields wherequotationsareusedfortheusual,normalpurposesofquotations. 

78 BC-10.11.Theobligationunderparagraph (3)–concerningtheindicationofthesource,and,ifit
appearsthereon,thenameoftheauthor–relatestobothparagraph (1)andparagraph (2).This
–asregardstheobligationtoindicatetheauthor’sname–mayberegardedasanobligation
derivedfromArticle 6 bis on moral rights.
Paragraphs (2) and (3): free use for teaching
BC-10.12. At the first and second Berne Diplomatic Conferences, in 1884 and 1885, lengthy 
debates took place on what kind of provision should be included in the convention on 
educational exceptions. Since, however, no substantive agreement was reached on how to 
define the conditions of such a limitation, this was left to national legislation and to special 
arrangements between the countries of the Berne Union. The following provision was included 
in the original, 1886 text of the Convention: 
As regards the freedom of including excerpts from literary or artistic works for use in 
publications destined for teaching or scientific purposes, or for chrestomathies, the effect 
of the legislation of the countries of the Union, and of special arrangements existing or to 
be concluded between them, is not affected by this Convention.
At the 1885 conference, where the original 1886 text of the Convention was, in fact, approved, 
itwasclarifiedthat,intheabove-quotedtext,”teaching”meansbothelementaryandhigher 
education, and that “publications […] for […] scientific purposes” also covered publications for 
self-education.149 At the 1908 Berlin, 1928 Rome and 1948 Brussels Diplomatic Conferences, 
several proposals were discussed to modify the text, but it was only at the latter conference 
where the text was somewhat changed; a new condition was added to the text of the provision: 
“to the extent justified by the purpose”.
BC-10.13.Thelatesttextofparagraph (2)hasbeenadoptedatthe1967StockholmDiplomatic
Conference. Two elements from the previous versions of the provision were maintained; namely, 
first, that the application of this free use is “a matter for legislation in the countries of the Union, 
and for special agreements existing or to be concluded between them”; and, second, that such 
use is only permitted “to the extent justified by the purpose”. At the same time, several changes 
were introduced: (i) the expression ”including excerpts” was replaced by the word “utilization”; 
(ii) the condition was included that the utilization may only be free if it is “by way of illustration”; 
(iii) thescopeofapplicabilityoftheexceptionwasextendedfrompublicationsalsotobroadcasts
and sound or visual recordings; (iv) in another dimension, the scope of applicability of the free 
usewasrestricted:nowitisonlyapplicableforteaching,andnotforpublications(or other
“utilizations”) “having a scientific character” (this, however, does not mean that the use of works 
previously covered in this respect may not be permitted, but that it rather may be based on 
some other provisions of the Convention on exceptions and limitations); (v) the reference to 
chrestomathies was left out (but this did not completely change the legal situation, since, in 
many cases, the utilization of works by way of illustration in chrestomathies may very well be 
covered by the new provision); and (vi) a proviso was added that the exception is only applicable 
“provided such utilization is compatible with fair practice”.
BC-10.14.Itseemsthatthenewexpression–“utilization[…]bywayofillustration”–isless
restrictive than the previous one: “including excerpts”, in the sense that it may also allow the 
utilization of entire works, provided that it does not go beyond the concept of “illustration” 
for teaching. However, entire works may only be shorter, because the free use of longer works 
would not conform to the concept of mere illustration and it would also conflict with the two 
restricting conditions (“justified by the purpose”; and “compatible with fair practice”).
BC-10.15.  The meaning of “teaching” is more precisely determined in the 1971 Paris Act of the 
Conventionthanunderthepreviousacts.ThereportofMainCommittee Iofthe1967Stockholm
Diplomatic Conference contains the definition of “teaching” in the form of a kind of agreed 
statement: “The wish was expressed that it should be made clear in this Report that the word 
‘teaching’wastoincludeteachingatalllevels–ineducationalinstitutionsanduniversities,municipal
149 Records of the 1885 Berne Diplomatic Conference , 84.

===== PAGE 78 =====
79
PART I. Guide to the Berne Convention
and State schools, and private schools. Education outside these institutions, for instance general 
teaching available to the public but not included in the above categories, should be excluded.”150
BC-10.16.  In the case of broadcasting to teaching institutions , specific problems may emerge 
because, unless appropriate measures are taken, the broadcast programs may be received not 
only by those institutions but, in principle, by any members of the public in the territory covered 
bythebroadcast.Atthetimeoftheadoptionofparagraph (2)inStockholmin1967,there
were only two possibilities for the participants in the Diplomatic Conference; either to apply 
arestrictedconceptof“broadcasting”–reducingitto“narrow-casting”inschools–thereby 
denying the possibility of fully using the benefits of broadcasting for teaching purposes; or to 
allow broadcasting in general “for teaching”, the option that was chosen. Under the conditions 
of the present digital and communications technologies, however, on the one hand, the 
consequencesofunrestrictedreceptionofsuchbroadcastsmaybemuchmoreeasilyinconflict 
with certain forms of normal exploitation of works or may otherwise unreasonably prejudice the 
legitimate interests of right owners, and, on the other hand, through an appropriate application 
ofnewtechnologies–suchasencryptiontechniques–itispossibletoreducetheimpactofthe
free use in such a way that the restricting conditions are fully respected.
BC-10.17.Thefreeuseunderparagraph (2)mayonlytakeplace“to the extent justified by the 
purpose”.Thetextofparagraph (2)determinesthepurposequiteclearly:“utilization[…]byway
of illustration […] for teaching”. This indicates that the condition is not simply that the utilization 
take place in a teaching institution; it should be for the purpose of teaching (of course, along 
with the usual educational functions of teaching) and, for example, not for mere entertainment 
without any relationship with the teaching activities. The expression “by way of illustration” also 
hasalimitingfactor.Itreflectstherequirementthattheutilizationmustbeorganicallybuilt 
into a teaching program and illustrate something in harmony with, and for the purpose of, such 
a program; it is not sufficient that it be part of some general cultural program in or around the 
institution. The two basic meanings of “illustration” seem to be, first, explaining something by 
offering examples, pictures, etc.; and, second, supplying a book, lectures, etc., with pictures, 
diagrams, etc. This also means that there should be an appropriate proportionality between 
what is supposed to be illustrated and the illustration. From this concept, therefore, certain 
limitations follow regarding the permissible purposes and extent of this free use.
BC-10.18.Asregardstherequirementofcompatibility with “fair practice ”, more or less the 
sameistrueofitasoffreeuseforquotation.Therecordsofthe1967StockholmDiplomatic
Conference do not contain any specific indication about the concept of fair practice. However, 
thethree-steptestunderArticle 9(2)oftheConventionisareliablebasisfordeterminingwhatis 
fair and what is not. Furthermore, in this case as well there is a close interrelationship between 
thisconditionandtherequirementthattheutilizationmustnotgobeyondtheextentjustified 
by the purpose; what is not justified by the purpose may not be regarded as fair, and, in turn, the 
concept of fairness certainly plays a role in determining the extent of use that may be justifiable.
BC-10.19.Asmentionedaboveinconnectionwithparagraph (1),paragraph (3)isequally
applicableconcerningparagraph (2).
Article 10 bis
[Further Possible Free Uses of Works: 1. Of certain articles and broadcast works; 2. Of works seen or 
heard in connection with current events]
(1) It shall be a matter for legislation in the countries of the Union to permit the reproduction 
by the press, the broadcasting or the communication to the public by wire of 
articles publishedinnewspapersorperiodicalsoncurrenteconomic,politicalorreligious
topics, and of broadcast works of the same character, in cases in which the reproduction, 
broadcasting or such communication thereof is not expressly reserved. Nevertheless, 
thesourcemustalwaysbeclearlyindicated;thelegalconsequencesofabreachofthis
obligation shall be determined by the legislation of the country where protection is claimed.

80 (2) It shall also be a matter for legislation in the countries of the Union to determine the 
conditions under which, for the purpose of reporting current events by means of 
photography, cinematography, broadcasting or communication to the public by wire, 
literary or artistic works seen or heard in the course of the event may, to the extent 
justified by the informatory purpose, be reproduced and made available to the public.
Free use of certain articles and broadcast works 
BC-10bis.1. The original 1886 Act of the Convention already took into account the specific 
informatorypurposereflectedinparagraph (1).ItsArticle 7providedforfreeuseofany 
articles publishedinnewspapersandperiodicalsunlesstheauthorsorpublishershadexpressly 
forbiddenit.Noprohibitionwasapplicableconcerningarticles ofpoliticaldiscussionornews 
of the day and miscellaneous facts. The 1908 Berlin Act took a step towards the elimination of 
absolutefreedomofreproductionofarticles ofpoliticaldiscussion.Itintroducedanewnorm 
initsArticle 9(2),underwhich,withtheexceptionofserialnovelsandshortstories(whichwere 
protectedasanyotherliteraryworks),itwasallowedtoreproduceanynewspaperarticle in 
another newspaper; but no free use was allowed if such reproduction was forbidden by the 
owner of copyright. The 1928 Rome Diplomatic Conference introduced further changes which 
advancedtherelevantprovision,atthattimestillinArticle 9(2),closertoitspresentform;it 
reducedthescopeoftheexceptiontoarticles oncurrenteconomic,politicalorreligioustopics
and thereby made clear that the purpose is to facilitate the dissemination of information by the 
press on certain socially important issues.
BC-10bis.2.Paragraph (1)receiveditsfinalformatthe1967StockholmDiplomaticConference
(whereitwasalsorenumberedasArticle 10bis(1)). The scope of works that may be covered by 
this exception was extended again. The direction of this extension was not, however, back to 
allkindsofnewspaperarticles irrespectiveoftheirimportanceforinformationaboutcurrent
matters, but rather towards the development of the genuine function of this provision; that is, 
facilitating the free flow of information on such matters. The permissible exceptions concerning 
works on current economic, political and religious topics were extended not only to reproduction 
ofnewspaperarticles innewspapers,butto“thereproductionbythepress,thebroadcastingor
thecommunicationtothepublicbywireofarticles publishedinnewspapersorperiodicalson
current economic, political or religious topics, and of broadcast works of the same character”.
BC-10bis.3.Underparagraph (1),nationallawsmayprovidethatthearticles andbroadcastworks
mentioned there may be used freely as described there unless their use is expressly reserved 
by the owner of rights. In other words, owners of rights may only enjoy certain rights in respect 
of such works if they formally and expressly reserve their rights. It is needless to deny that this 
isanelementofformality,theonlyminorand–consideringthenatureoftheseinformation-
relatedworks–harmlessexceptiontotheprincipleofformality-freeprotection.(Asisclearfrom 
its origins in the very first act of the Convention, it was adopted at a time when formalities still 
were acceptable under the Convention.)
BC-10bis.4.Thesecondsentenceofparagraph (1)beginsbystipulatingthat“thesource
must always be clearly indicated” and, put this way, the indication of the source seems an 
evenstrongerobligationthanunderArticle 10(3),butthesentencecontinueswith“thelegal 
consequencesofabreachofthisobligationshallbedeterminedbythelegislationofthecountry
whereprotectionisclaimed”.ItshouldbenotedthathereisnotaddedwhatinArticle 10(3)is:
“and of the name of the author if it appears thereon”.
BC-10bis.5.ThelegalconsequencesofabreachofobligationsundertheConventionare
supposed to be determined by the legislation where protection is claimed also in other 
cases,andtheConventiononlyexceptionallyprovidesforcertainconsequencesthatmust 
be applied (in fact, the liability of infringing copies to seizure is the only clear example of this; 
seeArticle 16).Thus,therelevantphraseinthesecondsentenceofparagraph (1)seemstobe
redundant. If its inclusion here nevertheless is still regarded as justified, and if it has a specific 
meaning, it is due to the nature of the obligation of indicating the “source”. The source here 
certainly means not just the title of the work; at least as important is the newspaper or other 
periodical publication or the broadcast program from which the work has been reproduced. 
Newspapers as such have different copyright status in the various countries; in some, they 
are regarded as collective works enjoying copyright protection; in some others, they are only

===== PAGE 80 =====
81
PART I. Guide to the Berne Convention
protected against unfair competition or on the basis of press and media legislation. This is 
likelythereasonwhythechoiceoflegalconsequencesislefttothelegislationofthecountry
whereprotectionisclaimed;somekindofconsequence,however,“shallbe”–thatis,mustbe–
determined (here the Convention does not use the usual term leaving more complete freedom: 
“it is a matter for legislation in the countries of the Union”).
BC-10bis.6. The fact that, in this provision, there is no direct reference to the obligation to also 
indicatethenameoftheauthorifitappearsonanarticle doesnotmeanthatthereisnosuch
obligation.Thereis,underArticle 6 bis containing the general provisions on moral rights.
Exceptions or limitations for reporting of current events
BC-10bis.7. It was the 1948 Brussels Diplomatic Conference which introduced this provision 
inwhatatthattimewasstillthesingleparagraph ofArticle 10bis: “It shall be a matter for 
legislation in countries of the Union to determine the conditions under which recording, 
reproduction, and public communication of short extracts from literary and artistic works 
may be made for the purpose of reporting current events by means of photography or 
cinematography.” The General Report of the Conference underscored that this was “a 
concession granted to the freedom of information”.151 It also stressed the limited nature of the 
free use by stating as follows: “We are convinced that we are interpreting the general sentiment 
of the Conference […] when we say that only short fragments can be involved, the borrowing of 
which seems essential to the accurate reporting of current events.” 152
BC-10bis.8. At the 1967 Stockholm Diplomatic Conference, the provision was modified and it was 
renumberedasArticle 10bis(2). The 1963 Study Group preparing the conference noted that the free 
use is only allowed for “the type of current events programme that transmits only a few episodes 
of an event, it being expressly provided that short extracts only may be used”.153 It also pointed out 
that ”[t]he rule should only be applicable to works which can be seen or heard in the course of the 
actualevent;itwillnotthereforeextendtothesubsequentsynchronizationofmusicforusewitha
current events film”.154 The Study Group observed that the condition expressed by the term ”short 
extracts” was not strictly suitable to the reproduction of works of art. The argument was raised that 
it could hardly have been the intention of the authors of the Convention to permit the reproduction 
ofonlyportionsofaworkofart–anactwhich,incertaincircumstances,couldinvolveinjurytothe
moral interests of the artist155–andthereforeitwasfoundnecessarytocompletethetextinsuch
a manner as to make it clear that in those cases it was permissible to reproduce entire works of art. 
The Study Group, accordingly, proposed that the possibility for allowing such free use, in addition 
to “short extracts from literary or artistic works”, should also be allowed for “works of architecture, 
isolated works of graphic, plastic or applied arts and isolated photographic works”.156 The 1963 
Committee of Experts shared the views of the Study Group, but recommended that, “instead of 
specifying the limits of the freedom allowed by the expression 'short extracts' and 'isolated works', 
the general concept of “the extent justified by the informatory purpose’ should be written into the 
text”.157 This was accepted and the conference adopted the present provision.
BC-10bis.9.Whatparagraph (2)leavestothelegislationofthecountriesoftheUnionis“todetermine
theconditions”–ratherthanjust“topermit”asinparagraph (1)ofthesamearticle –underwhich
certain acts may be carried out. As some commentators have pointed out, this language may be 
regarded as referring to the possibility of providing for non-voluntary licenses, since one of the 
“conditions” may be that, although such acts may be carried out without authorization, remuneration 
should still be paid.158 It seems, however, that, in these kinds of uses, the condition that remuneration 
must be paid is just an abstract possibility rather than something that the revision conferences 
intendedtosetasanormal,usualrequirement.Wherethiswastheintention–asinthecaseof
Articles 11bis(2)and13(1)–theConventionstatesclearlythatthe“conditions”applied“shallnot[…]
beprejudicial[…]tothe[rightoftheauthors][…]toobtainequitableremuneration”.Itseemsthat,in
this case, free use better corresponds to the considerations that served as a basis for this provision at

wasregardedtobethecaseherewasnotamarket-failuresituation–wherenon-voluntarylicenses

National laws, in general, correspond to this recognition; they allow free use for such purpose.
Article 11
[Certain Rights in Dramatic and Musical Works: 1. Right of public performance and of 
communication to the public of a performance; 2. In respect of translations]
(1) Authors of dramatic, dramatico-musical and musical works shall enjoy the exclusive 
right of authorizing:
(i) the public performance of their works, including such public performance by 
any means or process;
(ii) any communication to the public of the performance of their works.
(2) Authors of dramatic or dramatico-musical works shall enjoy, during the full term of 
their rights in the original works, the same rights with respect to translations thereof.
Paragraphs (1)(i) and (2): right of public performance of dramatic, dramatico-musical and 
musical works
BC-11.1.“Publicperformance”undertheBerneConvention–inrespectofwhichtheConvention
recognizedcertainrightsundercertainconditionsasearlyasinitsoriginal1886Act(inArticle 9(1)of
thattext)–clearlymeansperformanceofworksinthepresenceofthepublic,oratleastataplace
open to the public. The provision on the right of public performance of dramatic, dramatico-musical 
andmusicalworksappearedmoreorlessasitdoesnowinparagraph (1)(i),forthefirsttime,in
the 1948 Brussels Act of the Convention (along with the right of communication to the public of the 
performancesofsuchworksincertainwayscoveredbyparagraph (1)(ii)ofArticle 11).Atthattime,
paragraph (1)(i)simplyprovidedfortheexclusiverightofauthorsofsuchworkstoauthorize“the
publicperformanceoftheirworks”.Underasecondsentenceofparagraph (1),theapplicationofthe
provisionsofArticles 11bis and13was“reserved”.Article 11bis provided (already in that act) for the 
right of broadcasting and other communication-related rights; the “reservation” of its application 
onlyconcernedparagraph (1)(iii)discussedbelow.The“reservation”oftheapplicationofArticle 13,
however, meant that the right of public performance of mechanical reproductions of musical works 
wascoveredbythatArticle sinceitsparagraph (1)(ii)providedforsucharight.
BC-11.2. The 1967 Stockholm Diplomatic Conference modified the text on the right of public 
performanceexactlyinthelatteraspect.Itaddedtoparagraph (1)(i)ofArticle 11thefollowing 
phrase: “including such public performance by any means or process”. Performance “by any 
meansorprocess”obviouslyalsomeansperformancethroughtheuseofequipment,suchas 
inthecasementionedinArticle 13(1)(ii)oftheBrusselsAct.Asaconsequence,theprovisionon
publicperformancewasdeletedfromthecompletelytransformedArticle 13.
BC-11.3.Paragraph (2)containsaclarificationofwhatotherwisealsofollowsfromtherightof
translation:thattherightsunderparagraph (1)(andthismeansbothitemsoftheparagraph)
also extend to translations of the works as long as the term of protection of the original works 
has not expired yet. (Translators enjoy separate copyright protection for a separate term of 
protectionunderArticle 2(3)oftheConvention,providedthatthetranslationisoriginal,whichis 
in general the case.)
BC-11.4. The Convention does not provide a definition of the concept of “public”, either as an 
adjectiveorasanoun.Itis,however,quiteobviousthat,asregardstheadjective“public”,itisthe
opposite of the adjective “private” and, thus, what may not be characterized as “private” is to be 
regarded as “public ”. If “public” is used as a noun, it may similarly be regarded as the contrary of 
“private circle”; that is, those people who are beyond the private circle of the user. The definition 
of “public” in statutory law or through court decisions is left, in principle, to the countries of the

Union.Courtsmusttaketheseconsiderationsonthepublic–privateoppositionintoaccount,
and, obviously, are not allowed to artificially and arbitrarily reduce the scope of the concept of 
“public” and thereby the coverage of rights where the public element is decisive. In any case, the 
dominant position seems to be that all uses should be regarded “public”, and all acts directed “to 
thepublic”,thatgobeyondthecircleofafamilyanditsclosesocialacquaintances.Inthisrespect,
therearesimilarprovisionsinbothcivil-lawcountries(see,forexample.Article L122-5-1ofthe 
Intellectual Property Code of France160) and common-law countries (see, for example, section 
101 of the Copyright Act of the United States161). Where a work is communicated to the public, 
the members of the public do not need to be together; they may be separated in space and/
or in time. The right of public performance is not applied to all categories of works, but to all 
categories in respect of which, at the time of the last revisions, such a use seemed possible. The 
otherprovisionsonthisrightareasfollows:(i)Article 11ter(1)(i) on the exclusive right of authors 
of literary works to authorize “public recitation by any means or process” (this is not called right 
ofpublicperformancebutobviouslyitisavariantofthisright);(ii)Article 14(1)(i)ontheexclusive
right of the authors of any literary or artistic work to authorize, inter alia, the public performance 
of works having become the objects of cinematographic adaptation and/or reproduction (thus, 
italsoincludesmusicalworks);and(iii)Article 14bis(1), which provides that “[t]he owner of 
copyright in a cinematographic work shall enjoy the same rights as the author of an original 
work, including the rights referred to in the preceding Article”.
BC-11.5. In the case of the Berne Convention, the concept of “public performance” does not 
extend to communication to the public, either by wire or by broadcasting, since both of those 
actsinvolvethetransmissionofworkstoapublicthat–incontrastwithpublicperformance–is 
not present at the place from where the transmission is made. As regards the acts covered 
by the rights of public performance and public recital, the Convention does not use the term 
“communication to the public”.
BC-11.6. The fact that the Convention itself has never used the term in this sense may not fully 
rule out the possibility of regarding public performance as a kind of communication to the 
public on the basis of a very broad concept of “communication”. However, the principle that, in 
the interpretation of legal texts, one must not neglect the importance of the use of different 
terms should also be applied here. It seems that the drafters of the relevant provisions of the 
Convention wanted to differentiate between the act of performing a work in the presence of the 
public, on the one hand, and, on the other hand, communication of a work (or its performance 
or recital) to a public which may be found at a place other than from where the communication 
is made. This means that the Convention uses a narrower meaning of communication, in the 
senseofcommunicatingfromsomewhere–fromwherethecommunicationisinitiated–for
reception at a place different from the place of initiating the communication. This narrower 
meaning was identified in the “guided development” period mentioned in the Introduction, 
above.ItisalsoreflectedinthetextoftheWCT,whereArticle 8istitled“Communicationtothe 
Public”,andwhattheprovisioncoversareonlytwopossible–mutuallycomplementary–forms 
of communication (by wire, by wireless means or both) from one place to another.
Paragraphs (1)(ii) and (2): the right of communication to the public of dramatic, dramatico- 
musical and musical works
BC-11.7.Paragraph (1)(ii)wasincludedinthetextoftheConventionatthe1948Brussels
Diplomatic Conference. In this respect, the text of the Convention has not changed since then. 
Under it, “[a]uthors of dramatic, dramatico-musical and musical works shall enjoy the exclusive 
right of authorizing: [...] (ii) any communication to the public of the performance of their works.” 
This means any kind of communication other than broadcasting, since the latter is covered 
byArticle 11bis. (As mentioned above, in the Brussels Act, there was still a second sentence in

BC-11.8. Any communication to the public other than broadcasting and related communications 
means communication of the performance by loudspeaker, for example to a neighboring room, 
but most typically and importantly, communication to the public by wire (cable) in cases where 
the program is not already a broadcast program (in so-called “cable-originated programs”, the 
communicationbycableofbroadcastworksiscoveredbyArticle 11 bis(1)(ii)).
BC-11.9. The concepts of “public” and “to the public” are discussed above in connection with 
paragraph (1)(i).Itshouldbestressedherealsothatitisnotanindispensableconditionthat
members of the public be present, or that they watch and/or listen to the performance. It is 
sufficientthattheperformanceismadeinaplaceopentothepublic,orifitiscommunicated – as
describedinparagraph (1)(ii)–thatitismadeavailableforreceptionbythepublic,receptionitself
not being a condition for the act of communication to the public to take place. 
BC-11.10.Asindicatedabove,theclarificationinparagraph (2)abouttherightsofauthorsin
respectoftranslationsoftheirworksisalsoapplicabletotherightunderparagraph (1)(ii).
Implied exceptions to the right of public performance and certain other rights (“minor 
reservations”)
BC-11.11. The text of the Convention does not contain provisions on exceptions and limitations 
of the rights of public performance and communication to the public of performances 
under Article 11.However,thefollowingagreedstatementwasinsertedintotheGeneralReport
of the 1948 Brussels Diplomatic Conference:
Your Rapporteur-General has been entrusted with making an express mention of the 
possibility available to national legislation to make what are commonly called minor 
reservations. The Delegates of Norway, Sweden, Denmark and Finland, the Delegate of 
Switzerland and the delegate of Hungary have all mentioned these limited exemptions 
allowed for religious ceremonies, military bands and the needs of child and adult 
education.TheseexceptionalmeasuresapplytoArticles 11bis,11ter,13and14.Youwill
understand that these references are just lightly pencilled in here, in order to avoid 
damaging the principle of the right.162
The General Report refers to “minor reservations”, but it is obvious that they are, in fact, 
possible minor exceptions. Those countries which wish to apply them do not have to make any 
formal reservation.
BC-11.12. Note that this statement was made within the framework of reporting about the 
newArticle 11oftheConvention,andthusthesentence”[t]heseexceptionalmeasures
applytoArticles 11bis, 11ter, 13 and 14” is to be read as ”[t]hese exceptional measures, in 
additiontoArticle 11,alsoapplytoArticles 11bis, 11ter, 13 and 14”. The idea that a statement 
should be made about these “exceptional measures” or “minor reservations” was raised by a 
SubcommitteeoftheconferenceonArticles 11and11ter. The report of the subcommittee added 
toitsproposalconcerningArticle 11(1)containedthefollowingclarification:
The various delegations in the Subcommittee formally declared that their agreement and 
hence unanimity on this text were subject to the condition that the following statement 
shouldappearinthegeneralreport:‘ThewordingasnowadoptedinArticle 11(1)makes
no substantial change to the import of the text as it appears in the Berne Convention 
according to the Berlin and Rome revisions, given that certain exceptions admitted by 
some Union countries for clearly defined cases have no international import.’163

BC-11.13. The records of the General Commission of the 1948 Brussels Diplomatic Conference 
offer further indication about what was meant by the delegates under the concept of 
these exceptions:
The majority of delegates expressed concern that the legal situation was not substantially 
changed by the substitution of an exclusive and conventional right for the provision of the 
Rome text under which unionist authors were assimilated to national authors. To obtain 
such a result, it was sufficient for the Conference to make it clear that this exclusive right 
was not incompatible with certain exceptions provided by national laws, exceptions already 
allowed under the Rome regime, for religious, cultural or patriotic purposes. The Conference 
declared itself in favour of this, in harmony with the position of several governments. In 
particular, the Delegation of Sweden expressed the opinion that such exceptions should be 
extendedtoArticles 11bis,13and14,aswellastoArticles 11and11ter, andrequested,inthe
name of the Nordic governments, that this remark be included in the General Report. On the 
proposal of […] the rapporteur of the Sub-Committee, the Conference noted, however, that 
these exceptions should be of a limited nature and, in particular, that it was not sufficient 
that the performance or recitation was ‘not for profit’ in order that it be excepted from the 
exclusiverightoftheauthor.ConcerningthequestionofhowthetextoftheConvention
should be interpreted, the Conference was of the opinion that a mention of this matter 
should be inserted in the General Report, taking account of this, and, in particular what had 
been expressed by the Delegation of Sweden.164
BC-11.14. The issue of “minor reservations” was not raised during the preparatory work of the 
1967 Stockholm Diplomatic Conference, and no mention was made of them in the program of 
theconference.However,atoneofthesessionsofMainCommittee I,againtheDelegationof
Sweden, on behalf of the Nordic countries, proposed that a sentence be included in the report 
of the Committee to the effect that “the possibility given in the general report of the Brussels 
ConferencetomakeminorreservationstotheexclusiverightsprovidedforinArticles 11and
11ter was still valid”.165 This proposal was accepted, and the following statement was included 
inthereportofMainCommittee I:“ItseemsthatitwasnottheintentionoftheCommitteeto
prevent States from maintaining in their national legislation provisions based on the declaration 
contained in the General Report of the Brussels Conference. It accordingly seems necessary 
to apply to these ‘minor reservations’ the principle retained for exceptions to the right of 
translation,asindicatedinconnectionwithArticle 8(seeparagraph 205).” 166
BC-11.15.Thecontextinwhichtheabove-quotedstatementswereincludedintherecordsof
the Brussels and Stockholm Diplomatic Conferences clearly indicates that they were “agreed 
statements”, which are legitimate supplementary sources of interpretation of the Convention. 
The way these agreed statements were proposed, discussed and adopted and their inclusion in 
the records of the conferences do not leave any doubt that they are indispensable parts of the 
agreement adopted by the delegates concerning the rights involved and the possible exceptions 
to them. Therefore, any bona fide interpretationoftheConventionrequiresthattheybefully
taken into account. Thus, these statements correspond to the concept of “agreed statements” 
underArticle 31.2(a)oftheVCLT(“agreementrelatedtothetreaty”).
BC-11.16. The records of the revision conferences speak of “minor reservations”, but, as 
mentioned above, they are in fact possible minor exceptions. Those countries which wish to 
apply these kinds of restrictions of rights do not have to make any formal reservation.

86 Scope of rights to which “minor reservations” are allowed
BC-11.17. As discussed above, the agreed statement included in the general report of the 
BrusselsDiplomaticConferencecoveredtherightsprovidedforinArticles 11,11bis, 11ter, 13 and 
14 of (the Brussels Act of) the Convention. These were the following rights:
 – Article 11(1):theexclusiverightofauthorizing[…](i)thepublicperformanceof
[dramatic, dramatico-musical and musical] works; (ii) any communication to the public 
of the performance of [such] works;
 – Article 11bis(1): the exclusive right of authorizing: (i) the broadcasting of […] works 
or the communication thereof to the public by any other means of wireless diffusion 
of signs, sounds or images; (ii) any communication to the public, by wire or by 
rebroadcasting of the broadcast of the work, when this communication is made by an 
organization other than the original one; (iii) the public communication by loudspeaker 
or any other analogous instrument transmitting, by signs, sounds or images, the 
broadcastofthework(however,alongwithparagraph (2)whichallowstheapplication
ofnon-voluntarylicenses,andparagraph (3)whichprovidesforfreeuseornon- 
voluntary licenses for ephemeral recording for broadcasting purposes);
 – Article 11ter: the exclusive right of authorizing the public recitation of […] works;
 – Article 13(1):theexclusiverightofauthorizing:(i)therecordingof[musical]worksby
instruments capable of reproducing them mechanically; (ii) the public performance by 
meansofsuchinstrumentsofworksthusrecorded(however,alongwithparagraph (2)
which allows the application of non-voluntary licenses as discussed above);
 – Article 14(1):theexclusiverightofauthorizing(i)thecinematographicadaptation
and reproduction of […] works, and the distribution of the works thus adapted or 
reproduced; (ii) the public performance of the works thus adapted or reproduced.
BC-11.18.ThereportoftheStockholmDiplomaticConference,asquotedabove,statesthe
intention of the delegations to maintain the applicability of “minor reservations”. Although the 
Swedishdelegation,initsinterventionquotedinthesameparagraph above,referredonlyto
Articles 11and11ter of the Convention, the statement adopted as part of the report speaks of 
“provisions based on the declaration contained in the general report of the Brussels Conference”.
BC-11.19. Some of the provisions to which reference is made in the agreed statement adopted in 
Brusselshavebeenmodified.Namely,paragraph (1)ofArticle 13hasbeenremoved;atthesame
time, (i) the recording of musical works has been explicitly recognized as an act of reproduction 
underthenewArticle 9(3)oftheConvention;and(ii)thetextofbothArticle 11(1)andArticle 11ter 
(whichbecamethefirstparagraph ofanewArticle withthesamenumbering)hasbeenamended
to clarify that the exclusive right of authorizing public performance and recital, respectively, of 
the works covered by those provisions also includes “such public [performance][recitation] by any 
meansorprocess”.Furthermore,anewsubparagraph (ii)correspondingtosubparagraph (ii)of
Article 11hasbeenincludedinArticle 11ter(1), indicating that the exclusive right of authorization 
also applies to ”any communication to the public of the recitation of […] works”.
BC-11.20. It seems that the changes, in this respect, brought about by the Stockholm Diplomatic 
Conference, mainly consist in a re-characterization of rights. The recording of musical works 
hasbeenexplicitlyrecognizedasanactofreproduction–and,thus,theissueofpermissible 
exceptions to, and limitations of, the right of authorizing such an act has been transferred to the 
purviewofthethree-steptest.Asaresultofthis,thereferencetoArticle 13haslostitsvalidity 
(since now it only contains the provisions on non-voluntary licenses).
BC-11.21. The reference in the agreed statement in the General Report of the Brussels Diplomatic 
ConferencetoArticle 14oftheConventiondeservesspecialconsideration.Asquotedabove,that
Article wasinlinewiththeprovisionsonnon-copy-relatedrights(Articles 11,11bis and 11ter) in 
thesensethatitalsoprovided,initsparagraph (1)(ii),foranexclusiverightofauthorizingthe
public performance of the works that had become the objects of cinematographic adaptations. 
InStockholm,afurthernon-copy-relatedrightwasrecognizedinparagraph (1)(ii)oftheArticle;

namely, the right of authorizing the communication to the public by wire of the works thus adapted 
orreproduced.However,therightprovidedinparagraph (1)(i)ofArticle 14doesnotfitintothe
series of non-copy-related rights so far mentioned; it is a combination of a transformation right 
and of the basic copy-related right; the right of authorizing the cinematographic adaptation and 
reproduction of works. It may be stated that the applicability of “minor reservations” does not apply 
toparagraph(1)(i)–butonlytoparagraph(1)(ii)–ofArticle 14.Asfarasreproductionisconcerned,it
isArticle 9(2)thatdetermineswhatexceptionsandlimitationsarepermissible.
BC-11.22. From the viewpoint of the scope of applicability of “minor reservations”, it is also 
relevant that the 1967 Stockholm Diplomatic Conference inserted into the Convention a new 
Article 14bis whoseparagraph (1)provides:“Withoutprejudicetothecopyrightinanywork
which may have been adapted or reproduced, a cinematographic work shall be protected as an 
original work. The owner of copyright in a cinematographic work shall enjoy the same rights as 
the author of an original work, including the rights referred to in the preceding Article ” (emphasis 
added).Thismeansthat,throughtheextendedapplicationofArticle 14,theabove-identified 
non-copy-relatedrightsarealsoapplicableunderArticle 14 bis(1).
BC-11.23. Thus, in sum, as far as the 1971 Paris Act of the Convention is concerned, the option of 
“minor reservations” mentioned in the agreed statements adopted in Brussels and confirmed 
inStockholmcoversallthenon-copy-relatedrights–andonlythoserights–providedforin 
Articles 11(1),11bis(1), 11ter(1), 14(1) and 14bis(1) as discussed above.
The de minimis principle as the basis of “minor reservations”
BC-11.24. At the 1948 Brussels Diplomatic Conference, the idea of including a provision on the 
exceptions involved was discussed, and there was agreement about their permissibility, but the 
conference decided to settle this issue through a mere agreed statement. This in itself indicates 
that the general de minimis principle applies in this respect. It is emphasized in the text of the 
agreedstatementitselfquotedabove,sinceitspeaksof minor reservations, and also it points 
out that “these references are just lightly penciled in”.
BC-11.25. The repeated confirmation in the records of the Brussels Diplomatic Conference that only 
some minor exceptions are allowed, along with the examples mentioned in the agreed statement, 
suggests that no exceptions are permissible in the case of acts carried out for commercial, 
profit-making purposes. The report of the General Commission of the conference, however, also 
indicates the understanding of the conference in this respect: “the Conference noted, however, 
that these exceptions should be of a limited nature and, in particular, that, it was not sufficient that 
the performance or recitation was ‘not for profit’ in order that it be excepted from the exclusive right 
of the author” (emphasis added).167 Thus, the understanding of the Conference when adopting the 
agreed statement was that acts carried out for profit-making, commercial purposes must not be 
coveredbyany“minorreservation”,andthat–evenwithinthenot-for-profitactivities–onlythose
may be exempted that are of truly minor importance, in accordance with the de minimis principle.
Exhaustive or non-exhaustive list of “minor reservations”
BC-11.26.Theagreedstatementquotedabovementionsthefollowingexamplesasacts
permissible by “minor reservations”: acts carried out (i) in the framework of religious 
ceremonies;(ii)bymilitarybands;and(iii)forchildandadulteducation.Thequestioniswhether 
this may be regarded as an exhaustive list (and thus, a kind of “grandfathering” agreement to 
recognize certain existing minor cases) or as a non-exhaustive list. It seems that this cannot 
be regarded as a fully and rigidly closed exhaustive list, but it does indicate the approximate 
dimension and scope of permissible “minor reservations” where certain other cases may be 
identified through a reasonable and bona fide  applicationofthelegaltechniqueofanalogy
(for example, a national law might not be in conflict with the Convention if it allows exceptions 
not only for religious ceremonies but also for certain other similar events, such as official state 
ceremonies). It must be underlined again that, in the cases mentioned in the agreed statement, 
exceptions are only allowed if they are for not-for-profit purposes and if they, in all other 
aspects, correspond to the de minimis foundation of the concept of “minor reservations”.
