includes two thirds of the States which, at the time of the revision conference, are 
parties to the Convention.
3. In the event of adoption of a Convention revising this Convention in whole or in part, 
and unless the revising Convention provides otherwise:
(a) this Convention shall cease to be open to ratification, acceptance or accession as 
from the date of entry into force of the revising Convention;
(b) this Convention shall remain in force as regards relations between or with 
Contracting States which have not become parties to the revising Convention.
RC-29.1.TheConventionhasneverbeenrevised.Theupdatingoftheinternationalnorms–at
leastasfarastherightsofperformersandproducersofphonogramsareconcerned–hastaken
place in the WPPT and the BTAP.
Article 30 
[Settlement of disputes]
Any dispute which may arise between two or more Contracting States concerning the 
interpretation or application of this Convention and which is not settled by negotiation shall, 
attherequestofanyoneofthepartiestothedispute,bereferredtotheInternationalCourtof
Justicefordecision,unlesstheyagreetoanothermodeofsettlement.
RC-30.1.TheprovisionsofArticle 30aremutatis mutandis the same as or at least similar to the 
provisionsofArticle 33oftheBerneConvention.Thus,thecommentsmadeintheGuidetothe
Berne Convention in this collection apply in this case as well.
Article 31 
[Limits on Reservations]
Withoutprejudicetotheprovisionsofparagraph 3ofArticle 5,paragraph 2ofArticle 6,
paragraph 1ofArticle 16andArticle 17,noreservationmaybemadetothisConvention.
Article 32
[Intergovernmental Committee]
1. An Intergovernmental Committee is hereby established with the following duties:
(a) tostudyquestionsconcerningtheapplicationandoperationofthisConvention;and
(b) to collect proposals and to prepare documentation for possible revision of 
this Convention.
2. The Committee shall consist of representatives of the Contracting States, chosen with 
dueregardtoequitablegeographicaldistribution.Thenumberofmembersshallbe
six if there are twelve Contracting States or less, nine if there are thirteen to eighteen 
Contracting States and twelve if there are more than eighteen Contracting States.
3. The Committee shall be constituted twelve months after the Convention comes into force 
by an election organised among the Contracting States, each of which shall have one 
vote, by the Director-General of the International Labour Office, the Director-General of 
the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization and the Director of 
the Bureau of the International Union for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works, in 
accordance with rules previously approved by a majority of all Contracting States.

4. The Committee shall elect its Chairman and officers. It shall establish its own rules 
of procedure. These rules shall in particular provide for the future operation of the 
Committee and for a method of selecting its members for the future in such a way as to

5. Officials of the International Labour Office, the United Nations Educational, Scientific

RC-32.1.Ascanbeseen,Article 32providesforthejointadministrationoftheILO,UNESCOand
WIPO. It is to be noted, however, that since 2009 the ordinary sessions of the Intergovernmental 
Committee have been suspended. This is because the international norms on related rights 
(at least as regards the rights of performers and producers of phonograms) were updated in 
the WPPT and then in the BTAP; therefore, the WIPO  Standing Committee on Copyright and 
Related Rights (SCCR) has become the relevant forum (where there are also preparatory works 
in progress for a possible Broadcasters Treaty281).

[Languages]

beingequallyauthentic.

Italian and Portuguese.

PART II. Guides to the Older Generation of Related Rights Treaties – the Rome Convention, the Phonograms Convention and the Brussels, or Satellites, Convention
Convention for the Protection of Producers of Phonograms against 
Unauthorized Duplication of their Phonograms (Phonograms 
Convention), 1971
[Preamble]282
The Contracting States,
Concerned at the widespread and increasing unauthorized duplication of phonograms 
and the damage this is occasioning to the interests of authors, performers and producers 
of phonograms;
Convinced that the protection of producers of phonograms against such acts will also benefit 
the performers whose performances, and the authors whose works, are recorded on the 
said phonograms;
Recognizing the value of the work undertaken in this field by the United Nations Educational, 
Scientific and Cultural Organization and the World Intellectual Property Organization;
Anxious not to impair in any way international agreements already in force and in particular 
in no way to prejudice wider acceptance of the Rome Convention of October 26, 1961, which 
affords protection to performers and to broadcasting organizations as well as to producers 
of phonograms;
Have agreed as follows:
PhC-Pr.1.ThePhonogramsConventionisfrequentlycharacterizedasan“anti-piracyconvention”,
and this refers to the reasons for which the Convention was prepared and adopted. The 
text of the Convention including its Preamble (which normally identifies the objectives of a 
treaty), however, does not use the word “piracy”. The expression “widespread and increasing 
unauthorizedduplicationofphonograms”–isusedinstead.Thereportofthe1971Geneva
Diplomatic Conference indicates the reasons for this:
While recognizing that its purpose was the prevention of the piracy of phonograms, the 
Conference considered that the inclusion of the word ‘piracy’, as a description of the 
activities against which producers of phonograms should be protected, was not entirely 
appropriate in an international convention. It preferred to use the expression contained in 
the title, that is to say, unauthorized duplication.283
PhC-Pr.2.“Unauthorizedduplication”–or“unauthorizedreproduction”,whichmaybeconsidered
moreorlessasynonym–isaphenomenonbroaderthan“piracy”.Article 2oftheConvention, 
which identifies the acts against which protection must be granted, however, does not cover 
all cases of “unauthorized duplication”; it defines a narrower scope thereof: “the making of 
duplicates without the consent of the producer and […] the importation of such duplicates, 
provided that any such making or importation is for the purpose of distribution to the public, 
and […] the distribution of such duplicates to the public”. Making unauthorized duplicates, 
importing such duplicates for the purpose of distribution to the public, and distribution of such 
duplicatestothepublic,areusually–andquiterightly–called“piracy”.
PhC-Pr.3. Since the adoption of the Convention, the opinion of the international community 
seems to have changed concerning the appropriateness of using the word “piracy” in an 
internationaltreaty.TheTRIPSAgreementusesthistermandreferstoit,initsArticle 61,as
a form of infringement which is serious enough to incur criminal procedures and sanctions. 
TheAgreementalsooffersadefinitionofaderivativeexpression–“piratedcopyright 
282ThetitlesofthePreambleandarticles insquarebracketsarenotpartsofthetextoftheConvention.Thesetitles, 
however, appear in WIPO publications containing the text of the Convention.
283 Records of the International Conference of States on the Protection of Phonograms , Geneva, October 18 to 29, 1971 
(Geneva:UNESCO–WIPO,1975)(hereinafter: Records of the 1971 Geneva Diplomatic Conference ), 38, para. 31.

Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
176 good”–whichseemstobesomewhatbroaderthantheactscoveredbyArticle 2ofthe
Phonograms Convention.284
PhC-Pr.4.Thesecondparagraph ofthePreambledeservesaseparatemention.Itreflects
an important recognition concerning the relationship between the various categories of 
beneficiaries of protection. It draws attention to the fact that the protection of producers of 
phonograms against piracy also benefits the performers whose performances, and the authors 
whose works, are recorded on phonograms.
Article 1 
[Definitions]
For the purposes of this Convention:
(a) “phonogram” means any exclusively aural fixation of sounds of a performance or of 
other sounds;
(b) “producer of phonograms” means the person who, or the legal entity which, first fixes 
the sounds of a performance or other sounds;
(c) “duplicate”meansanarticle whichcontainssoundstakendirectlyorindirectlyfrom
a phonogram and which embodies all or a substantial part of the sounds fixed in 
that phonogram;
(d) “distribution to the public” means any act by which duplicates of a phonogram are 
offered, directly or indirectly, to the general public or any section thereof.
Phonogram and producer of phonograms
PhC-1.1. The definitions of “phonogram” and “producer of phonograms” in points (a) and (b) of 
Article 1ofthePhonogramsConventionarethesameasinpoints(b)and(c)inArticle 3ofthe
Rome Convention. Therefore, it is sufficient to refer to the comments to the latter provisions in 
the Guide to the Rome Convention.
PhC-1.2. Nevertheless, it should be noted that there was a debate at the Diplomatic Conference 
about the interpretation of the reference in the definition of “phonogram” as to an exclusively 
aural fixation. Two different interpretations of the Convention were discussed in relation to 
recordings made from the soundtracks of cinematographic works or other audiovisual works 
when the soundtrack is fixed simultaneously with the visual recording.
PhC-1.3. As the report indicates, under one view expressed at the Conference, the soundtrack 
constitutes the raw material for the recording, and when an exclusively aural fixation of 
the soundtrack is made, the resulting recording is a phonogram within the meaning of the 
Convention. The report states that this view is reinforced by the fact that the soundtrack almost 
invariably is edited or otherwise altered in the process of producing the recording, so that a new 
exclusively aural version is created. 285
PhC-1.4. According to the other view presented in the report, the sounds embodied in a 
recording produced from the soundtrack, having been first fixed in the form of an audiovisual 
work, do not have any separate character as an exclusively aural fixation, and thus the recording 
cannotqualifyasaphonogramundertheConvention,butispartoftheoriginalaudiovisual
work. It was pointed out that, even under this second view, the Convention provides only 
for minimum standards of protection and, therefore, it is within the competence of each 
284ThedefinitionisincludedinafootnotetoArticle 51oftheAgreement,whereitisusedinconnectionwiththespecial 
requirementsrelatedtobordermeasures.Itreads:“‘piratedcopyrightgoods’shallmeananygoodswhichare 
copies made without the consent of the right holder or person duly authorized by the right holder in the country 
ofproductionandwhicharemadedirectlyorindirectlyfromanarticle wherethemakingofthatcopywouldhave 
constituted an infringement of a copyright or a related right under the law of the country of importation.”
285 Records of the 1971 Geneva Diplomatic Conference , 38, para. 36.

Contracting State to protect recordings produced from soundtracks as phonograms under its 
national legislation.286
PhC-1.5. The report concludes: “[i]n any event, the Conference expressed the view that the 
person to be protected should be the person who first fixes the phonogram as such”. 287 This 
indeed is the essence. Under item (a), “‘phonogram’ means any exclusively aural fixation 
ofsoundsofaperformanceorofothersounds”.Thus,ifanexclusivelyaural–thatis,not
anaudiovisual–fixationismade,itisa“phonogram”.Itistobenotedthatthedefinitionof
“phonogram”underArticle 2(b)oftheWPPTisdifferentanditalsohasanimpactontheconcept 
of“audiovisualfixations”inArticle 2(b)oftheBTAP,asdiscussedintheGuidestothosetreaties.
Duplicate
PhC-1.6. Concerning the definition of “duplicate” in point (c), the Diplomatic Conference noted 
that“theessentialfeatureofaduplicatewasthefactthatthearticle containedsoundstaken 
directly or indirectly from a phonogram”. In the report it is pointed out that what was meant, 
particularly by the insertion of the word “indirectly”, was “the copying, by a machine or other 
appropriate apparatus, of recordings, even if the copying takes place from the broadcasting of 
a phonogram or from a copy of a phonogram”, and that “new recordings imitating or simulating 
the sounds of the original recording are not covered by the provisions of the Convention”. 288
PhC-1.7. Based on the text of the definition and this clarification, “duplicate” is used here as a 
synonym of “reproduction” and “copy”, and, at the time of the adoption of the Convention, there 
must not have been any substantive differences between the meanings of these terms. With 
the development of technology, however, a difference has emerged between “duplicate” as 
defined in point (c), on the one hand, and “reproduction” and “copy” on the other. The definition 
of “duplicate” is limited to “articles”, meaning tangible objects, while, as discussed in the Guide 
totheWCTconcerningArticle 1(4)ontheseconcepts(whicharethesame, mutatis mutandis, 
under the WPPT and the BTAP) “reproduction” and “copy” may now also take digital form when 
works and recordings are saved to electronic storage media, and this does not correspond to 
thenotionofan“article whichcontainssounds”.
PhC-1.8. The Diplomatic Conference also clarified that the adjective “substantial”, which appears 
inthedefinitionof“duplicates”ofaphonogram,expresses“notonlyaquantitativebutalsoa 
qualitativeevaluation”,andnotedthatasmallpartmayalsobesubstantial. 289
Distribution to the public
PhC-1.9.TheDiplomaticConferencedecidedtoaddtoArticle 1oftheConventionadefinitionof
the concept of “distribution to the public” in point (d). As noted in the report, in this definition, 
no specific reference is made to commercial purposes, in order not to restrict unnecessarily the 
field of application of the Convention, because “it was considered that commercial aims were 
understood in the terms of the definition as it appears therein”. The Conference also considered 
various examples of the “acts” by which duplicates of phonograms are offered directly or 
indirectly to the public, and found that such acts should include, for example, the supply of 
duplicates to a wholesaler for the purposes of sale to the public, directly or indirectly. 290
Article 2
[Obligations of Contracting States; Whom they must protect and against what]
Each Contracting State shall protect producers of phonograms who are nationals of other 
Contracting States against the making of duplicates without the consent of the producer and 
against the importation of such duplicates, provided that any such making or importation is for the 
purpose of distribution to the public, and against the distribution of such duplicates to the public.
286 Ibid., para. 37.

288 Ibid., para. 40.
289 Ibid., para. 41.

178 PhC-2.1.Article 2containsthemostsubstantiveprovisionoftheConvention.Therestof
the Convention may be considered to simply supplement or serve the application of this 
central norm (by defining concepts, referring to means of implementation, fixing the term of 
protection, and so on).
PhC-2.2. Protection must be granted to producers of phonograms who are “nationals” of 
other Contracting Parties. The meaning of “nationals” is sufficiently clear in the case of natural 
persons,butsince,byvirtueofthedefinitioninArticle 1(b),legalentitiesalsomaybe–and, 
infactveryfrequentlyare–phonogramproducers,intheircase,theconceptof“nationality” 
requiresinterpretation.Themostlogical“pointofattachment”thatmayserveasabasisfor 
identifyingthe“nationality”oflegalentitiesistheplaceoftheirheadquartersortheplacewhere 
they have their real and effective industrial or commercial establishments.
PhC-2.3. As mentioned above in the comments on the Preamble, protection must be granted 
against three kinds of piratical activities: (i) the making of duplicates without the consent of the 
producer, provided that it is for the purpose of distribution to the public; (ii) the importation 
of such duplicates, provided that it is for the purpose of distribution to the public; and (iii) the 
distribution of such duplicates to the public.
Article 3
[Means of Implementation by Contracting States]
The means by which this Convention is implemented shall be a matter for the domestic law of 
each Contracting State and shall include one or more of the following: protection by means of 
the grant of a copyright or other specific right; protection by means of the law relating to unfair 
competition; protection by means of penal sanctions.
PhC-3.1. It follows from the anti-piracy nature of the Convention that it does not specifically 
concentrate on the legal means through which protection may be granted against piratical 
activities. It is result- and performance-oriented; it leaves it to Contracting States to choose 
from among the legal means available, or to establish new ones, to achieve efficient protection 
againsttheactslistedinArticle 2.
PhC-3.2.Article 3identifiesfourpossibleoptionswhichmaybechoseneitheraloneorjointly; 
namely: (i) granting copyright (typical in common-law countries); (ii) granting a specific right 
(a “related right”, typical in civil-law countries); (iii) protection by means of the law on unfair 
competition (which tends to offer less efficient protection than copyright or a related right); and 
(iv) penal sanctions. 
Article 4
[Term of Protection]
The duration of the protection given shall be a matter for the domestic law of each Contracting 
State. However, if the domestic law prescribes a specific duration for the protection, that duration 
shall not be less than twenty years from the end either of the year in which the sounds embodied 
in the phonogram were first fixed or of the year in which the phonogram was first published.
PhC-4.1.Thisprovisionisquiteoutofdate.Itiswordedvaguelybecausegrantingprotection
bymeansoftherulesonunfaircompetitionisalsoanoptionunderArticle 3.Thepossibility 
mentionedintheArticle toprovidethatthetermofprotectionbecalculatedfromthe 
publicationofthephonogramismorefavorablethantheruleinArticle 14(a)oftheRome
Convention, according to which the term of protection is to be calculated from the fixation of 
the phonograms (because publication usually takes place later, the term of protection calculated 
from publication expires later). However, this is only one of the two options available. The 
minimumtermprovidedinthisarticle makesittotallyoutofdate(consideringthatboththe
TRIPS Agreement and the WPPT prescribes a 50-year minimum term).

Article 5 
[Formalities]
If, as a condition of protecting the producers of phonograms, a Contracting State, under its 
domesticlaw,requirescompliancewithformalities,theseshallbeconsideredasfulfilledifall
the authorized duplicates of the phonogram distributed to the public or their containers bear a 
noticeconsistingofthesymbol℗,accompaniedbytheyeardateofthefirstpublication,placed
in such manner as to give reasonable notice of claim of protection; and, if the duplicates or 
their containers do not identify the producer, his successor in title or the exclusive licensee (by 
carrying his name, trademark or other appropriate designation), the notice shall also include 
the name of the producer, his successor in title or the exclusive licensee.
PhC-5.1.ThisArticle containspracticallythesameprovisionasArticle 11oftheRome
Convention. Thus, the comments made on that provision above also apply here.
Article 6
[Limitations on Protection]
Any Contracting State which affords protection by means of copyright or other specific right, 
or protection by means of penal sanctions, may in its domestic law provide, with regard to the 
protection of producers of phonograms, the same kinds of limitations as are permitted with 
respect to the protection of authors of literary and artistic works. However, no compulsory 
licenses may be permitted unless all of the following conditions are met:
(a) the duplication is for use solely for the purpose of teaching or scientific research;
(b) the license shall be valid for duplication only within the territory of the Contracting 
State whose competent authority has granted the license and shall not extend to the 
export of duplicates;
(c) theduplicationmadeunderthelicensegivesrisetoanequitableremunerationfixed
by the said authority taking into account, inter alia, the number of duplicates which will 
be made.
PhC-6.1.InthedraftConvention,thisArticle wastopermitanyContractingStatewhichgrants
protection to producers of phonograms by means of a specific right to provide the same kinds 
of limitations with regard to the protection of producers of phonograms as those concerning 
the protection of authors of literary and artistic works. It was to be made clear that no 
compulsory licenses may be granted except in cases of duplication for the purpose of teaching 
or scientific research.
PhC-6.2. At the Diplomatic Conference, some delegations asked for the deletion of the provision 
prohibiting compulsory licenses. They expressed the view that such a provision could result in 
giving producers of phonograms a wider protection than compulsory licensing of the use of 
works.OtherdelegationswereinfavorofintroducingtheprovisionsofArticle 15oftheRome
Convention mutatis mutandis. The majority, however, was in favor of maintaining the prohibition, 
which sets limits to granting licenses. The view prevailed that it would not be justified to adopt 
Article 15oftheRomeConvention,becausethenewtreatyshouldbeopentoallStatesto
accede, whether or not they are party to a copyright convention, whereas this was not the case 
with the Rome Convention, to which only countries party to the Universal Copyright Convention 
may accede. 
PhC-6.3. The Conference agreed that the new treaty should not permit the establishment of a 
generalsystemofcompulsorylicensesexceptasspecifiedinArticle 6,andthatitshouldnot 
grant rights for “secondary uses” of phonograms through broadcasting and communication to 
the public.291
291 Ibid., para. 58.

===== PAGE 179 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
180 Article 7
[Savings. 1. Safeguard of Copyright and Neighboring Rights; 2. Protection for Performers; 3. Non- 
Retroactivity; 4. Substitution of the Criterion of Fixation]
(1) This Convention shall in no way be interpreted to limit or prejudice the protection 
otherwise secured to authors, to performers, to producers of phonograms or to 
broadcasting organizations under any domestic law or international agreement.
(2) It shall be a matter for the domestic law of each Contracting State to determine the 
extent, if any, to which performers whose performances are fixed in a phonogram are 
entitled to enjoy protection and the conditions for enjoying any such protection.
(3) NoContractingStateshallberequiredtoapplytheprovisionsofthisConventiontoany
phonogram fixed before this Convention entered into force with respect to that State.
(4) Any Contracting State which, on October 29, 1971, affords protection to producers of 
phonograms solely on the basis of the place of first fixation may, by a notification deposited 
with the Director General of the World Intellectual Property Organization, declare that it 
will apply this criterion instead of the criterion of the nationality of the producer.
PhC-7.1.Thesafeguardclauseinparagraph (1)isclearandself-explanatory;itdoesnotrequire
separate comments.
PhC-7.2.Inconnectionwithparagraph (2),theDiplomaticConferencedidnotadopttheproposal
of the Netherlands aimed at providing for the obligation to protect performers in such a way 
as to avoid a situation in which, if the producer of phonograms refrained from taking action 
against the infringer, the performers whose performances had been recorded would be without 
any remedy. The Conference considered that an obligation upon the producer to take action 
against the infringer, in a case where the performer shares in the receipts, should normally 
result from the contract between the producer and the performer; but it was in agreement in 
accepting that, in the case of default of the producer in the exercise of the rights deriving from 
the Convention, it is desirable that the contract be so drafted to permit the performers to take 
action directly against the infringer. 
PhC-7.3. In respect of the application in time of the Convention, the same kind of provision was 
adoptedinparagraph (3)asinArticle 20.2oftheRomeConvention.Thus,thecommentsmade
on that provision also apply here.
PhC-7.4.Thenotificationoptioninparagraph (4)issimilartothatprovidedforinArticle 17ofthe
Rome Convention.
Administrative and final clauses
TheprovisionsofArticles 8to13oftheConventioncontaintheusualadministrativeprovisions
and final clauses of WIPO treaties. They are self-explanatory and do not raise real interpretation 
questions.Therefore,commentsaremadeonlyonthosethatshowsomespecificityinthe 
context of the Convention.
Article 8 
[Secretariat]
(1) The International Bureau of the World Intellectual Property Organization shall 
assemble and publish information concerning the protection of phonograms. Each 
Contracting State shall promptly communicate to the International Bureau all new laws

PART II. Guides to the Older Generation of Related Rights Treaties – the Rome Convention, the Phonograms Convention and the Brussels, or Satellites, Convention
Convention Relating to the Distribution of Programme-carrying Signals 
Transmitted by Satellite (Brussels, or Satellites, Convention), 1974
[Preamble]292
The Contracting States,
Aware that the use of satellites for the distribution of programme-carrying signals is rapidly 
growing both in volume and geographical coverage;
Concerned that there is no world-wide system to prevent distributors from distributing 
programme-carrying signals transmitted by satellite which were not intended for those 
distributors, and that this lack is likely to hamper the use of satellite communications;
Recognizing, in this respect, the importance of the interests of authors, performers, producers 
of phonograms and broadcasting organizations;
Convinced that an international system should be established under which measures would be 
provided to prevent distributors from distributing programme-carrying signals transmitted by 
satellite which were not intended for those distributors;
Conscious of the need not to impair in any way international agreements already in force, 
including the International Telecommunication Convention and the Radio Regulations 
annexed to that Convention, and in particular in no way to prejudice wider acceptance of the 
Rome Convention of October 26, 1961, which affords protection to performers, producers of 
phonograms and broadcasting organizations,
Have agreed as follows:
SC-Pr.1. The first two paragraphs of the Preamble describe the reasons for which this Convention 
becamenecessaryandtheobjectivestobeachievedbyit.Thethirdparagraph referstothe 
interests the Convention is supposed to serve (even if, as discussed below in the comments to 
Article 2,theConventiondoesnotgrantspecificintellectualpropertyrights).Finally,thefifth 
paragraph referstotwoconventionsthatplayaroleintheregulationofactivitiesrelatedtothe
transmission of program-carrying signals. The International Telecommunication Convention 
and the Radio Regulations annexed to that Convention define and regulate the various forms 
of telecommunication, while the Rome Convention grants protection for three categories of 
beneficiaries and specifically for broadcasting organizations, to whom the prevention of “signal 
piracy” was particularly important.
SC-Pr.2.ThequestionmayberaisedwhetherthisConventionisa“specialagreement”under
Article 22oftheRomeConventionunderwhich”ContractingStatesreservetherighttoenter 
into special agreements among themselves in so far as such agreements grant to performers, 
producers of phonograms or broadcasting organizations more extensive rights than those 
granted by this Convention or contain other provisions not contrary to this Convention”. This 
questionshouldbeansweredintheaffirmative.Although,asdiscussedbelow,theSatellites 
Convention does not grant new specific rights to the beneficiaries of the Rome Convention, 
andthustheconditioninthefirstpartofArticle 22oftheRomeConventionisnotfulfilled, 
itcorrespondstothesecond–alternative–condition,sinceitcontains“otherprovisionsnot
contrary to the [Rome] Convention”; provisions which, despite not granting specific rights, 
serve the interests of the beneficiaries of the Rome Convention, and in particular broadcasting 
organizations. The provisions of the Satellites Convention certainly are not contrary to the Rome 
Convention (or, in fact, to the Berne Convention, and thus, if its indirect relevance for copyright 
isconsidered,italsosatisfiesthesimilarconditionsinArticle 20ofthatConventionconcerning 
“special agreements”).
292 The text of the Convention, as adopted and signed, does not contain titles. In the present guide to the Convention 
thosetitlesareincludedatthePreambleandeacharticle tofacilitatetheiridentificationwhichappearinthe Records of 
the International Conference of States on the Distribution of Programme-Carrying Signals Transmitted by Satellite, Brussels, 
6–21 May 1974(Paris:UNESCO–WIPO,1977)(hereinafter: Records of the 1974 Brussels Diplomatic Conference).

184 Article 1 
[Definitions]
For the purposes of this Convention:
(i) “signal” is an electronically-generated carrier capable of transmitting programmes; 
(ii) “programme” is a body of live or recorded material consisting of images, sounds or 
both, embodied in signals emitted for the purpose of ultimate distribution;
(iii) “satellite” is any device in extraterrestrial space capable of transmitting signals;
(iv) “emitted signal” or “signal emitted” is any programme-carrying signal that goes to or 
passes through a satellite;
(v) “derived signal” is a signal obtained by modifying the technical characteristics of the 
emitted signal, whether or not there have been one or more intervening fixations;
(vi) “originating organization” is the person or legal entity that decides what programme 
the emitted signals will carry;
(vii) “distributor” is the person or legal entity that decides that the transmission of the 
derived signals to the general public or any section thereof should take place;
(viii) “distribution” is the operation by which a distributor transmits derived signals to the 
general public or any section thereof.
SC-1.1. Considering that the Convention contains only very few operative norms, the definitions 
arequitenumerous.Thiswasnecessitatedbythespecifictechnologicalaspectsoftheissues 
covered by the Convention. The 1974 Brussels Diplomatic Conference, where the delegations 
included leading communications experts, tried to make the definitions and the use of 
terminology as technically accurate as possible, and in certain cases drew wording directly 
from the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) Radio Regulations. Nevertheless, it was 
agreed as a principle of drafting that, since the purpose of the Convention was fundamentally 
a juridical one, the terms used and their definitions should be made to serve legal objectives 
rather than conform to definitional standards developed for technical purposes.
Signal
SC-1.2. The term “signal” is intended to mean the electronic vector or “carrier” capable of 
transmitting a program from its point of origin. As long as a signal has the potential capacity of 
transmitting programs, it makes no difference what electronic means or combination of means 
are used to generate it.293
Program
SC-1.3. The report of the Diplomatic Conference describes the role of programs in the following way: 
The Brussels Convention deals with signals and not the messages those signals carry; as 
was often said, the subject of the treaty is the container and not the content. But the scope 
of the Convention is limited to those signals that carry ‘programmes’ and, as defined, this 
item refers to bodies of material put together for transmission through a satellite to the 
general public.294 
The definition makes clear that a program may be either live or recorded or a combination 
of both.
293 Records of the 1974 Brussels Diplomatic Conference , para. 63.
294 Ibid., para. 64.

===== PAGE 184 =====
185
PART II. Guides to the Older Generation of Related Rights Treaties – the Rome Convention, the Phonograms Convention and the Brussels, or Satellites, Convention
SC-1.4. There was a debate at the Diplomatic Conference on whether the Convention should 
be limited to television signals (“images or a combination of sounds and images”) or should 
also cover sound broadcasting as well (“images, sounds or both”). From the beginning of 
the preparatory work, the basic declared purpose of the Convention was to combat piracy of 
television transmissions by satellite. Since satellite transmissions of radio programming were 
rare and lacked a realistic economic basis, and since the ITU Convention seemed to be sufficient 
to deal with them, it was argued that programs consisting of sounds alone should not be 
included in the definition. However, a great many delegations argued the contrary view, and the 
Conference finally decided in favor of a broader definition. 295 
Satellite
SC-1.5. Since the 1974 Brussels Diplomatic Conference, the role and significance of satellites in 
telecommunication and broadcasting have become so obvious that now this definition does not 
seem necessary anymore. The report specifies that the word “extraterrestrial” in the definition 
means that, for at least a part of its orbit, the satellite must be located outside the earth’s 
atmosphere. It adds that the definition is not intended to exclude satellites like those in elliptical 
orbit that pass through the earth’s atmosphere during part of their orbital path. 296
Emitted signal and derived signal
SC-1.6. During the preparatory work of the Convention, it was accepted as a general principle 
that, as long as it was still possible to derive a message from it, a signal remained the same 
signalnomatterhowmanytimesitwasamplified,modulated,changedinfrequency,recorded,
re-recorded, or otherwise changed in its physical characteristics. Nevertheless, it was found 
desirable to differentiate between three different stages in the “life” of a signal: (i) emission; 
(ii) derivation; and (iii) distribution. The signal in its first two stages is defined separately in 
items(iv)and(v)ofArticle 1,whilethethird,“distributedsignal”,iscontainedinthedefinitionof 
“distribution” in item (viii).
SC-1.7. In the Nairobi text297 the term “emitted signal” was adopted, which meant a signal 
transmitted to a satellite, or that passes through a satellite. This concept was then further 
developed in complicated phrasing which distinguished between (i) emitted signals, (ii) signals 
derived from emitted signals, (iii) signals derived from fixations of emitted signals, and (iv) 
signals derived from signals derived from fixations of emitted signals. Considering this list, 
it is no surprise that the report of the Diplomatic Conference reviewed it thus: “No one was 
sure exactly what this meant, much less whether it covered all the possibilities”. 298 Thus an 
understandable desire emerged to simplify and clarify the text.
SC-1.8. A new term was adopted to cover several of the previously identified categories. This term 
was “derived signal”, which meant any signal whose physical characteristics have been modified 
insomewayfortechnicalrequirements,regardlessofhowmanytimesthemodificationshave
taken place or how many intervening fixations or duplications of fixations have been made.
SC-1.9. According to the finally adopted definitions, the term “emitted signal” covers any signal 
that travels to a satellite (the “up-link”) and any signal that passes through a satellite and is 
beamed back down to earth (the “down-link”). As soon as the signal has passed through the 
satellite, it is regarded as a “derived signal”, since technically it is necessary to change the 
signal’s physical characteristics to transmit it back to the earth without interference. Thus on the 
down-linkandthereafter,thesignalinfactqualifiesasbothan“emitted”anda“derived”signal. 
All this reflects the technology which existed at the time of the preparation and adoption of 
the Convention.

186 Originating organization
SC-1.10.Thedefinitionof“originatingorganization”–“thepersonorlegalentitythatdecides
whatprogrammetheemittedsignalswillcarry”–isclearandself-explanatory.Itisintendedto 
exclude telecommunications authorities and common carriers which exercise no control over 
what programs signals carry. The report of the Diplomatic Conference notes that the definition 
of “originating organization” is also intended to exclude the creators and producers of programs 
as such, because their control is over the content of programs, not the signals. 299
Distributor and distribution
SC-1.11. Obviously, the concept of “distribution” is the most important one in the Convention, 
since this is the act that Contracting States are obligated to prevent under certain circumstances. 
The decisive element in the concept of ”distribution” is that there must be a transmission of 
program-carrying signals “to the general public or any section thereof”. The “distributor” is the 
natural or legal person with ultimate decision-making responsibility in the distribution process.
SC-1.12. As the report of the Diplomatic Conference stresses, a transmission constitutes 
“distribution” under the Convention whether it is made simultaneously with the original emission to 
the satellite or from a fixation. The definition was regarded as broad enough to cover any existing 
or future telecommunications methods for transmitting signals, including not only traditional forms 
of broadcasting, but also transmission by cable or other fixed communications channels, laser 
transmission, and transmission by direct broadcasting satellites.300 The report also clarifies that 
Article 3,whichexcludesfromthescopeoftheConventionre-transmissionsofsignalstakenfrom
directbroadcasting satellites, does not affect the obligation of a Contracting State to prevent the 
distribution by means of a directbroadcast satellite (DBS), by an unintended distributor, of signals 
received from an “ordinary” (“point-to-point” or “distribution”) satellite. In other words, where the 
signals are transmitted from a DBS, their distribution is outside the coverage of the Convention by 
virtueofArticle 3,butwherethesignalsarereceivedfromanothertypeofsatellite,itisforbidden
for unintended distributors to retransmit them, even if they are using a DBS for the purpose.
SC-1.13. The concept of “distribution” under the Satellites Convention differs from the concept of 
“distribution” applied in the field of copyright and related rights. The latter basically means making 
available of copies –astangibleobjects–ofworksorsubjectmatterofrelatedrightstothepublic.
Article 2
[Scope of the Convention]
(1) EachContractingStateundertakestotakeadequatemeasurestopreventthe
distribution on or from its territory of any programme-carrying signal by any 
distributor for whom the signal emitted to or passing through the satellite is not 
intended. This obligation shall apply where the originating organization is a national of 
another Contracting State and where the signal distributed is a derived signal.
(2) In any Contracting State in which the application of the measures referred to in 
paragraph (1)islimitedintime,thedurationthereofshallbefixedbyitsdomesticlaw.
The Secretary-General of the United Nations shall be notified in writing of such duration 
at the time of ratification, acceptance or accession, or if the domestic law comes into 
force or is changed thereafter, within six months of the coming into force of that law or of 
its modification.
(3) Theobligationprovidedforinparagraph (1)shallnotapplytothedistributionof
derived signals taken from signals which have already been distributed by a distributor 
for whom the emitted signals were intended.

Subject matter and obligation
SC-2.1.Paragraph (1)ofArticle 2isanimportantprovisionbecauseitincorporatesthecontent
of the “Nairobi compromise”. The essence of the compromise was that, instead of granting 
broadcasting organizations an exclusive right of authorization with respect to distribution of 
signals transmitted by satellite, the Convention imposed an obligation on Contracting States to 
“takeadequatemeasurestopreventthedistributiononorfromitsterritoryofanyprogramme-
carrying signal by any distributor for whom the signal emitted to or passing through the 
satellite is not intended”.
SC-2.2. The report of the Diplomatic Conference states the understanding that the Contracting 
Statesarefreetoimplementthisbasicrequirementinanywaytheyseefit:“whiletheobligation
of the Convention might well be undertaken within the legal framework of intellectual property 
laws granting protection to signals under theories of copyright or neighbouring rights, a 
Contracting State could just as rightly adopt administrative measures, penal sanctions, or 
telecommunications laws or regulations on the subject”. 301
SC-2.3. The decisive factor for determining whether distribution must be prevented is whether 
the signal is intended for the distributor. In this context it was emphasized that “[w]hile it was 
true that the originating organization would often be the one making the decision as to the 
distributors for whom the signals were intended, this did not imply the creation of any economic 
rights under the Convention”.302
SC-2.4. The phrase “on or from its territory” means that there is an obligation of a Contracting State 
to prevent piratical transmission from a sending station located on its territory, even where the 
members of the public for whom the transmission is intended are entirely outside its territory.
SC-2.5. It was observed during the debates that the phrase “emitted to or passing through a 
satellite” could probably be deleted as a technical factor, but the Conference decided that, since 
paragraph (1)ofArticle 2isthebasicprovisionintheConvention,itshouldstateexplicitlythe
nature of the signals it deals with rather than only relying upon definitions which reflect this. It 
was made doubly clear that the Convention applies not only to poaching at the down-link end 
of a transmission or thereafter, but at any point on the up-link or down-link or from the storage 
unit of the satellite itself.
Duration of measures
SC-2.6. From the earliest beginnings of the preparatory work, opinion was divided as to whether 
a minimum limit should be fixed to the length of time a Contracting State must take the 
measuresrequired.AttheNairobimeeting,becauseofthefundamentalchangeinphilosophy,
additionalquestionswereraisedastowhetheraprovisionestablishingaminimumterm
remained appropriate, since the treaty was no longer based on private rights.
SC-2.7. In the debates, those favoring the retention of a minimum term argued that, without it, 
the Convention could be interpreted either as imposing a permanent obligation with respect 
to signals that have been recorded, or as presenting the opposite danger, namely, that States 
mightregardtheirobligationtotake“adequatemeasures”asfulfilledshortlyafterthesatellite
emission.AnumberofdelegationsurgedcompletedeletionoftheArticle onthegroundthata
provision creating a minimum term would be inconsistent with a treaty that does not carry any 
obligation to protect private property rights and that leaves States free to decide which is the 
most effective means to prevent distribution of satellite signals by unintended distributors. It was 
also pointed out that, although a specified minimum term may be relevant when it comes to the 
program content of a signal, it is difficult to apply it logically if only a signal as such is involved.
SC-2.8. After a very long debate, with several proposals and counter-proposals tabled, and 
withthedelegationsmoreorlessequallydividedonthisissue,finally,paragraph (2)was
adopted as a compromise text combined with a formal agreed statement included in the 
301 Ibid., para. 79.
302 Ibid., para. 80.

===== PAGE 187 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
188 report of the Conference which reads: “With respect to the duration of the measures referred 
toinArticle 1(1),itwasgenerallyconsideredthataperiodoftwentyyears could constitute a 
reasonable period”.303
Signals already distributed by intended distributors
SC-2.9.ThebasicconsiderationbehindArticle 2(3)isthattheConventionisintendedtodeal
primarily with space communications, and it is not to apply to situations that are essentially 
terrestrial. Therefore, if an unintended distributor derives the signals from an intended 
terrestrial distributor, the fact that the signals are emitted through a satellite does not make the 
Convention applicable. Such an act is rebroadcasting, which is covered by the Rome Convention. 
It was considered necessary to clarify that the new treaty does not cover such a situation. Of 
course, if none of the distributors along the line is intended to receive the signals emitted to or 
through the satellite, the situation is different and the Convention applies.
Article 3
[Distribution of Signals from Direct Broadcasting Satellites]
This Convention shall not apply where the signals emitted by or on behalf of the originating 
organization are intended for direct reception from the satellite by the general public.
SC-3.1. At the Diplomatic Conference, the delegation of Algeria proposed the exclusion from the 
scope of the Convention the distribution of signals taken from direct broadcast satellites. As was 
explained during the debate, a DBS system can be described as a service in which a broadcaster, 
instead of using an aerial located on the earth’s surface, uses an aerial located on a satellite in 
space with a very powerful transmitter capable of sending signals directly to individual receiving 
sets on the earth. Thus, in the context of the treaty, the originating organization and the 
distributor are one and the same, since no further distribution is needed to pick up signals from 
the satellite and send them on.
SC-3.2.Thisideawassupportedbyotherdelegations;thusArticle 3expresslyexcludesfrom 
the scope of the Convention signals that are “emitted by or on behalf of the originating 
organization” and are “intended for direct reception from the satellite by the general public”. The 
reference to the originating organization is needed to make clear that the exclusion does not go 
so far as to exempt the activities of a pirate distributor using a DBS system for distribution of 
conventional satellite signals.
SC-3.3. It followed from this limitation of the coverage of the Convention that relatively few 
countries acceded to it, and thus its relevance has substantially decreased. It does not apply to 
directbroadcastingsatellites,and,sinceitsadoption–withtheincreaseinthecapacityandpower
oftelecommunicationsatellitesandthegrowingcapacityofdevicestoreceivesignalsdirectly–an
increasing number of satellites have fallen outside the scope of the Convention. This trend became 
evenmoresignificantwiththeclarificationinArticle 2(f)oftheWPPTthatthetransmissionof
programs for reception by the public by wireless means by (direct broadcasting) satellite is also 
“broadcasting” in the sense of the right of broadcasting (and not mere telecommunication). 
Article 4 
[Exceptions]
NoContractingStateshallberequiredtoapplythemeasuresreferredtoinArticle 2(1)
where the signal distributed on its territory by a distributor for whom the emitted signal is 
not intended
(i) carries short excerpts of the programme carried by the emitted signal, consisting of 
reports of current events, but only to the extent justified by the informatory purpose 
of such excerpts, or

(ii) carries,asquotations,shortexcerptsoftheprogrammecarriedbytheemittedsignal,
providedthatsuchquotationsarecompatiblewithfairpracticeandarejustifiedbythe
informatorypurposeofsuchquotations,or
(iii) carries, where the said territory is that of a Contracting State regarded as a developing

distribution is solely for the purpose of teaching, including teaching in the framework 
of adult education, or scientific research.
SC-4.1.Duetothethoroughpreparatorywork,Article 4wasadoptedwithlittledebateandno
substantive changes. The discussion of these provisions at the Diplomatic Conference consisted 
mainlyofstatementsapprovingthecontentof,andthebalanceachievedby,theArticle asdrafted.
SC-4.2. The Conference accepted the following interpretative statement included in the report:
Underparagraph (i),shortexcerptsofacontestorspectaclecouldbedistributedifthe
genuine purpose was the reporting of a newsworthy event, but only to the extremely brief 
extent ‘justified by the informatory purpose’. To warrant the use of a short excerpt under 
this provision, the programming must be done as part of a report of general news of the 
day and would therefore, as a rule, have to be transmitted on the basis of a fixation. The 
possibilitiesofdistributingalloranypartofasportingeventunderparagraph (iii)seemto
be even more limited, since the sole purpose of the distribution must be teaching.304
SC-4.3. The meaning of “teaching, including teaching in the framework of adult education” as used 
initem(iii)ofArticle 4wasalsoclarified.ThedelegationoftheUnitedStatessuggestedthatthe
Conference interpret the term in a general way to include any kind of “systematic instructional 
activities”. The report of the Conference contains the following statements on this issue: 
This phrase, which also appears in the 1971 texts of both the Berne and Universal 
Copyright Conventions, includes all conventional forms of teaching at every level of 
educational and instructional television as distinguished from general programming that 
is cultural or informational in character. At the final plenary session it was agreed that the 
Conference as a whole should adopt this interpretation of the phrase.305
SC-4.4. An important point was also emphasized several times during the debates at the 
Conference,withspecificreferencetoArticle 4:theexceptionsallowedintheConvention 
haveapplicabilityonlywithrespecttothemeasuresthataStateisrequiredtotakeunder
the Convention itself. If the State has obligations under another treaty, such as the copyright 
conventions, the Rome Convention or the ITU Convention, those are not superseded by the 
exceptionsinArticle 4. 306
Article 5
[Non-retroactivity]
NoContractingStateshallberequiredtoapplythisConventionwithrespecttoanysignal
emitted before this Convention entered into force for that State.
SC-5.1.ThisArticle ispatternedonArticle 7(3)ofthePhonogramsConvention.Asthereportof
the Diplomatic Conference indicates, “[i]t means that, unless a Contracting State chooses to 
provide otherwise, the entry into force of the Convention in that particular State does not alter 
the legal status of signals that have already been emitted to a satellite”. 307
304 Ibid., para. 109.

190 Article 6
[Safeguard of Interests of Contributors to Programs]
This Convention shall in no way be interpreted to limit or prejudice the protection secured to 
authors, performers, producers of phonograms, or broadcasting organizations, under any 
domestic law or international agreement.
SC-6.1.Article 6wasconsideredanintegralpartofthe“Nairobicompromise”.Itsobjective
wastomakeclearthat,underthenewtreaty,noneofthe“adequatemeasures”adoptedby
a Contracting State could be allowed to impinge in any way whatsoever upon the present or 
future rights of authors, performers, phonogram producers or broadcasting organizations, 
whether the protection of those rights derived from domestic law, from the copyright 
conventions or from the Rome Convention.
SC-6.2.AttherequestofthedelegationsofAustriaandGermany,thefollowingstatementwas 
inserted in the report of the Diplomatic Conference: 
Among the governmental experts meeting in Paris (1972) and Nairobi (1973) it was 
undisputed that where a satellite is used for the distribution of programme-carrying 
signals made directly by the satellite itself, the originating organization, even without the 
insertion of such a provision in the Convention, is responsible for the distribution vis-à-
vis the authors, performers, producers of phonograms and broadcasting organizations 
and cannot plead that the distribution was made in space and thus outside the sphere of 
application of any national law.308
SC-6.3. The Conference also considered a proposal by the delegations of Denmark and Mexico 
to impose an obligation on broadcasting organizations to notify authors, performers, and other 
contributors to programs, in advance of a satellite broadcast using their contributions, of the 
distributors for whom the program-carrying signals were intended. The obligation would have 
arisen only in the case of the contributions protected against broadcasting in the Contracting 
State to which the broadcasting organization belonged, and it was also suggested that it might 
be made applicable only when the parties had not agreed otherwise. The Main Commission of 
the Conference, which discussed the proposal, expressed unanimous appreciation for the spirit 
behind this idea. Several delegations supported the proposal, and there was also widespread 
support for the general principle involved; namely, that, where the law of a broadcaster’s 
country recognizes broadcasting rights in a contribution to a program being transmitted by 
satellite, the contributors or their representatives should be able to know in advance where 
the signals carrying the program are intended to go, at least in cases where the contributors 
have not previously transferred or waived their rights. There was, however, opposition to the 
specific proposal on grounds that: (i) it would create insuperable practical difficulties in certain 
countries because of their legal framework or business or labor practices; (ii) even if not directly 
inconsistent with the compromise achieved in Nairobi, the proposal could upset the new balance 
of interests established under that compromise; and (iii) by limiting itself to an obligation to give 
advance notice, the proposal might adversely affect exclusive rights to control broadcasting 
already held by contributors under other international conventions. The proposal was therefore 
withdrawn on the understanding that the principle on which it was based, and the useful 
discussion of it, should be reflected in the report. 309

This Convention shall in no way be interpreted as limiting the right of any Contracting State to 
apply its domestic law in order to prevent abuses of monopoly.

Article 8 
[Reservations]
(1) Subject to paragraphs (2) and (3), no reservation to this Convention shall be permitted.
(2) Any Contracting State whose domestic law, on May 21, 1974, so provides may, by

(3) (a)  Any Contracting State which, on May 21, 1974, limits or denies protection with

United Nations, declare that, to the extent that and as long as its domestic law 
limits or denies protection, it will not apply this Convention to such distributions.
(b) AnyStatethathasdepositedanotificationinaccordancewithsubparagraph (a)
shall notify the Secretary- General of the United Nations in writing, within six 
months of their coming into force, of any changes in its domestic law whereby 
thereservationunderthatsubparagraph becomesinapplicableormorelimited
in scope.
SC-8.1. Although the Diplomatic Conference adopted the general principle reflected in 
paragraph (1),itfounditnecessarytoallowreservationsintwocases.
SC-8.2.Paragraph (2)wasinsertedbecause,underArticle 2(1),thenationalityoftheoriginating 
organization is provided as the sole criterion for the applicability of the Convention. The 
possibility of reservation was found necessary to deal with the situation in a few countries 
whose laws are based on the criterion of the place from which the signals are emitted.
SC-8.3.Paragraph (3)servesthetaskofreconcilingtheConventionwiththedomesticlawof
a few countries under which retransmissions of broadcasts to subscribers of wire and cable 
systems are considered to fall outside the control of the copyright owners. It was recognized 
that a provision allowing reservations on this point was needed to achieve widespread

Introduction to the Guides
From “guided development” of copyright to new binding norms
In Part I, the Introduction to the Guide to the Berne Convention outlines how the international 
copyright community tried to respond to the challenges of the new technological and social 
developments on the basis of the existing treaties, first and foremost the Berne Convention, in the 
form of model provisions, guided principles and the like. By the end of the 1980s, however, it had 
become clear that the non-binding soft-law solutions elaborated in that “guided development” 
period were insufficient. This was, first, because piracy was becoming an ever more dangerous 
phenomenon and the “toothless” WIPO conventions312 did not offer efficient means to combat 
it; and, second, because, as a result of the reaction of national legislators to the spectacular 
technological developments, the differences among national norms which had existed before 
began getting closer to the core elements of the copyright system (including the categories of 
works protected and rights granted). The preparatory work on new binding norms was initiated 
in the framework of the Uruguay Round of negotiations in the General Agreement on Tariffs and 
Trade (GATT), on the one hand, and in committees of governmental experts at WIPO, on the other 
hand, at more or less the same time.
GATT Uruguay Round of negotiations and the adoption of the TRIPS Agreement
The Uruguay Round of Multilateral Trade Negotiations of GATT (hereafter for the purpose of 
this Guide: the the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS 
Agreement) negotiations) was launched in Punta del Este, Uruguay, in September 1986, where the 
Ministerial Conference included in the agenda, inter alia, the following item: “trade-related aspects 
of intellectual property rights, including trade in counterfeit goods” which was described as follows:
In order to reduce the distortions and impediments to international trade, and taking into 
accounttheneedtopromoteeffectiveandadequateprotectionofintellectualproperty
rights, and to ensure that measures and procedures to enforce intellectual property rights 
do not themselves become barriers to legitimate trade, the negotiations shall aim to 
clarify GATT provisions and elaborate as appropriate new rules and disciplines.
Negotiations shall aim to develop a multilateral framework of principles, rules and 
disciplines dealing with international trade in counterfeit goods, taking into account work 
already undertaken in GATT.
These negotiations shall be without prejudice to other complementary initiatives that 
may be taken in the World Intellectual Property Organization and elsewhere to deal with 
these matters.313
312 UnderArticle 33(1)oftheBerneConventiontheonlypossiblewaytosettleadisputeistobringthecasebeforethe 
InternationalCourtofJustice.Thatforum,however,ratherservesasaforumbetweenvariouscountriestodealwith 
important political issues such as territorial disputes; it has not been found appropriate to solve copyright disputes; 
therefore, it has never been used in practice for such purposes.
313 DocumentMIN.DECdated20September1986,7–8.

===== PAGE 194 =====

PART III. Guides to the three WIPO “Internet Treaties” – the WCT, the WPPT and the BTAP
In the course of the TRIPS negotiations, the interpretation of the terms of reference also began 
to change. Up until the “mid-term” meetings to review the negotiation process, held in Montreal 
in December 1988 and then continued in Geneva in April 1989, the delegations’ positions on the 
coverage of a future agreement, the level of details to be settled and the relationship between 
the new agreement and the WIPO-administered conventions had differed greatly. And yet, the 
documentsadoptedinApril1989werealreadybasedonaquitebroadinterpretationofthe
mandate, on the basis of which the way was opened to extend the negotiations and the coverage 
of a future agreement to more or less all substantive aspects of intellectual property and also to 
enforcement of rights and dispute settlement.314 In March 1990, the European Community (EC)315 
submitted a “Draft Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property” in full harmony 
with the above-mentioned extensive interpretation of the terms of reference.316 This was followed 
by a similarly structured draft agreement tabled by the United States,317 and a number of other 
proposalsand/orcommentsfromSwitzerland,Japanandfromdevelopingcountries.318
Intensive negotiations started on these texts, the success of which depended, to a great extent, 
on the outcome of the negotiations about the numerous, and economically more important, 
other issues on the packed agenda of the Uruguay Round. The first really tangible result of the 
negotiationswasthetextpreparedasthe“Chairman’sdraft",inJune1990.Theconsultationsand
negotiationsspectacularlyaccelerated;increasinglycontradictoryvariantsandsquarebrackets
disappeared from the text, so much so that, by the time the Brussels Ministerial Conference took 
place in December 1990 (where an unsuccessful attempt was made to conclude the Uruguay Round 
inrespectofallissues)onlyveryfewquestionsremainedopen,and,infact,itwasnotduetothese
openquestionsinthedraftTRIPSAgreement,butrathertotheabsenceofagreementsinother
negotiation groups, that the Brussels Conference was unable to produce the desired final results.
The negotiations continued on the couple of still open issues in the TRIPS Negotiation Group 
with step-by-step progress, although the attention turned to the other negotiation groups. As 
a result of some new compromise solutions, it was possible to include an “option-free” “draft 
TRIPS Agreement” into the “Dunkel text", named for the then Director General of GATT and 
officially entitled “Draft Final Act Embodying the Results of the Uruguay Round of Multilateral 
Trade Negotiations". There were still some last efforts to introduce certain changes in the 
text, but, in December 1992, the TRIPS Agreement, in substance, reached the form in which 
it was then signed in Marrakesh in April 1994 along with the World Trade Organization (WTO) 
Agreement and the covered agreements 319 as its annexes.
As regards the protection of copyright and related rights, the most important new aspects 
of the TRIPS Agreement were the detailed regulation of the obligations of WTO Members 
concerning the enforcement of intellectual property rights in Part III and the extension of the 
WTO dispute-settlement mechanism to those rights. In contrast, as regards the substantive 
provisions–thosewhichdeterminethesubjectmatterandbasicconditionsofprotection,the 
minimum rights to be granted, the permissible exceptions to and limitations on rights, the term 
ofprotection,etc.–theAgreementdidnotbringaboutmanynewelements.
Concerningcopyright,theobligationsarebasedonthesubstantiveprovisions(Articles 1to 
21andtheAppendix)oftheBerneConvention,whichareincludedbyreference(Article 9.1;in
which, however, it is provided that the WTO Members “shall not have rights or obligations under 
theAgreementinrespectoftherightsconferredunderArticle 6 bis of [the Berne] Convention

Agreement and Treaties Administered by WIPO” 321preparedinOctober1996attherequestof
the General Assembly of the Organization.
Preparatory work for a “Berne Protocol” and a “New Instrument”
AtWIPO,theprojectofsettingnewcopyrightnormswaslaunchedattheSeptember–October
1989 sessions of the Organization’s governing bodies, that is, in a period when, after the Montreal 
and Geneva “midterm” meetings, the TRIPS negotiations were becoming more intensive, and 
thepossibilityofatrulysubstantiveagreementwasemerging.The1990–91programofWIPO
adopted at that session of the governing bodies included, inter alia, the following item:
The International Bureau will prepare, convene and service a committee of governmental 
experts in one or more meetings in order to examine whether the preparation of a protocol 
totheBerneConventionfortheProtectionofLiteraryandArtisticWorksshouldstart,and–
ifso–withwhatcontent,withaviewtosubmittingforadoptionthedraftofsuchaprotocol
to a Diplomatic Conference after 1991. The protocol would be mainly destined to clarify the 
existing, or establish new, international norms where, under the present text of the Berne 
Convention, doubts may exist as to the extent to which that Convention applies.
Theneedforsuchanexerciseliesinthefactthattherearecertainquestionsinrespect
of which professional circles have no uniform views and, what is of particular concern in 
international relations, even governments which legislated or plan to legislate on such 
questionsseemtointerprettheirobligationsundertheBerneConventiondifferently.
Such discrepancies in views already surfaced, or are likely to surface in the near future, in 
respect of certain subject matters of protection (e.g., computer programs, phonograms, 
computer-generated works), certain rights (e.g., right of rental, public lending right, right 
of distribution of copies of any kind of works, right of display), the applicability of the 
minima (no formalities, term of protection, etc.) and the obligation of granting national 
treatment (without reciprocity) to foreigners. In this connection, it will also be examined 
whether countries whose national law protects subject matters as works under their 
copyright law, or recognizes the protection of certain rights in their copyright law, may 
refuse the application of the minima or the granting of national treatment to foreigners 
or make the protection of foreign works or the application of certain rights to foreigners 
dependent on reciprocity.322
The legal nature of the would-be “protocol” had not been precisely determined. It was the 
working document prepared for the first session of the Committee of Experts on a Possible 
Protocol to the Berne Convention (hereinafter the Berne Protocol Committee) convened in 
November 1991 that tried to offer a substantive interpretation:

The expression “protocol” (to the Berne Convention) is used tentatively. Whether the 
new instrument, if any, will be called a protocol or by another name (for example, 
“Treaty Supplementing the Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic 
Works”) is not yet decided. In any case, the new instrument would be a multilateral treaty 
underArticle 20oftheBerneConvention,whichprovidesthat“[t]heGovernmentsof
the countries of the [Berne] Union reserve the right to enter into special agreements 
among themselves, in so far as such agreements grant to authors more extensive rights 
than those granted by the Convention, or contain other provisions not contrary to this 
Convention.”Inotherwords,thenewinstrument–thatfromhereonwardsiscalleda
Protocol–couldnotcontainprovisionsthatwoulddiminishtherightsofauthorsexisting
under the Berne Convention.323
At the first session of the Committee, there was no opposition to this interpretation. 
Nevertheless, several delegations suggested that the issue of the legal nature of the new 
instrument should be further studied and should not be decided upon yet. 324 Later, there was 
increasingagreementonaspecial-agreementapproach;andtheproposedtreaty–whichwas 
finallynamedtheWIPOCopyrightTreaty(WCT)–wasadoptedassuch.
Atthefirstsession,theBerneProtocolCommitteeelectedaChairman,JukkaLiedesofFinland, 
whothenwasre-electedatallthesubsequentsessionsoftheCommittee,andalsoelectedand 
re-elected at all the sessions of the so-called New Instrument Committee (see below), then was 
requestedtopreparethebasicproposalsforthe1996DiplomaticConference,andwaselected
there as the Chairman of Main Committee I. He played a decisive role in the success of the 
Conference and in the adoption of the two “Internet Treaties".
AtthesessionsoftheWIPOCommittee,referencewasmadequitefrequentlytotheongoing
TRIPS negotiations. The delegations preferred to slow down the work at WIPO to avoid any 
undesirable interference with, and impact on, the very complex negotiations in the framework 
of the Uruguay Round. Due to this, the work of the first two sessions of the Berne Protocol 
Committee325 only consisted in a kind of first reading with, at most, an attempt to identify the 
issues that might be addressed in a possible protocol.
At the first two sessions of the Committee, the most passionate debate took place on the issue 
of whether or not sound recordings might really be covered by a possible protocol to the Berne 
Convention. All the delegations that took the floor agreed that the rights of producers of sound 
recordings should enjoy strong intellectual property protection, duly adapted to new technological 
developments.326Viewsdiffered,however,astowhichwayandintheframeworkofwhatkind
of instrument the modernization of the protection of these rights should take place. Several 
delegations were in favor of sound recordings being included, and they saw no problem with the 
new instrument’s addressing certain issues concerning both copyright and related rights.327 One 
group of delegations was open to any solution for either joint or parallel provisions on copyright 
and related rights.328 A great number of delegations insisted, however, that the new provisions on 
the rights of producers of phonograms be adopted separately from copyright, since recordings 
were not works within the meaning of the Berne Convention. They stressed that only in that way 
could an appropriate balance be maintained between copyright and related rights.329
During the first two sessions of the Berne Protocol Committee, the same working methods 
were adopted as during the “guided development” period. The working documents were 
prepared–forthemostpart,withoutanyprevioussubstantiveinputbytheMemberStates 
oftheOrganization–bytheInternationalBureauofWIPO,wherethecommittees,groupsof
consultants and working groups discussed these documents, reports were adopted, sometimes 
with some recommendations; then the International Bureau prepared new working documents 
for the next meeting and the cycle started again. At the end of the second session of the Berne

This decision was taken in a period of important progress in the TRIPS negotiations, but when 
it was still not sure how they would end. There were still differing positions on many issues, 
includingthedesirablerelationship–and“distributionoflabor“–betweenWIPOandthefuture 
organization to be established for the administration of the agreements to be adopted. All this 
was reflected in this decision of the Assembly. From that time on, it was clear that, although 
that attention was focusing on the future TRIPS Agreement, the delegations found it a realistic 
objective to adopt new binding copyright and related right norms under the aegis of WIPO.

other Committee334 –wastakingplaceinaccordancewiththeabove-quoteddecisionofthe

The emerging “digital agenda”, preparation of what became the WCT and the WPPT
After the adoption of the TRIPS Agreement in April 1994, the international copyright community 
found itself faced with a new situation. It was around the time of the de facto finalization of the 
text of the TRIPS Agreement in December 1992 that the Internet started its really breathtaking 
career. By the time of the adoption of the Agreement, the application of digital technology 
andthequickexpansionoftheglobalinformationnetworkhadraisedweightynewissuesfor 
copyright and related rights. They had been addressed in national and regional studies and at 
WIPO brainstorming conferences, and they had also appeared as issues to be dealt with by the 
Berne Protocol and New Instrument Committees, where together they became the so-called 
“digital agenda” of the preparatory work. It was not a realistic idea to try to reopen negotiations 
on copyright and related rights in the WTO; therefore, the two WIPO Committees were the 
logicalalternativeforumstotrytogiveresponsestotheurgentquestionsposedbythese 
technological developments. The preparatory work was accelerated and became more effective.
A number of studies were prepared in various countries and regional integration bodies. 
Those which had the most substantive impact in the preparatory work were presented by the 
delegations of the United States, 335 the European Community336andJapan337 at the first joint 
meetings of the Berne Protocol and New Instrument Committees in September 1995 and copies 
were made available to all delegations.
The WIPO brainstorming conferences also greatly contributed to a thorough review of the 
challenges of online digital technology and to the outlining of possible solutions. These were 
worldwide events, in which a great number of representatives of governments, experts of non-
governmental organizations (NGOs), academics and technological specialists participated. WIPO 
hosted the symposia, which were truly of a worldwide nature; it also invited, at its own expense, 
government representatives of the various regions of the developing world. A compendium of 
the presentations was distributed to interested parties. Certain copyright-related issues raised 
by digital technology were touched upon at the WIPO Worldwide Symposium on Intellectual

The key preparatory work in which the “digital agenda” took the dominant role, of course, took 
place in the two Committees, which for a while held their sessions separately, but later jointly. 
While computer programs and (electronic) databases are also the results of the application of 
digital technology and the issues of their copyright protection were discussed by the Berne 
Protocol Committee and also in the “guided development” period before, they were not 
regarded as forming some kind of “digital agenda” yet. This term appeared when the use of 
digital technology and, in particular, the Internet, also extended to “traditional” categories of 
works and subject matters of related rights.
The preparatory work accelerated at the last three joint sessions of the two Committees. At the 
first of these sessions in September 1995, a breakthrough took place. 343 This was the session 
atwhichtheUnitedStates,theEuropeanCommunityandJapanpresentedtheirconcrete
proposals and the rich materials from the three worldwide symposiums held at Harvard, in Paris 
and in Mexico City were also made available. WIPO had also organized around that time the first 
wave of consultations in the three main regions of developing countries: Africa; Asia and the 
Pacific; and Latin America and the Caribbean.
A great number of proposals were submitted, and many of them concerned the “digital agenda”, 
which was identified explicitly in this way in the work program. In the reports of the joint 
sessions, the discussions on the relevant issues were also reflected under this title: “The digital 
agenda”.344AsproposedbytheChairman,JukkaLiedes,underthis“agenda”“[p]articularlythe 
questionsrelatingtoreproduction(ordistribution)bytransmissionorageneraltransmission
right, that is, the digital delivery issue, and [...] to technological protection measures and rights 
management information“ 345 were discussed. On the proposal of the European Community 
to adopt international norms on sui generis protection of databases, 346 only a preliminary 
discussion took place.347
The Committees asked the Director General of WIPO, the governments and the European 
Community to submit treaty-language proposals by the end of November 1995 for the following 
joint sessions of the Committees, and recommended that, after that session, “[t]he competent 
Governing Body of WIPO should be convened [and] the work be sufficiently advanced, to decide 
on the convocation and date of one or more Diplomatic Conferences for the conclusion of the 
appropriate treaties".348
The first joint sessions opened the way for an early Diplomatic Conference, while the second 
joint sessions held in February 1996 adopted practically all the decisions and recommendations 
that were necessary for the convocation of the Diplomatic Conference; the rest was more or less 
a mere formality. At the end of the second joint sessions, the Committees:
