204 The 1996 Diplomatic Conference and the adoption of the WCT and 
the WPPT
In December 1996, a diplomatic conference with the official title “Diplomatic Conference on 
Certain Copyright and Neighbouring Rights Questions” (CRNR/DC) was held (as per the decision 
of the Preparatory Committee and the competent WIPO governing bodies). The following 
documents were distributed to the participants:
CRNR/DC/1: Draft Agenda of the Diplomatic Conference;373
CRNR/DC/2: Draft Rules of Procedure of the Diplomatic Conference;374
CRNR/DC/3: Basic Proposal for the Administrative and Final Clauses of the Treaty to Be 
Considered by the Diplomatic Conference;375
CRNR/DC/4: Basic Proposal for the Substantive Provisions of the Treaty on Certain 
Questions concerning the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works to Be Considered by 
the Diplomatic Conference;376
CRNR/DC/5: Basic Proposal for the Substantive Provisions of the Treaty for the Protection 
of the Rights of Performers and Producers of Phonograms to Be Considered by the 
Diplomatic Conference;377
CRNR/DC/6: Basic Proposal for the Substantive Provisions of the Treaty on Intellectual 
Property in Respect of Databases to Be Considered by the Diplomatic Conference.378
Withthreedrafttreatiestobeconsidered,theDiplomaticConferencehadquiteanextensive 
agenda.Itistruethattherewasageneralfeelingthatoneofthethree–thatonsui generis 
protectionfordatabases–hadnorealisticchanceforadoptionatthisConferenceand,iftime
grewshort,mightquiteeasilybesetaside.Nevertheless,thediscussionsandnegotiationson 
theothertwo–betterprepared–drafttreatiesaloneseemedtobequiteatime-consuming 
task.Therefore,aquickstartwithrapidsettlementofalltheproceduralissueswouldhave 
been highly desirable, but it did not happen in that way. The Diplomatic Conference started 
on Monday, 2 December, in the morning, and it was unable to begin its substantive work on 
that day due to the negotiations on various procedural issues. Unfortunately, there was no 
progress on Tuesday, 3 December, either. What is more, the entire third day, Wednesday, 
4 December,wasalsousedforproceduralnegotiations;thus,about20percentofthenormal
–weekday–workingdaysofthethreeweeksoftheConferenceelapsedwiththesubstantive
issues untouched.379 There were three procedural issues that consumed so much time. First, the 
voting power of the “special delegation” of the European Community; second, the rules of the 
establishmentandcompositionofcertainbodiesoftheConferenceand,third–closelyrelated 
tothoserules–theelectionofofficers.ItwasonlyonThursday,5December,aroundnoonthat,
with the Rules of Procedure adopted and the officers elected, the Conference commenced its 
substantive work. 380
TheworkofMainCommitteeI–andwiththis,thetrulysubstantivework–startedonFriday, 
6 December,thelastdayofthefirstweekoftheConference.TheChairmansuggestedthat,first, 
the draft WCT and draft WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty (WPPT) be discussed, and 
the third draft treaty on sui generis protection for databases only later, depending on the time 
available. This was accepted without any opposition. 381
As suggested by the Chairman, the Committee proceeded with “clusters"; that is, draft 
provisions of more or less related content. Some clusters concerned only one of the two treaties, 
whileothers–andamongthemallthekeyissuesofthe“digitalagenda”,namely,therightof

at the same time. The weekend that followed was left free in order that the delegations and

on the more complex issues. From the morning of Monday, 9 December, until the morning 
of Wednesday, 11 December, however, Main Committee I was working at full speed in three 
sessions, in the morning, in the afternoon and in the evening, and it was able to complete a first 
debate on nearly all substantive provisions. 382 In the afternoon of Wednesday, 11 December, first 
the Steering Committee and then the Plenary held sessions. At the latter, the first report of the 
Credentials Committee was presented, and then the Chairman of the Plenary announced the 
decision of the Steering Committee according to which the Chairman of Main Committee I would 
produce consolidated texts of the substantive provisions of the two treaties which were to be 
discussed on the following day, Thursday, 12 December.383
As scheduled, in the afternoon on the following day, the Committee, in principle, started the 
debate on the consolidated texts, but this did not consist of much more than an explanation 
given by the Chairman.384 The delegations needed more time for consultations, and the 
followingtwodays–Friday,13December,andSaturday,14December–weresetasideforthis
purpose. On the morning of Sunday, 15 December (by now work was continued during the 
weekend, and there were also regular night sessions), Main Committee I started what was 
intended to be the final debate on, and the approval of, the texts of the draft treaties, but it did 
notgofar.Itadoptedtwoeasyparagraphs–paragraphs(2)and(3)ofArticle 1oftheWCT–and
then it found that the delegations were still not ready to proceed further. 385
The informal consultations on the substantive norms began on Sunday, 15 December in the 
afternoon,andcontinued–includinglatenightsessions–until18December.Thesesessions
were informal for various reasons: they took place in a smaller room where the atmosphere was 
much more easy-going; there were no name plates for the delegations in the usual alphabetical 
order, and the delegates belonging to the same regional groups were able to sit together and 
have sotto voce consultations even during the ongoing sessions; certain formalities concerning 
askingforandgivingthefloorandtheorderofinterventionswerenotrigidlykeptand–most
importantly–therewasanagreementthattheinterventionswouldnotberecordedandwould 
not be reflected in the minutes of the Diplomatic Conference. At the beginning, there was a 
tentative agreement that the various regional groups would be represented by a certain number 
of delegates; later, however, the consultations were made open to all interested delegations. 
Mostofthekeyissueswerediscussedduringtheseinformalconsultations–whichcouldmore
appropriatelyhavebeencallednegotiations–andcompromisesolutionswereworkedout
to solve them. The draft treaties were updated step by step as ever more issues were solved. 
These updated draft texts were then submitted to Main Committee I when it formally convened 
again.386 In certain cases, the compromise solutions also comprised agreed statements and 
it was also agreed upon at the informal consultations which delegations were to submit the 
proposed texts at the formal session of Main Committee I.
The sessions of Main Committee I which were intended to be the last ones took place on 
19 Decemberandthemorningof20December.Thecompromisesolutionsworkedoutthrough
the informal consultations were “proposed” one after the other concerning both the provisions 
of the treaties and the agreed statements related to them, and, since they had been already 
agreed upon during the informal consultations, they were adopted immediately by consensus 
without any further debate. 387
Therewerestillsomeopenquestions, 388 but then it seemed that they were also solved by noon 
on 20 December, which was the last day of the Diplomatic Conference, and what therefore 
remained was only the final polishing work, the formal adoption of the treaties by the Plenary 
and the signature ceremony.

Positive and negative impacts of the TRIPS Agreement on the preparatory work of the WIPO 
Treaties
The main features and provisions of the Treaty are discussed below in the Guide. What seems 
necessary to review in this introduction is the special relationship of the WCT (and partly of the 
WPPT) with the TRIPS Agreement.
As mentioned above, the negotiations in the Uruguay Round had a certain negative impact on the 
preparatory work in the Berne Protocol and New Instrument Committees in that the latter had to 
be slowed down in order to avoid any undesirable interference with the more complex negotiations 
in GATT. In addition to this procedural aspect, however, the TRIPS Agreement also had some 
substantive impact on the two “Internet Treaties”. It was of a double nature; partly positive and 
supportive and partly negative and restrictive. This is discussed below in detail along with the other 
complex issues of the relationship between the new treaties and the TRIPS Agreement.
By the time the preparatory work in the Berne Protocol and New Instrument Committees reached 
the decisive, final stage, the TRIPS Agreement had already been adopted and had entered into 
force. This turned out to be useful for the preparatory work concerning certain issues that 
had been more or less pending in the WIPO Committees before, but were solved in the TRIPS 
Agreement, such as the issues of the protection of computer programs393 and databases,394 the 
right of rental395 and the term of protection of the rights in performances and in phonograms.396

There was no need to negotiate these issues further; it was possible simply to transpose the 
relevant norms into the two treaties as parts of the new up-to-date international standards.
Beyond these concrete cases, the TRIPS Agreement was also helpful for providing the 
methodology of including the existing international norms in the newly adopted instruments. 
ThesubstantivenormsoftheBerneConvention–withtheexceptionofthoseonmoralrights
–wereincorporatedintotheWCTbyreferenceinthesamewayasintotheTRIPSAgreement; 397 
certain norms of the Rome Convention were included in the WPPT also more or less in the same 
way as in the TRIPS Agreement, either by reference 398 or expressly;399 furthermore, the non-
derogation clauses in the “Internet Treaties” in relation to the Berne Convention and the Rome 
Convention are also practically the same as in the TRIPS Agreement. 400
The negative impact of the TRIPS Agreement on the substantive provisions of the WCT and the 
WPPT was less important, but still it was felt in two aspects. The first aspect had its origins in 
thesamefactorsthatledtoapositiveimpact–albeitfromadifferentpointofview.Itistruethat
the adoption of some new provisions in the TRIPS Agreement facilitated the settlement, in the 
WCT and the WPPT, of the issues concerned, but this also set a limit to the scope and level of 
protection that could be granted in the new treaties. The delegations of some countries stated 
repeatedly that they were not ready to “reopen” negotiations on such issues with the possible 
consequenceofincreasingthelevelofprotection. 401 This does not mean that the wording of 
the relevant provisions was necessarily the same in the two WIPO Treaties as in the TRIPS 
Agreement; the TRIPS provisions were not included by reference in the new treaties but rather 
through the reproduction of their key elements, at times with some differences in the wording.
In the case of some of these provisions taken over from the TRIPS Agreement, the Diplomatic 
Conference adopted agreed statements clarifying that the provisions in the WIPO Treaties were 
intended to mean the same as the corresponding provisions in the TRIPS Agreement.
The other negative effect of the adoption of the TRIPS Agreement on the preparatory work 
intheWIPOCommittees–andonthecontentsofthe“InternetTreaties”–concernedthe
regulation of the enforcement of rights. As long as the final success of the TRIPS negotiations 
was not absolutely certain, there had been general support for the inclusion in the proposed 
treaties of detailed provisions on the enforcement of rights. 402 After the adoption of the TRIPS 
Agreement, this support became weaker, and finally the idea of detailed norms was dropped; 
only some very general obligations were prescribed in the WCT and the WPPT. 403 The main 
reasonforleavingoutthedetailedprovisionsonenforcementwasthatcertaindelegations– 
mainlyofindustrializedcountries–feltthatitwouldbebetterifthesegenuinelynewnorms 
were interpreted exclusively in the TRIPS context by TRIPS bodies (where the availability of the 
WTO dispute settlement mechanism was also a guarantee) without any possible interfering 
parallel interpretation that might emerge under the two WIPO Treaties.
Substantive relations of the TRIPS Agreement with the WCT and the WPPT – and their relations 
with the Berne Convention and the Rome Convention

notonlydidtheTRIPSAgreementhaveanimpactontheWIPOTreaties,but–atleastindirectly 
–possiblyalsoviceversa.SincetheexistingnormsundertheBerneConventionandtheRome
Conventionwereincluded–byreferenceorverbatim–inpracticallythesamewayintheTRIPS

208 AgreementandtheWCT,thequestionhasemergedhowthesenormsshouldbeinterpretedand
applied in the new context.
From this point of view, it seems that there is a slight difference between the inclusion of 
existing norms by a simple reference (as in the case of the substantive provisions of the Berne 
Convention and some provisions of the Rome Convention) and the incorporation of such norms 
through reproduction of the key elements (as in the case of some substantive provisions taken 
over from the Rome Convention and the three-step test “imported” from the Berne Convention 
with a scope of application broader than in the Convention).
As regards, for example, the substantive provisions of the Berne Convention included by 
referenceintheTRIPSAgreementandtheWCT(Articles 1to21alongwiththeAppendix,withthe
exception –inTRIPSonly–oftheprovisionsonmoralrights),thebasicquestioniswhetheronly
the text of those provisions should be considered to have been taken over or also some sources 
of interpretation that had emerged and developed during the “Berne life” of these provisions.
InthelightoftheprovisionsofArticles 31and32oftheViennaConventionontheLawof
Treaties(VCLT)quotedintheintroductiontothiscollectionofguides,thefundamentalquestion
concerning the provisions covered by the “Berne in TRIPS/WCT” provisions is whether the 
sourcesofinterpretationmentionedintheVCLT–the“context",thepossible“subsequent
agreements”and“subsequentpractice",the“specialmeaning”ofcertainwordsandexpressions,
“thepreparatorywork”ofthetreatiesand“thecircumstancesof[their]conclusion”–mean
the text and preparatory work of only the TRIPS Agreement and the WCT, or also of the Berne 
Convention. It is submitted that the correct answer is that all this should be taken into account. 
Otherwise, it would be impossible to adhere to the most basic principle of treaty interpretation 
laiddowninArticle 31.1oftheVCLT;namelythatatreatymustbeinterpretedingoodfaith.
Furthermore, the text of the substantive provisions of the Convention was not simply reproduced 
in the TRIPS Agreement and the WCT; rather it was made an obligation of the WTO Members and 
the Contracting Parties to the WCT to comply with these provisions of the Berne Convention.
This principle has also been recognized in the findings of a WTO dispute settlement panel report 
ontheapplicationofthethree-steptestfirstprovidedinArticle 9(2)oftheBerneConvention. 404 
Only few provisions of the Rome Convention were included by reference in the TRIPS 
Agreement and the WPPT, and to those provisions the same applies as to the substantive 
norms of the Berne Convention discussed above. In the case of the provisions included through 
“reproduction”–sometimeswithsomeslightchangesinthewording–thesamecannotbe
said. However, the reference to the context, the special meaning of the words and expressions, 
the preparatory work and the other relevant aspects of the Rome Convention may be helpful 
in interpreting some provisions of the Agreement and of the Treaty, since it is undeniable that 
thereisalink–evenifindirect–betweentheConventionandthesesubsequentinstruments. 
Thus, for example if a term is not sufficiently clear, but the same term is used in the Rome 
Convention, it seems justified on the basis of all the information concerning the Agreement or

Thereproductionofthekeyelementsofthethree-steptest–originallyprovidedforin 
Article 9(2)oftheBerneConvention–inArticle 13oftheTRIPSAgreementandinArticle 10
of the WCT, with some minor changes in the wording, but with a much broader scope of 
application than in the Berne Convention, 405 is a special case. This is so because the same test, 
with its original field of application, has also been incorporated by reference into the TRIPS 
AgreementbyitsArticle 9.1andintotheWCTbyitsArticle 1(4)(alongwiththedraftinghistoryof
theBerneprovision,whichisalsoanimportantsourcefortheinterpretationofTRIPSArticle 13 
andWCTArticle 10).Therefore,astheabove-mentionedWTOpanelhasalsorecognizedthis,the 
nature of the text imported from the Berne Convention may rightly be considered to be similar 
to that of the texts included by reference.
Some provisions of the TRIPS Agreement incorporated verbatim into the WCT may be considered 
tointerpretindirectlytheBerneConvention.Article 10.1oftheTRIPSAgreementissucha
provision: “Computer programs, whether in source or object code, shall be protected as literary 
worksundertheBerneConvention(1971)".Article 10.2oftheAgreement,on“compilationof
data”, may be regarded to be of the same nature, since, although it does not refer to the Berne 
Convention, it states an obligation that may be deduced from the Berne Convention. These 
provisionswerebasicallyreproducedinArticles 4(oncomputerprograms)and5(ondatabases)
of the WCT. This, as discussed below in this Guide, was done with slight changes in the wording. 
Thechanges–quiterightly–werenotconsideredtoresultinasubstantivemodificationinthe
scope and meaning of the relevant provisions of the TRIPS Agreement, which themselves are of 
an interpretative nature in relation to the Berne Convention.
This is clear from the two agreed statements which were practically identical (thus also underlining 
the de facto identical–interpretative–natureofthetwoprovisions)andreadasfollows:
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 4:Thescopeofprotectionforcomputerprograms
underArticle 4ofthisTreaty,readwithArticle 2,[406]isconsistentwithArticle 2ofthe
Berne Convention and on a par with the relevant provisions of the TRIPS Agreement.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 5:Thescopeofprotectionforcompilationsof
data(databases)underArticle 5ofthisTreatyisconsistentwithArticle 2oftheBerne
Convention and on a par with the relevant provisions of the TRIPS Agreement.
These agreed statements may be regarded as a kind of interpretation of the TRIPS Agreement, 
inthesensethat,althoughthelanguageoftheprovisionsofArticles 4and5oftheWCTseems
tobemoregeneralthanthatofArticle 10.1and10.2oftheTRIPSAgreement,theagreed
statements still indicate that these provisions of the WCT are regarded to be “on a par with 
the relevant provisions of the TRIPS Agreement". In the case of the provisions on computer 
programs and databases, diverging interpretations will hardly emerge depending on whether 
the Berne, TRIPS or WCT provision is taken as a basis. However, with respect to the interpretation 
of the relevant norms of the TRIPS Agreement, the legal nature of these agreed statements 
seemstobethesameasthatoftwootheragreedstatements–discussedbelow–thatseemto
interpret certain provisions of the TRIPS Agreement in a different situation; namely, in respect of 
provisions whose interpretation may or does involve differences of opinion.
There are certain provisions in the WCT and WPPT that were imported from the TRIPS Agreement 
and that go beyond the category of “Berne/in TRIPS/in WCT” elements discussed above, since 
they do not necessarily follow from the Berne Convention (or from the Rome Convention).

certain positions that were expressed during the debates and reject some others also discussed. 
These agreed statements may thus be regarded as attempting to settle the debates outside the 
TRIPS context, but in relation to the same kinds of provisions as in the TRIPS Agreement. All this 
mayraisequitecomplexquestionsconcerningtheinterpretationoftherelevantTRIPSnorms.
OneoftheseprovisionsandagreedstatementsconcernsArticle 7(1)oftheWCTontherental
right in respect of phonograms. As discussed in the analytic part below, the text of this 
provisiondoesnot–since,duetothedifferentcontext,itcannot–repeattherelevantprovision 
(Article 14.4)oftheTRIPSAgreementwordforword.Nevertheless,thefollowingagreed 
statement was adopted concerning this provision of the WCT:
ItisunderstoodthattheobligationunderArticle 7(1)doesnotrequireaContractingParty
to provide an exclusive right of commercial rental to authors who, under the Contracting 
Party’s law, are not granted rights in respect of phonograms. It is understood that this 
obligation is consistent with Article 14(4) of the TRIPS Agreement.409 
The most important special feature of this agreed statement is not just that it states that a 
provisionwordednotexactlythesameasinArticle 14(4)oftheTRIPSAgreementisnevertheless 
consistentwithit–althoughthisinitselfwouldbequiteanoteworthycross-interpretation. 
ItratherconsistsinthefactthatitinterpretsArticle 7(1)insubstance,suggestingthatthe
obligation is also consistent with this provision of the TRIPS Agreement. The special nature of 
the agreed statement becomes even more emphatic if one takes into account that, as discussed 
below, it reflects only one of the possible interpretations, aboutwhichtherewere–andthere
maystillbe–differencesofopinion.Althoughtheagreedstatementwasadoptedconcerning 
Article 7(1)oftheWCT,ithasthesamekindofeffectinconnectionwithArticle 9(1)oftheWPPT
on the rental right of performers.
InthecaseofanotherprovisionimportedfromtheTRIPSAgreement,onequestionissimply
whether or not it is a plus element in comparison with the Berne Convention. This provision 
isArticle 10(2)oftheWCT,whichreadsasfollows:“ContractingPartiesshall,whenapplying
the Berne Convention, confine any limitations of or exceptions to rights provided for therein 
to certain special cases that do not conflict with a normal exploitation of the work and do not 
unreasonablyprejudicethelegitimateinterestsoftheauthor".Article 13oftheTRIPSAgreement
does not seem to refer to the Berne Convention, since it reads as follows: “Members shall confine 
limitations or exceptions to exclusive rights to certain special cases which do not conflict with a 
normal exploitation of the work and do not unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of the 
right holder". Since, however, the exclusive rights to which this provision of the TRIPS Agreement 
refers include those which are provided for in the Berne Convention (with which the Members 
oftheWTOmustcomplybyvirtueofArticle 9.1oftheTRIPSAgreement),fromthepointofview
ofArticle 10(2)oftheWCT,itsmeaningisthesame.410Namely,anyexceptionorlimitation –
irrespective of whether it is specifically allowed by the Berne Convention or newly introduced 
–mayonlybeappliedifthecumulativeconditionssetinArticle 13oftheTRIPSAgreementandin
Article 10(2)oftheWCTonthe“three-steptest”arealsofulfilled.
ThisisthereasonwhythesecondsentenceoftheagreedstatementconcerningArticle 10(2)of
the WCT may also be regarded as another case of cross-interpretation between the WCT and the

Amajorquestioniswhetherornotthesecross-interpretingagreedstatements,alongwith 
the texts taken over from the TRIPS Agreement but not always in the same wording, may 
have any impact on the interpretation and application of the corresponding provisions of the 
TRIPSAgreement.Onethingseemstobequitesure:statementsadoptedinthiswayatWIPO 
outside theWTO–TRIPScontextconcerningtheTRIPSAgreementdonot–or,atleast,donot

asa“subsequentagreementbetweenthepartiesregardingtheinterpretationofthetreaty 

–althoughagreatnumberofcountriesadoptingtheWIPOTreatiesalongwiththeseagreed
statementsarethesameastheMembersoftheWTO–thereisnocompleteoverlapbetween 
the membership of the WTO and the said countries; thus, it would be difficult to speak of a 
subsequentagreementbetweenalltheMembersoftheWTO.
At the same time, it would also be difficult for a TRIPS body to completely neglect the fact that 
a great number of WTO Members participated in the adoption of these agreed statements 
atWIPO.Certainly,suchcross-interpretationsmayatleasthavetobetakenintoaccount–
irrespectiveofwhetherornottheyareeventuallyfoundtobedecisive–intheTRIPScontextas 
well. The above-mentioned WTO panel in its findings seemed to agree with this position. 411
Unfinished work of the Diplomatic Conference; long way to go to the adoption of the BTAP as 
the third “Internet Treaty”
The 1996 Diplomatic Conference left work unfinished on one and a half of the treaties to be 
drafted–inthesensethattheDraftTreatyonIntellectualPropertyinRespectofDatabases 
submittedtotheDiplomaticConferencewasnotconsideredatallinsubstance,while–and
thisisthehalftreaty–thealternativeoftheBasicProposalontheprotectionofperformers 
and producers of phonograms that would also have applied to “audiovisual performers” was 
not really discussed either. Instead, the Diplomatic Conference adopted a Recommendation 
suggesting further preparatory work on a possible treaty for the protection of databases, 412 
and a Resolution calling for the convocation of an extraordinary session of the competent WIPO 
GoverningBodiesduringthefirstquarterof1997todecideonthescheduleofthepreparatory 
work on a protocol to the WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty concerning audiovisual 
performances, with a view to the adoption of such a protocol no later than 1998. 413
The preparatory work on some form of database protection continued for a couple of years 
with limited support from the delegations and then it was abandoned. The preparatory work 
on the protection of the rights in audiovisual performances continued more persistently, first 
inaseparatecommitteeandthen–asoneoftheagendaitems–intheStandingCommittee
onCopyrightandRelatedRights(SCCR)–butitdidnotleadtoadiplomaticconferencein
1998.Itwasonlyin2000thatadiplomaticconferencewasconvened.Here19Articles were
adopted provisionally, but the delegations were not able to agree on the key provision on the 
questionoftheoriginalownershipandtransferofrights.Thishadalsobeentheobstacleat 
the 1996 Diplomatic Conference to a consensus on the protection of the rights of “audiovisual 
performers". Nevertheless, the work continued in the SCCR, where finally a compromise solution

WIPO Copyright Treaty (WCT), 1996
Preamble
The Contracting Parties,
Desiring to develop and maintain the protection of the rights of authors in their literary and 
artistic works in a manner as effective and uniform as possible,
Recognizing the need to introduce new international rules and clarify the interpretation of 
certainexistingrulesinordertoprovideadequatesolutionstothequestionsraisedbynew
economic, social, cultural and technological developments,
Recognizing the profound impact of the development and convergence of information and 
communication technologies on the creation and use of literary and artistic works,
Emphasizing the outstanding significance of copyright protection as an incentive for literary 
and artistic creation,
Recognizing the need to maintain a balance between the rights of authors and the larger 
public interest, particularly education, research and access to information, as reflected in the 
Berne Convention,
Have agreed as follows:
Introductory remarks
CT-Pr.1. The Preamble was adopted after the substantive provisions of the Treaty. Thus, it should 
not be supposed to reflect certain objectives or principles agreed upon by the delegations in 
an early stage of the preparatory work that then served as guidance for the adoption of the 
provisions of the Treaty. The Preamble is rather a kind of summary declaration of what had been 
discussed, negotiated and agreed upon at the 1996 Diplomatic Conference.
First paragraph
CT-Pr.2.Thefirstparagraph ofthePreambleconfirmsthattheContractingPartieshave 
the intention to follow the same objectives as those outlined in the Preamble of the Berne 
Convention.Thelatterbegins:“ThecountriesoftheUnion,beingequallyanimatedbythedesire 
to protect, in as effective and uniform a manner as possible, the rights of authors in their literary and 
artistic works”(emphasisadded).Thisparagraph oftheWCTPreamblecontainsthesamebasic
elements: “protection of the rights of authors in their literary and artistic works in a manner as 
effective and uniform as possible", and it only adds the intention of the Contracting Parties of 
the WCT “to develop and maintain” such protection. (As regards the meaning of the key words 
“effective” and “uniform", since they are the same as in the Preamble of the Berne Convention, 
the comments on them in the Berne Guide in this collection of guides apply here too.)
Second paragraph
CT-Pr.3.InthepreparatoryworkoftheTreaty,theimpactofnewtechnologies–and,in
particular,thatofdigitaltechnologyandtheInternet–wasthefocus.Theorderoftheadjectives
inthesecondparagraph doesnotseemtobeinharmonywiththis,becausetheadjective
“technological”ismentionedasthelastoneintheexpression“thequestionsraisedbynew 
economic, social, cultural and technological developments” (to which the Treaty is “to provide 
adequatesolutions”).Itmaybeinterpreted,however,toreflecttherecognitionthatitisnot
the new technologies themselves to which primary attention should be paid, but rather their 
economic, social and cultural impact. Furthermore, this also reflects a principle which had been 
adopted and consistently applied during the preparatory work; namely, that the new provisions 
should not be technology-specific, and should address the economic, social and cultural issues 
raised by these technologies in a more abstract manner.

===== PAGE 213 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
214 CT-Pr.4.Thesecondparagraph ofthePreambleidentifiesthetwomainformsofproviding
solutions to the new developments: “to introduce new international rules and clarify the 
interpretation of certain existing rules”. In fact, in the course of the preparatory work, an 
attempt was always made, first, to try to solve a given problem through interpretation of 
the existing norms or, failing this, through the adaptation of the existing norms to the new 
requirements.Thepreparationandadoptionofcompletelynewnormswasregardedonlyas
last resort, and it was relatively rare that it was chosen.
Third paragraph
CT-Pr.5.Thethirdparagraph ofthePreambleindicatesthespecificreasonwhytheTreatyhas
become necessary: “the profound impact of the development and convergence of information 
and communication technologies". The most spectacular result of this development and 
convergence was the Internet. The Internet is not mentioned in the text of the Treaty, but it is 
not by chance that the WCT and the WPPT have been referred to in the various comments as 
the “Internet Treaties". The fundamental reason why they are recognized as being important is 
exactly that they offer responses to the challenges raised by this global information network.
Fourth paragraph
CT-Pr.6.Thefourthparagraph underlineswhythemaintenanceanddevelopmentof“as
effective […] as possible” copyright protection is necessary; namely, because such protection 
has outstanding significance as an incentive for the creation of literary and artistic works. 
Theparagraph isusefulguidancefortheinterpretationoftheprovisionsoftheWCT;no
interpretation thereof would be acceptable that might undermine the efficiency of this incentive 
for creativity or weaken it in an unreasonable manner.
Fifth paragraph
CT-Pr.7. The fifth paragraph, similarly to the first, refers to the Berne Convention. It recognizes 
that, in the Berne Convention, there is “a balance between the rights of authors and the larger 
public interest", and that there is a need for maintaining this balance “as reflected in the 
Berne Convention".
CT-Pr.8. In the fifth paragraph, reference is made to “the rights of authors and the larger public 
interest”(emphasisadded).Itisquiteclearthatcertaininterestsaresupposedtobebalanced
withcertainotherinterests.Therefore,thebalanceinvokedinthisparagraph isinfacttobe 
achieved between the interests ofauthors–alongwiththeunderlyinglargerpublicinterestin
granting “protection of the rights of authors in their literary and artistic works in a manner as 
effective[…]aspossible”andprovidingbythis“anincentiveforliteraryandartisticcreation”– 
on the one hand, and, on the other hand, the “larger public interest”, that is, all the other relevant 
public interests.
CT-Pr.9.Thisparagraph makesitclearthatwhatisneededistomaintain the balance established 
intheBerneConvention.Therefore,thebalancingrequirementmustnotberegardedasa
newprinciple;ithasbeen–toborrowaphrasefromcomputertechnology–“decompiled”
from the existing balance of interests as manifested in the provisions of the Berne Convention. 
The balancing of interests is subsumed under the basic objective of the Convention; namely, 
the protection of copyright “in a manner as effective […] as possible”. The same principle of 
“balancing” must also prevail in the WCT.
CT-Pr.10.Certainaspectsofpublicinterests–namely,“education,researchandaccessto
information”–arealsoreferredtointhefifthparagraph.Itisexactlywithrespecttothese 
interests that the Berne Convention provides for certain specific exceptions and limitations. 
Thetextoftheparagraph itselfunderscoresthis,clarifyingthatwhatismeantisabalance 
“as reflected in the Berne Convention”. Therefore, it seems that the Diplomatic Conference 
did not intend to introduce new elements in contrast with the existing principles of the Berne 
Convention.AnagreedstatementconcerningArticle 10(2)oftheWCTconfirmsagainthe 
unchangedconceptofbalance:“ItisunderstoodthatArticle 10(2)neitherreducesnorextends 
the scope of applicability of the limitations and exceptions permitted by the Berne Convention".

Article 1
Relation to the Berne Convention
(1) ThisTreatyisaspecialagreementwithinthemeaningofArticle 20oftheBerne
Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works, as regards Contracting 
Parties that are countries of the Union established by that Convention. This Treaty shall 
not have any connection with treaties other than the Berne Convention, nor shall it 
prejudice any rights and obligations under any other treaties.
(2) Nothing in this Treaty shall derogate from existing obligations that Contracting Parties 
have to each other under the Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and 
Artistic Works.
(3) Hereinafter,“BerneConvention”shallrefertotheParisActofJuly24,1971,oftheBerne
Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works.
(4) ContractingPartiesshallcomplywithArticles 1to21andtheAppendixofthe
Berne Convention.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 1(4):Thereproductionright,assetoutinArticle 9of
the Berne Convention, and the exceptions permitted thereunder, fully apply in the digital 
environment, in particular to the use of works in digital form. It is understood that the storage 
of a protected work in digital form in an electronic medium constitutes a reproduction within 
themeaningofArticle 9oftheBerneConvention.
Paragraph (1): special agreement status
CT-1.1.Article 20oftheBerneConvention,initsfirstsentence,statesthat“[t]heGovernmentsof
the countries of the Union reserve the right to enter into special agreements among themselves, 
in so far as such agreements grant to authors more extensive rights than those granted by this 
Convention or contain other provisions not contrary to this Convention". The special agreement 
status of the WCT in itself is supposed to have a positive impact on the interpretation of its 
provisions, since it follows from this that any interpretation that would result in a decrease of the 
level of protection in contrast with the Berne Convention would be unacceptable. If there were 
twopossiblewaysofinterpretingtheTreaty–onebeinginharmonywithArticle 20oftheBerne
Convention and another one resulting in less extensive rights than under the Berne Convention, 
orotherwisecontrarytotheConvention–theformerinterpretationwouldhavetobeaccepted.
CT-1.2. The Treaty is open for ratification or accession by any WIPO Member State and also by 
some “intergovernmental organizations”. 414ThequestionmayemergewhetherArticle 20ofthe
Berne Convention is also applicable when a “special agreement” is concluded not only among 
the countries of the Berne Union but also with the participation of third parties. The answer 
shouldbeintheaffirmative;thereisnothinginthetextofArticle 20oftheBerneConvention 
that would create an obstacle to this.
Paragraph (1): no connection with other treaties
CT-1.3.Thefirstpartofthesecondsentenceofparagraph (1)seemsunnecessary,beacuse,ifa
treaty does not contain any provision establishing a connection with another treaty, obviously, 
it has no connection with that other treaty. No confirmation of a non-existing relationship 
isrequired.FromtherecordsoftheDiplomaticConference,ittranspires,however,thatthe
negativestatementincludedinthesecondsentenceofparagraph (1)wasintendedtoconfirm
specifically that there is no connection between the Treaty and the TRIPS Agreement. 415
CT-1.4. It should be noted that, as discussed above, during the preparatory work, a kind of de 
facto relationship was emerging between the WCT and the TRIPS Agreement. The relevant norms

CT-1.5. Although the WCT does not have such a special relationship with the TRIPS Agreement

Paragraph (2): safeguard clause
CT-1.6.Paragraph (2)containsasafeguardclauseguaranteeingthat,eveniftherewereany
conflict between the WCT and the Berne Convention, the Convention would be applied among 
those Contracting Parties that are also members of the Berne Union. In fact, however, it seems 
that there is no such conflict.
CT-1.7.Itistobenotedthatparagraph (2)hasarelevancenotonlyinrespectofthesubstantive
normsoftheBerneConvention(thatis,Articles 1to21oftheConventionanditsAppendix),but
alsoconcerningtheadministrativeandfinalclausesoftheConvention(Articles 22to38),which 
contain provisions on issues like the Assembly and Executive Committee of the Berne Union, 
finances, limited possibility of reservations, or settlement of disputes (through the International 
CourtofJustice).
CT-1.8.Article 2.2oftheTRIPSAgreementcontainsasimilarprovisionreferringtothe
BerneConvention,whichreadsasfollows:“NothinginPartsItoIVofthisAgreementshall
derogate from existing obligations that Members may have to each other under […] the 
Berne Convention". There is only similarity, since there are two substantive differences. First, 
Article 9.1oftheTRIPSAgreementprovidesthattheWTOMembers“shallnothaverightsor
obligationsunderthisAgreementinrespectoftherightsconferredunderArticle 6 bis of that 
[theBerne]Conventionoroftherightsderivedtherefrom”.Thus,Article 2.2oftheAgreement 
is a guarantee that those provisions could be fully applied, at least between those Members of 
the WTO that are also members of the Berne Union, even if moral rights are not enforceable 
under the TRIPS Agreement (with the arguable exception of the “right of paternity”, which may 
bededucedfromArticles 10(3)and10bis(1) of the Convention as an implied moral right not 
derivedfromArticle 6 bis, because they condition the applicability of the exceptions allowed by 
them on naming the author).418Second,Article 2.2,however,doesnotprovidearealsafeguard
for the Berne Convention; it implicitly allows the countries of the Berne Union to disregard their 
obligations under that Convention in a certain context, by stating only with regard to Parts I to 
IV of the Agreement that nothing in them derogates from existing obligations under the Berne 
Convention. Part V on dispute prevention and settlement is not mentioned. It is important to 
notethissince,underArticle 64.1oftheAgreement–whichmaybefoundinPart V –theWTO
dispute settlement mechanism is also applicable to the TRIPS Agreement, and it involves,

WIPO-administered conventions, including the Berne Convention) and, hopefully, this will be the 
typical effect. In principle, however, cross-retaliation is also possible in the case of violations of 
WTOobligationsoutsidethefieldofcopyright–orevenoutsidethefieldofintellectualproperty 
–throughsuspendingtheapplicationofcopyrightprotectionfortheworksoftheWCTMember 
concerned (whose legislation and the practical implementation thereof otherwise may happen 
to be in perfect harmony with the TRIPS Agreement (and the Berne Convention)).
Paragraph (3): reference to the 1971 Paris Act of the Berne Convention
CT-1.9.Paragraph (3)isself-explanatory.
Paragraph (4): obligation to comply with the substantive norms of the Berne Convention: 
general remarks
CT-1.10.Paragraph (4)obligatestheContractingPartiestocomplywithArticles 1to21andthe
AppendixoftheBerneConvention.IfthetextoftheseArticles hadbeensimplyreproducedinthe
Treaty–withoutanyreferencetotheConvention–theremightbeperhapsasomewhatdifferent
legalsituation;but,withthislegaltechnique(incorporationbyreference),itseemsthatArticles 1
to 21 of the Convention and the Appendix, except where the Treaty expressly provides otherwise, 
should be interpreted in the same way as in their original context within the Berne Convention.
CT-1.11. Interpreting these provisions in the same way as in the original context of the Berne 
Convention means, among other things, that the WCT has inherited not only the text but also 
the negotiating history of the provisions included by reference as reflected in the records of the 
various diplomatic conferences adopting and revising the Convention. This is a rich source of 
interpretationunderArticle 31and32oftheVCLT.
Articles 1 to 21 and the Appendix of the Berne Convention as applied in the context of the WCT
CT-1.12. In the following paragraphs it is discussed briefly how these provisions may be applied 
in the context of the WCT: where their application may follow the mutatis mutandis rule; where 
they should be applied in a somewhat different manner; and where a provision, although 
formallylistedinArticle 1(4),isnotinfacttobeapplied.
CT-1.13. Article 1:ConsideringthecontextintowhichthisArticle istofitintheWCT,itmustnot

theword“Union”appearsinArticles 2to6oftheWCT,theentiretyoftheContractingParties 
must be understood.
CT-1.14.Whileinalltheotherprovisionswheretheword“Union”isused–ingeneral,withinthe

the Berne Convention for the following reasons. Since the word “Union” means the entirety of

CT-1.15. Articles 2 and 2bis: No specific comments are necessary concerning the application

CT-1.16.Article 3oftheWCTprovidesformutatis mutandis application of, inter alia,Articles 2
and 2bisoftheBerneConvention.ThisseparateprovisionsupplementsArticle 1(4)oftheTreaty

C T-1.17. Articles 3 and 4:IntheBerneConvention,theseArticles fixtheconditionsofprotection 
(the“pointsofattachment”).Article 3oftheWCTprovidesthatthepointsofattachmentmust 
be applied, mutatis mutandis, inrespectoftheprotectionprovidedundertheTreaty,and–in

Articles shouldbeinterpretedinthecontextoftheWCT mutatis mutandis.
CT-1.18. The draft treaty which became the WCT contained provisions to adapt the definition of 
“publishedworks”(Article 3(3)oftheBerneConvention)tothedigitalenvironment.Underthe 
proposed provisions, the interactive making available of copies by wire or by wireless means 
“sothatcopiesareavailable”wouldhavequalifiedasanactofpublication,and,insuchacase,
the place “where the necessary arrangements have been made for ensuring availability of 
these works to members of the public” would have been regarded (in a kind of legal fiction) as 
the place of publication.420 The proposal implicitly recognized the fact that, through interactive 
transmissions, copies of works may be distributed to the public. The legal characterization of 
such transmissions, however, was the source of serious controversies during the preparatory 
work (which finally led to the “umbrella solution“ 421). Due to this, as well as to the not fully clear 
legalconsequences,theproposedprovisionswerenotadopted.Therefore,theconceptof
“publishedworks”undertheWCTremainsthesameasunderArticle (3)oftheConvention.
CT-1.19. Article 5:ThisArticle oftheBerneConventionincludescertainbasicprinciplesof 
copyright protection, such as national treatment, formality-free protection and independence of 
protection.TheagreedstatementadoptedconcerningArticle 3oftheWCT(seebelow)describes
how certain terms in these provisions are to be applied mutatis mutandis.
CT-1.20.Theagreedstatementmentionedintheprecedingparagraph contains,inter alia, 
the following instruction for the application mutatis mutandis of the provisions of the Berne 
Convention:“‘thisConvention’inArticles 2(8),2bis(2), 3, 4 and 5 of the Berne Convention will be 
read as if it were a reference to the Berne Convention and this Treaty". If this provision is applied 
forArticle 5(1)oftheBerneConvention,theadaptedtextissupposedtoreadasfollows:“Authors
shall enjoy, in respect of works for which they are protected under the Berne Convention and this 
Treaty, in Contracting Parties to this Treaty other than the country of origin, the rights which their 
respective laws do now or may hereafter grant to their nationals, as well as the rights specially 
granted by the Berne Convention and this Treaty” [emphasis added]. In this adapted text, the first 
combined reference to the Convention and the Treaty may lead to some interpretation problems, 
because it seems to suggest that authors enjoy national treatment in the framework of the 
Treaty “in respect of works for which they are protected under the Berne Convention and this 
Treaty in Contracting Parties to this Treaty other than the country of origin". Emphasis is added 
to the word “and” since the text may be understood to mean that only those works enjoy national 
treatment that are protected in a Contracting State both by the Berne Convention and by the 
Treaty. This meaning of the text would create a bizarre situation in the case of Contracting Parties

CT-1.21. No one intended such a result of the application of the above-mentioned agreed

CT-1.38.Theremaybetwopossibleanswerstothisquestion.Thefirstoneisthatthissimply 

Paragraph (4) and the agreed statement concerning it: application of Article  9 of the Berne 
Convention on the right of reproduction
CT-1.40. As discussed in the Guide to the Berne Convention in this collection of guides, by 
virtueofparagraph (1)ofArticle 9oftheBerneConvention,therightofreproductioncovers
reproduction “in any manner or form”. This language could hardly be interpreted in good faith in 
anymannerotherthanthat,unlessanexceptionorlimitationispermittedunderparagraph (2)
of the same Article, the right of reproduction is applicable to any kind of reproduction. In other 
words, if an act is reproduction, it is covered by the right of reproduction, and it may only 
be excluded from the operation of the right if it is done through appropriate exceptions and 
limitations. In other words, the scope of this right cannot be “overstretched” or “extended” 
further; there is simply no room for extending its scope because, in the absence of a permissible 
exception or limitation, the right of reproduction is applicable in the case of any imaginable (and 
even, for the time being, unimaginable) manner and form of reproduction.
CT-1.41. The first sentence of the agreed statement seems unnecessary, since it states the 
obvious:“Thereproductionright,assetoutinArticle 9oftheBerneConvention,andthe 
exceptions permitted thereunder, fully apply in the digital environment, in particular to the 
use of works in digital form". There is no reason for doubt to emerge that the expression “any 
manner or form” also covers digital form. If a work is transformed from analog into digital form, 
unless some substantive changes are made in the course of the transformation, reproduction 
takes place (while, in case of substantive changes, the applicability of the right of adaptation 
mayemerge).Theworkitself–thetext,thepicture,themusicalcreation–remainsthesame;
only the format in which it is embodied changes. If a new digital fixation of the work takes place, 
itmaynotbequalifiedinanyotherwaythanthatitisanewcopy,areproduction.
CT-1.42. It has been recognized since the 1970s, but definitively stated since 1982, when a special 
WIPO/UNESCO committee addressed this issue, that the inclusion of works in electronic storage 
is reproduction.423 Such storage fully corresponds to the concept of “reproduction” under the 
Berne Convention: it permits any indirect communication to the public or further reproduction 
of the work concerned. The fact that the copy of the work stored in the electronic storage 
mediumcannotbedirectlyperceived,butonlywithappropriateequipment,isirrelevant;itstill 
has all the criteria of a copy. It would seem to be in conflict with the Berne Convention (and, 
therefore, also with the TRIPS Agreement) not to recognize such storage as reproduction. This 
means that the second sentence of the agreed statement also reflects something that is the 
onlypossibleappropriateinterpretationofArticle 9oftheBerneConvention;whatitstates 
clearlyfollowsfromthatArticle oftheConvention.
CT-1.43.AlthoughthesecondsentenceoftheagreedstatementconcerningArticle 1(4)ofthe
WCT on the application of the right of reproduction was adopted only by a majority of the votes, 
thatmajority–undertheRulesofProcedureoftheDiplomaticConference–wassufficientfor
the adoption of the provisions of the treaties; and thus also of the agreed statements concerning 
theprovisions.ItsadoptionfulfilledtheconditionsofArticle 31.2(a)oftheVCLTunderwhich
“any agreement relating to the treaty which was made between all the parties in connexion with 
the conclusion of the treaty” is a relevant source of interpretation. The statement relates to the 
423 For the report of the session,  see Copyright (WIPO’smonthlyreview,September1982issue),245–246.

comment is that such an agreement must be made “between all the parties”. The adoption of an 
agreedstatementdidnotrequireunanimity.UnderArticle 9.2oftheVCLT,atreatymaybeadopted
by a two-thirds majority, and Rule 34(2)(iii) of the Rules of Procedure of the 1996 Diplomatic 
ConferencerequiredsuchamajorityfortheadoptionoftheTreaties.Itwouldnotbeanappropriate
interpretationofArticle 31.2(a)oftheVCLTthattheprovisionsofatreatymaybeadoptedbya
majorityofvotesbuttheadoptionoftheagreedstatementsrelatedtothemrequiresunanimity.
TheagreedstatementalsocorrespondstotheconditionunderArticle 31.2(a)oftheVCLTthatsuch
a statement must be adopted “between all the parties”; it was adopted, first at the session of Main 
Committee I, and then at the Plenary in that way, rather than at some separate forum. 
CT-1.44. The delegations which, at the Diplomatic Conference, opposed the second sentence of the 
agreed statement concerning storage of works in electronic media raised some arguments that 
did not relate to storage in general but only to certain temporary forms of storage, such as some 
technologicallyindispensable,but–intermsoftheexploitationoftheworksconcernedandthe
legitimateinterestsofownersofrights–irrelevantformsoftemporaryreproductionswhichtake
place during a transmission through interactive digital networks or incidentally to an authorized use 
of a work. Their idea was that “too temporary”, “too transient” reproductions must not be recognized 
asreproduction.This,however,wouldhavebeeninconflictwithArticle 9oftheBerneConvention
underwhichthedurationofthefixation(includingthestorageinanelectronicmedium)–whetherit
ispermanentortemporary–isirrelevant(aslongas,on the basis of the [new] fixation, the work may 
be perceived, reproduced or communicated). Nevertheless, there are commentators according to 
whom the term “storage” might be interpreted in a way that presumes more than a very short-lived 
fixation424–a“fleetingpassage”–althoughitisalsopointedoutbythesamecommentatorsthatthis
wouldnarrowtheconceptof“reproductioninanymannerorform”underArticle 9(1)oftheBerne
Convention,whichmightleadtoconflictswithArticle 20oftheConvention.425
CT-1.45.ItisanothermatterthatexceptionsallowedunderArticle 9(2)oftheBerneConventionon
the basis of the three-step test may be applied in the case of certain temporary reproductions. Where 
an exception to the right of reproduction is justified in accordance with the three-step test, the right 
method is what is offered by the Berne Convention; namely, to permit such an exception, rather 
thantryingtoapplythetechniqueoflegalfiction(bystatingthat,insuchcasesofreproduction,it
should be considered as if no reproduction had taken place). This seems to be the right method also 
as regards certain special cases of temporary reproduction that are technologically indispensable 
for carrying out certain authorized acts but which in themselves are irrelevant with regard to the 
exploitation of works and the legitimate interests of copyright owners.426
Article 2
Scope of Copyright Protection
Copyright protection extends to expressions and not to ideas, procedures, methods of 
operation or mathematical concepts as such.
CT-2.1.TheprinciplestatedinthisArticle hadalwaysbeenrecognizedandapplied–andhad
neverbeenquestioned–undertheBerneConventionasanindispensableelementofthe
concept of “work”, even if there was no explicit statement about it in the text of the Convention.
CT-2.2.TheinclusionofArticle 2intheWCTisaresultoftheimpactoftheTRIPSAgreementonthe
preparatory work and on the text of the WCT. It was decided that the same kinds of interpretative 
provisionsasthosecontainedinArticle 10oftheTRIPSAgreementshouldbeincorporatedintothe

Article 3
Application of Articles 2 to 6 of the Berne Convention
Contracting Parties shall apply mutatis mutandis theprovisionsofArticles 2to6oftheBerne
Convention in respect of the protection provided for in this Treaty.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 3:Itisunderstoodthat,inapplyingArticle 3ofthisTreaty,
theexpression“countryoftheUnion”inArticles 2to6oftheBerneConventionwillberead
as if it were a reference to a Contracting Party to this Treaty, in the application of those Berne 
Articles inrespectoftheprotectionprovidedforinthisTreaty.Itisalsounderstoodthatthe
expression“countryoutsidetheUnion”inthoseArticles intheBerneConventionwill,inthe
same circumstances, be read as if it were a reference to a country that is not a Contracting 
PartytothisTreaty,andthat“thisConvention”inArticles 2(8),2 bis(2), 3, 4 and 5 of the Berne 
Convention will be read as if it were a reference to the Berne Convention and this Treaty. 
Finally,itisunderstoodthatareferenceinArticles 3to6oftheBerneConventiontoa“national
ofoneofthecountriesoftheUnion”will,whentheseArticles areappliedtothisTreaty,mean,
in regard to an intergovernmental organization that is a Contracting Party to this Treaty, a 
national of one of the countries that is member of that organization.
CT-3.1.ThetextofArticle 3indicatesthewayinwhichtherelevantprovisionsoftheBerne
Convention should be applied mutatis mutandis; it is a useful clarification to eliminate any 
ambiguity about their application in the context of the WCT.
CT-3.2.Also,theagreedstatementconcerningArticle 3offersindicationsonhowcertain 
concretetermsappearinginArticles 2to6,withwhichtheContractingPartycomplies,should 
beappliedintheWCT.Itisself-explanatoryand,ingeneral,doesnotseemtorequirespecific
comments. It is sufficient to mention that the clarifications were needed for two main reasons: 
(i) to make it clear that the reference to the Berne Convention and to the countries of the Berne 
Union should be meant as reference to the Treaty and to the Contracting Parties of the Treaty; 
and (ii) to identify the changes that are necessary due to the fact that not only “countries” but 
also certain “intergovernmental organizations” may become party to the Treaty (the reference 
to Contracting Parties, in general, took care of this, but, in respect of the term “national of one of 
the countries of the Union” further clarification was needed).
CT-3.3.Theexpression“theprotectionprovidedforinthisTreaty”usedinArticle 3should 
be interpreted as meaning not only the new rights and aspects going beyond the level of 
protectionprescribedinArticles 1to21andtheAppendixoftheBerneConvention.Italso 
meanstheprotectionrequiredbytheseprovisionsoftheConventiontocomplywith–where
necessary mutatis mutandis andwiththewordingchangesinsomeprovisionsoftheWCT–
Article 1(4)oftheTreaty.Itshouldbenotedthatthelatterprovisionsincludebasicelementsof
“the protection provided for in this Treaty”.
Article 4
Computer Programs
ComputerprogramsareprotectedasliteraryworkswithinthemeaningofArticle 2ofthe
Berne Convention. Such protection applies to computer programs, whatever may be the mode 
or form of their expression.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 4:Thescopeofprotectionforcomputerprogramsunder
Article 4ofthisTreaty,readwithArticle 2,isconsistentwithArticle 2oftheBerneConvention
and on a par with the relevant provisions of the TRIPS Agreement.

224 The concept of “computer programs”
CT-4.1. The WCT does not contain a definition of “computer program”. In the course of the 
preparatory work of the Treaty, it was agreed that the definition of “computer program” adopted 
as part of the WIPO Model Provisions on the Protection of Computer Programs 427 was still 
valid. The definition reads as follows: “‘computer program’ means a set of instructions capable, 
when incorporated in a machine-readable medium, of causing a machine having information-
processing capabilities to indicate, perform or achieve a particular function, task or result".
CT-4.2. The definitions of “computer program”, where included in national laws, are, in general, 
inharmonywiththebasicsubstantiveelementsoftheabove-quoteddefinitionintheModel
Provisions.428 However, in the European Union (EU), a definition is used which, at first sight, seems 
tobebroader.Article 1.1oftheEUComputerProgramsDirective429 provides that “for the purpose 
of this Directive, the term ‘computer programs’ shall include their preparatory design material". 
Due to the broader phrasing, in fact, the term “computer programs” has a double meaning: 
first, productions that are really computer programs; that is, sets of instructions to cause a 
computer to perform certain functions and, second, in addition to computer programs proper, 
certain preparatory design materials that are not computer programs (yet) but, for the purpose 
of the Directive, are also covered by the provisions of the Directive on “computer programs”. In 
the Introduction of the Proposal for the Directive, this double meaning was pointed out by the 
European Commission, and also that not all kinds of preparatory materials fall under the definition: 
For the purposes of this proposal, the term ‘computer program’ is used. This means a set of 
instructions the purpose of which is to cause an information processing device, a computer, 
to perform its functions. The program, together with the supporting and preparatory 
design material which have made possible the creation of the program, can also be called 
‘computer software’. All such material is intended to be covered by the provisions of this 
proposalinsofarasitcanbedemonstratedthat,fromthematerialinquestion,aform
of program has been or could be created. However, it is not thought advisable to include 
a definition in the Directive to avoid it becoming outdated. Where the material is of a 
nature such that it could not lead to the creation of a program, for example, a user manual 
accompanying a program, although the material will not be protected as part of the 
computer program, protection by copyright or other means may nevertheless apply.430
InthecommentstoArticle 1oftheProposalfortheDirective,thisisstatedagain;and
concerning the preparatory design materials, further clarification is added: “Preparatory and 
designmaterialsuchasflowchartsordescriptionsofsequencesofstepsinplainlanguagewill
be included [but m]aterial such as user manuals or maintenance manuals will not”.431 
CT-4.3. One of the recitals of the Directive also clarifies to what sorts of materials the special 
regime applies: “for the purpose of this Directive, the term ‘computer program’ […] also includes 
preparatory design work leading to the development of a computer program provided that 
the nature of the preparatory work is such that a computer program can result from it at a 
later stage". This confirms that the provisions of the Directive concerning computer programs 
apply to preparatory design materials although they are not yet genuine programs; in order 
that they become computer programs, further acts are needed to transform them into sets of 
instructions enabling a computer to perform certain tasks.
CT-4.4.TwojudgmentsoftheCourtofJusticeoftheEuropeanUnion(CJEU)haveinterpreted
the status of preparatory design materials, although this was not the main issue in either of 
them. In Bezpečnostní softwarová asociace ,432 theCourtdealtwiththequestionofwhetheror

expression of combined instructions given to a computer so as to make it function and obtain a certain result.”

CT-4.5. In Bezpečnostní softwarová asociace , the Court stated as follows:
37. [T]heobjectofprotectionunderDirective91/250includestheformsofexpressionofa
computer program and the preparatory design work capable of leading, respectively, to the 
reproduction or the subsequent creation of such a program.
38. AstheAdvocateGeneralstatesinPoint61ofhisOpinion,anyformofexpressionof
a computer program must be protected from the moment when its reproduction would 
engender the reproduction of the computer program itself, thus enabling the computer to 
perform its task.435
Twofindingsareexpressedinthesestatements;first,thataproductiononlyqualifiesasa 
computer program when it consists in a set of instructions enabling a computer to perform a 
task;436 and second, that preparatory design material is not yet such a program; for it to become 
aprogramsomesubsequentcreativestepstillhastobemade.Concerningthelatteraspect, 
the Advocate General added the following clarification in his opinion: “Th[e] design work can 
include, for example, a structure or organisational chart developed by the programmer which is 
liable to be re-transcribed in source code and object code, thus enabling the machine to execute 
thecomputerprogram. […]Thatorganisationalchartdevelopedbytheprogrammercouldbe
compared to the scenario of a film".437 That is, a preparatory design material is not yet a real 
computer program in the same way as a scenario is not yet an audiovisual work, but it may be 
usedinsubsequentstepstocreateaprogramasascenariomayalsobeusedtoproducean
audiovisual work. 
CT-4.6. In SAS Institute Inc. concerning the concepts of computer programs proper and 
preparatorydesignmaterials,theCJEUagreesbyreferencetothefindingintheabove-quoted 
paragraph 37ofBezpečnostní softwarová asociace 438 (that preparatory material is not yet a 
computer program proper; in order to become a program further steps are needed). The Court 
also confirmed that user manuals are not to be regarded as preparatory design materials and, 
thus, are not covered by the concept of computer programs for the purpose of the Directive, 
though they may be protected as works if they are original intellectual creations. 439
CT-4.7. This means that from the viewpoint of the Directive there are three categories. First, 
computerprogramsproper–setsofinstructionseitherinsourcecodeorinobjectcode
enabling a computer to perform certain tasks - which are protected under the special regime of 
theDirective,inaccordancewithArticle 4oftheWCT(andArticle 10.1oftheTRIPSAgreement).
Second, preparatory design materials that are sufficiently developed to be transcribed into 
source code and object code and thus to be transformed into computer programs; which do not 
correspond to the concept of computer programs under the WCT (and the TRIPS Agreement) but 
to which the special regime of the Directive is extended, except those provisions that are only 
relevant to computer programs proper.440 Third, other preparatory or supporting materials that 
are not suitable to be transformed in that way, such as user manuals.

226 CT-4.8. A further issue is whether or not the images generated on screens as a result of the 
operation of a program (for example, in the case of video games) may or should be regarded 
as parts of a “computer program”. The dominant opinion is that the images generated by a 
computer program in the form of screen display fall outside the concept of “computer program” 
proper.Theconceptof“computerprogram”underArticle 4oftheWCTdoesnotcoverthe
images generated by computer programs on screens. Screen displays containing moving 
imagesmay,and,iftheycorrespondtotherequirementoforiginality,do,enjoycopyright
protectionasaudiovisualworks(andfixedimagesalsomaybe,andfrequentlyare,protected 
as graphic or photographic works).441 The copyright status of the different categories of works 
isnotnecessarilythesame(seethespecialprovisionsoncinematographicworksinArticles 14
and 14bis of the Berne Convention and the specific provisions concerning computer programs 
mentioned below). Therefore, the differentiation between computer programs and screen 
images generated by them has relevance for the scope of protection to be granted. 
Towards the recognition of computer programs as works protected by copyright
CT-4.9.WIPOstartedtodealwiththequestionoftheintellectualpropertyprotectionof 
computer programs in the 1970s, and, first, the idea of working out a sui generis system 
emerged.442 However, the Model Provisions, which provided for such a system, were not 
followed by national legislators, and the prevailing idea was that not a copyright-inspired sui 
generis system but copyright itself should be applied for the protection of computer programs. 
In February 1985, WIPO and UNESCO convened in Geneva a joint Group of Experts on the 
Copyright Aspects of the Protection of Computer Programs. At this meeting, on the basis of a 
thorough study443 and an animated debate, a breakthrough took place towards the recognition 
of computer programs as works protected by copyright. 444
CT-4.10. National laws that already provided for the copyright protection of computer programs, 
in general, granted the same kind of protection as for other categories of works. It is another 
matter that they also included certain “genre-specific” provisions, such as special exceptions 
for back-up copies or for “decompilation” of programs with the purpose of creating other, 
interoperable programs. There were, however, still some countries that, although ready to keep 
computer programs within the general copyright paradigm, wanted to apply certain regimes 
similar to the protection of works of applied arts or industrial designs (with a shorter term 
of protection and with the possibility of applying material reciprocity). There were then two 
developments which completed, at the level of binding regional and international norms, what 
had been worked out at the WIPO forums in the form of a soft-law model: first, the publication, 
inJuly1991,oftheComputerProgramsDirectiveoftheEuropeanCommunity;and,second,the
441 As discussed above, a graphic user interface is not a form of expression of a computer program within the meaning 
ofArticle 1(2)oftheComputerProgramsDirectiveandisnotprotectedunderthatdirective.Nevertheless,suchan 
interfacemaybeprotectedbycopyrightasanothercategory–particularlyasaudiovisual–work(see Bezpečnostní 
softwarová asociace ).  
Ingeneral,theCJEUdistinguishesbetweentheelementsinprogrammedform(setsofinstructions)andthosefalling 
within the executed form (audiovisual effects, icons, etc.). If they are original, the former are subject to copyright 
specific to computer programs while the latter are subject to common copyright law (general rules applicable in 
principle to all works with exceptions)  
The same may be said about the U.S. law as reflected in several court decisions. Paul Goldstein sums up the U.S. legal 
situation in the following way: 
Videogamestypicallyconsistoftwoseparableelements,eachindependentlycopyrightable:acomputer 
program, characteristically embodied in a semiconductor chip, and the animated audiovisual display that the 
computer program projects onto a video screen when activated by the player. Rights in the computer program 
can be infringed without infringing rights in the audiovisual display, and rights in the audiovisual display can be 
infringed without infringing rights in the computer program. Although the images in video game displays may 
appearinnofixedsequence,courtshavegenerallyheldthattheymeetsection101’srequirementina‘seriesof 
related images’ and thus constitute audiovisual works. 
(Paul Goldstein , Goldstein on Copyright(AlphenaandenRijn,Netherlands:WoltersKluwer,2025),2:144–145)Asimilar
treatment is provided for by Andean Decision 351 in its specific regulation for certain aspects of computer programs, 
leaving other aspects covered by the general standards.

adoption, in April 1994, of the TRIPS Agreement, both of which clarified that computer programs 
should be protected as literary works under the Berne Convention.
Article 4 of the WCT: adapted version of the clarification included in Article 10.1 of the TRIPS 
Agreement
CT-4.11.Article 10.1oftheTRIPSAgreementprovidesasfollows:“Computerprograms,whetherin
source or object code, shall be protected as literary works under the Berne Convention (1971)".445 
Thequestionmayemergewhythisprovisionreferstospecificformsofcomputerprograms
–sourcecodeandobjectcode–when,underArticle 2(1)oftheBerneConvention,aliteraryor
artistic work is protected “whatever may be the form or mode of its expression”. The reason 
seems to be that this was necessary in order to reject certain unfounded views that computer 
programs may only be protected by copyright as literary works as long as they are in source 
code, and that programs in object code, due to their utilitarian functions, are not protected. This 
position was badly founded, not only because the Berne Convention also protects works that 
serve utilitarian purposes, but also because it had failed to take into account that programs may 
be decompiled from object code into source code and that most users only have the program in 
its object code version (only executable by machine). Therefore, limiting copyright protection to 
the source code version alone or leaving a doubt about the protection of the code version would 
have risked undermining the copyright protection of computer programs.
CT-4.12.  There is only one provision in the Berne Convention in which the term “literary 
works”appearsratherthanthegenericterm“literaryandartisticworks”:Article 11 ter of the 
Convention on the public recitation of literary works (and the communication to the public of 
the recitation of such works). This provision is not relevant for computer programs because 
they are not susceptible of recitation. Why is there then a reference to literary works in this 
TRIPS provision? It seems that the intention is to discard any possibility of assimilating computer 
programstoworksofappliedart(whichhadbeenatechniquethatcertainnationallawshad
applied, on the basis of the philosophy that such programs are also works applied for utilitarian 
purposes).(RecallthatunderArticles 2(7)and7(4)oftheBerneConvention,theminimumterm
of protection of works of applied art is shorter than the general term of protection, and the 
protection of such works may be subject to reciprocity.)
CT-4.13.TheclarificationinArticle 4oftheWCT,accordingtowhichcomputerprograms“are
protectedasliteraryworkswithinthemeaningofArticle 2oftheBerneConvention",wastaken 
fromArticle 10.1oftheTRIPSAgreement.WhiletheTRIPSlanguageprovidesthatthey shall be 
protected as literary works, in terms of the respective obligations of the Contracting Parties of 
the WCT and the Members of the WTO, this different language does not make any substantive 
difference.Article 4oftheWCTmakesitsomewhatclearerthat,incomparisonwiththe 
existing provisions of the Berne Convention, no new obligation is involved; computer programs 
correspondtotheconceptofliterary(andartistic)worksunderArticle 2oftheBerneConvention 
and must enjoy protection as such.
CT-4.14. The protection of computer programs “as literary works” is discussed above with respect 
totheuseofthisterminArticle 10.1oftheTRIPSAgreement.SincethiselementinArticle 4ofthe
WCTwastakenfromthatprovision,itsmeaningissupposedtobethesame.Thequestionmay
be asked, however, whether a national law is only compatible with the WCT (and with the TRIPS 
Agreement) if it lists computer programs as a sub-category of “literary works”. It seems that this 
questionshouldbeansweredinthenegative.Whatisimportantisthatthelevel of protection 
for computer programs must not be lower than what the Berne Convention prescribes for the 
protection of literary and artistic works in general (“in general” meaning that no assimilation 
of computer programs to specific categories of works is allowed that would permit derogation 
from the generally prescribed level of protection, such as in the case of works of applied arts). 
Nevertheless, it is more appropriate to list computer programs as a sub-category of literary 
works. This does not mean that national laws are not allowed to include specific provisions on 
445 “Source code” is the original code of the computer programs written in program languages which can be read and 
understood by human beings, although only by those who are specialized in this field. “Object code” is a version of 
theprogramthatisdirectlyusablebyacomputer,inbinaryform–aseriesof“zeros”and“ones”–thatcomputer 
processors may understand, but human beings cannot unless it is “decompiled,” that is, transformed into source code.
