228 computer programs. As mentioned above, there are several examples of specific norms which, in 
spite of their specificity, must be in harmony with the general provisions of the Berne Convention.
CT-4.15.TheagreedstatementconcerningArticle 4wasadoptedattherequestofsome
delegations, mainly from developing countries, which wanted to make sure that the scope of 
applicationoftheprotectionofcomputerprogramsunderArticle 4doesnotchange–and,in
particular,isnotextended–withrespecttothatprovidedinArticle 10.1oftheTRIPSAgreement.
ThiswasfoundnecessarybecausethetextofArticle 10.1oftheTRIPSAgreementandthatof
Article 4oftheWCTarenotidentical.Theformerspeaksof“computerprograms,whetherin 
source code or object code”, and the latter of “computer programs, whatever may be the mode 
or form of their expression". The latter text seems more appropriate since it corresponds to 
theprovisionsofArticle 2(1)oftheBerneConvention(fromwhichtheexpression“whatever
may be the mode or form of their expression” was taken almost word for word). It also seems 
more appropriate considering the possibility that, in the future, the source code/object code 
categorization might become obsolete.
CT-4.16. If the latter possibility were realized (that is, if some new forms of computer programs 
emerged that could not be characterized on the basis of the source code/object code 
dichotomy), it might be asked whether the agreed statement could still be regarded as correct, 
sinceitmightbequestionedwhetherArticle 4oftheWCTweretruly“onapar”withArticle 10.1 
of the TRIPS Agreement. It seems, however, that, even in view of such a potential development, 
the agreed statement would continue to apply, for the following reasons. The reference to the 
mode and form of expression of computer programs is redundant and, in fact, unnecessary 
inviewofArticle 2(1)oftheBerneConvention,accordingtowhichthemodeandformof
expression of a work are irrelevant. At the time of the adoption of the TRIPS Agreement, the two 
categoriesmentionedinArticle 10.1oftheAgreement–sourcecodeandobjectcode–covered
computer programs in any form or mode. If some new productions or new aspects were 
identified that still correspond to the concept of “computer programs” beyond these two code 
formats,Article 10.1wouldstillapplytothem,first,duetotheintentiondulyexpressedinitthat 
itsscopeextendstoallkindsofcomputerprogramsand,second,duetotherequirementofthe
BerneConvention(whichisnotonlyincorporatedintotheAgreementunderArticle 9.1,butalso
referredtoinArticle 10.2)thatcopyrightprotectionmustextendtoworks“whatevermaybethe 
mode or form of [their] expression”.
CT-4.17.Intheagreedstatement,thereisalsoareferencetoArticle 2oftheWCT.Thereasons
forthisarediscussedinthecommentsonthatArticle above.
Article 5
Compilations of Data (Databases)
Compilations of data or other material, in any form, which by reason of the selection or 
arrangement of their contents constitute intellectual creations, are protected as such. This 
protection does not extend to the data or the material itself and is without prejudice to any 
copyright subsisting in the data or material contained in the compilation.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 5:Thescopeofprotectionforcompilationsofdata
(databases)underArticle 5ofthisTreaty,readwithArticle 2,isconsistentwithArticle 2ofthe
Berne Convention and on a par with the relevant provisions of the TRIPS Agreement.
Preparatory work; the impact of the TRIPS Agreement
CT-5.1. In the Committee of Governmental Experts working on what became the WCT, there was 
quitegeneralagreementthatcollectionsofmeredataorotherunprotectedmaterialshouldbe
protected by copyright in the same way as collections of literary and artistic works, provided 
there was originality in the selection or arrangement of the data or other materials. It was found 
that compilations of works werealreadyprotectedascollectionsunderArticle 2(5)oftheBerne 
Convention, while those compilations of data or other unprotected material  which–duetothe
selectionorarrangementthereof–areoriginalshouldbeprotectedunderArticle 2(1)(which
provides a non-exhaustive  list of protected works covering all original productions in the literary 
and artistic domain).

===== PAGE 228 =====
229
PART III. Guides to the three WIPO “Internet Treaties” – the WCT, the WPPT and the BTAP
CT-5.2. The TRIPS Agreement was adopted in April 1994 and had an impact on the way the 
questionoftheprotectionofdatabaseswasfurtherdiscussedintheCommitteeofExperts.The 
working paper prepared for the Committee for its first session after the adoption of the TRIPS 
AgreementreferredtoArticle 10.2oftheAgreementand,inharmonywiththat,proposedthe
inclusion of the same kind of provision in the treaty under preparation.
CT-5.3.Article 10.2oftheTRIPSAgreementprovidesasfollows: 
Compilations of data or other material, whether in machine readable or other form, which 
by reason of the selection or arrangement of their contents constitute intellectual creations 
shall be protected as such. Such protection, which shall not extend to the data or material 
itself, shall be without prejudice to any copyright subsisting in the data or material itself. 
ThisprovisioncoversbothcollectionsofworksmentionedinArticle 2(5)oftheBerneConvention
and compilations of data and other non-protected materials that “by reason of the selection 
or arrangement of their contents constitute intellectual creations”; that is, they are original for 
thisreason(and,thus,althoughnotcoveredbyArticle 2(5)oftheConvention,enjoyprotection
underthegeneralprovisionsofArticle 2(1)).SinceArticle 2(5)oftheBerneConventionisalready
incorporatedintotheAgreementbyArticle 9.1(TRIPSMembersareobligatedtocomplywithit), 
it would have been sufficient to include an interpretative provision on the copyright protection 
of databases in the narrower sense as mentioned above. The fact that this was not done does 
not create any substantive problem, but only some redundancy.
CT-5.4.ThelanguageofArticle 2(5)oftheBerneConventionandArticle 10.2oftheTRIPS 
Agreement differs. The former speaks of the “selection and arrangement” of the contents on 
the basis of which a collection may constitute intellectual creation, while the latter refers to the 
“selection or arrangement”ofthecontents.Fromtheviewpointoftherequirementoforiginality 
as the basic condition of copyright protection, the TRIPS version is more precise. It follows from 
the conjunction “or” that, no matter whether a compilation is original both for the selection 
and for the arrangement of its contents, or only for its selection or its arrangement alone, its 
originalitycounts;ifitisoriginal,itistobeprotectedunderArticle 2(1)orArticle 2(5).Inthe 
Berneprovision,theuseoftheword“and”issemanticallyimprecise.Since,however,Article 2(1)
of the Convention provides that every original production in the literary and artistic domain is 
protected, a compilation/database which is original, although only due to the selection or to 
thearrangementofitscontents,enjoysprotectionunderArticle 2(1),evenifitmightnotbe
protectedbyvirtueofArticle 2(5)oftheConventionalone.
CT-5.5.Theprotectionof“compilations”underArticle 10.2oftheTRIPSAgreement(and
“collections”underArticle 2(5)oftheBerneConvention)isprovidedonlytothosethat,dueto
the selection or arrangement of their contents, are original (and thus “intellectual creations”). 
Therefore, there is no obligation to provide protection for non-original databases by means of 
some sui generis rights as provided under Chapter III of the EU Database Directive.446 In addition to 
the draft WCT and the draft WPPT, a third draft treaty had been submitted to the 1996 Diplomatic 
Conference, on such sui generis protection.447 However, as mentioned in the Introduction to this 
Guide, it was not discussed in substance. A Recommendation was adopted to consider preparing 
such a treaty,448 but the idea did not receive sufficient support, and it was abandoned. 
CT-5.6.TwoclarificationsaremadeinthesecondsentenceofArticle 10.2oftheTRIPSAgreement:
first, that the protection of compilations is without prejudice to any copyright subsisting in 
any element of their contents (that is, those elements continue to enjoy copyright protection 
independentlyoftheprotectionofthecompilations).ThisisinaccordancewithArticle 2(5)ofthe
Berne Convention, which provides that the protection of collections is “without prejudice to the 
copyright in each of the works forming part of such selections". Second, the second sentence 
explicitly states that the protection granted for compilations does not extend to the data or 
material contained in them. That is, if an element is not protected by copyright, it does not obtain 
copyright protection by virtue of being included in a compilation protected by copyright.
446 Directive 96/9/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 March 1996 on the legal protection of 
databases,OJ L 77,March 27,1996.
447 See Records of the 1996 Diplomatic Conference ,DocumentCRNR/DC/6,332–374.
448 See Records of the 1996 Diplomatic Conference , 97.

230 Article 5 of the WCT: adapted version of the clarification in Article 10.2 of the TRIPS Agreement
CT-5.7. Although some other options were also discussed during the preparatory work of the 
WCT, in the end the 1996 Diplomatic Conference favored the adoption of the TRIPS version. The 
reasons were the same as for the clarification concerning the copyright protection of computer 
programs: this was a thoroughly negotiated text, and certain delegations were particularly keen 
on making sure that the corresponding provisions in the WCT did not lead to a different scope or 
level of protection.
CT-5.8.Nevertheless,thetextofArticle 5stillisnotexactlythesameasthatofArticle 10.2of 
the TRIPS Agreement. One difference is that, while the latter speaks of compilations “in machine 
readable and other form”, the former uses the more general term “in any form”. In practice, this 
means the same coverage of compilations, because the wording of the WCT provision means 
machine readable plus any other form, which amounts to “in any form” (both digital and analog). 
Nevertheless, the explicit reference to machine readable form is a useful clarification in the 
TRIPS provision, and it is not lost in the WCT despite the differing language. Due to the clear 
intentionoftheDiplomaticConference–whichisdulyandexplicitlyexpressedintheagreed
statementintheWCT–toapplyArticle 5oftheWCTwith the same coverage asthatofArticle 10.2
of the TRIPS Agreement, this clarification remains relevant in the context of the WCT.
CT-5.9.TheseconddifferencebetweenthetwoprovisionsisthatArticle 5oftheWCTsimply 
declares that the collections mentioned in it are protected,whileArticle 10.2oftheTRIPS
Agreement,asinthecaseofitsArticle 10.1oncomputerprograms,uses“shall”.Thesame
applies concerning this difference as is remarked above in respect of computer programs: as 
regards the obligations of the Contracting Parties of the WCT and the Members of the WTO, 
respectively, the differing language does not mean any substantive difference. The language 
ofArticle 5oftheWCT,however,makesitclearerthatthisisjustaninterpretativeprovision;in
comparison with the existing provisions of the Berne Convention, there is no new obligation. 449
Article 6
Right of Distribution
(1) Authors of literary and artistic works shall enjoy the exclusive right of authorizing the 
making available to the public of the original and copies of their works through sale or 
other transfer of ownership. 
(2) Nothing in this Treaty shall affect the freedom of Contracting Parties to determine the 
conditions,ifany,underwhichtheexhaustionoftherightinparagraph (1)appliesafter
the first sale or other transfer of ownership of the original or a copy of the work with 
the authorization of the author.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticles 6and7:AsusedintheseArticles,theexpressions
“copies” and “original and copies”, being subject to the right of distribution and the right of 
rental under the said Articles, refer exclusively to fixed copies that can be put into circulation as 
tangible objects.
CT-6.1.AspointedoutinthecommentsonArticle 8below,theactsofinteractivemaking
available to the public may also take the form of making available copies for downloading and 
thismayalsobecharacterizedasdistributionofcopies.Since,intheWCT,itisunderArticle 8
(on the right of communication to the public) that the issue of such rights has been settled, 
thepossibleapplicationoftherightofdistributionforsuchtransmissions–onthebasisof
the “umbrellasolution”–isdiscussedinthecommentsonthatArticle.Hereitissufficientto 
remark that, although those interactive acts may also be characterized as “distribution”, legally 
theymustbeprotectedunder(thesecondpartof)Article 8asinteractivemakingavailableto 
the public; therefore, no exhaustion of right takes place where such an act is performed. This 
is clear due to the fact that the effect of exhaustion of right concerns the right of distribution 
449 Nothing in the text of the Treaty excludes sui generis protection for the compilers of databases, however, as provided 
in Directive 96/9/CE of 11 March 1996 of the European Parliament and the Council on the legal protection of databases.

exclusively,andthatright–asisprovidedintheagreedstatementquotedabove–appliesonly
to making available to the public tangible copies; it does not apply to making digital copies 
available online; there is no such effect as online exhaustion of rights. The exhaustion (or first 
sale) doctrine has never applied to the making of additional copies, but only to the circulation 
of a particular physical copy. The recognition that digital copies are also covered by the right of 
reproduction does not change the basic character of the exhaustion doctrine; it does not permit 
the making of additional copies “in any manner or form”. A work embodied in a digital copy 
cannot be further disseminated without making more copies. The exhaustion doctrine does not 
apply to purely intangible digital copies. 
CT-6.2.InthecommentsonArticle 14intheGuidetotheBerneConventioninthiscollection,
it is pointed out that a kind of right of first distribution (which is exhausted with the first sale 
ofcopies),whichisprovidedforinArticle 6oftheWCT,mayalsobededucedfromtherightof
reproduction, and that it seems to be a defensible position that, under the Berne Convention, 
thisrightisrecognizednotonlyinrelationtocinematographicworks(onwhichArticles 14and
14bis contain explicit provisions on a right of distribution), but implicitly also to other categories 
of works. Nevertheless, the theory of “implicit recognition” did not receive unanimous support 
during the preparatory work; therefore, it is useful that the WCT also explicitly recognizes the right 
of (first) distribution.
CT-6.3. Concerning the right of distribution, the truly challenging issue is its exhaustion with 
the first sale of copies, and, in particular, the territorial effect of such exhaustion. During the 
preparatory work of the WCT, attempts were made to try to recognize a national or regional 
effect–withthecorollaryoftherecognitionofarightofimportation.Theattemptsfailed,and 
theissueofexhaustion–alongwithitsterritorialeffect–asprovidedforinArticle 6(2),wasleft 
to national legislation.
CT-6.4.ConcerningtheagreedstatementaddedtoArticle 6(andtoArticle 7)twothingsshouldbe
emphasized. First, it means that the right of distribution does not apply to intangible copies (and 
thus also, as noted above, the exhaustion doctrine does not apply to making available intangible 
digital copies). Second, although it is possible to characterize online interactive making available of 
copies as “distribution” (in the sense of distribution as reproduction through online transmissions) 
it does not change the obligation to provide protection in accordance with the second part of 
Article 8oftheWCTonanexclusive–andnon-exhausting–rightofonlineinteractivemaking
available to the public of works either through streaming or through downloading.
Article 7
Right of Rental
(1) Authors of
(i) computer programs;
(ii) cinematographic works; and
(iii) works embodied in phonograms, as determined in the national law of 
Contracting Parties,
 shall enjoy the exclusive right of authorizing commercial rental to the public of the 
originals or copies of their works.
(2) Paragraph (1)shallnotapply
(i) in the case of computer programs, where the program itself is not the essential 
object of the rental; and
(ii)  in the case of cinematographic works, unless such commercial rental has led 
to widespread copying of such works materially impairing the exclusive right 
of reproduction.
(3) Notwithstandingtheprovisionsofparagraph (1),aContractingPartythat,onApril
15,1994,hadandcontinuestohaveinforceasystemofequitableremunerationof
authors for rental of copies of their works embodied in phonograms may maintain that 
system provided that the commercial rental of works embodied in phonograms is not 
giving rise to the material impairment of the exclusive right of reproduction of authors.

The right of rental losing relevance
CT-7.1.Whentherightofrentalwasrecognizedintheinternationaltreaties–in1994by
Articles 11and14.4oftheTRIPSAgreementandthenin1996byArticle 7oftheWCTand
Articles 9and13oftheWPPT–rentalstillwasasignificantwayofexploitingfilms;first,in 
theformofrecordedvideocassettesand,then,bymeansofDVDsandBlu-raydiscs.Fromthe 
middle of the 2000s, however, the distribution model began changing to video-on-demand 
online “distribution”.450 The migration from physical to intangible copies has led to the decline 
not only of distribution by sales but also of rental of copies of films in the sense in which the 
rightofrentalisprovidedintheWCT,theWPPTandtheBTAP–thatis,asclarifiedintheagreed
statement, only applicable to the making available of tangible copies. Nevertheless, although 
this form of exploitation continues to lose significance, it has not yet disappeared completely; 
therefore,theprovisionsofArticle 9oftheBTAPstillareanalyzedbelow.Inthecaseof
computer programs, a similar migration has taken place from rental of tangible copies to online 
“distribution”,whiletherentalofcopies–withtheexceptionofsomecountries,suchasJapan–
has never become a significant use of phonograms.
No definition of “rental”
CT-7.2. No definition is provided either in the TRIPS Agreement or in the WIPO “Internet 
Treaties” of “rental” or “commercial rental”. In the Basic Proposal for what became the WPPT, 
Article 2(f)stillcontainedadefinitionwhichreadasfollows:“’rental’ofaphonogrammeans 
any transfer of the possession of a copy of a phonogram for consideration for a limited period 
of time”.451 This seemed to be the generally accepted concept of “rental”. The notes to the draft 
provisionintheBasicProposalpointedoutthatitdoesnotextendto“publiclending”–anact
not covered either by the TRIPS Agreement or by the new WIPO treaties, which, according to the 
notes, meant “transfer of the possession of an object for a limited period of time, free of charge, 
in a not-for-profit transaction”.452 It followed from this that the act of “rental” and “lending” was 
(rightly) regarded to be the same in that in both cases copies are made available for a limited 
periodoftime–withtheonlydifferencebeingthat“rental”was“forconsideration”andlending 
“free of charge in a not-for-profit transaction”. The expression “ commercial rental” [emphasis 
added]isusedinArticles 11and14.4oftheTRIPSAgreement;fromthereitwastransposed
intoArticle 7oftheWCT,Articles 9and13oftheWPPT,andArticle 9oftheBTAP.Theadjective
“commercial” is suitable to differentiate rental from lending, but it may also be understood to 
mean that “rental” is by definition for commercial “consideration”.
Article 7 of the WCT: an adapted version of the corresponding provisions of the TRIPS Agreement
CT-7.3. The Berne Convention does not provide for a right of rental. Thus, the obligation 
underArticle 7oftheWCTonthisrightisabovetheminimumlevelofprotectionunderthe
Convention. It is among those provisions that were adapted from the TRIPS Agreement.
CT-7.4. The extent and conditions of the protection of the right of rental was negotiated 
duringtheUruguayRoundofnegotiations,and,asaresult,quiteacomplexregulationwas
incorporated into the TRIPS Agreement. As mentioned above, it was a kind of guiding principle

during the preparatory work of the WCT and the WPPT that no agreement reached in the 
framework of the Uruguay Round should be altered. Therefore, although attempts were 
made at the 1996 Diplomatic Conference to recognize a general right of rental extending to 
all categories of works, those attempts failed; it was ultimately accepted that the scope and 
conditions of the protection of the rental right under the two new Treaties should be the same 
as under the relevant provisions of the TRIPS Agreement.
CT-7.5. In accordance with this agreement, the scope of works to be covered by the right of 
rental – as a minimum obligation – extends to the same categories as in the TRIPS Agreement: 
(i)computerprograms(firstsentenceofArticle 11intheTRIPSAgreement–Article 7(1)(i)inthe
WCT);cinematographicworks(firstsentenceofArticle 11intheTRIPSAgreement–Article 7(1)(ii) 
in the WCT); and (iii) “works embodied in phonograms, as determined in the national law”  (first 
sentenceofArticle 14.4intheTRIPSAgreement–Article 7(1)(iii)intheWCT).
CT-7.6. Concerning all three categories, the WCT contains the same provisions on certain 
limitations and conditions as those provided for in the TRIPS Agreement. As regards computer 
programs, the obligation to grant a right of rental does not apply where the program is not an 
essentialobjectoftherental(thirdsentenceofArticle 11intheTRIPSAgreement–Article 7(2)(i)  
in the WCT). Computer programs are included in cars, aircraft and various machines that 
arefrequentlyusedthroughrental.Insuchcasesacomputerprogramobviouslyisnotthe
essential object of the rental. It would be anachronistic to insist that, in addition to concluding a 
contract on the rental of a car, a separate authorization is needed for the rental of the computer 
programs built into the car. This exception does not apply to the rental of computers to which 
computer programs have been uploaded. In such a case, the computer is not a mere element of 
a complex machine, and, due to the fact that the function of the program is exactly to operate 
the computer, it cannot be said that the program is not an essential object of the rental.
CT-7.7. The right of rental in cinematographic works is more heavily limited since, in this case, it 
only applies if the commercial rental has led to widespread copying of such works, and through 
this,materiallyimpairstheexclusiverightofreproduction(secondsentenceofArticle 11in
theTRIPSAgreement–Article 7(2)(ii)intheWCT).Thereare,however,atleasttworeasonsfor 
which doubts may emerge about the justification of this limitation. First, although widespread 
reproduction, in the form of private copying, may be a side effect of rental of such works, it 
ispossibletotakeintoaccounttheeffectofprivatecopyingmoreadequatelythroughthe
applicationofaremunerationright–recognizedinseveralcountries–basedona “levy” on 
reproductionequipmentand/ormaterials.Therearegoodreasonstobelievethat,where
private copying becomes so widespread that it unreasonably prejudices the legitimate interests 
oftheownersofrights,itfollowsfromArticle 9(2)oftheBerneConventionthatsomeefforts 
shouldbemadetotrytoeliminate–oratleastreducetoareasonablelevel–theprejudice
through a remuneration system. Addressing this problem through a rental right does not 
seem to be sufficient (the more so because, for private copying, different sources may be used, 
among them off-air or online copying). It seems more appropriate to introduce guarantees to 
maintain the value of the right of reproduction when it is jeopardized. Second, it should also 
be taken into account that rental is a separate form of exploitation of works irrespective of 
whether or not it leads to private copying. These aspects, however, are losing relevance with the 
migration of works to online uses in the form of intangible copies.
CT-7.8. The limitation of the right of rental concerning phonograms is regulated in an even more 
complexmannerinArticle 7(3)oftheWCT.InthesecondsentenceofArticle 14.4oftheTRIPS
Agreement, in substance , the same provision may be found: 
Ifon15April1994aMemberhasinforceasystemofequitableremunerationofright
holders in respect of the rental of phonograms, it may maintain such system provided 
that the commercial rental of phonograms is not giving rise to the material impairment of 
the exclusive rights of reproduction of right holders. 
ThisprovisionwasincludedintheTRIPSAgreementattherequestofJapan,whichhadsucha
system, and, as with all the other elements of the relevant norms of the Agreement, this was 
also taken over without any substantive modification. The substantive identity of the two texts 
goes so far that the WCT text gives the same date as in the TRIPS provision, although this is 
the date of adoption of the TRIPS Agreement. The provision also includes an “impairment test”.

===== PAGE 233 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
234 Here, this test seems somewhat more appropriate because it is not linked to the copying of the 
rented phonograms but to the impairment of the right of reproduction in general.
No “online rental” (or “online lending”)
CT-7.9.TheagreedstatementconcerningArticles 6and7ontheconceptof“copies”inthe
applicationoftherightsofdistributionandrentalisdiscussedinthecommentsonArticle 6 
above. It follows from this that there is no “online rental”. If the copy of a work is made available 
to the public for a limited period of time (based on a specific software solution) in such a way 
that it may be accessed by the members of the public from a place and at a time individually 
chosen by them, it might be characterized as rental, but it is, in fact, an act of interactive online 
makingavailabletothepublic.Sincetheactisexactlythesame–justthecommercialnatureis
missing–thesameappliestolending.Therefore,whereinanationallawtherightoflending
is applied, it is limited to the making available of tangible copies. Similar to rental, there is no 
online lending either; the online making available to the public of copies for a limited time free 
of charge in such a way that members of the public may access them from a place and at a time 
individuallychosenbythemiscoveredbyArticle 8oftheWCT.Itisanothermatterthat,onthe
basisofArticle 10(1)oftheTreatyonthethree-steptest,broaderexceptionsorlimitationsmay
be provided to it than to the right of rental (concerning the same acts but for consideration).
The meaning of “works embodied in phonograms, as determined in the national law of 
Contracting Parties”
CT-7.10. As mentioned above, according to the intention of the Diplomatic Conference, the 
obligationsunderArticle 7oftheWCTweretobeexactlythesameasunderthecorresponding 
provisionsoftheTRIPSAgreement.However,quiteathornyproblememergedintheapplication
of this principle. While the provisions of the TRIPS Agreement are clear concerning the right 
ofrentalforcomputerprogramsandcinematographicworks,themeaningofitsArticle 14.4
on the right of rental of phonograms raised some problems, as it was interpreted in different 
ways at the Conference. The source of the problem was that, while this provision mentions 
producers of phonograms explicitly, concerning the other possible beneficiaries, it only uses the 
general term “and any other right holders in phonograms as determined in a Member’s law”. 
Thus,theinclusionofprovisionsonarightofrentalforauthorsandperformers–inrespect 
ofphonogramsinwhichtheirworksandperformances,respectively,areembodied–required 
interpretation of the relevant provisions of the TRIPS Agreement. The Diplomatic Conference 
triedtotransposethesomewhatambiguouslanguageofArticle 14.4oftheTRIPSAgreementin
as intact a manner as possible into the WCT (as well as into the WPPT), but it adopted an agreed 
statementthatcorrespondsonlytooneofthetwoconflictinginterpretationsofArticle 14.4(and 
of the new provisions in the WCT and the WPPT).
CT-7.11.ThefirstofthetwopossibleinterpretationsofArticle 14.4oftheTRIPSAgreement
was presented in the WIPO study on the “Implications of the TRIPS Agreement on Treaties 
Administered by WIPO” in the following way:
Asdiscussedabove,underArticle 11,inrespectofcomputerprograms,Membersare
obliged to provide for authors and their successors in title the right to authorize or to 
prohibit the commercial rental to the public of originals or copies of their copyright 
works. That obligation is applicable mutatis mutandis for phonograms in favor of 
producersofphonograms.Asregardsotherpossiblerightholdersinphonograms–such
as performers whose performances, and authors the performances of whose works, 
arefixedinphonograms–theexpression“anyotherrightholdersinphonogramsas
determined in a Member’s law” indicates that Members are free to extend or not to 
extend that right to those other right holders. 453
The ambiguous language made such an interpretation possible based on the phrase “as 
determined in a Member’s law”, which could be read to indicate “it is a matter for the legislation 
of Members”.
453 Implications of the TRIPS Agreement on Treaties Administered by WIPO , publication no. 464 (E) (WIPO, 1996), 28, 
para. 70.

===== PAGE 234 =====
235
PART III. Guides to the three WIPO “Internet Treaties” – the WCT, the WPPT and the BTAP
CT-7.12. The other interpretation was based on the argument that authors have an exclusive right to 
authorize the inclusion of their works in phonograms (and performers may have similar rights), and 
that such rights make the authors (and performers) concerned rightholders in phonograms. The 
problem with this argument (in addition to the above-discussed ambiguous term “as determined 
in a Member’s law”) is that the provision speaks of rights in phonograms, and not also in the works 
and/or performances embodied in the phonograms. The advocates of the first interpretation 
mentioned above may, and do, point out that the owners of rights in phonograms proper are the 
producers of phonograms, and the subject matter of the rights of other rightholders are not the 
phonograms but the works and performances that are embodied in them.
CT-7.13. As mentioned above, in accordance with the principle adopted at the Diplomatic 
Conference that nothing in the negotiated provisions of the TRIPS Agreement should be 
changed,theconsciousdecisionwasmadetotransposetheambiguoustextofArticle 14.4
oftheAgreementintoArticle 7oftheWCTintentionallywithaslittlechangeaspossible.Asa 
result,Article 7(1)(iii)oftheTreatyusestheexpression“worksembodiedinphonograms,as 
determined in the national law of Contracting Parties ”. In the new context (separated from the 
rights in phonograms), however, the provision became even more ambiguous.
CT-7.14. Since the intention was to maintain the same meaning of the provision as in the 
TRIPS Agreement, this, in principle, could also have brought with it the possibility of differing 
interpretations. However, during the informal consultations, several delegations insisted that 
a restrictive interpretation should be adopted in the context of the WCT and the WPPT. This 
wasdonethroughtheadoptionofthesecondagreedstatementconcerningArticle 7,quoted
above.Accordingtothisagreedstatement,“theobligationunderArticle 7(1)doesnotrequirea
Contracting Party to provide an exclusive right of commercial rental to authors who, under that 
Contracting Party’s law, are not granted rights in respect of phonograms”. This means practically 
thesameaswhatfollowsfromtheabove-quotedtextoftheWIPOstudy:“[ContractingStates]
are free to extend or not to extend” the right of rental granted in respect of phonograms to 
owners of rights other than producers of phonograms, such as authors (and performers).
CT-7.15. The agreed statement also states that the interpretation offered in it “is consistent 
withArticle 14.4oftheTRIPSAgreement”.ThisisakindofindirectinterpretationoftheTRIPS 
Agreement,whichmayraisespecificquestionsfortheWTObodies.Thosebodiesarenot 
obliged to accept the interpretation adopted by the WIPO Diplomatic Conference, but they 
can hardly fully neglect it either, taking into account that a great number of WTO Members 
participated in its unanimous adoption, albeit at a forum outside the WTO.
CT-7.16. In the Introduction to the guides to these three “Internet Treaties”, it is pointed out 
that the TRIPS Agreement had a mixed impact on the preparation of the WCT and the WPPT. 
The principle that the issues settled in it should not be renegotiated facilitated the adoption of 
some provisions, but it was also an obstacle to the reconsideration of certain aspects where 
thiswouldhavebeenjustified.TheambiguityofArticle 14.4oftheTRIPSAgreementwas 
recognized by the delegations, and it would have been reasonable to try to eliminate it. Instead 
of this, the “don’t touch what has been agreed in TRIPS” principle prevailed and, although the 
delegations were aware of it, the ambiguity was maintained. It is submitted that, if the problem 
had been addressed by the 1996 Diplomatic Conference, it could have led to making it clear that 
therightofrentalinphonograms–inviewoftheeconomicandculturalvalueofphonograms
andthecloseconnectionwiththerightofreproductiondulyreflectedinArticle 14.4ofthe 
TRIPSAgreement,Article 7(3)oftheWCTandArticles 9(2)and13(2)oftheWPPT–wasequally 
applicable not only for the producers of phonograms, but also for the performers and authors 
whose performances and works are embodied in the phonograms. It is submitted that this 
sort of application of these provisions of the WCT and the WPPT would be in accordance with 
the spirit of the treaties and the context in which the right of rental is provided. However, as 
mentioned above, the relevance of the issue is fading away with the migration of the use of 
phonograms from distribution of tangible objects to online making available to the public of 
digital copies (and increasingly by streaming rather than through downloading).

236 Article 8
Right of Communication to the Public
WithoutprejudicetotheprovisionsofArticles 11(1)(ii),11 bis(1)(i) and (ii), 11ter(1)(ii), 14(1)(ii) and 
14bis(1) of the Berne Convention, authors of literary and artistic works shall enjoy the exclusive 
right of authorizing any communication to the public of their works, by wire or wireless means, 
including the making available to the public of their works in such a way that members of the 
public may access these works from a place and at a time individually chosen by them.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 8:Itisunderstoodthatthemereprovisionofphysical
facilities for enabling or making a communication does not in itself amount to communication 
within the meaning of this Treaty or the Berne Convention. It is further understood that 
nothinginArticle 8precludesaContractingPartyfromapplyingArticle 11 bis(2).
Emergence of the “umbrella solution”; its modified application in Article  8 of the WCT
CT-8.1. In the course of the preparatory work of the WCT and the WPPT, there was 
agreement among the experts and government delegations that the placement of works 
on, and transmission through, the Internet should be made subject to an exclusive right of 
authorization.Therewasalsoquiteageneralwishtotrytoapplyexistingnorms(onthebasis
of which established practices had emerged and long-term contractual relations were based). 
However, when the existing rights were reviewed, it was seen that the digital interactive 
transmissions had confused the borderline between the two traditional groups of rights: copy-
related rights and non-copy-related rights. 454
CT-8.2. Making works available online for interactive use had confused the borderline between 
these two groups of rights in two aspects. First, it had become possible to make a work available 
through the Internet with the support of digital rights management (DRM) only allowing 
access to a work if the members of the public fulfill certain conditions. Thus, the actual uses of 
awork–dependingonwhatwasallowedunderwhatconditionsbytheDRMsystem–wasnot
necessarily determined at the moment of the making available of the work and by the person or 
entity alone who or which was carrying out the act of making available. It was the members of 
the public, who, through a virtual negotiation with the system, were to obtain access to and the 
possibility of using the work, and who were to choose whether the use would be deferred (by 
downloading a more than transient copy) or direct (through streaming just for watching a film 
or listening to music). Second, with online availability and interactive transmissions of works, 
hybrid forms of uses had emerged which did not respect the previously established border 
betweencopy-relatedandnon-copy-relatedrights(whenacopywasobtained–downloaded–it 
was also through transmission of electronic impulses, and, when a recording was streamed, also 
certain temporary copies were made).
CT-8.3.Inrespectofthequestionwhichrightsmightbeapplied,thekeynegotiatingdelegations
did not necessarily find themselves on the same side of the copy-related rights/non-copy-related 
rights border. Two major trends emerged, one trying to base the solution on the right of distribution 
and the other applying a broad right of communication to the public. It was not merely on some 
theoretical bases that a given country favored this or that option. The positions depended, to a 
great extent, on the existing national laws (which rights, for whom, and granted to what extent), 
454 Copy-related rights  (in addition to the basic right of reproduction) are the right of distribution, the right of rental, 
and the right of public lending (where recognized), covering acts by means of which copies are made available to the 
public; typically for deferred use, since the act of making available and the perception (studying, watching, listening 
to) of the signs, images and sounds in which a work or a sound recording is expressed (that is, the actual use) by the 
members of the public differ in time. Non-copy-related rights  (such as the right of public performance, the right of 
broadcasting, the right of communication to the public by wire), on the other hand, cover acts through which works 
orobjectsofrelatedrightsaremadeavailablefordirect–thatis,notdeferred–use(perceiving,studying,watching, 
listening to) by the members of the public.

the established practices, the position of the “reliance parties” (that is, those who have relied on the 
public domain status of works before they became protected),455 and the related national interests.
CT-8.4. When it had become clear that the international copyright community was faced with 
twobasicoptions–theapplicationoftherightofdistributionortheapplicationoftherightof
communicationtothepublic–(alongwith,ofcourse,somecombinationoftheseoptions),itwas
soonrecognizedthattheadoptionofanyoftheseoptionswasnotaneasymatterofrequiringa
simple decision after which the rest could be arranged automatically.
CT-8.5. The negotiating parties did not agree on the legal characterization of the acts of making 
works available online, and this led to a deadlock in the preparatory work. In order to eliminate 
the problem, the WIPO Secretariat worked out a compromise solution which contained the 
following elements: (i) the act of interactive making available to the public should be described 
as such in a neutral way, free of any specific legal characterization (for example, to be described 
as making a work available to the public by wire or by wireless means, for access by members 
of the public); (ii) such a description should not be technology-specific, but should express the 
interactive nature of digital transmissions by clarifying that a work is to be considered as having 
been made available “to the public” when the members of the public may access it at a time and 
in a place freely chosen by them; (iii) in respect of the legal characterization of the exclusive right 
or rights sufficient freedom should be left to national legislation; and (iv) the gaps in the Berne 
Conventiononthecoverageoftherelevantrights–therightsofcommunicationtothepublic
anddistribution–shouldbeeliminated.
CT-8.6.Thissolution–referredtoasthe“umbrellasolution”–wasofferedbytheWIPO 
Secretariat to the key negotiating parties, who decided to use it to eliminate the deadlock. The 
groupofindustrializedcountries–theso-called“StockholmGroup”–agreedthattheproposal 
would be presented by the delegation of the European Communities and supported by the 
other members of the group. It was also discussed and accepted at the regional consultation 
meetings organized by WIPO in the three major regions of developing countries (Africa, Asia and 
the Pacific, and Latin America and the Caribbean), and it was adopted by consensus at the 1996 
DiplomaticConferenceasprovidedinArticle 8oftheWCTandArticles 10and14oftheWPPT
(andmuchlater,in2012,itwasalsoincludedinArticle 10oftheBTAP).456 The adopted text in the 
provisions of the three Treaties is this: “exclusive right of authorizing […] the making available to 
the public of […] [works/performances fixed in phonograms/phonograms/performances fixed 
in audiovisual fixations], by wire or wireless means, [457] in such a way that members of the public 
may access these works from a place and at a time individually chosen by them".
CT-8.7. Had the Stockholm Group proposed the original “umbrella solution” worked out by the WIPO 
Secretariat, there would be fewer interpretation problems. However, in the proposal submitted by 
theEuropeanCommunitiesonbehalfofthegroupforwhatbecamelaterArticle 8oftheWCT,the
“umbrella” was opened only halfway; the solution was applied in a modified manner. The countries 
in the group that preferred the right of communication to the public as a general option seemed 
to be more numerous; therefore, first, the right of communication to the public was extended to

the application of a right other than the right of communication to the public or through the 
combination of different rights as long as the acts of interactive making available to the public 
were fully covered by the right or rights applied. 459 By a possible “other” right, first of all, the 
right of distribution was meant.
CT-8.9.TheUSstatementonthepossiblealternativewaysofimplementingArticle 8wasvalidnot
onlybecauseitwasnotopposedbyanydelegationattheDiplomaticConference,butalso–and
moreimportantly–becauseitwasinaccordancewiththewell-establishedpracticefollowed
in the application of the rights granted by the Berne Convention, whose compatibility with the 
Conventionhadneverbeenquestioned.Thatis,thatthelegalcharacterizationofarightmaydiffer
from the way it is characterized in the Convention. For example, in certain countries, “performing 
rights” (or the French provisions on the droit de “représentation”) cover not only those acts that are 
mentioned in the provisions of the Berne Convention as public performances of works, but also 
the right of broadcasting and the right of communication to the public which, under the Berne 
Convention, are separate rights. In other countries, the right of communication to the public (for 
example in the Andean countries)460 is applied as a general right covering all the three categories 
of the rights mentioned. In a third group of countries, it is the right of broadcasting which also 
extends to communication to the public by wire. With the “umbrella solution”, the differing legal 
characterizations were crossing the border between copy-related rights and non-copy-related 
rights–inaccordancewiththehybridnatureoftheactsofmakingworksavailableonline.
CT-8.10. However, it is important to underline again that the freedom of legal characterizations 
of the acts covered by the rights concerned is limited. The nature of the right (whether it is an 
exclusive right; as is the right of making available) and its level of protection (what exceptions or 
limitations may be applied) must be fully respected. 461

of relative freedom of” in this way [emphasis is added to the adjective “relative”]:
1. It is a broadly applied practice in national legislation to use terms other than those appearing in the international 
norms on copyright and related rightsconcerningcertainactscoveredbysuchrights,andconsequentlybythe

are characterized legally in the said international norms. For example, several countries grant a “right of public

broadcasting and the right of communication to the public by cable (wire), which, in the Berne Convention are construed as

scope of the right of broadcasting  determined in the Berne Convention (initsArticle 11bis(1)).

Online making available of copies characterized as act of “distribution”; no online exhaustion 
of rights
CT-8.11. Concerning the right of distribution, the WCT also eliminated the gaps in the Berne 
Convention.Article 6(1)oftheWCTprovidesforanexclusiverighttoauthorizethemaking
available to the public of originals and copies of works through sale or other transfer of 
ownership; that is, for an exclusive right of distribution. As analyzed above, an agreed statement 
addedtoArticles 6and7(ontherightsofdistributionandrental)–clarifiesthat “[a]s used in 
these Articles, the expressions ‘copies’ and ‘original and copies’, being subject to the right of 
distribution and the right of rental under the said Articles, refer exclusively to fixed copies that 
can be put into circulation as tangible objects ” (emphasis added).
CT-8.12. Therefore, although it is possible to characterize the acts of making works available 
online to the public for downloading as “distribution”, the principle of relative freedom of legal 
characterizationofactsandrightsrequiresthat,sincetheexhaustioneffectoftheexerciseof 
therightofdistributiononlyapplies,underArticle 6oftheWCT,totangiblecopies,itcannot 
beextendedtoactsofinteractivemakingavailableofdigital–thatis,intangible–copiesunder 
Article 8.NoonlinedigitalexhaustionisallowedundertheWIPOTreaties.Thisisexplicitly 
statedinArticle 3(3)oftheEUInformationSocietyDirective 462 and confirmed in the Tom Kabinet 
casebytheCJEU.463 In the United States, it was clarified in the ReDigi case that there is no online 
exhaustion (the 2nd Circuit Court rejected the appeal against the District Court judgment which 
stated this concerning online re-use of phonograms (“sound recordings”)). 464
An act of online interactive making available to the public takes place as soon as a work is 
made available to the public
CT-8.13. The expression “making available tothepublic”(emphasisadded)inArticle 8oftheWCT,
Articles 10and14oftheWPPTandArticle 10oftheBTAPmayhardlybeinterpreted–byvirtue
ofArticles 31and32oftheVCLT–inanywayotherthanthat, as soon as a work is uploaded on 
the Internet and thus becomes available to the members of the public to access it from a place 
and at a time individually chosen by them, an act of making available to the public takes place. 
Since the text of the treaty provisions is clear in this respect, there is not a need for its separate 
confirmation by the documents of the preparatory work.465 Nevertheless, the preparatory 
work does confirm this meaning of “making available to the public”. The documents of the 1996 
Diplomatic Conference make it clear that there was consensus about this among the delegations.
CT-8.14. When the delegation of the European Communities on behalf of the “Stockholm 
Group” of industrialized countries submitted the text to the Preparatory Committee before 
theDiplomaticConference–which,withminorwordingdifferences,wasthesameasinthe
provisionofArticle 8oftheWCT–itclarifiedthis:
[U]nder the proposal, for the completion of the act of communication to the public, it 
wouldnotberequiredthatanactualtransmissiontakesplace;forthis,themeremaking
available of works to the public (for example, the uploading of a work to a bulletin board) 
forsubsequenttransmissionwouldbesufficient.466
462 Article 3oftheDirective2001/29/ECoftheEuropeanParliamentandoftheCouncilof22May2001ontheharmonizationof
certainaspectsofcopyrightandrelatedrightsintheinformationsociety,OJL167,June22,2001(hereinafter:Information
Society Directive) provides as follows: “The rights referred to in paragraphs 1 and 2 shall not be exhausted by any act of 
communication to the public or making available to the public as set out in this Article.” The rights referred to are the right 
of communication to the public and the right of interactive making available to the public.

240 CT-8.15.ItisevenmoredecisivethatthenotesaddedtoArticle 10intheBasicProposal–which
becameArticle 8oftheWCTwiththesametext–statedthisclearlytoo:“Therelevantactisthe 
making available of the work by providing access to it. What counts is the initial act of making the 
work available”.467 [Emphasis added.] This is so in the same way as in the case of the exclusive 
rightofdistributionwhich,underArticle 6oftheWCT,Articles 8and12oftheWPPTand
Article 10oftheBTAP,appliesfor“makingavailable to the public” of copies [emphasis added]. 
The act of distribution takes place as soon as copies are made available; it is not a further 
conditionthatthemembersofthepublicbuythecopies–eveniftheyusuallydo.
CT-8.16.However,thefollowingquestionsmaybe–andsometimesare–asked.First,the
uploading of a work on the Internet is an act of reproduction, as also clearly recognized in 
the relevant agreed statements adopted at the Diplomatic Conference. If such an uploading 
is already covered by an exclusive right, why is there a need for a separate right of making 
available which takes place already with the uploading? Second, if an act of making available to 
the public takes place by uploading and thus by rendering a work or subject matter of related 
rightsaccessible,howarethesubsequentinteractivetransmissionsinwhichtheactualuseby 
the public consists taken into account?
CT-8.17.Theanswerstothesequestionsfollowfromthedialecticsofinteractivity.Theactismaking
a work available to access for use by the members of the public. The actual access by the members 
of the public consists in the realization of the possibility of gaining access. The final classification 
of the thus realized act depends on (i) the purpose of the use or uses for which the work is made 
available, and (ii) the use for which the work is accessed by the members of the public.
CT-8.18. For the concept of making available to the public, similar considerations apply as to the 
conceptofpublication,whichmayberegardedasaspecific,qualifiedformofdistributionof
copies.UnderArticle 3(3)oftheBerneConvention,aworkispublishedif“theavailability of […] 
copieshasbeensuchastosatisfythereasonablerequirementsofthepublic”[emphasisadded].
In this case too, the availability of copies is sufficient, as is pointed out on the basis of the analysis 
oftheprovisionandits“preparatorywork”inthetreatisebySamRicketsonandJaneGinsburg:
The wording of the definition indicates that it is the availability of copies that constitutes 
publication. Thus, if there is no public demand for copies, this should be irrelevant–the
copies are available to meet any demand that may reasonably be expected to exist, and 
the author’s Berne coverage should not be prejudiced by the fact that there is none at all 
[…]. [T]he status of ‘published work’ should not be denied to the work, simply because no one 
chooses to buy the book.468 [Emphasis added.]
CT-8.19.JörgReinbotheandSilkevonLewinski–whowereamongthenegotiatorsatthe1996
DiplomaticConferenceonbehalfoftheEuropeanCommunities–dealwiththisquestioninthe
following way:
[T]he act of “making available” to the public for access covers the offering of works for 
access and extends to the entire transmission to the user, if such transmission takes place. 
Accordingly, the mere establishment of a server which may be accessed individually by members 
of the public and at their choice regarding time and place constitutes the act of making available 
underArticle 8WCT.If a work is actually accessed, the whole act of communication is covered by 
the exclusive right, including the offering of the work in a server and its entire transmission 
up to the terminal from which the member of the public gets access to the work. This 
interpretation is confirmed by the wording: availability of the works is only accomplished when 
the work has been transmitted to the member of the public so that he or she may access it 
from his or her terminal. [Emphasis added, in particular to the words “only accomplished” 
to stress the similarity with the only accomplishment of the acts of distribution by actual 
buyingofcopies–notbythedistributorbutbythebuyersofcopies.]469

CT-8.20. The author of this collection of guides has also characterized the two elements of the 
concept (making available and its accomplishment by interactive transmission) in his book 
published on the WCT and the WPPT:
[U]nderArticle 8oftheWCTandArticle 3(1)oftheInformationSocietyDirective,the act of 
“communication to the public” in the form of making available is completed by merely making 
a work available for on-demand transmission. If then the work is actually transmitted in that 
way, it does not mean that two acts are carried out: “making available” and “communication 
to the public”.470 The entire act thus carried out will be regarded as communication to the 
public.Ofcourse,itisnotirrelevantfromthepointofviewoflegalconsequenceswhether
or not on-demand transmissions for which the work is made available are actually carried 
outandhowmanytimes,inwhichwayandwithwhatconsequences.Itisveryrelevant,for

CT-8.21.InspiteoftheclearmeaningofthetextofArticle 8oftheWCTandArticles 10and14of

theprovisions–nootherwell-foundedinterpretationispossiblethanthatanactofinteractive 
making available to the public does take place already when a work is made available to the 
public for access. Certain theories have been presented according to which this is not the case, 
claiming a mere making available to the public for access is not sufficient and a work made 
available for access must also to be accessed and transmitted.
CT-8.22. Such a theory was presented in an opinion by a group of academics under the name 
of “European Copyright Society” (ECS) in connection with the Svensson case472oftheCJEU(the

general should be regarded as an activity that is not covered by the right to communicate the 
worktothepublicembodiedinArticle 3ofDirective2001/29”andtheyofferedthisreason 
for their thesis: “Hyperlinks are not communications because establishing a hyperlink does not 
amount to ‘transmission’ of a work, and such transmission is a pre-requisite for ‘communication’ ”. 
[Emphasis added.]

expression is ‘la communication publique’.
[10.16] It seems clear that, at the treaty level, the term ‘communication’ can be used as 
a bridging term to ensure the international interoperability and mutual recognition of 
exclusive rights that have been or will be provided in national legislations using either the 
term ‘transmission’ or the term ‘communication’. The former refers to a technical transfer 
while the latter implies, in addition to the technical transfer, that something is communicated. 
For the purposes of the proposed Treaty, this slight difference between the terms is irrelevant. 
What is transferred or communicated is the work.475
CT-8.24. The second thing the authors of the ECS opinion disregarded is the principle of relative 
freedom of legal characterization in national laws of the acts and rights under the international 
treaties. The emphasis is on the adjective “relative”; as pointed out above, the different legal 
characterization must not result in changing the nature (such as compulsory license instead of 
exclusive right) or reducing the scope of application of the right as provided in a treaty.
CT-8.25. The third thing that they did not take into account was that, in the same Basic Proposal 
fromwhichtheyquotedthenotestoArticle 10,itismadeclearwhatfollowsfromthetextof
theprovisionquotedabove:“Therelevantactisthemakingavailableoftheworkbyproviding
access to it. What counts is the initial act of making the work available ”.476 [Emphasis added.]
CT-8.26. The Executive Committee of the International Literary and Artistic Association (ALAI) 
rebutted the theory presented in the ECS opinion:
The exclusive right of ‘making available’ under the WCT and the implementing EU legislation 
covers the offering to the public of a work for individualized streaming or downloading; in 
addition, where it takes place, the actual transmission of a work to members of the public 
also is covered, both irrespective of the technical means used for making available.477
CT-8.27.TheCJEU,inSvensson, also rejected the ECS theory, finding what seems obvious under 
Article 3(1)oftheInformationSocietyDirective:
AsisapparentfromArticle 3(1)ofDirective2001/29,fortheretobean“actof
communication,” it is sufficient, in particular, that a work is made available to a public in such 
a way that the persons forming that public may access it, irrespective of whether they avail 
themselves of that opportunity.478 [Emphasis added]
CT-8.28. In the United States, the miscomprehension of the concept of making available and 
the existing provisions of the U.S. Copyright Act have created certain problems. In 2016, the 
U.S. Copyright Office organized consultations on the status of implementation of the right of 
makingavailabletothepublic.TheopinionpresentedbyJaneGinsburgintheframeworkofthe
consultation characterized the existing situation in this way:
The WCT ‘making available’ right applies to the offering to the public of on-demand access 
to a work in the form of a stream or of a download. Compliance with the WCT requires a 
member state to cover both kinds of access (streaming and downloading), and to cover not 
only actual transmissions of streams and downloads, but also the offering to communicate the 
work as a stream or a download. […]
The ‘umbrella solution’ adopted at the 1996 Diplomatic Conference that yielded the 
WCT allows member states to implement the art. 8 making available right through a 
variety of means, including, for example, an all-embracing ‘making available’ right, or a 
combination of a public performance right covering streams and a digital distribution 
right covering downloads. Whatever the means chosen, however, the member state must

ensure that its law covers the offering to the public of on-demand access to a work both as a

The U.S. implementation has assigned the offering and communication of digital streams 
to the public performance right, and downloads to the reproduction and distribution 
rights. Although case law and statutory authority clearly establish that the U.S. 
distribution right embraces delivery of digital copies, decisions interpreting the scope 
ofthedistributionrightdifferregardingtheessentialquestionofcoverageofoffers 
todownload.Amajorityofcourtsaddressingthatquestionhavesofarheldthatthe
rightrequiresactualdeliveryofthedownload:amereofferingoftheworktothepublic
fordownloadingdoesnotsuffice.Inaddition,recentcaselawhascalledintoquestion
the scope of the public performance right in on-demand communications based on 
individualized storage copies […].
Unless courts consistently interpret the 106(3) distribution right to cover offers of digital 
downloads, and the 106(4)(5)(6) public performance and display rights to cover all kinds of 
on-demand offers of content for streaming access, the U.S. will not be in compliance with its 
international obligations. If courts persist in their current crabbed interpretations, Congress 
may need to step in. If Congress does legislate in this area, it would be preferable to provide 
for a true ‘making available right’, echoing WCT art. 8, rather than the piecemeal solution 
that currently pertains. The ‘umbrella solution’ was devised to enable the U.S. to adhere to 
the WIPO Copyright Treaties without amending the statute, but judicial interpretation to 
date has ripped the umbrella’s canopy from its spokes, leaving exclusive rights forlornly 
drenched by the torrent of uncompensated new uses and business models.479
CT-8.29. The conclusions of the study of the U.S. Copyright Office reflected the same problems 
created by the case law, but it sounded more optimistic:
[T]he Copyright Office concludes that the exclusive rights of copyright owners set forth 
under17U.S.C.§106collectivelymeetandadequatelyprovidethesubstanceofthe
making available right.
Consistent with the plain language of the Treaties, which defines the making available 
right in terms of whether members of the public ‘may access’ a copyrighted work, U.S. 
lawshouldbereadtoincludetheofferofpublicaccess,includingthroughon‐demand
services, without regard to whether a copy has been disseminated or received. Doing so is 
also consistent with the judicial opinions of foreign jurisdictions on this point.
Within the particular context of downloads, U.S. law provides the making available right 
through the exclusive right of distribution under Section 106(3). While some courts have 
failed to find distribution in the absence of evidence of completed transfers, and therefore 
declined to recognize claims based solely on making copies available to the public for 
download, the Copyright Office concludes that the appropriate reading of Section 106(3) 
in the context of making available claims is that it covers offers of access.480
CT-8.30. Thus, the study confirmed that the US legislation is suitable to apply the right of 
interactivemakingavailabletothepublicasprovidedinArticle 8oftheWCT.

CT-8.32. Since the text, in substance, is the same as what was proposed by the then European

andatatimeindividuallychosenbythem–irrespectiveofwhethertheinteractiveusethus 
made possible allows only perception or also the downloading of copies.
CT-8.33. The national laws of the EU Member States adhere to these concepts. This is so 
even where the national law has not been modified for the implementation of the right of 
making available to the public, but rather an existing right (in France, for example, the broadly 
interpreted “representation right” (“ droit de représentation”)) is considered to be suitable 
to absorb the broadly construed right of communication to the public, including the right 
of (interactive) making available of works. It is also true where a special term “electronic 
transmission” is used along with the term “communication to the public” and with the verbatim 
transpositionofthetextofthesecondpartofArticle 8oftheWCTontherightofinteractive 
makingavailabletothepublic–asinsection20(2)(b)oftheUKCopyright,Designsand
Patents Act:
(2)  References in this Part to communication to the public are to communication to the 
public by electronic transmission, and in relation to a work include:
(a)  the broadcasting of the work;
(b)  the making available to the public of the work by electronic transmission in such a 
way that members of the public may access it from a place and at a time individually 
chosen by them. [Emphasis added.]
In the case law, section 20(2)(b) has been applied without any problem not only to streaming but 
also to downloading.481

Inthatconnection–asalsoquotedabove–thenotesmentionedthattheFrenchtextofthe
Berne Convention484 uses the words “transmission”(inArticles 11(1)(ii),11ter(1)(ii) and 14(1)(ii)) and 
“communication”(inArticle 11bis) interchangeably in those cases where, in the English version, 
everywheretheword“communication”appears.Inviewofthis,thenotetotheArticle (atthat
time,stillArticle 10),characterizedtherelationshipofthetwotermsinthisway:“Theformer
refers to a technical transfer while the latter implies, in addition to the technical transfer, that 
something is communicated. For the purposes of the proposed Treaty, this slight difference 
between the terms is irrelevant. What is transferred or communicated is the work”.485
CT-8.35. This statement in the note that it is irrelevant which term is used in national laws has 
turned out to be too optimistic. It is true that “[w]hat is transferred or communicated is the 
work”,but–inthegivencontext–thequestioniswhat“transferring”and“communication” 
mean486 and not what is transferred and communicated. It is pointed out in the note itself that 
“[t]he former refers to a technical transfer while the latter implies, in addition to the technical 
transfer, that something is communicated”. That is, the meanings of the two terms do differ. 
CT-8.36. However, the differences between the acts of traditional non-interactive 
communicationtothepublicmentionedinthefirstpartofArticle 8oftheWCTandtheactof 
interactivemakingavailabletothepublicreferredtointhesecondpartoftheArticle areeven 
more complex. The act of making available to the public described in the second part of the 
Article isbasedon“pull”technology;andittakesplaceinaninteractivemanner.Theactisnot 
transmitting a work to be received by the members of the public, but making available a work in 
a way that, if the members of the public want to receive it , they have to cause it to be transmitted. 
It is another decisive difference that the acts of making available works to the public are of a 
hybrid nature. The transmissions triggered by the members of the public may be similar to 
theactsmentionedinthefirstpartofArticle 8(inthecaseofstreamingofworks),because 
the members of the public may apprehend the work simultaneously with its transmission. 
But it may also take place in such a way that, during the transmission, the members of the 
public cannot simultaneously listen to, watch or otherwise perceive the work. 487 Rather, the 
transmissiondeliversa“mute”file,andtheuser’ssubsequentopeningofthefilemakesit 
possible to see, hear or otherwise perceive the transmitted content. In such a case, the works 
aredownloadedanditisonthebasisof–atleasttemporary–copiesthattheymaybeusedby
the members of the public. There are certain categories of works (such as computer programs, 
e-books and other writings, sheet music, etc.) that are normally transferred online in that way. 
CT-8.37.InthesecondpartofArticle 8oftheWCT–aswellasinArticles 10and14oftheWPPT
andArticle 10oftheBTAPonastand-alonerightdifferentfromtherightofcommunication 
tothepublic–theexpression“makingavailabletothepublic”isusedwithameaningthat
is neutral from the viewpoint of whether a copy-related act (reproduction and what may be 
characterized as “distribution-through-reproduction-through-transmission”) or rather a non-
copy-relatedact(similarto–althoughwithrespecttotheinteractiveaspectstilldifferentfrom 
–broadcastingandanalogcommunicationtothepublic)takesplace.Itistobenotedthatthe
expressionusedinthesecondpartoftheArticle hasthesamekindofneutralmeaningaswhere 
thesameterm–“makingavailabletothepublic”–isusedintheBerneConvention;namely,in
Articles 7(2)and(3)and10(1).
CT-8.38. Nevertheless, although it is not an optimal solution to use the same expression to 
refertosubstantiallydifferentacts,Article 8maystillbeappliedappropriatelyiftheabove-
mentioned differences between the acts mentioned in the first and second parts of the 
Article aredulytakenintoaccount.Itseems,however,thatthisdoesnotalwayshappeninthis
way, and it may lead to interpretation problems. 
484Which,inthecontextoftheConvention,underArticle 37(1)(c)isdecisivefortheinterpretationoftheprovisionsof 
the Convention.
485 Records of the 1996 Diplomatic Conference , 204.
486 In the context of a copyright treaty, it is obvious that “what is transferred or communicated is the work”, but it is 
equallyobviousthat“whatistransferred,communicated,madeavailable,reproduced,distributed,translatedand 
adaptedisthework”,buttheseobviousstatementsdonotgiveanswertotherealquestionofwhat“transfer”, 

communication of the work in accordance with the ordinary meaning of “communication”.

246 CT-8.39.  Contracting parties have free choice of legal characterization of the right provided in the

andscopeoftheright–thatis,itisprovidedastheexclusiverightofinteractivemakingavailable

China,489 Montenegro,490 the Russian Federation491 and Ukraine492 in order to avoid interpretation

traditional manner and the hybrid forms of interactive making available to the public. In a special

CT-8.40. There are substantive differences in the implementation and application of the right

their interactive and hybrid nature. In the above-mentioned countries where the laws provide

communication to the public not only for performers and producers of phonograms but also for 
authors, this problem has not emerged. 494

248 CT-8.45. The Federal Court of Appeal (FCA), however, rejected the Board’s correct

first, that section 2.4(1.1) does not apply to interactive making available to the public of works 
for on-demand downloading, because it is not mere communication to the public in the 
traditional sense; second, that, for an act of making available to the public to take place, it is 
not sufficient to make a work available for interactive access as described in section 2.4(1.1); it 
is also necessary that the members of the public actually access the work made available. The 
Court even stated that “[s]ubsection 2.4(1.1) does not create a new exclusive right”, 500 by which 
it suggests that, since interactive making available to the public is called “communication to the 
public”, its status is the same as that of the non-interactive acts of communication to the public 
provided in the Copyright Act before the adoption of the new provision.

such a transmission is made to a public different from the public at which the original act of

CT-8.48. The Berne Convention, however, does not speak of communication to a “new public” 
or of “a public different from the public at which the original act of communication of the work 
isdirected”.Article 11bis(1)(ii)oftheConvention(alsoquotedbytheCJEU)readsasfollows:
“[a]uthors of literary and artistic works shall enjoy the exclusive right of authorizing: […] any 
communication to the public by wire or by rebroadcasting of the broadcast of the work, 
when this communication is made by an organization other than the original one ” [emphasis 
added].Themeaningofthistextisquiteclear:theonlyconditionisthattheretransmissionor
rebroadcasting be made by an organization other than the original one . There is no reference 
to any other criteria, such as a different or “new” public. The retransmission or rebroadcasting 
may be made to the same public; it may be made to a part of the same public only; it may be made 
to the same public or a part thereof along with a public not covered bytheoriginalbroadcast; and
it may be made to a completely new public.AllthesecasesarecoveredbyArticle 11bis(1)(ii) of 
the Berne Convention. It is an obligation under the Convention and (due to the inclusion of 
its substantive norms by reference) also under the TRIPS Agreement and the WCT to grant 
an exclusive right for all these acts. It is another matter that the authors may also “take into 
account” the retransmission of their works when they authorize the original transmission. That 
is, they may consent to the latter act as well by exercising their right to authorize it as a new act 
covered by their right of authorization (to which it should be added that the rights provided in 
paragraph (1)ofArticle 11bismaybelimitedbyvirtueofparagraph (2),ontheunderstanding
thatanylimitationmustbeaccompaniedbyequitableremunerationfortheauthors).
CT-8.49. In SGAE,theCJEUruledthattherightofcommunicationtothepublicwasapplicable,and,
in the given case, it was irrelevant whether the ruling was based on the finding that a new act 
of communication to the public or rather an act of communication to a “new public” had taken 
place.Nevertheless,theCourt’sanalysis–basedonaspecificunderstandingofacommentinan
old WIPO Guide published in 1978505–seemedtosuggestthat,fortheapplicabilityoftherightof
communication to the public, it is necessary that it be made to a “new public”.506
CT-8.50.TheauthoroftheformerGuide–ClaudeMasouyé,thethenDirectoroftheWIPO 
CopyrightDepartment–didnotreallysuggestthattherightofcommunicationtothe
public applies only where a work is communicated to a new public.507 A much more recent 
“interpretative document drawn up by WIPO” (as the Court refers to it) was already available 
whentheCourtwasdraftingitsjudgment –thenewGuidetotheBerneConvention,published
aquarterofacenturylater,in2003508 (the first edition of this Guide). The relevant part of the 
new guide was based on a thorough academic-style study 509 prepared by the team of WIPO’s 
504JudgmentoftheCourt(ThirdChamber)of7December2006, Sociedad General de Autores y Editores de España (SGAE) v.

506 As is explained in the Guide to the Berne Convention, an interpretative document drawn up by the WIPO  which, without 
being legally binding, nevertheless assists in interpreting that Convention , when the author authorises the broadcast 
ofhiswork,heconsidersonlydirectusers,thatis,theownersofreceptionequipmentwho,eitherpersonallyor 
within their own private or family circles, receive the programme. According to the Guide, if reception is for a larger 
audience, possibly for profit, a new section of the receiving public hears or sees the work and the communication of the 
programme via a loudspeaker or analogous instrument no longer constitutes simple reception of the programme itself but 
is an independent act through which the broadcast work is communicated to a new public . As the Guide makes clear, such 
public reception falls within the scope of the author’s exclusive authorisation right.  
The clientele of a hotel forms such a new public.  The transmission of the broadcast work to that clientele using 
television sets is not just a technical means to ensure or improve reception of the original broadcast in the catchment 
area.Onthecontrary,thehotelistheorganisationwhichintervenes,infullknowledgeoftheconsequencesofits 
action, to give access to the protected work to its customers. In the absence of that intervention, its customers, although 
physically within that area, would not, in principle, be able to enjoy the broadcast work . (Emphasis added.)
