CT-8.51. The 2003 WIPO Guide reflects the findings of the study prepared by Masouyé’s WIPO 
team. The following comment was made:
Thetextofparagraph (1)(ii)isveryclearinoneaspect.Therightprovidedforinitcovers
“any communication to the public by wire … of the broadcast of the work, when this 
communication is made by an organization other than the original one.” That is, the 
decisive criterion is that the communication is made by an organization other than the 
original one; if this is the case, the author or other owner of copyright has a right separate 
from the right to authorize the original act of broadcasting. There is no basis in the text 
of the Convention for which it would be justified to consider theories according to which 
“any” such communication only means “some,” in the sense that the […] communications 
in a “direct reception zone” or “service zone” would not be covered.513 
The study, published in 1984 in a special issue of Copyright,isquitevoluminous;itfills41pages.
Itseemssufficienttoquotetwoparagraphsreferringtothepreparatoryworkoftherelevant 
Berne provisions:
[T]he criteria of […] ‘new public’ were found to be impracticablewithregardtoqualifying
distinct activities of the organization authorized by the author to broadcast his work. 
No doubt had been raised during the Conference about the fact that distribution of the 
broadcast of a work by a third person always constitutes a new act of communication 
tothepublic.[…].Theprovision,asitstandsnowinArticle 11bis(1)(ii)oftheBerne
Convention, was adopted in the Subcommittee by 12 votes against 6 (Br. Doc. p. 290514), 
and later on unanimously by the Conference itself. 
In conclusion, Marcel Plaisant, the General Rapporteur of the Brussels Conference, 
summarized the result as follows: ‘The author has also a further right that covers any 
communication to the public which is made by an organization other than the original one. 
This is a right to an extension of the broadcast, of which, for the time being two methods 
areknown:therelayandtheradiodistribution [...]’(Br.Doc.p.101).Neither the wording of 
the relevant provision of the Berne Convention nor the respective conference documents offer 
any basis for the restriction of the scope of that special right of communication to the public 
according to particular criteria such as geographical or technological considerations or ‘must 
carry’ obligation under public law.515
CT-8.52. The “new public” theory has been analyzed by a working group of the Executive 
Committee of ALAI. The Committee in its opinion expressed the view that the theory is not 
in accordance with the relevant international and EU norms. 516 The opinion also deals with 
otherCJEUjudgmentsinwhichthetheorywasgivengreaternuanceandcombinedwithnew
elements, including, in particular, the TvCatchup and Svensson cases (see below).517

CT-8.53. The theory is somewhat modified in the TvCatchup518 judgment, where the Court 
recognizes the applicability of the right of communication to the public even in the absence 
ofa“newpublic”–butonlywheredifferent“specifictechnicalmeans”areusedforfurther 
communication. As the ALAI opinion referred to above points out, this corrective theory likewise 
does not seem to be in harmony with the Berne Convention, because just the contrary follows 
fromArticle 11bis(1)(ii),underwhichrebroadcastingofabroadcastwork–thatis,retransmission
of the work by the same technical means –iscoveredbyaseparateright.519 Nevertheless, in both 
SGAE and TvCatchup,thedecisivesubstanceoftherulings–recognizingtheapplicabilityofthe
rightofcommunicationtothepublic–certainlywouldnothavedifferediftheCourthadsimply 
stated that new acts of communication to the public had taken place.
CT-8.54. The joint application of the “new public” and “specific technical means” theories has led, 
however, to different results in the Svensson case mentioned above in another context. Here, 
the Court finds that the entire Internet population is a single public, and that, therefore, if a 
work has been made available online, any new act of making available of the work on another 
website and on another occasion necessarily takes place to the same public and by the same 
technical means; thus, the right of making available to the public in such a case is not applicable. 
TheCJEUhas,nevertheless,determinedapossiblewayofreservingtherightofinteractive
making available to the public; namely, by expressly restricting the availability of the works. The 
application of this condition seemed to reflect the recognition of the trend that a lot of people 
make their works and other protected materials available online and in doing so they expect, and 
accept, the free availability thereof and also allow the members of the public to interpret their 
intentions accordingly. As pointed out in the ALAI opinion, however, this solution is problematic 
for two reasons. First, it implies the exhaustion of the right of making available to the public in the 
absence of express restriction of access; second, the condition that the right may only survive if 
the authors restrict access to their works may be considered a kind of formality to be fulfilled in 
order to reserve the right, which does not seem to be in harmony with the international treaties.520
CT-8.55. In Svensson, it was not completely clear yet in which way the rightholders may restrict 
access to their works made available online; it might have meant a mere machine-readable 
reservation (which, under the WCT, would have meant rights management information,521 a 
form of preserving rights somewhat lighter than technological protection measures).522 In the 
subsequentcasesithasturnedout,however,thattheCJEUmeanttheapplicationoftechnological
protection measures. This was explicitly confirmed in BestWater,523wheretheCJEU–onthebasis
ofthejointapplicationofthethreeabove-mentionedtheories–foundittobeinorderthata
competitorhadwithoutpermissionusedtheaudiovisualworkoftherightholder–producedfor
advertisingpurposesofthelatter–byembeddingitonitsownwebsiteforthesamepurposes,
because no technological protection had been applied to reserve the rights in the work.
518 JudgmentoftheCourt(FourthChamber)of7March2013, ITV Broadcasting Ltd, ITV 2 Ltd, ITV Digital Channels Ltd, 
Channel 4 Television Corporation, 4 Ventures Ltd, Channel 5 Broadcasting Ltd, ITV Studios Ltd v TVCatchup Ltd , Case 
C-607/11, ECLI: EU:C:2013:147 (hereinafter: TvCatchup).
519 The ALAI Executive Committee has found that “the ‘specific technical means’ criterion is in conflict with international 
copyright norms regarding the scope of the minimum rights of communication to the public and making available to 
the public and the EU rules implementing them. There is no element of those norms and rules or of their ‘preparatory 
work’ that would support it”; see ALAI opinion on the “new public” and other theories , 21.

252 CT-8.56. The GS Media524–Soulier525 tandemofjudgmentsoftheCJEUhasraisedthepossibility
that the Court may rather use the implied license doctrine combined with the innocent 
infringement defense to adapt the exercise of rights to the realities of the online environment, 
rather than conditioning the preservation of the right of interactive making available to the 
public on the restriction of access by technological measures. Under this new approach, it would 
be recognized that, with any new act of making available of a work for interactive streaming 
or transmission for downloading, a new act of interactive making available to the public takes 
placeunderArticle 8oftheWCTandArticles 10and14oftheWPPT,but–intheabsenceofclear
indicationbytherightholdertothecontrary–theuserwhouploadsaworkthusaccessedto
make it available from their own website would not be liable for infringement if, in the given 
case, they have reason to believe that there is an implied authorization and, where it turns out 
that there is none, they might still claim that they did not have direct or constructive knowledge 
of this; that is, they are innocent infringers. 526
CT-8.57. With the new elements of GS Media and Soulier,thepossibilityemergedthattheCJEU’s
caselawcouldevolvetowardsgivingup“newpublic”asaconditionofanacttoqualifyas
communication or making available to the public. Then suddenly, with Renkhoff (or Córdoba), the 
Courtmadeaquantumleapinthatdirection. 527TheCJEUadopteditsjudgmentinaccordance
withArticle 3(1)oftheEU’sInformationSocietyDirectiveandArticle 8oftheWCTinruling 
that the right of interactive making available to the public may remain applicable in the case 
of making available a work that previously has been made available without any technological 
protection measure. The Court ruled as follows:
Theconceptof‘communicationtothepublic’,withinthemeaningofArticle 3(1)of
Directive 2001/29/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 May 2001 on 
the harmonisation of certain aspects of copyright and related rights in the information 
society, must be interpreted as meaning that it covers the posting on one website 
of a photograph previously posted, without any restriction preventing it from being 
downloaded and with the consent of the copyright holder, on another website.528
The effect of the recognition of a comprehensive right to communication to the public 
CT-8.58.Article 8,beforeprovidingforanexclusiverightofinteractiveonlinemakingavailable
of works, contains two elements. The first element is a mere non-derogation reference to 
those provisions of the Berne Convention that provide for rights to authorize different forms of 
communicationtothepublic(bywireorbywirelessmeans),thatis,Articles 11(1)(ii),11bis(1)(i) and 
(ii), 11ter(1)(ii), 14(1)(ii) and 14bis(1). It is clarified that these provisions continue to be applicable. It 
is to be noted that all these provisions cover traditional, non-interactive acts of communication to 
thepublic.Article 11bis(1)(i) on the right of broadcasting and related acts extends to all categories 
of works,buttheotherArticles listedgrantarightofcommunicationtothepublicbywireonly
for certain categories of works in certain forms:Article 11(1)(ii)onlyfordramatic,dramatico-
musicalandmusicalworksintheformofperformances;Article 11ter(1)(ii) only for literary 
worksintheformofrecitations;andArticles 14(1)(ii)and14bis(1) only for works in the form of 
cinematographic adaptations and for cinematographic (and other audiovisual) works themselves.

CT-8.59.ThesecondelementofthefirstpartofArticle 8,beforeprovidinginthesecondpart 
for an exclsusive right of (interactive) making available to the public, is that it extends the right 
of non-interactive communication to the public to all acts of communication, whether they are 
carried out by wire or by wireless means (or through the combination of the two) and without 
limiting it to the communication to the public of certain categories of works. Through this 
extension, the right of communication to the public by wire has become generally applicable 
alsoinrespectofthosecategoriesofworksthatarenotcoveredbyArticles 11(1)(ii),11ter(1)(ii),  
14(1)(ii) and 14bis(1)(ii) of the Berne Convention (such as musical works in the form of sheet 
music; literary works in any form other than in recitals, including computer programs; graphic 
works; photographic works; and so on).
CT-8.60.UnderthefirstpartofArticle 8,itisimplicitlyrecognizedthatbroadcastingisa 
specific form of communication to the public (rather than a mere “emission”). Thus, the new 
provision seems to confirm that, of the various “theories” referred to in connection with direct 
broadcastingbysatellitesinthecommentsonArticle 11bis of the Berne Convention in the Guide 
in this collection, the “communication theory” is the correct one.
CT-8.61.ThesecondsentenceoftheagreedstatementconcerningArticle 8(which,infact,is
a separate statement since its subject matter is different from that of the first sentence of 
theagreedstatement)makesitclearthatnothinginArticle 8precludesaContractingParty 
fromapplyingArticle 11bis(2) of the Berne Convention. As discussed in the comments on that 
provisionintheGuidetotheBerneConventioninthiscollection,Article 11bis(2) is interpreted, 
inter alia, as authorizing the application of non-voluntary licenses.
CT-8.62.Interactivetransmissionsdonotqualifyasbroadcasting(sincetheconceptofthelatter 
presupposesanactivecommunicatorandpassiverecipients)andthusArticle 11 bis does not 
applytothem.If,however,asaresultofnewtechnologies–suchasthroughsomevariantsof
“webcasting”,“simulcasting”,“streaming”,oranyotherexistingorfuturetechniques–anykind 
of non-interactive communication to the public takes place through the global digital network 
whichmayberegardedasbeingcoveredbyArticle 11bis,andthusalsobyArticle 11bis(2) 
the said “no export” proviso of the latter due to the global impact of such communication, 
would certainly not allow the application of non-voluntary licenses thereto . This is so because 
Article 11bis(2) provides that the “conditions” allowing such limitations “shall apply only in the 
countries where they have been provided”.
The first sentence of the agreed statement concerning mere provision of physical facilities; no 
liability, contributory liability
CT-8.63.Asreproducedabove,thefirstsentenceoftheagreedstatementconcerningArticle 8 
reads as follows: “It is understood that the mere provision of physical facilities for enabling or 
making a communication does not in itself amount to communication within the meaning of this 
Treaty [the WCT] or the Berne Convention”. This sentence of the agreed statement states the 
obvious: it has always been evident that those who carry out an act other than what is covered 
by a right provided for in a treaty (and in corresponding national laws) have no direct liability 
for any act covered by such a right. It is another matter that, depending on the circumstances, 
they may still be liable on the basis of some other forms of liability, such as contributory or 
vicarious liability. Liability issues are, however, very complex; the knowledge of a very large 
body of statutory and case law is needed in each country to judge a given case. Therefore, the 
international treaties on intellectual property rights, understandably and rightly, do not cover 
such issues of liability. The WCT follows this example (as do the WPPT and the BTAP).
CT-8.64. The sentence was adopted at the 1996 Diplomatic Conference as a result of an 
intensive lobbying campaign by non-governmental organizations of Internet service providers 
andtelecommunicationcompanies.Theywantedtoincludeinthetextofthetwotreaties–
or,atleast,inagreedstatements–someguaranteestoexemptthemfromtheliabilityfor
infringements committed by the users of their services, but they did not fully succeed in this, 
because the sentence has clarified only what amounts to the same exemption of liability that 
telephone companies have for the contents of their subscribers’ conversation.
CT-8.65.Twocommentsshouldbeaddedtothis.First,asincertainothercases,thequestion 
of contributory liability may emerge even if the intermediaries’ activity does not amount to

254 acts covered by copyright; and second, on the contrary, where the online actors also play an 
active role in the making available of works to the public, they may become users of the works 
and liable for infringements. The description and analysis of the national rules on liability of 
intermediaries–andtheconditionsoftheirexemptions–suchasthoseprovidedinsection
512oftheUSCopyrightActandinArticles 12to15oftheEUElectronicCommerceDirective529

conditions, certain acts covered by copyright take place.
Direct liability of certain online actors
CT-8.66.TheEUDigitalSingleMarketDirectiveinitsArticle 17regulatesthestatusof“online 
content-sharing service providers” (OCSSPs), referred to in the report prepared by Pierre 
Sirinelli and his team for the French Ministry of Culture as “false intermediaries”. 530 The study 
(which served as a basis for the initiation of the EU legislative process leading to the adoption 
ofArticle 17oftheDirective)pointedoutthatcertainhostingproviders’activitiesgobeyonda 
passive role of merely providing services, certainly beyond what the first sentence of the agreed 
statementconcerningArticle 8referstoas“themereprovisionofphysicalfacilitiesforenabling 
or making a communication”; so far beyond that they perform acts covered by the right of 
online making available to the public.
CT-8.67. The phenomenon of active hosting providers had already been the subject of court cases, 
includingbeforetheCJEU;inparticulartheL’Oréal judgment of the Court531 received great attention. 
Itwasnotaboutcopyrightbutabouttrademark,butitpointedoutinquitecleartermsthatthere
is a category of hosting providers to which the Sirinelli report referred as “false intermediaries”. 
Despite the fact that it was a trademark case, due to the horizontal application of the provisions 
of the liability rules in the Electronic Commerce Directive, its findings were also valid, mutatis 
mutandis, for copyright. Point 6 of the L’Oréal rulings was particularly relevant from this viewpoint:
Article 14(1)ofDirective2000/31/EC[…]mustbeinterpretedasapplyingtotheoperatorof
an online marketplace where that operator has not played an active role allowing it to have 
knowledge or control of the data stored.
The operator plays such a role when it provides assistance which entails, in particular, 
optimising the presentation of the offers for sale in question or promoting them. 
[Emphasis added.]
Where the operator of the online marketplace has not played an active role within the 
meaningoftheprecedingparagraph andtheserviceprovidedfalls,asaconsequence,
withinthescopeofArticle 14(1)ofDirective2000/31,theoperatornonethelesscannot,
in a case which may result in an order to pay damages, rely on the exemption from 
liability provided for in that provision if it was aware of facts or circumstances on the 
basis of which a diligent economic operator should have realised that the offers for sale in 
questionwereunlawfuland,intheeventofitbeingsoaware,failedtoactexpeditiouslyin
accordancewithArticle 14(1)(b)ofDirective2000/31.
CT-8.68. The activities of certain well-known big online platforms that make available huge 
amounts of works and other protected materials clearly correspond to the Court’s description 
of an active role, which makes them “false intermediaries” described in the Sirinelli report in

byArticle 14enablestheaboveserviceproviderstomakeconsiderableprofitsdueto

Article 2
(6) ‘online content-sharing service provider’ means a provider of an information society 
service of which the main or one of the main purposes is to store and give the public

Recital [64]
It is appropriate to clarify in this Directive that online content-sharing service providers 
perform an act of communication to the public or of making available to the public when 
they give the public access to copyright-protected works or other protected subject 
matteruploadedbytheirusers.Consequently,onlinecontent-sharingserviceproviders
should obtain an authorisation, including via a licensing agreement, from the relevant 
rightholders. [Emphasis added.]

533[Originalnoteinthequotedtext]Thisaccesscriterionisessentialinordertoconstitutetheactofmakingavailable. 
Indeed,theserviceprovidersinquestionenablethepublictoaccessprotectedcontent.Withouttheirintervention, 
the public would not have access to this content. Their role is therefore indisputable. The concept of access is

Thus,theserviceprovider’sinterventiontogiveaccesstotheworkpreventsArticle 14ofDirective2000/31from 

256 Article 17.Useofprotectedcontentbyonlinecontent-sharingserviceproviders
1.  Member States shall provide that an online content-sharing service provider performs 
an act of communication to the public or an act of making available to the public for 
the purposes of this Directive when it gives the public access to copyright-protected 
works or other protected subject matter uploaded by its users. 
 An online content-sharing service provider shall therefore obtain an authorisation from 
the rightholders referredtoinArticle 3(1)and(2)ofDirective2001/29/EC,forinstance
by concluding a licensing agreement, in order to communicate to the public or make 
available to the public works or other subject matter. [Emphasis added.]
2.  Member States shall provide that, where an online content-sharing service provider 
obtains an authorisation, for instance by concluding a licensing agreement, that 
authorisation shall also cover acts carried out by users of the services falling 
withinthescopeofArticle 3ofDirective001/29/ECwhentheyarenotactingona
commercial basis or where their activity does not generate significant revenues.
3.  When an online content-sharing service provider performs an act of communication 
to the public or an act of making available to the public under the conditions laid 
downinthisDirective,thelimitationofliabilityestablishedinArticle 14(1)ofDirective
2000/31/EC shall not apply to the situations covered by this Article. […]
4.  If no authorisation is granted, online content-sharing service providers shall be liable 
for unauthorised acts of communication to the public, including making available to 
the public, of copyright-protected works and other subject matter, unless the service 
providers demonstrate that they have:
(a)  made best efforts to obtain an authorisation, and
(b)  made, in accordance with high industry standards of professional diligence, best 
efforts to ensure the unavailability of specific works and other subject matter 
for which the rightholders have provided the service providers with the relevant 
and necessary information; and in any event
(c)  acted expeditiously, upon receiving a sufficiently substantiated notice from the 
rightholders, to disable access to, or to remove from their websites, the notified 
works or other subject matter, and made best efforts to prevent their future 
uploads in accordance with point (b).

CT-9.1.Article 7(4)oftheBerneConventionprovidesforaminimumtermofprotectionfor
photographicworks–“atleastuntiltheendofaperiodoftwenty-fiveyearsfromthemakingof
suchawork”–whichisshorterthanthegenerallyapplicableminimumtermsforliteraryand
artisticworks.SincetheapplicationofArticle 7(4)isruledoutbythisprovisionoftheWCT,the
Contracting States are obligated to apply the general norms on the term of protection. This means 
theapplicationofArticle 7(1)ifthereisanindividualauthor(atleasttheauthor’slifetimeplus50
years);orArticle 7(3)incaseofanonymousorpseudonymousphotographicworks(atleast50years
from the making available of the work, with the exceptions concerning the calculation of the 50-
yeartermprovidedinthatparagraph).TheapplicationofArticle 7bis of the Convention could also 
emerge (it is rare but not unheard of that a photographic work is created by co-authors).
CT-9.2.ItistobenotedthatitisonlyinrespectofphotographicworksthatArticle 9oftheWCT
excludestheapplicationofArticle 7(4)oftheBerneConvention.Article 7(4)providesforthe
same shorter term of protection for works of applied art. In respect of those works, the shorter 
term is also allowed under the WCT. The reason for this continued special treatment for works of 
appliedartistheutilitarianfunctionofsuchworks.Itisalsoduetothisthat,underArticle 2(7) 
oftheConvention,subjecttotheprovisionsofArticle 7(4),itisamatterforlegislationinthe
countries of the Berne Union “to determine the extent of the application of their laws to works 
of applied art and industrial designs and models, as well as the conditions under which such 
works, designs and models shall be protected” (it follows from this provision that it is allowed to 
protect only such works as designs and models).
CT-9.3.Article 9containsoneoftheveryfewprovisionsoftheWCTthathasnoconnection 
with the so-called “digital agenda” of the preparatory work. The adoption of the WCT offered 
an opportunity for this updating of the international norms on copyright to complete the long 
process of assimilating photographic works to the other categories of works. 539
Article 10
Limitations and Exceptions
(1) Contracting Parties may, in their national legislation, provide for limitations and 
exceptions to the rights granted to authors of literary and artistic works under this 
Treaty in certain special cases that do not conflict with a normal exploitation of the 
work and do not unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of the author.
(2) Contracting Parties shall, when applying the Berne Convention, confine any limitations 
or exceptions to rights provided for therein to certain special cases that do not 
conflict with a normal exploitation of the work and do not unreasonably prejudice the 
legitimate interests of the author.
539 A short summary of this process: (i) Although point 1 of the Final Protocol to the original, 1886 act of the Convention 
referred to photographic works, it left their protection to national legislation and allowed the application of material 
reciprocity for their protection. (ii) The 1896 Paris revision conference widened the basis of protection to photographic 
works and, at the same time, made it more uniform. National treatment was granted to photographs (except for the 
term of protection where material reciprocity was applicable) irrespective of whether they were placed on the same 
footing as artistic works, or were rather protected by a special law. Also a voeu was adopted by the Conference stating 
that it was desirable that, in all countries of the Union, the law protect photographic works and works produced by an 
analogous process and that the term of protection be at least 15 years. (iii) At the 1908 Berlin revision conference, it was 
agreed that all countries of the Union should protect photographs. In the Berlin act, however, photographic works 
werecoveredbyaseparateprovision(Article 3oftheConvention,ratherthanbeingincludedinthenon-exhaustive 
listof“literaryworks”inArticle 2).Consequently,theprovisionsoftheConventionon“literaryandartisticworks”did 
not apply to photographs; the law of each country was relevant. It was also allowed to national laws to determine 
freely the nature and duration of such protection. (iv) The 1928 Rome revision conference did not change the text of the 
Berne Convention in respect of photographic works. (v) At the 1948 Brussels revision conference, the term “photographic 
works and works produced by a process analogous to photography” was inserted in the non-exhaustive list of literary 
andartisticworksinArticle 2(1)oftheConvention.(vi) The 1967 Stockholm revision conference changed the wording of 
therelevantpartofArticle 2(1)oftheBerneConvention;itreplacedtheexpression“photographicworksandworks 
produced by a process analogous to photography” by the expression “photographic works to which are assimilated 
works expressed by a process analogous to photography.” By this modification, it was emphasized that the manner in 
which the work was expressed was the decisive factor in the definition, rather than the nature of the technical process. 
Anagreementwasreachedatlastaboutthetermofprotectionofphotographicworks.Article 7(4)providedasfollows: 
“It shall be a matter for legislation in the countries of the Union to determine the term of protection of photographic 
works [...]; however, this term shall last at least until the end of a period of twenty-five years from the making of such a 
work.” It was, at the same time, the last difference between the status of photographic works and literary and artistic 
worksingeneral,whichfinallywasremovedbyArticle 9oftheWCT.

Article 10 of the WCT: an extended application of the three-step test originally provided for by 
Article 9(2) of the Berne Convention
CT-10.1.Thethree-steptestwasprovidedforthefirsttimeinArticle 9(2)ofthe1967Stockholm
Act of the Berne Convention (then transposed without any change to the 1971 Paris Act). 
AlthoughitisquotedandanalyzedintheGuidetotheBerneConventioninthiscollection,it
seemsworthwhiletoquoteithereinordertodetailthestructureofits“steps”:“Itshallbe 
a matter for legislation in the countries of the [Berne] Union to permit the reproduction of 
[literary and artistic] works [first step:] in certain special cases, [second step:] provided that such 
reproduction does not conflict with a normal exploitation of the work and [third step:] does not 
unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of the author”. 
CT-10.2.InthecommentsonArticle 9(2)oftheBerneConventioninthiscollection,itisanalyzed
in detail how the three steps should be interpreted and applied. The most basic elements of that 
analysis may be summarized as follows:
First step: an exception or limitation must be a special case. This means that the use covered 
mustbespecific–preciselyandnarrowlydetermined–andthatnobroadlydetermined
cases are acceptable; and also that, as regards its objective, it must be “special” in the sense 
that it must be justifiable by some clear public policy considerations.540
Second step (which may only follow if the exception or limitation has not “failed” at the 
first step; that is, it is a special case): an exception or limitation must not conflict with 
a normal exploitation of works. This means that all forms of exploiting a work (that is, 
extracting value from the exclusive right of reproduction in the work through exercising 
it)thathas,orislikelytoacquire,considerableeconomicorpracticalimportancemustbe
reserved to the owner of the right; and that exceptions or limitations must not enter into 
economic competition with the exercise of the right of reproduction by the rights owner 
(in the sense that it must not undermine the market for the work).
Third step (which may only follow if the exception or limitation has passed the first two 
steps; that is, if it has been found that it is a special case and it does not conflict with 
a normal exploitation of the works): an exception or limitation must not unreasonably 
prejudice the legitimate interests of copyright owners. Legitimate interests means 
“legal interests” in the sense that it is in the interests of the owner of rights to enjoy 
and exercise the right of reproduction as fully as possible. An exception or limitation 
–inevitably,“bydefinition”–prejudicesthesekindsoflegitimateinterests,butsuch 
prejudice is allowed to occur in certain special cases not conflicting with any normal 
exploitation of the work; it must, however, be reasonable in the sense that it does not 
go beyond a certain level of prejudice that may still be justified in consideration of the 
underlying special, well-founded public policy considerations.
No more steps are needed. As the first WTO panel report that interpreted the three-step 
testpointedout,thereisnoneedtotrytotakeintoaccountcertain“externalities”–
suchasdevelopment,competitionorhumanrightsconsiderations–beyondthethree
cumulative conditions of the test.541 All those considerations can be duly assessed as part 
ofanadequateapplicationofthetest.
540ItismentionedinthecommentstoArticle 9(2)oftheBerneConventionthattherearecertaincommentatorswho– 
withreferencetoaWTOdisputesettlementpanelreport–donotconsiderthelegal–politicaljustificationofacaseas 
anindispensableconditionofitsqualifyingasspecial.
541 See thefindingsonthisinWTOpanelreportWT/DS/114/R,paras7.23–7.26.

Article 10 of the WCT: similarities and differences in comparison with Article 13 of the TRIPS 
Agreement
CT-10.3.Article 13oftheTRIPSAgreementhasadoptedthethree-steptestandextendedits 
scope to exceptions and limitations from the right of reproduction to any rights under copyright. 
It reads as follows: “Members [that is, Members of the WTO] shall confine limitations or exceptions 
to exclusive rights to certain special cases which do not conflict with a normal exploitation of the 
work and do not unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of the right holder” [emphasis 
is added to those parts of the provision which are worded in a way different from the relevant 
partsofArticle 9(2)oftheBerneConvention].Thesedifferencesarenotofasubstantivenature 
asconcernsthecriteriaofthethree-steptest.ThereallynewelementinArticle 13oftheTRIPS 
Agreement consists in its general applicability to all rights under copyright. This means both 
thoserightsthatareprovidedforundertheArticles oftheBerneConventionthathavebeen
includedintheAgreementbyreferenceinArticle 9.1andanynewrightprovidedforbythe
Agreement itself (which practically only means the right of rental). As regards the impact 
whichArticle 13mayhaveontheapplicationoftheexceptionsandlimitationsallowedinthe
Berne Convention and incorporated, by reference, into the Agreement, it may be regarded as 
an interpretation tool which, although it does not extend or restrict the applicability of those 
provisions, guarantees their appropriate interpretation, by excluding any possibility of a conflict 
with a normal exploitation of the works and any unreasonable prejudice to the legitimate 
interests of owners of copyright.
CT-10.4.ThecoverageoftheentireArticle 10oftheWCTissimilartothatofArticle 13ofthe
TRIPS Agreement in the sense that it is also applicable to all rights under copyright. Simply, while 
the latter consists of one single provision which is applicable for both the rights incorporated 
fromtheBerneConventionandthenewright–therightofrental–Article 10oftheWCTis
composed of two paragraphs which, at first sight, might seem to have different coverage. 542
CT-10.5.Infact,however,thereisanoverlapbetweenthetwoparagraphsofArticle 10.
Paragraph (1)coversall“therightsgrantedtoauthorsofliteraryandartisticworksunder
this Treaty”; that is, both those provided for in the provisions of the Berne Convention and 
incorporated into the Treaty by reference, and those that are new in comparison with the 
minimum obligations under the Berne Convention. This is so since the rights covered by the 
provisions included by reference are also granted under the Treaty. For this reason, in fact, 
paragraph (2)oftheArticle –whichrestatesthethree-steptestexclusivelyinrespectofthe
rightsbasedontheprovisionsoftheBerneConventionincorporatedintotheTreaty–seems
unnecessary.543 Nevertheless, this redundancy does not create any substantive problem; the 
coverageofthetwoparagraphsofArticle 10ispracticallythesameasthatofTRIPSArticle 13:
thethree-steptest–withthesameconditionsasunderArticle 9(2)–isapplicabletoallrights
under copyright.
CT-10.6.ThelanguageofthetwoparagraphsofArticle 10differsinoneaspect.Under
paragraph (1),ContractingParties“may [...] provide for” limitations and exceptions in certain 
specialcases;while,underparagraph (2),they“shall [...] confine” limitations and exceptions to 
certainspecialcases,whichcorrespondstothe“confine[...]to”languageofArticle 13oftheTRIPS
Agreement.Furthermore,thewordingofbothparagraphsdiffersfromthelanguageofArticle 9(2)
of the Berne Convention, which allows countries of the Berne Union “to permit [...] reproduction [...] 
in certain special cases”.
542 Thelanguageofthethirdconditionofthetestalsodiffers,butitisnotrelevantfortheinterpretationofArticle 10ofthe
WCT.InArticle 13oftheTRIPSAgreement,itisprovidedthatanexceptionorlimitationmustnotunreasonablyprejudice
thelegitimateinterestsofthe“rightholder”,whileunderArticle 9(2)oftheBerneConventionandArticle 10oftheWCT,
it is the legitimate interests of the “authors” which an exception or limitation must not prejudice. It may be argued that 
“rightholder”isasynonymof“ownerofright”usedinArticle 14bis(2) as a generic term to cover both authors and other 
originalownersofrights(inparticular,producersofaudiovisualworks).Furthermore,thesecondsentenceofArticle 2(6)
provides that “[t]his protection [the protection of the works mentioned in the article] shall operate for the benefit of the 
author and his successors in title” [emphasis added]; that is also for assignees of rights as “rightholders”. In the context of 
the TRIPS Agreement, however, the reference to “rightholder” instead of “author” is just one of the manifestations of the 
less author-centric and more production-, market- and trade-centric approach of the Agreement.
543 The language chosen for this does not seem to be fortunate, since it speaks about the application of the Berne 
Convention, while it is obvious that for the Contracting Parties, in this context, it is not the Berne Convention which 
applies,butonlythetreatyfromwhichitfollowstheobligationtocomplywithwhatisprovidedforinArticle 1to21ofthe
Convention (and this obligation also extends to those Contracting Parties which are not also party to the Convention).

260 CT-10.7.Thequestionmayemergewhetherornotthedifferentwordingmakesanydifference
in substance. It seems that the answer should be in the negative; the difference is simply 
due to a drafting inconsistency. There is no substantive difference for the following reasons: 
(i) under Article 9(2)oftheBerneConvention, permitting reproduction only in the cases that fulfill 
therequirementsofthethree-steptestalsomeansthatthecountriesoftheBerneUnion may 
provide for exceptions and limitations to the right of reproduction only in those cases; and (ii) 
sinceexceptionsandlimitationsmaybeprovidedonlyinthosecases–and,consequentlyinno
othercase–itmeansthat,alsounderArticle 9(2)oftheBerneConventionandArticle 10(1)of
the WCT, the countries of the Berne Union and the Contracting Parties of the WCT, respectively, 
must confine exceptions and limitations to those cases. 544 
Impact of Article 10(2) on the application of the provisions of the Berne Convention 
incorporated by reference into the WCT
CT-10.8.ItismentionedabovethatthecumulativeeffectofthetwoparagraphsofArticle 10is
practicallythesameastheeffectofthesingleprovisionofTRIPSArticle 13.Article 10,and,in 
particularitsparagraph (2),isaninterpretationtoolintheapplicationoftheprovisionsofthe 
Berne Convention on exceptions and limitations incorporated by reference. 
CT-10.9.InthecaseofArticle 13oftheTRIPSAgreement,thefindingthat,inrespectofthe
relevant norms of the Berne Convention, it does not have either an extending or a restricting 
effect on the scope of permissible exceptions and limitations, and that it is just an interpretation 
tool, is based on a possible interpretation of that provision of the Agreement. In the case of 
the WCT, in contrast, the Diplomatic Conference clarified, through the adoption of the agreed 
statementconcerningArticle 10(2),thatthisistheonlyadequateinterpretation.Asquoted 
above,itstated:“ItisalsounderstoodthatArticle 10(2)neitherreducesnorextendsthescopeof 
applicability of the limitations and exceptions permitted by the Berne Convention”.
Application of exceptions and limitations in the online digital environment
CT-10.10. The text ofArticle 10oftheWCTitselfdoesnotcontainanyspecificprovisionsabout 
the application of exceptions and limitations in the online digital environment. Nevertheless, 
the Diplomatic Conference adopted an agreed statement which addresses this issue specifically. 
Its first sentence is on the application of existing exceptions and limitations and it states: “It 
isunderstoodthattheprovisionsofArticle 10permitContractingPartiestocarryforward 
and appropriately extend into the digital environment limitations and exceptions in their 
national laws which have been considered applicable under the Berne Convention”. The second 
sentence refers to possible new exceptions and limitations: “Similarly, these provisions should 
be understood to permit Contracting Parties to devise new exceptions and limitations that are 
appropriate in the digital network environment”.
CT-10.11. The agreed statement should be interpreted in the light of the obligation to apply the 
three-steptestasprovidedforinArticle 10.Existingexceptionsandlimitationsmaybecarried 
forward to the new environment, but it should be guaranteed that they still correspond to the 
conditions of the test in the new circumstances. For example, educational exceptions obviously 
should be maintained, but, in the online digital environment for “distance education”, it should 
beensured–throughtechnologicalmeasuresandrightsmanagementinformation–thatthe
protected materials will be used only for the intended purpose and only by the beneficiaries 
oftheexception.Atthesametime,certainexceptions–suchas,forexample,thefreeuseof
quotations–maybecarriedforwardwithoutanysignificantchange.Asregardsthequestion 
of which exception is new, it depends, of course, whether the existing or the new elements are 
considered to dominate. Thus, for example, a distance education exception may seem to be

the exception to the right of reproduction concerning certain temporary acts of reproduction 
asunderArticle 5(1)oftheInformationSocietyDirectivewhich,likeanyotherexceptionsand
limitationsprovidedforinArticle 5,isalsosubjecttothethree-steptestbyvirtueofArticle 5(5).
Article 11
Obligations concerning Technological Measures
ContractingPartiesshallprovideadequatelegalprotectionandeffectivelegalremediesagainst
the circumvention of effective technological measures that are used by authors in connection 
with the exercise of their rights under this Treaty or the Berne Convention and that restrict acts, 
in respect of their works, which are not authorized by the authors concerned or permitted by law.
Application of technological protection measures: a key condition for the protection, exercise 
and enforcement of copyright in the online digital environment
CT-11.1. While the other provisions of the WCT consist mainly in the interpretation and certain 
adaptationsoftheexistinginternationalnormsoncopyright,Article 11,alongwithArticle 12,
includes truly new provisions. It was recognized during the preparatory work of the WCT and 
the WPPT that appropriate legal machinery must be available for effective application of the 
advice “the answer to the machine is in the machine” by Charles Clark to solve the problems 
posed by digital technology to copyright. 545 Namely, technological protection measures (such as 
encryption of the protected materials) and electronic rights management information (such as 
digital identifiers) should be used to prevent the unlawful functioning of the “machine”.
CT-11.2.Itwasacceptedasaprincipleatquiteanearlystageofthepreparatoryworkthatit
should be left to the interested owners of rights whether or not to use such measures and/or 
information and, if so, what types. It was recognized that the new treaties should not prescribe 
theinstruments,butonlygrantadequateprotectionfortheirapplicability.
The meaning of “effective technological measures”
CT-11.3. It is not necessary to try to offer a detailed description in this commentary of those 
technological protection measures that may be applied by the owners of rights. They are 
constantly developing as a result of technological advancements and the need for adaptations 
inresponsetotherepeatedattemptsatbreakingthem.Someofthemarequitewellknown,
such as, for example, “scrambling” of cable television signals in order to limit access to paid 
subscribers; the encryption of works or inclusion thereof into a tamper-resistant “software 
envelope” when transmitted through the global information network; or the inscription of 
electronic watermarks in digital material to help to prevent its unauthorized copying (and 
at the same time to trace such reproductions, a function that may be used for electronic 
rights management).
CT-11.4. What does need interpretation, however, is what it means that a technological measure, 
in order to be protected, must be effective.Itseemsquiteobviousthatitcannotbeconstrued
as meaning that, if it is possible to circumvent such a measure, it cannot be regarded as 
effective. This would be absurd since the objective of the provision is exactly to guarantee 
protection against acts of circumvention, which logically must be possible even with an effective 
technological measure in place, because if they were impossible, no protection would be 
needed. For a technological protection measure to be deemed effective, it seems sufficient 
that, in the ordinary course of its operation, some specific information, process or treatment 
should be necessary for gaining access to the work protected by it, and/or for carrying out an 
act controlled by it, such that said information, process or treatment is available only with the 
consent of the copyright owner.
545 See Charles Clark, Publishers and publishing in the digital era, in Worldwide Symposium on Copyright in the Global 
Information Infrastructure , publication no. 746 (E/S) (WIPO, 1995), 346.

===== PAGE 261 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
262 CT-11.5. It is not necessary to draw up a more detailed definition of “technological measures”, 
because it seems sufficiently clear. If a definition is still offered, it should be of a functional 
nature(ratherthantechnology-specific)inordertoavoid(probablyquiteearly)obsolescence.
The meaning of technological measures “used by authors in connection with the exercise of 
their rights under this Treaty or the Berne Convention”
CT-11.6.ThispartoftheArticle impliesthatitisuptotheauthors–“authors”,ofcourse,also
meaning their successor-in-title546–whetherornottousetechnologicalmeasuresandifsowhat
kindofmeasures.Buttheobligationtoprovide“adequatelegalprotectionandeffectivelegal 
remedies” applies as soon as such measures are applied.
CT-11.7.TheobligationunderArticle 11extendstotechnologicalmeasuresirrespectiveof
whichrighttheyareappliedinrespectof.Howtherightsareexercised–suchaswhetheronan
individualbasisorthroughcollectivemanagement–isalsoirrelevant.
The meaning of technological measures “that restrict acts, in respect of […] works”
CT-11.8. There are two basic forms of restricting acts: first, restricting access to works; and, 
second, restricting the carrying out of certain acts in respect of works. The obligations under 
Article 11coverbothofthesebasicforms.
CT-11.9.Itistobenotedthat,althoughArticle 11wasadoptedonthebasisofthe“digital
agenda” of the WCT and the WPPT, since its language is technologically neutral it is applicable 
not only to acts relating to uses of works in digital format, either online or offline, but, in 
principle, also to acts carried out in the “traditional” analog world. Thus it also provides an 
obligationto“provideadequatelegalprotectionandeffectivelegalremediesagainstthe 
circumvention of” the codes applied in coded broadcast programs. However, it is expected to be 
applied mainly in the digital, networked environment.
The meaning of “circumvention”
CT-11.10. Circumvention may be done in a number of different ways, including destroying, 
breaking or neutralizing technological protection measures; decrypting (“hacking”) an 
encrypted work; descrambling a scrambled work; “cracking” software envelopes; or tampering 
with digital watermarks. In general, “circumvention” means any act of avoiding, bypassing, 
removing, deactivating or impairing such a measure.
CT-11.11.Onthequestionofwhetheritisnecessarytoincludeaspecificdefinitionof
“circumvention”,thesameistrueasinrespectoftheabovequestionon“technological
measures”: the meaning of the term is sufficiently clear without it. What is important is that, if 
a definition is drafted in the future, it must be of a functional nature (rather than technology-
specific) in order to avoid foreseeable obsolescence.
The meaning of acts “not authorized by the authors concerned or permitted by law”
CT-11.12.Themeaningofthefirstpartofthephrase–“notauthorizedbytheauthorsconcerned”
–isclear.Theverypurposeofapplyingtechnologicalmeasuresisthatonlythoseactsmaybe
carried out that the “authors concerned” have authorized. In contrast, the second part of the 
phrase–“not[…]permittedbylaw”–requiresinterpretation.Thebasicquestioniswhetherthe
term “acts pemitted by law” is to be interpreted to mean any exceptions and limitations permitted 
by law or only those that are specifically permitted in this specific context. The first interpretation 
546AccordingtothesecondsentenceofArticle 2(6)oftheBerneConvention–which,underArticle 1(4)oftheWCTisalso 
applicableinthecontextofthetreaty–theprotectiongrantedtoauthorsalsoappliestotheauthors’successorsof 
title.Itisaquestionhowandwithwhateffectnon-exclusivelicensees(whoarenotsuccessors-in-title)mayapply 
TPMs. In general, there is no conflict of interests in this respect between the author and the licensee; after all, if the 
authors want to make available their works without TMP, they may do so, since the license is non-exclusive. At the 
same time, it is a legitimate interest of the licensees to control the dissemination of the works to the extent covered 
by the licenses, including by TPMs where it is necessary. Although national laws may regulate the issue in different 
ways, it seems justified to understand the phrase “used by authors in connection with the exercise of their rights” to 
also include use of TPMs by licensees on behalf of the authors who have exercised their rights by granting licenses.

263
PART III. Guides to the three WIPO “Internet Treaties” – the WCT, the WPPT and the BTAP
might make the protection to be provided by technological measures ineffective. For example, 
if a private copying exception were sufficient to remove technological protection of a new film 
without any further conditions, it would lead to immediate free availability of the film practically 
toeverybody;withthis,anumberofbusinessmethods–suchasvideoondemand–would
become untenable. Also, for example, it would be disproportionate to allow the circumvention of 
atechnologicalmeasureprotectinga750-pagetreatisetosomebodywhoonlywantstoquotesix
lines of it. Duly calibrated balance should be established that takes into account the rightholders’ 
interests and also ensures normal exploitation of their creations. In the online digital environment, 
thisrequirestechnologicalmeasures,andtheapplicabilityofonlythoseexceptionsorlimitations
that are justified by significant public or legitimate private interests.
CT-11.13. At the 1996 Diplomatic Conference, the delegations’ idea was to leave the task of 
the establishment of such a balance to the Contracting Parties. By the time of the adoption of 
theBTAP,however,sufficientexperiencehadbecomeavailabletodetermine–inanagreed
statement–certainkeycriteriatobetakenintoaccountforthebalancingtask.Thosecriteria 
may be duly applied also for the application mutatis mutandis of the same kinds of provisions 
ontechnologicalmeasuresasunderArticle 11oftheWCT.Theagreedstatementconcerning
Articles 13and15–analyzedbelowintheGuidetotheBTAP–readsasfollows:
ItisunderstoodthatnothinginthisArticle preventsaContractingPartyfromadopting
effective and necessary measures to ensure that a beneficiary may enjoy limitations and 
exceptions provided in that Contracting Party’s national law, in accordance with Article 13, 
where technological measures have been applied to an audiovisual performance and 
the beneficiary has legal access to that performance, in circumstances such as where 
appropriate and effective measures have not been taken by rights holders in relation 
to that performance to enable the beneficiary to enjoy the limitations and exceptions 
under that Contracting Party’s national law. Without prejudice to the legal protection 
of an audiovisual work in which a performance is fixed, it is further understood that the 
obligationsunderArticle 15arenotapplicabletoperformancesunprotectedornolonger
protected under the national law giving effect to this Treaty. [Emphasis added.]
CT-11.14. One of the guarantees for an appropriate balance, as pointed out below in the Guide 
to the BTAP in more detail, is the application of the three-step test. This ensures that not only 
the exceptions and limitations are in accordance with the three cumulative conditions of the 
test, but also the extent and the method of application of the measure to ensure that the 
beneficiaries can enjoy the exceptions and limitations where justified.
The requirement of providing “adequate legal protection and effective legal remedies” 
against circumvention
CT-11.15. Many acts of circumvention of technological protection measures may be carried out in 
private homes or in offices, where the enforcement of the prohibition of such unauthorized acts 
–bothforlogisticalreasonsandduetoprivacyconsiderations–isimpossibleorverydifficult. 
Therefore, if a national law only prohibits such acts, the legal protection and the remedies will 
not be effective.
CT-11.16. Due to the complexity of the technologies involved, in most cases the acts of 
circumvention may only be performed after the necessary circumvention device or service 
hasbeenacquired.Theiracquisitionnormallytakesplaceoutsidetheprivatesphereinthe
marketplace of such devices and services. Thus, the practical way of providing protection 
and remedies against unauthorized acts of circumvention is to cut the supply line of illicit 
circumvention devices and services by prohibiting the manufacture, importation and distribution 
of such devices and the offering of such services (the so-called “preparatory activities”).
CT-11.17. For these reasons, Contracting Parties may be sure that they are able to fulfill their 
obligationsunderArticle 11oftheTreatyonlyiftheyprovidetherequiredprotectionand
remedies: (i) against both unauthorized acts of circumvention and the above-mentioned 
“preparatory activities” that render such acts possible; (ii) against all such acts in respect of 
both technological measures used for access control and those used to control acts covered 
by certain rights, such as copy-control devices; (iii) not only against devices whose sole 
purpose is circumvention, but also against those that are primarily designed and produced

===== PAGE 263 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
264 for such purposes, that have only a limited, commercially significant objective or use other 
than circumvention, or that are obviously meant for circumvention because they are marketed 
(advertised, etc.) as such; and (iv) not only against an entire device of that nature, but also against 
individual components or built-in special functions that correspond to the criteria described above.
CT-11.18. It depends on the traditions and principles of the legal systems of Contracting Parties 
how they may guarantee “effective legal remedies” against both acts of circumvention and 
preparatory acts. It seems obvious, however, that in general civil remedies are indispensable. 
Furthermore, criminal penalties are also needed since the manufacture, importation and 
distribution of illicit circumvention devices is a kind of piratical activity. Against these 
“preparatory activities”, it seems justified to also apply those kinds of provisional and border 
measureswhichareprovidedforinArticles 50to60oftheTRIPSAgreement.
Article 12
Obligations concerning Rights Management Information
(1) ContractingPartiesshallprovideadequateandeffectivelegalremediesagainstany
person knowingly performing any of the following acts knowing, or with respect to civil 
remedies having reasonable grounds to know, that it will induce, enable, facilitate or 
conceal an infringement of any right covered by this Treaty or the Berne Convention:
(i)  to remove or alter any electronic rights management information 
without authority;
(ii)  to distribute, import for distribution, broadcast or communicate to the public, 
without authority, works or copies of works knowing that electronic rights 
management information has been removed or altered without authority.
(2) As used in this Article, “rights management information” means information which 
identifies the work, the author of the work, the owner of any right in the work, or 
information about the terms and conditions of use of the work, and any numbers or codes 
that represent such information, when any of these items of information is attached to a 
copy of a work or appears in connection with the communication of a work to the public.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 12:Itisunderstoodthatthereferenceto“infringement
of any copyright covered by this Treaty or the Berne Convention” includes both exclusive rights 
and rights of remuneration.
ItisfurtherunderstoodthatContractingPartieswillnotrelyonthisArticle todeviseor
implement rights management systems that would have the effect of imposing formalities 
which are not permitted under the Berne Convention or this Treaty, prohibiting the free 
movement of goods or impeding the enjoyment of rights under this Treaty.
Application of rights management information: a key condition for the protection, exercise 
and enforcement of copyright in the online digital environment
CT-12.1.Forthenatureandimportanceoftheprovisionsinthisarticle (andthoseincludedin
Article 11),seethefirsttwoparagraphsinthecommentsaboveonArticle 11.
Interpretation of Article  12
CT-12.2.TheprovisionsincludedinArticle 12are,ingeneral,self-explanatory;therefore,onlysome
points have to be emphasized. First of all, “any right covered by this Treaty or the Berne Convention” 
mentionedinparagraph (1)meansnotonlyanyeconomicrights,butalsoanymoralrights.
CT-12.3.WhileArticle 11fixestheobligationtoprovide“adequatelegalprotectionandeffective 
legalremedies”,Article 12obligatesContractingPartiesonlytoprovide“adequateandeffective 
legal remedies”. It seems that the lack of harmony between the two texts is the result of 
mere drafting inadvertence, and that the nature of the obligations of Contracting Parties is 
practically the same under the two provisions: providing adequate norms for the prohibition 
of the acts identified in them ( protection) and effective legal remedies in case of violation of 
suchprohibition.Itmaybeaddedthat,whileinthecaseofArticle 11itisanimportantissue

265

ofinterpretationtodeterminewhatprotectionmaytrulybe“adequate”againstunauthorized 
circumvention of technological measures (it is sufficient to refer to the issue of “preparatory 
activities”),thecomprehensiveanddetailednatureoftheprovisionsinArticle 12,whichalso 
include a definition, makes their implementation simpler. It is even possible to reproduce the 
provisionsofArticle 12innationallawwithoutanysubstantivechangewhatsoever;thenthe 
onlyremainingtaskwouldbetoadoptprovisionson“adequateandeffectivelegalremedies”.
CT-12.4.TherearethreelayersofknowledgeconditionsinArticle 12.First,theusersshouldknow
thattheyperformanactmentionedinitems(i)and(ii)ofparagraph (1);thatis,mereinadvertent
actsarenotcovered.Second,theyshouldknow–orinrespectofcivilremedies,shouldatleast
havereasonablegroundstoknow–thattheactperformedbythem“willinduce,enable,facilitate
or conceal an infringement”. Third, in the case of the acts listed in item (ii), they should also know 
that rights management information has been removed or altered without authority.
CT-12.5.TheprovisionsofArticle 12onlycoverelectronic rights management information. Such 
information is mainly embodied in “numbers and codes that represent such information” to 
whichthedefinitioninparagraph (2)refers.
CT-12.6.Inthedefinitionof“rightsmanagementinformation”providedinparagraph (2)of
thearticle,onlytheminimumaspectsofinformationaredeterminedforwhich“adequateand 
effectivelegalremedies”mustbeensuredagainsttheactsmentionedinparagraph (1).National 
laws may provide protection for a broader scope of rights management information.
The agreed statements: clarifying the coverage of the provisions and confirming the 
prohibition of formalities
CT-12.7.TheagreedstatementsadoptedconcerningArticle 12–agreedstatements in plural since 
thetwosentencescovertwodifferentissues–offersomeclarifications.Thefirstonemakes
evenclearerwhatisalreadyquiteclearinthetextofArticle 12(1)itself:that“anyrightscovered
by the Treaty” means both exclusive rights and possible rights to remuneration. The second 
sentence seems truly useful since it points out that the regulation and the application of rights 
management information may in no way undermine the principle of formality-free protection 
establishedinArticle 5(2)oftheBerneConventionandincorporatedbyreferenceintotheWCT.547 
Article 13 
Application in Time
ContractingPartiesshallapplytheprovisionsofArticle 18oftheBerneConventiontoall
protection provided for in this Treaty.
Correct title to avoid the use of the misleading term “retroactivity”
CT-13.1.AsmentionedinthecommentsonthatArticle intheGuidetotheBerneConventionin
thiscollection,theeffectofArticle 18(1)and(2)oftheConventionisfrequentlyreferredtoas
“retroactive protection”. As is stressed there, this reference is misleading because there is no 
retroactiveprotectionrequiredinthesensethatcertainactsallowedtobeperformedfreely 
before the entry into force of the Convention retroactively would be regarded as infringing. The 
provisionsofArticle 18onlymeanthattheobligationsundertheConventionmustbefulfilled 
from the very moment of the entry into force of the Convention for a given country. This includes 
the obligation to protect all works for which the term of protection has not yet expired (it is only 
from that moment that, for the performing of acts covered by exclusive rights, authorization is 
needed, and that the rights to remuneration apply). There is no retroactive obligation involved 
inthis,and,therefore,theapplicationofArticle 18(1)and(2)doesnotraiseanyconstitutionality
problem.Certainproblemsmayemerge,however,inrespectoftheacquiredrightsof“reliance
parties”.Article 18(3)oftheConventionoffersasolutiontosuchproblemsbyallowing 
547 Thatis,theprotection–orextentofprotection–ofworksmustnotbemadeconditionalontheapplicationofanyspecific
rights management information or rights management information at all (similarly, in this respect, to what is discussed 
aboveconcerningArticle 11onthequestionofapplicationornon-applicationoftechnologicalprotectionmeasures).

===== PAGE 265 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
266 transitionalprovisions,inordertorespectthe“acquiredrights”ofthosewhoreliedonthelegal 
situationbeforetheentryintoforceoftheConvention.Forthesereasons,thetitleofArticle 13
has been well chosen; there is no reference in it to any kind of retroactivity.
Article 18 of the Berne Convention and its mutatis mutandis application
CT-13.2.ItisnotjustifiedtorepeatheretheanalysisofArticle 18includedinthecommentsonit
in the Guide to the Berne Convention in this collection. It seems useful, however, to reproduce 
thetextoftheArticle thatshouldbeapplied“toallprotectionprovidedforinthisTreaty”:
(1)  This Convention shall apply to all works which, at the moment of its coming into 
force, have not yet fallen into the public domain in the country of origin through the 
expiry of the term of protection.
(2)  If, however, through the expiry of the term of protection which was previously 
granted, a work has fallen into the public domain of the country where protection is 
claimed, that work shall not be protected anew.
(3)  The application of this principle shall be subject to any provisions contained in special 
conventions to that effect existing or to be concluded between countries of the 
Union. In the absence of such provisions, the respective countries shall determine, 
each in so far as it is concerned, the conditions of application of this principle.
(4)  The preceding provisions shall also apply in the case of new accessions to the Union 
andtocasesinwhichprotectionisextendedbytheapplicationofArticle 7orbythe
abandonment of reservation.
CT-13.3.WhereArticle 13oftheWCTprovidesthat“Contracting Parties shall apply the provisions 
of Article 18 of the Berne Convention to all protection provided for in this Treaty” [emphasis 
added], obviously mutatis mutandis applicationismeant.Thus,inparagraph (1),“this Treaty” 
should be understood instead of “this Convention ”; inparagraph (3),“countries of the Union” 
should be understood as “Contracting Parties ”; and,inparagraph (4),“the Union” simply means 
“this Treaty”. In the mutatis mutandis applicationofparagraph (4),thereferencetoArticle 7is,
ofcourse,areferencetoArticle 7oftheBerneConvention,butnotonlytoit;alsotoArticle 9of
theWCT,whichexcludestheapplicationofArticle 7(4)oftheBerneConventiontophotographic
works, and, by this, extends the minimum term of protection of such works by assimilating them 
in this respect to other literary and artistic works.
Article 14
Provisions on Enforcement of Rights
(1) Contracting Parties undertake to adopt, in accordance with their legal systems, the 
measures necessary to ensure the application of this Treaty.
(2) Contracting Parties shall ensure that enforcement procedures are available under their 
law so as to permit effective action against any act of infringement of rights covered 
by this Treaty, including expeditious remedies to prevent infringements and remedies 
which constitute a deterrent to further infringements.
Measures necessary to ensure application
CT-14.1.Withonedifference,paragraph (1)ofArticle 14isaverbatimcopyofArticle 36(1)ofthe
Berne Convention, which reads as follows: “Any country party to this Convention undertakes to 
adopt, in accordance with its constitution, the measures necessary to ensure the application of 
this Convention”. The difference, as it can be seen in comparing the two texts, is that, while the 
Berne Convention refers to accordance with the constitutions of the countries concerned, the 
reference in the WCT is to accordance with the legal systems.
CT-14.2. A constitution contains the most fundamental elements, the macro aspects, of a legal 
system. The reference to the legal systems of the Contracting Parties suggests more freedom;

===== PAGE 266 =====
267
PART III. Guides to the three WIPO “Internet Treaties” – the WCT, the WPPT and the BTAP
it seems to allow the Contracting Parties to choose freely the legal means of implementing their 
obligations under the Treaty provided that those means are truly suitable for this purpose.
CT-14.3.Inaway,paragraph (1)ofArticle 14confirmstheprincipleofrelativefreedomof
legalcharacterizationwhichisdiscussedaboveinthecommentsonArticle 8oftheTreatyin
connection with the “umbrella solution”.
Obligations concerning enforcement of rights
CT-14.4. The draft treaty which later became the WCT still contained two alternatives concerning 
enforcement of rights. Alternative A consisted of the inclusion, as an integral part of the Treaty, 
ofatechnicallyadaptedversionofthefulltextofPartIII–Articles 41to61–oftheTRIPS
Agreement in an Annex. Alternative B would have achieved more or less the same result, but in 
a different way. It read as follows:
Contracting Parties shall ensure that the enforcement procedures specified in Part III, 
Articles 41to61,oftheAgreementonTrade-RelatedAspectsofIntellectualProperty
Rights, Including Trade in Counterfeit Goods, Annex 1C, of the Marrakesh Agreement 
Establishing the World Trade Organization, concluded on April 15, 1994 (the “TRIPS 
Agreement”), are available under their national laws so as to permit effective action 
against any act of infringement of the rights provided under this Treaty, including 
expeditious remedies to prevent infringements, and remedies that constitute a deterrent 
to further infringements. To this end, Contracting Parties shall apply mutatis mutandis the 
provisionsofArticles 41to61oftheTRIPSAgreement.548
CT-14.5.TheDiplomaticConferencedidnotadopteitherofthesealternatives.Viewsvery
much diverged in the course of the negotiations on various options. The deadlock was finally 
eliminatedbyacompromiseproposalofthedelegationofJamaica.Itconsistedofdeleting
both alternatives and replacing them by a text which, although not exactly in this form, but 
insubstance,appearedinArticle (1)ofthedraftAnnex.Thistextwasadoptedanditbecame 
paragraph (2)ofArticle 14oftheTreaty.
CT-14.6.Thisparagraph (2)isaveryslightlymodifiedverbatimcopyofthefirstsentenceofthevery
firstArticle –Article 41.1–ofPartIIIoftheTRIPSAgreementonenforcementofrights;itreadsas
follows(thedifferencesincomparisonwiththetextofparagraph (2)areindicatedinitalics):
Members shall ensure that enforcement procedures as specified in this Part are available 
under their law so as to permit effective action against any act of infringement of rights 
covered by this Agreement, including expeditious remedies to prevent infringements and 
remedies which constitute a deterrent to further infringements. 
CT-14.7.Itisanimportantfactorfortheinterpretationofparagraph (2)ofArticle 14oftheWCT
that it is a verbatim copy of this provision of the TRIPS Agreement, since it indicates that the 
enforcement provisions specified in Part III of the Agreement tend to be needed for achieving 
theresultmentionedinit–“effectiveactionagainstanyactofinfringementofrights”–andthat 
theyrequire“expeditiousremediestopreventinfringementsandremedieswhichconstitutea 
deterrenttofurtherinfringement”.Fromthiscontextandoriginofthetextofparagraph (2),and 
from the circumstances of its adoption, it seems to follow that only those Contracting Parties 
may fulfill the obligations under it that apply more or less the same kind of mechanisms against 
infringementsundertheTreatyasthoserequiredunderPartIIIoftheTRIPSAgreement.
Administrative and final clauses
TheprovisionsofArticles 15to25oftheWCTcontaintheusualadministrativeprovisionsand
final clauses of WIPO treaties. Due to their nature they are self-explanatory and do not raise 
questionsofinterpretation.Sincethesesameprovisionsandclausesarereproduced mutatis 
mutandis in all the treaties, though with some differences in the BTAP, comments are reserved 
for the end of Part III, where all three WIPO “Internet Treaties” are considered together.
548 Document CRNR/DC/55, Records of the 1996 Diplomatic Conference , 444.

(1) (a)  The Contracting Parties shall have an Assembly.
