WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty (WPPT), 1996
Preamble
The Contracting Parties,
Desiring to develop and maintain the protection of the rights of performers and producers of 
phonograms in a manner as effective and uniform as possible,
Recognizing theneedtointroducenewinternationalrulesinordertoprovideadequate
solutionstothequestionsraisedbyeconomic,social,culturalandtechnologicaldevelopments,
Recognizing the profound impact of the development and convergence of information and 
communication technologies on the production and use of performances and phonograms,
Recognizing the need to maintain a balance between the rights of performers and producers 
of phonograms and the larger public interest, particularly education, research and access 
to information,
Have agreed as follows:
First paragraph
PPT-Pr.1.Thefirstparagraph ofthePreamble,insubstance,isthesameasinthePreamble
to the WCT, with the only difference that here, of course, reference is made to the rights of 
performers and producers of phonograms rather than to the rights of authors.
PPT-Pr.2. In contrast, the Preamble of the WPPT differs from the Preamble to the Rome 
Convention. The latter is much simpler: “The Contracting Parties, moved by the desire to protect 
the rights of performers, producers of phonograms, and broadcasting organizations […]”.   
There is no reference in it to the development and maintenance of the protection of the 
categories of rights covered. This is certainly due to the fact that, at the time of its adoption, 
the Rome Convention was a “pioneer” treaty: it opened the way for the establishment of 
adequateprotectionofrelatedrights;thus,itwouldnothavebeenappropriatetoindicate
the development and maintenance of such protection as objectives. By 1996, the protection 
of the rights of performers and producers of phonograms had been established in a number 
of countries, and had also been developed at regional and international level, such as in the 
directives of the European Community and in the TRIPS Agreement. Thus, in the Preamble to the 
WPPT, it was justified to speak of maintenance and (further) development of the protection of 
the rights of performers and producers of phonograms.
PPT-Pr.3. There is one more difference between the Preambles to the Rome Convention and 
the WPPT; namely, that, while the former only refers to the desire to protect the rights covered 
by it, the latter adds that it is intended to be done “in a manner as effective and uniform and 
possible”. This text has been taken word for word from the Preamble to the Berne Convention. 
As analyzed in the comments on the Rome Convention in the Guide in this collection, at the time 
of the adoption of that Convention, due to its pioneer nature, it would have been badly founded 
to speak in the Preamble of protection “as efficient and uniform as possible”. The indication in 
the Preamble to the WPPT of the same kind of more ambitious objectives as in the Preamble 
totheBerneConventionissignificant;itreflectsatrendtowardsasortofconvergence–with 
stillexistingbutneverthelessdecreasingdifferences–betweenthelevelsofprotectionof 
copyright and related rights. It confirms the intention of those who adopted the WPPT to follow 
this trend, which is manifested in the Treaty in various aspects, such as, for example, in the 
recognitionofmoralrightsforperformers;andtheprovisions–textuallyinthesamewayasin 
theWCT,but(duetothedifferingcontext)stillmoreclearly–ontherightofinteractivemaking
available to the public, the right of distribution, the conditions for the application of exceptions 
and limitations, the obligations concerning technological protection measures and rights 
management information, and enforcement of rights.

===== PAGE 271 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
272 Second paragraph
PPT-Pr.4.Thelanguageofthisparagraph –withonedifference–isthesameasinthesecond
paragraph ofthePreambletotheWCT,andthesameappliestoitaswasdiscussedintheGuideto
the WCT above concerning that Preamble. The only difference is that the second sentence of the 
Preamble to the WCT refers not only to “the need to introduce new international rules”, but also to 
the need to “clarify the interpretation of certain existing rules”. This difference may be explained 
by the fact that the WPPT does not contain provisions that are worded as mere interpretations 
ofexistingnorms,incontrastwithArticles 4and5oftheWCT,whichsimplystatethatcomputer
programs and databases, respectively, are protected under the Berne Convention; the WPPT without 
exception uses “shall” constructions. This does not mean that the Diplomatic Conference did not 
clarify the application of certain existing norms concerning the rights covered by the WPPT. This, 
however, took place through the adoption of agreed statements, such as those on the application of 
the right of reproduction and the exceptions and limitations in the digital environment.
Third paragraph
PPT-Pr.5.Thisparagraph referstotheimpactofthedevelopmentandconvergenceofinformation
andcommunicationtechnologiesinthesamewayasthethirdparagraph ofthePreamble
to the WCT, with the only difference that it does so with regard to the production and use of 
performances and phonograms. Therefore, mutatis mutandis, the same applies to it as what is 
discussedinrespectofthatparagraph ofthePreambletotheWCTintheGuidetothatTreaty.
Fourth paragraph
PPT-Pr.6.Thisparagraph differsfromthecorrespondingparagraph –thefifthone–ofthe
Preamble to the WCT in two aspects. First, it does not refer, of course, to the balance “as 
reflected in the Berne Convention” and, second, it is not preceded by another paragraph, as in 
the WCT Preamble, which there reads as follows: “[e]mphasizing the outstanding significance 
of copyright protection as an incentive for literary and artistic creation”. As regards the first 
difference, it obviously would not have been appropriate to refer to the “balance of interests” 
offeredbythequiteout-of-dateRomeConvention,while,asfarastheseconddifferenceis
concerned, it does not seem justified to consider it as truly important, since it can hardly be 
denied that the protection of the rights of performers and producers of phonograms does have 
an outstanding significance (in fact, it is indispensable) as an incentive for new performances 
and the production of phonograms, regardless of whether this is stated explicitly.
Chapter I: General Provisions
Article 1
Relation to Other Conventions
(1) Nothing in this Treaty shall derogate from existing obligations that Contracting 
Parties have to each other under the International Convention for the Protection of 
Performers, Producers of Phonograms and Broadcasting Organizations done in Rome, 
October 26, 1961 (hereinafter the “Rome Convention”).
(2) Protection granted under this Treaty shall leave intact and shall in no way affect the 
protectionofcopyrightinliteraryandartisticworks.Consequently,noprovisionofthis
Treaty may be interpreted as prejudicing such protection.
(3) This Treaty shall not have any connection with, nor shall it prejudice any rights and 
obligations under, any other treaties.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 1(2):ItisunderstoodthatArticle 1(2)clarifiesthe
relationship between rights in phonograms under this Treaty and copyright in works embodied 
in the phonograms. In cases where authorization is needed from both the author of a work 
embodied in the phonogram and a performer or producer owning rights in the phonogram, 
the need for the authorization of the author does not cease to exist because the authorization 
oftheperformerorproducerisalsorequired,andviceversa.

===== PAGE 272 =====
273

ItisfurtherunderstoodthatnothinginArticle 1(2)precludesaContractingPartyfrom
providingexclusiverightstoaperformerorproducerofphonogramsbeyondthoserequiredto
be provided under this Treaty.
Title of the Article
PPT-1.1. The title does not fully cover the contents of the Article. Only paragraphs (1) and (3) of 
Article 1concerntherelationshipoftheWPPTwith“otherconventions”;paragraph (2),rather,
deals with the relationship of the protection granted under the Treaty with the protection 
ofcopyrightinliteraryandartisticworks.Also,althoughparagraph (1)trulydealswiththe 
relationshipwithaconvention–theRomeConvention–paragraph (3)refersto“othertreaties”.
Since “treaty” is the more generic term, a title like “Relation to other treaties and the protection 
of copyright” would have better corresponded to the contents.
No statement about the “special agreement” nature of the Treaty
PPT-1.2.TheWCT,initsArticle 1(1),statesthatitis“aspecialagreementwithinthemeaningof
Article 20oftheBerneConvention”. ThereisnosimilarstatementinArticle 1,orinanyother
provision,oftheWPPT,onitsspecialagreementnature“withinthemeaningofArticle 22ofthe
Rome Convention”. ThatArticle oftheRomeConventionprovidesthesamecriteriaofspecial
agreementsasArticle 20oftheBerneConvention. 549 The absence of a statement about it may 
hardly be regarded as decisive on whether or not the WPPT is a special agreement. It has been 
concluded among Contracting States of the Rome Convention, which is so despite the fact that 
it has not been concluded only among themselves but also with other countries. It is a treaty 
for the protection of the rights of two of the three categories of beneficiaries of the Rome 
Convention: performers and producers of phonograms. Therefore, from the viewpoint of the 
Contracting States of the Convention, the WPPT is a special agreement within the meaning of 
Article 22oftheRomeConvention.IntherelationshipbetweenRomeContractingStates,it 
must grant more extensive rights than those granted by the Convention, or it may contain other 
provisions, but they must not be contrary to the Convention.
PPT-1.3.TheWPPTseemstoconformtothecriteriaofArticle 22oftheRomeConvention.
Although it covers the rights of only two of the three categories of the beneficiaries of the 
Convention and, as regards the rights of performers, its coverage only extends to “aural” 
performances, it grants these beneficiaries rights that are more extensive than under the Rome 
Convention. It is not a problem in terms of the special agreement status of the Treaty that its 
protection does not cover all categories of beneficiaries, because there is nothing in the Treaty 
that is contrary to the Convention in respect of those beneficiaries.
PPT-1.4.Otherwise,asdiscussedbelow,theWPPTinArticle 1(1)containsasafeguardclausethat
precludesanyconflictwithArticle 22asfarastheContractingStatesoftheRomeConvention 
are concerned.
Safeguard clause for the Rome Convention
PPT-1.5.ThesafeguardclauseinArticle 1(1)oftheWPPTissimilartothesafeguardclausein
Article 1(2)oftheWCT.Theroleofthisprovision,however,forthereasonsjustmentioned,is
more important than that of the corresponding provision in the WCT. The importance of the 
safeguard clause follows not only from the narrower coverage of the WPPT, but also from the 
factthattheTreaty–withthemarginalexceptionsdiscussedinthecommentsonArticle 3below
–doesnotobligateContractingPartiestocomplywiththesubstantiveprovisionsoftheRome 
Convention (in contrast with the WCT, which does so concerning those of the Berne Convention). 
Although the WPPT includes provisions that in general seem to correspond, in substance at 
least, to the level of protection prescribed by the Rome Convention for the categories of rights 
covered, the text and the meaning of those provisions are not always the same as those of the 
corresponding provisions in the Rome Convention.
549Article 22oftheRomeConvention,discussedintheguidetothatconventioninthiscollection,readsasfollows: 
“Contracting States reserve the right to enter into special agreements among themselves in as far as such 
agreements grant to performers, producers of phonograms or broadcasting organisations more extensive rights 
than those granted by this Convention or contain other provisions not contrary to this Convention.”

Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
274 The WPPT and the protection of copyright
PPT-1.6.Article 1(2)oftheWPPTcorrespondstoArticle 1oftheRomeConvention;550 the only 
difference is that the Rome provision refers to the Convention, and the WPPT provision to the 
Treaty. Therefore, the same comments apply here mutatis mutandis as those concerning the 
provision of the Rome Convention in the Guide to the Convention in this collection.
PPT-1.7.ThefirstpartoftheagreedstatementconcerningArticle 1(2)confirmsthefindings
madeinthecommentsonArticle 1oftheRomeConventioninthatthenon-derogation
provision in relation to copyright does not establish a hierarchy between copyright and related 
rights. The words “vice versa” indicate that, the same way as the protection granted under 
the Treaty leaves intact and in no way affects the protection of copyright, the protection of 
copyrightequallyleavesintactandinnowayaffectstheprotectionoftherightsprovidedinthe 
Treaty. Where both copyright and related rights owners have an exclusive right of authorization 
in a production, the authorization of the copyright holder alone is not sufficient for the lawful 
use thereof; nor is the authorization of the owner of related rights alone.
PPT-1.8.Thesecondparagraph clarifiesthatgrantingexclusiverightstoperformersand
producers of phonograms beyond those to be granted under the Treaty is not in conflict with 
theprovisionsofArticle 1(2).Twocommentsshouldbeaddedtothissentence.First,whatis
stated in it goes without saying; it follows from the fact that the Treaty determines only the 
minimum level of protection to be granted. Second, since the sentence only mentions exclusive 
rights, on the a contrario principle of interpretation of legal provisions it might be understood 
toprecludeContractingPartiesfromprovidingrightstoremunerationbeyondwhatisrequired
byArticle 15oftheTreaty.Suchaninterpretation,however,wouldnotbewell-foundedforthe
reason mentioned in the first comment; that is, because the Treaty determines only the minimum 
obligations; if the protection is extended to another right to remuneration, no conflict emerges 
with the WPPT.551 It should be stressed, however, that the limitation of an exclusive right provided 
in the Treaty to a mere right to remuneration is a different matter; it is only allowed if it is 
permitted by the Treaty and it also fulfills the cumulative conditions of the three-step test.
No relation with other treaties
PPT-1.9.Article 1(3)issimilartothesecondsentenceofArticle 1(1)oftheWCT.Thereisonlyone
difference; namely, that the provision of the WCT implies a specific relationship with the Berne 
Convention; it reads as follows: “This Treaty shall not have any connection with treaties other 
than the Berne Convention […]”. This is not, however, a substantive difference. The specific 
connection with the Berne Convention follows from the special agreement status of the WCT in 
relationtotheBerneConventionasdeclaredinthefirstsentenceofitsArticle 1(1).However,as
discussed above, in spite of the fact that it is not stated in a similar way, the WPPT should also be 
regardedasaspecialagreementunderArticle 22oftheRomeConvention.Inviewofthis,the
WPPT does also have a certain relationship with the Rome Convention.
PPT-1.10.SinceArticle 1(3)oftheWPPTispracticallythesameasthesecondsentenceof
Article 1(1)oftheWCT,thepointsdiscussedconcerningthatsentenceintheGuidetotheWCT
above–thedoubtsastowhetheritistrulynecessary;thereasonsforitsinclusion(namely,to
make it absolutely clear that there is no relationship with the TRIPS Agreement); the de facto 
relationship of the Treaty with the TRIPS Agreement; the mutual impact of the Treaty and the 
TRIPSAgreementoneachother–applymutatis mutandis to this WPPT provision as well.
550Article 1oftheRomeConventiondiscussedaboveintheguidetothatConventionreadsasfollows:“Protection 
granted under this Convention shall leave intact and shall in no way affect the protection of copyright in literary and 
artisticworks.Consequently,noprovisionofthisConventionmaybeinterpretedasprejudicingsuchprotection.”
551 InReinbotheandvonLewinski,anotherargumentismadewhythissentenceoftheagreedstatementisequally 
applicable to the rights to remuneration. Namely that, “since exclusive rights are generally considered to represent 
thestrongestformofprotection,theprovisionofremunerationrightsbeyondtherightcoveredbyArticle 15ofthe 
WPPT must be all the more possible ( argumentum a maiore ad minus )”, at 258.

Article 2 
Definitions
For the purposes of this Treaty:
(a)  “performers” are actors, singers, musicians, dancers, and other persons who act, sing, 
deliver, declaim, play in, interpret, or otherwise perform literary or artistic works or 
expressions of folklore;
(b)  “phonogram” means the fixation of the sounds of a performance or of other sounds, 
or of a representation of sounds, other than in the form of a fixation incorporated in a 
cinematographic or other audiovisual work;
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 2(b):Itisunderstoodthatthedefinitionofphonogram
providedinArticle 2(b)doesnotsuggestthatrightsinthephonogramsareinanywayaffected
through their incorporation into a cinematographic or other audiovisual work.
(c)  “fixation” means the embodiment of sounds, or of the representations thereof, from 
which they can be perceived, reproduced or communicated through a device;
(d)  “producer of a phonogram” means the person, or the legal entity, who or which 
takes the initiative and has the responsibility for the first fixation of the sounds of a 
performance or other sounds, or the representations of sounds;
(e)  “publication” of a fixed performance or a phonogram means the offering of copies 
of the fixed performance or the phonogram to the public, with the consent of the 
rightholder,andprovidedthatcopiesareofferedtothepublicinreasonablequantity;
AgreedstatementconcerningArticles 2(e),8,9,12and13:AsusedintheseArticles,the
expressions “copies” and “original and copies” being subject to the right of distribution and 
the right of rental under the said Articles, refer exclusively to fixed copies that can be put into 
circulation as tangible objects.
(f)  “broadcasting” means the transmission by wireless means for public reception of 
sounds or of images and sounds or of the representations thereof; such transmission 
by satellite is also “broadcasting”; transmission of encrypted signals is “broadcasting” 
where the means for decrypting are provided to the public by the broadcasting 
organization or with its consent;
(g)  “communication to the public” of a performance or a phonogram means the 
transmission to the public by any medium, otherwise than by broadcasting, of sounds of 
a performance or the sounds or the representations of sounds fixed in a phonogram. For 
thepurposesofArticle 15,“communicationtothepublic”includesmakingthesoundsor
representations of sounds fixed in a phonogram audible to the public.
Introductory remarks
PPT-2.1. The WPPT follows the tradition of the Rome Convention in that it offers definitions of 
thekeytermsusedinitsprovisions.Moreorlessthesametermsaredefined–althoughnot
necessarilyinthesameway–asinArticle 3oftheRomeConvention.Thedifferencesarethese:
Article 2oftheWPPTalsocontainsdefinitionsof“fixation”and“communicationtothepublic” 
whicharenotincludedinArticle 3oftheRomeConventionwhile,intheConvention,there
aretwodefinitions–thoseof“reproduction”and“rebroadcasting”–whichdonotappearin 
the WPPT.
Performers
PPT-2.2. As discussed in the Guide to the Rome Convention in this collection of guides, the 
definitionof“performers”inArticle 3(a)oftheConventionislimitedtoperformancesofliterary 
andartisticworks,althoughArticle 9oftheRomeConventionprovidesthatContractingStates 

===== PAGE 275 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
276 may extend protection to artists who do not perform literary and artistic works. The definition 
inArticle 2(a)oftheWPPTfollowsthewordingofthatdefinition,butitdiffersintwoaspects.
PPT-2.3. The first difference is that it also includes the verb “interpret”. The intention seems to 
be to establish a better basis in the definition for the recognition of the “performer” status for 
those whose only contribution to performances is the interpretation of the works performed. 
Interpretation alone, without actual performance (for example, publishing a study on the way 
Beethoven’s symphonies should be interpreted) is not sufficient; in order that the interpreting 
personsmayqualifyas“performers”,theymustapplytheirinterpretationsthroughconcrete 
performances. The best example is the conductor of an orchestra, to which the report of the 
1961 Rome Diplomatic Conference refers as a “performer” without, however, establishing 
a specific category for this in the text of the definition. (For this, and for the differentiation 
between “artistes interprètes ” and “artistes éxécutants ” in the French version of the definition, see 
thecommentsonArticle 3(a)oftheRomeConventionintheGuideinthiscollection.)
PPT-2.4. The second difference is that the definition has been extended to performers of 
expressions of folklore.552 In this way, an unjustified limitation of the concepts of “performers” 
and “performances” has been eliminated and an indirect form of intellectual property protection 
has been granted for traditional cultural expressions. 
Phonograms; fixation of sounds in “audiovisual fixations” other than audiovisual works
PPT-2.5.InArticle 2(b)oftheWPPT,thedefinitionof“phonogram”containedinArticle 3(b)ofthe 
Rome Convention (which simply states that “‘phonogram’ means any exclusively aural fixation of 
thesoundsofaperformanceorofothersounds”)–hasbeenupdatedintwoaspects.
PPT-2.6. The first aspect is that the definition has been extended to those phonograms that 
arenotfixationsofsounds.Thisseemsnecessary,sincephonogramsmaybemadenow–by
applyingdigitaltechnology–alsothroughthefixationofdatathatareabletogeneratesounds 
withtheassistanceofappropriateelectronicequipment,suchthatthecorrespondingsounds 
did not exist before. It is this possibility to which the fixation of the “representation of sounds” 
refers in a technology-neutral manner.
PPT-2.7.Thesecondaspect–andthisismuchmoreimportant,inparticulargivenitsrelationship
(andapparentoverlap)withthedefinitionof“audiovisualfixation”inArticle 2(b)oftheBTAP–is
that the expression “exclusively aural” has been replaced by a longer phrase: “other than in 
the form of a fixation incorporated in a cinematographic or other audiovisual work”. In the 
Basic Proposal submitted to the 1996 Diplomatic Conference, another phrase was proposed: 
“an audiovisual fixation, the representation of sounds and images or the sound part of either 
is not a phonogram”.553Theabove-quotedphraseinArticle 2(b)oftheWPPTwasagreedupon
during informal consultations without any substantive explanation of the reasons behind it and 
without any debate.554 The effect of this phrase is that, in a case where an audiovisual fixation 
doesnotqualifyasawork,afixationofthesoundsofaperformanceorofothersounds,orof
a representation of sounds, incorporated in such an audiovisual fixation is to be regarded as a 
phonogram. For the apparent overlap with the definition of “audiovisual fixation” provided in 
theBTAPandthewayinwhichitmaybehandled,seethecommentsonArticle 2(b)intheGuide
to the BTAP below.
552 The term “expressions of folklore” has been used in the “Model Provisions on the Protection of Expressions 
ofFolkloreAgainstIllicitExploitationandotherPrejudicialActions”adoptedinJune1985byaWIPO–UNESCO 
CommitteeofGovernmentalExperts(ofwhichtheauthorofthisGuidewasthechairman).Itstextisavailable–with 
introductory comments, at www.wipo.int/export/www/tk/en/folklore/1982-folklore-model-provisions.pdf . In the 
comments added to the Model Provisions, it is stated that “copyright law is […] not the right kind of law for protecting 
expressions of folklore”, referred to as “productions consisting of characteristic elements of the traditional artistical 
heritage”. This is so “because, whereas an expression of folklore is the result of an impersonal, continuous and slow 
process of creative activity exercised in a given community by consecutive imitation, works protected by copyright 
must [...] bear a decisive mark of individual originality. Traditional creations of a community […] are generally much 
older than the duration of copyright so that, for this reason alone, a copyright-type protection, limited to the life of 
the author and a relatively short period after, does not offer to folklore a long enough protection.”, 5.

554 Ibid.,759,paras835–836.

PART III. Guides to the three WIPO “Internet Treaties” – the WCT, the WPPT and the BTAP
Interpretation of the agreed statement concerning Article 2(b); the status of the rights in 
preexisting phonograms incorporated in audiovisual works
PPT-2.8. Where the first fixation of the sounds is made by the producer of an audiovisual 
work,itfollowsfromthedefinitionof“phonogram”inArticle 2(b)oftheWPPTthatthereisno 
phonogram. It is another matter that, if the soundtrack is published separately, it is suitable 
toqualifyasaphonogram,becausethefixationofthesoundsisnolongerincorporatedinthe
audiovisual work. In accordance with this, in the debates in Main Committee I of the Diplomatic 
Conference, it was clarified that “the sound tracks of film, when detached from the film, that 
is,whenissuedasasoundrecording,shouldqualifyasphonograms”. 555 In such a case, where 
the producer of an audiovisual work has made the first fixation of the sounds, it becomes the 
producer of the soundtrack-turned-phonogram. In contrast, where a preexisting phonogram 
is copied into the soundtrack, it does not become a part thereof in the same way as the sounds 
first fixed by the producer of the audiovisual work; the first fixation has been made by the 
producerofthephonogram.Consequently,whenthephonogramisdistributedseparatelyfrom 
the audiovisual work, the owner of the right is the original producer of the phonogram.
PPT-2.9. The agreed statement clarifies this, but not only this; it also clarifies the status of the 
preexisting phonograms incorporated in (the soundtracks of) audiovisual works. It states that 
in such a case the rights in a phonogram are not affected; they are not lost just because the 
phonogram has been copied into the soundtrack of an audiovisual work.
PPT-2.10.Alongwiththisclarification,itisalsomadeclearthat,consequently,whenthe
phonogram is used separately, the owner of the right will be the original producer of the 
phonogram. However, the clarification of the latter alone would have hardly justified the 
adoptionofanagreedstatement.Hardly,becauseitmaynotreasonablybequestionedthat, 
when the phonogram first fixed in the soundtrack by the producer of phonograms is distributed 
separately, its authorization is needed.
PPT-2.11. It goes without saying that, when the producer of the preexisting phonogram 
authorizes the incorporation of the phonogram into an audiovisual work, it does license certain 
uses. It is normal that, with the authorization of such “synchronization” of the phonogram, 
the exclusive rights of reproduction and distribution are licensed, and the licensing of other 
exclusiverights–suchastherightof(interactive)makingavailabletothepublic–isalsousual.
The complex nature of audiovisual works justifies this; in order to make their normal exploitation 
possible, it is necessary to concentrate the rights of authorization in the hands of the producers. 
There is no legal or practical obstacle, however, to the application of rights to remuneration of 
the performers and producers of phonograms in spite of the transfer of the exclusive rights.
PPT-2.12.Thebasicquestioniswhatthepracticeinthefilmindustryisandhownational
lawsregulatethetransferofrights.Although–asclarifiedintheagreedstatement–the 
incorporation of preexisting phonograms in the soundtracks of an audiovisual work does 
notaffecttherightsinthem,therightsconcernedmaybeassignedor–whatseemsmore
common–licensedtotheproduceroftheaudiovisualwork,andnationallawsmayfacilitate
this by means of rebuttable (or even non-rebuttable) presumptions. Nevertheless, there are 
also national laws under which certain rights to remuneration are maintained for (authors and) 
performers when they transfer their exclusive rights to the producers of audiovisual works, and 
suchremunerationrightsarefrequentlyunwaivable.Theagreedstatementseemstoconfirm 
that at least those rights in the preexisting phonograms remain applicable also when they are 
incorporated (reproduced) in the soundtrack of audiovisual works.
PPT-2.13Inviewofthe“preparatorywork”oftheWPPT–inthesenseinwhichArticle 32ofthe
VCLTreferstoit–anuancedinterpretationoftheagreedstatementisjustified.Itwasatthe
2000 Diplomatic Conference that a debate took place on the status of rights in phonograms 
incorporated in audiovisual fixations. The following statements were made:
 – The US delegation did not specifically address the issue of the acts of incorporation of a 
phonogram in an audiovisual work, but stated that 
555 Ibid., 691, paras 400, 402.

===== PAGE 277 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
278 [t]he soundtrack of a motion picture or television production which formed part 
of the work was not a separate phonogram subject to separate remuneration, 
unlike a commercially published phonogram of the soundtrack or a selection 
from the soundtrack.556
 – The Australian delegation made the following statement: 
AccordingtothedefinitioninArticle 2(b)oftheWPPT,onceaphonogram
was incorporated in an audiovisual work, in that new context it ceased to be 
a phonogram, but the phonogram in the original format continued to enjoy 
itsstatusandprotection.Thus,ifitwasbroadcast,Article 15oftheWPPT
would continue to apply notwithstanding that it had been incorporated in 
the audiovisual fixation. However, if the audiovisual work incorporating the 
phonogram was used in a broadcast, the phonogram incorporated in it was not 
beingbroadcastforthepurposesofArticle 15.557
Theproblemwiththisstatementisthatitsbasicpremise–thataphonogramceasestobe
aphonogramwhenitisreproducedinthesoundtrack–isnotsupportedbythetextofthe
agreed statement. From the agreed statement just the contrary seems to follow: it is about the 
incorporation of the phonogram in an audiovisual work and not just about the incorporation of 
the sounds fixed in the phonogram. Furthermore, it is stated that through the incorporation of 
the phonogram, no rights are affected in it. The preposition “through” has two meanings that 
may be taken into account in this context: (a) “from one end or side of something/somebody to 
the other”; (b) “by means of; because of”. 558 If the first alternative is taken, the agreed statement 
means that throughout (from the beginning to the end of) the incorporation of the phonogram 
in an audiovisual work, the rights in it are not “in any way affected”. The second meaning 
suggests that, just because a phonogram is incorporated in an audiovisual work, the rights in it 
are not “in any way affected”. The agreed statement, under either of these two meanings, may 
hardly be understood such that the phonogram, because of its incorporation and throughout its 
being incorporated, does not exist.
 – TheJapanesedelegationofferedthemostcomplexanalysis:
[W]hen aural performances once fixed in a phonogram are incorporated in 
an audiovisual fixation, such aural performances do not fall under the new 
instrument but fall under the WPPT. On the other hand, aural performances 
fixed in an audiovisual fixation fall under the new instrument, however, 
when such aural performances are embodied in a phonogram, such aural 
performances embodied in a phonogram fall under the WPPT.559 
This analysis seems to correspond to the above-mentioned two meanings of the agreed statement.
 – Finally, the EC delegation stressed the flexibility available to the Contracting Parties: 
There were sound recordings that were accompanied by visual elements. That fact 
made such sound recordings an audiovisual fixation or made them phonograms, 
depending on how Contracting Parties would deal with these phenomena. The 
same went for the treatment of music videos. An important objective was that the 
new instrument would not prejudice the freedom of Contracting Parties to choose 
the appropriate category as they saw fit for those various phenomena.560
PPT-2.14. The comments made at the 2000 Diplomatic Conference on the rights of “audiovisual 
performers” may not be considered necessarily decisive for the interpretation of an agreed 
statement adopted four years earlier in 1996 concerning the definition of “phonogram”, but, since 
theoverwhelmingmajorityoftheparticipatingcountries–andallkeynegotiatingparties–were

557 Ibid., para. 319.

thesamein2000,thesestatementsmayberecognizedasthereflectionofsubsequentpractice
(inthesenseofArticle 31.3(b)oftheVCLT561)intheinterpretationofArticle 2(b)oftheWPPTand
the agreed statement. The rights in a phonogram are not “in any way affected” just because of 
its incorporation into, and through its being incorporated in, an audiovisual work; nevertheless, 
the Contracting Parties have some freedom “to choose the appropriate category” as the EC 
delegation put it, for the legal status of certain specific productions such as music videos.
PPT-2.15.Itshouldbestressed,however,thattherightsinthephonogramsmaybe–andinthe
majorityofcasesare–licensedtotheproducers.Thus,inpractice,thesurvivaloftherightsin 
phonograms throughout their incorporation does not cause a problem to the producers in the 
exploitation of the audiovisual works. Nevertheless, it follows from the agreed statement that, 
where national laws provide for an unwaivable right to remuneration for the performers in case 
of transfer of certain rights, such unwaivable rights are not “in any way affected” through the 
incorporation of the phonograms in audiovisual works. The same applies to any other rights 
in the phonograms that may not be transferred to the producers. The case of “performing 
rights” in musical works is a rare example, but it still is an example of survival of rights in this 
way; contrary to the rights of other authors of audiovisual works, these rights are usually 
maintained by the composers and lyricists of musical works and exercised through collective 
management organizations.
PPT-2.16.However,–aspointedoutbytheECdelegation–broadflexibilityseemstobeavailable
to the Contracting Parties in this respect. The EC delegation has also drawn attention to the 
special case of video clips, in connection with which it is particularly clear that, when they are 
broadcast or communicated to the public along with the visual elements (which may or may not 
qualifyasoriginalaudiovisualworks)thebroadcastingorcommunicationtothepublicofthe 
phonogramalsotakesplace;thus,forexample,therighttoanequitableremunerationunder
Article 8(2)ofEURental,LendingandRelatedRightsDirective 562 seems to be applicable along 
with any parallel rights in the accompanying visual elements.
Fixation
PPT-2.17.Thedefinitionof“fixation”inArticle 2(c)requiresthatthe“embodiment”ofsounds,orthe
representations thereof, be sufficiently stable for the possibility of its being perceived, reproduced 
or communicated through a device. It does not indicate what kind of “embodiment” may be 
relevant. In the absence of a restrictive criterion, it seems justified to interpret it as meaning any 
kind of material form on the basis of which it may be perceived, reproduced or communicated. 
This, inter alia, also means storage in an electronic memory. The notes added to this item in the 
BasicProposalclarifiedthat“thedefinitiondoesnotsetanyconditionsregardingtherequisite
permanenceorstabilityoftheembodiment;thereisnosetrequirementintheproposedTreaty”.563
PPT-2.18. In the Basic Proposal, it was noted that no definition of “reproduction” was proposed 
“becausethemeaningofthetermisdevelopedfullyinArticles 7and14”.564 Although these

Producer of a phonogram
PPT-2.19.AsnotedintheGuidetotheRomeConventioninthiscollection,inArticle 3(c)ofthat
Convention, “producer of phonograms” was defined as “the person who, or the legal entity 
which,firstfixesthesoundsofaperformanceorothersounds”.InthedefinitioninArticle 2(d) 
oftheWPPT,amoreprecisedefinitionalelement–theinitiativeofandresponsibilityforthe
fixation–hasbeenincludedand,forthereasonsmentionedaboveinconnectionwiththe
definition of “phonogram”, also a reference to “representations of sounds”.
PPT-2.20. In the Basic Proposal it was also noted that “[t]he producer is the person who takes 
the initiative, coordinates and assumes economic and other responsibility for the first fixation 
of a phonogram, regardless of the technology used. It is worth pointing out that digitizing 
or ‘re-mastering’ existing fixations of performances is not a ‘first fixation,’ irrespective of the 
investment made in corrections, noise removal and other such alterations”. 565
Publication
PPT-2.21.TheRomeConvention,initsArticle 3(d),defines“publication”as“theofferingof 
copiesofaphonogramtothepublicinreasonablequantity.”Item(e)ofArticle 2oftheWPPT
–inadditiontosomeinsubstantialchangeinthelanguage 566–hasaddedonlyoneelement
tothisdefinition;namely,ithasclarifiedthat“offeringcopies[…]inreasonablequantity”is 
only regarded as publication where it takes place with the consent of the owner of rights. In 
this respect, the concept of publication in the Treaty has been assimilated to the definition of 
“publishedworks”inArticle 3(3)oftheBerneConvention.
PPT-2.22.TheagreedstatementconcerningArticle 2(e)(aswellasArticles 8,9,12,and13)
regarding the concept of “copies” is mutatis mutandis the same as the agreed statement on the 
sameconceptconcerningArticles 6and7oftheWCT.Therefore,thecommentsmadeaboutthe
latter regarding those provisions in the Guide to the WCT above also apply here mutatis mutandis.
Broadcasting
PPT-2.23.Thefirstpartofthedefinitionof“broadcasting”inArticle 2(f)ispracticallythe 
sameasthedefinitionofthisterminArticle 3(f)oftheRomeConvention,accordingtowhich 
“‘broadcasting’ means the transmission by wireless means for public reception of sounds or 
of images and sounds”. The only difference is that the reference to the representations of 
sounds has been added here too, for the reasons indicated in connection with the definition of 
phonogramabove.SincethisdefinitionhasadoptedthelanguageofArticle 3(f)oftheRome 
Convention, it has inherited a drafting problem; namely, that the expression “public reception” 
seems to suggest that the act of reception takes place where members of the public are present 
or at a place that, at least, is open to the public. As discussed in the comments in the Guide 
to the Rome Convention in this collection, this expression was hardly intended to have such a 
meaning. There is no indication in the records of the 1961 Rome Diplomatic Conference that the 
conference wanted to adopt a term the meaning of which would have fundamentally differed 
fromtheconceptofbroadcastingunderArticle 11bis(1) of the Berne Convention (which is 
communication to the public by wireless means rather than reception in a public place).
565 Ibid.,250–252,para.2.19.
566ThelanguageofArticle 2(e)seemstohavebeenmadesomewhatcomplicatedsince,ifthestructureofArticle 3(d)of 
the Rome Convention had been followed, the definition could have read simply: “‘publication’ of a fixed performance 
or a phonogram means the offering of copies of the fixed performance or the phonogram to the public, with the 
consentoftherightholder,inareasonablequantity.”

PPT-2.24. The second part of the definition confirms that a transmission for reception by the 
public through satellites is also broadcasting if it otherwise corresponds to the definition (that 
is, if it is a transmission directly receivable by the public).
PPT-2.25. The third part of the definition deals with encrypted satellite broadcasts. It recognizes 
that, where the means for decryption are made available to the public, the transmission 
qualifiesasbroadcasting.Themeansfordecryptionmustbeprovidedtothepublicbythe 
broadcasting organization itself or with its consent.
PPT-2.26.Thereisnodefinitionof“rebroadcasting”inArticle 2.UnderArticle 3(g)oftheRome
Convention, “‘rebroadcasting’ means the simultaneous broadcasting by one broadcasting 
organizationofabroadcastbyanotherbroadcastingorganization”.ThenotestoArticle 2intheBasic
Proposal for what became the WPPT indicate the reason this definition was left out: “Rebroadcasting 
is broadcasting. In rebroadcasting, the relevant sounds or sounds and images have already been 
broadcast. To import the definition from the Rome Convention does not seem necessary”.567
Communication to the public
PPT-2.27. As discussed in the Guide to the Rome Convention in this collection, the concept of 
“communication to the public” under that Convention differs from what is used in the Berne 
Convention.WhiletheRomeConventiondoesnotcontainanydefinitionofthisconcept–itmayonly
be deduced from the context of the relevant provisions and from the negotiating history as reflected 
intherecordsofthe1961RomeDiplomaticConference–Article 2(g)oftheWPPTgivesadefinition.
PPT-2.28. The first phrase of item (g) defines “communication to the public” as transmission 
to the public by any medium other than broadcasting. The definition thus excludes wireless 
transmissions for reception by the public but also covers all retransmissions by wire of any 
other transmissions (including broadcasts). It does not cover interactive making available of 
performances (fixed in phonograms) and phonograms by wire (or wireless means) the way it is 
describedinArticles 10and14oftheWPPT.
PPT-2.29. The second phrase of item (g) extends the concept of “communication to the public” to 
“making the sounds or representations of sounds fixed in a phonogram audible to the public”. 
Such an act is carried out in the presence of the public or, at least, at a place open to the public, 
which,inthecaseoftheBerneConvention,qualifiesaspublicperformance(underArticles 11(1)(i)
and 11ter(1)(i))orpubliccommunicationofsoundsofabroadcastwork(underArticle 11bis(1)(iii)).
Article 3
Beneficiaries of Protection under this Treaty
(1) Contracting Parties shall accord the protection provided under this Treaty 
to the performers and producers of phonograms who are nationals of other 
Contracting Parties.
(2) The nationals of other Contracting Parties shall be understood to be those performers 
or producers of phonograms who would meet the criteria for eligibility for protection 
provided under the Rome Convention, were all the Contracting Parties to this Treaty 
Contracting States of that Convention. In respect of eligibility, Contracting Parties shall 
applytherelevantdefinitionsinArticle 2ofthisTreaty.
(3) AnyContractingPartyavailingitselfofthepossibilitiesprovidedinArticle 5(3)ofthe
RomeConventionor,forthepurposesofArticle 5ofthesameConvention,Article 17
thereof shall make a notification as foreseen in those provisions to the Director General 
of the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO).
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 3(2):FortheapplicationofArticle 3(2),itisunderstood

282 AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 3:ItisunderstoodthatthereferenceinArticles 5(a)and
16(a)(iv) of the Rome Convention to “national of another Contracting State” will, when applied 
to this Treaty, mean, in regard to an intergovernmental organization that is a Contracting Party 
to this Treaty, a national of one of the countries that is a member of that organization.
Protection provided to “nationals” of other Contracting Parties
PPT-3.1.Article 3(1)stipulatesthattheprotectionprovidedforintheWPPTisaccordedtothe
performers and producers of phonograms who are nationals of other Contracting Parties. Those 
who read this provision may be misled concerning the criteria of eligibility of protection. In fact, 
nationality is only one of the criteria of the protection of the rights of producers of phonograms, 
and it is not a decisive criterion concerning the protection of the rights of performers.
PPT-3.2.ThissomewhatmisleadingprovisionisasortofadaptedversionofArticle 1.3ofthe 
TRIPS Agreement on criteria of eligibility, which reads as follows:
Members shall accord the treatment provided for in this Agreement to the nationals of 
other Members. In respect of the relevant intellectual property right, the nationals of 
other Members shall be understood as those natural or legal persons that would meet 
the criteria for eligibility for protection provided for in the Paris Convention (1967), the 
Berne Convention (1971), the Rome Convention and the Treaty on Intellectual Property 
in Respect of Integrated Circuits, were all Members of the WTO members of those 
Conventions.AnyMemberavailingitselfofthepossibilitiesprovidedinparagraph 3of
Article 5orparagraph 2ofArticle 6oftheRomeConventionshallmakeanotification
as foreseen in those provisions to the Council for Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual 
Property Rights (the ‘Council for TRIPS’).
PPT-3.3.Article 3oftheWPPTfollowsthestructureoftheseTRIPSprovisions.First,paragraph (1)
statesthatthecriterionofeligibilityofprotectionisnationality;second,paragraph (2)determines
what“nationality”means–andonthisbasisitturnsoutthatitmaymeanmanycriteriaotherthan
nationalityasprovidedintheRomeConvention;and,third,paragraph (3)adaptstheprovisionsof
the Rome Convention on notifications to the context of the WPPT. Adopting the criteria of eligibility 
asprovidedundertheRomeConventionseemstobeanappropriatesolution.IntheWPPT–which
onlycoverstherightsofperformersandproducersofphonograms–itwas,however,unnecessary
tofollowthecomplexstructureofArticle 1.3oftheTRIPSAgreement(whichisontheeligibilityof
protection concerning all the different categories of intellectual property rights). The same result 
couldhavebeenachievedifthemisleadingstatementinparagraph (1)hadbeenleftout,andthe
presentparagraph (2)–toberenumberedasparagraph (1)–hadbegunasfollows:“Contracting
Parties shall accord the protection provided under this Treaty to those performers and producers 
ofphonogramswho[…]”,andfromherethetextcouldhavebeenthesameasnowinparagraph (2)
referring to the eligibility rules of the Rome Convention. The solution chosen in the WPPT achieves 
the same result, but in a more complicated way.
Criteria taken from the Rome Convention
PPT-3.4. The criteria for eligibility for the protection of the rights of performers and producers 
ofphonogramsprovidedundertheRomeConvention–towhichparagraph (2)refers–maybe
foundinArticles 4,5and17ofthatConvention,discussedintheGuidetothatConventioninthis
collection of guides.
PPT-3.5. These Rome provisions should be applied mutatis mutandis in the context of the 
WPPT. Two agreed statements offer some clarification for this purpose, in respect of the terms 
“fixation”and“nationalofanotherContractingState”.Furthermore,Article 3(3)indicateshow 
Articles 5(3)and17oftheRomeConventionshouldbeappliedforthepurposesoftheTreaty.
PPT-3.6. As regards the rest of the elements of the Rome provisions analyzed in the Guide 
inthiscollection,itisquiteclearwhattheirmutatis mutandis application means, with the 
exceptionofthecriterionmentionedinArticle 4(c)oftheRomeConvention:“theperformance, 
notbeingfixedonaphonogram,iscarriedbyabroadcastwhichisprotectedbyArticle 6of 
the Convention”. Because the WPPT does not apply to the protection of broadcasts, how this 
criterionmaybeappliedintheWPPTcontextrequiresinterpretation.

PPT-3.7. The first possible interpretation is that this criterion is not applicable for the WPPT since 
broadcasts are not protected under this Treaty, and it does not contain provisions similar to 
thoseincludedinArticle 6oftheRomeConvention.
PPT-3.8. The second kind of interpretation would conform to the principle of effectiveness, 
according to which a treaty provision must not be considered simply irrelevant; due efforts must 
be made for its application. However, it should be taken into account that the criterion under 
Article 4(c)oftheRomeConventionappliestophonogramscarriedbybroadcastscorresponding 
tothecriteriaofArticle 6oftheRomeConvention,whichreadsasfollows:
1.  Each Contracting State shall grant national treatment to broadcasting organisations 
if either of the following conditions is met:
(a) theheadquartersofthebroadcastingorganisationissituatedinanother
Contracting State;
(b)  the broadcast was transmitted from a transmitter situated in another 
Contracting State.
2.  By means of a notification deposited with the Secretary-General of the United 
Nations, any Contracting State may declare that it will protect broadcasts only if the 
headquartersofthebroadcastingorganisationissituatedinanotherContracting
State and the broadcast was transmitted from a transmitter situated in the same 
Contracting State. Such notification may be deposited at the time of ratification, 
acceptance or accession, or at any time thereafter; in the last case, it shall become 
effective six months after it has been deposited.
PPT-3.9.IfArticle 6consistedonlyofparagraph 1,thesecondinterpretationcouldbeeasily
applied.Paragraph 2,however,raisesaproblem,sincethenotificationsystemunderitisnot
applicable, even mutatis mutandis,intheWPPTcontext.Article 3(3)oftheWPPTonlycovers
notificationsmentionedinArticles 5.3and17oftheRomeConvention;itdoes not extend to 
whatisprovidedforinArticle 6.2oftheConvention.
PPT-3.10.Athirdpossibleinterpretationcanbeenvisaged;namely,thatthecriterioninArticle 6.2
of the Rome Convention would apply in the context of the WPPT whenever a Contracting Party 
grants protection for the rights of broadcasting organizations. There would also be difficulties 
withthisinterpretation,however.TherequirementofnotificationunderArticles 5.3,6.2,and17
of the Rome Convention indicates that the criteria of eligibility in a given Contracting Party should 
be known to the other Contracting Parties. In the absence of an appropriate notification system 
to take care of this, such a possible third interpretation certainly could not function.
PPT-3.11. In the absence of any guidance offered by the 1996 Diplomatic Conference on this 
issue, it seems difficult to suggest that the minimum obligations of the Contracting Parties 
concerning the scope of eligibility of protection would go beyond what follows from the first 
possible interpretation mentioned above.
Rome criteria and WPPT definitions
PPT-3.12.ByvirtueofthesecondsentenceofArticle 3(2)oftheWPPT,whentheabove-
mentionedRomecriteriaofeligibilityareapplied,thedefinitionsinArticle 2oftheTreaty 
ratherthanthedefinitionsinArticle 3oftheRomeConventionshouldbetakenintoaccount.
Consideringthetextsoftherelevantprovisions–Articles 4,5and17–oftheConvention,
thismeansthedefinitionsinthefirstfiveitems–items(a)to(e)–ofArticle 2oftheWPPT:
“performers”, “phonogram”, “fixation”, “producer of a phonogram” and “publication”.
Article 4
National Treatment
(1) Each Contracting Party shall accord to nationals of other Contracting Parties, as 
definedinArticle 3(2),thetreatmentitaccordstoitsownnationalswithregardto
theexclusiverightsspecificallygrantedinthisTreaty,andtotherighttoequitable
remunerationprovidedforinArticle 15ofthisTreaty.

Interpretation of paragraph  (1): special form of “national treatment”
PPT-4.1. At the Diplomatic Conference, two positions clashed: one wished to guarantee full 
national treatment, and another one reduced it to the minimum obligations under the Treaty. A 
number of amendments were submitted to the text of the draft treaty, then the issue was left 
to informal negotiations, and it was only addressed by Main Committee I on the morning of the 
last day of the conference. The passionate debate revealed that the delegates had not reached a 
generally acceptable agreement even by that time.
PPT-4.2. The delegation of Switzerland submitted at that session of Main Committee I the 
textwhichwasfinallyadoptedasArticle 4oftheWPPT.Thedelegationpointedoutthatits 
amendment was “based on the text of the TRIPS Agreement and this should constitute the 
basis for a compromise acceptable to all delegations”.568
PPT-4.3.ThecharacterizationoftheSwissproposalwascorrect.Thesolutionsuggested–and 
adopted–trulycorrespondedtotherelevantprovisionoftheTRIPSAgreement(thesecond 
sentenceofArticle 3.1),whichreads:“Inrespectofperformers,producersofphonogramsand 
broadcasting organizations, this obligation [that is, the obligation of each Member, under the 
first sentence of the same paragraph, to ‘accord to nationals of other Members treatment no 
less favorable that it accords to its own nationals with regard to the protection of intellectual 
property‘] only applies in respect of the rights provided under this Agreement”.
PPT-4.4. Treatment which only means the obligation to grant to the nationals of other 
Contracting Parties the rights specifically provided for in a treaty is a very special form of 
“national treatment” (in contrast with its traditional form, in which it means the obligation of a 
given country to grant the same treatment to the nationals of other Contracting Parties as to its 
own nationals, including in respect of the rights that go beyond the minimum obligations). 
PPT-4.5.WhileArticle 4oftheWPPTisinaccordancewithArticle 3.1oftheTRIPSAgreement,it 
differsfromtheprovisionsofArticle 2oftheRomeConventionasitwasunderstoodbythe1961
Diplomatic Conference, that is, as providing the same kind of fully fledged national treatment 
asundertheBerneConvention.However,asdiscussedinthecommentsonparagraph (2)of
thatarticle intheGuidetotheRomeConventioninthiscollection,forcertainlegal–political 
reasonsmentionedthere,asubsequentpracticehasemergedinthesenseofArticle 31.3(b)of
theVCLT;accordingtowhich,contrarytowhatwasstatedintherecordsoftheRomeDiplomatic
Conference, the provision should be interpreted to mean that the national treatment obligation 
only applies to the extent of the specifically provided rights along with specifically allowed 
exceptionsandlimitations.ThissubsequentpracticeofinterpretingArticle 2oftheRome 
ConventioninthatwayhasbeenadoptedalsoinrespectofArticle 4oftheWPPT.
PPT-4.6. The understanding on the validity of such an alternative interpretation was expressed at 
the1996DiplomaticConference–withdirectorimpliedagreementofalltheotherdelegationsof
theContractingStatesoftheRomeConvention–bythedelegationoftheEuropeanCommunities:
[The delegation] had submitted a proposal on national treatment with respect to [the 
draft WPPT], where it had taken the approach chosen by the Rome Convention, an approach 
that had been confirmed by the TRIPS Agreementafewyearsago[...][J]ustlikeinthose
two other agreements, the national treatment obligation should extend to those rights that 
were specifically granted and guaranteed in [the draft WPPT] itself. While [the] Delegation 
confirmed its proposal, it felt the need to arrive at a compromise that would suit all 
Delegations. Such a compromise should not deviate from the basic approach and the 
structure of the national treatment obligation as contained both in the Rome Convention 
and in the TRIPS Agreement with respect to related rights  […] [T]he proposal made by the 
Delegation of Switzerland was the approach that had been shared by all States party to

PPT-4.7.Theexpression“specificallygrantedinthisTreaty”requiressomecomments.Therights 
specifically granted under the Treaty should be considered together with the exceptions and/
orlimitationspermittedunderArticle 16oftheTreaty.Ifanexclusiveright–forexample,the
exclusiverightofreproductionprovidedforinArticles 7and11oftheWPPT–islimitedtoaright
to remuneration (as in the case of “private copying”), that exclusive right is still granted in the 
Treaty in spite of its limitation in the given case. Therefore, it does not seem to be justified to 
deny “national treatment” in such a case and, in that way, not only limit the right but, even in its 
limited form, to disapply it entirely for the nationals of other Contracting Parties. This analysis 
was made in various WIPO documents by the Secretariat of the Organization and, in the working 
document prepared for the third session of the “Berne Protocol” Committee, 570 the settlement 
of the issue of “private copying” was proposed in accordance with this. At the said session of the 
Committee, the Secretariat’s proposals received both support and opposition, and the majority 
of the delegations were rather of the view that the issue should not be included in the program 
of the preparatory work. Finally, the latter view prevailed; when the agenda was finalized (and 
narrowed) by the government delegations before the fourth session of the Committee, it did not 
include the issue of private copying. 571
PPT-4.8. Nevertheless, the issue of “private copying” and national treatment resurfaced at the 
1996 Diplomatic Conference. The Canadian delegation proposed that when the exclusive right 
in the case of private copying is limited to a right to remuneration, the obligation of national 
treatment should not be applied.572 The European Communities and their Member States went 
in the same direction, but they proposed the exclusion of all remuneration rights from the 
obligation to grant national treatment in this way: “A Contracting Party shall not be obliged 
toaccordtonationals,asdefinedinArticle 3(2),ofanotherContractingPartythetreatment 
providedforinparagraph (1)inrespectofrightswhichdonotderivefromexpressprovisions
of this Treaty or which might be recognized by national legislation in the context of limitations 
underArticles 13and20ofthisTreaty”.573 That is, it was proposed that when, in accordance with 
thethree-steptest(Articles 13and20,inthatstageoftheDiplomaticConference,stillcontained 
draft provisions on the test separately for the rights of performers and the rights of producers 
of phonograms) an exclusive right is limited to a right to remuneration (thus guaranteeing 
that there is no unreasonable prejudice to the legitimate interests of the nationals of other 
Contracting States) that right may be provided only to the nationals of the given Contracting 
Party and not to the nationals of other Contracting Parties. These proposals were simplified and 
further clarified in the Swiss proposal which was adopted by the Diplomatic Conference. 574
PPT-4.9. Before the adoption of the Swiss proposal, the delegation of the United States had 
presented orally certain compromise amendments; namely, the deletion of the adjective 
“specifically”fromparagraph (1)ofArticle 4andtheinsertionofanewparagraph (2)toread
asfollows:“Theobligationofparagraph (1)shallextendtoremunerationsystemsforprivate 
copyingofphonogramsinadigitalform,exceptthatContractingPartiesshallonlyberequired
to extend protection to nationals of another Contracting Party to the degree that the other 
Contracting Party has established such a remuneration system”. This would not have meant 
real national treatment but material reciprocity, and seemed to be a reasonable compromise. 
Nevertheless, when put to a vote, it was rejected by a large majority and the Swiss proposal was 
adopted to become part of the WPPT.575
PPT-4.10. It is not a surprise that the delegation of the United States, as a net exporter country 
of cultural and information productions, tried to ensure the applicability of national treatment

286 or,asaminimum,materialreciprocity,andthattheotherdelegations–intheiroverwhelming

also the rights provided for in the WPPT) “national treatment” to be granted to the nationals 
of other Contracting Parties applies only to the rights the protection of which is obligatory 
under a treaty; the obligation to grant the same treatment to the nationals of other Contracting 
Parties does not apply to the extent that the treatment enjoyed by a party’s own nationals is 
morefavorable.UnderArticle 31.3(a)oftheVCLT,suchanagreementshouldbebetweenall
the parties regarding the interpretation of a treaty or the application of its provisions, and the 
debates at the Diplomatic Conference have shown that there is no such full agreement on the 
rejection of national treatment and material reciprocity. But the WIPO Treaties do not offer an 
appropriate dispute settlement mechanism to those Contracting Parties that might wish to 
rejecttheexistenceandvalidityofsucha“subsequentagreement”.NorcantheTRIPSdispute 
settlement system be of assistance in this respect since, in the Uruguay Round, although the 
issues of private copying remuneration and national treatment were addressed in animated 
debates, its settlement ended in an agreement on not agreeing. There is, however, another 
possiblebasisintheVCLTtojustifytheapplicationofsuch“nationaltreatment”:thisisto
considerita“subsequentpractice”which,whileemerging,byitsverynature,doesnottakethe 
form a formal agreement, but may still imply an agreement between the parties. According to 
Article 31.3(b)oftheVCLT:“Thereshallbetakenintoaccounttogetherwiththecontext[…](b)
anysubsequentpracticeintheapplicationofthetreatywhichestablishestheagreementofthe 
parties regarding its interpretation”.
Interpretation of paragraph  (2): no obligation to the extent that another Contracting Party 
makes reservation
PPT-4.11.Article 15(3),towhichArticle 4(2)refers,provides:“AnyContractingPartymay,ina

ofparagraph (1)onlyinrespectofcertainuses,orthatitwilllimittheirapplicationinsome
otherway,orthatitwillnotapplytheseprovisionsatall”.Article 15(1),inrespectofwhichsuch
reservation may be made, provides for the right of performers and producers of phonograms 
toa“singleequitableremunerationforthedirectorindirectuseofphonogramspublishedfor
commercial purposes for broadcasting or communication to the public”.
PPT-4.12. Despite the different structure and language of this provision, the scope of the 
possiblereservationsissimilartowhatisprovidedinArticle 16.1(a)oftheRomeConvention
concerning the corresponding right of performers and producers of phonograms to a single 
equitableremunerationunderArticle 12ofthesameConventioninthesensethatitisalso
possible to completely exclude the application of such a right:
1.  Any State [...] may at any time, in a notification deposited with the Secretary-General 
of the United Nations, declare that:
(a) asregardsArticle 12:
(i)  it will not apply the provisions of that Article;
(ii) itwillnotapplytheprovisionsofthatArticle inrespectofcertainuses;
(iii)  as regards phonograms the producer of which is not a national of another 
Contracting State, it will not apply that Article;
(iv)  as regards phonograms the producer of which is a national of another 
ContractingState,itwilllimittheprotectionprovidedforbythatArticle to
the extent to which, and to the term for which, the latter State grants 
protection to phonograms first fixed by a national of the State making 
the declaration; however, the fact that the Contracting State of which 
the producer is a national does not grant the protection to the same

PPT-4.13. Although the scope of possible reservations is similar, there is still an important 
difference.UnderArticle 16.1(a)(iv)oftheRomeConvention,thereisaneedforareservation
also in those cases where another State makes use of a reservation (“deposits a notification”). 
In such a case, it is allowed to make use of a reservation (“deposit a notification”) notifying 
that the given State does not apply the right to the same extent. In contrast, it follows from 
Article 4(2)oftheWPPTthattheContractingPartiesdonothavetomakeareservationinsucha 
case; to the extent that another Contracting Party has made use of a reservation, the obligation 
underArticle 4(1)automaticallydoesnotapply.Insuchacase,theContractingPartiesarenot
obligated to grant the rights specifically provided in the Treaty to the same extent and, for this, 
they do not have to make any reservation (“declaration”); the obligation does not exist.
Chapter II: Rights of Performers
Article 5
Moral Rights of Performers
(1) Independently of a performer’s economic rights, and even after the transfer of those 
rights, the performer shall, as regards his live aural performances or performances 
fixed in phonograms, have the right to claim to be identified as the performer of his 
performances, except where omission is dictated by the manner of the use of the 
performance, and to object to any distortion, mutilation or other modification of his 
performances that would be prejudicial to his reputation.
(2) Therightsgrantedtoaperformerinaccordancewithparagraph (1)shall,afterhisdeath,
be maintained, at least until the expiry of the economic rights, and shall be exercisable 
by the persons or institutions authorized by the legislation of the Contracting Party 
where protection is claimed. However, those Contracting Parties whose legislation, at the 
moment of their ratification of or accession to this Treaty, does not provide for protection 
afterthedeathoftheperformerofallrightssetoutintheprecedingparagraph may
provide that some of these rights will, after his death, cease to be maintained.
(3) ThemeansofredressforsafeguardingtherightsgrantedunderthisArticle shallbe
governed by the legislation of the Contracting Party where protection is claimed.
Similarities to Article  6bis of the Berne Convention
PPT-5.1.AsthenotesaddedtodraftArticle 5intheBasicProposalforwhatbecametheWPPT
indicated,theprovisionsoftheArticle “aremodeledonArticle 6 bis of the Berne Convention”576 
onthemoralrightsofauthors.Thecommonelements–trulydifferingonlyin mutatis mutandis 
changes–areasfollows:
 – The moral rights granted to both authors and performers exist “independently of […] 
economic rights, and even after the transfer of those rights”. (This also implies that the 
economic rights are transferable, as under the Berne Convention, also under the WPPT.)
 – ThereisnolanguageeitherinArticle 6 bis oftheBerneConventionorinArticle 5ofthe
WPPT regarding the issue of inalienability (prohibition of inter vivos transfer) of moral 
rights.Inthisregard,thenotesintheBasicProposal–thevalidityofwhichwasnot
questionedatthe1996DiplomaticConference–offerthefollowingclarification:
The performer may exercise his moral rights, and he has the option not to 
exercise these rights; he may even waive them. To take an example, a performer 
may, in a contract, agree to refrain indefinitely from identifying himself as the 
performer of a particular performance. The position of a performer as the 
576 Records of the 1996 Geneva conference , 262, para. 5.02.

===== PAGE 287 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
288 performer of a given performance cannot, of course, be transferred; no one can 
step into his shoes in this sense.577
 – Theso-called“rightofrespect”bothinArticle 6 bis of the Berne Convention and in 
Article 5oftheWPPTincludestheright“toobjecttoanydistortion,mutilationorother 
modification of” the work/performance “that would be prejudicial to [the author’s/
performer’s] reputation”.
 – AsthenotesintheBasicProposaltodraftArticle 5pointedout,“alterationor
modification per se does not concern moral rights”.578 In the case of the WPPT, it is some 
prejudice to the performer’s reputation , while, in the case of the Berne Convention, it is 
some prejudice to the author’s honor or reputation by which modifications may come into 
conflict with the “right of respect”.
 – Paragraphs (2) and (3) contain the same provisions with changes made strictly on a 
mutatis mutandis basis.
Differences from Article  6bis of the Berne Convention
PPT-5.2.Therearesubstantivedifferencesinrespectofbothmoralrights–the “right of 
paternity”andthe“rightofrespect”–inthefollowingaspects.
PPT-5.3. As far as the right of paternity is concerned, the difference, although substantive, does 
notseemtobetrulyimportant.UnderArticle 6 bis(1) of the Berne Convention, an author has a 
right“toclaimauthorshipof[his]work”,while,underArticle 5(1)oftheWPPT,theperformer’s
right is “to claim to be identified as the performer of his performances, except where omission 
is dictated by the manner of the use of the performance”. The phrase “except where omission 
is dictated by the manner of the use of the performance” does not change in a substantial way 
thescopeandvalueofthismoralright.ThefactthatnosuchprovisoappearsinArticle 6 bis of 
the Berne Convention does not mean that authors’ names must always be indicated even if the 
manner of use of the work makes it impossible or highly impractical. As regards performers, at 
the 1996 Diplomatic Conference, the impossibility of identifying a large number of performers in 
an orchestra was mentioned as an example in a case of broadcasting the performance. 579
PPT-5.4. The difference is more important as regards the “right of respect”. First, this right, in 
Article 6bis of the Berne Convention, also extends to “other derogatory action in relation to […] 
thework”,whilethisisnotcoveredinArticle 5oftheWPPT.Second,while,underArticle 6 bis 
of the Berne Convention, an author may object to any action mentioned there not only where 
it would be prejudicial to his reputation but also where it would be prejudicial to his honor, the 
latterbasisforoppositionismissingfromArticle 5oftheWPPT.Thisdifferenceissubstantial, 
anditsjustificationisnotsufficientlyclear.Itisnotbecauseitseemsquiterarethatanaction 
would prejudice the reputation of a performer without a similar impact on his honor. During 
the informal negotiations, reference was made to parodies, and it was emphasized that it would 
not be appropriate to allow performers to oppose parodies by citing possible prejudice to their 
honor.Itmaybequestioned,however,whetherthereisarealdifferencewhereperformers
cannot oppose certain parodies prejudicing their honor, but the performer can oppose it 
citing prejudice to their reputation (although the performers’ reputation does not seem more 
important than their honor). Possibly the difference is that “reputation” may be important to a 
performer’s professional artistic activity, while “honor” is more relevant for the protection of the 
performer’s dignity in general (which, in the overwhelming majority of the Contracting Parties, 
is protected as part of general personality rights). 
PPT-5.5.Theexamplepresentedattheinformalnegotiationsisnot,however,quitepersuasive.A
parody relates more to the reputation of a performer than to his honor, since it in general tends 
torefertosomestylisticelementsthatareconsideredtobecharacteristicfortheperformer–at 
least, this may be suggested by the parody. It seems that the difference in the language was

Article 6
Economic Rights of Performers in their Unfixed Performances
Performers shall enjoy the exclusive right of authorizing, as regards their performances:
(i)  the broadcasting and communication to the public of their unfixed performances 
except where the performance is already a broadcast performance; and
(ii)  the fixation of their unfixed performances.
Similarities with the Rome Convention
PPT-6.1.TheactscoveredinthisArticle arepracticallythesameasthosementionedin
Article 7.1(a)and(b)oftheRomeConvention,althoughinthelattermorecomplexlanguageis
used.580Theonlypossiblesubstantivedifferencemayexistif,inthecaseoftheabove-quoted 
Article 6(ii)oftheWPPT,ofthetwopossibleinterpretationsoftheword“fixation”discussed 
below,therestrictiveoneisaccepted –tomeanonlyembodimentofsounds–since,in
Article 7.1(b)oftheRomeConvention,theword“fixation”isusedwithoutsuchlimitation,also
extending to the act of making an audiovisual fixation.
Differences from the Rome Convention
PPT-6.2.ByvirtueofArticle 7.1(a)and(b)oftheRomeConvention,“theprotectionprovided
forperformers”onlyhasto“includethepossibilityofpreventing”certainacts,whileArticle 6 
of the WPPT provides for a genuine exclusive right to authorize these acts. It is discussed in 
thecommentsontheabove-mentionedArticle intheGuidetotheRomeConventioninthis
collection what reasons served as a basis, in the context of the Convention, for only prescribing 
a “possibility of preventing”.
The meaning of “fixation”
PPT-6.3.Theexpression“thefixationof[…]unfixedperformances”inArticle 6(2)oftheWPPTis 
not interpreted in a uniform way; there are both restrictive and extensive interpretations.
PPT-6.4.Thequestioniswhethertherighttoauthorizethefixationofunfixedperformances
underArticle 6(ii)extendstoallfixationsoronlytofixationsonphonograms.Thetextofthe
provisionmaysuggestabroadercoverage;if,however,thedefinitionoffixationunderArticle 2(c)
is also taken into account, it seems that a narrower interpretation is justified. According to the 
said definition, “fixation” only means “the embodiment of sounds, or the representation thereof, 
from which they can be perceived, reproduced or communicated through a device” [emphasis 
added].Inviewofthisdefinition,Article 6(ii)onlyappliestofixationonphonograms.581
PPT-6.5. This interpretation, however, does not seem to be generally accepted. For example, 
the report of the first session of the WIPO Committee of Experts on a Protocol Concerning 
Audiovisual Performances, held in September 1997, reflects a different position of the 
delegationofJapaninthefollowingway:
ReferringtoArticle 6oftheWPPT,theDelegationtooktheviewthatitmightbeconsidered
that the right of performers to authorize the fixation of their unfixed performances

PPT-6.7. Two comments should be added to this. First, in the given stage of the debates,

thewithdrawalofthe“reservation”wasnottheonetowhichthedelegationofJapanreferred

informal consultations; namely that, with the adjective “musical”, the coverage of the WPPT 
wouldhavebeennarrowerthanthatoftheTRIPSAgreementwhich,initsArticle 14.1,extends
tothefixationofperformancesonphonogramsingeneral(sinceperformances–recitations–of 
literary works, such as poems, are also recorded on phonograms).
PPT-6.8. A more substantial argument raised in the above-mentioned debate at the first session of 
theCommitteeofExpertsonaProtocolconcerningAudiovisualPerformances–butnotreflected
inthereport–wasthatArticle 6(ii)mightbeinterpretedinamoreextensivewaysincetheword
“fixation” used in it refers to an act: fixing an unfixed performance; while the word “fixation” 
inthedefinitioninArticle 2(c)oftheTreatyisabouttheresult of an act: an “embodiment” of 
sounds. Although this is truly a more weighty argument, it still seems that the first interpretation 
mentioned above shows better the level of minimum obligations. If, in the same treaty, references 
toanactandtotheresultoftheact–or,moregenerally,averbformandanounformsoclosely
relatedtoeachother–areintendedtobedifferent,thisobviouslyshouldbeindicatedsomehowin
the negotiating history of the treaty. In the case of the WPPT, there is no such indication.
PPT-6.9. The generally shared agreement that, in respect of those issues that have been 
negotiated and settled in the TRIPS context, the two WIPO Treaties should not extend the 
obligations under the TRIPS Agreement, seems to confirm that the above-outlined restrictive 
interpretation may be considered more appropriate. It should, however, be stressed again 
that this only relates to the minimum obligations under the Treaty (and the TRIPS Agreement), 
since it is obvious that protection against “bootlegging” is, at least, as necessary in the case of 
unauthorizedaudiovisualfixationofperformancesasinthecasecoveredbyArticle 6(ii)(ifthe 
above-mentioned restrictive interpretation is taken as a basis). It is also worthwhile to note, 
however,thatwiththeadoptionofArticle 6oftheBTAPontherightsinunfixedperformances,
