and competition (c) intellectual property-related transfer of technology (d) potential 
flexibilities, exceptions and limitations for Member States and (e) the possibility of 
additional special provisions for developing countries and LDCs.
This recommendation concerns the way in which WIPO is supposed to prepare working 
documents in the stage of the preparation of a treaty. The same comments apply to this 
recommendationastotheothersofsuchnaturequotedandcommentedonaboveconcerning
the preparatory work leading to the adoption of new norms. With the adoption of the Treaty, 
the recommendations on how it was supposed to be prepared may be regarded to have been 
applied. Otherwise, it should be noted that the activities of WIPO were in accordance with these 
principles even before the proposal, preparation and adoption of the Development Agenda. 
Therefore, it might have been listed among the immediately applicable principles, since it had 
been already de facto applied.
BT-Pr.24.Thelastnotimmediatelyapplicablerecommendation–Recommendation23–isthe
closest to being suitable to recall how certain substantive issues were discussed and regulated 
in the BTAP:
To consider how to better promote pro-competitive intellectual property licensing practices, 
particularly with a view to fostering creativity, innovation and the transfer and dissemination 
of technology to interested countries, in particular developing countries and LDCs.
Article 12oftheTreatywasadoptedinsuchawaythatitcorrespondstothisrecommendation –
to the extent that it may apply for the protection of the rights of “audiovisual performers”. 
Through the issues of transfer of rights, it may also concern licensing practices, and its 
provisions–althoughnotrelevantforthepromotionofinnovationanddisseminationof
technology–aresuitabletofostercreativity.AsdiscussedbelowintheGuide,theprovisions 
ofArticle 12areflexible;somuchsothattheymaybesaidtoallownearlyeverything–andthe
contraryaswell–inregulatingornotregulatingtheissuesoftransferofrights.Therefore,there 
was good reason to “recall” that the Treaty had been prepared, inter alia, in accordance with 
these principles and should be applied keeping them in mind.
BT-Pr.25. It is worth noting, however, that the message of Recommendation 23 may not be 
fully relevant in the context of the BTAP. Pro-competitive licensing practices do favor those 
competitors who are more powerful and stronger. It is difficult to see why and how such 
practices might be particularly favorable to developing countries and the LDCs. In reality, 
for the development of these countries, preferential treatment and specific advantages are 
needed –exactlyinviewoftheirlowerstageofdevelopment–ratherthansubmittingthemto 
the Darwinian rules of competition.
Preparatory work of the BTAP and the Development Agenda
BT-Pr.26. The BTAP, due to its subject matter, is not best suited to reflect the role of the 
DevelopmentAgendainnorm-setting.Asquotedandanalyzedabove,technological 
innovation, transfer of technology and access to knowledge issues dominate its various 
recommendations. The objective of the BTAP, in contrast, is to protect the rights of performers 
in their performances fixed in audiovisual fixations, mainly in films and other audiovisual works; 
basically in entertainment productions. The right to access to entertainment is an aspect of 
therighttoparticipateintheculturallifeofthecommunityandtoenjoythearts–asdeclared
inArticle 27(1)oftheUniversalDeclarationofHumanRights,Therefore,itshouldbetakeninto
account in the provisions of copyright and related rights treaties. However, this does not seem 
to be a key aspect for the development considerations outlined in the Agenda. 604
604 Where development considerations may be particularly important concerning copyright is the access to knowledge and 
information for the purposes of public education and research. As discussed above, the need for a balancing of interests 
for this purpose has been recognized from the very first moments of treaty-making on copyright. The Appendix to the 
BerneConvention,thoughnowoutofdate,wasadoptedtofulfillspecificeducationalandresearchrequirements,and
there are also a number of other exceptions and limitations that are duly applied currently in both industrialized and 
developing countries to serve the same purposes. The accordance of those exceptions and limitations with the three-
step test (in particular with its first criterion that they must be limited to “certain special cases”) is guaranteed exactly 
through the condition that they are applied for the purposes of public education and scientific research.

===== PAGE 313 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
314 BT-Pr.27.TheoverwhelmingmajorityofthesubstantivenormsoftheBTAP–19ofthe20Articles –
were adopted (provisionally, but then they were not changed in Beijing) in 2000, while the adoption 
of the Development Agenda took place only in 2007. Therefore, it would be anachronistic to allege 
thatthose19Articles werepreparedandadoptedbytakingintoaccounttheconcretepointsofthe
Development Agenda. Nevertheless, as analyzed above, it may be said of the entire preparatory 
work of the BTAP that it took place in accordance with the principles laid down in the Agenda.
BT-Pr.28.Bytheinclusionofaparagraph inthePreamble“recalling”theimportanceof
theDevelopmentAgenda,inawayitwasimplicitlyrecognizedthatthe19Articles werein
accordance with the principles reflected in the Development Agenda. It is also worth noting 
thatthekeyprovisionsofthe19Articles wereadaptedversionsoftheWPPT,whichinturn
corresponded–alsomutatis mutandis –totherespectiveprovisionsoftheWCT.Therefore,
through the new preamble paragraph, it was also confirmed implicitly that the 1996 Treaties 
were likewise not in conflict with the relevant development considerations.
BT-Pr.29.Article 12–workedoutbasicallyin2011–andthenewagreedstatementsdidnot
change the nature of the BTAP from the point of view of the Development Agenda principles. 
The differences between the various countries that had emerged as an obstacle to reaching 
consensus on the issues of transfer of rights of “audiovisual performers” were not related to 
development aspects but to legal traditions and national solutions where industrialized and 
developing countries were found together in the same groups as advocating for this or that 
option.Article 12offersbroadflexibilityanditcertainlydoesnotexcludeanyoptionthateither 
may be dictated by or may be in conflict with any of the development considerations.
BT-Pr.30.ThenewagreedstatementconcerningArticle 1(1)ontherelationshipoftheTreatywith
the WPPT states the obvious (that nothing in the new Treaty affects any rights or obligations 
under the WPPT and that it does not obligate its Contracting Parties to ratify or accede to that 
Treaty), but it also includes the useful clarification that the new Treaty does not affect the 
interpretation of the provisions of the WPPT. This further confirms the continued validity of 
the principles and standards on which the 1996 WIPO Treaties were based; nothing in the new 
Treatymaybeinterpretedasservingtoquestionthoseprinciplesorweakenthosestandards.
BT-Pr.31.ThenewagreedstatementconcerningArticle 1(3)ontherelationshipoftheTreaty
with the TRIPS Agreement has no influence on the interpretation of the new Treaty since it 
is a “non-derogation” clarification from the viewpoint of the TRIPS Agreement, rather than a 
possible indirect means of interpretation of the new Treaty (on the basis of certain aspects 
of the TRIPS Agreement). The reference to the provisions of the TRIPS Agreement is also 
sufficiently well balanced; although competition aspects are mentioned specifically, it covers 
all the objectives and principles of the Agreement identified in its Preamble and in its various 
provisions (in fact, it covers in a general manner all its provisions on obligations, rights, the 
conditions and terms of protection, enforcement of rights, etc.)
BT-Pr.32.ThenewagreedstatementconcerningArticle 2(a)onthedefinitionof“performers”
clarifies that not only those who perform existing literary or artistic works (or expressions of 
folklore)qualifyasperformersbutalsothosewhocreate(improvise)suchworksinthecourse
of their performances. The statement does not include anything to do with the issue of “extras”. 
Itfollowsunequivocallyfromthetextofthedefinitionanditsnegotiationhistory(“preparatory
work”) as reflected in the records of the 2000 Diplomatic Conference that “extras” are not covered.
BT-Pr.33.ThenewagreedstatementconcerningArticle 15ontechnologicalprotection 
measures(TPMs)anditsrelationshipwithArticle 13onthethree-steptestoffersappropriate 
interpretation of the obligations concerning TPMs (which are the same, mutatis mutandis, under 
the new Treaty as under the WCT and the WPPT). In particular, it clarifies that not only the 
limitations and exceptions concerned must be in accordance with the three-step test, but the 
measures applied to ensure that beneficiaries may enjoy them are also only applicable where, 
and only in a way in which, the conditions of the test are fulfilled. As a further guarantee, the 
agreed statement limits the applicability of such measures to those beneficiaries who have legal 
access to performances and, although it does not state the absence of voluntary measures by 
the owners of rights as an absolute priority, it mentions it as the most typical (and, in the text, 
the only) example for situations where “measures” may be justified. The second sentence of 
the statement deals with possible “measures” in respect of performances in the public domain

PART III. Guides to the three WIPO “Internet Treaties” – the WCT, the WPPT and the BTAP
(whicharenotcoveredbytheTreatyand,thus,byitsArticle 15and,therefore,doesnotseemto
be relevant in the given context); in order to prevent any possible misinterpretation, it includes a 
phrase according to which it is without prejudice to the legal protection of audiovisual works in 
which such performances in the public domain might be included.
BT-Pr.34.Asmentionedabove,andasemphasizedinthecommentsonArticle 13below,where
the principles of the Agenda stating development considerations may truly have a role in the 
interpretation of the provisions of the BTAP is, in particular, the application of the three-step 
test, for the reasons mentioned there.
Article 1
Relation to Other Conventions and Treaties
(1) Nothing in this Treaty shall derogate from existing obligations that Contracting Parties 
have to each other under the WPPT or the International Convention for the Protection 
of Performers, Producers of Phonograms and Broadcasting Organizations done in 
Rome on October 26, 1961.
(2) Protection granted under this Treaty shall leave intact and shall in no way affect the 
protectionofcopyrightinliteraryandartisticworks.Consequently,noprovisionofthis
Treaty may be interpreted as prejudicing such protection.
(3) This Treaty shall not have any connection with treaties other than the WPPT, nor shall it 
prejudice any rights and obligations under any other treaties.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 1:ItisunderstoodthatnothinginthisTreatyaffectsany
rights or obligations under the WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty (WPPT) or their 
interpretationanditisfurtherunderstoodthatparagraph 3doesnotcreateanyobligations
for a Contracting Party to this Treaty to ratify or accede to the WPPT or to comply with any of 
its provisions.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 1(3):ItisunderstoodthatContractingPartieswhoare
members of the World Trade Organization (WTO) acknowledge all the principles and objectives 
of the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS Agreement) 
and understand that nothing in this Treaty affects the provisions of the TRIPS Agreement, 
including, but not limited to, the provisions relating to anti-competitive practices.
Title of the Article
BT-1.1.AspointedoutintheGuidetotheWPPTaboveconcerningthetitleofArticle 1(“Relation
to Other Conventions”), it is not well-formulated for two reasons, even if this does not create 
substantiveproblems.First,whileinparagraph (3),thecorrectgenericterm“treaties”isused, 
inthetitle,thenarrowerterm“conventions”appears.Second,paragraph (2)isnotabout
the relation to other treaties but about the relation of the protection of the rights covered 
intheTreatytotheprotectionofcopyright.ThetitleofArticle 1oftheBTAPisdifferentbut
not necessarily more precise: “Relation to Other Conventions and Treaties”. In fact, in this 
way, the terminological problem is only accentuated, because, while in the case of the WPPT, 
the impression that the conventions are not treaties might only emerge from the text of the 
provisions, in the BTAP, it is the title itself which suggests this.605
Similarities to, and differences from, Article 1 of the WPPT
BT-1.2. At first sight, the three paragraphs may seem to be verbatim versions of the 
correspondingparagraphsofArticle 1oftheWPPT.Inreality,althoughitistruethatthereare
similarelementsinthetwosetsofparagraphs–whichisunderstandablesincetheyarisefrom 
thesamepurposesandpartlyfromthesamekindsofprovisionsofthetwoTreaties–there
605ThislanguageisnotinaccordancewiththeterminologyoftheVCLT,inwhichtheterm“treaties”isusedasthe 
generic term to cover any international treaties, conventions, agreements, etc.

===== PAGE 315 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
316 are also differences. In the case of paragraphs (1) and (3), the texts differ and two new agreed 
statementsrelatetothem.Thetextofparagraph (2),incontrast,isexactlythesameinthe 
twoTreatiesandtheonlydifferenceisthattheagreedstatementconcerningparagraph (2)in
the WPPT does not appear in the BTAP, from which, in principle (and hopefully not in practice) 
certain a contrario inferences might follow.
Paragraph (1): non-derogation clause concerning the Rome Convention
BT-1.3.AsitrelatestotheRomeConvention,thetextofthenon-derogationclauseinArticle 1(1)
oftheBTAPisthesameasinArticle 1(1)oftheWPPT(thedifferenceisexactlytheextensionof
the clause to the relation with the WPPT itself). The role of the clause still somewhat differs due 
tothedifferentcontextsofthetwoTreaties.IncontrastwithArticle 19oftheRomeConvention –
under which, once the performers have consented to the incorporation of their performances in 
audiovisualfixations,theprovisionsontheirrightshavenofurtherapplication–theBTAPhas 
to do precisely with the rights of performers in their performances incorporated in audiovisual 
fixations. Therefore, it may seem that the BTAP cannot have any derogatory effect vis-à-vis the 
Rome Convention. On the basis of a more thorough analysis, it may be found, however, that 
thenon-derogationclausestillhasacertainrole–notregardingthelevelofprotection,but 
concerning the scope of beneficiaries of protection; it is relevant in at least in three aspects.
BT-1.4. One of the three aspects is clear without any special analysis. Obviously, the non-
derogation clause applies to the categories of rights covered in the Rome Convention (the rights 
of performers in their performances fixed in phonograms, the rights of producers of phonograms 
and the rights of broadcasting organizations) but not covered by the BTAP (in particular, the rights 
of broadcasting organizations which are not covered in either the WPPT or the BTAP).
BT-1.5. The second aspect of the possible role of the non-derogation clause depends on the 
interpretation of the provisions of the Rome Convention on national treatment. As discussed in 
the Guide to that Convention in this collection in the Guide to the WPPT above, the delegations 
atthe1961RomeDiplomaticConferencestatedtheunderstandingthat,inArticle 2.1(a)and
2.2oftheConvention,aBerne-typenationaltreatmentisprescribed,butunderArticle 3.1 
of the TRIPS Agreement, 606 the WTO Members are obligated to grant “national treatment” to 
the performers who are nationals of other Members of the WTO only for those rights that are 
explicitly provided under the Agreement. As pointed out in the comments in those Guides, the 
samekindof“nationaltreatment”obligationhasbeenprescribedinArticle 4oftheWPPTthe 
applicationofwhichhasbeenacceptedasa“subsequentpractice”inthesenseofArticle 31.3(b) 
oftheVCLT.Asdiscussedbelow,this“subsequentpractice”hasbeenfollowedalsoinArticle 4of
the BTAP on “national treatment”.
BT-1.6. The third aspect where the non-derogation clause may have a role is in the differences 
between the provisions on eligibility of protection. The provisions of the Rome Convention on 
the eligibility of performances for protection are extremely complex. In principle, the rules 
areincludedinArticle 4buttheyreferto–andmayonlybeinterpretedtogetherwith–the
provisionsofArticles 5and6ontheeligibilityofphonogramsandbroadcasts.Incontrast,the 
eligibilityrulesinArticle 3oftheBTAP,asdiscussedbelow,aremuchsimplerandnarrower.It
may follow from this that, in certain specific cases, a performance that would be eligible for 
protection under the Rome Convention may not be under the BTAP.607
The BTAP as a special agreement under Article 22 of the Rome Convention
BT-1.7.Article 1oftheBTAP,similarlytoArticle 1oftheWPPT,doesnotcontainastatementto
confirmthatitisaspecialagreementwithinthemeaningofArticle 22oftheRomeConvention–
606Article 3(1)oftheAgreementreadsasfollows:“Inrespectofperformers[…],thisobligation[toaccordrealnational 
treatment concerning other rights] only applies in respect of the rights provided under this Agreement.”
607SilkevonLewinskidescribessuchapossiblesituationinReinbotheandvonLewinski(481–482):  
ThismaybethecasewhereperformancesareprotectedunderArticle 4(a)RomeConvention,i.e.irrespectiveofthe 
nationality or habitual residence of the performer in a Contracting State. For example, where countries A and B are 
both parties to the Rome Convention and to the BTAP, and a performance of a national of a third country, which is not 
a party to the Rome Convention or the BTAP, takes place in country B, that performer is protected in country A under 
the Rome Convention, but not under the BTAP. In this case, the BTAP does not derogate from the Rome Convention, 
so that the performer continues to enjoy protection under the Rome Convention in country A.

PART III. Guides to the three WIPO “Internet Treaties” – the WCT, the WPPT and the BTAP
incontrastwithArticle 1(1)oftheWCTinwhichitisdeclaredthatitisaspecialagreementwithin
themeaningofArticle 20oftheBerneConvention.
BT-1.8.Article 22oftheRomeConvention–whichisasortofmutatis mutandis version of 
Article 20oftheBerneConvention–readsasfollows:
Contracting States reserve the right to enter into special agreements among themselves 
in so far as such agreements grant to performers, producers of phonograms or 
broadcasting organisations more extensive rights than those granted by this Convention 
or contain other provisions not contrary to this Convention.
Concerning the interpretation of this provision, its relation to the non-derogation clause and the 
accordanceoftheTreatywiththerequirementsofitsspecialagreementstatusthesameapplies
mutatis mutandis as what is discussed in the Guide to the WPPT above. That is, the nature of the 
new agreement is decisive; not a statement, or the absence thereof, according to which it is a 
specialagreementunderArticle 22oftheRomeConvention.
BT-1.9. The BTAP was concluded among the Contracting States of the Rome Convention. This is so in 
spite of the fact that it was not concluded only among them but also among them and other parties 
that are not Contracting States. Therefore, in the relationship between the Rome Contracting 
States,theBTAPissupposedtofulfillthecriteriaofArticle 22oftheConventioninthatitgrants
more extensive rights than those granted in the Convention or at least does not contain provisions 
contrary to it. It seems that the BTAP fulfills these criteria. Although it only covers the rights of one 
ofthethreecategoriesofthebeneficiariesoftheRomeConvention–ofperformers–and,although
as regards the rights of performers, it applies only to “audiovisual performances”, in the field of its 
coverage, it does grant rights that are more extensive than under the Rome Convention (as noted 
above,thisisobviousinviewofArticle 19oftheConvention).Asregardstheconditionthataspecial
agreement must not contain other provisions contrary to the Convention, it is also fulfilled in 
accordancewiththesafeguardclauseinArticle 1(1)oftheTreaty.
Paragraphs (1) and (3) and an agreed statement: relation to the WPPT
BT-1.10.Therearetwoparagraphs(paragraphs(1)and(3))ofArticle 1andanagreedstatement
todealwiththerelationoftheBTAPtotheWPPT.Thenon-derogationclauseinparagraph (1),in
addition to the Rome Convention, also applies to the WPPT. As discussed below in the comments 
onparagraph (3)oftheArticle,theoriginalideawastoregulatetheprotectionoftherightsof
“audiovisual performers” in a protocol to the WPPT. If that option had been chosen, due to the 
internal relationship between the WPPT and a protocol to it, the derogation clause, if it had been 
needed at all, certainly would have been worded in another way. However, since the BTAP was 
adopted as a stand-alone treaty, a non-derogation rule is needed also with respect to the WPPT.
BT-1.11. Both the WPPT and the BTAP were adopted for the protection of the rights of 
performers in their performances, but the WPPT covers the rights in performances fixed in 
phonograms (and in phonograms themselves), while the BTAP covers the rights in performances 
incorporated in audiovisual fixations. Therefore, at first sight, the role of the non-derogation 
clause seems to be limited since the subject matter of the two Treaties is not the same. A closer 
analysisoftherelevantprovisions,however,revealsthat–duetotheoverlapbetweenthe
definitionsof“phonograms”intheWPPTand“audiovisualfixations”intheBTAP–theclause 
may still have an important function. Furthermore, for example, although the provisions on 
theexclusiverightsconcerningunfixedperformancesarethesameinArticle 6oftheBTAPand 
Article 6oftheWPPT,stilltheymightbeinterpretedindifferentwaysunderthetwoTreaties.
The differences discussed below at the corresponding provisions of the BTAP may have an 
impact, inter alia, because the scope of beneficiaries is not the same under the two treaties. 
Ascanbeseenbelow,Article 3oftheBTAPprovidesprotectiononlytothenationalsofthe
other Contracting Parties (to which non-nationals of the other Contracting Parties who have 
theirhabitualresidenceinoneofthemareassimilated)while,underArticle 3oftheWPPT,the
broader categories of the Rome Convention apply.
BT-1.12.Inparagraph (3)ofArticle 1thereisamisleadingreferencetotheWPPTastheTreaty
with which the BTAP has substantive connection. Under one of the alternatives of the draft 
WPPT, the provisions of the Treaty would have also covered the rights of performers in the

===== PAGE 317 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
318 audiovisual fixations of their performances. Therefore, when the 1996 Diplomatic Conference 
adopted the other alternative not covering those rights, it was understandable that, in the 
Resolution on the continuation of the preparatory work to extend protection to performances 
incorporated in audiovisual fixations, the adoption of a protocol to the WPPT appeared to be a 
reasonable objective. If a Beijing Protocol on Audiovisual Performances had been adopted in 
2012,thereferenceinparagraph (3)toaspecificsubstantiveconnectionwiththeWPPTwould
have been appropriate (although in that case it would have been obvious and therefore not 
really necessary), but in Beijing a self-standing Treaty was adopted. In a protocol, but even in a 
self-standing treaty, it might have been a possible solution to provide for the mutatis mutandis 
application of certain provisions of the WPPT, which also would have established a sort of 
substantiveconnectionbetweenthetwoTreaties,butnosuchsolutionwaschosen.Some– 
althoughnotsubstantive–connectionscouldalsohavebeencreatedintheAdministrative 
and Final Clauses, by establishing a joint Assembly of the WPPT and the BTAP, or by limiting 
the eligibility for becoming party to the BTAP to Contracting Parties of the WPPT. However, as 
discussed below, no such connection was established. The only real reason for maintaining 
paragraph (3)inArticle 1seemstobethattheprincipleadoptedinthedecisionbeforethe2012
BeijingConferencethatthe19Articles “provisionally”agreeduponatthe2000Conferencewere 
not to be renegotiated has been somewhat rigidly applied here.
BT-1.13.Atthe2000DiplomaticConference,consensusemergedquiteearlythatthenatureof
the instrument (protocol or treaty) was not truly decisive. Although there were some delegations 
in Main Committee I that expressed preference either for a protocol or for a self-standing treaty, 
the issue of a possible connection between the two instruments was left to Main Committee II 
working on the Administrative and Final Clauses. At the sessions of Main Committee II, intensive 
debates took place over Alternative A (under which the instrument would have been a protocol 
or otherwise would have had close substantive connection with the WPPT) and Alternative 
B (the option of a stand-alone treaty). As a middle course, the idea of a joint assembly also 
emerged (although it would have only meant joint meetings of the Contracting Parties possibly 
with different voting rights depending on the treaty to which they were party). In the end, 
Alternative B seemed to have a majority, but no final decision had been adopted yet when the 
2000 Diplomatic Conference ended. In the Basic Proposal on Administrative and Final Clauses 
submitted to the Beijing Diplomatic Conference, there were no longer any alternatives; simply 
thegeneralmodelofsuchclausesinaWIPOtreatywereproposed–andlateradopted–which
were similar to the relevant clauses of the WPPT (separate Assembly, eligibility for becoming 
party, entry into force, etc.) and other recent WIPO treaties at that time (for example, in the 
Basic Proposal, reference was made to the way these clauses appeared in the Singapore Treaty 
on the Law of Trademarks (STLT) adopted in 2006).
BT-1.14.Asmentionedabove,theprovisionofparagraph (3)–referringtoaspecificconnection
withtheWPPT–doesnotseemconsistentwiththelegalstatusoftheBTAP.608 It is true that a 
number of provisions of the BTAP are identical or similar to the corresponding provisions of 
theWPPT,butthisisalsotrueofmanyprovisionsoftheWCT.Itgoeswithoutsayingthat–as
discussedbelowinthecommentsonArticle 12ontheissuesoftransferofrights–notonly
was the WPPT a source of inspiration for the BTAP, but also the WCT, as well as the substantive 
normsoftheBerneConventiontobecompliedwithunderArticle 1(4)oftheWCT.609
BT-1.15. With the adoption of the above-mentioned provisions among the Administrative and Final 
Clauses,thereferencetotheWPPTinArticle 1(3)oftheBTAPasatreatywithwhich,incontrast
withanyothertreaties,ithasasubstantiveconnectionbecameunjustified,but–asmentioned
above–duetotherigidapplicationofthepre-conferenceagreementbarringrenegotiationofthe
19provisionallyadoptedArticles,ithasremaineduntouched.Insteadofleavingoutparagraph (3),
anagreedstatementwasadoptedtonegate–inaself-contradictorymanner–thereferenceto
suchaconnectioninArticle 1(3).Theagreedstatementreadsasfollows:

PART III. Guides to the three WIPO “Internet Treaties” – the WCT, the WPPT and the BTAP
It is understood that nothing in this Treaty affects any rights or obligations under the 
WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty (WPPT) or their interpretation and it is 
furtherunderstoodthatparagraph 3doesnotcreateanyobligationsforaContracting
Party to this Treaty to ratify or accede to the WPPT or to comply with any of its provisions.
ThiswastheleastcontroversialagreedstatementinBeijingandthusitwasadoptedquite
quickly.Itstatestheobvious,butitwouldnothavebeennecessaryifparagraph (3)ofthe
Article hadbeendeleted.
BT-1.16. Nevertheless, there is a useful collateral effect of the agreed statement: it clarifies 
that not only are no rights and obligations under the WPPT (and it may be added, due to the 
similarity of many provisions of the two 1996 Treaties, also under the WCT) affected by anything 
in the BTAP, but that this is also true of the interpretation of those rights and obligations. This 
may be a guarantee against any attempts to revise and weaken the standards of the two 1996 
“Internet Treaties”. 
Paragraph (2) on relation with copyright
BT-1.17.ThetextofArticle 1(2)oftheBTAPandArticle 1(2)oftheWPPTisthesame.Thereisno
need even to refer to a mutatis mutandis application of the provision, because it only refers to “this 
Treaty” without identifying it (in the given context, it is obvious). Still there is a difference because, 
concerningArticle 1(2)oftheWPPT,anagreedstatementwasadopted–orrathertwostatements
combinedunderthesametitle–whileconcerningArticle 1(2)oftheBTAPthereisnone.
BT-1.18.ThedoubleagreedstatementconcerningArticle 1(2)oftheWPPTreadsasfollows:
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 1(2):ItisunderstoodthatArticle 1(2)clarifiesthe
relationship between rights in phonograms under this Treaty and copyright in works 
embodied in the phonograms. In cases where authorization is needed from both the 
author of a work embodied in the phonogram and a performer or producer owning rights 
in the phonogram, the need for the authorization of the author does not cease to exist 
becausetheauthorizationoftheperformerorproducerisalsorequired,andviceversa.
ItisfurtherunderstoodthatnothinginArticle 1(2)precludesaContractingPartyfrom
providing exclusive rights to a performer or producer of phonograms beyond those 
requiredtobeprovidedunderthisTreaty.
Thequestioniswhatkindofeffectitmayhavethatthisdoubleagreedstatementhasbeenleft
outfromtheBTAP.Theoptimisticanswer–fromperformers’pointofview–maybelittleor
nothing, because these statements just point out what is obvious. There is truly no reason to claim 
that, where international treaties and national laws subject the use of certain productions to the 
authorization of two or three different categories of contributors (such as authors, performers 
and producers) separately, it might somehow still be sufficient to obtain authorization from only 
one or two categories. Or in case of authorization by one category, that any other category might 
be constrained to also authorize the use of a given production in which the rightholders of that 
category also have a right of authorization. It can also be regarded as given that the absence of 
adeclarationaboutthepossibilityofprovidingahigherlevelofprotection–inviewoftheequal
absenceofadeclarationtothecontrary–isnotanobstacletotheContractingPartiestobemore
generous than what follows from the obligations under the Treaty.
BT-1.19.Itseemsthat,infact,thisisnotonlyanoptimisticanswerbut–ifthebasicprinciples
ofinterpretationoflegalnormsaredulytakenintoaccount–theonlyappropriateone.
Nevertheless, it is a pity that these statements were left out of the BTAP. This may be the source 
of faulty interpretations by citing a contrario consequences.Perhapsthereisaminordanger
of a conclusion that Contracting Parties are not allowed to provide for exclusive rights beyond 
whatisrequiredbytheBTAPjustbecausethisisnotstatedexclusively(sinceobviouslyitisnot

===== PAGE 319 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
320 prohibited either). However, the absence of the statement clearly rejecting the “cake theory” 610 
might lead to its emerging again.
Paragraph (3) of the Article and the agreed statement on the question of relation with 
treaties other than the WPPT, in particular with the TRIPS Agreement
BT-1.20.The(misleading)referenceinArticle 1(3)toaspecificconnectionoftheBTAPwiththe
WPPTisdiscussedabove.Apartfromthis,therestofthetextoftheparagraph isthesame 
asthetextofArticle 1(3)oftheWPPT.Therefore,thesamecommentsapplytothispartof
theparagraph asabovetoArticle 1(3)oftheWPPTintheGuidetothatTreaty,inparticular
concerning the relationship with the Rome Convention. As discussed above, whether or not it 
is explicitly stated, both the WPPT and the BTAP should be regarded as “special agreements” 
underArticle 22oftheRomeConvention.Therefore,itcouldhardlybedeniedthattheBTAP
has–atleastinthataspect–acertainrelationwiththeRomeConvention,atleastasfarasthe
Contracting States of the Convention are concerned; it may influence the interpretation of the 
BTAP provisions in the sense that it is not supposed to be in conflict with the Rome Convention; 
if the level of protection differs, it may only be more extensive. The non-derogation clause in 
paragraph (1)ofArticle 1oftheTreatyhasthesameeffect.
BT-1.21.ApartfromtheRomeConventionandtheWPPT,whenArticle 1(3)oftheBTAPstates
that it “shall not have any connection with [the other] treaties […] nor shall it prejudice any rights 
andobligationsunderanyothertreaties”,itisjustconfirmingwhatwouldhavebeenquite
obvious even without it. The contrary would only be the case if there were provisions in the 
BTAPtothateffect.Thesameistruewithrespecttothequestionofpossibleinfluenceonthe 
provisions of the BTAP by some other treaties.
BT-1.22. Although in the provisions of the BTAP, there is no indication of such influence by 
anotherTreaty,theagreedstatementconcerningArticle 1(3)oftheBTAPontherelationshipwith
the TRIPS Agreement should be examined for such an effect. If a relationship might be deduced 
from the agreed statement, a contradiction would emerge between it and the said provision of 
the BTAP according to which there is no connection with the TRIPS Agreement as with an “other 
treaty”. The answer is, however, clearly in the negative, since the statement is not about the 
questionofpossibleinfluencebytheTRIPSAgreementontheBTAPbutaboutanysuchinfluence
of the BTAP on the TRIPS Agreement; and it is confirmed that there is no such influence.
BT-1.23.ItisdulyclarifiedinArticle 1(3)thattheBTAP“shallnotprejudiceanyrightsand
obligations”’ (and, due to the absence of any connection, simply any provisions) under any 
other treaties, including the TRIPS Agreement. Therefore, in fact, there was no need for 
repeating in an agreed statement that “nothing in this Treaty affects the provisions of the 
TRIPS Agreement, including, but not limited to, the provisions relating to anti-competitive 
practices”. This redundant reference appears in the second part of the agreed statement. The 
first part reads as follows: “It is understood that Contracting Parties who are members of the 
World Trade Organization (WTO) acknowledge all the principles and objectives of the […] [TRIPS 
Agreement]”. This is a non-derogation statement and as such it has no substantive effect on the 
interpretation of either the BTAP or the TRIPS Agreement.
BT-1.24. While the agreed statement has no relevance as regards the interpretation of the BTAP, 
it may be regarded as an attempt to interpret the TRIPS Agreement in the BTAP. The reason for 
this, at first sight, is not clear. It is rather on the basis of certain proposals made in the course 
of the preparatory work that the original intention might be understood; such as the proposal 
under which the Contracting Parties of the BTAP would have “reaffirmed” their “commitments 
under the [TRIPS Agreement], in particular the provisions on principles, objectives and 
610 The “cake theory” refers to the reasons for the resistance of copyright owners against the recognition of related 
rights. It suggests that the users of certain productions (for example phonograms embodying the performances of 
musical works) cannot, or must not (e.g. budgetary entities or subsidiary companies with fixed budgets to be used 
forrightsrevenuepurposes)–orarenotwillingto–paymorefortheusethereofwhenanewrightisrecognized. 
Therefore, the “cake” should be divided, as a result of which the owners of copyright will receive less. In fact, it is 
arealitythattheuserscannotorarenotwillingtomakethe“cake”muchbigger.Thus,itisnotmerelya“theory”– 
although, it is still not a sufficient argument against the recognition of the rights of related rights beneficiaries.

competition policy”.611 If such proposals had been adopted, the agreed statement could 
not only have been read as a sort of interpretation of the TRIPS Agreement (in that it would 
have identified certain elements thereof as essential, but not mentioned others that are also 
important) but it could have been argued (although with dubious justification) that it might also 
serve as a source of interpretation of the BTAP.
BT-1.25. The agreed statement as adopted is not of this nature. It became a (redundant) non-
derogation clause and it refers not only to selected aspects of the TRIPS Agreement but, in 
a well-balanced manner, to the Agreement in general. The reference only to the “objectives” 
and“principles”couldhavebeeninterpretedtomeanjusttheprovisionsoftwoarticles of 
theAgreement(Articles 7and8)whichhavethesetitles.Incontrast,theexpressionusedin 
thestatement–“alltheprinciplesandobjectivesoftheAgreement[…]”meansnotonlywhat
isprovidedinthosetwoarticles butreferstoallprinciplesandobjectives.Theseinclude,for 
example, what is stated in the preamble of the TRIPS Agreement: “taking into account the need 
topromoteeffectiveandadequateprotectionofintellectualpropertyrights”;“[r]ecognizing[…] 
theneedfornewrulesanddisciplinesconcerning[…]theprovisionofadequatestandardsand
principles concerning the availability, scope and use of trade-related intellectual property rights 
[…] [and] the provision of effective and appropriate means for the enforcement of trade-related 
intellectual property rights”. There is a reference to all provisions of the TRIPS Agreement as not 
affected by the BTAP: (all) “the provisions of the TRIPS Agreement, including, but not limited to, the 
provisions relating to anti-competitive practices”. 612 
BT-1.26. Otherwise, it is not easy to understand why just the anti-competitive principles of the TRIPS 
Agreement are mentioned specifically as not being affected by the BTAP on the rights of “audiovisual 
performers” which, apart from the rights in unfixed performances, are not covered by the TRIPS 
Agreement. The reference to competition aspects of certain provisions adopted and applied in 
anotherorganization–theWTO–doesnotseemtobejustifiedeitherbecausethebasiccompetition
principles are also duly reflected in the treaties administered by WIPO, the organization under the 
aegis of which the BTAP has been adopted. The following statement (in fact, an agreed statement, 
even if it was not explicitly declared as one) was adopted at the 1967 Stockholm revision conference 
byMainCommittee IinconnectionwithArticle 17oftheBerneConvention:
The Committee accepted, without opposition, the proposal of its Chairman that mention 
shouldbemadeinthisReportofthefactthatquestionsofpublicpolicyshouldalwaysbe
a matter for domestic legislation and that the countries of the Union would therefore be 
able to take all necessary measures to restrict possible abuse of monopolies. Whereupon, 
the proposals of Australia and the United Kingdom relating to abuse of monopoly 
were withdrawn.613
Thus, if it was felt necessary to refer to the principles concerning anti-competitive practices, it 
could have been done by referring to the principles adopted long before the TRIPS Agreement 
under a treaty administered by WIPO (the Berne Convention) which, like the TRIPS Agreement, 
doesnotcovertherightsof“audiovisualperformers”,butwhich,duetoitssubjectmatter–also 
coveringaudiovisualworks–ismuchmorerelevantfromtheviewpointoftheprotectionofthe
rights of such performers than the general provisions of the TRIPS Agreement.
Article 2 
Definitions
For the purposes of this Treaty:
(a)  “performers” are actors, singers, musicians, dancers, and other persons who act, sing, 
deliver, declaim, play in, interpret, or otherwise perform literary or artistic works or 
expressions of folklore;
611 See the detailed description of this and other proposals, with the political agenda behind them, and the debate on the 
agreedstatementinReinbotheandvonLewinski,479–481.
612 Emphasis added.
613 Records of the Intellectual Property Conference of Stockholm, June 11 to 14, 1967 (WIPO, 1971), 1175, para. 263.

322 (b)  “audiovisual fixation” means the embodiment of moving images, whether or not 
accompanied by sounds or by the representations thereof, from which they can be 
perceived, reproduced or communicated through a device;
(c)  “broadcasting” means the transmission by wireless means for public reception of 
sounds or of images or of images and sounds or of the representations thereof; such 
transmission by satellite is also “broadcasting”; transmission of encrypted signals 
is “broadcasting” where the means for decrypting are provided to the public by the 
broadcasting organization or with its consent;
(d)  “communication to the public” of a performance means the transmission to the 
public by any medium, otherwise than by broadcasting, of an unfixed performance, 
orofaperformancefixedinanaudiovisualfixation.ForthepurposesofArticle 11,
“communication to the public” includes making a performance fixed in an audiovisual 
fixation audible or visible or audible and visible to the public.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 2(a):Itisunderstoodthatthedefinitionof“performers”
includes those who perform a literary or artistic work that is created or first fixed in the course 
of a performance.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 2(b):Itisherebyconfirmedthatthedefinitionof“audiovisual
fixation”containedinArticle 2(b)iswithoutprejudicetoArticle 2(c)oftheWPPT.
Comparison with the definitions in the WPPT
BT-2.1. It is a matter of logic that in the BTAP, which provides protection only for the rights of 
performers in audiovisual fixations of their performances, there is no definition of the terms 
“phonogram”or“producerofaphonogram”asinArticle 3(b)and(c)oftheRomeConvention
andArticle 2(b)and(d)oftheWPPT.Therewouldonlyhavebeenneedforeitherareferenceto
thedefinitionof“phonogram”inArticle 2(b)oftheWPPTorforitsrepetitionintheBTAPifthe 
Swissproposal –madeatthe2000DiplomaticConference–toreplacetheterm“audiovisual
fixation” by the term “fixations that are not phonograms” 614 had been adopted, but it was not.
BT-2.2.IncontrastwithArticle 2(e)oftheWPPT,intheBTAP,thereisnodefinitionof
“publication”. Its inclusion is not only not needed but would have been illogical, since the term is 
notusedintheBTAP;itisalsoonlyusedintheWPPTinArticle 17(2)onthetermofprotectionof
the right of producers of phonograms.615
BT-2.3. In principle, the term “fixation” may also be mentioned as not being defined in the BTAP 
incontrastwithArticle 2(c)oftheWPPT,butitseemsmoreappropriatetoconsiderthatthe
BTAP,initsArticle 2(b),includesthedefinitionofakindofmutatis mutandis version: “audiovisual 
fixation”asdiscussedbelow–a mutatis mutandisversion,becausewhatisdefinedinArticle 2(b)
of the WPPT is not “fixation” in general but only “aural fixation”: “embodiment of sounds, or of 
the representations thereof”.
BT-2.4.Thedefinitionsof“broadcasting”inArticle 2(f)oftheWPPTandArticle 2(c)oftheBTAP 
and“communicationtothepublic”inArticle 2(g)oftheWPPTandArticle 2(d)oftheBTAPmay
seem to be mutatis mutandis versions. As discussed below there is also an apparent overlap 
between the WPPT and the BTAP texts that needs due interpretation. It is another matter that, 
asanalyzedbelowatArticle 11oftheBTAP,therightsofbroadcastingandcommunicationtothe
publicarenotregulatedinthesamewayasinArticle 15oftheWPPT.
BT-2.5.Finally,thedefinitionof“performers”inArticle 2(a)oftheBTAPisidenticalwiththat 
inArticle 2(a)oftheWPPT.However,asdiscussedbelow,intheBTAP,anagreedstatement
was adopted on a less controversial issue (about the status of improvising performers) and

Article 2(a) and an agreed statement on the definition of “performers”
BT-2.6.SinceArticle 2(a)oftheBTAPisaverbatimrepetitionofArticle 2(a)oftheWPPT,ingeneral,
thecommentsintheGuidetotheWPPTaboveconcerningArticle 2(a)ofthatTreatyalsoapply
here. It may be remarked here too that the definition of “performers”, in its basic elements, 
correspondstothedefinitionofthesameterminArticle 3(a)oftheRomeConvention,butitdiffers
from it in two aspects. The first difference is that the definition in the BTAP, as also in the WPPT, 
includes the verb “interpret”. As mentioned in the Guide to the WPPT above, it allows the definition 
to be interpreted in such a way that it also covers (for example) conductors of orchestras. In 
connection with “audiovisual fixations”, however, it does not have a similar role. The second 
difference is that, while the Rome definition is limited to the performers of literary and artistic 
works, the WPPT and BTAP definitions are extended to performers of expressions of folklore.
BT-2.7. Although the definition of “performers” is the same in the WPPT and the BTAP, it is 
worthwhiletoanalyzeitwithregardtothesubjectmattersoftheTreatieswhich–apart
from the provisions on the rights in unfixed performances, do differ; the WPPT applies to the 
right of performers in their performances fixed in phonograms; the BTAP, to their rights in 
performances fixed in audiovisual fixations. Therefore, it may be asked whether the scope of 
performers as beneficiaries of protection in the two Treaties is also the same. If the answer 
wereinthenegative,afurtherquestionmightbewhythenthedefinitionwasnotadapted
accordingly.Itseems,however,thatthereisnoneedtodealwiththesecondquestion,
because, although certain acts listed in the definitions typically relate to performances fixed in 
phonograms and audiovisual fixations, respectively, practically all of them may be fixed in both 
kinds of fixations. The performances of singers and musicians may also be fixed in audiovisual 
fixations, and the sounds of performances of actors without the images may be published in 
phonograms. Dancers and pantomime actors may seem to be exceptions because, at first sight, 
their performances do not seem to be suitable to be fixed in phonograms. In extreme cases, 
however, this may not be excluded either; namely where they are fixed together with musical 
performances accompanying their movements in fixations not qualifyingasaudiovisualworks
which,therefore,forthereasonsdiscussedbelowinconnectionwithArticle 2(b)on“audiovisual 
fixation”, may fall in the category of phonograms rather than “audiovisual fixations”.
BT-2.8.TheagreedstatementconcerningArticle 2(a)isaboutthoseperformers“whoperforma
literary or artistic work that is created or first fixed in the course of a performance”. This means in 
practical terms those who produce improvisations in the course of their performances that, in view 
oftheiroriginalnature,qualifyasworks.TheEUdelegationexpresslystatedthisunderstandingin
its post-adoption declaration by saying that the European Union and its Member States welcomed 
the agreed statement on Article 2, which clarified that the definition of `performer' also covered 
those whose performances were improvisations, whether they remained unfixed or were fixed.616 
There may hardly be any doubt about the validity of this statement not only because no Contracting 
Partytriedtorebutit–whichshowedimplicitlythattheydidnotopposebutratheragreedwithit–
but also because it is undeniable that improvisation is the most obvious form of a performance of a 
literary or artistic work “that is created or first fixed in the course of a performance”.
BT-2.9.  The first version of the agreed statement was proposed by India before the beginning of 
the 2012 Diplomatic Conference (in accordance with the compromise agreement not to reopen 
the debate on the substantive provisions provisionally adopted in 2000, but with the possibility 
of including certain agreed statements, inter alia,concerningArticle 2).Itreadasfollows:“Itis
understood that the definition of the performer is an inclusive one and covers all audiovisual 
fixations of the performances”. 617 It was not clear what the Indian delegation meant by this text, 
sinceitcouldhavebeenunderstoodtostatesomethingwhich–inviewofthedefinitionsof
“performer”and“audiovisualfixation”inArticle 2(a)and(b)oftheBasicProposalonsubstantive 
provisionsofthedrafttreaty–wassupposedtobeclear.Therewasreasontopresumethat
perhapsthebroaddefinitionof“performer”insection2(qq)oftheIndianCopyrightAct–which 
616 See Summary Minutes of Main Committee I 2000 ,DocumentIAVP/DC/37.,para.277.

BT-2.10. In the course of the informal consultation, however, it was precisely the concept of 
inclusiveness that created the main problem, because this may have suggested that “extras” 
would be also covered. This was strongly opposed by the delegation of the United States. When 
it was clarified that basically improvisation was meant, the later adopted compromise text was 
agreed upon which describes such kinds of performances in more general language and, at the 
same time, in order to avoid a possible understanding that the definition also covers “extras”, 
omits the reference to “inclusiveness”.
The issue of extras discussed during the preparatory work of the Treaty
BT-2.11. Although the issue of extras emerged at the Beijing Conference in connection with 
theagreedstatementthatsettledthequestionofimprovisationsbyperformers,ithad 
been discussed intensively before in the preparatory work leading to the convocation of the 
Beijing Conference.
BT-2.12. Extras (which in a performance include members of a crowd or people moving in 
thescenebehindthefeaturedactors),ingeneral,hadnotbeen–andarenot–regardedas
performers in industry practice. It could have been considered as granted that they are not 
covered by the definition of “performers”, because they do not have a real role to perform 
a dialogue or a featured act. However, it was understandable that countries with big film 
industries such as the United States and India wanted to make it sure that this was the 
understanding under the new treaty and that the definition of “performers” could not be 
interpreted as also covering such non-performers. The US delegation submitted a definition 
with the purpose of making this clear as early as the second session of the Committee of Experts 
onaProtocolconcerningAudiovisualPerformancesheldinJune1998:
“performers” are actors, singers, musicians, dancers, and other persons who act, sing, 
deliver, declaim, play in, interpret, or otherwise perform literary or artistic works or 
expressions of folklore, but not including extra performers or background performers.618
Then in the preparatory document submitted for the first session of the Standing Committee on 
Copyright and Related Rights (SCCR) (which had taken over the tasks of the above-mentioned 
Committee of Experts) held in November 1998, the United States added the following comments 
to this proposal:
The May 18 U.S. Proposal [see above] excluded “extra performers and background 
performers” from the definition of performers. We now propose that this language be 
replaced by the exclusion of “ancillary performers, considered such by professional practice.” 
InresponsetotheconcernsraisedattheJunemeetingaboutthescopeof“extra
performers” and “background performers,” the revised language, which comes directly 
from the WIPO English translation of the French copyright statute, seeks to provide 
greater clarity. Further, it is sufficient to cover the basic concept while providing flexibility 
for national interpretation.619 
BT-2.13. India submitted to the second session of the SCCR held in May 1999 a proposed draft 
definition according to which “casual” or “incidental” performers would have been excluded and 
extras would have been mentioned as examples of such:
“performers” are actors, singers, musicians, dancers, and other persons who act, sing, 
deliver, declaim, play in, interpret or otherwise perform literary or artistic works or 
expressions of folklore but does not include performers whose performances are casual or 
incidental in nature such as extras.620

BT-2.15. In the discussion at the sessions of the SCCR, it was made clear, however, that extras are 
not really performers; thus, it would not be necessary to exclude them from the definition in the

During the work of the Committee of Experts and the SCCR proposals were made to 
exclude extras from the protection of the proposed Instrument. It was also proposed 
that the definition should expressly exclude “performers whose performances are casual

“ancillaryparticipants”donotqualifyforprotectionbecausetheydonot,intheproper

explicit provision concerning extras is necessary in the proposed Instrument. Accordingly, 
when implementing the proposed Instrument, Contracting Parties may determine 
in their national legislation the threshold at which a person becomes a performer 
entitled to protection. When making this determination, Contracting Parties may take 
into consideration established industry practice and, inter alia, whether a person has a 
speaking role or forms a background to the acting.625
BT-2.16. At the 2000 Diplomatic Conference, the delegation of the United States proposed that 
the main elements of the note in the Basic Proposal be transformed into an agreed statement to

It is understood that, in general, “extras”, “ancillary performers” or “ancillary participants” 
donotqualifyforprotectionunderthisInstrumentbecausetheydonot,intheproper
sense, perform literary or artistic works or expressions of folklore.626
The proposal had the advantage that it did not refer to extras as if they had been excluded –in
theformofanexception–fromthedefinition;itwouldhavesimplyclarifiedthat they are not 
performers. This was discussed in Main Committee I627anditreceivedquitebroadsupport. 628 
Some delegations, however, reserved their position and the European Community was rather

Article 2(b) and the agreed statement on the definition of “audiovisual fixation”
BT-2.18. The Basic Proposal submitted to the 2000 Diplomatic Conference contained the 
definition of “audiovisual fixation” which was adopted later verbatim in Beijing in 2012 (just 
not as item (c) as in 2000, but as item (b), because the definition of “audiovisual performer” still 
appearing in point (b) in the 2000 version had been left out):
“audiovisual fixation” means the embodiment of moving images, whether or not 
accompanied by sounds or by the representations thereof, from which they can be 
perceived, reproduced or communicated through a device.
BT-2.19. As discussed above, this is a kind of mutatis mutandis version of the definition of “fixation” 
inArticle 2(c)oftheWPPTtowhichanoteinthe2000BasicProposalreferredinthisway:
Item (c) defines the term “audiovisual fixation.” Its structure follows the definition of 
“fixation” in the WPPT, and all the technical elements (“embodiment,” “representations,” 
“from which they can be perceived, reproduced or communicated” and “through a device”) 
that are not dictated by the different subject matter addressed by the proposed Instrument 
are identical. What is embodied in an audiovisual fixation must be “moving images, whether 
or not accompanied by sound or by the representations thereof.” The expression “moving 
images” should be understood in a broad sense covering any visual material capable of 
incorporating or recording of visual material using whatever means and whatever medium.
[…] In the proposed Instrument the expression “audiovisual fixation” is used to refer to any 
firstfixationandanyfixationembodiedinasubsequentcopy.632
BT-2.20. However, the term “audiovisual fixation” should be compared not only with the term 
“fixation”butalsowiththeterm“phonograms”,asdefinedinArticle 2(b)and(c)oftheWPPT,
respectively (the latter along with an agreed statement):
(b)  “phonogram” means the fixation of the sounds of a performance or of other sounds, 
or of a representation of sounds, other than in the form of a fixation incorporated in 
a cinematographic or other audiovisual work;
(c)  “fixation” means the embodiment of sounds, or of the representations thereof, from 
which they can be perceived, reproduced or communicated through a device;
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 2(b):Itisunderstoodthatthedefinitionofphonogram
providedinArticle 2(b)doesnotsuggestthatrightsinthephonogramareinanyway
affected through their incorporation into a cinematographic or other audiovisual work.
BT-2.21. It can be seen that the word “fixation” as defined in the WPPT may be understood either 
tomeantheactoffixationofanunfixedperformance(asinArticle 6(ii)oftheWPPTonthe
exclusive right of fixation) or the result of the act of fixation (as in the definition of “phonograms”). 
UnderArticle 2(c)oftheWPPT,“fixation”maymeanthefixationof(i)thesoundsofaperformance;
631 See documentAVP/DC/14.
632DocumentIAVP/DC/3,22,para.2.05.

===== PAGE 326 =====
327
PART III. Guides to the three WIPO “Internet Treaties” – the WCT, the WPPT and the BTAP
(ii) sounds other than the sounds of a performance; and (iii) representation of sounds which 
necessarily are not the sounds of a performance (but electronically generated sounds). The latter 
two categories of sounds do not have any relevance regarding the rights of performers. It is a 
basicdifferencebetweentheWPPTandtheBTAPthat,whiletheformer–inadditiontotherights
ofperformers–alsocoverstherightsofproducersofphonograms,thelatterisonlyforthe
protection of the rights of (audiovisual) performers. If not the WPPT but just an imaginable WIPO 
Aural Performances Treaty (WAPT) had been adopted on the rights of performers in their aural 
fixations of performances (in phonograms) and not phonograms at the same time, there would 
not have been any need for a definition of “fixation” extending also to embodiment of sounds 
other than the sounds of performances and to representations of sounds.
BT-2.22. The coverage of the rights by the BTAP is different; it is only on the rights of (audiovisual) 
performers and not also on the rights of producers of audiovisual works and/or the makers of 
audiovisualfixationsnotqualifyingasworks.Therefore,thereisnoneedinthedefinitionof
“audiovisual fixation” to refer to the fixation of anything but the fixation of moving images of 
performers, and particularly not to some electronically generated representations of images. 
Thus, in fact, instead of the definition of “audiovisual fixation”, it would have been sufficient to 
define “audiovisual fixation of a performance” more narrowly (the more so because, in all the 
provisions on the rights in the BTAP, this term appears). For example: “‘audiovisual fixation of 
a performance’ means the embodiment of moving images of a performance, whether or not 
accompanied by sounds, from which they can be perceived, reproduced or communicated 
through a device”. In such a definition, there would not have been any reference to representation 
of moving images (other than, necessarily, moving images of a performance) which have no 
relevance in the BTAP; in contrast, it would have been indicated that the embodiment of a specific 
kindofmovingimages–namely,thoseofaperformance–aresolelyrelevant.
Overlap between the definitions of “audiovisual fixation” and “phonogram”
BT-2.23. At the 2000 Diplomatic Conference, intensive debates took place on the definition of 
“audiovisualfixation”concerningitspossibleoverlapwith–andthereforethepossibleneedfor 
itsdelimitationfrom–thedefinitionof(“fixation”ofaperformanceina)“phonogram”underthe 
WPPT. Since the attention was concentrated on this aspect, the delegations did not note another 
one;namelythattherewas–andintheBTAPstillthereis–nodefinitionof“fixation”.Below,
first, a reference is made to the less important issue of the absence of such a definition; then the 
problem of the overlap is addressed.
BT-2.24.Asdiscussedabove,inArticle 2(c)oftheWPPT,theterm“fixation”hasdouble
meanings; namely (i), as included in the expression “fixation of the sounds of a performance” 
inArticle 2(b),itmeanstheresultofanactoffixationand,assuch,thesubjectmatterof 
protection,and(ii)whenitisusedinArticle 6(ii)oftheWPPTconcerningtheexclusiverightof 
fixation of performers in their unfixed performances, it refers to the act of fixation. “Audiovisual 
fixation”asdefinedinArticle 2(b)oftheBTAPandasusedintheexpression“performancesfixed 
in audiovisual fixations” throughout the Treaty only means the result of an act of fixation and as 
such the subject matter of protection. Therefore, in the BTAP, in contrast with the WPPT, there 
is no definition of “fixation” with the same double meanings as in the WPPT (that is, both as a 
subject matter of protection and as an act covered by an exclusive right). This does not mean, 
however, that the 2012 Beijing Diplomatic Conference was wrong and that the 1996 Geneva 
Diplomatic Conference was right when it adopted a separate definition of “fixation”.
BT-2.25. As mentioned above, there was an animated debate at the 2000 Diplomatic Conference 
onthequestionofoverlap.Thenoteconcerningthedefinitionof“audiovisualfixation”inthe 
2000 Basic Proposal pointed out 633thatthemajorityofthekeyelements–“embodiment”,
“representations”, “from which they can be perceived, reproduced or communicated” and 
“throughadevice”–were(andintheadoptedtextoftheBTAPare)identicalwiththedefinition
of“fixation”intheWPPT.However,asstressedabove,“audiovisualfixation”–which,beyond 
its definition, only appears in the BTAP in the expression “performances fixed in audiovisual 
fixations”–isthesubjectmatteroftherightsof“audiovisualperformers”.Therefore,assuchit 
should rather be compared with, and delimited from, the definition of “phonogram” in the WPPT 
633 SeedocumentIAVP/DC/3,22,para.2.05.

===== PAGE 327 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
328 in connection with performers’ rights in the context of “performances fixed in phonograms”, the 
subject matter of the protection of the rights of performers under that Treaty.
BT-2.26. Concerning performances embodied in audiovisual works, there is no overlap between 
theWPPTandtheBTAPbecauseunderthedefinitioninArticle 2(b)ofWPPT“‘phonogram’ 
means [inter alia] the fixation of the sounds of a performance […] other than in the form of a 
fixation incorporated in a cinematographic or other audiovisual work”, that is, in such a case, 
clearlyjusttheBTAPappliessince,underitsArticle 2(b),an'audiovisualfixation'meansthe
embodiment of moving images, whether or not accompanied by sounds” [emphasis added]. The 
dynamic aspects of the relationship between audiovisual works and phonograms (that is, the 
status of preexisting phonograms incorporated in the soundtracks of films and the publication 
of the soundtracks) is another matter; they are discussed in the comments in the Guide to the 
WPPTaboveonArticle 2(b)andtheagreedstatementaddressingthesespecificissues.
BT-2.27. The situation is different in respect of “audiovisual fixations” that, in the absence of 
originality,donotqualifyasaudiovisualworks,becausetheWPPTdefinitionof“phonogram”only
excludes fixations in “audiovisual works”, while the BTAP definition of “audiovisual fixation”, at 
firstsight,coverssuchfixationsirrespectiveofwhetherornottheyqualifyasaudiovisualworks.
There seems to be an overlap, the size and importance of which seem to depend on how low or 
highaleveloforiginalitytestisappliedintheContractingPartiesconcerned.Thus,thequestion
is, in a country party to both Treaties, which provisions apply to performances incorporated in 
audiovisualfixationsnotqualifyingasaudiovisualworks:thoseoftheWPPT,theBTAPorboth?
BT-2.28.Thelastvariantmentionedabove–afixationqualifyingbothasphonogramand 
audiovisualfixation –wasnotdesirableandthedelegationswantedtoavoidit.Atthe2000
Diplomatic Conference, the Swiss delegation proposed a simple solution: to make it clear that 
audiovisual fixation under the new instrument means any fixations that are not phonograms. 
Thismighthavebeentheclearestsolutiontoavoidanoverlap.However,itraisedthequestion
ofhowtoapplyit,withvarioussub-questions.
BT-2.29. The Swiss delegation proposed that the term “audiovisual fixation” should be replaced 
with the term “fixations that are not phonograms”. 634 The delegation of Canada, however, 
rightly noted that, in this form, the term would have been too broad; it would have also included 
fixations of performance in a series of photographs; therefore, the reference to moving images 
still would have been necessary.635 In view of this, the Swiss proposal could have been improved, 
for example, in this way:
“audiovisual fixation of a performance” means the embodiment of moving images of a 
performance, whether or not accompanied by sounds, other than what is a ‘phonogram’ 
underArticle 2(b)oftheWPPT,fromwhichtheycanbeperceived,reproducedor
communicated through a device.
Or, if the intention had been to produce a stand-alone text, without the reference to the definition 
in the WPPT but still in accordance with it, the possible definition could have read in this way:
“audiovisual fixation of a performance” means the embodiment of moving images of a 
performance, whether or not accompanied by sounds, in a cinematographic or other 
audiovisual work, from which they can be perceived, reproduced or communicated 
through a device. 
This would have delimited the definition of “audiovisual fixation” of a performance from the 
definition of “phonogram” because, under the latter, the fixation of the sounds of a performance 
is a “phonogram” even when moving images of the performance are fixed together with the 
sounds–exceptwherethistakesplaceinaudiovisualworks. At the Diplomatic Conference, no 
such treaty-language proposal was made and, thus, no such definition was adopted, but still 
this kind of delimitation took place through an agreed statement concerning the definition 
of “audiovisual fixation” adopted provisionally in 2000 and then finally at the 2012 Beijing

BT-2.30.Thequestionishowdefinitivethissortofdelimitationmaybeinviewofthe 

statementdeniesinrespectof“audiovisualfixations”notqualifyingasworks.Thereare 
commentators who are of the view that the overlap of the definitions of “audiovisual fixations” 
and “phonograms” (prejudice to which is excluded by the agreed statement concerning the 
definition of “audiovisual fixation”) is not truly important and, to the extent it still exists, the 
BTAP is flexible enough to avoid real conflicts. 638
BT-2.31. Flexibilities are indeed available; certainly, to the greatest extent to those Contracting 
Parties of the BTAP that are not also Contracting Parties of the WPPT. Since they are not bound by 
the WPPT, it is up to them whether or not they take into account the agreed statement clarifying 
the relationship between “audiovisual fixations” and “phonograms”. This, however (at the time of 
writingtheseGuides),appliesonlytoasmallnumber–eight639–ofthe48ContractingPartiesof
the BTAP that are not also among the 114 Contracting Parties of the WPPT and, in general, they 
do not have a substantial role in the international markets of phonograms and audiovisual works.
BT-2.32. An important aspect in assessing the size of overlap between the definitions of 
“phonograms” and “audiovisual fixations”, and the available flexibilities, is what sort of 
originalitytestisappliedinthegivenContractingParties.Iftheoriginalitytestislow–oritis 
justakindofasweat-of-the-browtest–theproblemofoverlapmaybeminimal,ifitisrelevant
at all, while where a higher level originality is needed, it is bigger because, in that case, more 
non-original audiovisual fixations may fall in the category of phonograms. The status of 
videoclips or “music videos” may also be a source of possible flexibility, since much depends 
onwhethertheyarequalifiedasnon-originalaudiovisualfixationsofimagesaccompanying 
phonograms, or short audiovisual works accompanied by music, or as a production combined 
from phonograms and audiovisual works each to be protected as such, as pointed out by the 
European Community delegation at the 2000 Diplomatic Conference: “[T]here were sound 
recordings that were accompanied by visual elements. That fact made such sound recordings an 
audiovisual fixation or made them phonograms, depending on how Contracting Parties would 
deal with these phenomena. The same went for the treatment of music videos”. 640
BT-2.33. Nevertheless, as a summary of the analysis of the issues of the overlap between the 
definitionof“audiovisualfixation”inArticle 2(b)oftheBTAPandthedefinitionof“phonogram” 
inArticle 2(b)oftheWPPT,itshouldbestatedthat,fromtheprovisionsofArticles 31and32of
theVCLT–atleastfortheContractingPartiesoftheBTAPthatarealsoContractingPartiesof
theWPPT–itfollowsthat,wherean“audiovisualfixation”doesnotqualifyasanaudiovisual 
work, it is to be protected instead as a phonogram under the WPPT. Thus, where in the rest of 
this Guide the provisions on “audiovisual fixations” are analyzed and this expression is used, 
in this context, it tends to mean in effect fixations in audiovisual works; in particular for those 
countries that are party both to the WPPT and the BTAP. Nevertheless, it should be added 
again that there was an apparent understanding among the delegations in Beijing that the 
Contracting Parties have a certain flexibility in addressing the issue of the overlap.

provisionally after a long and animated debate. This, however, only concerned the level of

adoptionofthetwodefinitionswaseasyandquasi-automaticbecausethedefinitionsof the acts 
of“broadcasting”inArticle 2(f)oftheWPPTandArticle 2(c)oftheBTAPandof“communication 
tothepublic”inArticle 2(g)oftheWPPTandArticle 2(d)oftheBTAPareexactlythesame;only 
the subject matter in respect of which the acts are performed differs.
BT-2.35.AsinArticle 2(f)oftheWPPT,theactofbroadcastingisdefinedas“transmissionby
wireless means for public reception”. As discussed in the Guide to the WPPT above concerning 
thedefinitioninArticle 2(f),theexpression“forpublicreception”isnotwell-craftedbecauseit
suggests that the act of reception takes place publicly (as in the case of public performance or 
“publiccommunication”underArticle 11bis(1)(iii) of the Berne Convention, where the act is to 
be carried out at a place where public is present or which is open to the public). It would have 
beenbettertousethelanguageofArticle 11bis(1)(i) and (ii): “communication to the public”, rather 
than “public reception”; in particular in the BTAP as a stand-alone treaty. At the 2000 Diplomatic 
Conference,JukkaLiedes,thePresidentofMainCommitteeI,notedthisdiscrepancyoftheBasic
Proposal641 (which, at that time, was still explicable by the idea that the instrument might be a 
protocol to the WPPT), but it was not changed at that time, and then in Beijing it was not changed 
due to the application of the principle “do not touch the provisions provisionally adopted in 2000”.
BT-2.36. In spite of the same acts being covered by the WPPT and the BTAP definitions, the 
definitions still differ concerning the subject matter of the acts. In the WPPT definition, it is 
transmission “of sounds or of images and sounds or of the representations thereof”, while in 
the BTAP definition, the transmission is “of sounds or of images or of images and sounds or 
of the representations thereof”. Therefore, they might be regarded just as a pair of “ mutatis 
mutandis” versions. On the basis of a thorough comparison of the subject matter of the acts of 
broadcasting and communication to the public under the WPPT and BTAP definitions, it may be 
found,however,thatalthoughthedifferencesdonotraisespecificinterpretationquestions, 
there are identical elements in the two definitions which do. In both Treaties, the definition 
of “broadcasting” covers “the transmission by wireless means for public reception” of solely 
the sounds of the fixed performances and the definition of “communication to the public” 
also extends to “making [the fixed performances] audible” without making them visible at the 
sametime.Thesecommonelements–inadditiontotheabove-analyzedoverlapbetweenthe 
definitionsof“phonograms”and“audiovisualfixations” –seemtocreateafurtherpotential 
overlap between the WPPT and the BTAP. This was noted in the Basic Proposal submitted to 
the 2000 Diplomatic Conference, but a reasonable solution was outlined to eliminate it. It 
may be taken for granted that the delegations adopted the provisions on broadcasting and 
communication to the public in accordance with the understandings expressed in the following 
notes included in the Basic Proposal, even if it was not finally clarified in this way in the BTAP:
It may be observed that the definition of ‘audiovisual performances’ is broad enough to 
include performances that are exclusively aural. While this may at first seem surprising, 
it is necessary because any type of performance may be embodied in an audiovisual 
production. This arrangement is not inconsistent with the WPPT or any other treaty; the 
key is what use is made of the performance. Thus, an exclusively aural performance may 
fall under the WPPT if it is embodied by a producer in a phonogram, but it will fall under the 
proposed Instrument if the same performance is embodied as the audio portion of a film or 
other audiovisual production. The definitions of ‘broadcasting’ and ‘communication to the 
public’ likewise cover transmission of sounds alone. This too follows because, for example, 
the sound of a film may be broadcast via sound radio.642
BT-2.37. This note seems to reflect the recognition that, where exclusively the sounds of 
performances fixed in preexisting phonograms and then incorporated in an audiovisual 
fixation are broadcast or communicated to the public, in fact, the phonogram is broadcast or 
communicated to the public and, thus, such acts “fall under the WPPT”. It is another situation, 
as pointed out in the note, where the sounds incorporated by the producer of the audiovisual 
fixation into the “audio portion” (the soundtrack) are broadcast or communicated to the 
public; in that case (unless the producer has published the sounds fixed by it in the audiovisual
