Article 3
Beneficiaries of Protection
(1) Contracting Parties shall accord the protection granted under this Treaty to performers 
who are nationals of other Contracting Parties.
(2) Performers who are not nationals of one of the Contracting Parties but who have their 
habitual residence in one of them shall, for the purposes of this Treaty, be assimilated 
to nationals of that Contracting Party.
Nationals (and performers with habitual residence); Berne rather than the Rome and WPPT 
model
BT-3.1.IfonlythetextofArticle 3(1)oftheBTAPiscomparedwithArticle 3(1)oftheWPPT,it
may seem that the same basic criterion of eligibility for protection is determined: under both 
provisions, the beneficiaries are the nationals of other Contracting Parties. This is not the case 
however; it turns out from the rest of these WPPT and BTAP provisions that “nationals” are not 
defined the same in them. In the WPPT, the scope of beneficiaries is determined in a similar way 
asintheTRIPSAgreement.Article 3(1)oftheWPPTstatesthat“ContractingPartiesshallaccord 
the protection provided under this Treaty to the performers and producers of phonograms who 
arenationalsofotherContractingParties”,whichislikethefirstsentenceofArticle 1.3ofthe 
TRIPSAgreement.ThenArticle 3(2)oftheWPPT–liketherestofTRIPSArticle 1.3–providesthat 
“nationals” are to be understood as those who would meet the criteria of eligibility under the 
Rome Convention if all Contracting Parties were Contracting States thereof. This, as analyzed 
in respect of performers in the Guide to the Rome Convention in this collection, means that 
allthethreecriteriaprovidedinArticle 4oftheConventionareotherthanthenationalityof
theperformers(infact,nationalityisonlyoneofthecriteria–underArticle 5.1(a)oftheRome
Convention–oftheprotectionoftherightsinphonograms).
BT-3.2.InArticle 3oftheBTAP,incontrast,themodeloftheBerneConventionisapplied:
nationalsmentionedinparagraph (1)aresupposedtobetrulythenationalsofotherContracting
PartiesasunderArticle 3(1)(a)oftheBerneConvention(towhichperformerswithhabitual
residenceinotherContractingPartiesareassimilatedinArticle 3(2)oftheBTAPasprovidedfor 
authorsinArticle 3(2)oftheBerneConvention).
Debates at the 2000 Diplomatic Conference: preference for narrower or broader scope of 
beneficiaries
BT-3.3. In the Basic Proposal, the following arguments had been presented in favor of the points 
ofattachmentinArticle 3adoptedin2000provisionallyandthenin2012inBeijingfinally:
The criterion of nationality, supplemented by the criterion of habitual residence, is simple 
and manageable and well-adapted for a new form of international protection. This single 
criterion should also function as a better incentive for joining the proposed Instrument 
than additional criteria based on territoriality. Countries will obtain protection for their 
nationals in other Contracting Parties by joining the proposed Instrument.643
BT-3.4. At the 2000 Diplomatic Conference, there was broad support for the proposed provisions 
ofArticle 3.644 The European Community645 and its Member States and the Group of Central 
European and Baltic States646 (which, in general, supported the EC position), however, proposed 
thedeletionofparagraph (2)onhabitualresidence.Theyhadthreearguments.First,whileunder
the Berne Convention, due to the usually limited number of authors, this point of attachment

numerous, this is not the case. Second, although the application of the criterion of nationality 
might truly act as an incentive to adhere to the new instrument, this would not be necessarily 
be the case with performers’ habitual residence due to its easily changeable nature. Third, by 
granting protection on the basis of the habitual residences of performers, the application of the

broadenedtherangeofcriteriaforeligibility;butmaintaineditssupportforparagraph (2)–asa 
possiblealternativecriterion–onhabitualresidence.TheUSproposalreadasfollows:
1 Replacecurrentparagraph (1)withthefollowingnewparagraph:
“(1) Contracting Parties shall accord the protection granted under this Treaty to:
(a) performers who are nationals of other Contracting Parties;
(b) performers whose unfixed performance takes place on the territory of a 
Contracting Party;
(c) performers whose performance is fixed (other than in a phonogram) on 
the territory of another Contracting Party.”
2 Paragraph (2):SameasintheBasicProposal.647
If this proposal had been adopted, the range of points of attachment would have been 
significantlybroadened.However,neithertheEUproposaltodeleteparagraph (2)northe
alternative provisions suggested by the United States were adopted. In the spirit of compromise, 
boththeEuropeanCommunityandtheUnitedStateswithdrewtheirproposals,andArticle 3 
wasadoptedasitappearedintheBasicProposals–in2000provisionallyandthenin2012,
without amendment, finally.
Changing and multiple nationalities and habitual residences
BT-3.6. Since under the BTAP the protection of performers is granted in their performances, it 
seems obvious that, if a performer’s nationality or habitual residence changes after his or her 
performance, the nationality or habitual residence existing at the time of the performance 
still applies as a point of attachment. In the case of double or multiple nationalities or habitual 
residences, in principle, any of them may make the performer a beneficiary of protection. This 
is to be understood such that (i) only nationality of, or habitual residence in, a Contracting Party 
other than the one in which protection is claimed may serve as a point of attachment; (ii) in the 
case where a performer is a national of, or has habitual residence in, both a Contracting Party 
and a country that is not a Contracting Party, only the nationality of, or habitual residence in, 
the Contracting Party other than the one in which protection is claimed is relevant; (iii) between 
nationality and habitual residence, nationality is decisive (which means that the nationality of 
the performer of a Contracting Party is to be taken into account as a point of attachment even if 
he or she has a habitual residence in another Contracting Party).

of this Treaty.
(2) A Contracting Party shall be entitled to limit the extent and term of the protection 
accordedtonationalsofanotherContractingPartyunderparagraph (1),withrespect

Berne-type, Rome-type or TRIPS/WPPT-type national treatment?
BT-4.1. As analyzed in the Guide to the Rome Convention in this collection of guides in detail, the 
1961 Diplomatic Conference adopting the Convention understood the obligation to grant national 
treatment in a way similar to what is prescribed in the Berne Convention. In the records of the 
DiplomaticConference,itisstatedthatArticle 2(1)(a)and(2)meanthatthesametreatmentmust
begrantedtothenationalsofotherContractingStatesastoaState’sownnationals–alsofor
“rightsotherthantheminimarequiredbytheConvention”648–butnotlessthanthoseminima.
AsdiscussedinthatGuide–andalsointheGuidetotheWPPTconcerningArticle 4–intheTRIPS
negotiations another interpretation was adopted namely that the obligation to grant the same 
treatmentastonationalsonlyappliestogranttheminimarequiredbytheConvention;andthis
was called “Rome-type” national treatment, rather than “Berne-type” national treatment.
BT-4.2. As pointed out in the guides, this specific interpretation came to be accepted as 
“subsequentpracticeintheapplicationofthetreatywhichestablishestheagreementofthe 
partiesregardingitsinterpretation”asprovidedinArticle 31.3(b)oftheVCLT.
Debates on national treatment in preparation of the BTAP
BT-4.3. The first substantive discussions on the contents of the “New Instrument” took place 
atthesecond–andlast–sessionoftheCommitteeofExpertsonaProtocolConcerning
AudiovisualPerformancesinJune1998,wherethequestionofnationaltreatmentwasalready
among the most disputed issues. Two diametrically opposite proposals had been submitted to 
the Committee: one corresponding to the understanding of the delegations at the 1961 Rome 
Diplomatic Conference (a “Berne-type” national treatment) and another following the WPPT (and 
TRIPS) model which was referred to as “Rome-type” national treatment.
BT-4.4. The proposal corresponding to the original Rome model had been submitted by the 
United States:
With respect to performances for which they are protected under this Treaty as provided 
inArticle 3,performersshallenjoy,inotherContractingParties,thetreatmentthatthe
laws of such parties do now or may hereafter grant to their own nationals, as well as the 
rights specifically granted by this Treaty.649
In contrast, the European Community proposed the application mutatis mutandis oftheWPPT–
TRIPS model.650
BT-4.5. Before the second session of the Audiovisual Performances Committee, regional 
consultations had been organized in the three major groups of developing countries. Some 
membersoftheAfricanGroupsubmittedtreaty-languageproposalsforArticle 4.Thefirst 
paragraph lookedlikeaprovisionbasedontheoriginalRomemodelofrealnationaltreatment,
butthenitbecameclearfromthesecondparagraph thatitwouldnotbeobligatorytogrant
such treatment; Contracting Parties would be free to choose reciprocity:
(1)  Each Contracting Party shall accord to nationals of other Contracting Parties, in 
respect of the subject matter protected under this Protocol:
(a)  the rights specifically granted by this Protocol; and

provisionsoftheConvention–asprovidedinitsArticle 2(1)(a)and(2)–mighthavebeenan
obstacletoadoptinga“subsequentpractice”tolimitnationaltreatmenttotheminimum
obligationsundertheConvention.However,theUnitedStateshadnot–andevennowhasnot–
acceded to the Convention.

butthat“suchprotectionwouldbeinadequate[…]wheretherewereimportantdifferences

reciprocity principle with respect to certain additional rights recognized in national legislation,

(1) EachContractingPartyshallaccordtonationalscoveredinArticle 3,inrespectof

(2)  Any Contracting Party that, under its domestic law, provides for rights of 
remuneration or mandatory collective administration of exclusive rights with

rights to nationals of another Contracting Party. The Contracting Party making 
such Declaration shall provide in its national law measures that preclude collection 
for such rights in respect of audiovisual performances by nationals of any other 
Contracting Party in respect of which such Declaration is made.659
BT-4.10. The proposal constituted such a fundamental change in the US position that even the 
expression “compromise proposal” may not properly characterize it. It meant no less than the 
acceptance of the WPPT model by the United States, only in such a way that certain aspects 
of its application would have been clarified. The truly obligatory aspect of national treatment 
wouldhavebeenreducedtotheexclusiverightsprovidedintheTreaty;underitem (iii)of
paragraph (1),for"anyotherrights”,materialreciprocitywouldhavebeenapplicable.As
discussed below more in detail, what was stated in item (ii) seemed to be obvious: an exclusive 
right is usually provided in a treaty in such a way that certain exceptions to, or limitations 
of, it may be applied. If the right is limited in a certain way, it is still the right provided for 
intheTreaty,justlimitedinawayallowedbyit.Inparagraph (2),the“nocollectionwithout
distribution” principle was expressed. However, no real discussion took place on the US 
proposal.660 The SCCR proposed the convocation of the Diplomatic Conference for December in 
the same year, 2000; therefore, the proposal was left to be taken into account in the preparation 
oftheBasicProposalforthenewinstrument–aboutwhichitwasnotyetevendecidedwhether
it should be a protocol to the WPPT or a stand-alone treaty. 661
BT-4.11. The Basic Proposal prepared for the 2000 Diplomatic Conference contained two alternatives 
–AlternativesCandD662–thekeyaspectofwhich,however,didnotdiffer;neitherofthem
provided for national treatment beyond the minimum obligations under the Treaty. Alternative D 
corresponded directly to the WPPT model, while Alternative C, in essence, was a variant thereof:
Alternative C
(1)  Each Contracting Party shall accord to nationals of other Contracting Parties, in 
respect of the subject matter protected under this Treaty, the treatment it accords to 
its own nationals with regard to:
(i)  the rights specifically granted in this Treaty; and
(ii)  such additional rights as it accords to its own nationals.

“No collection without distribution” or “no collection without legal basis”?
BT-4.16. The principle of “no collection without distribution” was the very last issue discussed 
before the closure of the last session of Main Committee I in 2000 which ended with the 
adoption of a declaration that may be regarded as an agreed statement. The summary minutes 
reflect this in the following way:
423. […] The President made the following declaration: “during the work of Main Committee 
I, a proposal was made to include in the Treaty a provision stating that no Contracting Party 
should allow collection of remuneration in respect of performances of nationals of another 
Contracting Party, unless distribution of such remuneration is made to those nationals. 
Such rules have not been taken to the text of the Treaty. It is understood that there is no 
legal basis for collection of remuneration in a Contracting Party in respect of nationals of 
another Contracting Party for rights that it does not accord to those nationals. Collections in 
such circumstances would be inappropriate and without legal authority. Therefore all those 
from whom such remuneration is claimed should have legal remedies against the payment. 
Where remuneration is collected, on the basis of proper mandates, in a Contracting 
Party for rights that it accords to the nationals of another Contracting Party, but not 
distributed to them, those nationals should have legal means to ensure that they received 
the remuneration collected on their behalf.” The President asked the Committee whether 
Article 4couldbeadoptedwiththeunderstandingthatthedeclarationhehadjustmade
would be taken to the Records of the Diplomatic Conference.

BT-4.18. The clarification of the position of the European Community does not mean the denial 
of the principle that, without appropriate legal basis, no collection of remuneration is justified; 
this is evident and would be difficult to deny. The declaration seemed to rather justify it in view 
of certain domaine public-type systems applied in certain EC Member States (discussed in the 
commentsonArticle 4(2)oftheGuidetoWPPTabove).Asmentionedthere,suchasystem 
consists of collection for practically the entire world repertoire; distribution of the remuneration 
to nationals and foreigners whose rights are protected in the Contracting Party (either by 
virtue of an international treaty or on the basis of a reciprocity arrangement); and the use for 
cultural and/or social purposes of not only the non-distributable amounts (cases in which the 
rightholders cannot be identified or located) but also the amounts that are not covered by 
international obligations. If there are provisions in national laws under which such amounts 
are to be used for cultural and/or social purposes, the legal basis is not lacking; the legal basis 
is domaine public payant concerning the amounts corresponding to the performances not 
protected in the Contracting Party.
Interpretation of paragraph  (1)
BT-4.19.Article 4(1)oftheBTAPseemstobeamutatis mutandis versionofArticle 4(1)oftheWPPT:
“national treatment” only applies for the exclusive rights specifically granted in the BTAP (as in 
theWPPT)andtherighttoequitableremunerationforbroadcastingandcommunicationtothe
publicprovidedforinArticle 11(asinArticle 15oftheWPPT).Therefore,inthatrespect,thesame
comments apply as concerning the WPPT provision. That is, the term “national treatment” does not 
mean the same treatment as granted to nationals but only the obligation to grant the minimum 
level of protection prescribed in a treaty without the obligation to grant any further rights to the 
nationals of other Contracting Parties. It should also be pointed out that, where the Treaty provides 
for an exclusive right that may be limited under the Treaty to a right to remuneration, it is still an 
exclusiverightprovidedforintheTreaty,anditdoesnotlosethisbasicqualityifaContractingParty
makes use of the possibility under the Treaty of limiting it to a right to remuneration.
BT-4.20.However,althoughthetextofArticle 4(1)oftheBTAPappearstobeamutatis mutandis 
versionofArticle 4(1)oftheWPPT,insubstance,itsimpactisdifferent.Thisissobecause, 
althoughunderbothArticle 11oftheBTAPandArticle 15ofWPPT(towhichreferenceismade),
it is allowed to reduce, by “notification” (in fact, by reservation), the right of broadcasting and 
communicationtothepublic,whichmaygosofarastonotapplytherightatall,inArticle 11(1)
oftheBTAP,thisrightisanexclusiverightofauthorization,whileArticle 15(1)oftheWPPTonly
provides for it as a right to remuneration.
Interpretation of paragraph  (2)
BT-4.21.Paragraph (2)furtherconfirmsthematerialreciprocityapproachintheBTAP.Under
paragraph (1),“nationaltreatment”onlyappliestotheexclusiverightsthatmustbegrantedasa
minimumobligation;therefore,aspointedoutabove,thisisnottruenationaltreatment,but–in
668DocumentIAPV/DC/39. 

===== PAGE 338 =====
339
PART III. Guides to the three WIPO “Internet Treaties” – the WCT, the WPPT and the BTAP
respectofalevelofprotectionhigherthantheminimumobligation–itleavestheprotectionof
the nationals of other Contracting Parties to depend on the possibility of material reciprocity. In 
the case of the right of broadcasting and communication to the public, however, the minimum 
obligationisinfactnottheexclusiverightprovidedforinArticle 11(1)oftheTreatybutarightto
equitableremuneration,thelevelofprotectionofwhichmaybereducedfurtherunderArticle 4(3),
evendowntozero.Inthesecases,thequestionisnotwhetherornotaContractingPartyis
obligated to grant the higher level of protection provided to its own nationals also to the nationals 
of other Contracting Parties (which would be real national treatment) but rather whether or not 
its obligation to grant such a right must remain the same when another Contracting Party limits 
itinthewayallowedbytheTreaty.Insuchacase,itmayhardlybequestionedthatitisjustifiedto
applymaterialreciprocity.Paragraph (2)isinaccordancewiththisrecognition.
BT-4.22.Thereisstilloneaspectofparagraph (2)whichrequiresacomment.Inadditionto 
allowingthelimitationof“nationtreatment”totheextentoftheprotectionofArticle 11(1)and
11(2) of the Treaty “to those rights that its own nationals enjoy in the other Contracting Party” 
(that is, applying material reciprocity), it also allows the limitation of the term of protection for 
thesamereasons.Thisisincontrast–intwoaspects–withArticle 7(8)oftheBerneConvention 
on the principle of “comparison of terms” which reads as follows: “unless the legislation of [the 
country where protection is claimed] otherwise provides, the term [of protection] shall not 
exceed the term fixed in the country of origin of the work”.
BT-4.23. The first aspect that diverges from the Berne Convention does not seem to be 
significant; it consists in the difference that, in the case of the Berne Convention, the country 
where protection is claimed may automatically apply the shorter term provided in the country 
of origin of the works, and a contrary provision is only needed if the country is still willing 
to apply its longer term of protection, while under the BTAP, there is no such automatic 
application. A Contracting Party is allowed to limit the term in that way; if it does not make use 
of this permission, its longer term is supposed to apply. The reason this difference does not 
seem to be truly significant is that there is no obstacle to the Contracting Party’s providing for 
such limitation.
BT-4.24. The second aspect, however, may raise a specific interpretation problem, due to the a 
contrario principle of interpretation of legal texts: if a treaty reflects the position that permission 
is needed to limit an obligation, but it only limits it concerning certain specific rights, and not for 
other rights provided in the treaty, it means, in principle, that the limitation does not apply to 
theotherrights.ThisisthecaseinArticle 4(2):itisallowedtolimitthetermofprotectiononlyof 
the right of broadcasting and communication to the public; there is no such provision for other 
rights, such as the rights of reproduction, distribution, rental and (interactive) making available 
to the public.
BT-4.25. It is difficult to understand why the delegations would have wanted to apply the 
principle of “comparison of terms” for the right of broadcasting and communication to the 
public and not, for example, to the right of (interactive) making available to the public. It is 
probable that this differentiation between the rights was not intentional but just the result of 
some inadvertence which may be explained by the shortage of time caused by the protracted 
–andyetunsuccessful–negotiationsatthe2000DiplomaticConference.Duetothis,therewas
not sufficient time to eliminate such inconsistencies in the provisions (also an issue in Beijing 
with the principle “do not touch the 19 provisionally adopted articles”).
BT-4.26. The Basic Proposal submitted to the 2000 Diplomatic Conference did not yet contain 
thisaspectofthe“comparisonofterms”principle;AlternativeCofArticle 4,inwhichthetermof 
protection was mentioned, would have provided as follows:
1.  Each Contracting Party shall accord to nationals of other Contracting Parties, in 
respect of the subject matter protected under this Treaty, the treatment it accords to 
its own nationals with regard to:
(i)  the rights specifically granted in this Treaty; and
(ii)  such additional rights as it accords to its own nationals.
2.  A Contracting Party shall be entitled, in respect of nationals of any other Contracting 
Party, to limit the protection providedforinsubparagraph (ii)ofparagraph (1)tothe

Interpretation of paragraph (3)
BT-4.33.Thefirstpartofparagraph (3),withawordingchange(inclusionofthewords“toa 
Contracting Party” after the words “does not apply”) in substance is the same as (the entire text 
of)Article 4(2)oftheWPPT;thesoledifferencehereisthatintheBTAP,concerningthepossible
reservations,referenceismadenottoArticle 15(3),buttoArticle 11(3)withthefollowingtext: 
“Theobligationprovidedforinparagraph (1)doesnotapplytoaContractingPartytotheextent 
thatanotherContractingPartymakesuseofthereservationspermittedbyArticle 11(3)ofthis 
Treaty”. Therefore, in this respect, the same comments apply regarding the interpretation of 
theprovisionasintheGuidetotheWPPTaboveconcerningArticle 4(2)ofthatTreaty.Thatis,
what is involved in this case is not a reservation or a possible exception to the obligations under 
the Treaty, but a complete absence of any obligation; in such cases, the performances covered 
by said reservations made by other Contracting Parties simply remain outside the scope of 
protection, in the public domain. As also remarked there, it is another matter if a Contracting 
Party still extends protection on the basis of material reciprocity (and still another matter if it 
applies a domaine public payant system in this respect).
BT-4.34.ItisalsomentionedinthecommentsonArticle 4(2)intheGuidetotheWPPTthatthe 
sameappliestothoseperformances–fallingoutsidethescopeofprotection–whichforother 
reasons do not enjoy protection under any international treaty, which is obviously the case in 
the absence of treaty relations but also where a Contracting Party excludes performances, in 
general, or concerning the application of certain rights, from protection by using a reservation 
allowedbyatreaty.Infact,thisisrecognizedexplicitlyinthephraseinArticle 4(3)oftheBTAP: 
Theobligationprovidedforinparagraph (1)doesnotapplytoaContractingPartyto
the extent that another Contracting Party makes use of the reservations permitted by 
Article 11(3)ofthisTreaty,nordoesitapplytoaContractingParty,totheextentthatit
has made such reservation.
Article 5 
Moral Rights
(1) Independently of a performer’s economic rights, and even after the transfer of those 
rights, the performer shall, as regards his live performances or performances fixed in 
audiovisual fixations, have the right:
(i)  to claim to be identified as the performer of his performances, except where 
omission is dictated by the manner of the use of the performance; and
(ii)  to object to any distortion, mutilation or other modification of his performances 
that would be prejudicial to his reputation, taking due account of the nature of 
audiovisual fixations.

modificationwithinthemeaningofArticle 5(1)(ii).
Preparatory work in the WIPO Committees
BT-5.1. As on the majority of issues, the first substantive discussion on moral rights of 
“audiovisual performers” took place at the second session of the Committee of Experts on a 
ProtocolConcerningAudiovisualPerformancesinJune1998.Atthattime,thedeclaredobjective
–asstatedintheResolutionadoptedatthe1996DiplomaticConference–wasthepreparation
of a protocol to the WPPT. Therefore, it was not a surprise that the European Community and 
its Member States proposed the mutatis mutandis applicationofArticle 5ofWPPTonmoral
rights.676 Certain African countries proposed self-standing provisions, the effect of which, 
however, would have been the same, because they would have corresponded verbatim to the 
provisionsofArticle 5oftheWPPTandnotimplicitly. 677
BT-5.2. In contrast, the US delegation submitted a complex alternative proposal. The first 
partofArticle 5(1)ontherighttoclaimtobeidentifiedastheperformerofaperformance 
wasthesameasthecorrespondingpartofWPPTArticle 5(1)(whichwasnotdifficultforthe 
film industry to accept because traditionally all the performers are listed in their productions; 
usually the featured performers at the beginning of a film, and the others in the long credit lists 
at the end). For the provision on the right of integrity, however, the US delegation proposed 
a different language: “to object to any distortion, mutilation, or other modification of his or 
her performance that would be seriously prejudicial to the performer’s reputation, where such 
modification is not part of the normal exploitation of an audiovisual work by the producer of the 
work or its successors in interest, pursuant to the exercise of rights of authorization acquired by the 
producer in the performance”.678 At the session of the Committee, the US delegation explained 
thatthewords“pursuanttotheexerciseofrightsofauthorizationacquiredbytheproducer
in the performance” were aimed just to make it clear that the uses covered by a license are 
supposed to be allowed; it was not about a general waiver of moral rights. According to the 
explanation, the word “seriously” had been inserted before “prejudicial” because the audiovisual 
sector operated differently from the audio sector; the proposal was intended to recognize that 
adaptations are a routine part of making an audiovisual work. The word “other” before the 
words “modification of his or her performance” followed the texts of the Berne Convention 
and the WPPT and was deemed necessary because, according to the delegation, the terms 
“distortion” and “mutilation” also imply modifications. 679

BT-5.3. Neither of these diametrically opposite proposals seemed to be suitable for consensus. 
With the intention of working out a possible compromise, certain members of GRULAC submitted 
a proposal to the second session of the Audiovisual Performers Committee. It also consisted in a 
mutatis mutandis versionofArticle 5oftheWPPTasproposedbycertainmembersoftheAfrican
Group, but a new phrase was added at the end of the provision on the right of integrity: “and 
to object to any distortion, mutilation or other modification of his performances that would be 
prejudicial to his reputation, on the understanding, however, that the producer of the audiovisual 
fixation may make modifications necessary to facilitate the normal exploitations of the fixations”.680 
The reactions to the various proposals included support, opposition and expression of interest 
with some hesitation,681butnosubstantialprogresswasmade.JukkaLiedessimplyconcluded
that “the issue could be considered further in the next generation of working documents”.682
BT-5.4. The debates continued at the SCCR sessions. Solution was sought along the line 
of the GRULAC proposal to regulate the right of integrity on the basis of the principle of 
permitting “normal exploitation” of audiovisual works. Two countries with big film industries 
made proposals along those lines. India’s proposal on the right of integrity submitted to 
the second session of the SCCR held in May 1999 read as follows: “the right to object to any 
distortion, mutilation or other modification of his performance which would be prejudicial 
to his reputation, provided that a modification considered necessary by the producer of the 
audiovisual fixation for the normal exploitation of such fixation through any medium shall not 
be deemed to be prejudicial to the reputation of the performer”. 683 
BT-5.5. The US proposal presented for the third session of the SCCR, held in November 1999, 
essentially repeated the text that had already been introduced 18 months earlier before the 
CommitteeofExpertsonAudiovisualWorks(documentAP/CE/2/7,Annex,paragraph 10(f)), 
withoutsubstantivemodification.Itconsistedof(i)theinsertioninArticle 5(1)oftheadverb 
“seriously” before the words “prejudicial to the performer’s reputation”, (ii) the addition of a new 
sentence to indicate what is not to be considered “seriously prejudicial” and (iii) the inclusion of 
anewparagraph (4)todeterminewhatis“normalexploitation”.Theadditionalsentenceandthe
newparagraph readasfollows:
[…] Modifications consistent with the normal exploitation of an audiovisual work 
undertaken by the producer of the work or the producer’s successors in interest, pursuant 
totheexerciseofrightsofauthorizationacquiredbytheproducerintheperformance,
shall not be considered seriously prejudicial to the performer’s reputation […]
[…] The “normal exploitation of an audiovisual work” shall include the use of new or 
changed technology, media, formats, and/or methods of distribution, dissemination, 
making available or communication to the public. A performer shall give reasonable 
consideration to the interests of the other performers in the work, the writers of 
scenarios, dialogues or musical works created for the work, and the principal director 
of the work when seeking to exercise the above described rights with respect to 
such work.684
Although the US proposal largely reiterated an earlier approach rather than introducing new 
elements, it was perceived as an attempt to move towards a compromise, but it still did not 
seem to be acceptable by many countries, in particular by the European Community and 
its Member States. It still would have meant the acceptance of prejudice to the performer's 
reputation and would have only offered protection against seriously prejudicial acts which were 
to be determined in a complex manner.
At the 2000 Diplomatic Conference; “provisional” adoption of Article 5 with an agreed statement

BT-5.7. In the notes added to these provisions, reference was made to the various proposals 
made during the preparatory stages and then the reasons for the proposed text were outlined 
in this way:
[I]t should be emphasized that alteration or modification, such as abridgement, condensing,  
editing or dubbing, per se, does not concern moral rights. The same goes for new 
or changed technology, media, formats and methods of distribution, etc.. […] [T]he 
determination as to whether an act constitutes a violation of this moral right turns on 
whether the modification is objectively prejudicial to the performer’s reputation. This 
judgment should be made on objective criteria from the point of view of a reasonable viewer 
with experience in the pertinent category of audiovisual productions. Under standard 
interpretations of moral rights, a modification would not be considered a violation unless 
the prejudice were meaningful or substantial. For this reason it does not appear necessary 
toqualifytherequiredprejudiceintheArticle bysuchtermsas‘serious’or‘substantial.’[…]
‘Normal exploitation’ or standard industry practice, as such, therefore falls outside of the 
scope of moral rights.686 
BT-5.8.Theabove-quotedlastsentenceofthenotestothedraftArticle 5referredto“standard 
industry practice” as an alternative to “normal exploitation”. This was a significant conceptual 
change because concentrating only or mainly on the normal exploitation of audiovisual works 
–morerelevantforeconomicrights(andaconceptwithspecificmeaningusedinthesecond
condition of the three-step test for the applicability of exceptions to and limitations of those 
rights)–didnotseemtobetrulyfittingintheprovisionsontheprotectionofmoralinterestsof 
performers. “Standard industry practices” was a more appropriate concept determined by the 
specific nature of audiovisual productions; it became the key criterion in the text finally adopted.
BT-5.9. It was a significant step towards a possible consensus that the United States submitted 
a proposal in which there was no limitation of the protection of the right of integrity to serious 
prejudice to the performer's reputation and the criterion had been changed from “normal 
exploitation” to “customary practice”. The proposal consisted of the amendment of the second 
sentenceofArticle 5(1)(ii)basedonthe“customarypractice”approachandtheinsertionofan 
agreed statement defining in detail what is to be considered such practice:
I.Article 5(1)(ii)toread:
(ii)  to object to any distortion, mutilation or other modification of his performances that 
would be prejudicial to his reputation. Modifications of a performance consistent 
with customary practices in the course of a use authorized by the performer shall not 
be considered prejudicial to the performer’s reputation.
II.AgreedStatementconcerningArticle 5:
It is generally understood that modifications of any protected subject matter, including 
performances, which are “consistent with customary practices,” do not violate moral 
rights under treaties protecting any such works or performances. Moral rights are

in a meaningful or substantial way.
Customary practices in modifying a performance in an audiovisual work include practices 
such as editing, compression, dubbing, changes by censorship or in response to local 
sensibilities, and the mere use of new or changed technology, media, formats or methods 
of distribution.
Thereferencetothese“customarypractices”inArticle 5(1)(ii)isincludedinthis
instrument as a confirmation because such modifications are standard practice in the 
audiovisual industry.687
Although there were certain elements of this proposal that still did not have the chance to 
beacceptedbytheotherdelegations–inparticular,thatinthefirstparagraph oftheagreed
statement reference was made to treaties protecting audiovisual works or performances , which 
would also have implied the interpretation of the provisions of the Berne Convention, the WCT 
andtheWPPTonmoralrights(excludedintheTreatyadoptedbytheprovisionofArticle 1)–it
turned out to be a decisive step towards reaching consensus.
BT-5.10. The adoption of a compromise text was facilitated by the proposals made by Peru 
supported by various Latin American and Caribbean countries and by the European Community, 
which no longer insisted on the mere mutatis mutandis applicationoftheprovisionsofArticle 5
of the WPPT. Although the Peruvian proposal reverted to the use of the (normal) exploitation 
criterion,itwentinthesamedirectionastheUSproposal.Itconsistedofanewparagraph (2)to
beincludedafterparagraph (1):“Modificationsthataremadebytheproducerandarenecessary
for the exploitation of the audiovisual fixation, such as abridgement, condensing, editing or 
dubbing, shall not be considered modifications within the meaning of the forgoing paragraph”.688
BT-5.11.TheEuropeanCommunityproposedanagreedstatementconcerningArticle 5toread
as follows:
Itisunderstoodthatthemodificationsofanaudiovisualfixation,whicharerequiredin
the course of, or the preparation for, a use authorized by the performer, which form part 
of the exploitation of the performance as intended by the parties, such as formatting, 
editing, or the use of new or changed technology or media, and which are neither 
substantially nor objectively prejudicial to the performer’s reputation, do not concern the 
performer’s moral rights.689
Although in the proposed statement “exploitation” was also mentioned, it was in a different 
context, with the focus on the uses authorized by the performer and intended by the parties. 
The statement also included examples of such uses. It did not seem, however, to be clear how 
the alternative (but necessarily overlapping) criteria of no “substantially or objectively prejudicial 
[exploitation]” could have been jointly interpreted and applied.
BT-5.12.ThefinalversionofArticle 5whichwasthenapprovedbyMainCommitteeIand
adoptedbythePlenary–asthevariousotherdisputedprovisions–hadbeenagreeduponinthe
frameworkofinformalconsultations.Inthetextofparagraph (1)(ii)ontherightofintegrity,in
the final version neither the criterion of “normal exploitation” nor that of “customary practices” 
wasadopted,butanevenmoregeneral–andthereforemoresuitable–criterion:“takingdue
account of the nature of audiovisual fixations”. In the agreed statement, reference is made to 
the normal course of exploitation, but it is linked to those kinds of conditions that are included 
in the agreed statement proposed by the European Community.

consistsinthedivisionofparagraph (1)–whichintheWPPTisnotdividedinthisway–afterthe
introductory lines (“Independently of a performer’s economic rights, and even after the transfer 
of those rights, the performer shall, as regards his live performances or performances fixed in 
audiovisual fixations, have the right”) into subparagraphs (i) and (ii).
BT-5.14.Subparagraph (i),likethefirstpartofArticle 5(1)oftheWPPT,isontheright“toclaim
to be identified as the performer of his performances, except where omission is dictated by the 
manneroftheuseoftheperformance”.Subparagraph (ii),ontherightofintegrity,alsobegins
inthesamewayasthesecondpartofWPPTArticle 5(1):“toobjecttoanydistortion,mutilation 
or other modification of his performances that would be prejudicial to his reputation”. Then the 
substantivechangefollows,becausesubparagraph (ii)continuesandends,inaccordancewith 
the agreement reached at the informal consultations in 2000 as follows: “taking due account of 
the nature of audiovisual fixations”.
BT-5.15.Article 5(2)and(3)oftheBTAPonpost mortem protection and on the means of redress, 
respectively,areverbatimthesameasArticle 5(2)and(3)oftheWPPT.
BT-5.16. The most substantive adaptation of the right of integrity to the conditions of the 
audiovisual industry, however, cannot be found in the text of the Article, but in an agreed 
statement. The first sentence of the statement begins by stressing that its content is without 
prejudicetoanyothertreaty.Therestoftheagreedstatement–alongthelinesoftheagreed
statementproposedbytheEuropeanCommunitybutinasomewhatmoredetailedmanner–
clarifies, including through typical examples, what may be regarded as not conflicting with the 
right of integrity “taking due account of the nature of audiovisual fixations”. In contrast, the last 
twosentencesaremorelikelytosatisfytherequirementofthefilmindustry;thesemadethe 
overall regulation of moral rights acceptable to the US delegation.
Article 6
Economic Rights of Performers in their Unfixed Performances
Performers shall enjoy the exclusive right of authorizing, as regards their performances:
(i)  the broadcasting and communication to the public of their unfixed performances 
except where the performance is already a broadcast performance; and
(ii)  the fixation of their unfixed performances.
Same text as in Article 6 of the WPPT
BT-6.1.Inthepreparatorywork,therewasnorealdebateonArticle 6.Ithadbeenfound
indispensable to provide for such rights in unfixed performances (according to the synonym 
usedintheRomeConvention“liveperformances”)asinArticle 7.1(a)and(b)oftheRome
Convention,Article 14.1oftheTRIPSAgreementandArticle 6oftheWPPT.Theoriginalideawas
toincludethesameprovisionsasinArticle 6oftheWPPTwithoutchangingsubparagraph (i)and
onlyreplacingtheword“fixation”insubparagraph (ii)with“audiovisualfixation”.IntheBasic
Proposalsubmittedtothe2000DiplomaticConference,Article 6appearedinthisway.Atthe
2000 Diplomatic Conference, however, the adjective “audiovisual” was dropped and, thus, the text 
ofArticle 6hasbecomethesameasintheWPPT,andnotonlyinsubparagraph (i)ontheright
ofbroadcastingandcommunicationtothepublicbutalsoinsubparagraph (ii)ontherightof
fixation–but,inthecaseofthelatter,onlythetext;itsmeaningandcoveragediffer(seebelow).

===== PAGE 346 =====
347
PART III. Guides to the three WIPO “Internet Treaties” – the WCT, the WPPT and the BTAP
Right of broadcasting and communication to the public of unfixed performances: same text 
and same meaning as in the WPPT
BT-6.2.Subparagraph (i)oftheArticle remainedthesameduringthepreparatorywork; 
it was included in the Basic Proposal of the 2000 Diplomatic Conference and was adopted 
provisionally without any debate, and thus it also became part of the BTAP. Not only the text of 
thesubparagraph isthesameinthecontextoftheWPPTandtheBTAP,butalsoitsmeaning –
because“broadcasting”and“communicationtothepublic”aredefined,inArticle 2(f)and(g) 
oftheWPPTandArticle 2(c)and(d)oftheBTAP,respectively,inthesamewaytocoverboth
the aural and the visual elements of performances. Therefore, although there is an overlap 
regarding the scope of protection of the two Treaties, it does not create any problem in itself. 
Irrespective of which of the two Treaties a Contracting Party adheres to, it must provide such a 
rightforallkindsofunfixed–live–performances.
Right of fixation – same text as in the WPPT with different meaning and an overlap
BT-6.3.Asmentionedabove,therightoffixationprovidedinsubparagraph (ii),intheBasic 
Proposal, was to be applied only to audiovisual fixations of performances, that is, not to the 
fixation of the sounds alone. The notes added to the provision reflected the understanding 
thatArticle 6(ii)oftheWPPTonlycoversauralfixation. 690 As discussed in the Guide to the 
WPPT above, this is so because, although the provision of the WPPT is only about the right 
of performers to authorize “the fixation of their unfixed performances” (which, thus, seems 
tomeananysortoffixations,bothauralandaudiovisual),beforethat–inArticle 2(c)ofthe
WPPT–“fixation”isdefinedexclusivelyas“embodimentofsounds,oroftherepresentations 
thereof”.Thenotesinthe2000BasicProposalreferalsotoArticle 7.1(b)oftheRomeConvention,
wherethedefinition–andconsequentlytheright–offixationarenotlimitedinsuchaway;they
extend to both the aural and the visual aspects of the performances. According to the notes, 
thesameoverallcoverageoftherightoffixationasintheRomeConventioncould–andshould
–havebeenachievedthroughthecombinedprovisionsoftheWPPTandtheBTAP,and,forthis,
the latter would have had to provide a right to authorize “audiovisual fixation”.
BT-6.4.Ascanbeseenabove,intheadoptedtextofArticle 6(ii)oftheBTAP,contrarytothe
Basic Proposal, the adjective “audiovisual” does not appear; thus, the provision is verbatim the 
sameasinArticle 6(ii)oftheWPPT.IncontrastwiththeWPPT,thereisnoseparatedefinition
of “fixation” in the BTAP to reduce the right of fixation to certain aspects of the performances 
(in the BTAP, it certainly could have consisted in limiting it to audiovisual fixations to mirror the 
definitionintheWPPTlimitedtofixationsofsounds).Consequently,inspiteofthesametextof
subparagraph (ii),therightoffixation,intheWPPT,appliesonlytothefixationofsounds,while
in the BTAP, it applies to any fixation, audiovisual or of sounds. This means two things: first, 
differentmeaningandcoverage;and–inrespectoffixationsofsounds–anoverlap.
BT-6.5. It seems, however, that there is no substantive problem with the different meaning and 
coverage of the definition and the right of fixation, or with the overlap between the provisions. 
If there is a problem concerning the coverage of the right, it might be due to its limited scope 
in the WPPT. The correction in the BTAP seemed to be justified. After all, the main objective of 
the right of fixation is protection against illegal recording of performances (“bootlegging”); 
therefore, it would be difficult to explain why there is protection against unauthorized fixation 
of sounds of the performances only, and no protection against the fixation of the same, if the 
images of the performances are also recorded along with the sounds without authorization. 
Nevertheless, when the issue of the coverage of the right was discussed in the session of Main 
Committee I, there was still both support for 691 and opposition to, or at least hesitation about, 692 
the deletion of the adjective “audiovisual”. It was during the informal consultations that the 
690 The note read as follows:

BT-6.6. The overlap concerning the right of fixation exists where only the sounds of a 
performancearefixed.TheChairmanofMainCommitteeI,JukkaLiedes,gavethefollowing 
assessmentofthedeletionoftheadjective“audiovisual”fromthetextofArticle 6(ii):“Thismight 

not cause any harm and could remain as an understanding”.693 This is correct, including in view 
ofthenon-derogationrulesinArticle 1oftheBTAP,whicharesuitabletosettlethepossible
questionsofrelationshipbetweentheseTreatiesiftheyshouldstillemerge.
Article 7
Right of Reproduction
Performers shall enjoy the exclusive right of authorizing the direct or indirect reproduction of 
their performances fixed in audiovisual fixations, in any manner or form.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 7:Thereproductionright,assetoutinArticle 7,andthe
exceptionspermittedthereunderthroughArticle 13,fullyapplyinthedigitalenvironment,
in particular to the use of performances in digital form. It is understood that the storage of 
a protected performance in digital form in an electronic medium constitutes a reproduction 
within the meaning of this Article.
Same provision, mutatis mutandis, as in Article 7 of the WPPT
BT-7.1.Article 7ontherightofreproductionwasoneofthemostproblem-freeprovisionsduring
the preparatory work. In the Basic Proposal, it was presented as such and it was adopted as 
Article 7oftheBTAPwithoutanyrealsubstantivedebate.Althoughitistruethat,atthe2000 
DiplomaticConference,therewasaproposaltoamendthetextofArticle 7presentedinthe
Basic Proposal, it did not concern the act of reproduction but the subject matter of the act; and 
the proposal for the amendment was not adopted. (As discussed above, the Swiss delegation 
proposed the replacement of the term “audiovisual fixations” with the term “fixations that are 
not phonograms”.)
Confirmation of the agreed statement in the WPPT (and in the WCT) on storage of works in 
electronic medium
BT-7.2.TheagreedstatementconcerningArticle 7asadoptedintheBTAPismutatis mutandis 
thesameasintheWPPT–and,infact,asregardperformances,itisverbatimthesamesince,
in both versions, reference is made in general to “performances”; the agreed statement in the 
WPPT only differs because it also covers phonograms.
BT-7.3. The notes in the Basic Proposal added to the draft agreed statement refer to the fact that 
“the Diplomatic Conference adopted an agreed statement according to which the reproduction 
right,assetforthinArticles 7and11oftheWPPT,fullyappliesinthedigitalenvironment,andin
particular to the use of performances and phonograms in digital form” and simply add that “the 
agreedstatementreferredtoaboveisrelevantfortheconsiderationofArticles 7and13ofthe
proposed Instrument”. 694 The notes express no doubt about the validity of the agreed statement 
adopted in 1996.
693 Ibid.,para.278.Itistobenotedthattheoverlapisnotthesamewithallthreetreaties.Asmentioned,withArticle 6(ii) 

Article 8
Right of Distribution
(1) Performers shall enjoy the exclusive right of authorizing the making available to the 
public of the original and copies of their performances fixed in audiovisual fixations 
through sale or other transfer of ownership.
(2) Nothing in this Treaty shall affect the freedom of Contracting Parties to determine 
theconditions,ifany,underwhichtheexhaustionoftherightinparagraph (1)applies
after the first sale or other transfer of ownership of the original or a copy of the fixed 
performance with the authorization of the performer.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticles 8and9:AsusedintheseArticles,theexpression“original
and copies”, being subject to the right of distribution and the right of rental under the said 
Articles, refers exclusively to fixed copies that can be put into circulation as tangible objects.
Same provision, mutatis mutandis, as in Article 8 of the WPPT (and in Article 6 of the WCT)
BT-8.1.Article 8ontherightofdistribution–similartoArticle 7ontherightofreproduction–was
a problem-free provision during the preparatory work. In the 2000 Basic Proposal, it was proposed 
in this way, and it was adopted without any substantive debate. There is only a mutatis mutandis 
differenceincomparisonwithArticle 8oftheWPPT(andArticle 6oftheWCT);itreplacesthe
term “performances fixed in phonograms” appearing in the WPPT with the term “performances 
fixedinaudiovisualfixations”.Therefore,thecommentsmadeintheGuidetotheWCTabove–to
whichreferenceismadeintheGuidetotheWPPT–applyheretoo.Therearetwokeyissueswhich
shouldbementioned:thequestionofexhaustionoftheright,andtherelationshipoftherightof
distribution with the right of (interactive) making available to the public.
Exhaustion of the right of distribution
BT-8.2. In the course of the preparatory work leading to the 1996 Diplomatic Conference and at 
the Conference itself, the issue of the right of distribution was mainly addressed in connection 
with copyright, because there is a provision on the right of distribution in the Berne Convention 
but not in the Rome Convention. It emerged in connection with the “digital agenda” since it 
seemed to be possible to characterize the making available of copies by reproduction through 
online transmissions as distribution of copies. It was taken into account as a possible legal 
characterization of certain forms of interactive making available of works and, as such, also for 
the “umbrella solution” described in the Guide to the WCT above. It was, however, important to 
clarify that only legal characterization was involved which did not change the real nature of the 
acts covered by the rights of (interactive) making available. For this, it was necessary to analyze 
and regulate the right of distribution in the field where, in contrast, it was in fact applicable; 
namely in respect of the making available to the public of tangible copies, in connection with 
whichmainlythequestionofexhaustionoftherightwastobeaddressed.
BT-8.3. In the Guide to the Berne Convention and, with reference to it, in the Guide to the WCT 
above,itispointedoutthatBerneArticles 14and14bis may be interpreted as providing for 
a right of first distribution (exhausting with the first sale of copies, because it only applies to 
putting audiovisual works into circulation for the first time). Furthermore, it is noted that such a 
right of first distribution may also be deduced from the right of reproduction and, therefore, it 
seems to be a defensible position that the right may be recognized not only for cinematographic 
works(inrespectofwhich,Article 14and14bis contain explicit provisions), but implicitly also for 
other categories of works. However, the theory of implicit recognition of a right of distribution 
did not receive sufficient support during the preparatory work. Therefore, it was found to be 
necessary to explicitly recognize such a right in the WCT and likewise in the WPPT; the provision 
in the BTAP corresponds to this mutatis mutandis.
BT-8.4.Article 6(2)oftheWCT,Article 8(2)oftheWPPTandArticle 8(2)oftheBTAPleaveittothe
Contracting Parties to determine the conditions of the exhaustion of the right of distribution “after 
the first sale or other transfer of ownership of the original or a copy” of the work, phonogram 
or performance, respectively. This may mean territorial exhaustion (which implicitly means a

===== PAGE 349 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
350 right of importation), international exhaustion (allowing free parallel import) and, in principle, no 
exhaustion(which,however,onlyexistsinprinciple;thequestionoftheexhaustioneffectofthe
first sale of copies is in general settled in national laws). However, as mentioned above, the real 
importance of the regulation of the application of the right of distribution in the three “Internet 
Treaties” is its relationship with the right of (interactive) making available to the public.
The role of the agreed statement; no “online exhaustion”
BT-8.5. The agreed statement clarifies that the right of distribution applies only to the making 
available to the public of tangible copies as objects. The same is true concerning the right of 
rental, to which the agreed statement refers; furthermore, as discussed in the Guide to the 
WCTaboveandmentionedinthecommentsonArticle 9below,itcanapplytoapossibleright
of lending where this is granted. This excludes the application of the provisions on the right of 
distribution (as well as the right of rental and lending) to making copies available online (for 
downloading), because those copies are not tangible; they are not objects.
Article 9
Right of Rental
(1) Performers shall enjoy the exclusive right of authorizing the commercial rental to the 
public of the original and copies of their performances fixed in audiovisual fixations as 
determined in the national law of Contracting Parties, even after distribution of them 
by, or pursuant to, authorization by the performer.
(2) ContractingPartiesareexemptfromtheobligationofparagraph (1)unlessthe
commercial rental has led to widespread copying of such fixations materially impairing 
the exclusive right of reproduction of performers.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticles 8and9:AsusedintheseArticles,theexpression“original
and copies”, being subject to the right of distribution and the right of rental under the said 
Articles, refers exclusively to fixed copies that can be put into circulation as tangible objects.
Decreasing relevance of rental
BT-9.1.AsdiscussedinthecommentsonArticle 7intheGuidetotheWCT,themigrationfrom
physical to intangible copies has led to the decline not only of distribution by sales but also 
of rental of copies of films in the sense in which the right of rental is provided in the WCT, 
theWPPTandtheBTAP–thatis,asclarifiedintheagreedstatement,onlyapplicabletothe
making available of tangible copies. Nevertheless, although this form of exploitation is losing 
significance,ithasnotdisappearedyetcompletely;therefore,theprovisionsofArticle 9ofthe 
BTAP still are analyzed below.
No definition of “rental”
BT-9.2.Asalsomentioned,inthecommentsonArticle 7intheGuidetotheWCT,nodefinition
is provided either in the TRIPS Agreement or in the WIPO “Internet Treaties” of “rental” or 
“commercialrental”(thelattertermusedinArticles 11and14.4oftheTRIPSAgreement).The
expression “commercial rental”usedinArticles 11and14.4oftheTRIPSAgreementitwasadopted
fromit,first,intoArticle 7oftheWCTandArticles 9and13oftheWPPTandthenalsointoArticle 9
of the BTAP. The adjective “commercial” is suitable to differentiate rental from lending, but it may 
also be understood in such a way that “rental” is by definition for commercial “consideration”. 
Double orientation of the BTAP and the right of rental
BT-9.3. It is not only the adjective “commercial” that the WIPO “Internet Treaties” have inherited 
from the TRIPS Agreement provisions on the rights of rental. As is outlined in the Introduction 
of this Part III on the “Internet Treaties”, it served as a kind of guiding principle during the 
preparatory work of the WCT and the WPPT that no agreement reached in the framework of the 
Uruguay Round of negotiations should be altered. Therefore, although attempts were made at 
the 1996 Diplomatic Conference to recognize a general right of rental extending to all categories

===== PAGE 350 =====
351
PART III. Guides to the three WIPO “Internet Treaties” – the WCT, the WPPT and the BTAP
of works, these attempts ultimately failed; it was accepted during the informal consultations 
that the scope and conditions of the protection of the right of rental under the two new Treaties 
should be the same as under the relevant provisions of the TRIPS Agreement. This principle was 
also taken into account in the preparatory work of the BTAP.
BT-9.4.Inaccordancewiththisprinciple,thecategoriesofworksforwhich–asaminimum
obligation–arightofrentalistobegrantedundertheWCTarethesameasintheTRIPS
Agreement:(i)computerprograms(firstsentenceofArticle 11intheTRIPSAgreement–
Article 7(1)(i)intheWCT);cinematographicworks(firstsentenceofArticle 11intheTRIPS
Agreement–Article 7(1)(ii)intheWCT);and(iii)“worksembodiedinphonograms,asdetermined
inthenationallaw”(firstsentenceofArticle 14.4intheTRIPSAgreement–Article 7(1)(iii)in
the WCT). Concerning all three categories, the WCT contains the same provisions on certain 
limitations and conditions as those provided for in the TRIPS Agreement. Of these, in the context 
of the BTAP, only those are relevant that concern cinematographic (and other audiovisual) works. 
Inthiscase,thelimitationsarequitesubstantial:therentalrightonlyappliesifthecommercial
rental has led to widespread copying of such works materially impairing the exclusive right of 
reproduction(secondsentenceofArticle 11intheTRIPSAgreement–Article 7(2)(ii)intheWCT).
BT-9.5. In the preparatory work of the BTAP, there was some hesitation between two possible 
orientations. Since “audiovisual performers” were contributors to audiovisual works, it was 
necessary to take into account the status of such works as well as of the co-authors thereof. 
At the same time, the status of performers whose performances are fixed in phonograms was 
alsoajustifieddirectionoforientation–althoughthetheoryaccordingtowhichtherights 
of “audiovisual performers” should be directly assimilated to the rights provided in the WPPT 
did not seem to be well-founded due to the significant differences between the ways in which 
phonograms and audiovisual works are produced and the performers’ role in these productions. 
In principle, not only the WPPT provisions on a possible right of rental of performers whose 
performancesarefixedinphonogramswastobeconsideredasamodel,but–inparallel–also
such a possible right of authors the performances of whose works are recorded in phonograms, 
aswellastherightofrentalofproducersofphonogramsclearlyprovidedinArticle 13(1)ofthe
WPPT,althoughwitha“grandfathering”clauseinArticle 13(2)inaccordancewithArticle 14.4of
the TRIPS Agreement.
BT-9.6. In the Basic Proposal submitted to the 2000 Diplomatic Conference, the audiovisual 
works orientation was chosen rather than the assimilation to the status of performers whose 
performances are fixed in phonograms. In that stage, however, this was manifested only in the 
choiceoftheimpairmenttestinArticle 7(2)oftheWCTratherthanthetestinArticle 9(2)ofthe 
WPPT.DraftArticle 9readasfollows:
Performers shall enjoy the exclusive right of authorizing the commercial rental to the 
public of the original and copies of their performances fixed in audiovisual fixations even 
after distribution of them by, or pursuant to, authorization by the performer.
ContractingPartiesareexemptfromtheobligationofparagraph (1)unlessthe
commercial rental has led to widespread copying of such fixations materially impairing the 
exclusive right of reproduction of performers.695
Although the notes state that “[t]heoperativeelementsofparagraph (1)oftheproposed
Article 9areidenticaltotheelementsofthecorrespondingprovisionoftheWPPT”, 696 
paragraph (1)wasnottrulyidenticalanditwasnotjustamutatis mutandis versionofArticle 9of
theWPPT.Thesubjectmatterwasdifferent–“originalandcopiesof[…]performancesfixedin
audiovisual fixations” instead of “original and copies of […] performances fixed in phonograms” 
–butthetwoprovisionsalsodifferedinsubstanceinthatthephrase“asdeterminedinthe
national law of Contracting Parties” appearing in the WPPT version was missing.

If exclusive rental rights were provided with no impairment test to performers, it would 
have the effect of rewriting the TRIPS Agreement. It would mean granting to performers 
in respect of cinematographic works higher rights than those granted to authors. The 
impairment test did not occur in the context of the grandfathering clause. There was a 
grandfathering clause with respect to rental rights regarding sound recordings in the 
TRIPS Agreement, but it was intended only to deal with the situation of a very small 
number of countries which had already enacted the rights of remuneration with respect to 
rental rights before the TRIPS Agreement. It had no connection with the impairment test 
and it concerned sound recordings and not audiovisual works.705
BT-9.12. The US delegation made the same point as was stressed in the Basic Proposal: it is true 
that it would be a discrimination to provide different norms to regulate the rights of creators in 
thesameorsimilarpositions,butinthiscase–asinseveralothercases–thisprinciplejustified
similar or even the same norms for “audiovisual performers” as for “audiovisual authors” whose 
contributions usually merge inseparably in the complex audiovisual productions. 
BT-9.13.Finally,thedelegationsthatopposedthetextofparagraph (2)aspresentedintheBasic
Proposalshowedflexibility,andtheparagraph wasadoptedprovisionally,alongwiththeagreed 
statement, in 2000. It was then also adopted, in accordance with the deal serving as the basis for 
the re-convocation of the Diplomatic Conference, in 2012, as proposed, and as now it appears, in 
t he B TA P.
Interpretation of the term “as determined in the national law of Contracting Parties”
BT-9.14. The origin of the phrase “as determined in the national law of Contracting Parties” is a 
similarexpressioninthefirstsentenceofArticle 14.4oftheTRIPSAgreement,whichreadsas
follows:“TheprovisionsofArticle [ontherentalright]inrespectofcomputerprogramsshall
apply mutatis mutandis to producers of phonograms and any other right holders in phonograms as 
determined in a Member’s law”. (Emphasis added.) As discussed in the Guide to the WPPT above, 
the expression “right holders in phonograms” is not sufficiently clear. Normally it is intended to 
mean that the holders of the rights in phonograms are the producers of the phonograms. When 
performances of works are fixed in phonograms, the authors of those works and the performers 
of those performances have rights in their works and in their performances, respectively, and not 
in the phonograms. Nevertheless, since reference is made to rightholders other than producers 
of phonograms, there is good reason to interpret the expression as referring, even if in a peculiar 
way, to the rightholders of works and performances embodied in phonograms.
BT-9.15. The words “as determined in a Member’s law” in the TRIPS Agreement may be 
interpreted as a reference to the optional nature of the extension of the right of rental to such 
other rightholders. At the 1996 Diplomatic Conference, where it was a rigidly followed principle 
that the level of protection agreed upon in the TRIPS Agreement must not be renegotiated, it was 
understood in that way. The phrase has been included, in accordance with this understanding, 
bothinArticle 7(2)(ii)oftheWCTandinArticle 9(1)oftheWPPTontherentalrightofauthorsand
performers whose works and performances, respectively, are embodied in phonograms.
BT-9.16.TherightofrentalinArticle 9oftheBTAPisastand-alonerightof“audiovisual
performers” and, therefore, there did not seem to be any reason to use the same kind of 
ambiguouslanguageasinArticle 14.4oftheTRIPSAgreementand,followingit,inArticle 7(2)(ii)  
oftheWCTandArticle 9(1)oftheWPPT.Noreasonsweregivenbythedelegationswho
proposed the inclusion of the phrase other than that it was needed for an exact and complete 
assimilationtoArticle 9(1)oftheWPPT.Itispossiblethatthedelegationsdidnotreallyintend
to transform the provision into an optional one, but the importation of the what seems 
unnecessary language of “creative ambiguity” may have such an effect.
705 Ibid., para. 36.

354 “Rental” and “lending” through online transmission = (interactive) making available to the public
BT-9.17. Although the expression “online rental” is used sometimes to refer to the making 
available of intangible copies against remuneration for a limited time, it is not an act of rental 
under the WIPO Treaties, but an act of (interactive) making available to the public, because 
it corresponds to the description of such acts: “making available to the public of [works; 
performances fixed in phonograms; phonograms; under the BTAP: performances fixed in 
audiovisual fixations] in such a way that members of the public may access them from a place 
and at a time individually chosen by them”. In such a case, the purpose of interactive access is to 
allowacopytobeobtainedthroughonlinetransmissionforalimitedtime–asdeterminedbya
digitalrightsmanagementsystem–forpayment.
BT-9.18.Fortherightoflending–themakingavailableoftangiblecopiesforalimitedtime
withoutpaymentofremuneration–whichisnotcoveredbytheWIPOTreaties,thesame
applies, because the act of making available of copies is the same; what is referred to as “online 
lending”, in the case of intangible copies, is not lending but interactive making available to the 
public,asdiscussedintheGuidetotheWCTaboveconcerningArticle 7ontherightofrental.
Article 10
Right of Making Available of Fixed Performances
Performers shall enjoy the exclusive right of authorizing the making available to the public of 
their performances fixed in audiovisual fixations, by wire or wireless means, in such a way that 
members of the public may access them from a place and at a time individually chosen by them.
Mutatis mutandis version of the relevant provisions of the WPPT (and the WCT)
BT-10.1.Article 10oftheBTAPisamutatis mutandis versionofArticle 10oftheWPPT.While
in the course of the preparatory work of the WCT and the WPPT, the right of (interactive) 
makingavailabletothepublicwasadopted–onthebasisofthe“umbrellasolution”which
isdescribedindetailintheGuidetotheWCTabove–afteralongandintensivedebate,to
solveamajordeadlock,theadoptionofArticle 10oftheBTAPtookplacewithoutanyreal
debate,quasi-automatically.
BT-10.2.IntheproposalssubmittedasearlyasJune1998forthesecondsessionofthe
Audiovisual Performances Committee such a mutatis mutandis applicationofArticle 10ofthe
WPPT was already suggested,706 and since no real debate took place on it, Chairman Liedes 
announced that there was agreement on it.707 In a similarly smooth way, it was included in 
the Basic Proposal and adopted at the Diplomatic Conference in 2000 provisionally with an 
insubstantialamendment–orratherjustagrammaticalcorrectioninthetext 708–andthen,as
partofthe19articles onwhichnegotiationswerenottobereopened,alsoinBeijingin2012.
Confirmation of the justification and interpretation of the provisions on the right of 
(interactive) making available to the public
BT-10.3.Theprovisionsontherightof(interactive)makingavailabletothepublicunderArticle 8
oftheWCTandArticles 10and16oftheWPPTwereadoptedin1996inrecognitionoftheneedfor
aneffectivecontrolby–andthusforanexclusiverightofauthorizationof–therightholdersof
the acts of including a work or phonogram in the Internet and making it accessible to the public 
for on-demand use. By the adoption of a mutatis mutandis versioninArticle 10oftheBTAP,itwas
confirmed that the 1996 Diplomatic Conference adopted a correct decision and that this right (as 
anadaptationofexistingrightswithdifferentcharacteristics)adequatelyservesasthebasisofthe
exploitation of works and subject matters of related rights in the online digital environment.

BT-10.4. The meaning of the provision is the same as under the WCT and the WPPT; that is, the 
act takes place at the moment of making available of the works and objects of related rights. 
Theactualinteractivetransmissionisnotacondition–justasthereceptionofabroadcast 
programisnotaconditionofanactofbroadcasting.Theonlydifference–although,withregard 
tothequalificationoftheacts,itisimportant–isthatbroadcastingismadethrough“push” 
technology, while (interactive) making available to the public is based on “pull” technology with 
the key aspect that members of the public may access the protected material not only at a place 
chosen by them (which is possible also in the case of broadcasting with an appropriate receiving 
device) but also at a time individually chosen.
BT-10.5.ThenotesaddedtothedraftArticle inthe2000BasicProposalstatetheunderstanding –
notquestionedbyanydelegationattheDiplomaticConference–aboutanimportantfact.
Namely: although the making available to the public, and then the actual, on-demand 
downloadingofintangiblecopiesmaybecharacterizedcolloquiallyas“onlinedistribution”,thisis
anactofmakingavailabletothepublicandnotanactofdistributionundertheWIPOTreaties –
the WCT, the WPPT and the BTAP. The notes reflect this understanding in this way:
[…] A distinction is […] made between the distribution of copies of fixed performances 
inphysical,tangibleform,whichiscoveredbytherightofdistributioninArticle 8ofthe
proposed Instrument, and the making available of fixed performances by transmission. […]
No rights are exhausted in connection with the making available to the public. The 
performance may not be made further available or distributed to the public by the 
recipient without authorization. Exhaustion of rights may only be associated with the 
distribution of tangible copies put on the market by the rightholder or with his consent.709
Withthis,ithasbeenconfirmedthatundertheBTAP–asalsoundertheWCTandtheWPPT –there
is no such thing as “online exhaustion”. Exhaustion may apply to the distribution of tangible copies.
BT-10.6. It has also been confirmed that an act of (interactive) making available to the public is not 
really a simple act of communication to the public. It is discussed in the Guide to the WCT above 
how the “umbrella solution” is applied in that Treaty in such a way that the right of (interactive) 
makingavailable–inthehopeoffacilitatingtheapplicationofcertainlicensingsystems–hasbeen
includedinArticle 8onthe“[r]ightofcommunicationtothepublic”asifitwerealsosuchanact,
although it is different, for at least two reasons. First, it has an interactive nature and second, and 
more importantly, it also applies to certain acts in the course of which no real communication takes 
place, either in the ordinary or in the legal meaning of the term.710 As also discussed in the Guide to 
the WCT, this form of regulation providing for the right of interactive making available to the public 
together with the non-interactive communication rights, and in a way that implies the former might 
also be covered by the concept of the latter, has created certain misunderstandings; so much so 
thatincertaincountriesithasendangeredtheadequateapplicationoftheright.Therefore,itisa
safersolutiontofulfilltheobligationsprescribedinArticle 8oftheWCTbyprovidingforarightof
interactive making available to the public separately in parallel with the rights of broadcasting and 
communication to the public, also in the case of copyright.
BT-10.7.Articles 10and16oftheWPPTprovideforstand-alonerightsof(interactive)making
availabletothepublicandthustheydonotcreatethesamekindsofproblemsasArticle 8of
the WCT (at most, the misunderstandings of the latter might also have a negative effect for the 
application of the rights of performers and producers of phonograms provided in these WPPT 
provisions). In the BTAP, the same regulation has been chosen. There was a clear statement 
inthenotestoArticle 10intheBasicProposalreflectingtheunderstandingthatanactof 
(interactive) making available to the public is not communication to the public:
The right of making available to the public is limited to situations where members of the 
public may access performances fixed in audiovisual fixations from a place and at a time 
709DocumentIAVP/DC/3,46,paras10.02and10.05.
710 But interactive making available copies for downloading in such a way that, in the course of the transmission, the 
work or subject matter of related rights cannot be seen, heard or otherwise perceived.
