356 individually chosen by them. Thus, availability is based on interactivity and on-demand 
access; in this way, the making available right differs from the right of communication.711
Thischaracterizationoftherightof(interactive)makingavailabletothepublicisadequate
notonlyforArticle 10oftheBTAP,butlikewiseforArticles 10and16oftheWPPTandalsothe
secondpartofArticle 8oftheWCTonsucharight.
Article 11
Right of Broadcasting and Communication to the Public
(1) Performers shall enjoy the exclusive right of authorizing the broadcasting and 
communication to the public of their performances fixed in audiovisual fixations.
(2) Contracting Parties may in a notification deposited with the Director General of 
WIPOdeclarethat,insteadoftherightofauthorizationprovidedforinparagraph (1),
theywillestablisharighttoequitableremunerationforthedirectorindirectuseof
performances fixed in audiovisual fixations for broadcasting or for communication to 
the public. Contracting Parties may also declare that they will set conditions in their 
legislationfortheexerciseoftherighttoequitableremuneration.
(3) Any Contracting Party may declare that it will apply the provisions of paragraphs (1) 
or (2) only in respect of certain uses, or that it will limit their application in some other 
way, or that it will not apply the provisions of paragraphs (1) and (2) at all.
Right of broadcasting and communication to the public and the issue of transferability of 
rights in the preparatory work of the BTAP
BT-11.1. The proposals and the debates about these rights may serve as the best examples of the 
close interrelationship of the scope of economic rights and the issue of transferability of rights. 
At the second session of the Audiovisual Performances Committee, the United States proposed 
a broad exclusive right of broadcasting and communication to the public with the possibility 
of limiting it to a right of remuneration (and not fully denying it through reservation).712 This, 
however, like the recognition of other rights in audiovisual fixations, was linked to the condition 
of an appropriate provision on the transferability of these rights. The delegation of the European 
Community “recalled that in the Diplomatic Conference of 1996 it had been considered that the 
issue of rights in this area had not been ripe yet for being resolved, and said that still was the 
situation.Itquestioned,therefore,whethertheProtocolwastherightplaceforthissubject”.713
BT-11.2. The positions did not change fundamentally at the first two sessions of the SCCR. At the 
second session in May 1999, the delegation of the European Community did, however, explain 
in more detail the reasons for which, although it was a strong supporter of granting high-level 
protection for “audiovisual performers”, it still had reservations and doubts concerning the 
recognition of such rights in the proposed protocol. The European Community and its Member 
States did not yet have a specific proposal, but the EC delegation made the following points:
[D]ue consideration should be given to the fact that marketing mechanisms, contractual 
relations and payment mechanisms might be different here from the situation in the 
industry envisaged by the WPPT. A mutatis mutandisapplicationofArticle 15oftheWPPT
seemednotappropriate.Moreover,cautionwasrequiredinrespectofgrantingexclusive
rights[…]Article 15oftheWPPTmadereferencetoaparticularsituation,asdidArticle 12
of the Rome Convention, namely the broadcasting and communication to the public 
of phonograms published for commercial purposes. In the audiovisual industry, the 
situation was different. When a film was communicated to the public, the carrier would 
not be a videogram published for commercial purposes […] [I]f such a right would prove

Diverging proposals – from an exclusive right, through a right to remuneration, to no right
BT-11.3. At the third session of the SCCR in November 1999, although Canada submitted a 
new proposal,715 neither it nor the debate at the session produced any progress. Chairman 
Liedes, was forced to summarize that “there had not been much convergence”.716 At the last 
SCCR session in April 2000 before the Diplomatic Conference, there was no substantive debate 
on the rights of broadcasting and communication to the public. The issues of the form of the 
instrument (whether a protocol to the WPPT or a separate treaty), national treatment and the 
transfer of rights were the focus of the debates (which did have relevance for these rights). As 
discussedabove,sincethediametricallyoppositepositionsaroundthesequestions–mainly 
betweentheEuropeanCommunityandtheUnitedStates–werenoteliminatedeither,the
proposal on the convocation of the Diplomatic Conference seemed to be too early.
BT-11.4.Article 11inthe2000BasicProposal,wordedintheformofakindofa la carte menu, 
wasacombinationofArticle 11bis(1) and (2) of the Berne Convention in a mutatis mutandis 
version,Articles 12and 16.1oftheRomeConventionandArticle 15oftheWPPT.Althoughthe
language and the way in which the optional nature of the provisions was indicated were not yet 
exactlythesameasinArticle 11,whichhadbeenfinallyadopted,theoptionswerepractically 
thesame.Inparagraph (1),anexclusiverightwasprovidedfor,which,however,under
paragraph (2)wasallowedtobereducedtoarighttoequitableremuneration(inthatversion,
still without the need for any notification); and then a list of possible limited application or no 
applicationoftherightfollowedinparagraph (3).717
BT-11.5. The small number of insignificant amendments to the provisions suggested in the Basic 
ProposalmightcreatetheimpressionthattheadoptionofArticle 11waseasy.Infact,although
this had not manifested in the number and importance of the amendments, intense debate took 
place at the 2000 Diplomatic Conference with a broad spectrum of positions that extended from 
insistence on the need for an exclusive right as by the United States718 and the opposition to 
the possibility of full reservation by the African group 719 and the Russian Federation,720 through 
favoring mutatis mutandis applicationofthemodelofWPPTArticle 15asproposedbyChina, 721 
Norway722 and Switzerland,723 supporting the draft provisions in the Basic Proposal verbatim as 
byJapan724 or with certain improvements as by the European Community (the version proposed 
by it serving finally as the basis for the adoption of the Article) 725 up to suggestions to delete the 
entireArticle byarguingthattheobligationprescribedinitisminimalorevennon-existent,as 
by India,726 Thailand727orVietnam.728
BT-11.6.InviewofthegreatnumberofdifferentoptionsconcerningArticle 11,rangingfrom
an exclusive right to no right, filling an even broader spectrum than in the corresponding 
provisions of the Rome Convention, it became evident that such provisions may only be 
acceptable to the Contracting Parties that were ready to grant more generous protection 
than other Contracting Parties if the application of material reciprocity was to be allowed. 729 
Therefore,thedebateonArticle 11wasstronglylinkedto,andtoagreatextenttookplacein
parallelwith,thedebateonArticle 4analyzedabove.

Article 12 
Transfer of Rights
(1) A Contracting Party may provide in its national law that once a performer has 
consented to fixation of his or her performance in an audiovisual fixation, the exclusive 
rightsofauthorizationprovidedforinArticles 7to11ofthisTreatyshallbeownedor
exercised by or transferred to the producer of such audiovisual fixation subject to any 
contract to the contrary between the performer and the producer of the audiovisual 
fixation as determined by the national law.
(2) AContractingPartymayrequirewithrespecttoaudiovisualfixationsproducedunder
its national law that such consent or contract be in writing and signed by both parties 
to the contract or by their duly authorized representatives.
(3) Independent of the transfer of exclusive rights described above, national laws or 
individual, collective or other agreements may provide the performer with the right 
toreceiveroyaltiesorequitableremunerationforanyuseoftheperformance,as
providedforunderthisTreatyincludingasregardsArticles 10and11.
Introductory remarks
BT-12.1.Article 12isthekeyprovisionoftheBTAPformanyreasons.Theconsensustobe
reachedonthequestionsoforiginalownershipandtransferofrightswasindispensableto
make the Treaty acceptable to the delegations of countries with varied legal traditions and film 
industries at different levels of development. The absence of agreement on these issues led 
to the failure of the Diplomatic Conference in 2000 and it was the emerging consensus in 2011 
on the solution to eliminate the deadlock that opened the way for the re-convocation of the 
Conference in 2012. The scope of this Guide does not allow the preparatory work to be described 
in detail with its many ups and downs. In the comments below only those aspects are covered 
thatmayberelevantfortheinterpretationoftheprovisionsofArticle 12.
BT-12.2. This description of the preparatory work is followed by an analysis of the three 
paragraphs of the Article, of which only paragraphs (1) and (3) seem to raise real interpretation 
problems.Asregardsparagraph (2),ifthereisanyquestionaboutit,itdoesnotconcernits
meaning, but rather its function in the Treaty (whether it has any normative value or rather 
isofasoft-lawnature).Sinceparagraph (2)iscloselylinkedtooneelementoftheprovisionin
paragraph (1),thosetwoparagraphsarereviewedtogether.
Pre-BTAP regulations of transfer of rights
BT-12.3. The international treaties on copyright and related rights, in general, do not contain 
provisions on the transfer of rights. However, both the rights of performers and the rights 
of authors in their contributions to audiovisual productions were (and are) exceptions in this 
respect, and this had to be taken into account in the long and hectic preparatory work of what 
has become the BTAP.
BT-12.4. The description of the status of the rights of performers in their audiovisual fixations 
underArticle 19oftheRomeConventionisverysimple,butitisimportantfromtheviewpointof
730 Summary Minutes of Main Committee I 2000 ,DocumentIAVP/DC/37.,para.143.

thequestionoftheassessmentofthevalidityofthetriptychoftheJapanese–US–ECstatements 
mentionedbelow(becauseitseemsthattheJapanesedelegationaskedthequestionabout 
thepossibilityofapplyingrulesotherthanthoseprovidedinArticle 12oftheBTAPinviewof
theintentiontocontinueapplyingtheRomeArticle 19model).ByvirtueofArticle 19ofthe
Rome Convention, the rights are neither transferred nor granted directly to the producers, 
but “once a performer has consented to the incorporation of his performance in a visual or 
audio-visualfixation,Article 7[onperformers’rights]shallhave no further application ”.731 
Rights that are not applicable do not exist; they do not exist either for the performers or 
for the producers, and as non-existing rights they do not have a term of protection either. 
Simply, under the Rome Convention, the very notion of rights of performers in audiovisual 
fixations of their performances is unknown; no such rights emerge under the Convention. The 
performances simply become inseparable parts of the audiovisual fixations and, as such, they 
enjoyindirectprotection–notastherightsofperformersbutunderthecoverageoftherights 
of the producers of the audiovisual fixations. (The indirect protection may be based on the 
contracts concluded between the producers and the performers when the latter consent to the 
incorporation of their performances in an audiovisual fixation.)
BT-12.5. The characterization of the status of the rights of “audiovisual performers” under the 
TRIPS Agreement is even simpler. There is no word about them; no hint of them; as if they 
didnotexist.Article 14.1oftheAgreementprovidesforperformers’rightsonly“[i]nrespect 
of a fixation of their performances on a phonogram”. The Agreement goes so far in ignoring 
audiovisual performances as that it only grants protection to live performances against 
unauthorized fixation (“bootlegging”) if it is on a phonogram.
BT-12.6. The Berne Convention is not so rigid with regard to the rights of “audiovisual authors” 
astheRomeConventionto“audiovisualperformers”.Article 14 bis(2)(a) provides that the “ 
[o]wnership of copyright in a cinematographic work [= audiovisual work] shall be a matter 
for legislation in the country where protection is claimed”. The provision suggests complete 
freedom,butparagraphs (2)(b) to (d)and (3)oftheArticle containfurtherprovisionsonthebasis 
of which it turns out that, although the freedom is broad, it is not unlimited.
BT-12.7. As analyzed in the Guide to the Berne Convention in this collection of guides, the 
beginningofArticle 14bis(2)(b) of the Berne Convention suggests that the rule is the original 
ownership of producers (“makers”) and it is a kind of exception that the co-authors of 
audiovisualworksarerecognized–oralsorecognized–asownersofrights:
However, in the countries of the Union which, by legislation, include among the owners of 
copyright in a cinematographic work authors who have brought contributions to the making 
of the work, such authors, if they have undertaken to bring such contributions, may not, in 
the absence of any contrary or special stipulation, object to the reproduction, distribution, 
public performance, communication to the public by wire, broadcasting or any other 
communication to the public, or to the subtitling or dubbing of texts, of the work.732 
There is no rule in the Convention stating on what legal basis the producers of audiovisual 
works become the owners of copyright nor on the way in which the so-called “presumption of 
legitimation” (of the producers to perform and/or to authorize the acts listed in the paragraph) 
isobtained.Nevertheless,thenegotiationhistoryofArticle 14 bis indicates that, as regards 
the original ownership of film producers, the two basic legal systems taken into account 
were “film copyright” (where simply the producer is recognized as the “author” or at least the 
original owner of copyright) and “legal assignment”. In the case of the latter, in principle, the 
rights are granted to the co-authors of audiovisual works but, at the same moment, 733 they are 
transferred automatically to the producers. As regards “presumption of legitimation”, the text 
(taking account of the clause “in the absence of any contrary or special stipulation”) suggests 
that, normally, it may be obtained through a rebuttable presumption, but what is presumed 
is not necessarily the transfer of rights to the producer (although this is the normal way of 
guaranteeing smooth exploitation of audiovisual works) since it is only provided that the co-

360 authors may not oppose the performance of the acts listed, which may be the case also on the

BT-12.8.Paragraph (2)(c)and(d)includeprovisionsontheformofauthors’consentand
theconceptof“contraryorspecialstipulation”,respectively;theninparagraph (3)againa 
substantiveswitch–orratheradoubleoreventripleswitch–follows.Itisprovidedthat 
paragraph (2)(b)onthe“presumptionoflegitimation”isnotapplicabletothemainco-authorsof
cinematographic (and other audiovisual) works; namely, to the “authors of scenarios, dialogues 
and musical works created for the making of the cinematographic work, or to the principle 
director thereof”. That is, producers may only obtain the rights in the contributions of these co-
authors through individual or collective agreements. However, although this is the main rule, it 
maynotapply–andparagraph (2)(b)appliesinsteadasadefaultprovision–wherethenational
legislationprovidestothecontrary.Ifparagraph (2)(b)isnotappliedtotheprincipledirector,
the country concerned has to notify the Director General of the WIPO of this.
BT-12.9. At the 1967 Stockholm Diplomatic Conference, the objective was to harmonize the rules 
of original ownership and transfer of rights in the contributions of co-authors of cinematographic 
(andotheraudiovisual)works.ThecomplexprovisionsofArticle 14bis show that this objective 
was not fully achieved.734 Nevertheless, in a narrower field, real harmonization has still taken 
place; namely as regards authors other than thekeycontributorsmentionedinparagraph (3);for
the rights of those authors, the “presumption of legitimation” applies obligatorily.
BT-12.10.AsispointedoutintheGuidetotheBerneConvention,Article 14bis(2) does not 
raise any interpretation problem. It simply states that a Contracting Party may require,with
respect to audiovisual fixations produced under its national law, that the consent or contract 
mentionedinparagraph (1)beinwritingandsignedbybothpartiestothecontractorbytheir
dulyauthorizedrepresentatives.IfthereisanyquestionaboutArticle 12(3)oftheBTAP,itis
not about its meaning, but rather concerning its legal effect, because it reads like a soft-law 
suggestion rather than an operative norm.
The fate of Alternative B in the Basic Proposal for what became the WPPT
BT-12.11. The Basic Proposal for what was adopted at the 1996 Diplomatic Conference as the 
WPPT–asregardsperformers’rights–consistedoftwoalternativedrafttreaties:ontheone 
hand, a treaty only on the protection of the rights of performers in their performances fixed in 
phonograms (as Alternative A) and, on the other hand, a treaty on the protection of the rights of 
performers in respect of their “performances fixed in any medium” (as Alternative B). The latter 
alternative treaty with a broader coverage also contained a sub-alternative which consisted in 
the possibility of a reservation on the basis of which the audiovisual elements of performances 
could have been excluded from the scope of protection.735
BT-12.12.ThisquestionofthecoverageofthedraftWPPTwasoneofthemostcontroversial
issues at the 1996 Diplomatic Conference. The tension was so obvious that, when the 
consideration of the Basic Proposal for the treaty which was later adopted as the WPPT 
began,JukkaLiedes,ChairmanofMainCommittee Isuggestedthatthediscussionofthetwo 
alternatives should not be addressed yet at the formal session of the Committee, but rather 
left, for the time being, to informal consultations. The issue surfaced only once in a formal 
session. On Tuesday of the second week of the Conference, a debate on it took place in Main 
Committee I,which,however,didnotproduceabreakthrough;thus,itwastransferredback
to informal consultations, where the most important differences concerning the rights of 
performers in their audiovisual performances emerged between the European Community and 
its Member States and the United States.
BT-12.13. At the session of Main Committee I, the delegation of the European Community 
stressed that there should be no “discrimination” among performances and that “audiovisual 
performances” should enjoy the same high level of protection as “aural performances”. 736

BT-12.14. In contrast, the delegation of the United States was in favor of maintaining the 
international status quo –representedbyArticle 19oftheRomeConventionandArticle 14.1of
the TRIPS Agreement. It opposed the extension of the coverage of the Treaty to “audiovisual

industry and the film industry, and pointed out that, due to those differences, it is not a 
“discrimination” to have two different regimes for two different categories of fixations of 
performances. However, the US delegation showed readiness to participate in the efforts 
to work out a compromise solution, provided that the level of international protection of 
performers might be raised without the need for introducing fundamental changes in the 
well-functioning contractual system between the US film studios and the collective bodies of 
performers.741 The Group of Asian and Pacific countries, in general, supported the US position, 
as well as India, with its very big film industry based on a contractual system. 742
BT-12.15. The US delegation submitted a compromise proposal which was distributed on 
December 11,743thedayaftertheformaldebateontheissueinMainCommittee I,whereithad
alreadypresentedtheproposalorallyduringthedebate.Sincetheproposalwasquitecomplex
and contained cross-references to a number of draft provisions, it seems more appropriate to 
describe it on the basis of the following oral presentation by the US delegate as reflected in the 
Records of the Diplomatic Conference:
[The delegate pointed out that a] number of countries had pressed to expand the Treaty 
to cover performers of audiovisual works, rather than keeping the Treaty limited to sound 
recordings. He stressed that his country had consistently opposed extension of the Treaty 
in such a manner, and that it would continue to do so, unless serious problems that existed 
in making such extension were addressed. He saw two possibilities in that regard. Either the 
scope of the Treaty should be limited to exclude audiovisual performers, or an alternative 
approach should be developed that would permit the existing different systems to coexist.
[…] He said that his Delegation had developed a proposal that would accomplish that latter 
objective. The proposal had four interrelated and essential elements. First, the proposal 
would grant foreign performers statutory protection in the United States of America 
for their core economic rights. Those core economic rights were the rights of fixation, 
reproduction, distribution and making available to the public. The rights of modification 
and moral rights should be omitted. Second, each country should have flexibility under 
the Treaty as to how rights were to be implemented. With respect to its domestic 
performers, a country could implement the treaty obligations in a manner that would be 
consistent with its own existing system. He mentioned as an example that performers in 
the United States of America would realize their rights through the system of that country, 
which was based on collective bargaining agreements. Foreign performers, on the 
other hand, would receive specific statutory rights. The third element of his Delegation’s 
proposal was that the Treaty should contain provisions on transfer of rights. It should 
permit performers to freely transfer their economic rights. It would provide protection to 
performers beyond that provided by the Rome Convention, by allowing rights to continue 
to exist even after the performer consented to the fixation of his performance. Under the 
proposal, a presumption would apply that those rights were transferred to the producer 
once the performer agreed to participate in a film. The performer and producer would, 
however,befreetoagreeotherwise.Thefourthelementoftheproposalwouldrequire
each country to treat performers from other countries at least as well as it treated its own

BT-12.16. This seemed to be a major shift in the US position and raised the hope for a

world. The coverage of the WPPT was limited to live performances and performances fixed in 
phonograms (this was slightly broader than the coverage of the original Alternative A of the 
draft treaty which only extended to “musical performances”).

The issue of transfer of rights in the preparatory committees
BT-12.18. The work on the preparation of a “protocol” to the WPPT began in the Committee of 
Experts on a Protocol concerning Audiovisual Performances, which held its first session, as 
planned,inJune1997.Itwasakindofwarm-upmeetingwhereastocktakingofthe–otherwise
quitewell-known–positionstookplaceandwherethedelegationsstressedtheircommitment 
totrytoworkoutacompromisesolution.ThenatthesecondsessionoftheCommitteeinJune
1998 a number of proposals had been submitted747 which reflected that the delegations had 
taken their commitment seriously, but the basic differences of the positions concerning the key 
issue of transfer of rights still remained the most decisive obstacle to reaching consensus.
BT-12.19. For the second session of the Committee, the United States submitted the following 
treaty-language proposal:
Once a performer has consented to the fixation of his or her performance in an 
audiovisual work, he or she shall be deemed to have transferred all exclusive rights of 
authorization granted under this Treaty with respect to that particular audiovisual work 
to the producer of that work and its successors in interest, subject to contractual clauses 
to the contrary. The foregoing sentence shall not apply to any rights of remuneration 
aperformermayhaveunderthelawofanyContractingParty,norshallitrequirea
Contracting Party to establish any such rights of remuneration.748
BT-12.20. This proposal would have resulted in a more advantageous position for the performers 
thanArticle 19oftheRomeConventioninfourrespects:(i)theprovisionwouldhaveapplied
only to fixations in audiovisual works rather than to any audiovisual fixations; (ii) the rights of 
performers would have had application also after having consented to the incorporation of 
their performances in an audiovisual work; (iii) although there would have been a presumption 
of transfer, it would have been rebuttable; (iv) the rebuttable presumption would have only 
covered exclusive rights of authorization (and not mere rights to remuneration).
BT-12.21. The US delegation stated that the proposed presumption was a key element of its 
proposal as a whole, because it was a condition of granting wide-ranging exclusive rights. 
It considered it essential to ensure for producers of audiovisual works the legal certainty 
needed that they could exploit those works globally. The delegation stressed that, without due 
assurances that their contracts would be respected worldwide, it would be very difficult for 
the producers to do business. The delegation also informed the Committee that the proposal 
had won the acceptance of the audiovisual performers’ organizations in its country. 749 The 
delegation of India supported the US proposal and said that its country “did not want to kill 
producers and thereby murder performers”. 750
BT-12.22.TheGRULACcountriessubmittedaproposal–trendinginthesamedirection–
concerningthequestionoftransferofrights.Itsuggestedthatthestatusof“audiovisual 
performers” should be assimilated to that of “audiovisual authors” under the Berne Convention 
rather than to that of “aural performers” under the WPPT, and that in doing so the realities of 
the audiovisual industry should be taken into account rather than those of the phonographic 
industry. The Group presented the following draft provision: “In the case where a performer 
authorizes the inclusion of his performance in an audiovisual fixation, the Contracting Parties 
shall apply, mutatis mutandis, theprovisionsofArticle 14bis(2) of the Berne Convention”.751 The 
proposal was supported by the delegation of China “with reference to the massive investments

preparatory work of a “protocol” to the WPPT or a stand-alone treaty continued as one of the items 
on the agenda of the Standing Committee on Copyright and Related Rights (SCCR), which dealt with 
itinfoursessions–beforeanewDiplomaticConferencewasconvened–inNovember1998,May
1999, November 1999 and April 2000. At the first SCCR session, both the European Community and 
its Member States758 and the United States759 maintained their positions represented at the second 
session of the Audiovisual Performances Committee, as did the African Group760 and the GRULAC.761 
Onlythedelegationoftwocountries–JapanandCanada–submittednewproposals.
BT-12.25.TheJapaneseproposalwasacombinationofthe“presumptionoflegitimation”
provisionofArticle 14bis(2)(b)oftheBerneConventionandArticle 19oftheRomeConvention,
but in substance, it corresponded more to the former. It also intended to offer flexibility through 
the possibility of a reservation-type notification:
(1)  A performer who has undertaken to bring contributions to the making of an 
audiovisual fixation of his performance may not, in the absence of any contrary or 
special contract, object to the reproduction, distribution, rental and making available 
of his performance fixed in the audiovisual fixation.
(2) NotwithstandingtheprovisionsofArticle 4(1),anyContractingPartymay,as 
regards performers who are nationals of such Contracting Party, establish 
national legislation which does not contain rules providing for the application of 
paragraph (1).SuchContractingPartyshallnotifytheDirectorGeneralofWIPOby 
means of a written declaration, which will be immediately communicated by him to 
all the other parties of this Protocol.762
This proposal was put forward as a basis for a possible compromise, but for all its flexibility, it 
still did not fully satisfy those delegations that wanted the new instrument to be silent about the 
issue of transferability, nor was it acceptable for those, such as the United States and India, that 
wanted some guarantee for the recognition of the producer’s ownership of rights under their 
contractual systems.

BT-12.26. The Canadian proposal consisted in further development of the idea presented at 
the second session of the Audiovisual Performances Committee to try to solve the issue of 
transfer of rights through some kind of private international law provisions. The draft provisions 
suggested by Canada read as follows:
Atthetimeofratifyingoraccedingtothis[Protocol]/[Treaty]oratanysubsequenttime,
a Contracting Party may declare by an instrument deposited with the Director General 
that once a performer [who is a national of [that]/[any] Contracting Party]/[regardless of 
nationality] has consented to the fixation of his or her performance in an audiovisual work 
by a national of that Contracting Party, he or she shall be deemed to have transferred all 
exclusive rights of authorization granted under this [Protocol]/[Treaty] with respect to that 
particular audiovisual work to the [author]/[producer]/[first owner of copyright] of that work 
[provided such [author]/[producer]/[first owner of copyright] is a national of a Contracting 
Party] and [his, her or] its successors in interest subject to any written [contractual [clause]/
[provision]]/[agreement] to the contrary. The foregoing sentence shall not apply to any 
rights of remuneration a performer may have under the law of any Contracting Party, nor 
shallitrequireaContractingPartytoestablishanysuchrightsofremuneration.
Where a Contracting Party makes such a declaration it shall apply [and be binding] in all 
other Contracting Parties of this [Protocol]/[Treaty].
For purposes of this article, the term ‘an audiovisual work by a national of that Contracting 
Party’ means an audiovisual work where the [author]/[producer]/[first owner of copyright] 
is a national of the Contracting Party which made the declaration [regardless of the place 
of fixation or publication of the audiovisual work].
[[For purposes of this article] ‘producer’ shall include both individuals and legal entities 
[and the identity of the producer shall be determined by the law of the Contracting Party 
which made the declaration]].
Adeclarationmadeunderthisarticle mayberevokedatanytime.763
The most important element of this proposal was the obligation to recognize the transfer of 
rights in the “country of origin” as being valid in the other Contracting Parties.
BT-12.27. The first session of the SCCR, despite all the joint efforts, did not produce a 
breakthrough in solving the complex issue of transfer of rights, but it was again on the agenda 
at the second session in May 1999. All the previously submitted proposals were on the table. 
Inaddition,Indiapresentedanewproposal.ItcorrespondedtoArticle 14 bis(2)(b) of the Berne 
Convention based on the concept of “presumption of legitimation”, but it would have eliminated 
the casuistic nature of that provision:
In the absence of any contract to the contrary, once the performer has by written 
agreement consented to the audiovisual fixation of the performance, he shall not object to 
the enjoyment by the producer of the exclusive rights of authorization specifically granted 
to the performer under this Treaty in respect of such fixation, for the purpose for which 
such fixation was made.764
Such a provision would have assimilated the status of “audivisual performers” to that of the co-
authors of audiovisual works without differentiating as between key authors and “secondary” 
authors, and as such it could not count on the support of those delegations that preferred a 
WPPT orientation.
BT-12.28. Nevertheless, another proposal also landed on the table at the second SCCR session, 
and it had a major impact. The international NGO of “audiovisual performers”, the International 
Federation of Actors (FIA), with the assistance of the International Bureau of WIPO, distributed 
a “non-paper” (a paper without any document number; mainly due to the fact that, according to

Itpresentedthefollowingcomments–stillnotintreatylanguage:
[I]f this Instrument expressly recognises the possibility of a presumption of transfer, and 
inturnrequiresitsrecognitioninothercontractingpartieswhichmaythemselvesnot

1.  The transfer must be rebuttable (as in the US proposal).
2.  It must be expressed in a written contract and state which rights are to be

3.  The performer must receive remuneration in return for the transfer.
4.  Rights for uses that do not yet exist cannot be presumed transferred (as in the

5.  The transfer can only apply to the exclusive rights provided in the Instrument and not 
to remuneration rights or to moral rights.

audiovisual work, which we understand to be the intent of the US proposal.

of transfer in the instrument. However, in the interest of compromise and to move the 
process forward, we are prepared to consider the possibility for countries to choose 
this option in their national legislation and have it recognized by other countries. The 
conditions we have stated for such international recognition are those that we regard 
asessentialforanysuchoptiontobeacceptableandfairtoperformerswhoare–aswe
continuallyremindgovernmentshere–theweakestpartyinanybargaining.
BT-12.29. The FIA also offered ideas to work out some private international law rules to solve the 
issue of transfer of rights:
[An] area of difficulty in the Canadian Government proposal is the point of attachment to 
the producer. We recognise that this may seem the most obvious solution, and no doubt 
the producers will say that as the body which invests in the production, the producer is the 
logical point of attachment.
However we see this as open to easy and obvious abuse. There is nothing to prevent 
a production company from incorporating in a particular country in order to avoid the 
obligations related to copyright and indeed other obligations. The establishment of shell 
companies is already a major problem for performers’ trade unions and therefore the 
nationality of a producer is something that cannot be relied upon in this process.
We do not propose that the nationality of the performer be the point of attachment. This 
wouldbeimpracticaltoadministerasitisquitenormaltoseeperformersofanumberof
nationalities within the same audiovisual production.
Usinganotherpointofattachment–thecountryinwhichtheproductionisprimarily
shot–wouldoffertheleastopportunityformanipulationbutisalsocomplextodetermine
in international production. We have examined this element and consider that it may still 
offer a way forward.
BT-12.30. At the third session of the SCCR held in November 1999, only one new proposal had been 
submitted on this issue; namely by Canada, which had presented a new variant of the proposal it

BT-12.31. In view of the slow progress towards a compromise solution, the SCCR adopted a

BT-12.35.Thevalueofadoptionofthe19articles wasreducedbecauseeverythingdependedon

BT-12.36.TheBasicProposalcontainednolessthanfouralternativesforArticle 12,ofwhich

Alternative E. Transfer
Once a performer has consented to the incorporation of his performance in an audiovisual 
fixation, he shall be deemed to have transferred all exclusive rights of authorization 
provided for in this Treaty with respect to that particular fixation to its producer, subject to 
written contractual clauses to the contrary.
Alternative F. Entitlement to Exercise Rights
In the absence of written contractual clauses to the contrary, once the performer has 
consented to the audiovisual fixation of his performance, the producer shall be deemed to 
be entitled to exercise the exclusive rights of authorization provided for in this Treaty with 
respect to that particular fixation.

BT-12.37. Alternative E corresponded to the proposal of the United States made during the 
preparatory work, which was supported by some delegations but strongly opposed by some 
others, including in particular those of the European Community and its Member States. In 
contrast, Alternative H reflected the position of certain delegations, in particular those of the 
European Community and its Member States, but it seemed unacceptable for some others, 
including the delegation of the United States (due, inter alia, to its potential to serve as a 
basis for the application of “rule of law” theories to deny the recognition of rights granted to 
producers–ratherthantoperformersasnaturalpersons).Thesealternativesdidnothave 
any reasonable chance to become the basis of consensus. Only Alternative F and, even more, 
Alternative G seemed to have some chance. Concerning these two alternatives, the notes in the 
Basic Proposal read as follows:
12.10DuringthepreparatorystagesamodelthattookitsinspirationfromArticle 14bis(2)(b)  
of the Berne Convention was considered by some delegations. Alternative F is based on this 
approach […].
12.11 One aspect of obscurity has been removed from the provision in Alternative F 
compared to the corresponding provisions of the Berne Convention. The legal operation 
oftheso-calledclauseon‘presumptionoflegitimation’ofArticle 14bis(2)(b) of the Berne 
Convention is based on the expression ‘authors … may not … object’. Authors continue 
to be owners of their respective rights, but the rights are not exercisable against the 
user. Alternative F is similar in its effect but is phrased as a presumption of entitlement. 
The producer would be expressly and properly ‘entitled to exercise the exclusive rights 
of authorization provided for in this Treaty’ […]. Producers would have certainty in their 
ability to exploit the audiovisual production in the marketplace.
12.12 In the same way as Alternative E, Alternative F would be mandatory for the 
ContractingParties.Note12.09isequallyvalidastoAlternativeF.
12.13 […] The purpose of Alternative G is to build a bridge between different legal systems, 
leaving each country to determine its own policy concerning transfer, while still providing 
business certainty. It is based on the principles of private international law.
12.14 The main function of Alternative G would be to guarantee the recognition of 
different arrangements for the transfer of rights that are in use in different Contracting 
Parties. It does so providing in paragraph (1) that a transfer of any of the exclusive rights 
of authorization to the producer shall be governed by the law of the country most 
closely connected with the audiovisual fixation, a principle well established in private

BT-12.38. The issue of transfer of rights surfaced twice777 at the level of formal sessions of Main 
Committee Iforshortandnottrulysubstantivedebates.Therealworkwasdoneintheworking 

stillshowed,however,thatnoteverydelegation–and,inparticular,notthedelegationsofthe

Still,onDecember 20,somelasteffortsweremadeandvariousvariantswereraised,butin 

above-quotedrecommendationofthePlenary,thefateofthe“WIPOAudiovisualPerformances 
Treaty” was returned into the hands of the Assemblies of Member States of WIPO which were

Conference.TheWIPOAssembliesdidso–notattheSeptember2001session,but10fullyears
later, at their 2011 sessions.
Breakthrough in 2011; (re)convocation of the Diplomatic Conference and adoption of the BTAP
BT-12.39. After the half success/half failure of the 2000 Diplomatic Conference a gloomy mood 
and pessimism prevailed at the sessions of SCCR and the WIPO Assemblies regarding the 
chance to agree on the issue of transfer of rights and thus for the hope of an instrument on 
the rights of “audiovisual performances”. Thus, although the issue was retained on the agenda, 
and even “ad hoc informal meetings” were organized to discuss it, for a while no real progress 
was made. In that period, mainly background activities (and some lukewarm consultations, 
rather than serious negotiations) took place in which the International Bureau of WIPO played 
a significant role by ordering and publishing studies and by preparing surveys of national 
provisions on the protection of “audiovisual performances” and of contractual systems on the 
basisofquestionnairesaddressedto,andrespondedtoby,agreatnumberofMemberStates.
Inter alia, a survey was published covering the national legislation of 98 Member States 780 with a 
summary prepared by the WIPO Secretariat. The most thorough and comprehensive document 
waspreparedbyJaneC.GinsburgandAndréLucasandwasentitled“StudyonTransferofthe
RightsofPerformerstoProducersofAudiovisualFixations–Conclusion”. 781 In the “Conclusion” 
version,theytookintoaccountalsotheresponsestotheabove-mentionedquestionnaireand 
the studies prepared by experts on these issues from Egypt (Hassan Badrawi 782), from Germany

BT-12.40. In spite of the availability of rich background documentation and the organization 
of regional and national seminars by WIPO, the fronts between the various positions did not 
move.TheadvanceddraftAudiovisualPerformersTreaty–withits19“provisionally”adopted 
articles andonlyonemissing–wokeupfromalongcomain2011justtofindthattwoopposing
scenarios were waiting for it: either to fall back again into regression and fade away from the 
agenda or, as a result of a concentrated last effort, to recover and succeed.
BT-12.41.ThedangerofregressionemergedinJanuary2011whenBrazilsubmittedanumber

a complete revision);

was to be applied under the provisionally adopted Article, as likewise not under the

To also raise the possibility of transforming the obligation of protection into a mere option 
of protection of technological measures (by indicating “may” as an alternative to “shall” in 
paragraph (1)oftheArticle).

remuneration schemes to be applied in their favor.

Interpretation of Article  12: introductory remarks
BT-12.50.WhenthebasicrulesoftheVCLTontheinterpretationoftreatiesareappliedthe
interpretationofthekeyaspectsofArticle 12seemstobeclear.Atthe2000Diplomatic
Conference,however,analternativeinterpretationemerged–inparticularconcerning
paragraph (1)–supportedbycertaindelegations(andapparentlynotopposedbyothersinthe
debate).Below,theelementsofthearticle areinterpretedinthisorder:(i)thetitleoftheArticle; 
(ii)paragraph (1)onthebasisoftheVCLTrules;(iii)alternativeinterpretationofparagraph (1);
(iv)paragraph (2);and(v)paragraph (3).
Interpretation of the title of the Article
BT-12.51.ThetitleofArticle 12is“Transfer of Rights”. It does not seem to fully correspond to 
thecontentsoftheprovisionsofthearticle because,inparagraph (1),thetransferofrights
is only one of the possibilities permitted; in addition, it is allowed to provide for the original 
ownership or the right of exercising the exclusive rights. The negotiation history of the 
article describedaboveclearlyshows,however,thattheexpression“transferofrights”has 
always been understood in this broader sense. It is necessary to note this, because, although in 
paragraph (1)allthreepermittedforms–originalownershipoftheproducer,legitimationofthe
producertoexercisetherights,andtransferofrightstotheproducer–areclearlyprovided,in
paragraph (3),onlytheterm“transferofexclusiverights”appearsanditrequiresinterpretation 
whetheritisusedinanarrowersenseorinthesamebroadersenseasinparagraph (1).
Interpretation of paragraph (1) on the basis of the VCTL: “once a performer has consented to 
fixation of his or her performance in an audiovisual fixation”
BT-12.52.Thisisthesituationtowhichtheprovisionofparagraph (1)–and,infact,theentire
article –applies.Thewordingofthephrasehardlyraisesanyinterpretationissues;suffice 
it to remark that “consenting” is a synonym of “authorizing”, the term used in the provisions 
oftheBTAPontheexclusiverightofauthorizationofperformers.ItisArticle 6(ii)ofthe 

Treaty by virtue of which the performers have an exclusive right to authorize such fixation of 
their performances.
BT-12.53. It is worth noting how the provision does not continue after this phrase. It does not 
continue the same way the phrase “once a performer has consented to the incorporation of 
hisperformanceinavisualoraudio-visualfixation”inArticle 19oftheRomeConventiondoes, 
namely,withthestatementthattheprovisionsonperformers’rightsprovidedforinArticle 7of 
the Convention “shall have no further application”. With this they cease to exist; the users of the 
audiovisual fixations do not have any obligation to the performers, but only to the producers 
ofthefixations.WhatperformersmayhaveunderArticle 12,incontrast,iswhattheyhave 
agreed upon in contracts with the producers; they only have contractual claims. In the context 
oftheBTAP,Article 12(1)simplycannotcontinueinthesameorsimilarwaysincetheprovisionis
about the rights in “audiovisual fixations” which according to the BTAP “by definition” exist when 
performers consent to the fixations of their performances; in fact, instead of no longer having 
application, they rather just come into existence.
BT-12.54.Thisisthekeyelementofthe“context”inwhichArticle 12“shallbeinterpretedingood
faithinaccordancewiththeordinarymeaningtobegiventothetermsofthetreaty”asrequired
byArticle 31.1oftheVCLT.Thepreambleisalsopartofthe“context”asclarifiedinArticle 31.2
oftheVCLTanditalsoindicatestheobjectandpurposeoftheTreatyinthelightofwhichits
provisions are to be interpreted. In this regard, the very first clause of the preamble seems to 
offer guidance: “[d]esiring to develop and maintain the protection of the rights of performers in 
their audiovisual performances in a manner as effective and uniform as possible”.
Interpretation of paragraph (1) on the basis of the VCTL: “[a] Contracting Party may provide in 
its national law that the exclusive rights […] shall be owned or exercised by or transferred to 
the producer”
BT-12.55. In a treaty, the phrase “a Contracting Party may provide”–inaccordancewiththe
ordinarymeaningoftheterms(seeArticle 31.1oftheVCLT)–normallymeansthatwhat
follows after the phrase is something the Contracting Parties are  permitted to do. Where what 
is permitted consists in an exception to or limitation of a right or in any other decrease of the 
level of protection to be granted by a treaty as a minimum obligation, it implies that there is a 
need for such permission and that, a contrario, where no such permission is provided, such an 
exception or limitation or other decrease of protection is not permitted.
BT-12.56. Here, what is thus permitted relates to the provisions of the BTAP on the performers’ 
exclusive rights of authorization in the audiovisual fixations of their performances which 
they“shallenjoy”.ThreethingsarepermittedunderArticle 12(1)inrespectoftheseexclusive
rights: (i) to provide that the rights are owned by the producer; (ii) to provide that the producer 
is authorized to exercise the rights; and (iii) to provide that the rights to be enjoyed by the 
performers are transferred to the producer. Due to the complex nature of “audiovisual 
fixations”, in particular of audiovisual works (to which, for the reasons discussed in connection 
with the definition of “audiovisual fixation” above, the BTAP in fact applies), the consolidation of 
the exercise of rights in the hands of the producer is justified in the same way as in the case of 
the rights of co-authors of such works. Therefore, it is not a realistic option for the performers 
to maintain their exclusive rights of authorization and exercise the rights by themselves 
individuallyeachtimeanaudiovisualworkistobeused.Inthecontextofparagraph (1),the
needfortheconsolidationoftheexclusiverightsisnotaquestion.Thequestionisinwhich
way the consolidation may take place. From the above-mentioned a contrario principle, the 
answer seems to follow that it may take place only in these three ways specifically permitted 
by the BTAP. It certainly may not take place in such a way that it would result in the abolishing 
of the rights in the sense that they cease to apply as soon as an “audiovisual fixation” is made 
with the performer’s consent, because this would deny the existence of the BTAP as a treaty on 
performers’ rights in “audiovisual fixations ”. It should also be taken into account that it offers 
a stronger negotiation position to the performers if what they consent to is that the rights of 
authorization to be enjoyed by them are transferred to the producers rather than consenting 
to the termination of their rights and, at most, their transformation into contractual claims. The 
transferofexistingexclusiverights–insteadoftheterminationthereofwiththeconsenttothe 
fixationoftheperformances–isalsomorefavorablewithregardtotheapplicationofpossible 

===== PAGE 375 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
376 “best-seller” clauses. 803 And it is particularly relevant from the viewpoint of the systems of 
unwaivable rights to remuneration maintained at the transfer of the exclusive rights.
Interpretation of paragraph (1) on the basis of the VCLT: “subject to any contract to the 
contrary”
BT-12.57. The meaning of the provision is straightforward. In a legal norm, no interpretation 
thereofispossible–“ingoodfaithinaccordancewiththeordinarymeaningtobegiventothe
termsofthetreatyintheircontextandinthelightofitsobjectandpurpose”–otherthanthat
what is provided does not apply if, and to the extent that, there is a contract to the contrary.
BT-12.58. Although the meaning of the proviso is clear in that what appears in the foregoing may 
berebuttedbycontract,thequestionmayariseofitsexactreference;whethertherebutting 
effectonlyappliestothelastofthethreeoptions–transferofrights–mentionedbeforethe 
proviso, or to all three options appearing before it, that is, ownership and exercise of the rights 
by the producers. The structure of the text shows that rather the latter is the case; it applies 
to all three options. That is, if the contrary is provided in a contract, not only does the transfer 
of rights not take place, but the rights also cannot be owned or exercised by the producer. It is 
another matter whether or not such contrary provisions are truly made in contracts. Due to the 
characteristics of the audiovisual industry and the exploitation of audiovisual works, it seems 
inevitable that the ownership and/or exercise of rights be consolidated in the producers’ hands. 
But it is not irrelevant, with regard to the performers’ legal position, whether or not they enjoy 
certain exclusive rights that may not be owned or exercised by or transferred to the producers 
unless, and to the extent that, they give their consent in a contract.
BT-12.59. The structure of the provision from which the above-mentioned full coverage of 
the proviso may be derived is this: “the exclusive rights […] shall be owned or exercised by or 
transferred to the producer […] subject to any contract to the contrary [emphasis added]”. If the 
intention had been to reduce the scope of the proviso to the last of the three options, it would 
have had to be expressed somehow. It could have been constructed as: “the exclusive rights 
[…] shall be owned or exercised by or, subject to any contract to the contrary, transferred to the 
producer”. But the structure of the provision is not like this.
Interpretation of paragraph (1) on the basis of the VCLT: meaning of the proviso “as 
determined by the national law ”
BT-12.60.Thequestionistowhatthelastproviso“asdeterminedbythenationallaw”refersas
to be determined. It seems clear, however, that the national law may not determine anything 
contrarytowhatisprovidedforinparagraph (1).
BT-12.61.Therearethreeissuesintheprovisionofparagraph (1)thatrequiredeterminationin
nationallaw.First,whetherornotanyofthethreeoptionspermittedinparagraph (1)isapplied;
second, which, if any, is applied; and third, how a contract may rebut the effect of any of the 
three options (in particular whether it must be concluded in writing and if so in which way and 
with what contents to be valid). The proviso may refer to all of them or any of them; in fact all 
three issues need legislative decision and regulation. What it may not mean is to allow national 
rules to conflict with the contents of the provision the application of which is to be determined.
Summary of the interpretation of paragraph (1) on the basis of the VCLT
BT-12.62.OnthebasisoftheapplicationofArticles 31and32oftheVCLT,thefollowing
interpretationofArticle 12(1)maybeestablished:(i)ContractingPartiesarepermittedtoprovide,
as determined in their national laws, that the exclusive rights enjoyed by performers under the 
BTAP, once they have consented to the fixation of their performances in audiovisual fixations, are

owned or exercised by, or transferred to, the producers, unless otherwise provided (rebutted) 
in contract; (ii) a contrario, it follows from the text, the context, the object and the purpose of 
the provision that the same is not permitted without the possibility of rebutting it by contract; 
and (iii) it also follows from the same principle that other kinds of legislative provisions on the 
consolidation of the performers’ exclusive rights in the hands of the producers are not permitted.
BT-12.63. This reading of the provision seems to be in accordance with the context, object and 
purpose of the BTAP. There is no agreed statement and no separate instrument that would 
concernitinaccordancewithArticle 31.2(a)and(b)oftheVCLT.SincetheBTAPhasrelatively
recentlyenteredintoforceandmanykeynegotiatingparties–suchastheEuropeanUnionand
itsMemberStates(withtheexceptionofSlovakia)ortheUnitedStates–havenotratifiedityet,it
wouldhardlyberealistictospeakofaspecial“subsequentpractice”(Article 31.3(b)oftheVCLT),
and there does not seem to be another international treaty that would have had to be taken into 
accountasasourceofinterpretation(Article 31.3(c)).Thestandardtermsusedintheprovisions
are well known in the field of copyright and related rights; thus, one could hardly speak of a 
“specialmeaning”tobegiventothetermsasintendedbytheparties(Article 31.4oftheVCLT).
BT-12.64.Theinterpretationofparagraph (1)issufficientlyclearaboutthepermittedoptions.
It hardly needs a separate confirmation by any supplementary sources referred to in 
Article 32.Norisitthecasethatsuchsourcesareneededtodetermineitsmeaningbecause
itsinterpretationonthebasisofArticle 31wouldbeambiguousorobscureorwouldleadtoa
manifestly absurd or unreasonable result.
BT-12.65. One possible source of interpretation has not yet been reviewed above: “any 
subsequentagreementbetweenthepartiesregardingtheinterpretationofthetreatyorthe 
applicationofitsprovisions”(Article 31.3(a)oftheVCLT).ThisprovisionoftheVCLTseemsto
mean an agreement between all the parties after the adoption of the Treaty. There does not 
seem to be such a post-conference subsequent agreement. Nevertheless, as can be seen below, 
analternativeinterpretationofparagraph (1)isbasedoncertainstatementsmadebysome

of interpretation”.

BT-12.71.  Any differences between the ordinary meaning of the text of a treaty and what follows 
from it according to the generally accepted rules of interpretation, on the one hand, and, on 
the other hand, an understanding among the parties that contradicts it does not facilitate the 
interpretation, implementation and application of the treaty. In such a situation, in general, 
there are two tasks: first, trying to choose a reasonable interpretation on the basis of which the 
difference is less significant; second, reconciling the interpretation with the ordinary meaning 
of the text, and the context, object and purpose of the provision, as well as with the rules of 
interpretationofinternationaltreatiesascodifiedinArticles 31and32oftheVCLT.Inviewofthe
factthat,accordingtotherecords,therewasagreementwiththeJapanesestatementbycertain
keynegotiatingparties –thathavestrongpositionsinthemarketswheretheapplicationofthe
rightsof“audiovisualperformers”isrelevant–andapparentlytherewasnooppositiontoit,
significant deference is justified in assessing its validity. It seems, however, that the chance to 
reconcile the purported agreement adopted at the informal consultations with the provisions 
oftheBTAPdoesdifferinrespectofthethreepossiblemeaningsoftheJapanesestatement
outlined in the preceding paragraph. It would be relatively easy in the case of the first meaning 
–astatementabouttheapplicabilityofsomepossiblevariantsoftheoptionsprovidedin
Article 12(1)–butitseemsthatthedelegationsrathermeantthesecondorthethirdmeanings.808
BT-12.72.ItisworthwhiletostarttheanalysiswiththethirdpurportedmeaningoftheJapanese
statement,accordingtowhichJapanaskedforandreceivedaguaranteethat,inspiteofthe
provisionsinArticle 12(1),itmaystillapplyasystemcorrespondingtoArticle 19oftheRome
Convention. It is submitted that, if a Contracting Party applied this Rome provision exactly in 
the way that it is provided in that Convention, it would be in conflict not only with the provisions 
ofArticle 12butwiththeentireBTAPonperformers’rightsinaudiovisualfixations,exceptwith
Article 6ontherightsinunfixedperformances.Thisissobecause,insuchacase,bydefinitionno
rights would emerge in the authorized audiovisual fixations; the performers would lose those rights 
before they could emerge at all. It would have been meaningless to speak of a term of protection as 
providedinArticle 14sincetherightsthat,inprinciple,weretobegrantedwouldceasetoexistat
the very moment when they, in principle, were supposed to be born. Therefore, any understanding 
accordingtowhichaContractingPartymayapplytheRomeArticle 19modelmustbereconciled
withArticle 12(1)oftheBTAPanditmayonlydosoifitisunderstoodinsuchawaythat,although
the rights really cease to be applicable in favor of the performers, they do not cease to be applicable 
ingeneralbecausetheproducersbecometheirownersautomatically–withoutthepossibilityof
acontracttothecontrarywhich,however,wouldbeinconflictwiththeprovisioninArticle 12(1)
according to which such effect may be “subject to any contract to the contrary”.
BT-12.73.Inviewofthis,itisonlythesecondmeaningoftheJapanesestatementthatmight

interpretationrulesoftheVCLT.Theabove-mentionedcommentatorsreferringtotheinformal

may be subject to a contract to the contrary, are permitted to not provide for such contractual 
rebuttal; that is, the presumption of transfer may be made non-rebuttable. With due respect 
totheeffortsbythosewhosuggestthisinterpretation–andirrespectiveofwhatmighthave 
beentheintentionofsuchanunreportedinformalagreement–callingaprovisiononthe
non-rebuttable nature of an effect provided in a treaty just a matter of “ determination” of the

theJapanesestatementinthewaydescribedabove,itwillcertainlybemanifestedinsuch 
subsequentpractice.

BT-12.76.Underparagraph (1)ofthearticle “onceaperformerhasconsentedtofixationofhisor

however,onlyprovidesthatContractingParties“mayrequire”writtenform.
BT-12.77.Theprovisionofparagraph (2)mighthavehadadecisivenormativeeffectifwritten
formhadbeenmadeageneralrequirement,butitisnotthecase.TheContractingPartiesare
only allowed to prescribe such a condition for the validity of the transfer of rights. Therefore, 
theeffectofparagraph (2)–asaguaranteetotheperformersthattheirconsentmayonlybe
recognized as a basis for the transfer of their rights if it is granted in such a duly controllable 
way–islimited.
809Here,themeaningofthephrase“asdeterminedbythenationallaw”isdifferentthaninArticle 14.4oftheTRIPS 
