Interpretation of paragraph (3): “Independent of the transfer of exclusive rights described 
above”
BT-12.78. The meaning of the words “independent of the transfer of exclusive rights” is clear: 
whatisprovidedafteritintheparagraph (apossiblerighttoremunerationfortheuseofthe
performances) is applicable independently or in spite of the transfer of the exclusive rights. It 
is also clear that it is not the exclusive rights but the transfer of the exclusive rights of which the 
possible right to remuneration is independent. It simply cannot be any other way because the 
owner of an exclusive right does not have two parallel rights: the right to authorize (or prohibit) 
the acts covered by the right and a right to remuneration for the acts authorized; the payment 
of remuneration is usually a condition of the authorization of the acts.
BT-12.79. It is worth comparing the expression “[i]ndependent of the transfer of exclusive rights” 
inArticle 12(3)oftheBTAPwiththeexpression“[i]ndependentlyoftheauthor’srights,and 
evenafterthetransferofthesaidrights”appearinginArticle 6 bis(1) of the Berne Convention 
on“moralrights”.IntheBerneprovision,“moralrights”doreallyexistindependentlyof–and 
theirnaturedoesdifferfrom–theeconomicrights.Itfollowsfromthisthattheycontinueto
be applicable even when the economic rights are transferred for the same acts. In contrast, 
inArticle 12(3)oftheBTAP,theissueisthetransferoftheperformers’exclusiverightsof
authorization, an integral part of which is the right to claim and receive remuneration for the 
authorized acts.
BT-12.80.Themeaningof“thetransferofexclusiverights”atthebeginningofparagraph (3)(of
whichthepossiblerighttoremunerationis“independent”)alsorequiresinterpretation.Itmight
only mean transfer of rights in a narrower sense, because only it is mentioned explicitly. There are, 
however,well-foundedreasonstobesurethattheothertwooptions–ownershipandexercise
oftheexclusiverightsbytheproducers–arealsomeant.First,thetitleofthearticle isalsojust
“TransferofRights”,andunderit,inparagraph (1),thereareprovisionsnotonlyontransferof
rights in a narrower sense but also on other two options. Second, the phrase “transfer of exclusive 
rights as described above” also confirms that all options described above are covered.
Interpretation of paragraph  (3): “individual, collective or other agreements may provide the 
performer with the right to receive royalties or equitable remuneration for any use of the 
performance, as provided for under this Treaty including as regards Articles  10 and 11”
BT-12.81.Itseemsappropriatetoconsiderthispartoftherestoftheparagraph separately,
because–contrarytoarighttotheotheroptionunderwhicha national law may provide for 
equitableremuneration–itiseasytodealwithit.Easybecause,iftherewerenotreatyprovisions
to state that these agreements may provide performers with a right to remuneration, they still 
could.Thispartofparagraph (3)doesnothaveatruenormativerole.Thewayitiswordeddoes
not even read like a recommendation; the possibility to guarantee, through contracts, a share 
of the remuneration obtained for the authorization by the producer of the acts covered by the 
transferredrightsissimplydescribedasapossibility–although,inthecontextoftheBTAP,and
inviewofitsobjectandpurpose,suchasharetotheperformersseemstobequitejustified.
Whatneedsspecificcommentsisthereferenceto“royaltiesorequitableremuneration”as
alternatives. The two terms are in broad overlap with each other. The ordinary meaning of 
“royalty” is “a sum of money that is paid to someone who has written a book, piece of music, etc. 
each time that it is sold or performed”811 (that is, a recurrent payment due any time a use of the 
subject matter takes place), while the ordinary meaning of “remuneration” is “an amount of money 
that is paid to somebody for the work that they have done”.812 It follows from this that “royalty” 
is “remuneration” but not every kind of “remuneration” is “royalty”. Therefore, in the Treaties on 
copyrightandrelatedrights(andalsointheBTAP–withthesoleexceptionofArticle 12(3))–the
word “remuneration” is used as a generic term which also covers royalties. It follows from this 
that mentioning the two terms as alternatives seems unfortunate phrasing that may lead to 
somemisunderstandings.Sincetheadjective“equitable”appearsonlybefore“remuneration”,
therequirementofequitablenessmaybeunderstoodnottoapplyto“royalties”,forinstance,or
811 See https://www.oxfordlearnersdictionaries.com/definition/english/royalty.
812 See https://www.oxfordlearnersdictionaries.com/definition/english/remuneration.

===== PAGE 381 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
382 even that “royalties” do not fall in the category of remuneration, which obviously is not the case. 
Itisjustifiedtosimplyunderstand“royaltiesandequitableremuneration”tobeintendedtomean
“royaltiesandotherequitableremuneration”orsimply“royaltiesorotherremuneration”.
BT-12.82.Thispartofparagraph (3)referstocertainpossiblewaysofexercisingtheexclusive
rights of performers. In principle, when their performances are incorporated in audiovisual 
fixations–which,undertheBTAP,areaudiovisualworks–theycouldpreservetheirexclusive
rights to exercise them in parallel with the producers, the co-authors of the works and the other 
performers.Butthisonlyinprinciple,becausethecomplexityofsuchworksrequiresconsolidation
of the exclusive rights in the hands of the producers. Therefore, the performers usually transfer 
theirexclusiverightstotheproducersonthebasisofanagreement–collectiveand/orindividual
–thatmayguaranteethemappropriateremuneration.Itmaytaketheformofaone-timeadvance
payment, which means that no right to remuneration remains after the transfer of the rights, and, 
therefore,itdoesnotseemtobecoveredbyparagraph (3).Oritmaybearecurringpaymentfor
the uses of the performances authorized by the producers, either as a share of the remuneration 
obtainedbytheproducersordirectlyfromtheusers(althoughthisisfrequentlycombinedwith
an initial advance payment). Since such a right to remuneration is based on agreements, normally 
no double payment emerges in the sense that the users of audiovisual fixations would have to 
pay twice for the same production. When the performers receive payments from the producers, 
this is obvious, since it may be taken for granted that the producers set and obtain remuneration 
that corresponds to the value of the production in which the performances are incorporated, and 
the performers receive a share in accordance with their agreement with the producers. The end 
result is similar in cases where the producers authorize the use of the audiovisual fixations against 
payment, but allow the performers, under the agreement, to also obtain a recurring remuneration 
from the users directly. In such a case, the combined remuneration is supposed to correspond to 
the value of the work and its use; since the performers receive their share directly, the payment to 
the producers is to be proportionally lower.
Interpretation of paragraph (3): “national laws […] may provide the performer with the right 
to receive royalties or equitable remuneration for any use of the performance, as provided for 
under this Treaty including as regards Articles  10 and 11”
BT-12.83. At first superficial sight, it might seem that the same applies to such provisions 
in national laws as what is discussed above concerning individual, collective or “other” 
arrangements. To a certain extent, this is true: the application of both systems is just a 
possibility. However, where a national law provides for such remuneration to the performers for 
the same uses covered by the exclusive rights transferred to the producers along with the right 
toremunerationbuiltintothoserights,itraisesseveralquestions.Itisnecessarytoanalyzethe 
relationship of the right to remuneration transferred as an integral element of the exclusive 
rights and the right to remuneration provided to the performers for the same uses authorized 
bytheproducers.Theanalysismayextendtoatleastthreequestions:(i)whichsystemismore 
advantageous from the point of view of the object and purpose of the BTAP; that is, which one 
serves better “the protection of the rights of performers in their audiovisual performances in a 
manner as effective […] as possible”;813 (ii) how may it be achieved that the protection is “as […] 
uniform as possible” such that the nationals of the various Contracting Parties may enjoy the 
rights provided for in the BTAP under each other’s legal systems; and (iii) how can the double 
paymentofremunerationbytheusersforthesameusesbeavoidedwherethequestionof
combination of the agreement-based and statutory-law-based systems emerges.
BT-12.84. As regards the advantages or disadvantages of the two systems , their comparison is only 
meaningful if it is presumed that both are applied in complete, fully fledged form. A statutory 
right to remuneration has an obvious advantage to the performers in their negotiations with 
theproducers;theydonothavetonegotiatesucharightsincetheyhaveit;thequestionis
how it is combined with a possible advance payment. For the appropriate operation of such 
a system, the performers need a collective management organization that carries out its 
activitiesintheirfavorinaccordancewiththerequirementsofgoodgovernance,transparency 
and accountability. An efficiently functioning collective body to represent the interests and 
rights of “audiovisual performers” is also indispensable in an agreement-based system. These 
813 See thefirstpreambleparagraph oftheBTAP.

===== PAGE 382 =====
383
PART III. Guides to the three WIPO “Internet Treaties” – the WCT, the WPPT and the BTAP
organizations are needed to successfully negotiate a framework agreement within which the 
various performers may get appropriate remuneration. Without this, the individual performers 
are in a much weaker position, and only those have a real chance to negotiate a reasonable 
agreement who are already well-known and popular. It cannot be said, however, that the 
agreement-based systems are not beneficial both for the performers and the producers; where 
they are well-established, they do serve appropriately.
BT-12.85. By according exclusive rights to “audiovisual performers” to be granted as a minimum 
obligation of the Contracting Parties irrespective of whether they have agreement-based or 
statutory-right-based systems, the BTAP has established a basis for protection “as […] uniform 
as possible” (as stated in the Preamble). It is in itself a basic benefit of the BTAP that, in this way, 
the value of the performers’ contribution to the audiovisual productions is duly confirmed. It 
strengthens their position not only where they enjoy a statutory right to remuneration but 
also where they obtain remuneration on the basis of negotiations with the producers. This is 
so because, with the recognition of the underlining exclusive rights, they have a solid basis to 
claim that their remuneration must correspond to the value reflected by those rights. The BTAP, 
however, is not about domestic systems that may function appropriately in parallel despite 
their differences; it is about the obligation of the Contracting Parties to “accord the protection 
granted under this Treaty to performers who are nationals of other Contracting Parties” 
(Article 3oftheBTAP).Therefore,themostimportantquestionoftherelationshipofthetwo 
systemsishowtherightsoftheperformers –inparticular,theirrightstoremuneration–may 
prevail if the audiovisual fixations in which their performances are incorporated are used in a 
Contracting Party with a different legal system.
BT-12.86. The idea of solving the issue of the transfer of rights on the basis of private 
internationallawprincipleswasabandoned.Nevertheless,withtheadoptionofArticle 12on
the transfer of rights, at least one issue that may emerge in the application of those principles 
has been solved. By virtue of the provisions of the article, the Contracting Parties recognize 
that the obligations under the Treaty may be fulfilled through any of the systems mentioned 
there. A country cannot adhere to the BTAP without accepting that it is among the possible 
options that the producers of audiovisual fixations may be the owners of, or may exercise 
otherwise, the authors’ exclusive rights transferred to them. Therefore, they cannot cite “public 
order” implications by arguing that, under their laws, the original ownership of producers is 
not acceptable. As far as the agreement-based Contracting Parties are concerned, they are not 
obligated to introduce a specific statutory right to remuneration (which is only a possibility under 
Article 12(3)oftheBTAP);however,inordertofulfilltheirobligationtogranttheexclusiverights
prescribed in the Treaty along with the right to remuneration as an integral part thereof to the 
nationals of other Contracting Parties, they are certainly supposed to establish a legal framework 
to facilitate the application of their right to remuneration in the agreement-based system.
BT-12.87.Thequestionofrelationshipofthetwosystemsemergeswithgreatereffectinthe
Contracting Parties with a statutory right to remuneration, such as what is applied in the 
EU. There are two possible solutions, in principle, to try to solve the problems raised by the 
differences of the various systems that might be in accordance with the provisions and the 
declaredpurposeoftheBTAP.Thefirstoneisthattheproducersofagreement-basedcountries–
astheownersoftheexclusiverightsofperformers–claimandreceiveremunerationcalculated
in such a way that it also includes a part of the remuneration for the use of the entire audiovisual 
production also corresponding to their (the producers’) obligation to pay “residuals” to their 
performers. This option would presuppose that the producers could collect the remuneration 
provided to the performers in a statutory-law country that corresponds to the performers’ 
contractual right to receive “residuals”. The second possibility would be to allow the performers 
who are nationals of other Contracting Parties with agreement-based systems to collect 
remuneration due to the performers by virtue of statutory laws directly from the users on the 
understanding that, due to this, the producers’ contractual obligation to pay “residuals” does not 
extend to the uses authorized by them for which their performers collect remuneration directly.

===== PAGE 383 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
384 BT-12.88. There is a theory,814 however, according to which the part of the right to remuneration 
provided to performers by a national law is independent not only of the transfer of the 
exclusive rights to the producers, but also of the exclusive rights transferred. It is independent 
in spite of the fact that it is due for the uses authorized by the producers on the basis of the 
performers’ exclusive rights owned, exercised by or transferred to them. It is independent in 
the sense that the producers are not allowed to receive the entire remuneration for the use 
oftheaudiovisualfixationsalthough,inaccordancewithArticle 12oftheBTAP,theyown,or
may exercise, the performers’ rights fixed in those fixations. The performers whose exclusive 
rights have been transferred to the producers have a statutory right to remuneration carved 
out from the remuneration for the uses covered by their exclusive rights, authorized by the 
producers who own or may exercise those exclusive rights. The performers may collect that 
part of the remuneration for the uses authorized by the producers on the basis of their (the 
performers’)exclusiverightstransferredtothem.Furthermore–andmoreimportantly– 
according to such a theory, because the performers have the right to receive remuneration 
directly from the users (for the uses authorized by the producers as the rightholders of the 
performers’ exclusive rights) this right has nothing to do with the exercise of their exclusive 
rights transferred to the producers; it is an independent right to remuneration. And, still 
according to the theory, it is decisive that, although it follows from the provisions of the BTAP, it 
isnotarighttoremunerationprovidedinArticle 11oftheTreatywhich,byvirtueofArticle 4(1)
of the BTAP, is the only right to remuneration that the nationals of other Contracting Parties may 
enjoy. Therefore, under such a theory, the nationals of other Contracting Parties do not enjoy 
therighttoremuneration(inspiteofthefactthat,inArticle 12,itisstressedthattherightto
remuneration for the acts for which the performers may have a statutory right to remuneration 
doescover–“include” –theactscoveredbyArticle 11).
BT-12.89. This theory denying national treatment does not seem to be in accordance with 
Article 12orwiththeobjectandpurposeoftheBTAP.Itisnotjustamatterofnationaltreatment
to recognize the performers’ right to receive remuneration as an integral part of their exclusive 
rightsunderArticles 7to11oftheBTAP,butitisalsoaminimumobligationundertheTreaty.
It would not correspond to the concept of exclusive rights if the right to claim and receive 
remuneration for the authorization of the acts covered by such rights were not recognized 
as deriving from the exclusive nature of the rights. If a Contracting Party prescribes that a 
part of the remuneration for the acts covered by the exclusive rights must be received by the 
performers, it may be regarded as a justified measure to protect their interests as presumed 
weakerpartiesinthenegotiationswiththeproducers.However,thenthisright–asapartofthe
right to remuneration for the uses authorized by the producers as holders of the performers’ 
exclusiverightsaswellunderArticle 12oftheBTAP–issupposedtobegrantedalongwiththe
exclusive rights, as an integral element thereof, also to the nationals of other Contracting Parties.
BT-12.90. In principle, one may imagine a “solution” in accordance with the above-mentioned 
theory that the performers’ right to remuneration for the uses authorized on the basis of the 
exclusive rights is not covered by the right to remuneration as part of the exclusive rights but 
is a separate right to remuneration. In view of this, the right to remuneration which is separate 
from, and “independent” of, the exclusive rights for the application of which such remuneration 
is due, both the exclusive right and the separate, “independent” right to remuneration may 
be applied in parallel for the same acts authorized by the producers as the owners of the 
performers’ rights concerned. The description of such an imaginable “solution” in itself 
showsthatitishardlyacceptablesinceitwouldbeinconflictwiththebasiclegal–political 
considerations for which double payments for the same acts are not acceptable.
BT-12.91. In spite of what is outlined above on the basis of the traditional methods of 
interpretationoftheprovisionsofinternationaltreatiesascodifiedinArticles 31and32,it 
cannotbeexcludedthata“subsequentpractice”willbeformedalsointhiscasewithoutany 
opposition.A“subsequentpractice”(seeArticle 31.3(b)oftheVCLT)maybebasedonthelegal
fiction that, when a statutory right to remuneration is granted to those who have transferred 
their exclusive rights, that right to remuneration is not due for the acts covered by the exclusive 
814 For example, basically such a theory is outlined in Reinbothe and von Lewinski (it is argued that a right to 
remuneration–althoughnolongeranexclusiveright-isstilldueforactsauthorizedbytheownersoftheexclusive 
rights of which the right to claim remuneration is an integral part, even if no national treatment applies); see 541.

notapplytoit.A“subsequentpractice”maybeformedalongtheselinesevenifitsaccordance 
withArticle 12wouldbemorethandubious(itsdescriptionaboveshowshowcontradictoryit 
mightbe),butthisisthenatureofa“subsequentpractice”;ifitisacceptedbyalltheparties–or
atleastnotopposedbyanyofthem–itmayprevailinpractice.
BT-12.92. In summary, it may be said that the BTAP is to have a positive impact for the position 
of“audiovisualperformers”byprovidingcertainminimumrightstobegranted–whichthen
may be applied and exercised in different ways in the various Contracting Parties. It may also 
facilitatetheestablishmentofadequaterelationsbetweentheContractingPartiesbyobligating
them,throughArticle 12,torecognizetheownershiportheexerciseoftheperformers’exclusive
rights by the producers as being in accordance with the Treaty (thus, excluding the possibility to 
deny the recognition of such ownership or right to exercise by citing “public order” implications). 
However,theTreatymighttrulyfulfillitspurposedeclaredinthefirstparagraph ofthePreamble
only if it results also in mutual application of the performers’ rights in the relationship between 
Contracting Parties with agreement-based and statutory-rights-based systems, respectively.
Article 13
Limitations and Exceptions
(1) Contracting Parties may, in their national legislation, provide for the same kinds of 
limitations or exceptions with regard to the protection of performers as they provide 
for, in their national legislation, in connection with the protection of copyright in 
literary and artistic works.
(2) Contracting Parties shall confine any limitations of or exceptions to rights provided for 
in this Treaty to certain special cases which do not conflict with a normal exploitation 
of the performance and do not unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of 
the performer.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 13:TheAgreedstatementconcerningArticle 10(on
Limitations and Exceptions) of the WIPO Copyright Treaty (WCT) is applicable mutatis mutandis  
alsotoArticle 13(onLimitationsandExceptions)oftheTreaty.
BT-13.1.ThetextofArticle 13oftheBTAPisverbatimthesameasthetextofArticle 16ofthe
WPPT; therefore, the same comments apply to it as in the Guide to the WPPT above concerning 
saidarticle ofthatTreaty,whichinturnrefertothecommentsonArticle 9(2)oftheBerne
Conventionasthemodelofthethree-steptestprovidedinparagraph (2)ofthesearticles ofthe 
WPPT and the BTAP.
BT-13.2. It seems sufficient to refer to the main points of the comments made in the Guide to the 
BerneConventioninthiscollectionofguidesontheprototypeprovisionofArticle 9(2)onthe 
three-step test; as they likewise apply here. 
 – Thethreeconditionsofthetest–confinementtocertainspecialcases,noconflict
with a normal exploitation (there of the works, here of the performances), and no 
unreasonable prejudice to the legitimate interests of the rightholders (there of the 
authors,hereoftheperformers)–arecumulative;anexceptionorlimitationmayonly
be applied if all of them are fulfilled;
 – The first condition itself includes two cumulative conditions: (i) an exception or limitation 
mayonlycoveralimited–preciselyandnarrowlyconfined–caseand(ii)itmustbe
“special”inthesensethatitmustbejustifiablebysoundlegal–politicalreasons;815
815 This seems to be the dominant opinion among the commentators. There is, however, contrary opinion too, as 
discussedinthecommentstoArticle 9(2)oftheBerneConventionintheGuidetotheConventioninthiscollection 
(they refer to a WTO report in which the panel expressed the view that, in the context of the WTO agreements and 
theGATT–WTOdisputesettlementcaselaw,itisnotjustifiedtomakevaluejudgmentsingeneraland,thus,itisnot 
justified either to judge which case is special (and not just limited)).

===== PAGE 385 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
386  – Thesecondcondition–accordingtowhichanexceptionorlimitationmustnotconflict
withanormalexploitationoftheperformances–meansthatallformsofexploiting
awork–andhereaperformance–(thatis,extractingvalueoftheexclusiveright
ofreproductionintheworkthroughexercisingit)whichhas,orislikelytoacquire,
considerable economic or practical importance, must be reserved to the holder of the 
right, in such a way that the exceptions or limitations must not enter into economic 
competition with the exercise of the rights by the rightholder (in the sense that it must 
not undermine, to the detriment of the rightholder, the market);
 – Thethirdcondition–namelythatanexceptionorlimitationmustnotunreasonably
prejudicethelegitimateinterestsoftherightholders–expressesmostfullythatthe
objective of the three-step test is to strike a balance between various well-founded 
public and private interests. Legitimate interests mean the interests of the rightholders 
to enjoy and exercise their rights as fully as possible. It is inevitable that an exception 
or limitation tends to prejudice these interests; the prejudice must be, however, 
reasonable in the sense that it must not go beyond a certain level that may still be 
justifiedinconsiderationoftheunderliningsoundlegal–politicalconsiderations.
No more steps are needed. As the first WTO panel report that interpreted the (slightly adapted 
version) of the three-step test in a patent case pointed out, there is no need to take into account 
certain“externalities”–suchasdevelopment,competitionorhumanrightsconsiderations– 
beyond the three cumulative conditions of the test. 816 All those considerations are supposed to 
be taken into account and can be duly assessed as part oftheadequateapplicationofthetest.
BT-13.3.InthesamewayasinthecaseofArticle 16oftheWPPT,anagreedstatementrefers
totheagreedstatementconcerningArticle 10oftheWCTonexceptionsandlimitationsinthe
digitalenvironment.ThecommentsonthatagreedstatementintheGuidetotheWCT–the 
essence of which is that the three-step test is to govern the applicability of the exceptions and 
limitationsinthenewenvironment–applyalsointhecontextoftheBTAP.
Article 14
Term of Protection
The term of protection to be granted to performers under this Treaty shall last, at least, until the 
end of a period of 50 years computed from the end of the year in which the performance was fixed.
BT-14.1. Since the performances fixed in audiovisual works become integral parts of the works, 
it would have seemed reasonable to provide for the same term of protection of the rights in 
performances fixed in such works as for those works and for the contributions of the co-authors 
thereof. The Canadian delegation raised this idea at the 2000 Diplomatic Conference, 817 but did 
notultimatelysubmitaproposaltothiseffect.TheChairmanofMainCommittee I,JukkaLiedes, 
however, stated that, since the term of protection under the Basic Proposal was just a minimum, 
those Contracting Parties that find it justified may provide for the same term of protection as for 
the audiovisual works (or the co-authors thereof). 818
BT-14.2.Thus,theWPPTmodelhasbeenapplied;theprovisionofArticle 14oftheBTAPis
verbatimthesameastheprovisionofArticle 17(1)oftheWPPT.

Article 15
Obligations concerning Technological Measures
ContractingPartiesshallprovideadequatelegalprotectionandeffectivelegalremediesagainst
the circumvention of effective technological measures that are used by performers in connection 
with the exercise of their rights under this Treaty and that restrict acts, in respect of their 
performances, which are not authorized by the performers concerned or permitted by law.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 15asitrelatestoArticle 13:Itisunderstoodthat
nothinginthisArticle preventsaContractingPartyfromadoptingeffectiveandnecessary
measures to ensure that a beneficiary may enjoy limitations and exceptions provided in that 
ContractingParty’snationallaw,inaccordancewithArticle 13,wheretechnologicalmeasures
have been applied to an audiovisual performance and the beneficiary has legal access to 
that performance, in circumstances such as where appropriate and effective measures have 
not been taken by rights holders in relation to that performance to enable the beneficiary 
to enjoy the limitations and exceptions under that Contracting Party’s national law. Without 
prejudice to the legal protection of an audiovisual work in which a performance is fixed, it is 
furtherunderstoodthattheobligationsunderArticle 15arenotapplicabletoperformances
unprotected or no longer protected under the national law giving effect to this Treaty.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 15:Theexpression“technologicalmeasuresusedby
performers” should, as this is the case regarding the WPPT, be construed broadly, referring 
also to those acting on behalf of performers, including their representatives, licensees or 
assignees, including producers, service providers, and persons engaged in communication or 
broadcasting using performances on the basis of due authorization.
The same provisions as in the WPPT
BT-15.1.TheprovisionofArticle 15oftheBTAPisverbatimthesameastheprovisionofArticle 18
of the WPPT, which, in turn, is a mutatis mutandis versionofArticle 11oftheWCT.Therefore,the
same comments apply to this provision as those made in the Guide to the WCT and the Guide 
totheWPPTaboveconcerningtherespectivearticles ofthosetreaties.However,inthecontext 
of the BTAP, to the same provision two agreed statements were added. The second one was 
adopted earlier and without any substantive debate since it was regarded to state what seemed 
to be obvious. The agreed statement presented as the first one above was adopted only at the 
Beijing Diplomatic Conference after intensive debates as is described below.
Agreed statement concerning “technological measures that are used by performers”
BT-15.2. It was clear also with respect to the provisions of the WCT and the WPPT that, while they 
refer to “technological measures that are used by [authors][performers]”, this also means those 
measures that are used on their behalf to protect their rights directly or indirectly when they are 
incorporated in other productions, such as audiovisual works, collections, published editions or 
phonograms.ThiswasmadeclearinthenotesaddedtothedraftofArticle 15inthe2000Basic
Proposal with respect to “audiovisual performers”. 819 At the Diplomatic Conference, however, 
the delegation of Canada suggested that this clarification be transformed into an agreed 
statement.820Itwasnotcontroversial–andinthecaseof“audiovisualperformers”particularly 
obvious,sincenormallynottheybuttheproducerstakecareofsuchmeasures–anditwas
adopted in 2000 provisionally and then in 2012 finally without any real debate.
Agreed statement “concerning Article 15 as it relates to Article 13”
BT-15.3. It was agreed upon as part of the compromise adopted in 2011 which opened the

articles wouldnotbeopenforfurthernegotiations,threeagreedstatementswouldstillbe 
adopted,oneofthethreeconcerningArticle 15ontechnologicalmeasures.

388 BT-15.4. At the start of the Beijing Diplomatic Conference, there were three competing 
proposals.Twoofthem–thejointproposalbyBrazil,MexicoandtheUnitedStates,ontheone

BT-15.5. Brazil, Mexico and the United States proposed the following agreed statement:
It is understood that in the absence of voluntary measures taken by rights holders 
in relation to a particular performance protected under this treaty, nothing in this 
Article shallpreventaContractingPartyfromadoptingappropriatemeasures and permit 
that a beneficiary of a limitation or exception provided in its national law in accordance 
with Article 13 may benefit from such limitation or exception where technological 
measures have been applied to an audiovisual performance and the beneficiary has legal 
access to that performance. Without prejudice to the legal protection of an audiovisual 
work in which a performance is fixed, it is further understood that the obligations under 
Article 15arenotapplicableto performances unprotected concerning the economic rights 
under the national legislation giving effect to this Treaty, including but not limited to the expiry 
of the term of protection of the economic rights.821 
BT-15.6.Intheabovetext,thosepartsareemphasizedinwhichtheEU–Kenyan–Nigerian
proposal differed. In that proposal, (i) the word “procedures” was used instead of “measures” 
and the verb “ensure” instead of “permit”; (ii) a comma appeared after (but not before) the 
crucialphrase“inaccordancewithArticle 13”;and(iii)thelastpartofthesecondsentenceread
as follows: “to performances unprotected or no longer protected under the national legislation 
giving effect to this Treaty”.822
BT-15.7. India proposed this text:
Itisunderstoodthattheadequateprotectionoftechnologicalmeasuresappliedtoa
particular audiovisual performance shall not prevent contracting parties from adopting 
adequateandeffectivemeasuresnecessarytoensureexerciseoflimitationsand
exceptionsinaccordancewithArticle 13tothatperformanceandaccesstoperformance
in the public domain.823
The Indian proposal differed from the two joint proposals in the following aspects: (i) it used the 
adjectives“adequateandeffective”referringtomeasuresratherthantheadjective“appropriate”
referring to measures/procedures; (ii) it did not state that those measures may only be applied 
in the absence of voluntary measures; (iii) it did not reduce the applicability of such measures 
to those cases where the beneficiary has legal access to the performance; (iv) it contained the 
phrase“inaccordancewithArticle 13”aftertheshorttext“toensureexerciseoflimitations
and exceptions” rather than just directly after the text “a limitation or exception provided in its 
national law”; and (v) instead of the complete respective second sentence of each of the joint 
proposals, it simply referred to “access to performance in the public domain” to be ensured.
BT-15.8. As can be seen, in the adopted text of the agreed statement, the expression “effective 
andnecessarymeasures”isusedratherthan“appropriatemeasures”asintheBrazilian–
Mexican–USproposal,“appropriateprocedures”asintheEU–Kenyan–Nigerianproposal,and 
“adequateandeffectivemeasures”asintheIndianproposal.Thecombinationofadjectives 
“effective and necessary ” before the word “measures” is the result of a compromise reached after 
intensive negotiations. The adjective “necessary” was not used in any of the three proposals; 
it relates to the idea emerging during the informal consultations that it should be made clear 
that the “measures” are only applicable where necessary; in particular, where the rightholder 
applying technological measure does not make the protected material accessible voluntarily.
821 DocumentAVP/DC/10;emphasisadded.
822 SeedocumentAVP/DC/11.
823DocumentAVP/DC/14.

===== PAGE 388 =====
389
PART III. Guides to the three WIPO “Internet Treaties” – the WCT, the WPPT and the BTAP
BT-15.9. In the adopted text, the principle of the priority of voluntary measures to make the 
protected materials accessible, rather than immediate use of an intervention mechanism, is not 
reflected as clearly as in the two joint proposals. Nevertheless, it is still expressed in the phrase 
“in circumstances such as where appropriate and effective measures have not been taken by 
rights holders in relation to that performance to enable the beneficiary to enjoy the limitations 
and exceptions” which indicates this as the most typical (and, probably, the only) example of 
situations where the intervention measures may be necessary.
BT-15.10. It is a basic criterion that the intervention “measures” may only be applied where 
the beneficiary of the exception or limitation has legal access to the performance. This seems 
to correspond to one of the conditions of the applicability of such “measures” provided in the 
fourthnon-numberedsubparagraph ofArticle 6(4)oftheEUInformationSocietyDirective:
The provisions of the first and second subparagraphs [on the intervention mechanisms to 
ensure the applicability of certain limitations and exceptions] shall not apply to works or 
other subject matter made available to the public on agreed contractual terms in such a 
way that members of the public may access them from a place and at a time individually 
chosen by them.
BoththeBrazilian–Mexican–USproposalandtheEU–Kenyan–Nigerianproposalreferredto 
the objective of the intervention “measures” as ensuring that the beneficiaries may benefit 
from the exceptions or limitations. In the adopted text the synonymous expression “ to enable 
the beneficiary to enjoy the limitations and exceptions” is used. Although the verb “to enjoy” 
islessfrequentlyusedintheprovisionsconcerninglimitationsandexceptionsthantheverb
“to benefit”, its meaning is practically the same. The beneficiaries benefit from the possibility 
that they are allowed to use freely the protected subject matter and enjoy, in this way, the 
advantages of the exception or limitation. In contrast, the use of the expression of “exercising” 
an exception or limitation as suggested in one of the proposals would not correspond to the 
concepts of an exception or limitation; those who are allowed by it to do something freely do 
benefit from and enjoy it, they do not “exercise” something.
BT-15.11. The relationship between Article 15 and Article 13 –towhichthetitleoftheagreement
refers–wasakeyissueaddressedintheagreedstatement.Theadoptedtextmakesitclear
thattheconditionsofthethree-steptestprovidedinArticle 13oftheTreatyapplybothforthe
questionofwhatkindsoflimitationsandexceptionsmaybeprovidedinnationallawsandfor
thequestionofinwhichcasesandhowthe“measures”mentionedinthestatementmaybe
applied. This is expressed clearly in the structure of the text. The phrase “in accordance with 
Article 13”appearsbetweencommasand,thus,thethree-steptestcontrolsnotonlythetext 
immediately before it (in which case it could have been read and understood also in this way: 
“limitationorexceptionprovidedinitsnationallawinaccordancewithArticle 13”)buttheentire 
sentence before it. It is clarified in this way (i) that any “measures” may only be applied in case of 
limitations and exceptions that are provided in accordance with the three-step test; and (ii) that 
the cases where the “measures” are applied and the way they are applied also must correspond 
to the three cumulative conditions of the test. 824
BT-15.12. The second sentence on performances in the public domain seems to be unnecessary 
sinceArticle 15onlycoverstechnologicalmeasures“thatareusedbyperformersinconnection 
with the exercise of their rights under this Treaty”; therefore, since no rights exist in such 
performances,Article 15hasnoapplication.Thequestionmayberaisedwhatkindsof 
performances are “unprotected” other than those “no longer protected” in the expression 
“unprotected or no longer protected”. A possible answer may be that the performances of those 
performersaremeantwhoarenotbeneficiariesofprotectionunderArticle 3oftheTreaty 
(since they are not nationals of, nor have their habitual residence in, any Contracting Party). It 
is needless to say that, from this viewpoint, the second sentence is also unnecessary because 
there are no rights in such performances under the Treaty.

390 BT-15.13. The second sentence could potentially have had an unintended effect in the sense that, 
on its basis, someone might have claimed that the inclusion of an unprotected performance in 
an audiovisual work would permit the application of “measures” in respect of that otherwise 
protected audiovisual work as well. The basis for such a potential claim has been eliminated by 
the phrase at the beginning of the second sentence: “Without prejudice to the legal protection 
of an audiovisual work in which a performance is fixed”.
Article 16
Obligations concerning Rights Management Information
(1) ContractingPartiesshallprovideadequateandeffectivelegalremediesagainstany
person knowingly performing any of the following acts knowing, or with respect to civil 
remedies having reasonable grounds to know, that it will induce, enable, facilitate, or 
conceal an infringement of any right covered by this Treaty:
(i)  to remove or alter any electronic rights management information 
without authority;
(ii)  to distribute, import for distribution, broadcast, communicate or make available 
to the public, without authority, performances or copies of performances fixed 
in audiovisual fixations knowing that electronic rights management information 
has been removed or altered without authority.
(2) As used in this Article, “rights management information” means information which 
identifies the performer, the performance of the performer, or the owner of any 
right in the performance, or information about the terms and conditions of use 
of the performance, and any numbers or codes that represent such information, 
when any of these items of information is attached to a performance fixed in an 
audiovisual fixation.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 16:TheAgreedstatementconcerningArticle 12(on
Obligations concerning Rights Management Information) of the WCT is applicable mutatis 
mutandis alsotoArticle 16(onObligationsconcerningRightsManagementInformation)of
the Treaty.
BT-16.1.TheprovisionsofArticle 16onrightsmanagementinformationusedfortheexercise
and enforcement of rights are mutatis mutandis thesameastheprovisionsinArticle 12ofthe
WCTandArticle 19oftheWPPT–andthesameistrueoftheagreedstatementsconcerning
these provisions. Therefore, the comments made in the Guide to the WPPT and the Guide to the 
WCT above on those provisions likewise apply here mutatis mutandis.
Article 17 
Formalities
The enjoyment and exercise of the rights provided for in this Treaty shall not be subject to 
any formality.
BT-17.1.Thisprovision–verbatimthesameastheprovisionofArticle 20oftheWPPT–isclear
and self-explanatory. By this provision, both the WPPT and the BTAP follow the same principle of 
formality-freeprotectionasstatedinArticle 5(2)oftheBerneConventionconcerningcopyright. 
It is worth noting this because the Rome Convention and the Phonograms Convention still allow 
theapplicationofformalitiesinrelationtophonograms,providing,however–intheirArticle 11
andArticle 5,respectively–thatanyformalitiesareconsideredtobefulfilledifthebriefnotice 
described in those provisions is indicated on the copies of the phonograms in commerce or on 
their containers.

Article 18
Reservations and Notifications
(1) SubjecttoprovisionsofArticle 11(3),noreservationstothisTreatyshallbepermitted.
(2) AnynotificationunderArticle 11(2)or19(2)maybemadeininstrumentsofratification
or accession, and the effective date of the notification shall be the same as the date of 
entry into force of this Treaty with respect to the Contracting Party having made the 
notification. Any such notification may also be made later, in which case the notification 
shall have effect three months after its receipt by the Director General of WIPO or at 
any later date indicated in the notification.
Declarations as reservations
BT-18.1.ItmaybesaidthatArticle 18(1)oftheBTAPismutatis mutandis thesameasArticle 21of
the WPPT since the only difference is that the BTAP provision makes the no-reservation principle 
subjecttoArticle 11(3),andtheWPPTprovision,toArticle 15(3).However,theprovisionsto
which the principle is subject differ both in substance and, in a certain aspect, regarding 
thelanguage.UnderArticle 15(3)oftheWPPT,aContractingParty“may,inanotification
[…]declare”thatitonlyappliesarighttoequitableremunerationprovidedinArticle 15(3),
whileunderArticle 11(3)oftheBTAP,aContractingParty“maydeclare”(withoutmentionofa
notification)thatit“willapplytheprovisionsofparagraph (1)or(2)[ofArticle 11]onlyinrespect
of certain uses, or that it will limit their application in some other way, or that it will not apply the 
provisionspfparagraphs (1)and(2)atall”(andinparagraph (1)anexclusiverightisprovidedfor,
whichunderparagraph (2)maybelimitedtoarighttoremunerationbyanotification).
BT-18.2.Suchdeclarationsaretoberegardedasreservations,asthetitleofArticle 18(1)ofthe
BTAPandthewords“[s]ubjectto”inboththeWPPTandtheBTAPrefertothis.Article 19ofthe
VCLTprovidesthat,whereitisallowed,areservationmaybeformulated(only)“whensigning,
ratifying,accepting,approvingoraccedingtoatreaty”.Thisalsoappliestothe“declarations”– 
asreservations–intheabove-mentionedprovisionsoftheWPPTandtheBTAP.
Notifications
BT-18.3.IncontrastwithArticle 21oftheWPPT,Article 18alsohasasecondparagraph.The
meaningofArticle 18(2)isclear.Theonlycommentthatisnecessaryistodrawattentionto
the difference between these “notifications” and “reservations”: while reservations may be 
formulatedintheinstrumentsofratificationoraccession(seetheprovisionofArticle 19ofthe 
VCLT),thenotificationsreferredtoinArticle 18(2)–asexpresslystatedinthesecondsentence– 
may also be made later and they enter into force after three months.
Article 19 
Application in Time
(1) Contracting Parties shall accord the protection granted under this Treaty to fixed 
performances that exist at the moment of the entry into force of this Treaty and to all 
performances that occur after the entry into force of this Treaty for each Contracting Party.
(2) Notwithstandingtheprovisionsofparagraph (1),aContractingPartymaydeclare
in a notification deposited with the Director General of WIPO that it will not apply 
theprovisionsofArticles 7to11ofthisTreaty,oranyoneormoreofthose,tofixed
performances that existed at the moment of the entry into force of this Treaty for each 
Contracting Party. In respect of such Contracting Party, other Contracting Parties may 
limittheapplicationofthesaidArticles toperformancesthatoccurredaftertheentry
into force of this Treaty for that Contracting Party.
(3) The protection provided for in this Treaty shall be without prejudice to any acts 
committed,agreementsconcludedorrightsacquiredbeforetheentryintoforceofthis
Treaty for each Contracting Party.

===== PAGE 391 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
392 (4) Contracting Parties may in their legislation establish transitional provisions under 
which any person who, prior to the entry into force of this Treaty, engaged in 
lawful acts with respect to a performance, may undertake with respect to the same 
performanceactswithinthescopeoftherightsprovidedforinArticles 5and7to11
after the entry into force of this Treaty for the respective Contracting Parties.
Application for existing audiovisual fixations
BT-19.1.Paragraph (1)oftheArticle isbasedonthesameprincipleasArticle 18oftheBerne
ConventionandArticle 22(1)oftheWPPT,whichsimplyreferstotheBerneprovisionsinthis
respect. This means that the Treaty is applicable to the subject matter existing at the moment of 
its entry into force for the given Contracting Party, but only with respect to the acts performed 
afteritsentryintoforce.Therefore,theTreaty–similarlytotheBerneConventionandthe
WPPT–isnotappliedretroactively,despiteanypossibleerroneousreferencetotheeffectof 
these provisions as “retroactive protection”. Nevertheless, although these provisions are not 
retroactive, they are retrospective in the sense that the application of the protection to the 
existingfixationsalsomeanstheapplicationofArticle 14onthetermofprotection,which 
means that the protection applies to all fixed performances for which the 50-year term of 
protection has not yet expired.
Possible exclusion of application for existing audiovisual fixations
BT-19.2.TheprovisionsoftheBTAP,duetowhatisprovidedinArticle 19(2),differfromthe
provisionsofArticle 18oftheBerneConvention,Article 13oftheWCTandArticle 22oftheWPPT.
Article 19(2)oftheBTAP,incontrastwiththerelevantprovisionsoftheseotherWIPO-administered
treatiesandwhatisprovidedinArticle 19(1)oftheBTAPitself,allowstheContractingPartiesto
notapplytheeconomicrightsprovidedinArticles 7to11tofixedperformancesthatexistatthe
timeoftheentryintoforceoftheTreaty.Thus,thisprovisionisnotapplicabletoArticle 5onmoral
rights(ortoArticle 6ontherightinunfixedperformances,whichsimplycannotapply,sincethe
applicationofArticle 19(1)mayonlyemergewherethereisanexistingfixation,andthis,inthecase
ofliveperformances,isexcluded).ItisworthnotingthatArticle 22(2)oftheWPPTalsoprovides
foranexceptiontothegeneralruleonapplicationintime–butonlyconcerningArticle 5onmoral
rights(which,incontrast,arenotcoveredbyArticle 19(2)oftheBTAP).
BT-19.3.Underthesecondsentenceofparagraph (2),ifaContractingPartyexcludesthe
application of the economic rights to performances fixed already at the moment of entry into 
force of the Treaty, other Contracting Parties may limit its application for the fixations of that 
Contracting Party in the same way.
No retroactivity; transitional provisions
BT-19.4. The purpose of the provisions of paragraphs (3) and (4) is to clearly exclude any real 
retroactive effect of the protection of the BTAP when it enters into force for a Contracting Party. 
Whatisprovidedinparagraph (3)istrulyjustclarificationofwhatfollowsfromparagraph (1),
namely that the Treaty applies from the moment of its entry into force also to the fixed 
performancesalreadyexistingatthatmoment–butonlyfromthatmoment.Consequentlyit 
does not apply to the acts previously performed concerning the existing fixations, and it does 
notmakevalidpreviousagreementsnon-applicableretroactively.Thisisstatedinparagraph (3).
BT-19.5.Paragraph (4)hasaconnectionwithparagraph (3),becauseitregulates,inter alia, the 
questionofapplicabilityofagreementsconcludedpriortheentryintoforceoftheTreatyafter 
its entry into force. The provision reflects the recognition that contracts have been concluded 
and investments have been made in the period when the protection did not yet apply to certain 
acts. Those who have engaged in such activities need to adapt to the new legal situation. The 
transitionalmeasuresthatmaybeallowedunderparagraph (4)makesuchadaptationpossible.
It follows from the very concept that the measures are supposed to be transitional: they should 
be limited in time just to ensure that those who engaged in lawful activities before do not suffer 
unreasonable prejudice due to the immediate application of the Treaty. The comments made 
concerningthetransitionalprovisionsofArticle 18oftheBerneConventionintheGuideto
the Convention in this collection of guides apply mutatis mutandis to the relevant provisions of 
Article 19oftheBTAPaswell.

Article 20
Provisions on Enforcement of Rights
(1) Contracting Parties undertake to adopt, in accordance with their legal systems, the 
measures necessary to ensure the application of this Treaty.
(2) Contracting Parties shall ensure that enforcement procedures are available under their 
law so as to permit effective action against any act of infringement of rights covered 
by this Treaty, including expeditious remedies to prevent infringements and remedies 
which constitute a deterrent to further infringements.
BT-20.1.TheprovisionsofArticle 20areverbatimthesameastheprovisionsofArticle 14of
theWCTandArticle 23oftheWPPT.Theywereadoptedwithoutanysubstantivedebatefirst 
provisionally in 2000 and then finally in 2012 in Beijing. The same comments apply to them, 
mutatis mutandis, as those made above in the Guide to the WCT and the Guide to the WPPT to 
the said provisions of those Treaties.
Administrative and final clauses
TheprovisionsofArticles 21to30oftheBTAPcontaintheusualadministrativeandfinalclauses
of WIPO treaties. They are by nature self-explanatory and do not raise real interpretation 
questions.Therefore,commentsaremadeonlyonthoseprovisionsthatshowsomespecificities.
Article 21 
Assembly
(1) (a)  The Contracting Parties shall have an Assembly.
(b)  Each Contracting Party shall be represented in the Assembly by one delegate 
who may be assisted by alternate delegates, advisors and experts.
(c)  The expenses of each delegation shall be borne by the Contracting Party that 
has appointed the delegation. The Assembly may ask WIPO to grant financial 
assistance to facilitate the participation of delegations of Contracting Parties 
that are regarded as developing countries in conformity with the established 
practice of the General Assembly of the United Nations or that are countries in 
transition to a market economy.
(2) (a)  The Assembly shall deal with matters concerning the maintenance and 
development of this Treaty and the application and operation of this Treaty.
(b) TheAssemblyshallperformthefunctionallocatedtoitunderArticle 23(2)in
respect of the admission of certain intergovernmental organizations to become 
party to this Treaty.
(c)  The Assembly shall decide the convocation of any diplomatic conference for 
the revision of this Treaty and give the necessary instructions to the Director 
General of WIPO for the preparation of such diplomatic conference.
(3) (a)  Each Contracting Party that is a State shall have one vote and shall vote only in 
its own name.
(b)  Any Contracting Party that is an intergovernmental organization may 
participate in the vote, in place of its Member States, with a number of votes 
equaltothenumberofitsMemberStateswhicharepartytothisTreaty.No
such intergovernmental organization shall participate in the vote if any one of 
its Member States exercises its right to vote and vice versa.
(4)  The Assembly shall meet upon convocation by the Director General and, in the 
absence of exceptional circumstances, during the same period and at the same 
place as the General Assembly of WIPO.

394 (5)  The Assembly shall endeavor to take its decisions by consensus and shall 
establish its own rules of procedure, including the convocation of extraordinary 
sessions,therequirementsofaquorumand,subjecttotheprovisionsofthis
Treaty,therequiredmajorityforvariouskindsofdecisions.
BT-21.1.TheprovisionsofArticle 21(1)to(3)correspondtotheprovisionsofsimilarWIPOtreaties
ontheAssembliesoftheContractingPartiesandtheyareverbatimthesameasArticle 15(1)to
(3)oftheWCTandArticle 24(1)to(3)oftheWPPT(onlythenumbersoftheprovisionsreferredto
aredifferent).Paragraphs (4)and(5),however,differtoacertainextentfromthecorresponding
paragraphs in the WCT and the WPPT.
BT-21.2.AccordingtoArticle 15(4)oftheWCTandArticle 24(4)oftheWPPT,theAssembliesof
the Contracting Parties of those Treaties are to meet in ordinary session once every two years. It 
has since become practice for the Assemblies established under the various WIPO-administered 
treaties to have their sessions at the same place (usually in Geneva) and at the same time as 
the General Assembly of WIPO. This practice, in principle, was formally in conflict with those 
provisions of WIPO treaties that provided for one ordinary session every two years. However, 
because they did not exclude the possibility of extraordinary sessions this was not a real conflict. 
ItwasalreadyinArticle 23(6)oftheSingaporeTreatyontheLawofTrademarks(STLT)that
annualsessionsweremadetheofficialrule.Asnote21.01addedtothedraftArticle inthe
Basic Proposal prepared for the Beijing Diplomatic Conference indicated, 825 the STLT model was 
followed in the BTAP.826
BT-21.3.ThechangeintheprovisionofArticle 21(5)oftheBTAP,incomparisonwiththesame
paragraphs in the WCT and WPPT Articles, is of a similar nature. Under these provisions, the 
Assemblyestablishes,aspartoftherulesofprocedure,whatmajorityisrequiredforthevarious 
decisions. It follows from this that those decisions may also be adopted by a majority vote. In 
Article 21(5)oftheBTAP,thisisalsomentionedasaruletobedeterminedbytheAssembly–
thus, the possibility of the adoption of the decisions by a majority vote has been maintained 
–but,inaccordancewiththeemergingprinciplethat,ifpossible,theWIPObodiesadopttheir 
decisions by consensus, this is indicated as an objective to which the Assembly should aspire. 827
Article 22 
International Bureau
The International Bureau of WIPO shall perform the administrative tasks concerning the Treaty.
Article 23
Eligibility for Becoming Party to the Treaty
(1) Any Member State of WIPO may become party to this Treaty.
(2) The Assembly may decide to admit any intergovernmental organization to become 
party to this Treaty which declares that it is competent in respect of, and has its own 
legislation binding on all its Member States on, matters covered by this Treaty and 
that it has been duly authorized, in accordance with its internal procedures, to become 
party to this Treaty.
(3) The European Union, having made the declaration referred to in the preceding 
paragraph intheDiplomaticConferencethathasadoptedthisTreaty,maybecome
party to this Treaty.

Article 24
Rights and Obligations under the Treaty
Subject to any specific provisions to the contrary in this Treaty, each Contracting Party shall 
enjoy all of the rights and assume all of the obligations under this Treaty.
Article 25
Signature of the Treaty
ThisTreatyshallbeopenforsignatureattheheadquartersofWIPObyanyeligiblepartyfor
one year after its adoption.
BT-25.1.Article 25followstheSTLT–ratherthantheWPPT–model.Article 28oftheWPPT
provides that the Treaty was to be open until December 31, 1997, for signature by any Member 
StateofWIPOandbytheEuropeanUnion;thatis,bythosewhich,accordingtoArticle 26ofthe
WPPT(thetextofwhichisidenticalwithArticle 23oftheBTAP),wereeligibletobecomepartyto 
theTreaty.UnderArticle 31(2)oftheSTLT,incontrast,theTreatyremainedopenforsignature
attheheadquartersoftheOrganizationforoneyearafteritsadoption.Since,inthatrespect, 
Article 25hadthesameprovisionandbecausetheBTAPwasadoptedonJune24,2012,itwas
openforsignatureuntilJune26,2013.
Article 26
Entry into Force of the Treaty
ThisTreatyshallenterintoforcethreemonthsafter30eligiblepartiesreferredtoinArticle 23
have deposited their instruments of ratification or accession.
BT-26.1.Article 26oftheBTAPdiffersfromArticle 29oftheWPPTinthatitprovidesfor30
eligible parties, rather than 30 States, to have deposited their instruments of ratification for the 
entryintoforceoftheTreaty.This(inviewoftheprovisionsofArticle 23)meant,inadditionto
the Member States of the WIPO, also the EU.828
Article 27
Effective Date of Becoming Party to the Treaty 
This Treaty shall bind:
(i) the30eligiblepartiesreferredtoinArticle 26,fromthedateonwhichthisTreatyhas
entered into force;
(ii) eachothereligiblepartyreferredtoinArticle 23,fromtheexpirationofthreemonths
from the date on which it has deposited its instrument of ratification or accession with 
the Director General of WIPO.
BT-27.1.Article 30onEffectiveDateofBecomingPartytotheWPPTincludesfourparagraphs:

intergovernmental organization. The rules on the entry into force for the Member States, the 
EC and other possible intergovernmental organizations have not changed in substance, but

Depositary
The Director General of WIPO is the depositary of this Treaty.

PART IV. Guide to the 
Marrakesh VIP Treaty
Introduction
TheofficialtitleoftheTreatyadoptedinMarrakesh,Morocco,onJune17,2013is“Treatyto
FacilitateAccesstoPublishedWorksforPersonsWhoAreBlind,VisuallyImpaired,orOtherwise 
PrintDisabled”.Itisquitesurethatitwillberarelyreferredtobythislongtitle.Onthewebsite
of the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), under the treaties administered by the 
Organization,itislistedas“MarrakeshVIPTreaty”andthisabbreviatedtitleisusedincertain 
commentaries as well.829Insomeothercommentariesashorterabbreviation–MT–appears, 830 
and in still others it is just called the “Marrakesh Treaty”. 831 This Guide uses the title “Marrakesh 
VIPTreaty”orshortenedversionsofthis.Also,theshortforms“thevisuallyimpaired”and 
“visually impaired and other print disabled persons” are generally used in place of “persons who 
are blind, visually impaired, or otherwise print disabled” as it appears in the title of the Treaty.
In the statements made at the adoption session of the Marrakesh Diplomatic Conference and 
immediately after it, the Marrakesh Treaty was characterized by various adjectives to emphasize its 
importanceandtodescribeitsspecialnature,suchas“exceptional”,“unique”andeven“historical”.
The Marrakesh Treaty is certainly historical from the viewpoint of the visually impaired 
and other print disabled people in that the international community has devoted a special 
treaty exclusively to facilitate their access to works both by legal provisions and through an 
organizational framework of enhanced worldwide cooperation.
The Treaty is also historical in another respect. With its adoption, a troubled historical period in 
international copyright relations seems to have ended in a reasonable manner. It began not long 
after the adoption of the two WIPO “Internet Treaties” (the WIPO Copyright Treaty (WCT) and 
the WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty (WPPT)) and lasted for more than a decade. 
Certain poorly informed and badly founded allegations were spreading about the international 
copyright system, such as that it does not guarantee due balance of interests, that it only 
concentratesontheprotectionofrights,thatitdoesnotallowtheapplicationofadequate
exceptions and limitations in recognition of important public and legitimate private interests, 
that it is an obstacle to due access to works, and so on.
Itwouldrequireaseparatevoluminousstudytoanalyzetheideologicalorspecial-interests-
driven reasons behind these attacks against copyright. 832 Nevertheless, two visible reasons may 
stillbementionedwhichplayedaroleinthisperiod.First,that–partlyasacollateraleffectof 
tradenegotiations–newtensionshadappearedinthefieldofintellectualpropertyandnew 
ideas on how the IP system could better serve development. Second, new powerful interest 
groups and a number of new organizations suddenly started participating in the copyright 
829 See,forexample,JørgenBlomqvist,Primer on International Copyright and Related Rights  (Cheltenham: Edward Elgar, 2014) 
(hereinafter:Blomqvist).
830 See,forexample,LaurenceR.Helfer,MollyK.Land,RuthL.OkedjiandJeromeH.Reichman, The World Blind Union 
Guide to the Marrakesh Treaty, available at https://www.wipo.int/edocs/mdocs/copyright/en/wipo_cr_mow_17/
wipo_cr_mow_17_topic_2_c.pdf  (hereinafter: WBU Guide).
831 See,forexample,JörgReinbotheandSilkevonLewinski, The WIPO Treaties on Copyright: A Commentary on the WCT, the 
WPPT, and the BTAP, Second edition (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2015) (hereinafter: Reinbothe and von Lewinski).
832 For a description of these aspects that emerged in the preparatory work of the Marrakesh Treaty, see Reinbothe and 
vonLewinski,616–617.

398 meetings of WIPO, many of which did not yet have sufficient information and experience about 
WIPO’s activities and the operation of the international copyright system, and they had some 
biased preconceptions about it.
Time was needed for a new consolidation. It has taken place gradually as a result of (i) smoothly 
integrating new development-oriented emphases into the activities of the Organization 
in a well-balanced manner avoiding ideology-based exaggerations (this development was 
manifested in the adoption of the WIPO Development Agenda in 2007); and (ii) a welcome 
recognitionthattheexistinginternationalcopyrightnorms–ratherthanraisinganyobstacles 
–doofferanadequatebasisforestablishingandoperatingasystemsuitablebothtograntthe 
necessary incentives for creation of valuable works and due reward for the creators and, at the 
sametime,toensure–throughappropriatelimitationsandexceptions–availabilityofthose
works to the general public.
At the closure of the Diplomatic Conference which adopted the Marrakesh Treaty, the 
participants spoke of a “Marrakesh miracle”. In the euphoria of the success of the Conference, 
this was understandable. Nevertheless, the success was due to the above-mentioned 
graduallybuilt-up new consolidation through joint efforts of the delegations supported by the 
professional and diplomatic contribution by the WIPO Secretariat. In Marrakesh, the efficient 
work of the Conference Bureau and, in particular Martin Moscoso of Peru as the facilitator of 
the key informal negotiations, as well as the suitable setting guaranteed by the government of 
the host country, Morocco, made it possible to reach consensus. Most of the non-governmental 
organizations(NGOs)–althoughtheyrepresentedmoreorlessdiverginginterests–alsoacted 
in a way that strengthened the chance to reach reasonable compromises. It is well known, 
for example, how substantially the joint statement of the United States National Federation 
oftheBlind(NFB)andtheMotionPictureAssociationofAmerica(MPAA)–publishedbefore 
theDiplomaticConference–contributedtoremovingsomefinalobstaclesbyclarifyingthat 
they both opposed the attempts at keeping the treaty hostage of some loudly promoted 
extraneous agendas. 833
Although it is stated above that the Marrakesh Treaty is historical also because it seems to 
have put an end to a restless decade in the field of the international copyright relations, the 
“Marrakesh miracle” could not have taken place without the momentum created by the “Beijing 
spirit”. The success of the adoption of the Beijing Treaty on Audiovisual Performances (BTAP) 
and the Marrakesh Treaty within a year was due to a great extent to the neutralization of certain 
misconceptions created in the post-WCT/WPPT period. One such misconception was that the 
three-steptestisanobstacletotheestablishmentandmaintenanceofanadequatebalanceof 
interests and, therefore, its scope of application should be narrowed through reinterpretation; 
another was that the application of technological protection measures (TPMs) do not make it 
possible for beneficiaries to take advantage of the limitations and exceptions necessary for the 
public interests.
In Beijing, the provisions of the existing international treaties both on the three-step test 
and the protection of TPMs were included in the BTAP in a mutatis mutandis manner in the 
same way as they appear in the two other WIPO “Internet Treaties”’ (the WCT and the WPPT), 
thereby rejecting implicitly the theories presented against them. It has also been clarified how 
833 See, Joint Statement by National Federation of the Blind President Marc Maurer and MPAA Chairman Senator Chris Dodd 
on Importance of Completing Visually Impaired Treaty  published on May 30, 2013. In the statement, the NFB President 
and the MPAA Chairman underscored that “this important Treaty must not be a vehicle for extraneous agendas. 
The goal remains, as it has been since the outset, a meaningful treaty to create greater access to published works 
for the visually impaired.” They summed up the following basic principles which they had found indispensable 
forthesuccessoftheDiplomaticConference–amongwhichtheneedtoavoidaddressingextraneousissueswas 
further emphasized:
1. Support a legally-binding access Treaty which will allow more published works to be converted into accessible 
formats used by the blind and print disabled.
2. Allow those accessible copies to be shared across international borders.
3. Take account of countries’ level of development, in line with existing international provisions.
4. Ensure that the treaty will be fully consistent with international copyright norms.
5. Avoid addressing extraneous copyright issues not directly related to creating greater access to published works 
for the blind and print disabled.
(See https://nfb.org/index.php/about-us/press-room/joint-statement-national-federation-blind-president-marc-maurer-
and-mpaa)

itispossibletograntadequateprotectionforTPMsandinparalleltomaketheapplicationof
limitations and exceptions possible with proper balance. Since, thus, the issue of TPMs had been 
satisfactory settled in Beijing, the scope of application of the three-step test became the focus 
of negotiations in Marrakesh, but the Diplomatic Conference here confirmed again that the 
existinginternationalnormsofferasolidbasisforanadequatebalanceofinterests,withthe 
three-step test as an indispensable guarantee for both allowing the necessary limitations and 
exceptions and controlling their reasonable application.
Any characterization of the Marrakesh Treaty as “the first treaty to deal with copyright 
limitationsandexceptions”–orevenas“thefirstaccess-to-knowledgetreaty”wouldcontradict 
certain basic historical facts. The international copyright treaties, since the moment of the 
adoption of the very first such treaty, the Berne Convention, have always recognized the 
needforadequatelimitationsandexceptionsandhavealwaysfunctionedas“access-to-
knowledge” treaties 834 in two ways. First, they ensure the creation of “knowledge” (valuable 
works embodying knowledge 835) through effective protection of copyright, without which there 
would not be “knowledge” to be accessed through limitations and exceptions. Second, they 
establish a balance between the public interest to offer due incentives and rewards to authors 
to produce such “knowledge”, on the one hand, and, on the other hand, other public interests 
and legitimate private interests through appropriate limitations and exceptions.
The Treaty is not historical in the sense that it would have introduced previously missing 
international copyright norms on limitations and exceptions for the benefit of visually impaired 
people to ensure availability of accessible format copies. It was already mentioned in the 
preparatory documents of the 1967 Stockholm Diplomatic Conference that such exceptions 
and limitations were to be recognized in connection with the new regulation of the right of 
reproduction.836ThentheModelProvisionsadoptedbyaWIPO–UNESCO(UnitedNations
Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization) Working Group in 1982 837 and approved by 
the Executive Committee of the Berne Union 838 not only confirmed this but placed the need 
for special treatment for the visually impaired in the focus of attention by adopting soft-
law provisions.
The Model Provisions adopted by a Working Group (of which the author of this commentary 
happened to be the Chairman839) and later approved by the Executive Committee already 
followedthesame–or,atleast,similar–principlesasthoseonwhichtheMarrakeshTreaty
is based:
(i)  There was complete agreement in 1982 as well that the exceptions or limitations for 
the visually impaired should be “subject to the obligations under the international 
conventions”840 (including the key obligation to respect the conditions of the three-
step test).
(ii) Theprincipleofabalancedapproach–“aproperbalancebetweentheneedsof
handicapped persons and the legitimate interests of copyright owners”841–wasalso
stressed at that time.

determinedinparagraph (1),ifthereareappropriateguaranteesthattheworkwillbe

The two versions differed in that one provided for completely free use, and the other consisted 
in the limitation of the exclusive rights to a right to remuneration. The reference to the 
international norms to be taken into account indicated that, although the model provisions, in 
general, had been found to be in accordance with those norms, they should be interpreted and 
applied in accordance with certain general provisions of the international copyright treaties, 848 
inparticularoftheBerneConventionwiththethree-steptestinitsArticle 9(2).
The Model Provisions reflected the possibilities offered by the technologies available in the 
pre-digital environment where the accessible formats still mainly meant braille and, to a certain 
extent, sound recordings (“audio books” or “talking books”). Nevertheless, the basic principles 
on the need for, and the justification of, specific exceptions or limitations for the benefit of the 
visually impaired were laid down in the Model Provisions on the basis of which new norms were 
introduced in several national laws to facilitate access of the visually impaired to books and 
other publications. Unfortunately, it was not in many national laws; still certain governments did 
not make use of these possibilities allowed by the existing international norms.
The advent of digital technology has brought about fundamentally new opportunities to 
ease the “book famine” of visually impaired and other print disabled people. It has not only 
made access to books and other works easier, including across national borders but, due to 
thesearchableandmanageablequalitiesofdigitalcopies,ithasalsoopenedupanumber
of previously unimaginable ways in which the beneficiaries of exceptions or limitations can 
use accessible format copies, making their scope of access ever more like that of sighted 
people. With digitization, however, the works available in accessible format are also useable 
by sighted people. With original braille versions, it did not emerge as a real challenge that the 
copies produced on the basis of exceptions or limitation for the beneficiaries were, in principle, 
equallyavailabletosightedpeople.Evenwithtraditional“audiobooks”noseriousproblems 
emerged. But with the digitization of the recordings and with the ever more sophisticated digital 
applications, it has become a complex task to establish a proper balance between providing as 
easy access as possible to the beneficiaries and ensuring due guarantees for the rightholders 
against uncontrolled use of the accessible format copies by the general public.
In view of the limited scope of this Guide it is not possible to present a complete overview of 
the technological developments and new distribution models. 849 Suffice it to refer to the Digital 
Accessible Information System (DAISY) 850 which was known and taken into account in the course 
of the preparatory work and at the Marrakesh Diplomatic Conference. On the WIPO website not 
long after the adoption of the Marrakesh Treaty, DAISY was referred to as follows: “The Digital 
Accessible Information System (Daisy) converts original texts to audio books that can be easily 
navigated by persons who are blind, visually impaired, or otherwise print disabled. Based on 
open standards, Daisy is run by a non-profit international consortium of talking book libraries 
and others”.851 This short description points out the key features of the system: transformation 
of books and other publications into digital format and, with the assistance of the necessary 
computer programs, making the digital copies easily searchable and navigable. As soon as 
protected materials exist in a digital version, not only is access to them rendered much easier 
but also several new uses are made possible. The beneficiaries may navigate in the DAISY files 
not only chapter by chapter and section by section but also line by line; they can regulate the 
listening speed, place bookmarks, etc., and certain navigational levels provide access to tables 
and other not purely textual information about non-text-based creations.
These were the rich opportunities the exploitation of which a new WIPO instrument was 
supposed to facilitate. Although copyright issues were to be dealt with, in fact, the problem was 
not that the existing international norms would not have offered an appropriate framework. 
The above-mentioned Model Provisions had proved that, at last, in the analog environment,
