Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
402 there was no obstacle to applying appropriate exceptions and limitations in favor of the visually 
impaired–orwiththeexpressionusedin1982,“visuallyhandicapped”–persons.Thedigital
format of works has raised new challenges and, in the new environment, the establishment of 
adequatebalanceofinterestsrequiredefforts.Itsubmittedthatthiscouldhavebeenpossible
even on the basis of the existing treaties, since in the meantime, through the WCT, the norms 
necessary for recalibrating and fine-tuning the balance of interests in the digital environment 
hadalsobeenmadepossible.However,theadoptionofaseparateinstrument–atthebeginning
itwasstillanopenquestionwhethermoredetailedmodelprovisions,arecommendationora
treatywouldbethesuitableform–waspreferredasashortandclear-cutsolution.
One of the advantages of a treaty rather than a soft-law instrument is that, in this way, the 
cause of the blind, visually impaired, and other print disabled people receives greater attention. 
Afterall,oneoftheproblemswasthat,asmentionedabove,although–astheadoption
andpublicationoftheModelProvisionsin1982hadmadeclear–itwaspossible,stillmany
governments had not introduced exceptions or limitations to facilitate access to knowledge, 
information, and entertainment productions for these people. The lacuna in using the available 
legal options was also revealed in the Sullivan report, 852 which was presented as the most 
important study serving as the basis for the preparatory work in the Standing Committee on 
Copyright and Related Rights (SCCR).
Therewerecertainfactorsthat–inspiteoftheavailableoptionsintheinternationaltreaties –
complicatedthetask.AsystemlikeDAISYneededcopiesinextensiblemarkuplanguage(XML)
format,theproductionofwhich –bothfromprintedcopiesbyscanningandfromportable
documentformat(PDF)toXML–requiredadvancedtechnologyandwasquitecostly.Therefore,
itwouldnothavebeenenoughforcertaincountries –inparticularforthedevelopingandleast-
developedcountries–tointroduceexceptionsandlimitationsbyvirtueofwhichtheycouldhave
produced accessible format copies; they did not have the financial resources and the necessary 
technologicalcapacities.Inprinciple,allowingparallelimport–throughinternationalexhaustion
–theycouldhaveimportedsuchcopiesrelativelyfreelyfromthosewhoproducetheminother
countries, but the authorities and the rightholders of some of those countries were reluctant 
to export the copies; the authorities, because they had invested in the mass digitization and 
recording of books and other publications from public resources and thus wanted to satisfy 
first of all the demands of the visually impaired and other print disabled population in their own 
countries, and the rightholders because digital format copies were more vulnerable to viral 
unauthorized uses. This raised the need for some kind of international instrument to facilitate 
trans-border availability of accessible format copies with due guarantees and an appropriate 
organizational framework of international cooperation.
Due to this nature of the task of the preparatory work, it was left open for several sessions of the 
SCCR (practically, until the last one held before the convocation of the Diplomatic Conference) 
whether the instrument under preparation should take the form of a treaty or a robust 
recommendation (or some similar soft-law instrument). It was a broadly shared opinion among 
the participants that what was truly important was the content of the would-be instrument 
and that its legal form was a less significant aspect. Finally, some emotional and humanitarian-
oriented political considerations contributed to the choice of the treaty form. The representatives 
of visually impaired and other print disabled people, understandably, insisted on such a form as 
asymbolofhumansolidarity;andtheinternationalcommunity–includingthosegovernment
delegationsthatpreviouslyhadnotbeenconvincedofthenecessityofsuchaform–responded
positively to this demand by expressing full empathy for people with these impairments.
It is worth noting that the modification of the title, replacing the expression “improve access” 
withtheexpression“facilitateaccess”–whichwasthelastamendmentadoptedintheplenary
sessioninwhichtheTreatywasadopted–madethetitlemoresuitabletoexpresstherelationship
between the existing international norms and the provisions of the Treaty. Specifically, the existing 
internationalnorms,asdiscussedabove,hadanadequatebasisforintroducinglimitationsand
exceptions for the visually impaired in national laws and, thus, what was needed was only to 
facilitate the making use of the possibilities offered by those norms as effectively as possible 
through establishing a legal and organizational framework for effective cross-border cooperation.
852JudithSullivan,Study on Limitations and Exceptions for the Visually Impaired , document SCCR/15/7 (WIPO, 2007).

===== PAGE 402 =====
403
PART IV. Guide to the Marrakesh VIP Treaty
The Treaty offers really new means to ensure better and easier availability of accessible format 
copies not mainly by providing for limitations and exceptions that the Contracting Parties 
aretoapply–sinceanygovernmentwithdueresponsibilitytowardsitsvisuallyimpairedand
other print disabled population could have made use of the flexibilities offered by the existing 
international treaties also without being “constrained” to do so by a separate treaty. Nor has 
it mainly contributed to the availability of accessible copies produced in other countries by 
providingforfreeimportation–becausethequestionwasratherwhethertherewouldbe 
such copies available to import. It has rather contributed to easing and, as much as possible, 
eliminating the “book famine” in the countries in need by means of two features that were new 
in comparison with the usual normative frameworks of the copyright treaties.
Thefirstnewfeatureconsistedintheprovisionsonexportofcopies–whichmeantboth 
export of tangible accessible copies and cross-border online making available of such copies. 
No copyright treaties had contained yet such norms, but only provisions on the rights of 
reproductionanddistribution.Theexceptionallowingfreeexport–undercertainconditions–is 
a specific form of exception to the right of distribution.
The second new feature was even more important; namely, the establishment of a network of 
“authorized entities” to facilitate smooth trans-border supply of accessible format copies and 
also to offer guarantees to rightholders that the exceptions and limitations function solely for 
the interests of the beneficiaries and not also for sighted people.
The Marrakesh Treaty has also been characterized by some commentators as a “human-rights 
treaty”. It is true that the human rights of the visually impaired and other print disabled persons 
were the focus in the preparation and adoption of the Treaty, but this does not change the 
basicnatureoftheinstrument.Itisanintellectualproperty–moreclosely,acopyright–treaty
establishing a fine-tuned balance of interests. The basic structure is the same as in the case of other 
copyrighttreaties:toguaranteeadequateprotectionofcopyrightinordertoensuresustainable
creation of valuable works, but also to provide for limitations and exceptions where, and to the 
extent that, they are necessary to ensure due access to the works to satisfy certain public and 
legitimate private interests. In this sense, if the Treaty is characterized as a “human-rights treaty”, 
the copyright treaties, since the very beginning, have also been “human-rights treaties”.
The three-step test plays the same key role in the Marrakesh Treaty as in every other new-
generation copyright treaty adopted since its first version appeared in the 1967 Stockholm Act 
of the Berne Convention. Despite attempts, mainly on the part of certain NGOs, to eliminate it, 
or at least to limit its application, it has again been confirmed as an indispensable element of the 
international copyright norms. The flexibilities allowed by the test make it possible to provide for 
well-justified limitations and exceptions in such a way that they do not go so far as to endanger 
the very sources from which the beneficiaries may enjoy free or easier access to the protected 
creations. In accordance with this key function of the test, several references are made to it in 
thisGuide,inparticularconcerningArticle 11oftheMarrakeshTreaty.Inthiscollectionofguides
to the WIPO-administered treaties, the most complete analysis of it is given in the Guide to the 
BerneConventioninthecommentsonArticle 9(2).
When describing the legal nature of the Marrakesh Treaty, it is also important to discuss why 
those participants in the Diplomatic Conference and commentators were right who stressed 
the exceptional and unique nature of the Treaty. The Marrakesh Treaty is truly exceptional, due to 
its specific format-centric orientationdictatedbythespecialstatusanduniqueneedsofvisually 
impaired and other print disabled persons. Its focus is not simply works protected by copyright 
and copies of such works but accessible format copies–accessibletopeoplelivingwiththese
grave impairments. This is why it was justified to regulate the exceptions and limitations in such 
anexceptionalmanner:insuchawaythattheContractingPartieshaveto–andarenotjust
allowedto–applythem.
ThequestionmayemergewhethertheMarrakeshTreatyisinaccordancewithArticles 19and
20oftheBerneConvention.UnderArticle 19,amembercountryoftheBerneUnionisfree
toprovideforagreater–ahigher-level–protection.Thelevelofprotectionisdeterminedby
the rights to be granted and the exceptions or limitations permitted to the rights. Under the 
Marrakesh Treaty, the Contracting Parties accept that they do not grant higher protection than 
what follows from the exceptions or limitations provided in it. It is clear, however, that a country

===== PAGE 403 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
404 that does not provide for greater protection, by this alone, does not violate its obligations under 
theConvention.MaytherethenbeaconflictwithArticle 20oftheConvention,whichprovides 
that if the countries of the Union enter into special agreements among themselves (or among 
themselves and also with other countries), those agreements must grant more extensive rights 
than those granted by the Convention “or other provisions not contrary to this Convention”? 
It is submitted that there is no conflict with this provision either, due to the latter phrase 
on “other provisions”. As pointed out above, the exceptions and limitations provided in the 
Marrakesh Treaty are submitted to the three-step test and are not contrary to, but allowed by, 
the Convention.853
InviewofthevariousweightyquestionsstillopenatthebeginningoftheDiplomatic
Conference, the adoption of the Treaty is a great achievement of the negotiating delegations 
and those who helped them as catalysts in reaching a reasonable consensus. Considering the 
complexityoftheissuesstilltobesettled–asalsoreflectedinthecontentsandthestructure 
ofthedraft–alongwiththeshorttimeavailabletotransformthenegotiatedagreementsinto 
treaty language, the Treaty is also a respectable drafting accomplishment. Nevertheless, as is 
inevitable under such circumstances, it still contains certain elements of “creative ambiguity”, 
redundanciesandopenquestionswhichrequireinterpretation.
It is also an important aspect that the adoption of the Marrakesh Treaty has been beneficial 
for the “public relations” of copyright. It has proved again in a spectacular way, and amid 
great public and media attention, that the existing copyright system is able to function “as 
advertised”; it serves as an effective means for the protection of the rights of the creators, but 
itisalsocapableofsatisfyingtherelatedpublicandlegitimateprivateinterests–includingthe 
protectionandrespectofhumanrights–throughadequateexceptionsandlimitations.
853 See the comments by Silke von Lewinski in Reinbothe and von Lewinski (who seems to be of the same opinion 
concerningthequestionofaccordanceoftheMarrakeshTreatywiththeseBerneprovisions),629–630.

Marrakesh Treaty to Facilitate Access to Published Works for 
Persons who are Blind, Visually Impaired, or Otherwise Print 
Disabled, 2013
Preamble
The Contracting Parties:
Recalling theprinciplesofnon-discrimination,equalopportunity,accessibilityandfulland
effective participation and inclusion in society, proclaimed in the Universal Declaration of 
Human Rights and the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities
MT-Pr.1. The Marrakesh Treaty has a much higher number of preamble paragraphs than 
the WIPO-administered copyright treaties in general: thirteen, in contrast with the Berne 
Convention and the WCT, which have only four (but in the case of the Berne preamble, only one 
isofasubstantivenature).ThisinitselfshowstheuniquenatureoftheTreaty.
MT-Pr.2.Thefirstpreambleparagraph referstotheprinciplesoftheUniversalDeclarationand 
the UN Convention in accordance with the strong human-rights justification of the exceptions 
andlimitationsprovidedforintheTreaty.Theprinciplesof“non-discrimination,equal
opportunity,accessibilityandfullandeffectiveparticipationandinclusioninsociety”require 
special treatment for the visually impaired and otherwise print disabled persons; they must 
be kept in mind in the application of all the provisions adopted in Marrakesh. Nevertheless, as 
underlined in the Introduction to the Guide above, the strong human rights justification of the 
exceptions and limitations provided in it does not change the fact that the Marrakesh Treaty is 
anintellectualproperty–andmorespecifically,copyright–treaty.
MT-Pr.3. The principles of non-discrimination and equal opportunity have double significance. On 
theonehand,theyserveasthelegal–politicalbasisfortheexceptionsandlimitationsprovided 
forintheTreaty–accordingtowhich,asmuchaspossible,thesameopportunitiesshouldbe
guaranteedtoitsbeneficiariesoftheTreatywithoutdiscrimination–and,ontheotherhand,
they determine the scope within which they are justified.
Mindful of the challenges that are prejudicial to the complete development of persons with 
visual impairments or with other print disabilities, which limit their freedom of expression, 
including the freedom to seek, receive and impart information and ideas of all kinds on an 
equalbasiswithothers,includingthroughallformsofcommunicationoftheirchoice,their
enjoyment of the right to education, and the opportunity to conduct research,
MT-Pr.4.Thenatureofthispreambleparagraph isthesameasthepreviousone;butitrefers
more concretely to the reasons justifying exceptions and limitations in favor of the visually 
impaired and otherwise print disabled persons.
Emphasizing the importance of copyright protection as an incentive and reward for literary and 
artistic creations and of enhancing opportunities for everyone, including persons with visual 
impairments or with other print disabilities, to participate in the cultural life of the community, 
to enjoy the arts and to share scientific progress and its benefits,
MT-Pr.5.Thisparagraph underlinestheimportanceofestablishingandmaintainingaproper
balance–onwhichtheinternationalcopyrightnormshavealwaysbeenbased–between,onthe
one hand, the public interest of providing incentive and reward for the creation of works that 
may then be made accessible to the public and, on the other hand, other public and legitimate 
private interests, including those underlined by human-rights considerations. In a way, it may be 
regardedasaparaphraseoftheprovisionsofArticle 27(1)and(2)oftheUniversalDeclarationof
Human Rights, here with the visually impaired and print disabled persons in focus:
(1)  Everyone has the right freely to participate in the cultural life of the community, to 
enjoy the arts and to share in scientific advancement and its benefits.
(2)  Everyone has the right to the protection of the moral and material interests resulting 
from any scientific, literary or artistic production of which he is the author.

406 Aware of the barriers of persons with visual impairments or with other print disabilities to access 
publishedworksinachievingequalopportunitiesinsociety,andtheneedtobothexpandthe
number of works in accessible formats and to improve the circulation of such works,
MT-Pr.6.Thispreambleparagraph referstothereason–discussedintheIntroductiontothe
Guideabove–forwhichtheTreatyisexceptionalanduniqueinthesystemofintellectual
copyright norms; namely, that its main objective is to guarantee the availability of special format 
copies of works to the beneficiaries of the exceptions and limitations provided in it.
Taking into account that the majority of persons with visual impairments or with other print 
disabilities live in developing and least-developed countries,
MT-Pr.7.Thisparagraph statesanimportantfactthatwastakenintoaccountinthepreparation
and adoption of the provisions of the Treaty (and, as mentioned in the Introduction to the 
Guide, also recognized already at the adoption of the 1982 Model Provisions). Beyond the 
basic provisions on exceptions and limitations, the trans-border measures and the established 
organizational framework are of particular relevance for the developing and least-developed 
countries.Theproductionofaccessibleformatcopiesisquitecostly,butwhentheyare
available, the extra costs of sharing them with the beneficiaries of these countries afflicted by 
the “book famine” should not be high.
Recognizing that, despite the differences in national copyright laws, the positive impact of new 
information and communication technologies on the lives of persons with visual impairments 
or with other print disabilities may be reinforced by an enhanced legal framework at the 
international level,
MT-Pr.8. A basic objective of the Treaty is emphasized in this preamble paragraph; to offer a 
legal framework for co-operation agreements to promote practical availability of accessible 
format copies by making use of advanced information and communication technologies. From 
this viewpoint, the need for easy availability of books and other publications to the visually 
impaired and otherwise print disabled persons has a double aspect: first, availability for the 
purpose of scanning and digitizing of the works; and, second, availability of the digitized works 
to the beneficiaries of the exceptions and limitations.
Recognizing that many Member States have established limitations and exceptions in their 
national copyright laws for persons with visual impairments or with other print disabilities, yet 
there is a continuing shortage of available works in accessible format copies for such persons, 
andthatconsiderableresourcesarerequiredfortheireffortofmakingworksaccessibleto
these persons, and that the lack of possibilities of cross-border exchange of accessible format 
copies has necessitated duplication of these efforts,
MT-Pr.9.Theparagraph recognizesthat,although–bymakinguseoftheflexibilitiesofferedby
theexistinginternationaltreaties–agreatnumberofcountrieshaveprovidedforappropriate
exceptions or limitations for visually impaired or otherwise print disabled persons, the 
accessible format copies produced and made available on the basis of such exceptions and 
limitations so far have not been used efficiently. In particular, they have not become available in 
many developing and least-developed countries that do not have an appropriate infrastructure 
to produce such copies.
MT-Pr.10.Theparagraph alsoreferstooneofthemainreasonswhytheTreatyisexceptional
andunique;namely,thatitisaninternationalco-operationagreementtoofferanadequate
legal and organizational framework for enhanced co-operation to promote practical availability 
of accessible format copies.
Recognizing both the importance of rightholders’ role in making their works accessible 
to persons with visual impairments or with other print disabilities and the importance of 
appropriate limitations and exceptions to make works accessible to these persons, particularly 
when the market is unable to provide such access,

MT-Pr.11.Thispreambleparagraph isofspecificimportanceinviewoftheanimateddebates
during the preparatory work and at the Diplomatic Conference on the issue of commercial 
(market)availabilityofaccessibleformatcopies.Intheend,Article 4(4)oftheTreatywas
adoptedonthisissue.Theparagraph statesthesameprincipleaswhatwasemphasizedatthe
adoption of the 1982 Model Provisions mentioned above; namely, that preference should be 
given to access provided, under reasonable conditions, by the owners of rights and that the 
exceptions and limitations have a key role mainly when the access to available format copies 
cannot be ensured in that way.
Recognizing the need to maintain a balance between the effective protection of the rights 
of authors and the larger public interest, particularly education, research and access to 
information, and that such a balance must facilitate effective and timely access to works for the 
benefit of persons with visual impairments or with other print disabilities,
MT-Pr.12.Thisparagraph andthefollowingoneaddresstheneedformaintainingduebalance
between the public interest to grant effective protection of authors’ rights in order to promote 
the creation of the works needed by the general public and the related private interests, on the 
one hand, and the general public interest to receive access to those works, in particular by the 
beneficiariesoftheTreaty,ontheotherhand.Inthisparagraph thisisrecognizedasageneral
principle, while in the following one it is reaffirmed that the balance is to be established in 
accordance with the three-step test.
Reaffirming  the obligations of Contracting Parties under the existing international treaties 
on the protection of copyright and the importance and flexibility of the three-step test for 
limitationsandexceptionsestablishedinArticle 9(2)oftheBerneConventionfortheProtection
of Literary and Artistic Works and other international instruments,
MT-Pr.13.Theparagraph drawsattentiontoakeyaspect;namely,thatanyexceptionsor
limitations provided under the recent international copyright treaties, including this one, 
areonlyapplicableiftheyfulfillthethree-steptest.Theparagraph referstoArticle 9(2)of 
theBerneConventionandthecorrespondingprovisionsintheothertreaties,and–byusing
theexpression“three-steptest”–itmakesitclearthatthethreeconditionsofthetestmust 
be applied cumulatively such that an exception or limitation may only be applied if all the 
conditions are fulfilled. 854 
Recalling the importance of the Development Agenda recommendations, adopted in 2007 by 
the General Assembly of the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), which aim to 
ensure that development considerations form an integral part of the Organization’s work,
MT-Pr.14. Development considerations have always been a key part of WIPO’s activities. In 
2007, the Development Agenda recommendations adopted by the WIPO Assembly specifically 
confirmed their importance and determined how they should be taken into account under the 
current conditions.
MT-Pr.15. It seems that the majority of the recommendations of the Development Agenda do 
not directly concern the specific subject matter of the Marrakesh Treaty in the sense that the 
provisionsofthelatteraretoservethespecialrequirementsofvisuallyimpairedandprint 
disabled persons. Nevertheless, some of the recommendations of a more general nature are 
relevant for the special human-rights justification of the exceptions and limitations provided by 
the Treaty; they should be kept in mind in the course of their practical application.
Recognizing the importance of the international copyright system and desiring to harmonize 
limitations and exceptions with a view to facilitating access to and use of works by persons with 
visual impairments or with other print disabilities.

It is supposed to facilitate access to and use of works by the visually impaired and other print

exceptionspermittedbytheexistinginternationalnorms–insuchawaythattheimportanceof 

Have agreed as follows:
Article 1
Relation to Other Conventions and Treaties
Nothing in this Treaty shall derogate from any obligations that Contracting Parties have to each 
other under any other treaties, nor shall it prejudice any rights that a Contracting Party has 
under any other treaties.
MT-1.1. This is a usual non-derogation provision but, in the context of the Marrakesh Treaty, it 
also has a specific function. The main purpose of the Treaty is to provide appropriate exceptions 
and limitations in order to ensure accessible format copies for the beneficiaries. However, it 
would have been illogical to try to adopt an instrument on limitations of and exceptions to 
copyright without clarifying what rights are involved that the Contracting Parties are obligated 
to protect and enforce, but in respect of which the exceptions and limitations are to apply. One 
may only really speak of an exception to, or a limitation of, a right if its subject matter, nature 
(whether it is an exclusive right or a mere right to remuneration) and extent (the coverage of the 
acts to which it relates) are precisely determined.
MT-1.2. Through this provision, it is confirmed that the Marrakesh Treaty is part of the system 
of international copyright treaties and that the basic nature of the exceptions and limitations 
provided for in it is the same as those permitted by the other treaties (in fact, they are not only 
of the same nature but they are based on, and must be interpreted on the basis of, certain key 
provisions of the other copyright treaties, particularly those on the three-step test).
Article 2 
Definitions
For the purposes of this Treaty:
(a) “works”meansliteraryandartisticworkswithinthemeaningofArticle 2(1)ofthe
Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works, in the form of text, 
notation and/or related illustrations, whether published or otherwise made publicly 
available in any media;
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 2(a):ForthepurposesofthisTreaty,itisunderstoodthat
this definition includes such works in audio form, such as audiobooks.
MT-2.1. The definition of “works” is limited to those works in respect of which the application of 
the exceptions and limitations provided for in the Treaty is truly justified; those to which visually 
impaired or other print disabled persons may only receive access if the works are made in, or 
transformed into, a special format available to them. These are the works to which, through the 
expression“bookfamine”,referencewasmadefrequentlyduringthepreparatorywork;thatis, 
first of all, books and other publications consisting mainly of texts. 855 (Since notations normally 
also include text, they do not significantly broaden the scope of works “in the form of text”. 856)
855AccordingtotheinterpretativeprovisionsofArticle 10.1oftheTRIPSAgreementandArticle 4oftheWCT,computer 

any indication to the contrary, the term “works” as used in the Marrakesh Treaty also covers computer programs.

MT-2.2. The reference to “related illustrations” extends the coverage of the works to a certain

MT-2.3. An agreed statement was adopted concerning the definition of “works” to clarify that  
“[f]or the purposes of this Treaty, it is understood that this definition includes such works in 
audio form, such as audiobooks”. Since audio recordings of texts are potentially accessible

Audiobooks were identified already in the 1982 Model Provisions as such copies. 857
MT-2.4. Although works protected by copyright are the basic objects of the limitations

MT-2.5. The definition covers only works that have been published or have been otherwise made 
“publicly available” by the author or other rightholder. It does not apply to works made available 
illegally without the consent of the author or other rightholder. 858
MT-2.6. In connection with the definitional element of works “published” or otherwise “made 
publicly available”, it should be noted that publishers often grant pre-publication licenses to 
organizations that use technologies to make accessible format copies in order that simultaneous 
publication of non-accessible format copies and accessible format copies may take place. It 
followsfromthegoverningprinciplesoftheTreaty–non-discriminationandequalopportunity 
–that,incaseswheretheaccessibleformatcopiesareequallyaffordableonreasonableterms
(bringingthewould-bebeneficiariesandsightedpeopleintoequalposition)thelegal–political 
and social justification of the limitations and exceptions is somewhat weakened. Affordability, 
however, is not the same in different markets; what under certain conditions is affordable in one 
country may not be affordable in another, which is a significant factor from the viewpoint of the 
export and import of accessible format copies. 
(b)  “accessible format copy” means a copy of a work in an alternative manner or form 
which gives a beneficiary person access to the work, including to permit the person 
to have access as feasibly and comfortably as a person without visual impairment or 
other print disability. The accessible format copy is used exclusively by beneficiary 
persons and it must respect the integrity of the original work, taking due consideration 
of the changes needed to make the work accessible in the alternative format and of the 
accessibility needs of the beneficiary persons;
MT-2.7. The definition concerns the central element of the Marrakesh Treaty, the only treaty to 
havetheobjectiveofprovidingforanadequatelegalandorganizationalframeworktofacilitate 
availability of such copies of works.
MT-2.8. It makes it clear that there is a difference between works that, due to their form, are ab 
initio accessible to persons both with and without visual impairment, on one hand, and, on the

exceptionsundertheTreatylessjustifiedand–incertainfactualsituations–evenmakesit
questionablewhethertheyarejustifiedatall.InviewofthepurposeoftheTreaty–clearly 
statedinvariouspreambleparagraphs–inthecaseswhereanydoubtsemergeinthisrespect,a
solution more favorable for the beneficiaries of the Treaty should be preferred. 
MT-2.10. The nature of the two sentences of point (b) differs. Only the first sentence reads like 
a real definition, but it begins in a circular way. It states that an “accessible format copy” is “a 
copy […] which gives a beneficiary person access to the work” “in an alternative manner or 
form”. In the given context, “alternative form” is to be understood as a form other than any form 
regularly usable by sighted people. The form is supposed to be “alternative” in the sense that 
the alteration is needed to make the copies of the works accessible for the visually impaired.
MT-2.11. The second part of the first sentence adds somewhat more substance based on the 
principlesofnon-discriminationandequalopportunity.Itclarifiesthatanaccessibleformat 
copy is supposed to ensure that a person with visual impairment “have access as feasibly and 
comfortably as a person without visual impairment or other print disability”. In view of the 
principle of impossibilium nulla est obligatio, the term “as feasibly and comfortably” certainly is to 
mean as feasibly and comfortably as possible under the given circumstances.
MT-2.12. The second sentence of point (b), at first sight, does not appear to further define 
“accessible format copies”, but rather to determine two basic rules that must be respected when 
the alterations are made and when the copies are used. First, they may be used exclusively 
only by beneficiary persons; second, they must respect the integrity of the original work. 
Nevertheless, these rules do have some indirect definitional role, because they indicate the 
nature of alterations necessary to make the format of the copies accessible. First, the purpose 
of the alterations must be kept in mind; and second, how the alterations may impact the works 
altered, summed up in this way: “it must respect the integrity of the original work, taking due 
consideration of the changes needed to make the work accessible in the alternative format and 
of the accessibility needs of the beneficiary persons”. 
MT-2.13.Theseelementsofpoint(b)oftheArticle alsoclarifythatthelimitationsandexceptions
under the Treaty may be applied only if they relate to such copies, only for the beneficiary 
persons,andonlytotheextentnecessaryforensuringequalopportunitytovisuallyimpairedor 
other print disabled people. 859
MT-2.14. The scope of persons to whom copies of works are made accessible is decisive from 
the viewpoint of whether or not the application of limitations or exceptions provided for in the 
Marrakesh Treaty is in accordance with the three-step test. If works are accessible exclusively 
to beneficiary persons, the exception or limitation will probably pass the three cumulative 
conditions of the test. However, as soon as they may be used in the same way by persons who 
are not visually impaired or otherwise print disabled (practically by the general public), they may 
more easily come into conflict with the test.
MT-2.15. Point (b) emphasizes the need to respect authors’ moral right to protect the integrity of 
their works when changing the format to make the copies accessible. This does not mean, however, 
859Therearecommentatorswhopointoutthat,wherecopiesofaworkaremadeavailableonthemarketonequal 
termsbothforpersonswithimpairmentandforthosewithoutimpairment–and,thus,they may be used not only by 
the beneficiaries and without the need for alternative copies –onecannotreallyspeakof“accessibleformatcopies”; see 
Reinbothe and von Lewinski (arguing that in such a case, the copies are not “used exclusively by beneficiary persons” 
and,inaddition,arenot“inanalternativemannerorform”asrequiredbythedefinitionof“accessibleformatcopy”), 
see at 632.

PART IV. Guide to the Marrakesh VIP Treaty
thatonlytherightofintegrityapplies;theotherbasicmoralrightprovidedinArticle 6bis of the 
BerneConvention–therighttoclaimauthorshipinworks–mustnotbeneglectedeither.
(c)  “authorized entity” means an entity that is authorized or recognized by the government 
to provide education, instructional training, adaptive reading or information access to 
beneficiary persons on a non-profit basis. It also includes a government institution or 
non-profit organization that provides the same services to beneficiary persons as one 
of its primary activities or institutional obligations.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 2(c):ForthepurposesofthisTreaty,itisunderstoodthat
“entities recognized by the government” may include entities receiving financial support from 
the government to provide education, instructional training, adaptive reading or information 
access to beneficiary persons on a non-profit basis.
(d) An authorized entity establishes and follows its own practices:
(i)  to establish that the persons it serves are beneficiary persons;
(ii)  to limit to beneficiary persons and/or authorized entities its distribution and 
making available of accessible format copies;
(iii) to discourage the reproduction, distribution and making available of 
unauthorized copies; and
(iv)  to maintain due care in, and records of, its handling of copies of works, while 
respectingtheprivacyofbeneficiarypersonsinaccordancewithArticle 8.
MT-2.16. The “authorized entities” have a key role both in the domestic application of exceptions 
and limitations and in the international co-operation for cross-border availability of accessible 
format copies. They ensure, on the one hand, that accessible format copies may be available to 
the beneficiaries and, on the other hand, that they may only be available to the beneficiaries as 
providedinpoint(b)ofArticle 2.
MT-2.17.ByvirtueofArticle 2(c),theContractingPartiesareobligatedtoensurethatonlythose
entities operate as “authorized entities” that are suitable to fulfill the above-mentioned double task. 
This is the reason for which government authorization is needed. Government “recognition”, in 
the context of the definition of “authorized entity”, may only be understood as a concept similar to 
“authorization”; otherwise it would not be justified, in their case, to speak of “authorized entities”. 
ThisisconfirmedbytheagreedstatementadoptedconcerningArticle 2(c),whichmentionsthose
entities as examples of being “recognized” that are in close links with the government, so much so 
that they are “receiving financial support from the government to provide education, instructional 
training, adaptive reading or information access to beneficiary persons on a non-profit basis”.
MT-2.18. Authorization is a guarantee that an “authorized entity” will work in the interest of 
visually impaired and other print disabled persons and will also respect the rights and legitimate 
interests of copyright owners, thus only a non-profit organization may be authorized as such.
MT-2.19. Under the first sentence of point (c), those entities may be authorized or recognized 
that “provide education, instructional training, adaptive reading or information access to 
beneficiary persons”; thus, publicly accessible educational institutions and libraries established 
for the visually impaired certainly will be among such entities. The second sentence of the 
point adds that a “government institution or non-profit organization that provides the same 
services to beneficiary persons as one of its primary activities or institutional obligations ” may 
only be authorized or recognized as “authorized entities”. 860 This applies in a situation where 
the government cannot afford to establish and operate institutions exclusively for the purpose 
of offering services for beneficiary persons. Such service, however, must be not only one of 
manyequallysignificantfunctionsofthegovernmentinstitutionornon-profitorganization 
concerned, but one of their primary activities or institutional obligations.
MT-2.20. When read in isolation, the four conditions listed in items (i) to (iv) of point (d) seem 
like normative provisions, because they determine the tasks of “authorized entities” for the 
860 Emphasis added. For a detailed review of such possible entities, see WBU Guide,52–59.

===== PAGE 411 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
412 fulfillment of which they must establish and follow their “own practices”. However, these 
provisions are closely linked to point (c) on the definition of“authorizedentity”inanarticle with
the title “Definitions”, and their function seems to be in fact definitional. The Contracting Parties 
may only authorize (or “recognize”) any entities as “authorized entities” that “establish and 
follow […] practices” suitable to fulfill the tasks listed in the four items (or, to put it another way, 
the entities only fall under the definition of “authorized entities” and guarantee due application 
of the limitations or exceptions provided for in the Treaty if they establish and duly follow 
practices as prescribed in items (i) to (iv)).
MT-2.21. A Contracting Party does not fulfill its obligations under the Treaty if it authorizes an 
entity (or recognizes it as authorized) that then does not function as prescribed. Some measures 
are needed to ensure that the “authorized entities” comply with the conditions prescribed in 
items (i) to (iv) and other treaty provisions (including the possibility of suspending or withdrawing 
the authorization or recognition in case of grave or repeated violation of those conditions).
MT-2.22. Under item (i), an entity may be authorized if it makes it sure that the persons it serves 
are beneficiaries. Item (ii) closely relates to this, because it indicates the reason for which the 
entity must identify the beneficiary persons; it is obligated to guarantee that the persons to 
whom the authorized entity distributes or otherwise makes available accessible format copies 
correspond to the definition of beneficiaries.
MT-2.23. According to item (iii), an entity only fulfills the criteria of authorization if it applies 
adequatepractices“todiscouragethereproduction,distributionandmakingavailableof 
unauthorized copies”. The entity must discourage any kind of infringing acts in connection with 
accessible format copies; that is, any acts of reproduction, distribution or making available 
of such copies in a way that it is not allowed under the exceptions and limitations provided 
for in the Treaty, as well as any acts performed in respect of the copies that would go beyond 
the scope of exceptions and limitations without due authorization. To “discourage” such acts, 
certainly it is not sufficient to simply inform the interested persons of the illegal nature of 
the acts; it presupposes proactive measures and sanctions that are suitable to effectively 
discourage infringements.
MT-2.24. Item (iv), as part of the definition, prescribes procedural criteria that an entity must 
fulfilltoqualifyasanauthorizedentity.“Duecare”requiresproceduresandpracticestoensure 
the fulfillment of the double obligation of the entity: to make available accessible format 
copies to beneficiaries and, at the same time, discourage infringing acts. The other procedural 
obligation is “to maintain due records of its handling of copies of works”. This is indispensable 
for the government to be able to guarantee that the entities authorized or recognized by it duly 
fulfill the tasks prescribed in the Treaty.
MT-2.25.Consequentprescriptionandapplicationoftheserequirementsisanindispensable 
precondition of the application of trans-border making available of accessible format copies. It 
is only in this way that the exporting countries may trust that, in the importing countries, the 
copiesdulyservetherequirementsofbeneficiarypersons–andonlybeneficiarypersons. 861
MT-2.26.Fortheprotectionofprivacy,seethecommentsonArticle 8,below.Inconnectionwith 
Article 2(d)(iv),sufficeittoremarkthat,inthecontextoftheMarrakeshTreaty,noactsmay 
be regarded as being in conflict with the protection of privacy that are indispensable for the 
application of the Treaty; these include acts that are necessary to identify, and maintain records 
of,beneficiarypersonsandtomakesurethattheyqualifyassuchunderArticle 3.Withoutthis, 
thebasicconditionstatedintherelevantprovisionsoftheTreaty–thataccessibleformatcopies
may only be made available to the beneficiaries and the limitations and exceptions provided for 
intheTreatymayonlybeappliedifthisisguaranteed–cannotbefulfilled.
861 Silke von Lewinski also stresses this aspect of the definition and the role of authorized entities in Reinbothe 
andvon Lewinski:WhileContractingPartiesarefreetodeterminetheproceduresorwaysinwhichentitiesare 
authorized or recognized to provide the relevant tasks, the purpose of such government involvement is to create a 
certain degree of credibility and reliability for the relevant institution, and thereby to enhance the trust among the 
institutionsandconsequentlytofacilitatecross-borderexchangeforthebeneficiarypersons. See at 633.

MT-2.27. In sum, under the definition in point (d), no entity is allowed to be authorized, or 
recognized as an “authorized entity”, that does not establish and apply practices to fulfill the 
definitional criteria under points (i) to (iv).
Article 3 
Beneficiary Persons
A beneficiary person is a person who:
(a)  is blind;
(b)  has a visual impairment or a perceptual or reading disability which cannot be improved 
togivevisualfunctionsubstantiallyequivalenttothatofapersonwhohasnosuch
impairment or disability and so is unable to read printed works to substantially the 
same degree as a person without an impairment or disability; or
(c)  is otherwise unable, through physical disability, to hold or manipulate a book or to 
focus or move the eyes to the extent that would be normally acceptable for reading;
regardless of any other disabilities.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 3(b):Nothinginthislanguageimpliesthat“cannotbe
improved”requirestheuseofallpossiblemedicaldiagnosticproceduresandtreatments.
MT-3.1.Article 3determinesabroadscopeofbeneficiarypersons.Inviewofthis,the
requirementsensuringthattheexceptionsandlimitationsundertheMarrakeshTreatyare
applied to provide availability of accessible format copies only to such persons appear to be 
even more justified. The authorized entities must guarantee this and they may only do so if they 
duly identify these persons as such on the basis of sufficient proof that they have one or more 
forms of impairment listed in the article.
MT-3.2.Ofthethreecategoriesofbeneficiarypersonslistedinthearticle,thefirst–“blind” 
persons–isobvious;itdoesnotneedspecificcomments.Thesecondcategoryhasmore 
complexcriteria.Visuallyimpairedpersons”bydefinition”arenotblind,buttheyare“unable 
to read printed works to substantially the same degree as a person without an impairment or 
disability” (emphasis added). People with “a perceptual or reading disability” (dyslexia was 
mentionedmostfrequentlyinthecourseofthepreparatorywork)formasubcategoryofthose 
who are unable to read in the same way as persons without an impairment or disability. In all 
these cases, a further criterion is that their impairment or disability cannot be improved to make 
theirvisualfunctionsubstantiallyequivalenttothatofsightedpeoplewithoutreadingdisability. 
The agreed statement clarifies this criterion in that the term “cannot be improved” does not 
requiretheuseofallpossiblemedicaldiagnosticproceduresandtreatments.Thiscertainlymay 
not be understood to suggest that no medical diagnostic procedure is needed to determine 
whetheragivenpersontrulyqualifiesasabeneficiary.Thereareobviouscaseswherethe 
persons concerned should make efforts to improve their condition, such as obtaining glasses or 
contact lenses, while at the other end of the spectrum they certainly must not be expected to 
undergo treatments that may imply high risks. 862
MT-3.3. The third category was inserted in the definition “beneficiary persons” in a later stage of 
the preparatory work because, in this case, it is not blindness or visual impairment that justifies 
the preferential treatment. Those who fall into this category are unable to hold or handle 
normally a book or cannot use their eyes for reading for reasons other than visual impairment; 
thus, they likewise cannot obtain access to published works. 863
862 For a detailed overview of the various possible cases within this spectrum, see WBU Guide,63–66.
863 In the WBU Guide,suchexamplesarelistedas”quadriplegia,cerebralpalsy,tremor,brainorspinalinjury,ormotor-
neuron and neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)”, 66.

414 Article 4
National Law Limitations and Exceptions Regarding Accessible Format Copies
1. (a)  Contracting Parties shall provide in their national copyright laws for a limitation or 
exception to the right of reproduction, the right of distribution, and the right of making 
available to the public as provided by the WIPO Copyright Treaty (WCT), to facilitate the 
availability of works in accessible format copies for beneficiary persons. The limitation 
or exception provided in national law should permit changes needed to make the work 
accessible in the alternative format.
Introductory remarks
MT-4.1. As discussed in the Introduction to this Guide, the exceptions and limitations 
providedforinsubparagraph (a)arethosepresumedtobeapplicablebyvirtueoftheexisting
international norms (provided they also correspond to the cumulative conditions of the three-
steptestasprescribedinArticle 11).Anygovernmentrespectingthehumanrightsofpersons
with visual impairments and other print disabilities may be expected to follow the examples of 
thenumerousnationallawswhich–inrecognitionofthespecificneedsofsuchpersons–have
made use of the possibilities offered by the existing international norms. It is also discussed in 
the Introduction to this Guide above (i) why these provisions originally appeared in two versions 
using “should” and “shall” language, respectively,; (ii) why it was not regarded to be of great 
importance which of the two versions would be finally adopted (but rather the contents of the 
provisions and the necessary guarantees were considered decisive); (iii) why this instrument was 
tobeexceptionalandunique;and(iv)whyandhowthispersuadedgovernmentdelegationsto
choose to give it the form of a treaty rather than recommendations.
MT-4.2.Itisworthnoting–asasignthatashall-languagetreatyandarobustsetofshould-
language recommendations with practically the same contents were long regarded as having a 
similarchancetoensurethatgovernmentswouldintroduceandapplyadequateprovisionsin
nationallaws–that,inthesecondsentenceofsubparagraph (a)ofArticle 4(1)oftheTreaty,the
should language has been maintained.
Rights to be covered
MT-4.3.UnderArticle 4(1)(a),theexceptionsandlimitationsclearlyapplytotherightsof 
reproduction and distribution which cover acts indispensable for producing and making 
available accessible format copies to the beneficiary persons. The third right mentioned is “the 
right of making available to the public as provided in the WIPO Copyright Treaty (WCT)” which, 
inthecontextofArticle 4(1)(a),certainlymeanstherightofinteractivemakingavailabletothe 
public provided in the second part of Article 8 of the WCT.
Meaning of the rights provided in subparagraph (a)
MT-4.4.Twointerpretationsseemtobepossibleconcerningthequestionofwhatthephrase
“as provided by the WIPO Copyright Treaty (WCT)” refers to: only to the last-mentioned right, 
“the right of making available to the public”, or also to the right of reproduction and the right of 
distribution before it. If the first interpretation were accepted, it would imply that the drafters 
were not sufficiently precise in Marrakesh; they wanted to refer to the WCT only in order to 
determine the meaning of “making available to the public” but they neglected to refer to the 
concreteprovisionintheWCT.However,thereisanotherarticle intheWCTthatprovidesforan
“exclusive right of authorizing the making available to the public” of works (in that case, in the 
formoftangiblecopies);namely,Article 6oftheWCTontherightofdistribution.
MT-4.5. There is, however, another possible interpretation which is more logical and for which 
it is not necessary to presume any drafting imprecision; namely that “as provided in the WIPO 
Copyright Treaty (WCT)” refers to all three rights listed. It is more logical because all three 
rights are provided for and determined in the WCT; the right of reproduction and the right of 
distributionalsobymeansofagreedstatementsconcerningArticles 1(4)and6,respectively. 
Also, it would be difficult to explain why it happened that the drafters rightly enough found it

===== PAGE 414 =====
415
PART IV. Guide to the Marrakesh VIP Treaty
necessary to determine the meaning of the acts covered by the rights to which the exceptions 
and limitations were to be applied but then did so only with respect of one of the three rights.
MT-4.6.TheinterpretationthatWCTismeantingeneralratherthanjustitsArticle 8alsomakesthe
reference to “the right of making available to the public” more precise, because it is through the 
agreedstatementconcerningArticle 6oftheWCTthatitsdifferencefromtherightofdistribution
is clarified.864Article 31.1oftheViennaConventionontheLawofTreaties(VCLT)providesthatthe
terms of a treaty must be interpreted in “good faith”. It follows from this that, if one interpretation 
implied an assumption that the drafter chose an imprecise language but, under another 
interpretation, the text becomes more logical and it does not entail an assumption about the 
drafters’ imprecision, the latter interpretation should be adopted in good faith. Therefore, it may 
be established that the phrase “as provided by the WIPO Copyright Treaty (WCT)” refers to all three 
rightsmentionedbeforeit,whichexplainsalsowhyArticle 8isnotmentionedspecifically.
Permitted changes in making alternative format
MT-4.7.Thesecondsentenceofsubparagraph (a)clarifiesthatchangesmaybemadetorendera
work accessible in an alternative format, but only to the extent that it is needed for this purpose. This 
means that the changes may only consist in technical/technological transformations indispensable 
to make copies accessible to the visually impaired. The limitations and exceptions provided for in the 
Marrakesh Treaty do not extend to substantive modifications that would amount to adaptations. 
Article 4(1)(a)oranyotherprovisionsoftheTreatydonotapplytotherightofadaptationprovided
inArticle 12oftheBerneConventionunderwhich“[a]uthorsofliteraryandartisticworksshallenjoy
the exclusive right of authorizing adaptations, arrangements and other alterations of their works”.
The meaning of “limitation” and “exception“
MT-4.8.InArticle 4(1)(a)andotherprovisionsoftheTreatytheterms”limitation”and”exception”
appear. In accordance with the ordinary meaning of these words, as is clarified in the Glossary in 
PartVofthiscollectionofguides,“limitation”meansthattherightisapplicablebutinalimited 
form (usually an exclusive right limited to a non-voluntary license or otherwise to a mere right 
to remuneration), while ”exception” means that, in the given special case, the right concerned is 
not applicable in any form (the use is free; no authorization is needed and no remuneration has 
tobepaid).Itshouldbestressedheretoothat,asprovidedinArticle 11oftheTreaty–andas
requiredbytheexistinginternationalnorms–thelimitationsandexceptionsundertheTreaty
are only applicable if they correspond to the cumulative provisions of the three-step test.
(b)  Contracting Parties may also provide a limitation or exception to the right of 
public performance to facilitate access to works for beneficiary persons.
Right that may be covered (“performance”  recital)
MT-4.9. The Treaty covers works ”in the form of text, notation and/or related illustrations”. 
Such works are, in general, literary works that are not performed in the sense in which the 
Berne Convention uses the term performance. That term is only applicable to musical, 
dramatic,dramatico-musicalandaudiovisualworks(seeArticles 11(1)(i),14(1)(i)and14bis(1) 
of the Convention). The texts of literary works are rather recited underArticle 11ter(1)(i) of the 
Convention, while the related illustrations cannot be used in the form of a performance or 
recitation. Illustrations may only be displayed, which presumes visual perception; therefore, 
displays are not accessible to the visually impaired. They may only become accessible if they are 
transformed into accessible form, which might allow perception through touching (the same 
way as braille transcripts, but this does not consist in performance or recitation and their use 
does not involve a public act; it may only take place individually) or into textual description, 
whichmaybeprotected–asaliterarywork–ifitisofanoriginalnature.
864 SeethecommentstoArticles 6and8intheGuidetotheWCTpointingouttheimportanceoftheclarificationinthe 
agreedstatementconcerningArticle 6,accordingtowhichtherightofdistributionappliesonlytomakingavailable 
to the public tangible copies. Thus, although the online making available to the public of copies (for downloading) may 
becharacterizedas”distribution”,stilltherightofmakingavailabletothepublic–andnottherightofdistribution 
(andwiththerightofdistributionthepossibleexhaustionoftheright)–applies.

416 Use of dramatic works in writing; sheet music
MT-4.10. Dramatic works normally are created in the form of writing; that is, as text. Therefore, 
in that form, they are covered by the definition of ”works” in the context of the Marrakesh Treaty. 
The possibility of transformation of dramatic works published in writings into accessible format 
copiesiscertainlycoveredbyArticle 4(2)(a).Itisanotherquestionhowbeneficiarypersonsmayuse
dramatic works in that form. One way of using such works is feasible and may take place in practice; 
such as reading on the basis of braille. In principle, the written text of dramatic works may also be 
transformed into a recording specifically for Marrakesh beneficiaries, but the practicability of such 
form is limited. It is imaginable, however, that visually impaired persons perform dramatic works 
(the same way as they may recite literary works) on the basis of accessible format copies, such as 
in an event in their schools or other special institutions. It is in this context that also the need for 
an exception to or limitation of the right of public performance may emerge in principle. But such 
kinds of public performances of dramatic works usually take place in such specific circumstances 
and in the presence of such a specific public that certain exceptions and limitations other than 
those provided in the Marrakesh Treaty may also apply; such as educational exceptions, exceptions 
and limitations for social institutions, or just so-called “minor reservations”.865
MT-4.11. Sheet music is covered by the concept of ”notation” and, thus, the definition of ”work”. 
Consequently,theexceptionsandlimitationsprovidedinArticle 4(1)(a)applytoit.Sheetmusic
may be transformed into an alternative accessible format and may be distributed. It then may 
be used for public performance by beneficiary persons.
Extension of the application of Article 4.1. to related rights
MT-4.12.AnagreedstatementwasaddedtoArticle 10(2)oftheTreatyonthelegalmethodsof
implementation of the Marrakesh Treaty which reads as follows: “It is understood that when a 
workqualifiesasaworkunderArticle 2,includingsuchworksinaudioform,thelimitationsand 
exceptions provided for by this Treaty apply mutatis mutandis to related rights as necessary to 
make the accessible format copy, to distribute it and to make it available to beneficiary persons”. 
TheanalysisinthecommentonArticle 10(2)discussestheimpactthisagreedstatementmay 
haveontheinterpretationofArticle 4(1).
2. AContractingPartymayfulfillArticle 4(1)forallrightsidentifiedthereinbyprovidinga
limitation or exception in its national copyright law such that:
(a)  Authorized entities shall be permitted, without the authorization of the copyright 
rightholder, to make an accessible format copy of a work, obtain from another 
authorized entity an accessible format copy, and supply those copies to beneficiary 
persons by any means, including by non-commercial lending or by electronic 
communication by wire or wireless means, and undertake any intermediate steps 
to achieve those objectives, when all of the following conditions are met:
(i)  the authorized entity wishing to undertake said activity has lawful access 
to that work or a copy of that work;
(ii)  the work is converted to an accessible format copy, which may include 
any means needed to navigate information in the accessible format, but 
does not introduce changes other than those needed to make the work 
accessible to the beneficiary person;
(iii)  such accessible format copies are supplied exclusively to be used by 
beneficiary persons; and
(iv)  the activity is undertaken on a non-profit basis; 
and 
Introductory remarks
MT-4.13. Paragraph(2)(a) has two parts: first, it indicates further what sorts of acts are permitted 
underparagraph (1);andsecond,itdetermineswhatconditionsmustbefulfilledforthose
actstobepermitted.Inthefirstpart,theactscoveredbyparagraph (1)areparaphrased 
865 Seetheconceptof“minorreservations”intheGuidetotheBerneConventioninthiscollectionofguidesatArticle 11(1).

inasomewhatcolloquialway,andthusrequireinterpretation.Inthesecondpart,thefour
items differ in terms of whether they provide new conditions or more details concerning the 
requirementtobefulfilled,butingeneraltheyareratherredundant;theyconfirmorrephrase 
what is provided in other provisions of the Treaty.
Permitted acts: ”to make an accessible format copy of a work”’
MT-4.14.Thefirstactmentionedinthelistofparagraph (2)(a)isasynonymoftheactto
reproduce a work in accessible format: ”to make an accessible format copy of a work”. It does not 
addanythinginsubstancetoparagraph (1)anddoesnotneedinterpretation.
Permitted acts: ”[to] obtain from another authorized entity an accessible format copy”
MT-4.15.  In contrast, the phrase “[to] obtain from another authorized entity an accessible format copy” 
needs some explanation. An entity may obtain a copy in various different ways; it may buy a copy, 
rentacopy,loanacopy,receiveitfreeofcharge–nosuch”act”hascopyrightrelevance;therefore,
this does not really fit in a provision on exceptions to or limitations of copyright. In the context of 
the Marrakesh Treaty, it means the importation of a copy where the element of obtaining a copy 
concernsaright.TheexceptiontotherightofimportationisprovidedinArticle 6.
Permitted acts: ”[to] supply […] copies to beneficiary persons by any means […]”
MT-4.16. The phrase ”[to] supply […] copies to beneficiary persons by any means, including by 
non-commercial lending or by electronic communication by wire or wireless means ” was not 
draftedinaccordancewiththeterminologyusedinthecopyrighttreaties;thereforeitrequires 
interpretation. This applies, first of all, to the key term ”to supply”, which is not used in the 
copyright treaties. From the context of the provision, it seems to follow that the concept 
of ”supplying” copies means making available copies through acts covered by two rights 
mentionedinArticle (1)(a)and(b):therightofdistributionandthe”rightofmakingavailable
to the public as provided in the WIPO Copyright Treaty (WCT)” (for the comments on this, see 
above). ”Supplying copies” probably does not refer to exceptions to or limitations of the right 
of reproduction because it seems to mean making available already existing copies and also 
because making copies as a synonym of reproduction appears in the text before (and certainly 
no acts of public performance (recital) is meant because by those acts no copy is ”supplied”).
Permitted acts: ”[to] supply […] copies to beneficiary persons by […] non-commercial lending”
MT-4.17. The term ”non-commercial lending”raisescertainquestionsbecausethereisnoprovision
in the Marrakesh Treaty on the right of lending; in fact, no copyright treaty provides for such a 
right. Interestingly enough, due to this provision, it is just this Treaty which seems to recognize it 
implicitly in the sense that the provision on exceptions and limitations suggests that there is such a 
right.Theclosestrightonwhichthereareprovisions,inArticle 7(1)oftheWCT,istherightofrental
(at least for certain categories of works). The very act of lending and rental is the same; it consists 
in “making available for use [of tangible copies of works]866 for a limited period of time”. The only 
difference is that rental is for commercial advantage, while lending is not.867 It follows from this 
also that the expression ”non-commercial lending” is a pleonasm. “Lending” by definition is a non-
commercial act: non-commercial making available of a copy for use for a limited time. If the same 
act is performed for commercial advantage, it is not lending, but rental.
MT-4.18.InordertointerprettheprovisioninArticle 4(2)(a)onexceptionsorlimitationsallowing
freelendingofaccessibleformatcopies,itisnecessarytotakeintoaccountthedifferences– 
866 SeethecommentsonArticle 8oftheWCTproviding, inter alia, for the right of (online interactive) making available to 
the public, in the Guide to the WCT in this collection. As is discussed there, although the acts of online making works 
available to the public for a limited period may be characterized as rental or lending, for such acts the provision of 
Article 8oftheWCTontherightofonlinemakingavailabletothepublicstillapplies.
867 SeethedefinitionsinArticle 2(1)(a)and(b)oftheRental,LendingandRelatedRightsDirectiveoftheEU 
(Directive 2006/115/EC):
(a) “rental” means making available for use, for a limited period of time and for direct or indirect economic or 
commercial advantage;
(b) “lending” means making available for use, for a limited period of time and not for direct or indirect economic or 
commercial advantage, when it is made through establishments which are accessible to the public.

418 concerning the relationship between the right of distribution and the right of rental (along with 
therightoflendingwhereitisgranted)–betweentheWCTandthenationallawsfollowing
the WCT model, on the one hand, and, on the other hand, some national laws that apply other 
models.UnderArticles 6and7oftheWCT,therightsofdistributionandrentalaretwostand-
alone rights (the right of distribution meaning making available copies by sale or other transfer 
of ownership). For example, the Rental, Lending and Related Rights Directive of the European 
Union (EU)868 applies this model and it also provides for a right of (public) lending. In contrast, for 
example,undersection 106(3)oftheU.S.CopyrightAct, 869 the right of distribution covers rental 
and lending in addition to the sale or other transfer of ownership of copies, but, while the right 
of distribution is exhausted with the first sale of copies, this is not necessarily so regarding the 
rights of rental and lending.870
MT-4.19. Having clarified this, it may be presumed that, although the right of lending is not 
mentionedinArticle 4(1)amongtherightstowhichtheexceptionsandlimitationsapply,the
drafters of the Treaty probably were thinking of the provisions of the EU Directive and certain 
national laws, like the U.S. Copyright Act, where the right of lending is part of the right of 
distribution–arightcoveredbyArticle 4(1).Inanyway,whetherornotitistakenforgranted
that,insuchanindirectway,therightoflendingisalsocoveredbyArticle 4(1),nosubstantial
problem emerges; no matter whether an exception applies to such a right or not, lending of 
accessible format copies is allowed freely.
Permitted acts: ”[to] supply […] copies to beneficiary persons by […] electronic communication 
by wire or wireless means”
MT-4.20. No provision may be found in any international copyright treaty on ”electronic 
communication”, but only communication to the public which, if it is by wireless means, is 
broadcasting. The expression seems to suggest that also the rights of (non-interactive) 
communication to the public and broadcasting are covered if these acts take place 
”electronically” (which is ever more widespread technology used also for non-interactive 
communication to the public, including broadcasting). In principle, it might have been justified 
to extend the exceptions and limitations to these rights. However, this would have had to be 
providedinArticle 4(1)andnotinArticle 4(2)(a),whichisonlyonthedetailsoftheapplicationof 
Article 4(1).Ithasnotbeenprovidedso.871 It is another matter that, although not by virtue of the 
Marrakesh Treaty, but under other copyright treaties, certain exceptions and limitations might 
be applied also concerning these rights.
MT-4.21.Therefore,bycomparingArticle 4(1),wheretheexceptionsandlimitationstocertain 
rightsareprovidedandArticle 4(2)(a),whichisabouttheapplicationofArticle 4(1),itmaybe 
found that the expression ”electronic communication by wire or wireless means” is probably a 
–notquitefortunate–paraphraseofwhatismentionedinArticle 4(1)(a)as“therightofmaking
availabletothepublicasprovidedbytheWIPOCopyrightTreaty(WCT)”–asdiscussedabove, 
somewhatimprecisely–andwhatcertainlymeanstherightof(interactive)makingavailableto 
thepublicasprovidedinthesecondpartofArticle 8oftheWCT.
Permitted acts: ”[to] undertake any intermediate steps to achieve those objectives”
MT-4.22. In the provision, no objectives are mentioned, but only acts permitted in the application 
oftheexceptionsandlimitationsprovidedinArticle 4.1oftheTreaty.Itwouldnothavebeen
necessary to provide that such intermediary steps are also permitted if such acts were to 
be meant that are not covered by copyright. Nor would it have been necessary to refer to 
intermediatestepsifthosestepscorrespondedtoactsotherwisecoveredinArticle 4(1)and(2)(a). 
For example, before distribution or online making available of copies, those copies have to be 
made, and making copies implies the right of reproduction, or, for the making available of an 
audio book, a performance or recital of the work before, but all this is supposed to be covered

Conditions to be met for the acts to be permitted
MT-4.23.ThelistofpermittedactsinArticle 4(2)(a)continuesinthisway:“whenallofthe
following conditions are met”; then conditions are determined in four points. These do not 
requirespecialinterpretation;theyareself-explanatoryandtoagreatextentredundantin
view of other provisions of the Marrakesh Treaty. Point (i) states what should be obvious for any 
exceptions and limitations; namely that they must be based on lawful sources. Point (ii) repeats 
insomewhatmoredetailwhatisprovidedinthesecondsentenceofArticle 4(1)(a)onwhatkinds
of changes are allowed for the making of accessible format copies. Under point (iii), the accessible 
format copies are to be ”supplied” exclusively to be used by beneficiary persons, which is a 
condition prescribed in several other provisions of the Treaty before and after, including in the 
definitionof”accessibleformatcopies”inArticle 2(b)oftheTreaty.Finally,point (iv)isredundant
inviewofthecriterionstatedinthedefinitionof“authorizedentity”inArticle 2(c)oftheTreaty
according to which these entities must carry out their activities on a non-profit basis.
(b)  A beneficiary person, or someone acting on his or her behalf including a 
primary caretaker or caregiver, may make an accessible format copy of a 
work for the personal use of the beneficiary person or otherwise may assist 
the beneficiary person to make and use accessible format copies where the 
beneficiary person has lawful access to that work or a copy of that work.
MT-4.24.Copyingforprivate,personalpurposesisfreeundermanynationallawsinquitea 
broad scope of acts of reproduction even for persons without impairment, although in certain 
cases not as a full exception to the exclusive right of reproduction but as a limitation to a right 
toremuneration.InArticle 4(2)(b),itisclarifiedthateitherthebeneficiarypersonsorthose 
who act on their behalf may make accessible format copies freely for the personal use of the 
beneficiary persons of works to which they have lawful access.
3. AContractingPartymayfulfillArticle 4(1)byprovidingotherlimitationsorexceptions

AgreedStatementconcerningArticle 4(3):Itisunderstoodthatthisparagraph neitherreduces

Application of Article  4(1) in manners other than mentioned in Article  4(2)
MT-4.25.InthecontextofArticle 4,whereparagraph (2)providesforcertainconcretewaysof 
applyingtheprovisionofparagraph (1),theexpression”otherlimitationsorexceptions”may
onlymeanthosethatarealsosuitabletoapplyparagraph (1)althoughnotinthesameconcrete
ways. Such ”other limitations or exceptions” may also be those that are applicable in favor of any 
members of the public, including the beneficiaries under the Marrakesh Treaty, in such a way 
thattheyfulfilltherequirementsprovidedinArticle 4(1).
MT-4.26. Such ”other” ways of applying the exceptions and limitations must also be in 
accordance with the international norms and with the other provisions of the Treaty; in 
particular–asthisismadeclearinthisparagraph byreferencetoArticle 11–withthe
cumulative conditions of the three-step test.

420 Possible limitations of and exceptions to the right of translation
MT-4.27. An agreed statement was added to this paragraph. It states that its provision neither 
reduces nor extends the scope of applicability of limitations and exceptions permitted under the 
Berne Convention, as regards the right of translation, with respect to the visually impaired. The 
statementisinaccordancewith–and,infact,followsfrom–theprinciplesofnon-discrimination 
andequalopportunityinvokedinthefirstpreambleparagraph.Itstatesnomorethanthatthe 
same treatment applies in respect of the right of translation for beneficiary persons under the 
Marrakesh Treaty as for other persons. This means that, if a translation is available, it should 
also be available under the same conditions to the beneficiary persons.
MT-4.28. This also means that if, for example, a developing country applies compulsory 
translation licenses in accordance with the Appendix to the Berne Convention, the translations 
are supposed to be made available also to visually impaired or other print disabled persons 
in accessible format copies. In contrast, if no translation exists in a given language (since 
the holder of the exclusive right of translation has not authorized one and no compulsory 
license is applicable in accordance with the Appendix) and, therefore, none is available either 
to beneficiary persons or to other persons, in general, it would not be in accordance with 
theprinciplesofnon-discriminationandequaltreatmenttoclaimthatatranslationmustbe
made available just to the beneficiary persons through a specific limitation or exception. Only 
in general, because it is possible that there are certain works that specifically interest the 
beneficiaries under the Treaty and, therefore, its availability in translated form is justified.
4. AContractingPartymayconfinelimitationsorexceptionsunderthisArticle toworks
which, in the particular accessible format, cannot be obtained commercially under 
reasonable terms for beneficiary persons in that market. Any Contracting Party availing 
itself of this possibility shall so declare in a notification deposited with the Director 
General of WIPO at the time of ratification of, acceptance of or accession to this Treaty 
or at any time thereafter.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 4(4):Itisunderstoodthatacommercialavailability
requirementdoesnotprejudgewhetherornotalimitationorexceptionunderthisArticle is
consistent with the three-step test.
Paragraph (4) in the light of the eighth preamble paragraph
MT-4.29.Theeighthpreambleparagraph oftheMarrakeshTreatyreadsasfollows:“Recognizing 
both the importance of rightholders’ role in making their works accessible to persons with visual 
impairments or with other print disabilities and the importance of appropriate limitations and 
exceptions to make works accessible to these persons, particularly when the market is unable to 
provide such access”. It stresses the importance of the rightholders’ role in making their works 
accessible to the beneficiary persons, which seems to have two aspects. First, it means that, for 
theavailabilityoftheworkstosatisfycertainrequirementsandexpectationsofthemembersof
the public, including visually impaired and otherwise print disabled persons, their creative efforts 
are needed. Second, they are expected to be willing to make available their works in ab ovo 
accessible format copies on reasonable conditions allowing affordable access by the beneficiary 
persons. This implies that the application of exceptions and limitations is particularly justified 
when the market is unable to provide due access, in this way, to accessible format copies.
MT-4.30.Boththeseaspectsofthepreambleparagraph arerelevantfortheinterpretation
andapplicationofparagraph (4).Itishardlyquestionablethatforsustainablecreativity,itis
indispensable that the authors and other rightholders receive appropriate remuneration for 
the use of their works. This may also be ensured, however, if the remuneration is differentiated, 
taking into account the specific conditions of the different categories of users and, in the case 
of trans-border distribution of accessible format copies, the economic and social conditions 
in the various countries. What is affordable in an industrialized country may not be in a 
developing country and certainly not in a least-developed country. It seems that the preamble 
paragraph referstothisconsiderationwhenitstatesthatexceptionsandlimitationsare
important where the availability of accessible copies cannot be guaranteed through the usual 
market conditions, and that this is particularly true in the case of the cumulatively disadvantaged 
persons–thevisuallyimpairedandotherprintdisabled–livingincountrieswithpooreconomic

===== PAGE 420 =====
