and social conditions. These and the related human-rights and humanitarian considerations 
shouldbedecisiveinconsideringthequestionofwhethertheabsenceofcommercialavailability
may be made a condition of the application of the exceptions and limitations under the 
Marrakesh Treaty.
MT-4.31.Nevertheless,theprovisionofparagraph (4)isbasedontherecognition–also
reflected in the 1982 Model Provisions, as mentioned above, and also stressed in the Preamble 
oftheTreaty–thatthebestwayofprovidingabroadandup-to-datesupplyofaccessibleformat
copies is by encouraging the owners of rights to arrange for this under reasonable conditions.
MT-4.32.  One may be tempted to presume that those Contracting Parties will apply 
paragraph (4)inordertoofferadequateincentivesfortheirownersofrightstopromote
proactively the production and distribution of accessible format copies. Through the 
application of the provisions to facilitate cross-border use of such copies, the beneficiary 
personsofimporting–mainlydeveloping–countriesmayalsobenefitfromsuchincentivizing 
legislative measures.
MT-4.33. Quick and effective commercial availability of accessible format copies with affordable 
conditions ensured by the publishers themselves rather than applying limitations and 
exceptions to make such copies available may also be in the interest of developing countries. 
This recognition was reflected, for example, in the position paper of the Publishers Association 
of South Africa (PASA) on the Marrakesh Treaty:
[F]or meaningful progress in closing the gap [between the availability of non-accessible 
formats and accessible formats], it is vital to keep incentives to publish alive and 
specifically incentives to format and mainstream content to make it “born-accessible;” 
that is, in a format that lends itself to full accessibility by using the right software and 
navigational tools.
Commercialavailabilityisanimportantconcerntopublishers:onlypublisherscanquickly
and efficiently provide books to persons with print disability at the same time and under 
the same terms as to persons without a print disability. Wherever we do this already, there 
is no need for copyright exceptions.873
Agreed statement: stating the obvious
MT-4.34.Anagreedstatementwasadoptedconcerningparagraph (4):”Itisunderstood 
thatacommercialavailabilityrequirementdoesnotprejudgewhetherornotalimitationor
exceptionunderthisArticle isconsistentwiththethree-steptest”.Intheagreedstatement, 
theexpression”commercialavailabilityrequirement”soundsasifitweresuggestingthat 
commercialavailabilityisarequirementoftheapplicabilityoflimitationsandexceptions. 
However,thestatementconcernsArticle 4(4),underwhichaContractingParty may subject 
theapplicabilityofthelimitationsandexceptionsprovidedforinArticle 4(1)tothecondition 
that a given work cannot be obtained commercially in the market in a particular accessible 
formatunderreasonableterms.Thismeansthatcommercialavailabilityisnotarequirement
for the application of limitations and exceptions. Due to this, the statement should rather be 
understood to mean that the absence of commercial availability alone is not a decisive factor in 
the applicability of limitations or exceptions with regard to the three-step test.
MT-4.35. The agreed statement seems to be neutral from the viewpoint of what role commercial 
availability or its absence may have in terms of the three-step test. It only states that this in 
itself does not prejudice the application of the test. Therefore, it seems to only mean that the 
applicationoftheabsence-of-commercial-availabilityrequirementalone does not necessarily 
meanthatthelimitationsorexceptionscorrespondtothethree-steptest.Thisisquiteobvious 
because a complex analysis is needed in order to establish whether or not an exception or 
limitation corresponds to the three conditions of the test (which in the case of the exceptions 
and limitations to be applied for visually impaired and other print disabled persons rather 
only means the second and third conditions, because it is granted that they correspond to the

5.  It shall be a matter for national law to determine whether limitations or exceptions 
underthisArticle aresubjecttoremuneration.
Interpretation of paragraph  (5): mutatis mutandis as paragraph  (4)
MT-4.36.Fortheinterpretationandapplicationofparagraph (5)inthelightoftheeighth 
preambleparagraph –sinceitiscloselyconnectedtothecommercialaspectsofavailabilityof 

thecommentsonparagraph (4)above.
Paragraph (5) and the meaning of “limitations” and “exceptions”
MT-4.37.SincetheprovisionsofArticle 4coverbothexceptionsandlimitations, in view of the 
commentsonArticle 4(1)above,thisprovisionmayberegardedasamereclarification:inthe
case of a limitation, the right concerned is still maintained but in a way that what is originally 
provided for as an exclusive right is limited to a mere right to remuneration (or to a non-voluntary 
license, which is similar to a right to remuneration since there is no need for prior authorization).
MT-4.38. The use of the term ”exception” does not seem to be appropriate in this 
paragraph takingintoaccounttheordinarymeaningoftheword,asalsoclarifiedinthe
Glossary. As discussed, in the case of an exception to a right, free use is allowed in the sense 
that neither any authorization is needed nor any remuneration is to be paid. Therefore, if no 
authorization is needed for the performance of acts covered by a certain right but remuneration 
must be paid, it is not an exception to, but a limitation of, the right.
Article 5
Cross-Border Exchange of Accessible Format Copies
1.  Contracting Parties shall provide that if an accessible format copy is made under a 
limitation or exception or pursuant to operation of law, that accessible format copy 
may be distributed or made available by an authorized entity to a beneficiary person or 
an authorized entity in another Contracting Party.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 5(1):ItisfurtherunderstoodthatnothinginthisTreaty
reduces or extends the scope of exclusive rights under any other treaty.
Article 5 on export and Article 6 on import: twin rights for cross-border exchange
MT-5.1.TheprovisioninArticle 5(1)–alongwiththerelatedprovisionsonthedetailsand
conditionsofitsapplicationinArticle 5(2)–isakeyelementoftheMarrakeshTreatybecause
itisuniquelyformat-oriented.Itreflectstherecognitionthat,byavoidingduplicationof 
investments in the making of accessible format copies of the same works in the same language 
in various countries, the objective to be served by the Treaty may be more efficiently fulfilled; 
as well as that the availability of accessible copies may only be ensured in the least developed 
andcertaindevelopingcountriesiftheyimportsuchcopiesfromother–mainlyindustrialized 
–countries.Article 5(1)appliesfortheContractingPartieswhereaccessibleformatcopiesare 
made;suchContractingParties–usingageneralterm–aresupposedto”export”copiesto
otherContractingPartiesinaccordancewiththeprovisionsofArticle 5(1).Article 6ontheright 
toimportmirrorsArticle 5withregardtotheContractingPartiestowhichaccessibleformat 
copies are exported.
Interpretation of Article 5(1): “if an accessible format copy is made under a limitation or 
exception or pursuant to operation of law”
MT-5.2. The phrase ”if an accessible format copy is made under a limitation or exception or 
pursuant to operation of law” (emphasis added) means that the provision applies only in this 
case. It is only in this case that “that accessible format copy may be distributed or made available

===== PAGE 422 =====
423
PART IV. Guide to the Marrakesh VIP Treaty
by an authorized entity to a beneficiary person or an authorized entity in another Contracting 
Party”.Consequently,whenanaccessibleformatcopyismadenotinthiswaybutbasedonthe
authorizationoftherightholder,Article 5(1)isnotapplicable. 874
Interpretation of Article 5(1): “accessible format copy […] made […] pursuant to operation of law”
MT-5.3.TheprovisionofArticle 5(1)isapplicableonlywhereanaccessibleformatcopyismade
under a limitation or exception or “pursuant to operation of law”. The other provisions of the Treaty 
only mention limitations or exceptions; therefore, this term needs interpretation. Since it is linked 
by the conjunction ”or” to exceptions or limitations, it is an alternative to these; it logically cannot 
mean a limitation of, or an exception to, a right. Thus “pursuant to the operation of law” seems to 
refer to certain productions that, although they qualify as literary or artistic works, are excluded from 
copyright protection under the legislation of a Contracting Party (where such exclusion is allowed 
underspecificprovisionsoftheBerneConvention).Articles 2(4)and2bis(1) contain such provisions:
Article 2(4):ItshallbeamatterforlegislationinthecountriesoftheUniontodetermine
the protection to be granted to official texts of a legislative, administrative and legal 
nature, and to official translations of such texts.
Article 2bis(1): It shall be a matter for legislation in the countries of the Union to exclude, 
whollyorinpart,fromtheprotectionprovidedbytheprecedingArticle politicalspeeches
and speeches delivered in the course of legal proceedings.
Interpretation of Article 5(1): “that accessible format copy may be distributed or made available”
MT-5.4.ThisphraseshouldbeinterpretedtogetherwithArticle 5(4)(c),whichreads:“Nothing
inthisArticle affectsthedeterminationofwhatconstitutesanactofdistributionoranactof
making available to the public”. This seems to be a non-derogation clause, but it can hardly be 
construedassuch,becausethereisnothinginArticle 5thatmightberegardedasdirectorindirect
determination.Thisleadstothequestionofwhereitisthendeterminedwhattheseactsmean.The
answermaybefoundpartlyinArticle 1,whichcontainsthebasicnon-derogationclause,andpartly
–andalsomoreconcretelyinthecontextoftheMarrakeshTreaty–inArticle 4(1)asanalyzedabove.
MT-5.5.UnderArticle 1,“[n]othingintheTreaty[derogates]fromanyobligationsthat
Contracting Parties have to each other under any other treaties, nor shall it prejudice any rights 
that a Contracting Party has under any other treaties”. Therefore, for the Contracting Parties 
oftheWCT–andtheoverwhelmingmajorityofthepresentandpotentialfutureContracting 
PartiesoftheMarrakeshTreatyarepartytotheWCT–thereislikelynodoubtwheretheymay
find these acts determined.
MT-5.6.FromArticle 4(1),however,itisclearthat,foranyContractingPartyoftheMarrakesh
Treaty, irrespective of whether it is also party to the WCT, its concepts of distribution and 
making available to the public apply. As discussed above, there are two possible readings of 
Article 4(1).Oneofthem–and,basedonthetextandthecontextoftheprovision,itseems
tobethecorrectoneunderArticle 31.1oftheVCLT–isthatthephrase”asdeterminedinthe
WIPO Copyright Treaty (WCT)” refers to all three rights mentioned before it; that is, to the 
right of reproduction, the right of distribution and the right of making available to the public. 
Nevertheless, even if the other possible interpretation were accepted, it would not change the 
essence of the determination of the acts of distribution and making available to the public. 
Under that other interpretation, the phrase ”as determined by the WIPO Copyright Treaty 
(WCT)” would be considered to refer only to the last mentioned act of ”making available [to the 
public]”.875 The concept of ”making available [to the public]” would have to be understood as 
provided in the WCT, while the meaning of the term “distribution” of copies might be considered 
asitfollowsfromArticle 6oftheWCTandtheagreedstatementconcerningit(accordingto
which the right of distribution only applies to the making available of tangible copies and 
that it is exhausted with the first sale thereof). It is hardly a troubling effect in terms of the 
874 In Reinbothe and von Lewinski, Silke von Lewinski expresses the same opinion, see 641.
875Thewords“tothepublic”areaddedinsquarebracketsalthough,whiletheyappearinthiswayinArticle 4(1)(a),they 

MT-5.7.Therefore,inthecontextoftheTreaty,thenon-derogationclauseinArticle 5(4)(c)

public]”underArticle 4(1)(a).
Interpretation of the agreed statement
MT-5.8.AnagreedstatementwasappendedtoArticle 5(1):“Itisfurtherunderstoodthatnothing
in this Treaty reduces or extends the scope of exclusive rights under any other treaty”. It is not 
clear why such a statement was found necessary and why it has been adopted solely concerning 
Article 5(1),becauseitaddressesthegeneralquestion–ifitisaquestionatall–whether
anything in the Treaty may reduce or extend the scope of exclusive rights under any other treaty.
MT-5.9.Intheprecedingparagraph,whether“itisaquestionatall”iscalledintoquestionbecause
what is stated in the agreed statement clearly follows from other provisions of the Treaty. The 
agreed statement covers an issue of the relationship of the Marrakesh Treaty with other treaties. 
Thisissue,however,issettledbythenon-derogationclauseofArticle 1oftheTreaty.
MT-5.10. Therefore, if such an agreed statement had been necessary, it would have been more 
appropriatetoadoptitconcerningArticle 1.Butitisnotnecessary.Itfollowsunequivocally 
fromArticle 1andthusdoesnotchangethescopeofanyexclusiverightsprovidedforin
those treaties (of course, in the sense that it does not concern it in a way other than through 
limitations and exceptions provided in the Treaty). As for the extension of rights provided in 
other treaties, there is no provision in the Marrakesh Treaty from which this might be deduced; 
which is understandable, because the purpose of the Treaty is exactly to provide limitations and 
exceptions to the existing rights provided in other treaties.
2. AContractingPartymayfulfillArticle 5(1)byprovidingalimitationorexceptioninits
national copyright law such that:
(a)  authorized entities shall be permitted, without the authorization of the rightholder, 
to distribute or make available for the exclusive use of beneficiary persons 
accessible format copies to an authorized entity in another Contracting Party; and
(b)  authorized entities shall be permitted, without the authorization of the 
rightholderandpursuanttoArticle 2(c),todistributeormakeavailable
accessible format copies to a beneficiary person in another Contracting Party;
provided that prior to the distribution or making available the originating authorized 
entity did not know or have reasonable grounds to know that the accessible format 
copy would be used for other than beneficiary persons.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 5(2):Itisunderstoodthat,todistributeormakeavailable
accessible format copies directly to a beneficiary person in another Contracting Party, it may 
be appropriate for an authorized entity to apply further measures to confirm that the person it 
isservingisabeneficiarypersonandtofollowitsownpracticesasdescribedinArticle 2(c).
Interpretation of Article  5(2)(a)
MT-5.11.Subparagraph (a)doesnotaddanytrulynewsubstantivecriteriafortheapplicationof
paragraph (1);itmerelyrepeatsinotherwordsandmoredetailwhatfollowsfromparagraph (1)
and the other provisions of the Treaty:
 – Paragraph (1)providesthat,whereanaccessibleformatcopyismadeunderalimitationor
exception or pursuant to operation of law, it may be distributed or made available by an 
authorized entity to a beneficiary person or an authorized entity in another Contracting 
Party. As can be seen, point (a) repeats this in terms of distribution or making available of 
accessible copies to an authorized entity.
 – Itistruethat,intheclosinglinesoftheparagraph itisaddedthatsubparagraph (a)(like
subparagraph (b))appliesonlyiftheauthorizedentitydoesnotknoworhavereasonablegrounds

===== PAGE 424 =====
425
PART IV. Guide to the Marrakesh VIP Treaty
to know that the accessible format copy would be used for persons other than beneficiaries. This, 
however, follows from the very definitions of “accessible format copy” and “authorized entity” in 
Article 2(b),(c)and(d).Underthoseprovisions,anaccessibleformatcopybydefinitionmaybe
usedexclusivelybybeneficiarypersons(Article 2(b))andanauthorizedentity,alsobydefinition,
must “establish that the persons it serves are beneficiary persons” and must “limit to beneficiary 
persons and/or authorized entities […] distribution and making available of accessible format 
copies”(Article 2(d)).Therefore,theclosinglinesofArticle 5(2)onlyconfirmwhatisclarifiedinthe
provisionsofArticle 2(ofcourse,suchredundancydoesnotcreateanyinterpretationproblem).
Article 2appliesintheseaspectstoowithouttheneedtobeseparatelyconfirmed.Inaccordance
with this, it is more than obvious that, if an authorized entity knows or has reasonable grounds 
to know that an accessible format copy will be used by others than beneficiary persons, it is not 
allowed to distribute or make available accessible format copies to them.
Interpretation of Article  5(2)(b)
MT-5.12.Thesamecommentsapplytosubparagraph (b)mutatis mutandis astosubparagraph (a)
above –withtheimportantdifference,however,thattheresponsibilityoftheauthorizedentity 
of the “exporting” Contracting Party is much greater if it distributes or makes available online 
accessible format copies to beneficiary persons directly. In such a case it is not only “appropriate 
for an authorized entity to apply further measures to confirm that the person it is serving is 
abeneficiaryperson”asstressedintheagreedstatementaddedtosubparagraph (b),but,in 
general, it is highly desirable.
3. AContractingPartymayfulfillArticle 5(1)byprovidingotherlimitationsorexceptions
initsnationalcopyrightlawpursuanttoArticles 5(4),10and11.
“Other” limitations and exceptions: with the same meaning as Article  5(1)
MT-5.13.ThesamekindofcommentmaybemadeonthisprovisionasonArticle 4(3).In
the context of the Treaty, the purpose of this provision is only to clarify the possible ways of 
implementingthelimitationsorexceptionsprovidedforinArticle 5(1).Thatis,“otherlimitations
orexceptions”mayonlymeanthosethataresuitabletoimplementArticle 5(1)althoughnotinthe
formsmentionedinArticle 5(2).TheTreatydoesnotregulate“otherlimitationsorexceptions”in
the sense that they do not provide specifically for the beneficiaries under the Marrakesh Treaty.
Bottom line: accordance with the three-step test
MT-5.14. Such “other” exceptions or limitations must also be in accordance with the international 
normsandwiththeotherprovisionsoftheMarrakeshTreaty,inparticular–asisalsomade
clearinparagraph (3)byareferencetoArticle 11aswellastoArticle 5(4)tobridgethe“Berne
gap”andthe”WCTgap”(seebelow)–withthecumulativeconditionsofthethree-steptest.
4.  (a)  When an authorized entity in a Contracting Party receives accessible format 
copiespursuanttoArticle 5(1)andthatContractingPartydoesnothave
obligationsunderArticle 9oftheBerneConvention,itwillensure,consistent
with its own legal system and practices, that the accessible format copies are 
only reproduced, distributed or made available for the benefit of beneficiary 
persons in that Contracting Party’s jurisdiction.
Interpretation of Article  5(4)(a)
MT-5.15.Subparagraph (a)ofArticle 5(4)isintendedtosolvetheproblemwhichwasreferred
to in the course of the preparatory work and at the Diplomatic Conference as the “Berne gap”. 
ItaddressesthesituationofthecountriesthatarenotboundbyArticle 9(2)oftheBerne
Convention, which subjects any exception to or limitation of the right of reproduction to the 
three-step test. The number of such countries is very limited since the substantive provisions of 
the Convention bind not only the member countries of the Berne Union but, by reference, also 
theMembersoftheWorldTradeOrganization(WTO)(onthebasisofArticle 9(1)oftheTRIPS
Agreement)andtheContractingPartiesoftheWCT(byvirtueofArticle 1(4)ofthethatTreaty).
Thus,thedescriptioninArticle 5(4)(a)addressesonlythecountriesthatarenotboundbyanyof
these instruments; furthermore, those least developed countries that are not party either to the

===== PAGE 425 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
426 Berne Convention or to the WCT and are only Members of the WTO (but, due to the transitional 
provisionsunderArticle 66(1)oftheTRIPSAgreement,maynotyetbeboundbysuchprovisions
oftheBerneConventionasArticle 9).
MT-5.16.Article 5(4)(a)ensuresthatthebasicprincipleoftheMarrakeshTreaty,according
to which accessible format copies may only be reproduced, distributed or made available 
to beneficiary persons, is duly respected. Furthermore, the phrase “are only reproduced, 
distributed or made available for the benefit of beneficiary persons in that Contracting Party’s 
jurisdiction” (emphasis added) means not only that these acts may be performed exclusively for 
beneficiary persons but also that the authorized entities are not allowed to distribute or make 
available accessible format copies to a beneficiary person or an authorized entity in another 
Contracting Party. They must limit the distribution or making available of such copies to the 
jurisdiction of the Contracting Party concerned.
MT-5.17.TheprovisionofArticle 5(4)(a)accordingtowhichtheContractingPartyconcernedmust
ensure the personal and territorial limitation of the scope of distribution or making available 
of accessible format copies “consistent with its own legal system and practices” seems to be 
redundant,becauseArticle 10oftheTreatyprovidesasfollows:
1.  Contracting Parties undertake to adopt the measures necessary to ensure the 
application of this Treaty.
2.  Nothing shall prevent Contracting Parties from determining the appropriate 
method of implementing the provisions of this Treaty within their own legal system 
and practice.
MT-5.18.UnderArticle 10(2),notonlytheimplementationofArticle 5(4)(a),butthe
implementation of the entire Treaty must be “consistent with the legal system and practice” 
of the given Contracting Party. It must be stressed, however that, irrespective of the kind of 
legal system and practice the Contracting Party may have, it should be in accordance with 
Article 5(1).Itcannotusethespecialfeaturesofitslegalsystemorpracticeasanexcusefornot
implementing duly the provisions of the Treaty.
(b)  The distribution and making available of accessible format copies by an 
authorizedentitypursuanttoArticle 5(1)shallbelimitedtothatjurisdiction
unless the Contracting Party is a Party to the WIPO Copyright Treaty or 
otherwise limits limitations and exceptions implementing this Treaty to the right 
of distribution and the right of making available to the public to certain special 
cases which do not conflict with a normal exploitation of the work and do not 
unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of the rightholder.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 5(4)(b):ItisunderstoodthatnothinginthisTreaty
requiresorimpliesthataContractingPartyadoptorapplythethree-steptestbeyondits
obligations under this instrument or under other international treaties.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 5(4)(b):ItisunderstoodthatnothinginthisTreatycreates
any obligations for a Contracting Party to ratify or accede to the WCT or to comply with any 
of its provisions and nothing in this Treaty prejudices any rights, limitations and exceptions 
contained in the WCT.
Interpretation of Article  5(4)(b)
MT-5.19.WhileArticle 5(4)(a)fillsthe“Bernegap”,inArticle 5(4)(b),theproblemofthe“WCT
gap” is settled. The limitations and exceptions provided in the Marrakesh Treaty beyond the 
rightofreproductionregulatedinArticle 9oftheBerneConventionalsoapplytotherights 
of distribution and making available to the public which are provided for by the WCT. Under 
Article 10oftheWCT,bothexceptionstoandlimitationsoftheserights–alongwiththespecific
limitationsandexceptionsprovidedbytheBerneConvention–mayonlybeappliediftheymeet
the cumulative conditions of the three-step test.

MT-5.20.Article 5(4)(b)appliesnotonlytothoseContractingPartiesthatreceiveaccessible 
format copies from another Contracting Party but also to those that might wish to distribute or 
make available such copies to the beneficiary persons in another Contracting Party through an 
authorized entity or directly. Unless the receiving Contracting Party is also party to the WCT (and 
thusobligatedtoapplythethree-steptestunderArticle 10ofthatTreaty)orotherwisesubmits 
the application of the limitations and exceptions to the three-step test, it must limit distribution 
and making available of accessible format copies to the beneficiary persons within its own 
jurisdiction. Such a Contracting Party is not allowed either to distribute or to make available 
such copies to the beneficiary persons of another Contracting Party. 876
Interpretation of the first agreed statement concerning Article  5(4)(b)
MT-5.21.TwoagreedstatementsareappendedtoArticle 5(4)(b).Thefirststatesthatnothingin 
the Marrakesh Treaty implies that a Contracting Party is to adopt or apply the three-step test 
beyonditsobligationsunderthisTreatyorotherinternationaltreaties.Itisauniqueprovision
in an international copyright treaty. What it states is not only obvious but the most obvious 
aspectoftheconsequenceofbecomingpartytoacopyrighttreaty;itgoesalongwiththe 
acceptance of certain minimum obligations. When an obligation is provided in a treaty, it is not 
necessary to state that it must be fulfilled, nor to add that this is so only to the extent that there 
is an obligation.
MT-5.22. The countries party to the Berne Convention, the Members of the WCT and the 
Contracting Parties of the WCT are all obligated to limit copyright exceptions and limitations 
to the fulfillment of the three-step test. This includes the overwhelming majority of potential 
Contracting Parties of the Marrakesh Treaty, and is particularly relevant for those with the 
capacity for production and making available of accessible format copies.
MT-5.23.TheMarrakeshTreatycontainsclearprovisionsinArticle 5(4)(b)concerningthose
Contracting Parties that are not party to the WCT. They are not obligated to become party to it 
(althoughthenthequestionmayemergewhytheyneedexceptionstoandlimitationsofcertain
rights if they do not grant those rights) and, thus, are not obligated to apply the three-step test 
byvirtueofitsArticle 10.ItisexactlyArticle 5(4)(b)oftheMarrakeshTreaty,towhichthisagreed
statement is appended, that bridges the gap that emerges in this case. Therefore, it is clear in 
this context that the first agreed statement declares what is obvious.
Interpretation of the second agreed statement concerning Article  5(4)(b)
MT-5.24. The second agreed statement seems to be unnecessary. Nothing in the interpretation 
of the Marrakesh Treaty would be different if this statement had not been adopted. There is no 
provision in the Treaty that might be interpreted as an obligation to accede to the WCT or to 
fulfill any obligation under it although a Contracting Party has not accepted it, and as far as the 
non-derogation clause in the second part of the statement is concerned, it merely repeats what 
isprovidedinArticle 1oftheTreaty.
MT-5.25.ThefactthatthisagreedstatementwasadoptedspecificallyconcerningArticle 5(4)(b)
makesitevenmoreconspicuouslyunnecessary.Itisinthisprovisionthatitismadeevenclearer –
ifitwerenototherwisecompletelyclear–thataccessiontotheWCT(andthustheacceptanceof
any obligation under that treaty) is not a precondition of becoming party to the Marrakesh Treaty. 
ThisisimpliedinthekeyphraseofArticle 5(4)(b):“unlesstheContractingPartyisaPartytothe
WIPO Copyright Treaty”. Thus, it cannot emerge that a country may not become party to the 
Marrakesh Treaty without first being party to the WCT. This puts it beyond all doubt that it may.
(c) NothinginthisArticle affectsthedeterminationofwhatconstitutesanactof
distribution or an act of making available to the public.

Article 6
Importation of Accessible Format Copies
To the extent that the national law of a Contracting Party would permit a beneficiary person, 
someone acting on his or her behalf, or an authorized entity, to make an accessible format 
copy of a work, the national law of that Contracting Party shall also permit them to import an 
accessible format copy for the benefit of beneficiary persons, without the authorization of 
the rightholder.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 6:ItisunderstoodthattheContractingPartieshavethe
sameflexibilitiessetoutinArticle 4whenimplementingtheirobligationsunderArticle 6.
What may be made may also be imported
MT-6.1.TheprovisionofArticle 6logicallyfollowsfromtheotherprovisionsoftheMarrakesh
Treaty.Thequestionmayemergewhyitprovidesthattheimportisallowed“[t]otheextentthat
the national law of a Contracting Party would permit [someone] to make an accessible format 
copy of a work”. The answer may be found in the words “to the extent”, and it is a reference 
toArticle 4(4),whichallowslimitationsorexceptionstobeconfinedtoworksthatcannot 
beobtainedcommerciallyunderreasonableterms,andtoArticle 4(5),accordingtowhich 
limitations877 may be subject to remuneration.
Agreed statement on the application to Article  6 of the “flexibilities” under Article  4
MT-6.2.TheagreedstatementappendedtoArticle 6readsasfollows:“Itisunderstoodthat 
theContractingPartieshavethesameflexibilitiessetoutinArticle 4whenimplementingtheir 
obligationsunderArticle 6”.Inthecontextoftreatyobligations,therearetwobasictypesof 
“flexibilities”. First, permission is provided in certain cases under certain conditions not to apply 
a certain rule or to limit its application (exceptions and limitations fall into this category, but 
permission to exclude certain categories of works from copyright protection, for example, is 
of the same nature). Second, although there is no exception to or limitation of the obligation 
to apply a certain rule, it is left to the Contracting Parties how they fulfill it (the latter kind of 
“flexibilities” do not allow them to not fulfill the obligation at all or not completely). It is in the 
lightofallthisthatthe“flexibilities”offeredbyArticle 4shouldbeconsideredandthatthe 
possibilityoftheirapplicationinthecontextofArticle 6mayemerge.Theidentificationofthe 
provisions providing such “flexibilities” is, in general, facilitated by the fact that such provisions 
use may language,allowingtheContractingPartiestomakeuseofthem.InArticle 4,thereare
four such provisions, which are discussed below.
MT-6.3.Article 4(1)(b)isthefirstsuchprovisionbut,sinceithasnothingtodowiththeright 
ofdistribution(orimportation)–butonlywithpublicperformance(recitation)–theagreed 
statement is irrelevant.
MT-6.4.Article 4(2)isthesecondsuchprovision.Ituses may language in respect of how the 
provisionofArticle 4(1)isimplemented.Thosewhotriedtoapplythiskindof“flexibility”in 
thecaseofArticle 6wouldhavetoacknowledgethatthereisnoneedforitinthecontext
ofimportationofaccessibleformatcopies,becauseArticle 6determinesallthesubstantive 
conditions;thereisnoroomfordetailsasintherelationshipofArticle 4(1)andArticle 4(2).
877 For the reasons why only limitations are involved rather than exceptions, seethecommentsonArticle 5(5)above.

===== PAGE 428 =====
429
PART IV. Guide to the Marrakesh VIP Treaty
MT-6.5.Article 4(3),incontrast,mayreallyoffer“flexibilities”thatapplytoArticle 6.Asdiscussed 
in the comments to that provision, it clarifies that, as long it guarantees the implementation of 
Article 4(1),thelimitationsandexceptionsprovidedforinit may also be implemented through 
“other exceptions or limitations”. If one considers this “flexibility” regarding the method of 
implementationofArticle 6,whatmightoccurisapossibilityofabroaderregulationconcerning 
the right of importation and possible limitations of or exceptions to it.
MT-6.6.Article 4(4)alsousesmay languageinrespectofquiteanimportantaspectofthe
applicationornon-applicationofthelimitationsandexceptionsprovidedforinArticle 4(1).Itallows
a Contracting Party to disapply the limitations and exceptions as long as accessible format copies 
may be obtained commercially under reasonable terms. Making use of this “flexibility” in respect 
ofArticle 6wouldmeanthataContractingPartymaydecidenottoapplyArticle 6where,onits
market, accessible format copies are available under reasonable terms. As mentioned above, this 
kindof“flexibility”,towhichtheproviso“totheextent”refers,appliesinthetextofArticle 6.
MT-6.7.ThelastprovisionofArticle 4thatusesmay languageisArticle 4(5),underwhich,inthe
casescoveredbyArticle 4(1),itisuptoeachContractingPartytoprovideforremunerationasa
condition of the application of the limitations. As discussed above, this is the other “flexibility” to 
which the proviso “to the extent” refers. 878
Article 7
Obligations Concerning Technological Measures
Contracting Parties shall take appropriate measures, as necessary, to ensure that when they 
provideadequatelegalprotectionandeffectivelegalremediesagainstthecircumventionof
effective technological measures, this legal protection does not prevent beneficiary persons 
from enjoying the limitations and exceptions provided for in this Treaty.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 7:Itisunderstoodthatauthorizedentities,invarious
circumstances, choose to apply technological measures in the making, distribution and making 
available of accessible format copies and nothing herein disturbs such practices when in 
accordance with national law.
Technological measures and the application of exceptions and limitations under the WIPO 
“Internet Treaties”
MT-7.1. The WCT and the WPPT, adopted in 1996, were the first international treaties to obligate 
ContractingPartiestoprovideadequatelegalprotectionandeffectivelegalremediesagainst 
the circumvention of effective TPMs. Sixteen years later, in 2012, the international community, 
in the BTAP as the third “Internet Treaty”, confirmed that, in the online digital environment, the 
application of TPMs, in certain cases, is an indispensable means of normal exploitation of works 
andsubjectmattersofrelatedrights.Article 15oftheBTAPcontains( mutatis mutandis, adapted 
tothesubjectmatteroftheTreaty)thesameprovisioninthisrespectasArticle 11oftheWCT
andArticle 18oftheWPPT.
MT-7.2. By the time the preparation and adoption of the BTAP took place, sufficient experience 
was available on the implementation of the TPMs provisions of the WCT and the WPPT. It had 
beenprovedthatappropriatebalancemaybeestablishedbetweenadequateprotectionofTPMs
and the application of certain exceptions and limitations that are important from the viewpoint 
of public interests, including the protection of human rights. An agreed statement adopted 
concerningArticle 15onTPMsandArticle 13ofthethree-steptestclarifiedthisasfollows:
ItisunderstoodthatnothinginthisArticle preventsaContractingPartyfromadopting
effective and necessary measures to ensure that a beneficiary may enjoy limitations and 
exceptionsprovidedinthatContractingParty’snationallaw,inaccordancewithArticle 13,
where technological measures have been applied to an audiovisual performance and 
878FortheapplicationoftheflexibilitiesprovidedinArticle 4whenimplementingArticle 6, seealsoBlomqvist,172
(analyzingthemay-languageprovisionsofArticle 4intermsoftheirapplicationconcerningArticle 6).

430 the beneficiary has legal access to that performance, in circumstances such as where 
appropriate and effective measures have not been taken by rights holders in relation to 
that performance to enable the beneficiary to enjoy the limitations and exceptions under 
that Contracting Party’s national law.
MT-7.3. As discussed in the Guide to the BTAP in Part III of this collection of guides, while the 
statement stresses that it is justified to adopt measures to ensure the applicability of limitations 
or exceptions where TPMs are used, it also clarifies that this should be done in due accordance 
withthethree-steptestinadoublesense:first,asprovidedinArticle 13oftheBTAP,any
limitation or exception must fulfill the three cumulative conditions of the test and, second, 
measures to ensure limitations or exceptions may only be applied where, and to the extent that, 
they do not create conflicts with the test. 879
MT-7.4.Thereis,however,afundamentaldifferencebetweenArticle 11oftheWPPT,Article 18
oftheWPPTandArticle 15oftheBTAP,ontheonehand,andArticle 7oftheMarrakeshTreaty
on the other. While the provisions of the three Internet Treaties obligate Contracting Parties 
to“provideadequatelegalprotectionandeffectivelegalremediesagainstthecircumvention 
of effective technological measures that are used by [owners of rights] in connection with the 
exerciseoftheirrights”,Article 7oftheMarrakeshTreatydoesnotprescribethisobligation.
Itonlyprovidesthat,wheretheContractingPartiesprovideadequatelegalprotectionand 
effective legal remedies against the circumvention of TPMs, they have to ensure the applicability 
of the limitations and exceptions provided for in the Treaty.
Technological measures and application of exceptions and limitations under Article  7 and the 
agreed statement concerning it
MT-7.5. The agreed statement adopted a year before in Beijing on the relationship of the 
protection of rights through the use of TPMs and the application of exceptions and limitations 
seems to offer some guidance in the context of the Marrakesh Treaty on how “to ensure 
thatwhentheyprovideadequatelegalprotectionandeffectivelegalremediesagainstthe 
circumvention of effective technological measures, this legal protection does not prevent 
beneficiary persons from enjoying the limitations and exceptions provided for in [the] Treaty”.
MT-7.6. Rightholders may adopt specific TPMs to ensure that only the beneficiaries may have 
accesstotheirworks.Thiswouldcorrespondtowhatisimpliedintheabove-quotedagreed
statementconcerningArticles 13and15oftheBTAP;thatitisadvisabletogivepreferenceto
rightholders to take appropriate and effective measures to enable the beneficiaries to enjoy the 
limitations and exceptions.
MT-7.7.TheagreedstatementconcerningArticle 7isnot,however,abouttheuseofTPMsbythe
rightholders, but by the authorized entities. It goes without saying that the objective of the use 
of TPMs by those entities is certainly the same as that mentioned in the preceding paragraph. 
AlthoughtheTPMsarenotusedinconnectionwiththeexerciseofrightsinthiscase–andthus
donotcorrespondtotheprovisionsofthethreeInternetTreatiesmentionedabove–itmaybe
themosteffectivewayoffulfillingtheobligationofauthorizedentitiesunderArticle 2(d)(ii)“to 
limit to beneficiary persons and/or authorized entities [the] distribution and making available 
of accessible format copies”.880 In fact, such limitation of access to the beneficiaries by the 
authorized entities does serve the interests of rightholders; it is a guarantee that the exceptions 
and limitations provided for may be applied to the full benefit of visually impaired and other 
print disabled persons such that it may be also in accordance with the three-step test.
MT-7.8.Itistobenotedthat,unlikeArticle 12oftheWCT,Article 19oftheWPPTandArticle 16
oftheBTAP,whichalsoobligateContractingPartiestograntadequateprotectionforelectronic
rights management information, the Marrakesh Treaty does not contain such provisions. 
Nevertheless,itfollowsfromArticle 1oftheTreatythat,asregardstheContractingPartiesthat 
879 See the comments on the agreed statement in the Guide to the BTAP.
880JørgenBlomqvistnotesthesame,andheanalyzesinmoredetailhowtechnologicalprotectionmeasuresmaybe 
applied in the context of the Marrakesh Treaty; seeBlomqvist,209–210.

are also party to these other WIPO Treaties, nothing derogates from their obligation to provide

Article 8
Respect for Privacy
In the implementation of the limitations and exceptions provided for in this Treaty, Contracting 
Partiesshallendeavortoprotecttheprivacyofbeneficiarypersonsonanequalbasiswithothers.
Redundant confirmation of the principle of equal treatment
MT-8.1.TheArticle isredundant;whatisstatedinitisobvious.Itfollowsdirectlyfromthebasic
principlesoftheMarrakeshTreaty–non-discriminationandequalopportunity–declaredinthe 
firstpreambleparagraph withreferencetotheUniversalDeclarationofHumanRightsandto 
the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. There is no reason this 
principlemightnotbeequallyapplicableconcerningtheprotectionofprivacy.
Protection of privacy in the application of the Treaty
MT-8.2. Such a provision in a copyright treaty is unusual. It seems necessary to discuss the 
aspects of the application of copyright and the exceptions and limitations concerning certain 
rights in which the need for the protection of privacy may emerge at all. Certainly such issues 
may emerge in connection with the obligation of the competent authorities “to limit to the 
beneficiary persons […] its distribution and making available of accessible format copies” 
(Article 2(d)(ii))and“tomaintainduecarein,andrecordsofthehandlingofcopiesofworks, 
whilerespectingtheprivacyofbeneficiarypersonsinaccordancewithArticle 8”(Article 2(d)
(iv)). The fulfilling of these obligations for which an authorized entity must establish and follow 
“its own practices” seems to determine how the protection of privacy may be ensured. The 
authorized entities have to make sure that the persons to whom accessible format copies are 
distributed or made available are in fact visually impaired or otherwise print disabled persons. 
To prove this, it is not justified to apply some intrusive procedure, but as a minimum the 
authorizedentitiesaresupposedtorequiresomecertificateissuedbyadoctor,oramedical
or other competent institution. In the case of cross-border distribution and making available 
of such copies, this may only be ensured, in general, through due cooperation between duly 
established and functioning authorized entities. For the same purpose, some databases and 
records also seem to be needed through which the beneficiary persons may be identified and 
theuseoftheadequateuseofaccessibleformatcopiesmaybeshown.
Article 9
Cooperation to Facilitate Cross-Border Exchange
1.  Contracting Parties shall endeavor to foster the cross-border exchange of accessible 
format copies by encouraging the voluntary sharing of information to assist authorized 
entities in identifying one another. The International Bureau of WIPO shall establish an 
information access point for this purpose.
MT-9.1.InviewofthekeyobjectiveoftheMarrakeshTreaty–toofferalegalandorganizational
framework to foster international cooperation facilitating as broad and efficient availability of 
accessibleformatcopiesaspossiblethroughasystemofauthorizedentities–theapplication 
of this provision is indispensable. The international cooperation system provided by the Treaty 
may only duly function if it is ensured that information is shared to identify authorized entities. 
It is an obligation of Contracting Parties to encourage such information exchange.
2.  Contracting Parties undertake to assist their authorized entities engaged in activities 
underArticle 5tomakeinformationavailableregardingtheirpracticespursuant
toArticle 2(c),boththroughthesharingofinformationamongauthorizedentities,
and through making available information on their policies and practices, including 
related to cross-border exchange of accessible format copies, to interested parties and 
members of the public as appropriate.

Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
432 MT-9.2.Paragraph (2)providescertaindetailsonhowContractingPartiesmayfulfilltheir 
obligationsunderparagraph (1).Theprovisionsseemself-explanatory.
3.  The International Bureau of WIPO is invited to share information, where available, 
about the functioning of this Treaty.
MT-9.3. The information hub provided by WIPO is necessary to foster cross-border exchange. 
The Treaty may only be applied in an effective and transparent manner if the Contracting 
Parties, in accordance with their obligation to encourage information exchange, duly make 
information available to be used through the information access point of WIPO mentioned 
inparagraph (1).
4.  Contracting Parties recognize the importance of international cooperation and its 
promotion, in support of national efforts for realization of the purpose and objectives 
of this Treaty.
AgreedstatementconcerningArticle 9:ItisunderstoodthatArticle 9doesnotimplymandatory
registration for authorized entities nor does it constitute a precondition for authorized entities 
to engage in activities recognized under this Treaty; but it provides for a possibility for sharing 
information to facilitate the cross-border exchange of accessible format copies.
MT-9.4.Paragraph (4)statesthereasonwhyitisindispensablethattheContractingParties
fulfilltheobligationsunderArticle 9toencouragethesharingandeffectivemakingavailableof 
information about authorized entities.
MT-9.5.AnagreedstatementappendedtoArticle 9,clarifyingthatitdoesnotimplymandatory 
registration for authorized entities nor constitute a precondition for authorized entities to 
engageinactivitiesrecognizedunderthisTreaty–butthatitprovidesforapossibilityfor
sharinginformationtofacilitatethecross-borderexchangeofaccessibleformatcopies–maybe
interpreted in this way:
First:“ItisunderstoodthatArticle 9doesnotimplymandatoryregistrationforauthorized
entities.” It should be acknowledged, however, that reliable sources are needed to allow 
due identification of authorized entities. This is so since, where authorized entities have 
a role in the application of the limitations and exceptions provided for in the Treaty, only 
thoseentitiesareallowedtoactthatfulfillalltherequirements,includinginparticular
thosedeterminedinArticle 2(c)and(d).Atthelevelofinternationalcooperation,
it is particularly important to know which entities of other Contracting Parties are 
authorized. In view of this, although the Treaty does not obligate Contracting Parties 
to maintain a registry of authorized entities, this seems necessary as a stable basis for 
international cooperation.
Second:“ItisunderstoodthatArticle 9doesnot[…]constituteapreconditionfor
authorizedentitiestoengageinactivitiesrecognizedunderthisTreaty”.Article 9ofthe
Treaty serves the facilitation of cross-border exchange. It is true that authorized entities 
may engage in activities recognized under the Treaty in a given Contracting Party provided 
theyfulfilltheconditionsprescribedinArticle 2(c)and(d),andthusareauthorizedinthat
Contracting Party. It is also true that an authorized entity of a Contracting Party may find 
some way to find out which entity may be regarded as authorized in another Contracting 
Party to which it may distribute or make available accessible format copies by virtue of 
Article 5(orfromwhichitmayimportsuchcopiesinaccordancewithArticle 6).However,
underArticle 9,ContractingPartiesareobligatedtoendeavortofostercross-border
cooperationbyencouragingsharingofinformation.Theabove-quotedelementofthe
agreed statement should be interpreted in the light of this obligation.
Third:“ItisunderstoodthatArticle 9[…]providesforapossibilityforsharinginformation
to facilitate the cross-border exchange of accessible format copies”. This element of 
the agreed statement should be interpreted in the same way as the preceding one. 
Where there is a reasonable possibility for sharing information to facilitate cross-border 
exchange of accessible format copies, it follows from the obligation of Contracting Parties 
underArticle 9thattheyshouldmakeuseofthispossibilityasfullyaspossible.

MT-9.6. It is hoped that Contracting Parties will not only encourage voluntary information 
exchange,butwillproactivelyguaranteeconditionsconducivetoadequatecross-border 
information exchange. Where necessary, introducing obligatory information exchange is also a 
“possibility” to make use of.
Article 10
General Principles on Implementation
1.  Contracting Parties undertake to adopt the measures necessary to ensure the 
application of this Treaty.
Basis principle: pacta sunt servanda
MT-10.1. This kind of provision is usual in WIPO treaties. It means no less than the statement of 
application of the basic principle of any treaty: pacta sunt servanda.
2.  Nothing shall prevent Contracting Parties from determining the appropriate method of 
implementing the provisions of this Treaty within their own legal system and practice.
AgreedStatementconcerningArticle 10(2):Itisunderstoodthatwhenaworkqualifiesas
aworkunderArticle 2,includingsuchworksinaudioform,thelimitationsandexceptions
provided for by this Treaty apply mutatis mutandis  to related rights as necessary to make the 
accessible format copy, to distribute it and to make it available to beneficiary persons.
Methods of implementing the Treaty
MT-10.2. The usual provisions in WIPO treaties generally also state what indeed is self-evident: 
that the Contracting Parties may ensure the application of the Treaty in accordance with their 
constitution or in accordance with their national legal system in general. The variants of the 
references to the legal mechanisms of Contracting Parties do not have much importance; 
thus,itlikewisedoesnothavemuchimportancethatArticle 10(2)oftheMarrakeshTreatyalso
mentions legal practice. Whether its basis is the constitution, the legal system or legal practice, a 
Contracting Party is obligated to fully implement and apply the Treaty.
Extension of the limitations and exception to related rights
MT-10.3. It is surprising that what is actually a new substantive provision appears in a mere agreed 
statementconcerningArticle 10(2).Underthestatement,whenworksdefinedinArticle 2(a)are
involved, including works in audio form, the limitations and exceptions provided for by the Treaty 
apply mutatis mutandis to related rights to the extent necessary to make the accessible format 
copy,todistributeitandtomakeitavailabletobeneficiarypersons.Article 10(2)isaboutthe
methods through which Contracting Parties may implement the provisions of the Treaty. They 
cover only limitations of and exceptions to copyright in a narrow category of works; there is no 
provision in the Treaty on limitations of and exceptions to related rights. Therefore, in reality, there 
is no provision in this respect that Contracting Parties would have to implement.
MT-10.4.Inviewofthis,itdoesnotseemtobeanidealdraftingtechniquetostatelightlythat,
when the provisions on exceptions to and limitations of copyright are implemented, they should 
beunderstoodasalsorequiringimplementationofcertainlimitationsandexceptionsonwhich 
there is no provision in the Treaty. If there was truly agreement at the Diplomatic Conference 
about what is stated in the agreed statement (and there must have been, since the Treaty was 
adopted unanimously with this agreed statement included), there would not have been any 
obstacle to settling this issue in determining the subject matter covered by the exceptions and 
limitations provided for in the Treaty correspondingly.
MT-10.5. The remarks above about the suboptimal manner of settling the issue of related rights 
do not mean that there might be any serious doubt about the validity and applicability of the 
agreed statement or that this issue would not have to be addressed. However, the agreed 
statement, instead of facilitating the interpretation of the provisions of the Treaty (which is the 
normalpurposeofsuchstatements)ratherraisessomeinterpretationquestions.

===== PAGE 433 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
434 MT-10.6.Thefirst–andperhapstheeasiest–questioniswhatsortsofrelatedrightsare
concerned, since they are not identified. There are three traditional categories of such 
rights: the rights of performers, producers of phonograms and broadcasting organizations. 
Nevertheless,theagreedstatementofferssomeguidanceinthisrespectsinceit–inharmony 
withwhatissupposedtofollowfromthecontextoftheTreaty–onlyspeaksofthoserelated
rights that it may be necessary to limit or grant an exception to so as to make accessible format 
copiesofworkscoveredbythedefinitionof“work”inArticle 2,todistributethesecopiesandto 
make them available to beneficiary persons.
MT-10.7. In the case of the rights of performers what seems to be sufficiently clearly covered 
are their rights in recitations of works in the form of texts, such as poems, short stories or 
evennovels(as“talkingbooks”).Inadditiontothis,thequestionofthecoverageofcertain 
“moretraditional”productionsofperformingartists–suchastheirperformancesinradio 
plays or even in traditional dramatic works the theater presentations of which are transmitted 
through radio in such a way that, by sotto voce commentaries, the essential visual elements of 
thepresentationsaredescribedsimultaneously–mightalsoemerge,sincetheyexistinforms 
accessible to visually impaired and other print disabled persons. In the case of such “traditional” 
performances, there are truly certain interpretation problems for which some guidance would 
be helpful (which might have been offered in an agreed statement).
MT-10.8. Performers have two basic sets of rights; one in their live performances and another 
inthefixations(recordings)oftheirperformances.Therightsinliveperformancesarequite 
strong exclusive rights. One of those exclusive rights is the right of fixation of unfixed (live) 
performances. The exceptions to and limitations of copyright provided for in the Marrakesh 
Treaty cover the rights of reproduction, distribution and making available to the public; 
performers enjoy these rights under the relevant international treaties in respect of sound 
recordings (fixations) of their performances (partly depending on whether or not they are 
authorized fixations) separately from their right of fixation.
MT-10.9. It would be difficult to claim that the limitations of and exceptions to the rights in works 
covered by the Marrakesh Treaty might be extended, mutatis mutandis, to rights not covered. 
For example, there is no reference in the Treaty to the right of fixation. In view of this, it seems 
evident that the mutatis mutandis application of the Treaty’s provisions on limitations of and 
exceptions to copyright is not supposed to imply the application of limitations and exceptions to 
thisrightofperformers.Ifthisisaccepted–andtherearequitesolidreasonstoacceptit–this
may also negatively influence the mutatis mutandis extension of limitations of and exceptions 
to the three rights as provided for in respect of copyright. This is so since the provisions of the 
Treaty(see,inparticularArticle 4(2(a)(i)and(b),wherethisisstatedverbatim)clarifythatthe 
exceptions and limitations may only be applied where the basis of the acts is “lawful access 
to a work or a copy” (here the mutatis mutandis meaning of “copy” seems to be the fixation of 
a performance/recitation).
MT-10.10.However,theanalysismayhardlyendhere.Forexample,onemayciteArticle 9(3)of
the Berne Convention, which provides that “any sound […] recording shall be considered as a 
reproduction for the purposes of this Convention”. In view of this, one might try to argue (i) that 
what is covered by the right of reproduction under the Berne Convention in this manner may be 
understood to be covered by the right of fixation from the viewpoint of the rights of performers, 
in addition to the right of reproduction they enjoy as such. One might then conclude (ii) that it 
is justified to extend mutatis mutandis the limitations and exceptions provided for in the Treaty 
concerning the authors’ right of reproduction to the performers’ right of fixation as well (thus 
paving the way for producing lawful “copies” and, from that, for mutatis mutandis application of 
other limitations and exceptions based on such “copies”). Nevertheless, it is easy to recognize 
thatthisisquiteanoverstretchedwayofinterpretinghowfar mutatis mutandis application may 
go without providing explicit rules.
MT-10.11. Beyond these basic aspects, there are other interpretation problems, in particular if 
the status of “traditional performances” also is considered; performances which typically are not 
made specifically for the purpose of visually impaired or other print disabled persons but for the 
general public.

===== PAGE 434 =====
435
PART IV. Guide to the Marrakesh VIP Treaty
MT-10.12. As long as live oral public performances/recitations of texts take place, the special 
status of the visually impaired is hardly relevant; the principles of non-discrimination and 
equalopportunitysuggestthattheymayenjoysuchperformances/recitationsbasicallyunder 
the same conditions as the persons without such impairment. The same may be said about 
performances/recitations transmitted by radio, including radio plays or the above-mentioned 
radio transmissions from theaters (in terms of which, of course, it should also be noted that just 
listeningtotheperformances/recitationsisnotaqualifiedact).
MT-10.13. The use of sound fixations of such “traditional performances” is another matter, since 
it may concern the rights of reproduction, distribution and making available to the public. With 
thesekindsofrecordings,another–alsoquitebasic–interpretationproblememerges;namely,
whether, in the case of such recordings of performances/recitations intended for the general 
public, one could speak at all of special accessible format copies produced to make works accessible 
to the visually impaired. Quiteprobablyanegativeanswershouldbegiventothisquestionin
accordancewiththebasicprinciplesofnon-discriminationandequalopportunity.
MT-10.14. As regards the rights of producers of phonograms, the scope of the rights of 
performers covered by the Treaty may, to a great extent, determine the coverage of the possible 
exceptions to and limitations of these rights, too. This is because what is be relevant for mutatis 
mutandis application of the exceptions and limitations provided in respect of works in text 
format may be just the recordings of recitations of such works. For the reasons discussed above, 
phonograms consisting in recordings of “traditional”, general-purpose performances/recitations 
do not seem to be covered.
MT-10.15. More or less the same considerations apply regarding the rights of broadcasting 
organizations. In this case, due to the very nature of broadcasting, the general-purpose nature 
of the transmissions may be a decisive aspect. Thus where recitations of works in accessible 
formatcopies–forexampleintheformofaudiobooks–aretransmitted,the mutatis mutandis 
application of the limitations and exceptions provided for in the Treaty might only emerge at 
all if what is involved is not broad- but narrowcasting, available exclusively for persons with 
visual impairment. (It should be stressed that here only the specific limitations and exceptions 
providedforintheTreatyareconsidered;otherlimitationsandexceptions–suchas,for
example,thoseforeducationalpurposes–applyalsoforthevisuallyimpaired.)
3.  Contracting Parties may fulfill their rights and obligations under this Treaty through 
limitations or exceptions specifically for the benefit of beneficiary persons, other 
limitations or exceptions, or a combination thereof, within their national legal system 
and practice. These may include judicial, administrative or regulatory determinations 
for the benefit of beneficiary persons as to fair practices, dealings or uses to meet their 
needs consistent with the Contracting Parties’ rights and obligations under the Berne 
Convention,otherinternationaltreaties,andArticle 11.
Exceptions and limitations not specifically provided for the benefit of beneficiary persons
MT-10.16.Thisparagraph doesnotaddanytrulynewruletowhatfollowsfromtheprovisionsof
the Treaty and from the legal situation under the existing international norms.
MT-10.17.Thefirstsentenceisredundantinallaspects.Article 10(2)clarifiesalreadythatthe
Contracting Parties may implement (that is: fulfill their obligations and exercise their rights 
under) the Treaty “within their own legal system and practice”. This covers the implementation of 
all aspects of the Treaty; beyond any doubt, it includes the key aspects of applying limitations and 
exceptions. Therefore, in this respect, the first sentence does not provide anything new. It has 
already been provided that the limitations or exceptions for the beneficiary persons may also be 
appliedthrough“other”limitationsorexceptions;seetheprovisionsofArticles 4(3)and5(3).
Providing limitations or exceptions through “judicial, administrative or regulatory 
determinations for the benefit of beneficiary persons as to fair practices, dealings or uses“
MT-10.18.ThesecondsentenceofArticle 10(3)statesinthecontextoftheMarrakeshTreaty
what has always been recognized concerning the provisions on exceptions and limitations in 
national laws. The parties to the international copyright treaties may apply exceptions and

===== PAGE 435 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
436 limitationsthatareallowedunderthetreaties–totheextentthattheyareallowed–through
specific exceptions or limitations subject to “fair practice”, through “fair dealing” or through “fair 
use” (based on well-developed specific criteria established through case law and also codified 
in statutory law). The proviso “to the extent that they are allowed” is, however, a key criterion 
which also means that the exceptions or limitations must be in accordance with the cumulative 
conditionsofthethree-steptestasprovidedinArticle 11oftheTreaty.
MT-10.19.Inthecontextoftheprovision,itseemsquitesurethattheintentionwastoreferto
fair practice, fair dealing and fair use, rather than “fair practices”, “fair dealings” and “fair uses” in 
plural. There are legal systems that apply one or other of these concepts and criteria. However, 
when they do, in general, they refer to and apply them as “fair practice”, ”fair dealing” or “fair use”.
MT-10.20. It is to be recognized that applying limitations or exceptions in these forms rather 
than on the basis of specific, duly targeted provisions in the statutory law might only be an 
appropriateoptionifthereiswell-establishedcourtpracticebasedonadequatelydeveloped 
criteria. For example, in the United States, the fair use system is the result of two centuries’ 
development of case law. A simple copying of the statutory codification of that voluminous and 
stilldevelopingcaselawoffairuseinsection107oftheU.S.CopyrightAct–andthentrying
tosettlethequestionsoflimitationsandexceptionsonthatbasisinacountry without similar 
legaltraditionsandwithoutabodyoflawthathasthusemergedasasolidbasis–mayhardly
produce the same satisfactory result.
MT-10.21. The fair use system is not an alternative to the application of the three-step test. When 
it truly exists as well-established practice, it may be just a means to fulfill the conditions of the 
test. In the fair use system, a court may also find that, in a given case, there is no infringement 
of copyright (in other words, there is an exception or limitation) even if not all the codified 
factorsequallyspeakinfavorofthis;thatis,thefairusefactorsare not necessarily cumulative. 
Incontrast,asdiscussedbelowinthecommentsonArticle 11oftheMarrakeshTreaty,the
conditions of the three-step test are cumulative; if one of the three conditions is not fulfilled, 
alimitationorexceptioncannotbeapplied.TheUSfairusesystemissupposedto–and,as
experienceshows,itdoes–correspondtothecumulativeconditionsofthethree-steptest 
through the application of various not necessarily cumulative criteria developed through a rich 
case law and partly codified also in statutory law. What has been discussed concerning fair use 
applies mutatis mutandis to fair practice and fair dealing, too.
Article 11
General Obligations on Limitations and Exceptions
In adopting measures necessary to ensure the application of this Treaty, a Contracting Party 
may exercise the rights and shall comply with the obligations that that Contracting Party has 
under the Berne Convention, the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property 
Rights and the WIPO Copyright Treaty, including their interpretative agreements so that:
(a) inaccordancewithArticle 9(2)oftheBerneConvention,aContractingPartymaypermit
the reproduction of works in certain special cases provided that such reproduction 
does not conflict with a normal exploitation of the work and does not unreasonably 
prejudice the legitimate interests of the author;
(b) inaccordancewithArticle 13oftheAgreementonTrade-RelatedAspectsofIntellectual
Property Rights, a Contracting Party shall confine limitations or exceptions to exclusive 
rights to certain special cases which do not conflict with a normal exploitation of the 
work and do not unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of the rightholder;
(c) inaccordancewithArticle 10(1)oftheWIPOCopyrightTreaty,aContractingPartymay
provide for limitations of or exceptions to the rights granted to authors under the WCT 
in certain special cases, that do not conflict with a normal exploitation of the work and 
do not unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of the author;
(d) inaccordancewithArticle 10(2)oftheWIPOCopyrightTreaty,aContractingPartyshall
confine, when applying the Berne Convention, any limitations of or exceptions to rights

===== PAGE 436 =====
437
PART IV. Guide to the Marrakesh VIP Treaty
to certain special cases that do not conflict with a normal exploitation of the work and 
do not unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of the author.
The three-step test and the non-derogation clause
MT-11.1. The three-step test has become the standard basis to establish a proper balance of interests 
inrespectofcopyright.Ontheonesideofthebalance,thereisthepublicinteresttoadequately
protect copyright and thus to ensure sustainable creation and production of works (to which 
membersofthepublicmaythenreceiveaccess)andtoofferadequaterewardstotheirauthors
(and, in this way, recognize both their legitimate private interest and their human rights laid down in 
Article 27(2)oftheUniversalDeclarationofHumanRights).Ontheotherside,thereareotherpublic
interests and legitimate private interests in terms of which due respect for human rights (including 
thosetowhichthefirstpreambleparagraph oftheTreatyrefers)isakeyrequirement,alongwith
more general public interests concerning economic, social, and cultural development.
MT-11.2.WhatisstatedinthisArticle followsdirectlyfromthenon-derogationclauseofArticle 1.
TheobligationsquotedinArticle 11areamongthosefromwhichnothingintheMarrakesh
Treaty derogates. Thus, the member countries of the Berne Union, the Members of the WTO, 
and the Contracting Parties of the WCT are obligated to ensure that the limitations and 
exceptions provided for in the Marrakesh Treaty are applied only if, and to the extent that, they 
fulfill the cumulative conditions of the three-step test.
Quoting the provisions on the three-step test: justified redundancy
MT-11.3.Still,therearetworeasonswhythissomewhatredundantarticle maystillbejustified.
First, the Treaty provides for exceptions and limitations allowed by the existing international norms 
to fulfill its objective of facilitating availability of accessible format copies to visually impaired and 
other print disabled persons. Since these exceptions and limitations cannot be applied if they 
do not correspond to the conditions of the three-step test, it is understandable that the specific 
confirmation of this key element of the system of limitations and exceptions has been found 
necessary.Thus,thisredundancyinArticle 11isjustifiedanduseful.Second–andthisseemsto
bethemoresubstantialreason–inthecourseofthepreparatoryworkandevenattheDiplomatic
Conference,asmentionedintheIntroductionabove,thereweresomeattemptstoquestionthe
applicabilityofthetestconcerningthelimitationsandexceptionscoveredbytheTreaty.Article 11
confirms that those attempts were badly founded and that, if they had succeeded, they would 
have led to conflicts with key provisions of the existing international treaties binding the sweeping 
majority of the negotiating parties and would-be Contracting Parties.
The role of “interpretative agreements”
MT-11.4.TheprovisionsofArticle 11consistalmostentirelyofverbatimquotationsofthe
relevant provisions of the Berne Convention, the TRIPS Agreement and the WCT. There is only 
oneelementofthetextthatcannotbefoundinthoseprovisionsandwhich,thus,requires
separate remarks. There is a reference to “interpretative agreements”, suggesting that those 
“agreements” should also be taken into account for the application of the relevant provisions 
of the three instruments. This reference to such a possible basis of interpretation of the said 
provisionsseemstobeunnecessary.AsquotedintheIntroductiontothiscollectionofguides, 
fortheinterpretationofthetreatiesArticles 31and32oftheVCLTapply.Thoseprovisions
list the possible sources of interpretation and, to the extent that there are “interpretative 
agreements” concerning the application of the relevant provisions, they would have to be taken 
intoaccountevenwithoutsuchareferenceinthisarticle oftheTreaty.
MT-11.5.Inthiscontext,theveryexpression“interpretativeagreements”requires
interpretation.AsquotedintheIntroduction,Article 31oftheVCLTinitsparagraphs(2)and(3)
refers to certain sources of interpretation that might be meant by this expression:
2.  The context for the purpose of the interpretation of a treaty shall comprise, in 
addition to the text, including its preamble and annexes:
(a)  any agreement relating to the treaty which was made between all the parties in 
connection with the conclusion of the treaty;

===== PAGE 437 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
438 (b)  any instrument which was made by one or more parties in connection with the 
conclusion of the treaty and accepted by the other parties as an instrument 
related to the treaty.
3.  There shall be taken into account, together with the context:
(a) anysubsequentagreementbetweenthepartiesregardingtheinterpretationof
the treaty or the application of its provisions;
(b) anysubsequentpracticeintheapplicationofthetreatywhichestablishesthe
agreement of the parties regarding its interpretation[.]
MT-11.6.InrespectoftheprovisionsofthethreetreatiesquotedinArticle 11,thereisno
separateagreementinthesenseofArticle 31(2)(b),noranysubsequentagreementas
referredtoinArticle 31(3)(a)oraseparatepractice-basedagreementofamodifyingeffect 
thatcorrespondstoArticle 31(3)(b).Thus,onecannotspeakofanykindofagreementsthat
wouldmodifyinanywaywhatsoeverwhatfollowsfromArticle 31(1)oftheVCLTconcerningthe
interpretationofthethree-stepprovisionsquotedinArticle 11oftheTreaty.
MT-11.7.Incontrast,thereisanagreedstatementconcerningArticle 10oftheWCT.Under
Article 31.2)(a)oftheVCLT,”[t]hecontextforthepurposeofinterpretationofthetreatyshall
comprise, in addition to the text, including its preamble and annexes” also such statements.881 
Therefore,asremarkedabove,therewasnoneedtorefertoitintheintroductorylinesofArticle 11
asasourceofinterpretation;itsapplicationfollowsdirectlyfromthisprovisionoftheVCLT.The
agreedstatementconcerningArticle 10oftheWCTquotedinpoints3and4ofArticle 11ofthe
Treaty reads as follows:
ItisunderstoodthattheprovisionsofArticle 10permitContractingPartiestocarry
forward and appropriately extend into the digital environment limitations and exceptions 
in their national laws which have been considered acceptable under the Berne Convention. 
Similarly, these provisions should be understood to permit Contracting Parties to devise 
new exceptions and limitations that are appropriate in the digital network environment.
ItisalsounderstoodthatArticle 10(2)neitherreducesnorextendsthescopeof
applicability of the limitations and exceptions permitted by the Berne Convention.
This agreed statement contains the only “interpretative agreement” to which the introductory 
linesofArticle 11mayrefer.Itconfirmsthattheexceptionstoandlimitationsoftherights
provided in the WCT must correspond to the three-step test.
MT-11.8. The three-step test plays a decisive role in the Marrakesh Treaty; it is the basis on which the 
existing international norms make it possible to apply the limitations and exceptions provided for 
in it and, at the same time, it also determines the conditions, and thus the limits, of the application 
of those limitations and exceptions. Therefore, it inevitably warrants some comments. Such 
comments are also justified to rebut certain badly informed allegations about the test presented 
–mainlybysomenon-governmentalorganizationsNGOs–duringthepreparatoryworkofthe
Treaty. A detailed analysis of the test may be found in the Guide to the Berne Convention in this 
collectionofGuidesconcerningArticle 9(2),whichisthefirstincarnationofthetest.Hereonlythe
main points of that analysis are summed up as they apply in the context of the Marrakesh Treaty:
(i) The truly relevant specific exceptions and limitations provided for in the Marrakesh 
881Paragraph 2of31oftheVCLTalongwithparagraph 1,accordingtowhichthetermsofatreatymustbeinterpretedin 
their context in the way provided there, reads as follows:
1. A treaty shall be interpreted  in good faith in accordance with the ordinary meaning to be given to the terms of the 
treaty in their context and in the light of its object and purpose.
2. The context  for the purpose of the interpretation of a treaty  shall comprise, in addition to the text, including its 
preamble and annexes:
(a) any agreement relating to the treaty which was made between all the parties in connection with the conclusion of 
the treaty ;
(b) any instrument which was made by one or more parties in connection with the conclusion of the treaty and 
accepted by the other parties as an instrument related to the treaty. 
(Emphasis added.)
