Treaty follow from the three-step test in the sense that there are no specific limitations 
and exceptions in the Berne Convention in this respect (no such specific exceptions as 
forillustrationforteachingunderArticle 10(2)orsuchspecificlimitationsasconcerns 
broadcastingunderArticle 11bis(2) of the Convention). The limitations of and exceptions 
totherightofreproductionarebasedonArticle 9(2)oftheBerneConventionandthe
limitations of and exceptions to the rights of distribution and making available are based 
onArticle 10(1)oftheWCT.
(ii) Thetest–asitclearlyfollowsfromthestructureofitsvariousversionsquotedinArticle 11
of the Marrakesh Treaty and as is also confirmed in an agreed statement adopted in 
connectionwiththeadoptionofitsfirstversioninArticle 9(2)oftheBerneConvention–
must be applied step by step such that, if a limitation or exception does not fulfill the first 
condition, its application is ruled out. If the limitation or exception passes the first “step” but 
is not consistent with the second condition, it must not be applied. Then the limitation and 
exception may only be applied if it also satisfies the third condition.
(iii)Thefirstofthethreecumulativeconditions–thatalimitationorexceptionmustbeconfined
tocertainspecialcases–inthecontextoftheBerneConventionandtheotherWIPOtreaties
–meansthatitisapplicableinthoselimitedcaseswherethereisasoundlegal–political
justification for it (the human-rights considerations concerning the availability of accessible 
formatcopiesforthevisuallyimpairedarecertainlysuchalegal–politicaljustification).882
(iv)Thesecondcondition–noconflictwithanormalexploitationofworks–asconfirmed
bythepreparatoryworkofArticle 9(2)oftheBerneConvention–meansthata
limitation or exception must not “enter into economic competition with [a possibility of 
extractingeconomicvaluefromtherightsin]works”“whichhaveorarelikelytoacquire
considerable economic or practical importance”.
(v) Itisonthebasisofthethirdcondition–nounreasonableprejudicetothelegitimate
interestsoftherightholders–thatthefine-tuningoftheduebalanceofinterestsmay
take place. An exception or limitation may cause certain prejudice to the legitimate 
interest of rightholders in obtaining remuneration to recoup their creative and financial 
investments with reasonable profit that may guarantee sustainable creation and 
production of works; but it must not be of an unreasonable nature. The principle of 
reasonable proportionality should prevail.
(vi)AsdiscussedalreadyinthecommentonArticle 10(3)oftheMarrakeshTreaty,thefair
use system is not an alternative to the international system of limitations and exceptions 
subject to the three-step test. Under the international norms, and thus also under the 
Treaty, the exceptions and limitations are only applicable if, and to the extent that, 
they–throughacasebycaseapplicationofcertainwell-establishedandnotnecessarily
cumulativefactors–fulfillallthreecumulativeconditionsofthetest.Theexceptionsand
limitations based on the fair use system (like the systems based on fair dealing and fair 
practice) are only consistent with the existing international treaties if, and to the extent 
that, they are also in accordance with the three-step test.
(vii) The existing limitations and exceptions may be extended to the online digital 
environment, but only in such a way that, when they are extended, they correspond to 
the three-step test in the different conditions of the new environment.
(viii) The provisions of the treaties (including their preambles) that contain general principles 
and/orreflectingobjectives(suchasthatcorrespondingtotheprovisionsofArticles 7and
8 of the TRIPS Agreement) may be taken into account in the application of limitations and 
exceptions. This, however, should take place not in addition to, but within the framework 
of, the application of the cumulative conditions of the three-step test (and cannot serve as 
a basis for “re-interpretation” of the test itself).883
882 SeethecommentsonArticle 9(2)intheGuidetotheBerneConventioninthiscollectionofguidesfortheanalysison 
which this interpretation is founded, but also the references to an alternative position according to which, as it has 
beenfoundinaWTOdisputesettlementreportmentionedthere,thelegal–politicalconsiderationarenottobetaken 
into account yet in the first step; this is rather a matter for the other two steps, in particular the third step.

440 Commercial availability of accessible format copies and the three-step test
MT-11.9. Specific comments are necessary concerning the role of commercial availability of 
accessible format copies as concerns the three-step test.
MT-11.10. One of the preamble paragraphs of the Marrakesh Treaty confirms the recognition 
of “both the importance of rightholders’ role in making their works accessible to persons with 
visual impairments or with other print disabilities and the importance of appropriate limitations 
and exceptions to make works accessible to these persons, particularly when the market is 
unabletoprovidesuchaccess”.Thepreambleparagraph confirmsthe potential relevance of 
the aspect of availability of copies ensured by the owners of rights (normally, in the form of 
commercial availability ) from the viewpoint of the application of limitations and exceptions.
MT-11.11.AnagreedstatementwasadoptedconcerningArticle 4(4)whichaddressesthis
issue:“Itisunderstoodthatacommercialavailabilityrequirementdoesnotprejudgewhether 
ornotalimitationorexceptionunderthisArticle isconsistentwiththethree-steptest”.As 
analyzedinthecommentsonArticle 4(4)above,the“commercialavailabilityrequirement”in 
factmayonlybeunderstoodreasonablyas“absence-of-commercial-availabilityrequirement” 
of the application of limitations and exceptions provided for in the Treaty. It is what, according 
to the agreed statement, is not supposed to prejudge in itself the consistency of limitations 
and exceptions with the three-step test. Thus, a separate analysis is needed of the role of 
commercial availability as regards the three-step test, in particular considering the second and 
third conditions of the test.
MT-11.12.Thenon-derogationprovisionofArticle 1oftheTreatyappliesalsototheagreed
statement adopted concerning the provisions of the Treaty. This means that neither the agreed 
statement nor any other provision of the Treaty or any other agreed statement derogates from 
thethree-steptest,asprovidedintheexistingtreatiesandasconfirmedinArticle 11.Thus,the 
analysisofthequestionofwhethertheapplicationofalimitationorexceptionisconsistent 
with the test in a concrete context where accessible copies are available in a given market on 
reasonable terms may hardly be dispensed with.
Making copies commercially available undoubtedly has relevance from the viewpoint of the 
normal exploitation of works and this, in certain cases, may influence the judgment of whether 
a given limitation or expression can pass the second “step” of the test. The fact that the copies 
areavailableonreasonableterms–ifitisalsoconsideredinthelightofwhatfollowsandwhat
doesnotfollowfromtheprinciplesofnon-discriminationandequalopportunity–mayinfluence 
the assessment of the normalcy of a means of exploitation of the works concerned. It may also 
influence the finding of whether a limitation or exception is consistent with the third condition 
of the test (that it is only applicable if and to the extent that it does not unreasonably prejudice 
the legitimate interests of owners of rights).
MT-11.13. This means that it depends on a thorough analysis where and in which way commercial 
availability or its absence may play a role in whether or not a limitation or exception is consistent 
with the cumulative conditions of the three-step test.
Article 12
Other Limitations and Exceptions
1.  Contracting Parties recognize that a Contracting Party may implement in its national 
law other copyright limitations and exceptions for the benefit of beneficiary persons 
than are provided by this Treaty having regard to that Contracting Party’s economic 
situation, and its social and cultural needs, in conformity with that Contracting Party’s 
international rights and obligations, and in the case of a least-developed country taking 
into account its special needs and its particular international rights and obligations and 
flexibilities thereof.

Other limitations and exceptions
MT-12.1.Paragraph (1)refersagainto“othercopyrightlimitationsandexceptions”afterseveral
otherprovisionsoftheTreatyhavereferredtosuchlimitationsandexceptions(seeArticles 4(3), 
5(3), and 10(3)). The comments made on the concept of such other limitations and exceptions 
concerningthoseprovisions,inparticularconcerningArticle 10(3),applyhereaswell.
Special rules for least-developed countries
MT-12.2. There is also a reference to the transitional provisions concerning least-developed 
countries,whicharediscussedinthecommentstoArticle 9(2)intheGuidetotheBerne
Convention in this collection; that is, to those “flexibilities” under the TRIPS Agreement that are 
providedinArticle 66(1)oftheAgreement.Underthetransitionalarrangementsprovidedthere, 
least-developedcountriesthatareMembersoftheWTOarenotrequiredtoapplytheprovisions 
oftheAgreementotherthanArticles 3,4and5. 884 This means that if they are not members of 
theBerneUnionand/ortheWCT,theyarenotobligatedtocomplywithArticles 1to21andthe
AppendixoftheBerneConvention.Therefore,theyarenotobligatedtoapplyArticle 9(2)ofthe 
Conventiononthethree-steptestorArticle 13oftheAgreementextendingtheapplicationof 
the test to all limitations of and exceptions to copyright. The problem of the “Berne gap” and the 
“WCTgap”thatemergesinsuchacase,whicharesettledinArticle 5(4)(a)and(b),arediscussed 
above in the comments to those provisions.
2.  This Treaty is without prejudice to other limitations and exceptions for persons with 
disabilities provided by national law.
Limitations and exceptions for persons with disabilities in general
MT-12.3.Itisdoubtfulwhetherthereisanyneedforthisclarificationinparagraph (2).Totheextent
that Contracting Parties apply the limitations and exceptions by respecting all the provisions of 
the Treaty, it is hardly a relevant issue whether or not they also apply additional limitations and 
exceptions. Even without such a clarification, there is nothing in the Treaty to give rise to the 
interpretation that, since it contains provisions on limitations and exceptions for visually impaired 
and other print disabled persons, it prohibits Contracting Parties from applying, in accordance 
with the international copyright norms, certain limitations and exceptions for a broader scope of 
beneficiaries in which the beneficiary persons under the Marrakesh Treaty are also included.
Administrative and final clauses
TheprovisionsofArticles 13to22oftheMarrakeshTreatycontaintheusualadministrativeand
final clauses of WIPO treaties. Due to their nature they are self-explanatory and do not raise 
realinterpretationquestions.Therefore,commentsaremadeonlyonthosethatdisplaysome 
specificity in the context of the Treaty.
Article 13 
Assembly

MT-13.1.TheprovisionsofArticle 13areverbatimthesameastheprovisionsofArticle 21of
the BTAP on the BTAP Assembly. Paragraphs (1) to (3) correspond to what is provided in the 
similar WIPO treaties on the assemblies of the Contracting Parties and they are verbatim the 
sameasArticle 15(1)to(3)oftheWCTandArticle 24(1)to(3)oftheWPPT(onlythenumbersof
the provisions referred to are different). Paragraphs (4) and (5) differ to a certain extent from 
the corresponding paragraphs in the WCT and the WPPT; in contrast, they are the same as 
Article 21(4)and(5)oftheBTAP.
MT-13.2.AccordingtoArticle 15(4)oftheWCTandArticle 24(4)oftheWPPT,theAssembliesof
the Contracting Parties of those treaties were to meet in ordinary session once every two years. 
It has become, however, a practice that the Assemblies established under the various treaties 
administered by WIPO have their sessions at the same place (usually in Geneva) and at the same 
time as the General Assembly of WIPO. Although this practice was not in conflict with those 
provisions of WIPO treaties that provided for one ordinary sessioneverytwoyears–because
they did not exclude the possibility of extraordinary sessions–itwasalreadyinArticle 23(6)of
the Singapore Treaty on the Law of Trademarks (STLT) that the annual session was made the 
officialrule.AsmentionedintheGuidetotheBTAP,Article 21(4)oftheBTAPfollowedtheSTLT
model;sodidtheMarrakeshTreatyoneyearlaterinitsArticle 13(4).
MT-13.3.Thechangeintheprovisionofparagraph (5)–anotherpost-STLTinnovation–in
contrast with the same paragraphs in the WCT and WPPT articles, is of a similar nature. Under 
theprovisions,theAssemblyestablishes,amongitsotherrulesofprocedure,therequired 
majority for the various decisions. It follows from this that those decisions may also be adopted 
byamajorityvote.InArticle 21(5)oftheBTAP,andalsoinArticle 13(5)oftheMarrakeshTreaty,
thisisalsomentionedasaruletobedeterminedbytheAssembly–thus,thepossibilityofthe
adoptionofthedecisionsbyamajorityvotehasbeenmaintained–but,inaccordancewiththe
emerging principle that, if possible, the WIPO bodies adopt their decisions by consensus, this is 
indicated as an objective which the Assembly should endeavor to achieve.

instruments was provided as the condition of entry into force. This number, in the case of the

===== PAGE 443 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
444  MT-18.2. In the Basic Proposals containing the drafts of what later became the WCT and the 
WPPT submitted to the 1996 Diplomatic Conference, the “standard” number from the older 
WIPO-administeredtreaties–five–appeared.AttheDiplomaticConference,however,different 
higher numbers of instruments (15, 20 and even one-third of the then number of member 
countries of the Berne Union, which would have meant nearly 50) were proposed. Finally, in the 
informal consultations, the delegations agreed on 30. Those delegations who proposed higher 
numbers presented two basic arguments. First, the two treaties were intended to regulate the 
protection of copyright and two categories of related rights in the online digital environment, 
and this justified the participation of a more significant number of countries when the treaties 
entered into force. Second, the treaties contained certain provisions the due implementation 
andapplicationofwhichwastorequirelongerperiodsofpreparationinthevariouscountries.
MT-18.3.BeforetheMarrakeshDiplomaticConference,inthepreviousyearinBeijing,Article 26
oftheBTAPalsorequired30instrumentsofratificationoforaccessiontotheTreatyforitsentry 
intoforce.Ascanbeseen,thenumberofinstrumentsindicatedinArticle 18oftheMarrakesh
Treaty–20–liesbetweentheold“standard”(fiveorsix)andthemorerecentoneadopted
in 1996 and in 2012: 30. It seems that the negotiating parties set this number by taking into 
accounttwo–notnecessarilyconverging–considerations.Thefirstwastheirwishtotryto 
fulfillthemainobjectiveoftheTreaty–facilitatingavailabilityofaccessibleformatcopiesfor 
thevisuallyimpaired–assoonaspossible.Thiswasanargumentinfavorofalowernumber.
However, the other criterion was that, in order to fulfill the function of the Treaty to serve as a 
basis for enhanced international cooperation, a relatively substantial number of Contracting 
Parties was needed. The number chosen may appear to be a reasonable compromise between 
these criteria. Although it should be recognized that the treaty may not have full value without 
the participation of the European Union and its Member States, in view of the fact that they 
are rich sources of works whose availability in accessible format is important to effectively 
mitigate the “book famine”. For this reason and because the EU and its Member States were to 
deposit their instruments jointly, as a result increasing the number of instruments on one single 
day–basedoncurrentEUmembership–by27(plusone),the“standard”oftherecentWIPO
copyrightandrelatedrightstreatiescouldhavebeenamoreadequatenumber.

Effective Date of Becoming Party to the Treaty 
This Treaty shall bind:
(a) the20eligiblepartiesreferredtoinArticle 18,fromthedateonwhichthisTreatyhas
entered into force;
(b) eachothereligiblepartyreferredtoinArticle 15,fromtheexpirationofthreemonths

theBTAPsimplifiedthestructureontheprovisionsonthisquestion,incontrastwithprevious 
WIPO treaties, such as the WCT and the WPPT). In point (i), however, not 30 but 20 eligible 
partiesarementionedasadirectconsequenceofthecorrespondingprovisioninArticle 18.

Denunciation of the Treaty
This Treaty may be denounced by any Contracting Party by notification addressed to the 
Director General of WIPO. Any denunciation shall take effect one year from the date on which 
the Director General of WIPO received the notification.

PART V. Glossary of 
copyright and related 
rights terms
Access (right to ~)
1. In certain countries, a “right to access” the originals of works of fine art is granted for the 
authors of such works. The authors may, under reasonable conditions, demand that the 
proprietors of the originals of their works make them available temporarily where this is 
indispensable for the exercise of certain rights, such as the right of reproduction or the 
right of display (or exposition); the latter, in general, only in exceptional cases, such as for 
the purpose of presenting an author’s entire oeuvre or a given period of his or her creative 
activity. It is a kind of residual right of the author, and, from another viewpoint, it is a 
restriction of the proprietary right of the owner of the original of the work. For this reason, 
under the law of some countries, the access to the original of a work can only be legally 
requiredincasesofabusiverefusalbytheowner.
2. The expression “right to access” is used in legal literature to refer to a purported exclusive 
right of the owners of copyright or related rights to control access to their works or subject 
matters of related rights. According to some theories, if access to the work is protected by 
technological protection measures (TPMs) and if, in accordance with the WCT, the WPPT and 
the BTAP, their circumvention is prohibited, the result may be that users need an authorization 
from the rightholders to access the works or subject matters of related rights, and, thus, it may 
be said that the owners of rights have an exclusive right to authorize access. In fact, with the 
protection of TPMs against unauthorized circumvention no new right is granted; it just serves 
the protection, exercise and enforcement of rights which are otherwise granted. 
3. “Right to access” is used in the context of copyright and related rights to refer to the right of 
members of the public to have access to information and to cultural products and services 
as human rights enshrined in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights: “Everyone has the 
right to freedom of opinion and expression; this right includes freedom to hold opinions 
without interference and to seek, receive and impart information and ideas through any 
mediaandregardlessoffrontiers”(Article 19);“Everyonehastherightfreelytoparticipate
in the cultural life of the community, to enjoy the arts and to share in scientific advancement 
anditsbenefits”(Article 27(1)).Insuchadirectform–asarighttohaveunconditionalfree
accesstoanyworkorsubjectmatterofrelatedrights–itisnotapplicable,butitisafactorin
balancing interests to be taken into account in the establishment and application of certain 
exceptions and limitations, in accordance with the three-step test (see below). 
Access (to ~ works/ subject matters of related rights by members of the public)
Theword“access”appearsinArticle 8oftheWCT,Articles 10and14oftheWPPT,andArticle 10
of the BTAP in the text: “making available to the public of […] works/performances fixed in 
phonograms/audiovisual fixations in such a way that members of the public may access them 
from a place and at a time individually chosen by them”. It means the act by members of the 
public of obtaining or retrieving a work or subject matter of related rights in order to perceive 
and use it. Both access to, and use of, works or subject matters of related rights may be made 
conditional by the rightholders by means of technological protection measures (TPMs). (For the 
applicability of exceptions and limitations where TPMs are used, see paragraphs 15.3 to 15.13 of 
the Guide to the BTAP, Part III).

PART V. Glossary of copyright and related rights terms
Accessible format copy
UnderArticle 2(b)oftheMarrakeshTreaty,an“accessibleformatcopy”means“acopyofa
work in an alternative manner or form which gives a beneficiary person access to the work, 
including to permit the person to have access as feasibly and comfortably as a person without 
visual impairment or other print disability. The accessible format copy is used exclusively 
by beneficiary persons and it must respect the integrity of the original work, taking due 
consideration of the changes needed to make the work accessible in the alternative format and 
of the accessibility needs of the beneficiary persons”. (For further details, see paragraphs MT-2.7 
toMT-2.15oftheGuidetotheMarrakeshTreaty,PartIV.)
Adaptation; right of ~
1. The act of altering a pre-existing work (either protected or in the public domain) or an 
expression of folklore, for a purpose other than that which it originally served, in such a 
way that a new work comes into being in which the elements of the pre-existing work or 
expression of folklore and the new elements merge together. The purpose may be to produce 
the work in the form of a new genre (such as a novel in the form of a dramatic work or an 
audiovisual work, or a folk song in the form of a symphonic work) or to make it suitable to 
use in another context (such as creating a shorter and/or simpler variant). There are specific 
terms for the alteration of a musical work for the purpose of a new way of performing it, and 
for the expression of a literary work in another language: “arrangement” and “translation”.
2. “Rightofadaptation”isashortenedreferencetotherightprovidedunderArticle 12of
the Berne Convention under which authors must enjoy the exclusive right of authorizing 
adaptations, arrangements and other alterations of their works. (For further details, see 
paragraphs BC-12.1 to BC-12.3 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.)
3. The result of an act of adaptation. Adaptations are covered by the generic category of 
“derivativeworks”andareprotectedunderArticle 2(3)oftheBerneConvention“asoriginal
works without prejudice to the copyright in the original work.” (For further details, see 
paragraphs BC-2.30 and BC-2.38 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I). 
Agreed statement
1. Asourceofinterpretationofinternationaltreaties.TheViennaConventionontheLawof
Treaties(VCLT)provides,initsArticle 31.1:“Atreatyshallbeinterpretedingoodfaithin
accordance with the ordinary meaning to be given to the terms of the treaty in their context 
andinthelightofitsobjectsandpurpose”.InArticle 31.2(a)itadds:“Thecontextforthe
purpose of the interpretation of a treaty shall comprise, in addition to the text, including its 
preamble and annexes: (a) any agreement relating to the treaty which was made between all 
the parties in connexion with the conclusion of the treaty”.
2. The new generation of copyright and related rights treaties of WIPO include such agreed 
statements: the WCT nine, the WPPT ten, the BTAP twelve and the Marrakesh Treaty thirteen. 
Ingeneral,theseagreedstatementscorrespondtotherequirementsofArticle 31.2(a)quoted
above, and thus they may serve as sources to interpret the provisions concerned. 
Alteration of a work; other ~
1. The act of modifying a work; a generic term which covers both those modifications that, due 
to their original nature, enjoy copyright protection (including adaptations and arrangements), 
and those that do not include new creative contributions.
2. There are certain alterations that are not covered by the terms “adaptation” and 
“arrangements”,butthatstillqualifyasoriginalcontributionstothealteredoriginalworks.
This arises, inter alia,fromArticles 2(3)and12oftheBerneConvention,bothofwhichrefer,in
addition to adaptations and arrangements, to “other alteration[s]” (caricatures and parodies 
may be considered as such “other alterations”). (For further details, see paragraphs BC-2.38 
and BC-12.1 to BC-12.3 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
3. “Alteration” also means the result of an act of alteration mentioned in points 1 and 2. 
Alterations, where they are original creations, are covered by the generic term “derivative 
works”andareprotectedunderArticle 2(3)oftheBerneConvention“asoriginal
works without prejudice to the copyright in the original work”. (For further details, see 
paragraph BC-2.38oftheGuidetotheBerneConvention,PartI.)

===== PAGE 447 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
448 4. UnderArticle 6bis of the Berne Convention, authors have the moral right to oppose any 
alteration (modification) of their works which may be prejudicial to their honor or reputation. 
(For further details, see paragraphs BC-6 bis.3 and BC-6bis.5 of the Guide to the Berne 
Convention, Part I.) 
Alteration of electronic rights management information
AtermusedinArticle 12(1)(i)oftheWCT,Article 19(1)(i)oftheWPPT,andinArticle 16(1)(i)of
the BTAP. It means any act that results in any substantive modification in “rights management 
information”, against which, if they are carried out without authorization in the manner set forth 
intheseprovisions,adequateandeffectiveremediesaretobeapplied.(Forfurtherdetails,see 
paragraphs CT-12.2 and CT-12.6 of the Guide to the WCT, Part III.)
Analog format/technology
1. The analog format of a work or subject matter of related rights means its fixation and/or 
transmission in the form of continuously changing values, rather than in the form of discrete 
numeric values, or “digits”.
2. Analog technology is applied for the fixation, reproduction, distribution, and transmission of 
works and subject matters of related rights in analog format.
3. The terms “analog format” and “analog technology” are used in contrast with the terms 
“digital format” and “digital technology”.
Anonymous work
1. A work giving no indication of its author, whether by name or pseudonym, on the copies of 
the work or in connection with its use.
2. Article 7(3)oftheBerneConventioncontainsspecificprovisionsonthetermofprotection
ofanonymousworks,andArticle 15(3)oftheConventionprovidesforapresumptionthat
a publisher whose name appears on such a work is the representative of the author, and 
is entitled to protect and enforce the author’s rights. These provisions of the Convention 
cease to apply when the author’s identity is revealed and claim to authorship of the work is 
established. (For further details, see paragraphs BC-7.18 to BC-7.24 of the Guide to the Berne 
Convention, Part I.) 
Application in time
1. Thetimefromwhichatreatyisapplicable,asregulatedinArticle 18oftheBerneConvention.
The term’s application mutatis mutandis isprescribedbyArticle 16.6oftheTRIPSAgreement
concerningcertainrelatedrights,byArticle 13oftheWCT,Article 22oftheWPPT,and
Article 19oftheBTAP.
2. TheessenceoftheprovisionsofArticle 18oftheBerneConvention(includedinparagraphs(1)
and (2) of the Article) is that the Convention must be applied in a country of the Berne Union 
from the time of the entry into force of the Convention for that country for all works which have 
not yet fallen into the public domain, neither in the country of origin nor in the country where 
protection is claimed, due to the expiry of the term of protection previously granted. This also 
meansthataworkorsubjectmatterofrelatedrightsthathasneverbeenprotected–since,for
example,therewasnointernationaltreatyunderwhichitwouldhavehadtobeprotected–but
in respect of which the term of protection provided for by the above-mentioned treaties has not 
yetexpired,mustbeprotected,inaccordancewithArticle 18oftheBerneConvention,untilthe
expiry of the term of protection prescribed. However, if a work was previously not protected, 
orifarightwaspreviouslynotapplied,andbyvirtueofparagraphs(1)and(2)ofthearticle the
workbecomesprotectedortherightapplicable,onthebasisofparagraph (3)ofthearticle,
certain transitional provisions may be introduced. (For further details, see paragraphs BC-18.3 
to BC-18.11 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
3. SinceArticle 18oftheBerneConventionprescribestheapplicationoftheprovisionsof
theConvention–alsoconcerningtheworksandsubjectmattersofrelatedrightsexisting
atthemomentofitsentryintoforce–onlyfromthemomentoftheentryintoforceof
a treaty mentioned above, it does not have retroactive effect. Such an effect would only 
exist if the application of the provisions of the Convention extended to acts performed 
beforetheentryintoforceoftheConventionwhichatthattime–intheabsenceofthe

applicabilityoftheprovisionsoftheConvention–werestilllawful.Theeliminationofthis
kindofretroactiveeffectismadepossibleunderparagraph (3)ofArticle 18oftheConvention
through the adoption of transitional provisions (which, however, must not conflict with the 
basic provisions under paragraphs (1) and (2) of the same Article). (For further details, see 
paragraphs BC-18.1 and BC-18.2 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
Arrangement (of a musical work)
1. The act of altering a musical work (either protected or in the public domain) to be performed in 
a new form (such as the transcription to piano of a work originally composed for orchestra). (For 
further details, see paragraphs BC-12.1 and BC-12.3 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
2. The result of an act of arrangement mentioned in point 1 above. Arrangements, if they 
are original creations, are covered by the generic category of “derivative works”, and are 
protectedunderArticle 2(3)oftheBerneConvention“asoriginalworkswithoutprejudiceto
thecopyrightintheoriginalwork”.(Forfurtherdetails,seeparagraph BC-2.38oftheGuideto
theBerneConvention,Part I.)
“Article 12 rights”
1. TherightsgrantedunderArticle 12oftheRomeConvention,byvirtueofwhich“[i]fa
phonogram published for commercial purposes, or a reproduction of such phonogram, is 
useddirectlyforbroadcastingorforanycommunicationtothepublic,asingleequitable
remuneration shall be paid by the user to the performers, or to the producers of the 
phonograms,ortoboth”.However,Article 16oftheRomeConventionallowsreservations
toArticle 12,whichmaygosofarastocompletelydisapplytheprovisionsoftheArticle.(For
further details, see paragraphs RC-12.1 to RC-12.5 of the Guide to the Rome Convention, Part II.)
2. Article 15oftheWPPTprovidesforthesamekindofrighttoasingleequitableremuneration,
with the same kinds of reservations. For further details, see paragraphs PPT-15.1 to PPT-15.10 
of the Guide to the WPPT, Part III.) 
Artificial intelligence (AI)
1. A term commonly used to designate computer systems that are able to perform certain tasks 
thatnormallyrequirehumanintelligence.
2. AIraisesthreekindsofissuesconcerningcopyrightprotection.Thefirstisthequalificationof
the acts of training artificial intelligence systems for which a large amount of materials and 
data are used, including protected works. This involves, at least, acts of reproduction which 
requireeitherauthorizationbytherightholdersortheapplicabilityofcertainexceptions
or limitations in accordance with the three-step test. The second issue is the protection of 
artificial intelligence systems themselves. They may be regarded as computer programs; 
therefore, the rules of protection of such programs apply to them. The third issue concerns 
thequestionofcopyrightprotectionofartificialintelligenceproductions.Itfollowsfrom
the general definition of a “work” (as discussed in the comments in the Guide to the Berne 
ConventiononArticle 2oftheConvention)–accordingtowhichaworkisanoriginal
creationofhumanintellect–thatgenerativeAIproductionsthatdonotincludeoriginaland
determinativehumancontributionsdonotqualifyasworksprotectedbycopyright.
Artistic works
Under the Berne Convention, all works that are not to be regarded as literary works. However, 
the overwhelming majority of the provisions of the Convention apply, in general, to “literary and 
artistic works”. It is very rare that a provision only covers either literary works or artistic works, 
or a specific category or subcategory of works. Although some works may be regarded as 
exclusively literary (such as, for example, short stories, poems or scientific studies) or exclusively 
artistic (such as paintings or sculptures), this is not necessarily the case; encyclopedias and 
multimedia works (such as video games) are obvious examples of hybrid works. (For further 
details, see paragraphs BC-2.8 to BC-2.10 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.)

===== PAGE 449 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
450 Assignment of copyright and related rights
Transfer of the right of authorization of the use of the work or subject matter of related rights 
ratherthanjustauthorizing–grantingalicensefor–theusethereof.
Audiovisual adaptation
1. Theactofcreatinganaudiovisualworkonthebasisofapre-existingwork(mostfrequently
anovel,ashortstory,adramaticordramatico-musicalwork).UnderArticle 14(1)(ii)of
the Berne Convention, authors of literary or artistic works have the exclusive right of 
authorizing “the cinematographic adaptation […] of these works”. In this provision, the 
term “cinematographic adaptation” should be understood to have the same kind of 
broader meaning as “cinematographic works” as used in the Convention; that is, any kind of 
“audiovisual adaptation”. (For further details, see paragraphs BC-14.8 to BC-14.11 and BC-14.16 
of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
2. The result of the act mentioned in point 1 above. An audiovisual adaptation is normally 
anaudiovisualworktheprotectionofwhichisgovernedbyArticle 14bis of the Berne 
Convention. 
Audiovisual fixation
1. The act of fixation of the images and sounds of something (a performance, a stage 
production, a sport event, etc.).
2. The result of the act mentioned in point 1 above. If the audiovisual fixation contains original 
elements,itqualifiesasanaudiovisualwork.
3. ThesubjectmatterofprotectionundertheBTAPdeterminedinArticle 2(b)as“the
embodiment of moving images, whether or not accompanied by sounds or by the 
representation thereof, from which they can be perceived, reproduced or communicated 
through a device”. As the agreed statement concerning the definition clarifies, it is “without 
prejudicetoArticle 2(c)oftheWPPT”,where(forthereasonsdiscussedinthecommentson
Article 2(b)oftheGuidetotheBTAP,PartIII),thereferenceto“2(c) oftheWPPT”istoberead
actuallyas“2(b) oftheWPPT”onthedefinitionof“phonogram”(underwhichanyfixationof
sounds of a performance other than in the form of a fixation incorporated in an audiovisual 
work is a “phonogram”). (For further details, see paragraphs PPT-2.5 to PPT-2.16 of the Guide 
to the WPPT and paragraphs BT-2.18 to BT-2.33 of the Guide to the BTAP, Part III.)
Audiovisual performances/performers
1. Expressions which are often used to refer to certain categories of performances and 
performers, but which are not suitable to differentiate them from certain other categories. 
Thisissobecause–withsomeexceptions,suchasvoiceactorsinanimatedfilmsorpantomime
actors–performancesusuallyincludebothauralandvisualelements.Theyratherdifferentiate
performances (and their performers) according to what elements thereof are fixed; whether 
only the aural elements (on phonograms) or both aural and visual elements (in audiovisual 
works or in non-original audiovisual fixations), on the understanding that the concept of 
“audiovisual” also covers the fixation of mere visual elements (such as in the case of silent films).
2. UnderArticle 19oftheRomeConvention,“onceaperformerhasconsentedtothe
incorporationofhisperformanceinavisualoraudio-visualfixation,Article 7[ontherights
of performers] shall have no further application”. The TRIPS Agreement and the WPPT do 
not cover performers’ rights in audiovisual fixations, although the definition of “phonogram” 
inArticle 2(b)oftheWPPT–underwhichonlythefixationofthesoundsofperformancesin
audiovisualworksarenot“phonograms”–isinoverlapwiththeprotectionoftherightsof
performers in audiovisual fixations. (For further details, see paragraphs RC-19.1 to RC-19.3 of the 
GuidetotheRomeConvention,PartII,andparagraph PPT-2.5toPPT-2.16oftheGuidetothe
WPPT, Part III.) 
3. The rights of performers in their performances fixed in audiovisual fixations are protected 
bytheBTAP.Althoughthearticles oftheBTAPdonotusetheexpressions“audiovisual
performances” or “audiovisual performers”, the title and the Preamble of the Treaty do refer 
to “audiovisual performances”. In the context of the BTAP, “audiovisual performers” are to 
be understood as those whose performances are fixed in audiovisual fixations. (For further 
details,seeparagraph BT-Pr.1oftheGuidetotheBTAP,PartIII.)

===== PAGE 450 =====
451
PART V. Glossary of copyright and related rights terms
Audiovisual work
1. A work consisting of “a series of fixed related images, with or without accompanying sounds, 
susceptible of being made visible and, where accompanied by sound, susceptible of being 
made audible” by means of an appropriate device. (In the preceding sentence, the text 
betweenquotationmarksisfromthedefinitionof“audiovisualworks”inArticle 2oftheFilm
Register Treaty which has been adopted, but is not in force.)
2. It is also an element of the concept of “audiovisual works” that, when the series of fixed related 
images are made visible by means of an appropriate device, it imparts the impression of motion.
3. “Audiovisual work” is a shorter synonym of the expression “cinematographic works to which 
are assimilated works expressed by a process analogous to cinematography” appearing in the 
non-exhaustivelistofliteraryandartisticworksinArticle 2(1)oftheBerneConvention.Itcovers
works fixed either traditionally, chemically on film or in any other way, such as in particular 
electronically/digitally, irrespective of their objective or the way they are used, such as for 
cinema presentation or in television, as well as irrespective of their genres, such as fiction films 
or documentaries, feature films or short films, with featured or voice actors, etc. (For further 
details,seeparagraph BC-2.20oftheGuidetotheBerneConvention,PartI.)
Author
1. The intellectual creator of the work; thus, necessarily a human creator. Some national laws, 
however,alsorecognizetheauthorshipoflegalentities–suchasemployers,producers,etc.
–whotaketheinitiativeandresponsibilityforthecreationofthework(andwho,ingeneral,
through determining the objectives and certain features of the work to be created, may also 
have a direct or indirect impact on the nature, style and contents of the work).
2. UnderArticle 2(6)oftheBerneConvention,theprotectionofworks“shalloperateforthe
benefit of the author and his successors in title”. (For further details, see paragraphs BC-2.2 
and BC-2.45 to BC-2.51 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
Authorization
Permission to perform an act in respect of a work or subject matter of related rights. The 
exclusive rights to grant (or not grant) authorization are key elements of authors’ rights and, 
where granted, the rights of beneficiaries of related rights.
Authorship; right to claim ~
Authorshipisthequalityofbeingtheauthorofawork.Therighttoclaimauthorshipofaworkis
oneofthemoralrightsofauthorsunderArticle 6 bis of the Berne Convention. It is also referred 
to as the “right of attribution” (For further details, see paragraphs BC-6 bis.1 and BC-6bis.2 of the 
Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
Authors’ rights
Rights granted to authors in respect of their works. Authors have two kinds of rights: economic 
rightsandmoralrights.Theexpression“authors’rights”isusedfrequentlyasasynonymof 
“copyright”. In certain countries following the common law tradition, however, “copyright” 
hasanarrowermeaning;itonlycoverseconomicrights(takingintoaccountthedifferent–
personalityrights–natureofmoralrightsunderthelawsofthosecountries).
Automatic protection (the principle of)
See “formality-free protection (the principle of)”.
Backdoor protection
1. Protection enjoyed under the Berne Convention by an author who is not a national of a 
country of the Berne Union by virtue of the first publication of that author’s work having 
takenplaceinacountryoftheBerneUnion(underArticle 3(1)(b)and3(4)oftheConvention).
2. WhereacountryoutsidetheBerneUnionfailstoadequatelyprotecttheworksofauthorswho
are nationals of one of the countries of the Union, the country of the Union concerned may

===== PAGE 451 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
452 restrictprotectionundercertainconditionsfixedinArticle 6oftheBerneConvention.(For
further details, see paragraphs BC-6.1 and BC-6.2 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
3. The significance of backdoor protection has decreased recently as a result of a decisive 
increase in the number of countries of the Berne Union.
Back-up copy
A copy of a computer program (also called “archival copy”) made to prevent loss of the 
applicability of the program by deterioration or unintentional deletion. Under many copyright 
laws, making a back-up copy is permitted as an exception to the exclusive right of reproduction 
if it is made by the lawful owner of the copy. It is also generally provided that if the owner’s 
possession of the copy ceases to be lawful, the back-up copy must be destroyed.
Beijing Treaty on Audiovisual Performances (BTAP)
TheBeijingTreatyonAudiovisualPerformanceswasadoptedinBeijingonJune24,2012.It
provides protection for the rights of performers in their performances fixed in audiovisual 
fixations. It is administered by WIPO.
Beneficiaries of exceptions or limitations
1. Those who are permitted to use works and subject matters of related rights without the need 
to ask the permission of the rightholders and without the obligation to pay remuneration 
(exceptions) or permitted to use works and subject matters of related rights without the need 
to ask the permission of the rightholders, but with the obligation of paying remuneration or 
otherwise subject to conditions (limitation).
2. TheMarrakeshTreatyhasdeterminedaspecificscopeofbeneficiaries.UnderArticle 3,
in the application of the Treaty, a beneficiary is a person who (a) is blind; (b) has a visual 
impairment or a perceptual or reading disability which cannot be improved to give visual 
functionsubstantiallyequivalenttothatofapersonwhohasnosuchimpairmentordisability
and so is unable to read printed works to substantially the same degree as a person without 
an impairment or disability; or (c) is otherwise unable, through physical disability, to hold 
or manipulate a book or to focus or move the eyes to the extent that would be normally 
acceptable for reading. (For further details, see paragraphs MT-3.1 to MT-3.3 of the Guide to 
theMarrakeshTreaty,PartIV.)
Beneficiaries of protection
1. Those natural persons who, and legal entities which, may enjoy and exercise copyright or 
related rights under international treaties on copyright and related rights and/or national 
copyright laws. They are: (i) in the case of the Berne Convention and the WCT, authors and 
other original owners of copyright, and their successors in title; (ii) in the case of the Rome 
Convention, performers, producers of phonograms, broadcasting organizations, and their 
successors in title; (iii) in the case of the TRIPS Agreement, authors, other original owners 
of copyright, performers, producers of phonograms, broadcasting organizations, and their 
successors in title; (iv) in the case of the WPPT, performers in respect of their live performances 
and their performances fixed in phonograms, producers of phonograms, and their successors 
in title; and (v) in the case of the BTAP, performers in respect of their live performances and 
their performances fixed in audiovisual fixations and their successors in title.
2. In a wider sense, also those who enjoy protection of their rights, at least indirectly, as a 
result of the prohibition of certain acts. At the level of the international norms on copyright 
and related rights, these are: (i) in the case of the Phonograms Convention, producers of 
phonograms (possibly along with performers whose performances are fixed in phonograms) 
and their successors in title; and (ii) in the case of the Brussels, or Satellites, Convention, 
broadcasting organizations and their successors in title.
Berne Convention
1. The Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works was adopted in Bern in 
1886, completed in Paris in 1896, revised in Berlin in 1908, completed in Berne in 1914, revised 
in Rome in 1928, in Brussels in 1948, in Stockholm in 1967, and in Paris in 1971, and amended

===== PAGE 452 =====
453
PART V. Glossary of copyright and related rights terms
(in non-substantive aspects) on September 28, 1979. When reference is made in this Glossary 
to the Berne Convention, it is to the latest text of the Act, adopted in Paris in 1971.
2. UnderArticle 9.1oftheTRIPSAgreementandArticle 1(4)oftheWCT,itisanobligationof
Members of the WTO and the Contracting Parties to the WCT, respectively, to comply with 
Articles 1to21oftheBerneConvention(but,byvirtueofArticle 9.1oftheTRIPSAgreement, 
the Members of the WTO “shall not have rights or obligations under this Agreement in 
respectofthe[moral]rightsconferredunderArticle 6 bis of that Convention or of the 
rights derived therefrom”). Thus, when reference is made in this Glossary to any of these 
provisions of the Berne Convention, it is indirectly also a reference to the TRIPS Agreement 
andtheWCT,underwhichtheyareequallyapplicable.
Berne Union
TheUnionconstitutedunderArticle 1oftheBerneConventionby“[t]hecountriestowhich 
thisConventionapplies.”ThemaingoverningbodyoftheUnionistheAssembly(seeArticle 22 
of the Berne Convention) which, inter alia, is competent to “deal with all matters concerning 
[...]theimplementationofthisConvention”(paragraph 2(a)(i)ofArticle 22).TheAssemblyhas 
anExecutiveCommittee(seeArticle 23oftheBerneConvention).Theadministrativetasks 
with respect to the Union are performed by the International Bureau of the World Intellectual 
PropertyOrganization(WIPO)(Article 24(1)(a)and(b)oftheBerneConvention).TheDirector 
GeneralofWIPOisthechiefexecutiveoftheUnionandrepresentstheUnion(Article 24(1)(c)of
the Berne Convention).
Book
1. The term “book”, as subject matter of copyright protection, does not mean a physical object, 
that is, a number of sheets of paper fastened together within a cover, but the literary work 
(such as a novel or short story) and/or artistic works (such as drawings or photographic 
works)thatfillthatobject.Consequently,itcoversbooksintraditionalprintedformandin
any other form, such as in particular the digital form of “electronic books” (e-books).
2. Under certain copyright laws, the typographical arrangement of a published edition of 
a book is the subject matter of a separate related-rights-type of protection ( sui generis) 
enjoyed by publishers.
Broadcast
A program-carrying signal transmitted by an act of broadcasting. As such, it is the subject 
matterofrelatedrightsgrantedtobroadcastingorganizations(seeArticle 13oftheRome
Convention). (For further details, see paragraphs RC-13.1 to RC-13.5 of the Guide to the Rome 
Convention, Part II.) 
Broadcasting; right of ~
1. “Broadcasting” is communication of sounds or of images and sounds to the public by wireless 
transmission. It covers both terrestrial broadcasting and satellite broadcasting. The term 
“broadcasting” does not include interactive making available of works and subject matters 
of related rights over computer networks (where the time and place of reception may be 
individually chosen by members of the public).
2. The Berne Convention does not offer an explicit definition of “broadcasting”, but its meaning 
maybededucedfromArticle 11bis(1) of the Convention, which provides for an exclusive right of 
“communicationtothepublicofworksbywirelessmeans”.Underparagraph (2)ofthearticle,
conditions may be determined for the exercise of this right, which may serve as a basis for the 
application of non-voluntary licenses or mandatory collective management (both of which are 
“conditions” allowed to be determined “under which the rights mentioned in the preceding 
paragraph maybeexercised”).(Forfurtherdetails,seeparagraphsBC-11bis.2 to BC-11bis.11 of 
the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
3. For an act of broadcasting to take place it is sufficient to transmit the signals carrying a 
program making it possible for members of the public to receive them; actual reception is not 
a condition and it is not a relevant act from the viewpoint of copyright or related rights.
4. The TRIPS Agreement does not contain separate provisions on the definition of broadcasting 
or the right of broadcasting. It only obligates members of the WTO to comply, inter alia, with

===== PAGE 453 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
454 Article 11bis of the Berne Convention.
5. ThesamemaybesaidoftheWCT.However,italsoreferstoArticle 11bis of the Berne 
ConventioninitsArticle 8onthe“RightofCommunicationtothePublic”–confirmingthat
the provision on that broad right does not prejudice the application of those provisions of 
the Berne Convention which provide for a right of communication to the public of certain 
categories of works in certain forms. This reference confirms the interpretation mentioned in 
point 2 above that broadcasting is one form of communication to the public.
6. Article 3(f)oftheRomeConventioncontainsanexplicitdefinition:“‘broadcasting’meansthe
transmission by wireless means for the reception by the public of sounds or of images and 
sounds”. It is to be noted that the expression “transmission […] for public reception” is not 
precise.Asmentionedinpoint3above,foratransmissiontoqualifyas“broadcasting”,itisnot
necessarythatitsreceptionbe“public”–thatis,thatittakeplaceinthepresenceofagroup
of people corresponding to the concept of “public”, or at least at a place open to the public. 
ByvirtueofArticle 7(1)(a)oftheRomeConvention,theprotectionforperformersincludesthe
“possibility of preventing” the broadcasting of their live performances without their consent. 
Concerning the right to remuneration of performers and/or producers of phonograms in 
respectofbroadcastingofphonogramspublishedforcommercialpurposes,see“Article 12
rights”. (For further details, see paragraphs RC-7.6 to RC-7.9 and RC-12.1 to RC-12.5 of the Guide 
to the Rome Convention, Part II.) 
7. At the international level, the most up-to-date definition of “broadcasting” is contained in 
Article 2(f)oftheWPPTandArticle 2(c)oftheBTAP(which,however,hasinheritedfromthe
Rome Convention the misleading expression “transmission […] for public reception”). It reads 
as follows: “‘broadcasting’ means the transmission by wireless means for public reception 
of sounds or of images and sounds or of the representations thereof; such transmission by 
satellite is also ‘broadcasting’; transmission of encrypted signals is ‘broadcasting’ where the 
means for decrypting are provided to the public by the broadcasting organization or with its 
consent”.TheWPPTalsoprovidesfor“Article 12”-typerights(Article 15),asdoestheBTAP
forbroadcastingandcommunicationtothepublic(Article 11).Inrespectofbroadcastingof
unfixed performances, both Treaties provide for an exclusive right rather than a “possibility of 
preventing”(Article 6inbothTreaties).(Forfurtherdetails,seeparagraphsSC-3.1toSC-3.3of
the Guide to the Brussels, or Satellites, Convention, Part II; paragraphs PPT-2.23 to PPT-2.38 
of the Guide to the WPPT, Part III; and paragraphs BT-2.34 to BT-2.37 of the Guide to the BTAP, 
Part III.)
Broadcasting organization
1. The only category of the three groups of beneficiaries of the Rome Convention (the other 
two being performers and producers of phonograms) of which the Convention contains no 
definition. Nevertheless, the meaning of the term is self-evident; it may be derived from the 
concept of “broadcasting”; that is, it is a radio or television organization which by its signal 
communicates programs to the public. This is made possible by the organization by the activity 
necessary for the preparation of a program flow; that is, the assembling and scheduling of the 
program content. The term does not include those organizations that simply rebroadcast the 
program of a broadcasting organization thus assembled, scheduled and broadcast. 
2. The General Report of the 1961 diplomatic conference, which adopted the Rome Convention, 
contains the following clarification of the concept of “broadcasting organization”: “[I]f 
thetechnicalequipmentinaContractingStateisownedbythepostaladministration,but
what is fed into the transmitter is prepared and presented by such organizations as the 
Radiodiffusion-Television Francaise or the British Broadcasting Corporation, the latter, and not 
the postal administration, is to be considered the broadcasting organization.” (For further 
details, see paragraphs RC-3.21 to RC-3.23 of the Guide to the Rome Convention, Part II.) 
Brussels Convention
The Brussels Convention Relating to the Distribution of Programme-Carrying Signals 
Transmitted by Satellite was adopted in 1974 and entered into force in 1979. See also 
“Satellites Convention”.
Cablecast
Program transmitted by “cablecasting”.

===== PAGE 454 =====
455
PART V. Glossary of copyright and related rights terms
Cablecasting
Communication to the public of a cable-originated program. Transmission by cable of encrypted 
signals carrying a cable-originated program is “cablecasting” where the means for decrypting 
are provided to the public by the cablecasting organization or with its consent. “Cablecasting” 
is not to be understood as including making available to the public through transmissions in an 
interactive manner through a computer network.
Cablecasting organization
1. An organization that communicates to the public cable-originated programs. This, implicitly, 
also includes the activities necessary for such communication; that is, the assembling and 
scheduling of the program to be communicated to the public. On the other hand, the concept 
does not include those organizations which simply retransmit the program of a broadcasting 
or cablecasting organization thus assembled, scheduled and communicated to the public.
2. There is, for the time being, no international treaty to protect the rights of cablecasting 
organizations. Some national laws have, however, assimilated cablecasting to broadcasting, 
and have granted to cablecasting organizations the same kinds of related rights as to 
broadcasting organizations.
Cable-originated program
1. A program communicated to the public by cable (wire) when what is so communicated is not a 
program of a broadcasting or cablecasting organization retransmitting simultaneously with 
the original broadcast or cablecast and without changes.
2. The communication to the public of cable-originated programs is covered by the exclusive 
rights of communication to the public provided for by the Berne Convention in respect of 
communication to the public of performances of dramatic, dramatico-musical and musical 
works(Article 11(1)(ii)),recitationsofliteraryworks(Articles 11ter(1)(ii)), and audiovisual works 
(Articles 14(1)(ii)and14bis(1)). (For further details, see paragraphs BC-11.7 to BC-11.9 and BC-14.8 
to BC-14.11 of the Guide to Berne Convention, Part I.) 
Cable retransmission
1. Retransmission to the public by cable (wire) of a broadcast work in a simultaneous and 
unchanged manner. Where the broadcast is not simultaneous or is changed, it is a cable-
originated program.
2. UnderArticle 11bis(1)(ii) of the Berne Convention, copyright holders have an exclusive right to 
authorize any communication (retransmission) to the public by cable (wire) of the broadcast 
of a work, whenever it is made by an organization other than the original broadcaster (subject 
topossiblelimitationsunderArticle 11bis(2)). (For further details, see paragraphs BC-11bis.15 
to BC-11bis.19 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.)
Characters
Identifiable persons or other figures in fictional literary or artistic works, which, when they form 
substantial elements of such a work, with a clearly identifiable identity and with specific original 
features, are to be protected by copyright as such. Several national laws contain clarification to 
this effect.
Choreographic work
1. A category of works mentioned in the non-exhaustive list of literary and artistic works in 
Article 2(1)oftheBerneConvention,consistingofaseriesofstepsandmovements,ingeneral
in the form of dances in ballets, usually accompanied by music. (For further details, see 
paragraph BC-2.18oftheGuidetotheBerneConvention,PartI.)
2. Several national laws protect choreographic works only if they have been fixed in some 
materialformbyspecificnotationtechniques(suchasbyLabannotation),orbyaudiovisual
fixation (a condition of copyright protection the application of which is permitted by 
Article 2(2)oftheBerneConvention).

===== PAGE 455 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
456 Cinematographic adaptation
See “audiovisual adaptation”.
Cinematographic work
1. In a narrow sense, a work created through the use of a specific technology, namely 
cinematography, which means the fixation of a series of related images, with or without 
accompanying sounds chemically on a celluloid strip (or other similar medium), susceptible 
of being made visible and, where accompanied by sound, susceptible of being made audible 
by means of an appropriate device, creating the effect of movement (hence the expression: 
“motion picture”).
2. When used in the provisions of the Berne Convention, it is understood to mean not only 
cinematographic works in the narrow sense mentioned in point 1 above, but also the broader 
categoryindicatedinthenon-exhaustivelistofliteraryandartisticworksinArticle 2(1)of
the Berne Convention as “cinematographic works to which are assimilated works expressed 
by a process analogous to cinematography”. In that way, it corresponds to the concept of 
“audiovisualworks”.(Forfurtherdetails,seeparagraph BC-2.20oftheGuidetotheBerne
Convention, Part I.) 
Circumvention (of a technological protection measure)
The act of avoiding, bypassing, removing, deactivating or otherwise impairing a technological 
protection measure. For the obligation of Contracting Parties of the WCT, the WPPT and the 
BTAPtoprovideadequatelegalprotectionandeffectivelegalremediesagainsttheactsofsuch 
circumvention, see “technological protection measures (TPM)”.
Claim authorship of a work; right to ~
1. Torequiretherecognitionoftheauthorshipofawork.Ingeneral,itinvolvesrequiringthat
the name of the author be indicated on the copies and in connection with any public use of 
the work, unless this is impossible or unreasonable under the given circumstances.
2. TherighttoclaimauthorshipofaworkisoneofthemoralrightsgrantedunderArticle 6bis 
of the Berne Convention. It is also referred to as the “right of attribution”. (For further details, 
see paragraphs BC-6bis.1 and BC-6bis.2 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.)
Claim to be identified as the performer of a performance; right to ~
The right to claim to be identified as the performer of one’s performances is a moral right of 
performers,recognizedbyArticle 5oftheWPPTandArticle 5(1)(i)oftheBTAP,similartothe
righttoclaimauthorshipofawork.Paragraph (1)oftheArticle providesexplicitlythatthe
right does not extend to those cases “where omission is dictated by the manner of use of the 
performance”. (For further details, see paragraphs PPT-5.1 to PPT-5.5 of the Guide to the WPPT, 
Part III.)
Cloud technology
1. Remote availability of computing resources and services to a client computer (such as 
a desktop or laptop personal computer). The data is processed and stored by the client 
remotelyoninfrastructurecalled“cloud”–notownedorpossessedbytheclient,butused
only as a service through the Internet. (This describes the Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) 
model; the other main models are Software-as-a-Service (SaaS), by means of which a client 
may use a software application, and Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS), which allows the client to 
use an entire computing platform, such as Windows, remotely.)
2. There are private and public cloud services. Copying a work or subject matter of related 
rights in a private cloud storage from which it may only be accessed by the client computer 
(“private locker”) is an act of private copying. Where, however, a work or subject matter of 
related rights is stored in such a way that it is directly or through a clickable link accessible by 
membersofthepublic,itqualifiesasanactof(interactive)makingavailabletothepublic.

457
PART V. Glossary of copyright and related rights terms
Co-authors, work of co-authorship
Twoormoreauthorswhojointlycreateawork.UnderArticle 7bis of the Berne Convention, 
the term of protection of a work of co-authorship is the lifetime of the co-authors and 50 years 
measuredfromthedeathofthelastsurvivingauthor.(Forfurtherdetails,seeparagraph   
BC-7bis.1 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.)
Coding
See “encryption; encrypting”.
Collection/compilation (of works/data)
1. The two terms are used as synonyms in the international norms on copyright. A collection or 
compilation of works, data or other materials, in any form, is protected as a work if, by reason 
of the selection or arrangement of its contents, it constitutes an intellectual creation. 
2. Such collections/compilations are protected by the Berne Convention, the TRIPS Agreement 
and the WCT:
 – Article 2(5)oftheBerneConventionprovides:“Collectionsofliteraryorartistic 
works such as encyclopedias and anthologies which, by reason of the selection and 
arrangement of their contents, constitute intellectual creations shall be protected as 
such, without prejudice to the copyright in each of the works forming part of such 
collections.” In this provision, the conjunction “or” is inclusive, that is, it should be read 
as“and/or”:ifthereisonereasonforwhichanyproduction–includinganycollection/
compilation–constitutesanintellectualcreation,itissufficient;thereisnoneedfor 
another reason. Thus, if a collection/compilation constitutes an intellectual creation 
by reason of the selection or by reason of the arrangement of its contents alone, it 
isprotected.Collections/compilationsofdataandothermaterialsnotqualifyingfor 
copyrightprotectionarenotprotectedbyvirtueofArticle 2(5),but,sincetheground 
for protection of collections/compilations is the original nature of the selection or 
arrangement of their contents, such collections/compilations as productions in the 
literary and artistic domain constituting intellectual creations are to be protected by 
virtueofthegeneralprovisionofArticle 2(1)oftheBerneConvention.(Forfurther 
details, see paragraphs BC-2.41 to BC-2.44 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.)
 – Article 10.2oftheTRIPSAgreementandArticle 5oftheWCTcontainsimilarprovisions.
Theyreadasfollows(thedifferingelementsinsquarebrackets):“Compilationsofdataor
other material, [whether in machine readable or other form,] [in any form] which by reason 
of the selection or arrangement of their contents constitute intellectual creations [shall be] 
[are] protected as such. [Such protection, which shall] [This protection does] not extend 
to the data or material itself [ shall be] [is] without prejudice to any copyright subsisting in 
the data or material [itself] [in the compilation].” The Articles’ titles are misleading, as they 
refer only to “Compilations of Data”, and this is further aggravated by the fact that the word 
“Databases” is added in parentheses. However, these provisions cover not only original 
databases but also original collections/compilations of works and any other material. (For 
further details, see paragraphs CT-5.7 to CT-5.9 of the Guide to the WCT, Part III.)
3. See also “data; database”. 
Collective work
1. A work embodying the works of several authors created at the initiative and under the 
responsibility of a person or legal entity who or which publishes the work under his or its 
name (who or which then becomes the original owner of copyright), in which the various 
contributions–becauseoftheirgreatnumberorindirectnature–aremergedintothe
totality of the work so that it is impossible, or at least impracticable, to identify the individual 
works and their authors. 
2. In certain national laws, however, the term “collective work” is used as a synonym of “collection 
of works”. Under section 101 of the U.S. Copyright Act, a “collective work” is a work, such as a 
periodical issue, anthology, or encyclopedia, in which a number of contributions, constituting 
separate and independent works in themselves, are assembled into a collective whole.
