the Guide to the WPPT, and paragraphs BT-10.1 to BT-10.7 of the Guide of the BTAP, Part III.)
Mandatory collective management
Collective management of rights under copyright or related rights in respect of which the law 
prescribes the condition that they can only be exercised through collective management. If 
mandatory collective management is prescribed in respect of exclusive rights, it is a limitation 
on such rights (see also “exceptions and limitations”).
Marrakesh Treaty
TheMarrakeshTreatytoFacilitateAccesstoPublishedWorksforPersonsWhoAreBlind,Visually
Impaired or Otherwise Print Disabled was adopted in Marrakesh, Morocco, in 2013.
Mechanical right
1. The right to reproduce works in recordings (phonograms or audiovisual fixations).
2. Article 13oftheBerneConventionallows,undercertainconditions,theapplicationof,and
some copyright laws provide for, non-voluntary licenses for sound recording of musical works 
and any words pertaining thereto. (For further details, see paragraphs BC-13.1 to BC-13.7 of 
the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
Minor exceptions; “reservations”
1. A term referring to those exceptions to the right of public performance provided for in the 
BerneConvention(Articles 11(1)(i),11ter(1)(i), 14(1)(ii) and 14bis(1)) which are not expressly 
mentioned in the text of the Convention, but which follow from the application of the de 
minimis principle of interpretation of legal provisions. The General Report of the 1948 
Brussels revision conference referred, in a kind of agreed statement to “limited exemptions 
[...] allowed for religious ceremonies, military bands and the needs of child and adult 
education” as such “minor exceptions”. The 1967 Stockholm revision conference confirmed 
that the principle of minor exceptions was considered valid. The records of the revision 
conferences use the term “minor reservations”, but it is obvious that what is involved are, 
in fact, possible minor exceptions. Those countries which wish to apply these kinds of 
restrictions of rights do not have to make any formal reservation. (For further details, see 
paragraphs BC-11.11 to BC-11.25 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.)
2. The legitimacy of such exceptions is also subject to the three-step test. 
Modification
Asynonymof“alteration”.ItisusedinArticle 6 bis of the Berne Convention, which provides, inter 
alia, for a right of the author to object to any distortion, mutilation or other modification of his 
work which would be prejudicial to his honor or reputation.
Moral rights
1. At the level of the international norms of copyright and related rights (i) the rights of authors 
providedforinArticle 6bis of the Berne Convention, that is, the right to claim authorship (also 
referred to as the “right of authorship” or the “right of attribution”) and the right to object 
to any distortion, mutilation or other modification of a work, or other derogatory action 
in relation to it, which would be prejudicial to the honor or reputation of the author (also 
referred to as the “right of respect” or the “right of integrity”), and (ii) similar (but not the 
same)rightsofperformers–asregardstheirunfixedauralperformancesorperformances
fixedinphonogramsorinaudiovisualfixations–providedforinArticle 5oftheWPPTand
Article 5oftheBTAP,respectively:therighttoclaimtobeidentifiedastheperformerof
their performances, except where omission is dictated by the manner of the use of the 
performance, and the right to object to any distortion, mutilation or other modification of 
his performances that would be prejudicial to the performer’s reputation (though under

===== PAGE 477 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
478 the BTAP, specific norms apply to the latter right taking into account the special aspects of 
audiovisual performances and the audiovisual works in which they are fixed). (For further 
details, see paragraphs BC-6bis.1 to BC-6bis.10 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I, 
paragraphs PPT-5.1 to PPT-5.5 of the Guide to the WPPT, and paragraphs BT-5.13 to BT-5.16 of 
the Guide to the BTAP, Part III.) 
2. Several copyright laws following the civil law legal tradition provide for further moral 
rights for authors (not provided for in the Berne Convention), such as the right to decide 
whether the work should be made available to the public (also referred to as the “right 
of disclosure”), and the right to withdraw copies from circulation (also referred to as the 
“right of withdrawal”). The exercise of the latter right, in general, goes together with the 
author’s obligation to pay appropriate compensation to those who have in stock copies 
for distribution.
Motion picture
See “cinematographic work”; “audiovisual work”.
Multimedia production
1. Atermfrequentlyusedwithwidelydifferingmeaningsandsometimeswithmeanings
not sufficiently clear. A multimedia production seems most generally understood to be a 
collection in digital format of, typically, more or less all kinds of works, except for three-
dimensional works (that is, literary works, graphic works, audiovisual works and musical 
works,etc.)Phonogramsindigitalformataswellasmeredataalsomaybe,andfrequently
are, parts of such collections. An indispensable feature of any multimedia production is that 
it may be used in an interactive, non-linear way, which is made possible by the other basic 
elementofmultimediaproductions–whichisalwayspresentinsuchproductions–namely,a
computerprogram.Videogamesarethemosttypicalexamplesofsuchproductions.
2. MultimediaproductionsthatconstituteintellectualcreationsareprotectedunderArticle 2(1)
and/or (5) of the Berne Convention, irrespective of their legal characterization (most 
frequentlyascollections,audiovisualworksand/orcomputerprograms)underthevarious
national laws.
National treatment (principle of ~)
1. A basic principle under the international norms on copyright and related rights according to 
which a country must accord to the nationals of other countries party to the same treaties 
no less favorable protection than what is accorded to its own nationals. National treatment is 
usually subject to the minimum level of protection prescribed by the given instruments, which 
must be granted to the nationals of other countries party to the same treaties, irrespective 
ofwhetherthegivencountrygrantssuchalevelofprotectiontoitsownnationals–asin
Article 5(1)oftheBerneConvention.(Forfurtherdetails,seeparagraphsBC-5.1toBC-5.3ofthe
Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
2. ForthespecificwayinwhichtheobligationofnationaltreatmentisprovidedinArticle 2ofthe
Rome Convention on related rights, how it is interpreted in the light of the relevant provisions 
of the TRIPS Agreement, the WPPT and the BTAP, and how it is applied under the latter 
treaties, see paragraphs RC-2.2 to RC-2.8 of the Guide to the Rome Convention, Part II, and 
paragraphs PPT-4.1 to PPT-4.13 of the Guide to the WPPT, and paragraphs BT-4.1. to BT-4.34 of 
the Guide to the BTAP, Part III. 
Near-on-demand transmission
1. A transmission of works and subject matters of related rights (in particular with respect to 
phonograms–andworksandperformancesembodiedinthem),intheformofbroadcasting
or cablecasting, whose impact is the same as, or is very close to, that of an on-demand 
transmission, without fully corresponding to the concept of the latter, such as certain 
subscriptionsystemsthroughwhichentiredigital-qualityrepertoiresofauthors,performers
and producers of phonograms are delivered in a systematic way.
2. ThereisareferencetothisintheagreedstatementadoptedonArticle 15oftheWPPT,which,
in general, only provides for a right to remuneration to performers and producers for the 
broadcasting and cablecasting of phonograms. It reads as follows: “It is understood that

===== PAGE 478 =====
479
PART V. Glossary of copyright and related rights terms
Article 15doesnotrepresentacompleteresolutionofthelevelofrightsofbroadcastingand
communication to the public that should be enjoyed by performers and phonogram producers 
in the digital age. Delegations were unable to achieve consensus on differing proposals for 
aspects of exclusivity to be provided in certain circumstances or for rights to be provided 
without the possibility of reservations, and have therefore left the issue to future resolution.” 
(For further details, see paragraphs PPT-15.11 to PPT-15.15 of the Guide to the WPPT, Part III.) 
Neighboring rights
See “related rights”.
Non-copy-related rights
1. One of the three main categories of economic rights in the framework of copyright and 
related rights (along with copy-related rights and transformation rights). The term non-
copy-related rights means those rights which do not relate to the making (reproduction) and 
distribution of copies, in particular the right of reproduction, the right of (first) distribution, 
the right of rental and the public lending right. Non-copy-related rights (such as the right 
of public performance, the right of broadcasting, the right of communication to the public 
by wire), cover acts through which works or objects of related rights are made available 
fordirect–thatis,notdeferred–use(perceiving,studying,watching,listeningto)bythe
members of the public.
2. On the blurring of the borderline between copy-related rights and non-copy-related rights, 
see “making available to the public; right of ~” and “umbrella solution”.
Non-voluntary licenses
A reference to “compulsory licenses” and “statutory licenses”. See “exceptions and limitations”.
Normal exploitation (no conflict with ~ of works and subject matters of related rights)
See “three-step test”.
Object code
1. That version of a computer program which is already compiled from the source code of 
the program and thus it is ready to be run on a computer. The object code file contains 
asequenceofinstructionswhichthecomputerprocessor“understands”,butwhichis
impossible or very difficult for human beings to read and understand. When a copy of the 
computer program is obtained by a user, it is usually in the form of compiled object code, 
and the source code (which may be read and understood by humans; at least, by experts) is 
not made available. This has made it necessary to permit “decompilation” for the creation of 
interoperable programs under certain conditions.
2. Article 10.1oftheTRIPSAgreementclarifiesthat“[c]omputerprograms,whetherinsourceor
object code, shall be protected as literary works under the Berne Convention”. The reference 
to the two basic forms of computer programs is a matter of redundancy since, under 
Article 2(1)oftheBerneConvention–which,byvirtueofArticle 9.1oftheTRIPSAgreement,
mustalsobecompliedwithbytheMembersoftheWTO–aliteraryorartisticworkmustbe
protected “whatever may be the mode or form of its expression”. In accordance with this, 
Article 4oftheWCTstatesasfollows:“Computerprogramsareprotectedasliteraryworks
withinthemeaningofArticle 2oftheBerneConvention.Suchprotectionappliestocomputer
programs, whatever may be the mode or form of their expression.” (For further details, see 
paragraphs CT-4.11, CT-4.15 and CT-4.16 of the Guide to the WCT, Part III.) 
Original; originality
In relation to a work, originality means that it is the author’s own intellectual creation, and is 
not copied from another’s work. In certain countries following the common law tradition, for a 
productiontoqualifyasaworkitis,however,sufficientthatitistheresultof“skillandlabor” 
or merely the “sweat of the brow”; that is, of any intellectual effort, even if not of a creative 
nature. In contrast, in some countries following the civil law tradition, it is also a condition that

===== PAGE 479 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
480 the work bear the impact of the author’s personality. Originality is not to be confused with the 
patentrequirementof“novelty”;thepreexistenceofasimilarworkunknowntotheauthor–in 
particular,onetowhichtheauthorhashadnoaccess–doesnotaffecttheoriginalityofan
independently created work. (For further details, see paragraphs BC-2.1 to BC-2.5 of the Guide to 
the Berne Convention, Part I.)
Original of a work
The material object in which the work is first fixed. It should not be confused with the concepts 
of originality and of original works. For literary works, the original is the manuscript.
Original work
1. All works are, by definition, original productions (intellectual creations); thus, it would not be 
appropriate to use the adjective “original” as a reference to the originality of works (since, 
in fact, in that way, the term would have the following meaning: “original productions”. The 
term “original work” is not used in that way, but simply in contrast with the term “derivative 
work”, as a synonym of “pre-existing work”, or “underlying work” that is, the work which 
has been transformed, through translation, adaptation or other alteration, into a derivative 
work.ThetermisusedinthatsenseinArticle 2(3)oftheBerneConvention.(Forfurther 
details, see paragraphs BC-2.1 to BC-2.5 and BC-2.31 and BC-2.32 of the Guide to the Berne 
Convention, Part I.)
2. The term “original work” has a specific meaning in the provisions on the resale right (droit de 
suite) in the expression “original works of art”. In this context, the expression has the same 
meaningas“originalofawork”.(Forfurtherdetails,seeparagraph BC-14ter.2 of the Guide to 
the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
Owner of copyright
1. The natural person to whom, or the legal entity to which, the copyright in a work belongs. 
Except for a few special cases under certain copyright laws, the original owner of copyright 
is the author in whom copyright is vested by operation of law upon his creation of the work. 
Certain copyright laws grant original ownership of copyright to a person other than the 
author or to a legal entity (such as the producer of an audiovisual work, the publisher of a 
collective work or the employer of the author). This is provided for in the Berne Convention 
specificallyforcinematographic(andotheraudiovisual)works;Article 14bis(2)(a) provides that 
the ownership of copyright in such works “shall be a matter for legislation in the countries 
where protection is claimed”. (For further details, see paragraphs BC-14bis.2 to BC-14bis.5 of 
the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
2. Owners of copyright may also be the heirs of the authors, or the legal successors to those 
legal entities as original owners of copyright.
3. The overwhelming majority of copyright laws allow transfer (assignment) of copyright, 
in whole or in part, as a result of which the transferee (assignee) becomes the owner of 
copyright.TheBerneConventioninArticle 2(6)clarifiesthataprotectiontobegrantedunder
the Convention applies both to authors and to their successors in title. (For further details, 
see paragraphs BC-2.47 to BC-2.51 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
Owner of related rights
1. The natural person to whom, or the legal entity to which, related rights belong. The original 
owners of related rights are the following: for the rights of performers, the performers 
concerned; for the rights of producers of phonograms, the producers concerned; for the 
rights of broadcasting organizations, the organizations concerned; for the rights of makers 
of databases, the makers of databases concerned; and for the rights in typographical 
arrangements in published editions, the publishers concerned.
2. Owners of related rights may also be the heirs of the natural persons who were the original 
owners of related rights and the legal entities which become legal successors to those legal 
entities which were original owners of related rights.
3. In the case of assignment (transfer) of related rights, the assignee (transferee) becomes the 
owner of the related rights concerned.

PART V. Glossary of copyright and related rights terms
Performance; performer
1. A performance is simply what is performed by a performer. This term, in general, is 
broader than the term “performance of a work” since it also applies to the performances 
of expressions of folklore and may also extend, for example, to performances by variety 
artistes. Performances are the subject matters of the rights of performers, a category of 
related rights under the Rome Convention, the TRIPS Agreement, the WPPT and the BTAP. 
2. Themostup-to-datedefinitionof“performers”isofferedinArticle 2(a)oftheWPPTand
Article 2(a)oftheBTAP:“actors,singers,musicians,dancers,andotherpersonswhoact,sing,
deliver, declaim, play in, interpret, or otherwise perform literary or artistic works or expressions 
offolklore”.TheRomeConventioncontainsasimilardefinitioninitsArticle 3(a)thatis,however,
narrower since it covers only the performers of literary and artistic works (it does not cover 
expressionsoffolklore,whichdonotqualifyassuchworks).Inanothersense,theconceptof
“performer”isbroaderundertheRomeConventioninthatArticle 9oftheConventionprovides
for the possibility of extending it to variety and circus artistes. (For further details, see paragraphs 
BC-3.1 to BC-3.9 of the Guide to the Rome Convention, Part II, paragraphs PPT-2.2 to PPT-2.4 of the 
Guide to the WPPT, and paragraphs BT-2.2 to BT-2.4 of the Guide to the BTAP, Part III.) 
Performing a work; right of public performance
1. Performing a work means the act of a performer concerning a work as a result of which 
the work becomes audible and/or visible for those who are present at the place of the 
performance. Furthermore, it also means the making audible or visible of an audiovisual work 
oraworkembodiedinaphonogramthroughappropriateequipment.
2. UnderArticle 11(1)oftheBerneConvention,ownersofcopyrightmusthavetheexclusive
right of authorizing the public performance of their dramatic, dramatico-musical and 
musical works. The provision clarifies that the concept of such public performance extends 
to “public performance by any means or process”, which means that the public performance 
of such works fixed in audiovisual fixations or in phonograms is also covered. The term 
“publicperformance”isusedinthelattersense–thatis,inthesenseofperformingworksby
meansofequipment–inArticles 14(1)(ii)and14bis(1).Article 14(1)(ii)provides,withrespect
to cinematographic works (which also mean other audiovisual works): “[a]uthors of literary 
or artistic works shall have the exclusive right of authorizing [...] the public performance [...] 
oftheworksthusadaptedorreproduced”.Article 14 bis(1) adds that “the owner of copyright 
in a cinematographic work [which also means other audiovisual work] enjoys the same rights 
as the author of an original work, including the rights referred to in the preceding Article”, 
that is, also the right of public performance. (For further details, see paragraphs BC-14.8 and 
BC-14.11 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
3. It is to be noted that, although the Berne Convention mentions separately the recitation of 
literaryworks,andprovidesforaseparaterightofpublicrecitationinitsArticle 14ter(1)(ii), 
recitation should be regarded to be covered by the general concept of “performance”.
4. Thenatureoftherightof“publiccommunication”providedforinArticle 11bis(1)(iii) of the 
Berne Convention is similar to the right of “public performance” and the right of “public 
recitation” for the reasons mentioned under those expression below.
5. If works are made audible and/or visible to those who are not present at the place from 
where this takes place (in other words, from where the act originates), it is not performance 
but communication, and, provided it is “to the public”, it is covered by the right of 
broadcasting, the right of communication to the public by cable (wire), and, in certain cases, 
the right of making available to the public.
6. For a broader concept of the right of public performance, see “performing rights”.
Performing rights
1. A commonly used term, mainly in the context of collective management of copyright 
and related rights, to mean more or less all non-copy-related rights: the right of public 
performance, the right of public recitation, the right of broadcasting and the right of 
communication to the public by cable (wire).
2. In certain countries, the scope of the right of public performance extends to all the rights 
mentionedinpoint1above;thatis,itisbroaderthanwhatisprovidedinArticle 11(1)(i)of
the Berne Convention. See “legal characterization of acts and rights; principle of relative 
freedom of ~)”.

482 Personal use
See “private use; private reproduction.”
Petits droits
Frenchtermfrequentlyusedtodenotethe“performingrights”innon-dramaticmusicalworks, 
with or without words, which, in general, are managed on a collective basis. The English term 
“small rights” is also used in this context.
Phonogram
1. Attheinternationallevel,thebroadestdefinitionof“phonogram”isofferedinArticle 2(b)
of the WPPT, according to which it means “the fixation of the sounds of a performance 
or of other sounds, or of a representation of sounds, other than in the form of a fixation 
incorporated in a cinematographic or other audiovisual work”. (For further details, see 
paragraphs RC-3.10 to RC-3.13 of the Guide to the Rome Convention, Part II.)
2. ThedefinitionintheWPPTisbroaderthanthedefinitionintheRomeConvention(Article 3(b))
andthePhonogramsConvention(Article 1(a)):“anyexclusivelyauralfixationofsoundsof
a performance or of other sounds”, since it also covers audiovisual fixations that are not 
original,andthusdonotqualifyascinematographicorotheraudiovisualworks.(Forfurther
details, see paragraphs PPT-2.5 to PPT-2.16 of the Guide to the WPPT, Part III.) 
3. In countries following the civil law tradition, phonograms are regarded as subject matters 
of related rights and producers of phonograms are granted related rights protection. In 
countries following the common law tradition in general, phonograms are recognized as 
works, and copyright protection is granted in respect of them. In those countries, in general 
the term “sound recording” is used rather than the term “phonogram”.
Phonogram notice
ThenoticementionedanddescribedintheprovisionsofArticle 11oftheRomeConventionand
Article 5ofthePhonogramsConvention.Undertheseprovisions,if,asaconditionofprotecting 
the rights of producers of phonograms, or of performers, or both, in relation to phonograms, 
aContractingState,underitsdomesticlaw,requirescompliancewithformalities,theseare 
considered as fulfilled if all the copies in commerce of the published phonogram, or their 
containers,bearanoticeconsistingofthesymbol℗accompaniedbytheyeardateofthefirst
publication, placed in such a manner as to give reasonable notice of a claim of protection. If 
the copies, or their containers, do not identify the producer or the licensee of the producer (by 
carrying his name, trade mark or other appropriate designation), the notice also is to include 
the name of the owner of the rights of the producer. If the copies or the containers do not 
identify the principal performers, the notice must also include the name of the person who, in 
the country in which the fixation was effected, owns the rights of such performers. (For further 
details,seeparagraph RC-11.1oftheGuidetotheRomeConventionandparagraph PhC-5.1of
the Guide to the Phonograms Convention, Part II.) 
Phonograms Convention
The Convention for the Protection of Producers of Phonograms Against Unauthorized 
Duplication of Their Phonograms, adopted in Geneva on October 29, 1971. Sometimes referred 
to as the “Geneva Phonograms Convention”. It is administered by the United Nations, in respect 
of depositing of instruments and notifications, by WIPO in respect of the establishment of 
official texts, and otherwise by WIPO, ILO and UNESCO together.

See “criteria of eligibility for protection”.
“Post mortem auctoris ” (p.m.a.)
Latinexpressionmeaning“afterthedeathoftheauthor”.Thistermisfrequentlyusedinthe 
Latinversion–sometimesinanabbreviatedformas“p.m.a”–inreferringtoatermofprotection

lasting during the life of an author and for a certain duration after his death. Thus, the term of 
protectionprovidedforinArticle 7(1)oftheBerneConventionasabasicruleisreferredtoas50
years post mortem auctoris. (For further details, see paragraphs BC-7.5 to BC-7.7 of the Guide to 
the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
Prejudice (no unreasonable ~ to the legitimate interests of owners of rights)
See “three-step test”.
Preventing (possibility of ~ certain acts)
AtermusedintheRomeConvention(Article 7.1)andtheTRIPSAgreement(Article 14.1).
Originally, in the Rome Convention, the use of this expression, rather than a reference to an 
(exclusive) right of authorizing or prohibiting certain acts, became necessary since, at that 
time, some countries following the common law legal tradition were not ready to grant explicit 
intellectual property rights to performers, and they were only in a position to protect them 
against certain acts performed without their consent on the basis of other legal institutions, such 
as the protection of personality rights. (For further details, see paragraphs BC-7.1 to BC-7.3 of the 
Guide to the Rome Convention, Part II.) The ever more prevailing international trend, however, is 
that performers are granted fully fledged intellectual property rights; this trend is reflected also 
intherelevantprovisionsoftheWPPT(seeitsArticles 6to10)andArticles 6to11oftheBTAP.
Private use; private reproduction
1. Use of works and subject matters of related rights (such as reproduction, translation, 
adaptation, arrangement or other transformation) for private, personal and non-commercial 
purposes, such as research, learning or entertainment. As a rule, it is regarded as a broadly 
permitted free use. In certain cases of private use, however, the exclusive right involved 
(such as the right of reproduction in computer programs) must not be limited since it would 
conflict with a normal exploitation of the work. In other cases of private use, the exclusive 
right involved may be limited to a right to remuneration (as in the case of private copying of 
phonograms and audiovisual works). From this viewpoint, it should be taken into account 
that private reproduction is also under the control of the “three-step test” provided for in 
Article 9(2)oftheBerneConvention,Article 13oftheTRIPSAgreement,Article 10oftheWCT,
Article 16oftheWPPTandArticle 13oftheBTAP.(Forfurtherdetails,seeparagraph PPT-4.8
of the Guide to the WPPT, Part III.) 
2. Private copying through the Internet has specific aspects. First, the inclusion of works 
in “private lockers” by means of “cloud” technology is also private copying, provided the 
access to the works and subject matters of related rights include is limited to the private 
sphere (if access by the members of the public is allowed, an act of interactive making 
available to the public takes place). Second, as it is made clear by statutory and/or case law 
in certain countries, copying from (at least, obviously) illegal sources, makes the otherwise 
free acts of private copying infringing. Third, due to the great number of people who may 
and do make private reproduction from online sources tending to conflict with the normal 
exploitation of the works and subject matters of related rights concerned (which may only 
bepreventedoreliminated–oratleastreduced–throughtheapplicationofcopy-protection
technological measures).
Producer of an audiovisual work
1. The person who, or legal entity which, takes the initiative and responsibility for making an 
audiovisual work.
2. Under some copyright laws following the common-law tradition, the producer of an 
audiovisual work is the original owner of copyright, and, under some of those laws, is even 
recognizedastheauthorofthework.Article 14bis(2)(a) of the Berne Convention provides 
that the “[o]wnership of copyright in a cinematographic [and other audiovisual] work shall be 
a matter for legislation in the country where protection is claimed”. (For further details, see 
paragraphs BC-14bis.2 to BC-14bis.10 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.)

Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
484 Producer of a phonogram
1. The broadest and most up-to-date definition of “producer of a phonogram” is offered 
inArticle 2(d)oftheWPPT,underwhichit“meanstheperson,orthelegalentity,whoor
which takes the initiative and has the responsibility for the first fixation of the sounds of a 
performance or other sounds, or the representations of sounds”. The definition is up-to-date; 
it includes electronically (digitally) generated sounds. Its broader nature follows not only from 
this,butaswell–andevenmore–fromthebroadernatureofthedefinitionof“phonogram”
inArticle 2(a)oftheWPPT.Italsocoversaudiovisualfixationsotherthanthosewhichare
originalandthusqualifyasaudiovisualworks.(Forfurtherdetails,seeparagraphsPPT-2.19
and PPT-2.20 of the Guide to the WPPT, Part III.) 
2. TheRomeConvention,inArticle 3(c),definesthetermas“thepersonwho,orthelegalentity
which,firstfixesthesoundsofaperformanceorothersounds”.UnderArticle 3(b)oftheRome
Convention, however, “phonograms” are exclusively aural fixations of sounds. (For further 
details, see paragraphs RC-3.10 to RC-3.15 of the Guide to the Rome Convention, Part II.) 
Program (carried by programme-carrying signals); ~ of a broadcasting organization
1. ProgramisdefinedintheBrussels,orSatellites,Convention(Article 1(ii))–whereitisspelled 
as“programme”–inthefollowingway:“abodyofliveorrecordedmaterialconsistingof
images, sounds or both”. By this, one of the two substantive elements of the subject matter 
oftheprotectiontobeofferedundertheSatellitesConvention–“programme-carrying 
signals” is defined.
2. The term somewhat differs from the concept of the “program of a broadcasting organization” 
which is a synonym of “broadcast”, since the Brussels, or Satellites, Convention does not 
coverdirectbroadcastingsatellites–butonlyfixed-servicesatellites–andthus,initscontext,
a program is supposed to be still at a pre-broadcasting stage. (For further details, see 
paragraphs SC-1.3 and SC-1.4 of the Guide to the Brussels, or Satellites, Convention, Part II.) 
Programme-carrying signal
The subject matter of protection to be granted under the Brussels, or Satellites, Convention: a 
“signal” which is carrying a “programme”. (For further details, see paragraphs SC-1.2 to SC-1.4 of 
the Guide to the Brussels, or Satellites, Convention, Part II.) 
Pseudonymous work
1. A work of an author who discloses and makes available a work under a pseudonym; that is, a 
name other than the official civil name of the author. 
2. Such a work, irrespective of the use of a pseudonym, is protected by copyright, and the 
beneficiaryoftheprotectionistheauthor.Article 7(3)oftheBerneConventioncontains
specific provisions on the term of protection of pseudonymous works. If, however, the 
pseudonym leaves no doubt as to the identity of the author, or if the author himself 
subsequentlyrevealshisidentitytothepublic,thisprovisionisreplacedbytherelevant
generalrules(see,inparticular,Article 7(1)and7bis of the Convention) applicable to works 
whose authors are identified by their real names. (For further details, see paragraphs BC-7.18 
to BC-7.21 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
Public; the ~
1. “Public” means a substantial number of persons outside the normal circle of a family and its 
closesocialacquaintances.Itisnotdecisivewhetherornotthepersonsarepresentinone
place; the availability of works or subject matters of related rights to them suffices. In cases 
of communication to the public (including broadcasting) and interactive making available to 
the public, it is irrelevant whether the members of the public capable of receiving the works 
or subject matters of related rights may receive them at the same place or at difference 
places, and at the same time or at different times.
2. As an adjective in reference to an act, “public” (such as performance or recitation) means that 
the act is performed in the presence of the public, or at least at a place open to the public. 
(Forfurtherdetails,seeparagraph BC-11.4oftheGuidetotheBerneConvention,PartI.)

===== PAGE 484 =====
485
PART V. Glossary of copyright and related rights terms
Publication; published work
1. The Berne Convention does not define the concept of “publication” directly. It does so, 
however,indirectlywhenitprovidesinArticle 3(3)asfollows:“Theexpression‘published
works’ means works published with the consent of their authors, whatever may be the means 
of manufacture of the copies, provided that the availability of such copies has been such as 
tosatisfythereasonablerequirementsofthepublic,havingregardtothenatureofthework.
The performance of a dramatic, dramatico-musical, cinematographic or musical work, the 
public recitation of a literary work, the communication by wire or the broadcasting of literary 
or artistic works, the exhibition of a work of art and the construction of a work of architecture 
shall not constitute publication.” From this definition, it follows that, under the Convention, 
“publication”means“makingavailableofcopies(thatis,distribution)inaquantityand
mannerthatissuitabletosatisfythereasonablerequirementsofthepublic”.(Forfurther
details, see paragraphs BC-3.6 to BC-3.9 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
2. TheRomeConvention(inArticle 3(d))offersadirectdefinitionwhichreflectsasimpler
conceptthanwhatfollowsfromArticle 3(3)oftheBerneConvention,sinceitreadsasfollows:
“'publication’ means the offering of copies of a phonogram to the public in reasonable 
quantity”.ThecorrespondingdefinitionoftheWPPT(inArticle 2(e))isbroader,inthesense
that it also covers separately the publication of a fixed performance, but it is essentially similar 
to the definition in the Rome Convention: “'publication’ of a fixed performance or a phonogram 
means the offering of copies of the fixed performance or the phonogram to the public, with 
the consent of the rightholder, and provided that copies are offered to the public in reasonable 
quantity”.(Forfurtherdetails,seeparagraphsRC-3.16toRC-3.18oftheGuidetotheRome
Convention, Part II, and paragraphs PPT-2.21 and PPT-2.22 of the Guide to the WPPT, Part III.) 
3. The TRIPS Agreement does not contain any definition of “publication” (but compliance with 
Article 3(3)oftheBerneConventionisanobligationoftheMembersoftheWTO).
Public communication
1. Theterm“publiccommunication”isusedinArticle 11bis(1)(iii) of the Berne Convention; 
it provides that the owners of copyright enjoy the exclusive right to authorize “the public 
communication by loudspeaker or any other analogous instrument transmitting, by signs, 
sounds or images, the broadcast of the work”. The use of this term, rather than the term 
“communication to the public”, is appropriate, since this act does not involve the transmission 
of the work to another place: it is an act carried out in a place where the public is or may be 
present, and, in that sense, it is similar to “public performance” and to ‘’public recitation”. It 
means the reception of a broadcast work in a way that it becomes audible and/or visible to 
those who are present and correspond to the concept of “(the) public”.
2. The term differs from the expression “communication to the public”, since in the case of the 
latter, those to whom works or subject matters of related rights are transmitted for reception, 
and who correspond to the concept “the public”, are usually at different places. (For further 
details,seeparagraph BC-11bis.13 the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
Public display; right of ~
See “displaying/display; right of public display”.
Public domain
The scope of those works and objects of related rights that can be used and exploited by 
everyone without authorization, and without the obligation to pay remuneration to the 
ownersofcopyrightandrelatedrightsconcerned–ingeneral,duetotheexpiryoftheirterm
of protection or to absence of an international obligation to protect them. It is to be noted, 
however, that in certain countries, moral rights remain applicable also after the expiry of the 
term of protection of the economic rights. 
Public lending right
Right granted in some national laws in respect of the lending of copies of works (usually books 
and other publications) by not-for-profit libraries open to the public. No such rights are provided 
in the international norms on copyright and related rights.

===== PAGE 485 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
486 Public performance; right of ~ 
See “performing a work; right of public performance”.
Public recitation; right of ~
See “performing a work; right of public performance”.
Published edition
The given version of a work, whether it is protected or not, or of other material, as published 
in printed format. Some countries, mainly those with a common law tradition, grant sui generis 
related-right-type protection to publishers in respect of their “typographical arrangements of 
published editions”.
Rebroadcasting; right of ~
1. The simultaneous and unchanged broadcasting by one broadcasting organization of the 
broadcast of another broadcasting organization. 
2. UnderArticle 11bis(1)(ii) of the Berne Convention, authors enjoy the exclusive right to 
authorize such rebroadcasting when it is done by an organization other than the original one. 
Article 11bis(2) of the Convention permits limitations on such a right, such as the application 
of non-voluntary licenses or submitting its exercise to the condition of mandatory collective 
management.(Forfurtherdetails,seeparagraph BC-11bis.13 of the Guide to the Berne 
Convention, Part I.)
3. UnderArticle 13(a)oftheRomeConvention,broadcastingorganizationsenjoytheright
to authorize or prohibit the rebroadcasting of their broadcasts. (For further details, see 
paragraph RC-13.2oftheGuidetotheRomeConvention,PartII.)
Reception
The act of receiving a program broadcast or cablecast (communicated to the public by cable 
(wire)), usually for the purpose of watching, listening to and/or reproducing the works or subject 
matters of related rights included in the program. Reception is not part of, or a condition for the 
completion of, an act of broadcasting or cablecasting.
Reciprocity
The principle of making protection, or the extent of protection, of copyright or related rights of 
nationals of another country conditional on the existence of the same (or at least similar) extent 
of protection granted in that other country, to the nationals of the country concerned. Where 
a treaty obligates contracting parties to grant national treatment to the nationals of other 
contracting parties, the treatment is not allowed to be reduced to the level of reciprocity.
Recording of a work or subject matter of related rights
A “fixation of a work or a subject matter of related rights”.
Related rights
In the traditional narrower sense, the term “related rights” (or its synonym “neighboring rights”) 
means the rights of performers with respect to their performances, the rights of producers of 
phonograms with respect to their phonograms, and the rights of broadcasting organizations 
with respect to their broadcasts. In the EU the producers of a “first fixation of films” also enjoy 
related rights. The broader meaning of the expression extends to the rights of publishers in the 
typographical arrangements of their published editions, and to the sui generis rights of makers 
of databases.

===== PAGE 486 =====
487
PART V. Glossary of copyright and related rights terms
Remuneration; right to ~
1. “Remuneration” is payment to be made by those who perform an act concerning a work or a 
subject matter of related rights. On the basis of an exclusive right of authorization, the owner 
of rights is in a position to subject the authorization of any act covered by the right to the 
payment of an appropriate remuneration; therefore, in the case of an exclusive right, it is not 
necessary to state that the owners of rights have the right to receive remuneration for the 
authorization of the acts concerned.
2. A “right to remuneration” may be granted on two differing legal bases. Either an exclusive right 
of authorization is limited in certain specific cases to a mere right to remuneration, subject to 
the three-step test; or remuneration is provided for in the treaties and national laws. 
Rental; right of ~
1. The transfer of the possession of a copy of a work or a subject matter of related rights for a 
limited period of time for direct or indirect economic or commercial advantage.
2. The Berne Convention and the Rome Convention do not provide for a right of rental, while the 
TRIPSAgreement(initsArticles 11and14.4),does–undersomeconditionsandwithsome
exceptions–inrespectofcomputerprograms,audiovisualworksandphonograms.The
obligationtograntarentalrightisthesameundertheWCT(Article 7),theWPPT(Articles 9and
13)andtheBTAP(Article 9)asundertheTRIPSAgreement.(Forfurtherdetails,seeparagraphs
CT-7.3 to CT-7.16 of the Guide to the WCT, paragraphs PPT-9.1 to PPT-9.3 and PPT-13.1 to PPT-13.3 
of the Guide to the WPPT, and paragraphs BT-9.3 to BT-9.18 of the Guide to the BTAP, Part III.)
3. In general, rental is regarded to be covered by a broader concept of distribution, and in 
certain countries, a general right of distribution extends to it. In those countries, what is in 
other countries a separate right of rental is granted through an exception to the exhaustion 
of the right of distribution with the first sale of (or other first transfer of property in) the 
copies concerned in respect of their rental. In other countries, a separate right of rental, 
usually restricted to specific categories of works and/or subject matters of related rights, is 
providedinparallelwiththerightof(first)distribution–thelatterbeingappliedonlytothe
sale or other transfer of property (and exhausted with the first such act).
Reproduction; right of ~
1. “Reproduction” is a [new] fixation of the work or subject matter of related rights sufficiently 
stable for the work or subject matter of related rights to be perceived, (further) reproduced 
and communicated on the basis thereof. Storage of works in electronic form (computer 
memory) is also reproduction, since it fully corresponds to this concept.
2. Article 9(1)oftheBerneConventionprovidesthatownersofcopyrightmustenjoyan
exclusive right to authorize the reproduction of their works “in any manner or form”. In 
harmony with this, from the viewpoint of the concept of “reproduction” and the coverage of 
the right of reproduction: (i) the method, manner and form of the reproduction are irrelevant; 
(ii) it is irrelevant whether the copy of the work may be perceived directly or only through a 
device; (iii) it is irrelevant whether or not the copy is embodied in a tangible object that may 
be distributed; (iv) it is irrelevant whether the reproduction is made directly (for example, on 
the basis of a tangible copy) or indirectly (for example, off air from a broadcast program); and 
(v) the duration of the fixation (including the storage in an electronic medium as clarified in 
theagreedstatementsconcerningArticle 1(4)oftheWCT,Articles 7and11oftheWPPTand
Article 7oftheBTAP)–whetheritispermanentortemporary–isirrelevant(aslongas,on
the basis of the [new] fixation, the work may be perceived, reproduced or communicated). 
3. SinceunderArticle 9.1oftheTRIPSAgreementandunderArticle 1(4)oftheWCT,compliance
withArticle 9oftheBerneConventionisanobligation,thesameconceptof“reproduction”
isapplicable–withthesamescopeoftherightofreproduction–underthoseinstruments
asundertheBerneConvention.Articles 7and11oftheWPPTandArticle 7oftheBTAPon
the exclusive right of reproduction of performers and producers of phonograms apply the 
languageofArticle 9(1)oftheBerneConventionmutatis mutandis, including the clarification 
that the rights provided for in them cover reproduction “in any manner or form”. Thus, under 
that treaty, the concept of “reproduction” and the scope of the right of reproduction is also the 
same as what is outlined in point 1 above. The agreed statements concerning these provisions 
mentionedinpoint2aboveclarifythattherightofreproduction–alongwiththeexceptionsto
andlimitations–fullyappliesinthedigitalenvironmentaswell,includingthestoragethereof

===== PAGE 487 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
488 in electronic media. (For further details, see paragraphs BC-9.6 to BC-9.10 of the Guide to the 
Berne Convention, Part I, and paragraphs CT-1.40 to CT-1.45 of the Guide to the WCT, Part III.)
4. In contrast with the other instruments mentioned above, the Rome Convention contains an 
explicitdefinitionofreproductioninitsArticle 3(e).However,itisverysimple:“‘reproduction’
means the making of a copy or copies of a fixation”. Since “reproduction”, “copying” and 
“making a copy or copies” are synonyms, this is not a truly substantive definition. Only 
Article 10oftheConventionaddsacertainclarifyingelementinthesensethatitspeaksof
“direct or indirect reproduction”. In spite of this, it may hardly be presumed that the concept 
of ”reproduction” in the Rome Convention differs from what is applicable under the above-
mentioned other instruments. (For further details, see paragraphs RC-3.19 and RC-3.20 of the 
Guide to the Rome Convention, Part II.) 
Reprographic reproduction
Reproduction of works by photocopying or analogous procedure in the form of facsimile copies.  
Making reduced or enlarged facsimile copies is also reprographic reproduction.
Resale right
1. The inalienable right of authors or, after their death, the persons or institutions authorized by 
nationallegislation,toaninterestinanysaleoftheiroriginalworksofartsand–muchmore
rarely–theiroriginalmanuscripts,subsequenttothefirsttransferthereofbytheauthor.It
usually takes the form of a specific percentage of the sale price, or the difference between the 
resale price and the previous sale price. The applicability of the right is usually restricted to 
publicauctionsandtosalesthroughartdealers.UnderArticle 14ter of the Berne Convention, 
granting such a right is optional, and its application may be subject to reciprocity. (For further 
details, see paragraphs BC-14ter.2 to BC-14ter.4 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.)
2. TherightisfrequentlyreferredtobyitsFrenchterm,droit de suite.
Residual right
Aright–ingeneral,arighttoremuneration–(usuallyinalienable)ofauthorsandperformers
which is maintained for them under the law when they transfer their exclusive rights to others. 
UnderArticle 12(3)oftheBTAP,nationallawsorindividual,collectiveorotheragreementsmay
provide for performers such a right in case of the transfer of exclusive rights under the Treaty. 
(For further details, see paragraphs BT-12.83 to BT-12.92 of the Guide to the BTAP, Part III.)
Respect (right of)
See “moral rights”.
Retroactivity
In the context of the international norms on copyright and related rights, a misnomer since 
none of the treaties on copyright or related rights provides for its retroactive application. The 
correct“applicationintime”providedforinArticle 18oftheBerneConvention–the mutatis 
mutandis applicationofwhichisprescribedintherelevantprovisionsoftheothertreaties–is
that, subject to the conditions determined there, all works and subject matters of related rights 
for which the term of protection has not yet expired enjoy protection from the moment of the 
entry into force of the Convention. 
Right of adaptation
See “adaptation; right of ~ ”.
Right of attribution
See “moral rights”.

Rights management information (RMI)
1. DefinedinArticle 12(2)oftheWCT,Article 19(2)oftheWPPTandArticle 16(2)oftheBTAP,
in a mutatis mutandis manner, practically in the same way: “information which identifies 
[the work, the author of the work, the owner of any right in the work] [the performer, the 
performance of the performer, the producer of the phonogram, the owner of any right in 
the performance or phonogram], or information about the terms and conditions of use 
of [the work] [the performance or phonogram], and any numbers or codes that represent 
such information, when any of these items of information is attached to a copy of [a work] 
[a fixed performance or a phonogram] or appears in connection with [the communication 
of a work to the public] [the communication or making available of a fixed performance or a 
phonogram to the public]”.
2. UnderArticle 12(1)oftheWCT,Article 19(1)oftheWPPTandArticle 16(1)oftheBTAP,
“ContractingPartiesshallprovideadequateandeffectivelegalremediesagainstanyperson
knowingly performing any of the following acts knowing, or with respect to civil remedies, 
having reasonable grounds to know, that it will induce, enable, facilitate or conceal an 
infringement of any right covered by this Treaty [or the Berne Convention]: (i) to remove 
or alter any electronic rights management information without authority; (ii) to distribute, 
import for distribution, [broadcast or communicate to the public] [broadcast, communicate 
or make available to the public] without authority, [works or copies of works] [performances, 
copies of fixed performances or phonograms] knowing that electronic rights management 
information has been removed or altered without authority.” (For further details, see 
paragraphs CT-12.1 to CT-12.6 of the Guide to the WCT, Part III.)

Rome Convention
The International Convention for the Protection of Performers, Producers of Phonograms and 
Broadcasting Organisations, adopted in Rome on October 26, 1961. It is administered by the 
United Nations in respect of depositing instruments and notifications, and otherwise by WIPO, 
ILO and UNESCO jointly. 
Satellites Convention
The Convention Relating to the Distribution of Programme-Carrying Signals Transmitted by 
Satellite, adopted in Brussels on May 21, 1974. It is administered by the United Nations as 
regards depositing of instruments and notifications, and otherwise by WIPO, UNESCO, ILO and 
the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) jointly.
Scientific works
A category of “literary and artistic works” the use of which, in some national laws and indirectly 
alsointheBerneConvention(inArticle 2(1)intheexpression“everyproductionintheliterary, 
scientific and artistic domain”), is unnecessary and misleading, since the scientific subject 
matter of work is irrelevant from the viewpoint of its copyright protection. For example, 
articles orbooksonscientifictopicsareprotectednotbecauseoftheirtopic,butbecausethey 
arearticles andbooks,thatis,literaryworks.(Forfurtherdetails,seeparagraph BC-2.8ofthe 
Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.)

PART V. Glossary of copyright and related rights terms
Sheet music
1. Expression of a musical work through notes and other symbols, usually with certain standard 
instructions, either in handwriting (which thus is to be regarded as a manuscript) or in printed 
form, and either with or without accompanying words.
2. In some national laws, there are specific provisions on sheet music, for example, concerning 
a right of rental in musical works in such form or on the exclusion of the applicability of the 
exception for private reproduction thereof.
Simultaneous publication of a work
UnderArticle 3(3)oftheBerneConvention,aworkistobeconsideredashavingbeenpublished
simultaneously in two or more countries if it has been published in them within 30 days of its 
first publication. This provision is of relevance in connection with eligibility for protection under 
theBerneConvention.(Forfurtherdetails,seeparagraph BC-3.5oftheGuidetotheBerne
Convention, Part I.) 
Small rights
See “petits droits ”.
Software
See “computer program”.
Sound recording
1. A phonogram. In countries following the common law tradition in which phonograms 
are recognized as works, the term “sound recording” is generally used, rather than the 
term “phonogram”.
2. The act of aurally fixing sounds of performances (inter alia, performances of works) or other 
sounds. Under copyright, the sound recording of (performances of works) is covered by 
the“mechanicalright”versionoftherightofreproduction(Articles 9and13oftheBerne
Convention).Inrespectofperformances,theRomeConvention(Article 7.1(b))andtheTRIPS
Agreement(Article 14.1)prescribethe“possibilityofpreventing”suchanactifdonewithout
theconsentoftheperformer,whiletheWPPTandtheBTAP(inboth,Article 6(ii))providesfor
an exclusive right of authorization in this respect. (For further details, see paragraphs BC-13.1 
toBC-13.5oftheGuidetotheBerneConvention,Part I,andparagraphsRC-7.11toRC-7.15of
the Guide to the Rome Convention, Part II.) 
Source code
1. Source code is that version of a computer program which has not yet been compiled to run on 
a computer. It may still be read and understood by humans; at least, by experts.
2. Article 10.1oftheTRIPSAgreementclarifiesthat“[c]omputerprograms,whetherinsourceor
object code, shall be protected as literary works under the Berne Convention”. The reference 
to the two basic forms in which computer programs are expressed is a matter of redundancy 
since,underArticle 2(1)oftheBerneConvention–which,byvirtueofArticle 9.1oftheTRIPS
Agreement,mustbecompliedwithalsobytheMembersoftheWTO–aliteraryorartistic
work must be protected “whatever may be the mode or form of its expression”. In accordance 
withthis,Article 4oftheWCTstates:“Computerprogramsareprotectedasliteraryworks
withinthemeaningofArticle 2oftheBerneConvention.Suchprotectionappliestocomputer
programs, whatever may be the mode or form of their expression.” (For further details, see 
paragraphs CT-4.11 to CT-4.17 of the Guide to the WCT, Part III.) 
Special cases (covered by exceptions and limitations)
See “three-step test”.

Storage of works and subject matters of related rights in electronic medium (computer memory) 
See “reproduction; right of”.
Streaming
Online transmission of a work or subject matter of related rights over the Internet in the form of 
a steady, continuous flow of digital data allowing the transmission to be played while the rest of 
the data is still being received. Streaming is covered by the right of interactive making available 
to the public if the work or subject matter of protection is made available in such a way that the 
members of the public may access it from a place and at a time individually chosen by them and 
by the right of communication to the public if it is made in the form of webcasting.
Subject matter of related rights
Subject matter in respect of which related rights are granted (performances, phonograms,  
broadcasts).
Subscription services
See “near-on-demand transmission”.
Subtitling
1. The act of superimposing a written text on an audiovisual work (usually in a language other 
than the language spoken in the audiovisual work).
2. UnderArticle 14bis(2)(b) of the Berne Convention, “in the countries of the Union which, by 
legislation, include among the owners of copyright in a cinematographic work [as well as 
other audiovisual works] authors who have brought contributions to the making of the work, 
such authors, if they have undertaken to bring such contributions, may not, in the absence 
of any contrary or special stipulation, object to the […] subtitling […] of texts […] of the work”. 
(Article 14bis(3) contains exceptions to this provision.) 
Successor in title
A natural person or legal entity succeeding by assignment (transfer) of rights or by inheritance 
(operation of law) the original owner of copyright or related rights as the owner of the rights 
concerned.UnderArticle 2(6)oftheBerneConvention,“[t]hisprotectionshalloperateforthe 
benefit of the author and his successor in title”. (For further details, see paragraphs BC-2.45 to 
BC-2.51 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.)
Technological protection measure (TPM)
1. Any technology, device or component that is designed in such a way that, in the normal 
course of its operation, it prevents or restricts acts, in respect of works or subject matters 
of related rights that are not authorized by the owner of rights. A technological measure 
is “effective” where the use of a protected work or subject matter of related rights is 
controlled by the owner of rights through the application of an access control process, such 
as encryption or other transformation of the work or subject matter of related rights, or 
ofacopycontrolmechanism,which–inthenormalcourseofitsoperation–achievesthe
protection objective.
2. UnderArticle 11oftheWCT,Article 18oftheWPPTandArticle 15oftheBTAP,Contracting
Partiesmustprovideadequatelegalprotectionandeffectivelegalremediesagainstthe
circumvention of effective technological measures that are used by owners of rights in 
connection with the exercise of their rights under those treaties, and that restrict acts in 
respect of their works, performances or phonograms, respectively, which are not authorized 
by them or permitted by law.

===== PAGE 492 =====
493
PART V. Glossary of copyright and related rights terms
3. DuringtheimplementationoftheTreaties,ithasbecomeclear–andthisisreflectedin
therespectiveprovisionsinnationallaws–thatitisnotpossibletoprovideadequatelegal
protection and effective legal remedies against acts of circumvention if the protection and 
remedies are not also applied to the so-called “preparatory activities”. That is, against the 
manufacture, import, distribution, sale, rental, advertisement for sale or rental, or possession 
for commercial purposes of devices, products or components, or the provision of services 
which: (i) are promoted, advertised or marketed for the purpose of circumvention of; or (ii) 
have only a limited commercially significant purpose or use other than to circumvent; or 
(iii) are primarily designed, produced, adapted or performed for the purpose of enabling or 
facilitating the circumvention of any effective technological measures. (For further details on 
TMPs, see paragraphs CT-11.3 to CT-11.9 of the Guide to the WCT, Part III.) 
Term of protection
The period of time during which copyright in works is, and related rights in subject matters 
thereof are, protected. With the expiry of the term of protection, the work or the subject matter 
of related rights falls into the public domain.
Three-step test
1. Test to determine whether or not an exception or limitation is permissible. The test includes 
three cumulative conditions (“steps”) to be fulfilled. An exception or limitation: (i) may only 
cover certain special cases; (ii) must not conflict with a normal exploitation of the works 
or subject matters of related rights (in fact, exploitation of the rights in works and subject 
matters of related rights); and (iii) must not unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of 
owners of rights. (For further details, see paragraphs BC-9.11 and BC-9.65 of the Guide to the 
Berne Convention, Part I.)
2. ThetestwasoriginallyprovidedforinArticle 9(2)oftheBerneConventionconcerning
exceptions to and limitations on the right of reproduction. It has been extended by 
Article 13oftheTRIPSAgreement,andthenalsobyArticle 10oftheWCT,forexceptions
toandlimitationsonalleconomicrightsundercopyright.Finally,Article 16oftheWPPT
andArticle 13oftheBTAPhaveextendedittotherightsofperformersandproducersof
phonograms covered by that Treaty. It is also applicable to the exceptions and limitations 
providedintheMarrakeshTreaty(seeArticle 11).
3. Thefirststepofthetest–thatanyexceptionorlimitationmayonlycover“certainspecial
cases”–meanstwocumulativerequirements:first,thatanyexceptionorlimitationmustbe
limited in its coverage; no broad exception or limitation with a general impact is permitted; 
and, second, it must also be special, in the sense that there must be some specific and sound 
legal–politicaljustificationforitsintroduction(forthereasonsandfordifferentpositions,see
paragraphs BC-9.19 to BC-9.49 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I).
4. As regards the second step, the meaning of the term “exploitation” is the activity by which the 
owners of copyright or related rights employ their rights to extract the value thereof. Combined 
with the adjective “normal”, the condition that exceptions or limitations must not “conflict with 
a normal exploitation” means that they must not amount to a form of exploitation that has, or 
islikelytoacquire,suchconsiderableimportancethatitmayenterintoeconomiccompetition
with the exercise of the rights of the owners of the copyright or related rights concerned (in 
other words, that may undermine the possibility of a normal exploitation of the rights in works 
or subject matters of related rights in a significant way). (For further details, see paragraphs 
BC-9.50 to BC-9.56 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.)
5. Thethirdstep–thatanexceptionorlimitationmustnotunreasonablyprejudicethe
legitimateinterestsoftheauthorsorotherownersofrights–indicatesthatcertainprejudice
may be tolerated to the legitimate interests of owners of rights, but that it must not go 
beyond what may be regarded as reasonable. The issue of a reasonable or unreasonable 
level of prejudice may be judged on the basis of the relevant, sound social norms and public 
policies taken into account in the first step. “Legitimate interests” means legal interests of 
owners of rights to enjoy, exercise, and benefit from their rights. (For further details, see 
paragraphs BC-9.57 to BC-9.60 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
Traditional cultural expressions (TCEs)
See “expressions of folklore”.

494 Transfer/transferability of copyright and related rights
1. The assignment of copyright or related rights by the owner of such rights (assignor) to a 
natural person or legal entity (assignee) as property. In contrast with a license, which involves 
only granting permission to perform certain specified acts, transfer (assignment) of a right 
means that the right of authorization or prohibition of acts covered by the right itself is 
transferred to the transferee (assignee). 
2. Under the international norms on copyright and related rights, economic rights, in particular 
the exclusive rights, are generally construed as transferable rights (in contrast with moral rights, 
which are not transferable). In harmony with this, the overwhelming majority of copyright 
laws allow authors or other owners of copyright and related rights to transfer or assign their 
economic rights, while under some copyright laws, at least in certain cases, only licenses may be 
granted, but the rights themselves may not be transferred/assigned (this is provided in this way 
mainly for the purpose of protecting the interests of authors and performers who are presumed 
to be the weaker parties in the negotiations with powerful users).
3. Even in the countries where economic rights are transferable (which are in significant 
majority),thisisnotapplicabletocertaininalienable–orevenunwaivable–rightsto
remuneration. At the level of the international treaties, see the inalienable right of resale 
(droit de suite)underArticle 14ter(1)oftheBerneConventionandtherighttoequitable
remuneration of performers maintained independently of the transfer of their exclusive 
rightsmentionedinArticle 12(3)oftheBTAP.(Forfurtherdetails,seeparagraphsBT-12.62to
BT-12.92 of the Guide to the BTAP, Part III.) 
Translation; right of ~
1. As an act, translation is generally considered to mean the transformation of a text written 
or spoken in one language into another language. (Under some national laws, the concept 
is extended to the transformation of a computer program from one programming language 
into another one.)
2. UnderArticle 8oftheBerneConvention,ownersofcopyrightmustbegrantedanexclusive
righttoauthorizethetranslationoftheirworks.UnderArticle 2(3)oftheBerneConvention,
the “[t]ranslations […] of […] a [...] work, shall be protected as original works without prejudice 
to the copyright in the original work”. (For further details, see paragraphs BC-2.31 to BC-2.37 
of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.) 
TRIPS Agreement
1. The Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights Including Trade in 
CounterfeitGoods,adoptedinMarrakesh,Morocco,in1994,asAnnexVIItotheAgreement
Establishing the World Trade Organization (WTO). It is administered by the WTO.
2. “CopyrightandRelatedRights”(PartII,Section1,Articles 9through14)formthefirstofeight
branchesofintellectualpropertyrightscoveredbytheTRIPSAgreement.PartIII(Articles 41
to61)oftheAgreementcontainsdetailedprovisionsonenforcementofrightsandPartVison
the prevention and settlement of disputes along with the “WTO Understanding on Rules and 
Procedures Governing the Settlement of Disputes”. 
Umbrella solution
1. The solution chosen by the 1996 Geneva Diplomatic Conference, which adopted the 
WCT and the WPPT, to eliminate the problems which had emerged concerning the legal 
characterization of uploading a work or subject matter of related rights and making it 
accessible for interactive digital transmissions through the Internet, and the rights to be 
applied for such transmissions (certain countries preferred the application of the right of 
communication to the public, while others the right of distribution). The “umbrella solution” 
includes the following elements: (i) describing such acts of making accessible protected 
contents for interactive digital transmissions in a neutral, legal-characterization-free 
manner, as “making available to the public of works/performances fixed in phonograms/
phonograms, by wire or wireless means, in such a way that the members of the public 
may access them from a place and at a time individually chosen by them”; (ii) providing an 
exclusive right to owners of copyright and related right to authorize such acts; but (iii) leaving 
toContractingPartiesthelegalcharacterizationofsuchacts–whetherascommunicationto

===== PAGE 494 =====
495
PART V. Glossary of copyright and related rights terms
thepublicordistributionorboth,orjustasmakingavailabletothepublic–andthechoiceof
corresponding right or rights to be applied, as long as the same acts are covered by the same 
kind of right(s) (that is, exclusive right(s)).
2. InArticles 10and14oftheWPPTonthe“rightofmakingavailableoffixedperformances/
phonograms”,this“solution”isapplieddirectly(lateralsoinArticle 10oftheBTAP),whilein
theWCT,thisneutraldescriptionoftheinteractiveactsisincludedinArticle 8onabroadly
construed “right of communication to the public” likewise covering non-interactive acts 
of communication to the public, but with a clarification in the records of the diplomatic 
conference that the obligation to grant an exclusive right with respect to such acts may 
also be fulfilled by granting a right other than the right of communication to the public 
(in particular, the right of distribution) or a combination of rights. (For further details, see 
paragraphs CT-8.1 to CT-8.10 of the Guide to the WCT, Part III.)
UNESCO
The United Nations Educational, Cultural and Scientific Organization, based in Paris. It 
administerstheUniversalCopyrightConvention(UCC),aswellas–jointlywiththeUnited 
Nations, WIPO and ILO, the Rome, Phonograms and Brussels, or Satellites, Conventions. See the 
entries on the UCC and the other three conventions.
Universal Copyright Convention (UCC)
TheUniversalCopyrightConvention–adoptedinGenevain1952,andrevisedinParisin1971.In
principle,itisadministeredbyUNESCO,but–sinceallthecountriespartytotheUCChavejoined
theBerneConvention(andbecause,undertheAppendixdeclarationrelatingtoArticle XVIIof 
theUCC,onlytheBerneConventionbindsthem)–ithaslostrelevance.
Unreasonable prejudice (no ~ to the legitimate interests of owners of rights)
See “three-step test”.
Uploading
1. Theactoftransferringaworkorsubjectmatterofrelatedrightsonline–throughdigital
transmission –fromasmall(“client”)device(suchasapersonalcomputer)toalarger(“host”
or“server”)system,usuallyforthepurposeofofferingthepossibilityofsubsequentacts
of “downloading”.
2. Uploading is an act of reproduction, but, in general, it is an intermediary step of (interactive) 
making available to the public. 
Use of a work or subject matter of related rights
1. In a narrow sense, performing an act covered by economic rights under copyright or 
related rights.
2. In a broader sense, using a work or a subject matter of related rights in any manner and for 
any purpose, including any use by a lawful owner of a copy, such as reading a book, listening 
to a phonogram, or watching an audiovisual work. Such uses of works or subject matters of 
related rights are not covered by copyright or related rights.
User (of a work or subject matter of related rights)
1. In a narrow sense, a natural person who, or legal entity which, performs an act covered by 
economic rights under copyright or related rights.
2. In a broad sense, anyone who performs an act of using a work or subject matter of related 
rights in any manner or form, including an owner using a lawful copy , such as reading a 
book, listening to a phonogram, or watching an audiovisual work.
Videogram
In certain national laws, it is used as a synonym of “first fixation of films” as a subject matter of 
related rights (specifically provided under EU law). Since the level of protection of the rights of

===== PAGE 495 =====
Guide to the Copyright and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO
496 producers in “first fixations of films” is lower than that of audiovisual works, it must be ensured 
thattherightsinaudiovisualworks–forthefirstfixationofwhichrelatedrightsaregranted– 
remain intact and applicable in parallel with the related rights.
Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (VCLT) 
TheViennaConventionontheLawofTreatieswasadoptedin1969andenteredintoforce
in1980.ItsArticles 31to33includeprovisionsontheinterpretationoftreaties.Theyare
considered as codification of the generally accepted principles and rules of interpretation of 
international norms; thus, they are taken into account and applied even by those countries that 
may not recognize them as obligatory. 
Webcasting
The act of making accessible for reception by the public transmissions of sounds, images, or 
sounds and images or the representations thereof, by wire or wireless means over the Internet 
in a way other than making available to the public interactively. Such transmissions, where 
encrypted, are considered as “webcasting” only where the means for decrypting are provided to 
the public by the webcasting organization or with its consent. From the viewpoint of copyright, 
webcastingiscoveredbythefirstpartofArticle 8oftheWCT,whichprovidesforanexclusive 
right of non-interactive transmissions of works.
Webcasting organization
The natural person or the legal entity who or which takes the initiative and has the 
responsibility for the transmission to the public of sounds, images, or sounds and images or the 
representations thereof, in the form of webcasting.
WIPO Copyright Treaty (WCT)
One of the WIPO “Internet treaties”: adopted in Geneva in 1996, it entered into force in 2002. As 
its name indicates, it is administered by WIPO.
WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty (WPPT)
One of the WIPO “Internet treaties”: adopted in Geneva in 1996, it entered into force in 2002. As 
its name indicates, it is administered by WIPO.
Withdrawal (right of)
See “moral rights”.
Work made for hire
1. Under the copyright law of at least one country, a specific term covering both works created by 
employed authors under their employment, and certain works ordered or commissioned. The 
latter works are covered by the concept of “work made for hire” if they are specially ordered or 
commissioned for use as a contribution to a collective work, as part of a motion picture or other 
audiovisual work, as a translation, as a supplementary work, as a compilation, as an instructional 
text, as a test, as answer material for a test, or as an atlas, if the parties expressly agree, in a 
written instrument signed by them, that the work is to be considered a work made for hire.
2. The employer or other person for whom the work is prepared is considered the author 
for purposes of the copyright law of the country, and, subject to written agreement to the 
contrary, owns all the rights comprised in copyright.
Work of applied art
1. An artistic work embodied in or applied to a subject matter for utilitarian purposes, whether 
handicraft or produced on an industrial scale.
2. Theterm“worksofappliedart”appearsinthenon-exhaustivelistofworksinArticle 2(1)of
the Berne Convention. However, the Convention also provides that “[s]ubject to the provisions

ofArticle 7(4)ofthisConvention,itshallbeamatterforlegislationinthecountriesofthe
Union to determine the extent of the application of their laws to works of applied art [...] as 
wellastheconditionsunderwhichsuchworks[...]shallbeprotected”(Article 2(7)).Article 7(4)
reads: “It shall be a matter for legislation in the countries of the Union to determine the term 
of protection of photographic works and that of works of applied art insofar as they are 
protected as artistic works; however, this term shall last at least until the end of a period of 
twenty-five years from the making of such a work.” (For further details, see paragraphs  
BC-2.52 to BC-2.55 of the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.)
Work of architecture
A creation in the field of the art of constructing buildings, bridges and similar structures. Such 
creations are usually understood as comprising both the plans, designs, sketches and models 
serving as a basis for construction, and the completed buildings, bridges and similar structures 
themselves. The term “works of architecture” appears in the non-exhaustive list of literary and 
artisticworksinArticle 2(1)oftheBerneConvention.(Forfurtherdetails,seeparagraph BC-2.22 
the Guide to the Berne Convention, Part I.)
Works
See “literary and artistic works”.
World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) 
1. WIPO is an intergovernmental organization and a specialized agency of the United Nations 
system. It was established by the Convention Establishing the World Intellectual Property 
Organization (WIPO Convention), which was adopted in Stockholm in 1967 and entered into 
force in 1970. 
2. UnderArticle 3oftheWIPOConvention,theobjectivesoftheOrganizationare:“(i)topromote
the protection of intellectual property throughout the world through cooperation among 
States and, where appropriate, in collaboration with any other international organization, 
(ii)toensureadministrativecooperationamongtheUnions”.AccordingtoArticle 4ofthe
Convention,“[i]nordertoattaintheobjectivesdescribedinArticle 3,theOrganization,
through its appropriate organs, and subject to the competence of each of the Unions: (i) 
shall promote the development of measures designed to facilitate the efficient protection of 
intellectual property throughout the world and to harmonize national legislation in this field; 
(ii) shall perform the administrative tasks of the Paris Union, the Special Unions established 
in relation with that Union, and the Berne Union; (iii) may agree to assume, or participate in, 
the administration of any other international agreement designed to promote the protection 
of intellectual property; (iv) shall encourage the conclusion of international agreements 
designed to promote the protection of intellectual property; (v) shall offer its cooperation 
toStatesrequestinglegal–technicalassistanceinthefieldofintellectualproperty;(vi)shall
assemble and disseminate information concerning the protection of intellectual property, 
carry out and promote studies in this field, and publish the results of such studies; (vii) shall 
maintain services facilitating the international protection of intellectual property and, where 
appropriate, provide for registration in this field and the publication of the data concerning 
the registrations; (viii) shall take all other appropriate action”.
3. WIPO administers, inter alia, the Berne Convention, the WCT, the WPPT, the BTAP, and the 
MarrakeshTreaty,andjointlyadministers–alongwiththeUnitedNations,ILOandUNESCO–
the Rome, Phonograms and Brussels, or Satellites, Conventions. 
World Trade Organization (WTO)
The WTO is an intergovernmental organization established by the Marrakesh Agreement 
Establishing the World Trade Organization (WTO Agreement), signed at Marrakesh, Morocco, 
in 1994. The Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS 
Agreement),AnnexVIIoftheWTOAgreement,isoneofthecoveredagreementswithwhichall 
Members of the Organization are obliged to comply.

This new edition of the Guide to the Copyright 
and Related Rights Treaties Administered by WIPO 
is the most authoritative publication on WIPO’s 
copyright treaties.
The publication presents an updated legal 
commentary on all eight WIPO copyright and 
related rights treaties, adding the two newest 
(Beijing Treaty and Marrakesh Treaty). It includes 
background information as well as article by 
article explanation on, and interpretation of, 
each instrument, particularly in relation to new 
technological developments.
The publication provides key information and 
guidelines to a large audience, for example, policy 
makers, government officials, legal practitioners, 
judges, scholars, academics and students.
